The pre-operative work

Anaemia is the item with the strongest evidence and the longest lead time. Pre-operative anaemia affects 15 to 39% of elective hip and knee patients and is associated with transfusion, infection, longer stay and readmission; the ERAS consensus grades correcting it as high evidence with a strong recommendation, and it is the single pathway item that cannot be done on the morning of surgery. A haemoglobin below 130 g/L in either sex is the trigger for ferritin and transferrin saturation; iron deficiency is treated with intravenous iron at least two to three weeks before the date, and a cause is looked for. Intravenous iron given at wound closure is a weaker version of the same idea: in a randomised trial of 89 knee arthroplasties it halved the rate of anaemia at 30 days (34% versus 62%). The day-case programme in particular depends on this, because the post-discharge transfusion is the complication that the outpatient cohorts in the American NSQIP data had more of than their inpatient matches (4.1% versus 0.1% after discharge), and a transfusion at home is a readmission.

Prehabilitation has less behind it than the enthusiasm suggests. Pre-operative physiotherapy improves early pain and function slightly and does not shorten stay or accelerate discharge criteria; the ERAS consensus does not recommend it as an essential intervention, and a 2026 meta-analysis of 38 trials found a small average benefit in performance-based function, none in patient-reported function, and no evidence that frail patients gain more. The honest advice is that a patient who can do stairs before surgery will do stairs after it, and that the four to six weeks before an arthroplasty are better spent on haemoglobin, glucose, weight, smoking and the drugs than on a supervised exercise class.

Fasting is clear fluids to two hours and solids to six, with the time written for the patient’s actual slot, because a patient who has been nil by mouth since midnight for an afternoon list arrives dehydrated and orthostatic before the spinal has done anything. Carbohydrate loading reduces insulin resistance and improves pre-operative hunger and nausea in small trials, but has not been shown to accelerate discharge in hip or knee replacement, and the ERAS consensus does not recommend it as essential. A clear carbohydrate drink two hours before is harmless and reasonable; it is not what makes the pathway work. Sedative premedication is not given routinely, because it sedates the patient on the afternoon they are supposed to be walking.

Patient education is low-evidence and strongly recommended, which is the right grade for an intervention that costs nothing and determines the patient’s expectations. The expectation that matters most for same-day discharge is that they will walk on the day of surgery and go home that evening; a patient who was told to expect three nights will take three nights.

The anaesthetic skeleton

The ERAS consensus accepts general and neuraxial anaesthesia equally, on moderate evidence, and the reasoning is in the neuraxial chapter. The pathway’s practical preference is a spinal, because it removes intraoperative opioid, lowers blood loss, and in the same-day discharge meta-analysis was protective against failure while general anaesthesia increased it (OR 0.58 for success). The spinal has to be dosed for recovery: a 15 mg bupivacaine spinal at 14:00 is a patient who stands at 20:00 and voids at midnight, which is a one-night stay. The options are low-dose bupivacaine (7.5-10 mg), mepivacaine where it is available (motor recovery 210 versus 229 minutes and urinary retention 36% versus 57% against isobaric bupivacaine 10 mg in a randomised knee trial), or chloroprocaine for the shortest cases. Spinal opioid is not recommended for routine use in the ERAS consensus, because it delays what the pathway is trying to bring forward.

The analgesic skeleton is the same for hip and knee and is now well defined by PROSPECT: paracetamol and an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor started before or during surgery and continued regularly, a single intravenous dose of dexamethasone, a motor-sparing regional technique, and opioid only as rescue. For the knee that technique is a single-shot adductor canal block plus surgeon periarticular infiltration; the ERAS consensus grades local infiltration analgesia for the knee as high evidence and says nerve blocks have not shown superiority over it and are not an essential component, which is a statement about femoral blocks and quadriceps weakness rather than about the adductor canal. For the hip it is a supra-inguinal fascia iliaca block or a PENG block, with infiltration as the fallback when a block cannot be done; the ERAS consensus does not recommend infiltration for the hip, PROSPECT allows it when a block is impossible, and the difference between the two reflects how little the hip needs beyond a spinal and a good oral regimen. Gabapentinoids are not recommended by either body; they sedate, they add to orthostatic intolerance, and in the same-day discharge data gabapentin is a risk factor for failure.

Dexamethasone is the cheapest and most useful drug in the pathway. In the DEX-2-TKA trial of 485 knee arthroplasties, a single 24 mg dose reduced 48-hour morphine from 43 mg to 38 mg, with better pain scores, and a second 24 mg dose at 24 hours added nothing. The dose question is unsettled: 8 to 10 mg is what most guidelines name, 24 mg is what the Danish trials used, and a trial of 1 mg/kg against 0.3 mg/kg in low-pain-responder knee patients found no difference at all (moderate-to-severe pain on walking at 24 hours in 56% versus 53%). The author’s practice is 8 mg at induction for every arthroplasty without a specific contraindication, and a higher dose in the patient predicted to have a bad pain course; the diabetic patient gets the same dose and a glucose check on the ward, because the antiemetic and analgesic benefit outweighs a day of hyperglycaemia. The ERAS consensus recommends screening for and giving multimodal PONV prophylaxis, and dexamethasone covers both purposes.

Tranexamic acid is high-evidence and strongly recommended: 1 g IV before incision, with a second dose or topical application as the surgeon prefers. It is the reason the day-case programme can promise not to transfuse. The tourniquet is not recommended routinely for the knee in the ERAS consensus, because of the pain and the quadriceps dysfunction that follow a long inflation; surgeons vary, and the anaesthetic consequence of a tourniquet is covered in the tourniquet chapter. Fluids are given judiciously and stopped after surgery in favour of oral intake, and warmth is maintained throughout.

No drains, no catheters

Drains are not recommended for hip or knee replacement on moderate evidence: level 1 data show they increase blood loss and transfusion without reducing haematoma or infection. Urinary catheters are not recommended routinely, and when used are removed as soon as the patient can void, ideally within 24 hours. The single most useful number in the ERAS consensus is the catheterisation threshold: in a large randomised trial within an enhanced recovery pathway, scanning and catheterising at 800 mL rather than 500 mL significantly reduced the need for catheterisation without increasing urological complications. Retention is largely iatrogenic: in 378 fast-track arthroplasties, 40% of knees and 36% of hips were catheterised for retention, and the strongest associations were intraoperative catheter placement itself and, for hips, age over 60 and more than 1,350 mL of intraoperative fluid. A short-acting spinal, no catheter, restrained fluids, a bladder scanner on the ward and an 800 mL threshold are the whole of the prevention.

Day 0 mobilisation and the discharge criteria

Mobilisation on the day of surgery is the pathway item that converts all the others into a shorter stay, and the ERAS consensus grades it as strong. It requires that the block be motor sparing, that the spinal has receded, that the pressure holds when the patient sits, and that a physiotherapist is on the ward in the afternoon rather than the next morning. The patient who is asked to stand four hours after a low-dose spinal with a working adductor canal block and an NSAID on board usually can; the patient who has had 15 mg of bupivacaine, a femoral block and a morphine PCA cannot, and the difference is entirely the anaesthetist’s.

Discharge is by objective, team-based functional criteria rather than by the calendar: pain controlled on oral medication, independent transfers and walking with the aid they will use at home, stairs if they have them, voiding, tolerating diet, a wound that is dry, and a responsible adult at home for the first night. Written criteria stop the two-day default from reasserting itself, and the ERAS consensus recommends them on low evidence and a strong grade. For a same-day discharge the criteria are the same with a time limit: if they are not met by the evening, the patient stays, and that is a planned outcome rather than a failure.

Day-case arthroplasty: the decision tree

patient meets selection criteria   --no--> inpatient pathway (same skeleton,
   |yes                                     no time limit)
pre-op complete: Hb, drugs, home,  --no--> defer, fix, rebook
   |yes  expectations set
morning list                       --no--> inpatient (an afternoon spinal is
   |yes                                     a next-day walk)
spinal low dose + block + LIA + dex + TXA, no catheter, no drain
   |
by about 18:00: block receded, standing, pain controlled on oral, voided
   |yes                                    |no
home with written plan, phone call AM      stays the night (planned, not failed)

Patient selection and the Australian context

The outpatient cohorts in the literature were younger, lighter and fitter than the inpatients they were compared with; that is the first thing every meta-analysis says and it is the reason the safety data are reassuring rather than proof. The 41-study review found no difference in complications, readmission or patient-reported outcomes between outpatient and inpatient pathways, with a moderate-to-high risk of bias. The unicompartmental knee data are the cleanest: 88% successful same-day discharge across 9,694 patients, 91% in selected and 76% in unselected cohorts, readmission 3%, complications 4%. The selected patient is the one the programme should start with: ASA 1 or 2, body mass index below about 40, no insulin-requiring diabetes out of control, no sleep apnoea that is untreated, no anticoagulant that cannot be managed, a haemoglobin above 120 g/L, a house without a staircase they cannot manage, an adult at home, a mobile phone, and a willingness to go home. In the same-day failure meta-analysis the risks were female sex, ASA 3 and 4, smoking, more than two allergies, and general anaesthesia.

In Australia the same-day joint sits almost entirely in private hospitals, where the surgeon, the anaesthetist and the physiotherapist can agree a pathway without a committee, and where the funder’s interest in avoiding a two-night stay aligns with the patient’s. The public system runs the same enhanced recovery skeleton with a one- or two-night stay, because its patients are older and sicker and because the ward, not the theatre, sets the pace. Nothing in the evidence suggests that a two-night public stay is unsafe or that a same-day private discharge is unsafe; the difference is selection and logistics. A programme that works has a named clinician who takes the evening phone call, a pathway back to the ward that does not go through the emergency department, and an honest audit of who went home and who came back.

The failure modes

Orthostatic intolerance is the commonest reason a same-day discharge fails and the commonest reason an inpatient is still in bed on day 1. It is dizziness, nausea and presyncope on sitting or standing, occurs in up to half of arthroplasty patients, and is associated with female sex, age, comorbidity, pain above 5/10, gabapentin, spinal anaesthesia, hip rather than knee, and opioid. The mechanism is a failure of vasoconstriction in a patient who is relatively hypovolaemic from blood loss and fasting, vasodilated from the spinal and the inflammatory response, and bradycardic from opioid and lying flat. Prevention is the whole pathway: euvolaemia without overload, tranexamic acid, no gabapentinoid, minimal opioid, a short spinal, and sitting up early rather than lying flat for six hours and standing suddenly. Midodrine 10 mg four to five doses over the first day halved orthostatic intolerance at first mobilisation (18% versus 33%) in a randomised trial of 159 arthroplasties, with syncope only in the placebo group and a median stay of two rather than three days; it is a reasonable addition for the patient with a history of it, not yet a routine.

Pain at the point the block recedes is the second failure, and it is predictable to the hour. A chloroprocaine or mepivacaine spinal is gone before the patient reaches the ward; if the oral regimen has not been given in recovery and the adductor canal block or infiltration is not working, the patient will be in severe pain at 17:00 and will not go home. The fix is timing (first oral doses in recovery, not on the ward), a block that outlasts the spinal, and a written rescue plan for the first night at home that the patient has in their hand. The rebound phenomenon after a single-shot block is discussed in the procedure cards; dexamethasone reduces it.

Nausea is less common than it was because the spinal removes the volatile agent and most of the opioid, and dexamethasone and ondansetron cover the rest. The nauseated patient after a spinal is usually hypotensive; treat the pressure before the next antiemetic.

Urinary retention is prevented as above; the patient who cannot void by the evening with a scan under 800 mL goes home with instructions and a phone number, and the one over 800 mL is catheterised and stays. Neither is a disaster.

The failures that matter are the ones the pathway cannot see: the bleed at home that becomes a transfusion, the wound that dehisces, the pulmonary embolus in a patient whose prophylaxis depended on an injection they did not give themselves. The post-discharge complication rate in the NSQIP outpatient data (6.3% versus 1.1% for matched inpatients, mostly transfusion) is the figure that keeps the programme honest. It is why the haemoglobin is fixed beforehand, why tranexamic acid is not optional, and why the first phone call is the next morning.

Edge cases

  • The afternoon case. A low-dose spinal at 15:00 can still go home, but the margin is gone; a general anaesthetic with blocks and infiltration, or an inpatient pathway, is often the more honest plan for a late list.
  • Bilateral arthroplasty. Not a day case. The blood loss, the duration and the orthostatic load are each doubled.
  • Revision. Not a day case; the pathway’s analgesic skeleton still applies, the stay does not.
  • The patient on an anticoagulant. The spinal interval is in the neuraxial chapter; the discharge question is who gives the next dose and when.
  • The diabetic patient. Dexamethasone is given, the glucose is checked at six hours, and the patient on insulin stays the night unless the programme has a specific protocol for them.
  • Sleep apnoea. Treated apnoea with a device at home and an opioid-sparing regimen is compatible with same-day discharge; untreated or severe apnoea with an opioid requirement is not.
  • Frailty. The frail patient gains the most from the pathway and is least likely to go home the same day. The skeleton is the same; the time limit is removed.

Key sources

The ERAS Society consensus of 2020 is the backbone and gives an evidence level and grade for each of its 17 items; most of what is in this chapter is a restatement of it with the anaesthetic reasoning attached. The Copenhagen “why still in hospital” study explains the list. The same-day discharge evidence is almost entirely observational and selected, with the unicompartmental knee data the best of it; the failure-mode meta-analysis and the orthostatic intolerance trial are the two most useful recent additions. Where the chapter gives a dose or a threshold without a citation (the 800 mL bladder threshold is cited; the 130 g/L anaemia trigger and the 8 mg dexamethasone dose are convention), it is standard practice rather than trial evidence.

Part A

The orthopaedic patient: frailty, hip fracture pathways, rheumatoid and ankylosing spondylitis, obesity

Five patient phenotypes recur across the orthopaedic list and each breaks the standard plan in a predictable place. The frail older patient dies or loses independence according to frailty, delirium and time to theatre, not anaesthetic technique, so the pathway (block in the emergency department, surgery within 36 hours, orthogeriatric care, day 1 mobilisation) is the treatment. Rheumatoid arthritis is an airway and a cervical spine problem before it is a joint problem. Ankylosing spondylitis is a fixed neck and a difficult neuraxial space. Obesity changes positioning, dosing, block technique and the day-case question. The young trauma patient is the one in whom compartment syndrome and fat embolism are real.

The frail older patient

Frailty is the loss of physiological reserve across several systems at once, so that a stressor of fixed size (a fracture, an anaesthetic, a night of hypotension) produces a disproportionate and often irreversible decline. It is not age, and it is not comorbidity, although both track with it. The Clinical Frailty Scale was built to make it measurable in a clinic in under a minute: a 9-point picture scale from very fit to terminally ill, in which each one-category increase raised the medium-term risk of death by about a fifth and of institutional care by about a quarter in the original cohort, independent of age, and outperformed measures of cognition, function and comorbidity. In hip fracture it predicts what the anaesthetist is asked to predict: in a meta-analysis of 11 studies and 45,979 patients, frailty carried an odds ratio of 1.46 for complications, 1.68 for inpatient death, 1.46 for death at six months and 2.24 for death at a year or more.

The scale is worth using because it changes behaviour. A CFS of 2 having a hemiarthroplasty is a 70-year-old who will walk out; a CFS of 7 having the same operation is someone for whom the operation is analgesia and nursing, the goal is comfort and transfer, and the family conversation about what the next year looks like belongs before theatre, not after the delirium. The Australian hip fracture standard asks for frailty, cognition, delirium risk and nutrition to be screened at presentation, and the reason is that these four, not the ASA grade, are what the discharge destination depends on.

Delirium is the complication the anaesthetist is blamed for and can least control. The pooled prevalence after hip fracture is about 23%; dementia (OR 3.42), ASA 4 (OR 4.19), age over 80 and diabetes are the risks that matter, and the anaesthetic technique is not one of them (REGAIN: 20.5% after spinal, 19.7% after general). What does reduce it is the pathway: orthogeriatric care reduced delirium by 19% and in-hospital mortality by 28% across 37 studies, and a peripheral nerve block reduced postoperative delirium (RR 0.68) in a meta-analysis of 12 trials in patients without pre-existing cognitive impairment, which is the one anaesthetic intervention with a delirium signal and the reason the fascia iliaca block belongs in the emergency department rather than the anaesthetic room. Beyond that the measures are old-fashioned: glasses and hearing aids on, a clock and a window, a family member, no anticholinergics, no benzodiazepines, a bladder that is empty and a bowel that moves, oxygen saturation that is normal, pain treated with paracetamol and a block rather than a morphine infusion, and a night that is dark and quiet.

Cognitive assessment at presentation is a baseline, not a diagnosis. A 4AT or an abbreviated mental test on arrival lets the ward recognise the hypoactive delirium that is otherwise charted as “quiet” and lets the anaesthetist know whether the patient in front of them has capacity for the consent conversation, which the Association of Anaesthetists’ dementia guideline sets out in detail. The practical trap is the patient who scores badly because of pain, opioid or the ambulance ride and is then labelled demented; score again after the block.

Medication reconciliation is where the avoidable harm sits. The hip fracture patient arrives on an anticoagulant, an antiplatelet, an antihypertensive, a diuretic, a sulfonylurea, a benzodiazepine and a statin, and each has a decision attached. The anticoagulant decides the anaesthetic technique rather than the timing (see the neuraxial chapter); the antihypertensive and diuretic are held on the morning of surgery in a patient who has been lying on a floor; the sulfonylurea is held because the patient is fasting; the benzodiazepine is continued because withdrawal is a delirium; the anticholinergics for the bladder are stopped. A pharmacist on the orthogeriatric round does this better than the anaesthetist at 07:00, which is part of why orthogeriatric care works.

The time-to-surgery target is the pathway’s hard number. The 2023 Australian standard moved it from 48 to 36 hours from first presentation (from the fracture itself for an inpatient fall), with the explicit instruction that correctable problems (anaemia, anticoagulation, electrolytes, uncontrolled diabetes or heart failure) are optimised promptly rather than used as reasons to wait, and that transfer from a remote site is a reason for delay only in the sense that surgery still happens as soon as possible. In 2022, before the change, 78% of Australian patients had surgery within 48 hours and the hospital averages ranged from 16 to 92 hours; only 45% walked on day 1. HIP ATTACK, which randomised 2,970 patients to surgery at a median of 6 hours against 24 hours, found no difference in mortality (9% versus 10%) or major complications (22% versus 22%), which tells you that heroic acceleration adds nothing and that the harm sits in the long tail beyond a day or two, not in the difference between tonight and tomorrow morning. What justifies delay is a short list: a condition that will be materially better in 24 hours and is dangerous now (decompensated heart failure, a potassium of 6.5, a haemoglobin of 70 g/L with active bleeding, sepsis, an INR above 1.5 that vitamin K will correct), and a decision, made with the patient, to palliate. An echocardiogram for a murmur in a patient who was walking last week is not on the list; the Association of Anaesthetists’ guideline names echocardiography as an area of controversy precisely because it so often delays rather than changes management. The author’s rule is that a hip fracture is never delayed for an investigation that would not change the operation, and that “waiting for the anticoagulant to wear off” means a general anaesthetic tonight, not a spinal in three days.

Hip fracture: the first 36 hours

ED arrival ---> pain scored, paracetamol, fascia iliaca or femoral block
            |   within the hour; cognition, frailty, delirium risk, nutrition
            |   screened; medicines reconciled
            v
orthogeriatric review ---> correctables fixed in parallel, not in series
            |              (Hb, K, glucose, fluids, anticoagulant plan)
            v
theatre within 36 h ---> spinal (low dose) or GA; pressure near baseline;
            |             cement precautions for the hemiarthroplasty
            v
day 1 ---> out of bed, full weight bearing, delirium screened, bone health
            plan, discharge plan written with the family

The anaesthetic itself is covered on the neck of femur card. The chapter-level points are three. The block before surgery is the intervention with the best evidence for both pain and delirium. Intraoperative hypotension is associated with death and should be prevented with a low spinal dose and a vasopressor started early rather than treated after the event. And the hemiarthroplasty that is cemented in a frail patient is the setting for bone cement implantation syndrome, which has its own chapter.

Rheumatoid arthritis

Rheumatoid arthritis presents to the orthopaedic list as a patient needing a joint, but it is a systemic disease of synovium, and synovium lines joints the anaesthetist uses. The cervical spine is the first. Atlantoaxial subluxation (anterior, from erosion of the transverse ligament; vertical, from erosion of the lateral masses letting the odontoid rise into the foramen magnum; subaxial, from facet and disc destruction below C2) was present in 42% of 220 outpatients in a 2014 Japanese series despite modern treatment, associated with disease of more than 10 years, advanced radiographic stage and multiple narrowed disc spaces, and neck pain was associated only with the vertical form. The relevant consequence is that a third or more of long-standing rheumatoid patients have an unstable neck and most of them do not know it. The practical rule is that any rheumatoid patient with disease over 10 years, erosive disease, neck pain, neurological symptoms or a planned airway intervention has flexion and extension lateral cervical radiographs before an elective arthroplasty, and that a patient in whom they cannot be obtained in time is managed as unstable: no extension at laryngoscopy, a videolaryngoscope or awake fibreoptic intubation, manual in-line stabilisation, and a neutral neck in the head holder for shoulder surgery. The beach chair position for a rheumatoid shoulder is the case where this matters most, because the head is fixed and out of sight for two hours.

Below the neck the airway is still rheumatoid. The temporomandibular joints limit mouth opening, the cricoarytenoid joints can be fixed by arthritis so that the glottis is narrow and the voice hoarse, and a tube that passed easily can leave a patient with stridor after extubation because the arytenoids have been pushed against a joint that does not move; the case reports of acute airway obstruction from cricoarytenoid arthritis are rare but recurrent. A hoarse voice, dyspnoea on exertion or stridor on a rheumatoid patient’s history earns a smaller tube, a gentle laryngoscopy, and a plan for extubation that assumes swelling. Supraglottic airways and regional techniques avoid most of this, and a spinal for a rheumatoid knee is a good anaesthetic.

Steroid cover has changed. The 2022 American College of Rheumatology and AAHKS guideline for hip and knee arthroplasty recommends continuing the patient’s usual daily glucocorticoid dose through surgery rather than giving supraphysiological stress doses, on the grounds that the evidence for stress dosing is weak and the harms (infection, hyperglycaemia, poor wound healing) are not. The author’s practice follows it: the morning prednisolone is given, hydrocortisone is available for unexplained hypotension, and the patient on a dose above about 20 mg of prednisolone equivalent or with a known adrenal problem gets a specific plan agreed with their rheumatologist. The same guideline continues methotrexate, sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine and leflunomide through surgery, withholds biologics by scheduling the operation at the end of the dosing interval (a drug given four-weekly is skipped and surgery falls in the fifth week), restarts them when the wound is healing at about 14 days, and withholds JAK inhibitors for a short interval before surgery. The infection risk from a biologic is real and is the surgeon’s and rheumatologist’s problem to balance against a flare; the anaesthetist’s job is to notice that the dose timing was not planned and to ask before the patient is asleep.

Anaemia in rheumatoid arthritis is the anaemia of chronic disease with iron deficiency from NSAIDs layered on top, and it is common enough that every rheumatoid arthroplasty patient has a ferritin and transferrin saturation in the pre-admission clinic; the chronic disease component does not respond to iron and the deficiency component does. The rheumatoid patient also bleeds more than their haemoglobin suggests because the tissues are friable and the surgery is often revision or complex, so tranexamic acid and a group and hold are routine. Positioning is a separate problem: a patient with fixed, deformed and painful joints cannot be put into the position the surgeon wants without first finding out, awake, which positions they can tolerate, and a joint subluxed by a careless transfer is a real complication.

Ankylosing spondylitis

Ankylosing spondylitis fuses the axial skeleton from the sacroiliac joints upward into a rigid kyphotic column, and the anaesthetic problems follow from that single fact. The cervical spine is fixed, often in flexion, so that the patient cannot look up, cannot extend the neck for laryngoscopy and may not be able to lie flat without a stack of pillows; the fused spine is also brittle and fractures with little force, so forcing extension to get a view risks a cervical fracture with cord injury. The airway plan is decided from the chair in the pre-admission clinic: if the patient can be positioned with a videolaryngoscope and has adequate mouth opening, that is reasonable with a fibreoptic scope in the room; if the chin is on the chest, an awake fibreoptic intubation is the default and the chapter will not pretend otherwise. The temporomandibular joints are involved in a minority and add trismus to the list.

Neuraxial anaesthesia is difficult and not impossible. The interspinous ligaments ossify and the interlaminar spaces close, so the midline approach meets bone. In a 10-year series of 82 procedures in 51 patients, spinal anaesthesia succeeded in 10 of 13 attempts and the epidural failed in all three, which is the usual experience: a spinal through a paramedian or lateral approach, aiming through the gap that remains at the lower lumbar levels, often works; an epidural catheter rarely threads and the spread when it does is unpredictable because the ossified ligamentum flavum and the epidural fat behave differently. Ultrasound finds the interspace that is still open. A spinal placed is a good anaesthetic for a hip replacement in a patient whose airway is hard; a failed spinal in a patient whose airway is hard is the scenario that needs a plan before the needle, which is to say that the fibreoptic scope and a second anaesthetist are in the room for the spinal, not called for afterwards.

The chest wall is fused and the vital capacity reduced, so ventilation is diaphragmatic and the patient tolerates the prone and lateral positions poorly; apical fibrosis is a late complication. The heart is involved in a minority: aortic root dilatation and aortic regurgitation, and conduction defects, are the classic associations and are looked for with an echocardiogram in a patient with a murmur or with long-standing disease, because aortic regurgitation changes the pressure targets (keep the heart rate up, avoid a slow full ventricle) and conduction disease occasionally needs pacing. Hip replacement in ankylosing spondylitis is also one of the operations with heterotopic ossification as a specific risk, which the surgeon may address with a single dose of radiotherapy or an NSAID course, and the surgeon’s view on NSAIDs should be known before the anaesthetist writes them up.

Positioning a fused kyphotic spine on a flat table breaks it. The patient’s own posture is reproduced with pillows and gel under the head and the knees, the table is broken rather than the patient, and the operative position for a hip is confirmed with the patient awake if there is any doubt. A fracture of a fused spine is a catastrophic injury and the mechanism is usually a transfer.

Obesity

Obesity changes four things on the orthopaedic list: the position, the block, the dose and the discharge. The position first. A patient of 140 kg in the lateral decubitus for a hip has a dependent arm, a dependent peroneal nerve and a brachial plexus that each carry more weight than the padding was designed for; the beach chair sits the abdomen against the diaphragm; the prone position for spine surgery has the whole weight on the chest and the abdomen compressed against the frame unless the bolsters leave it free, which is also the condition for keeping the epidural veins empty. The table weight limit is a real number. Pressure areas, brachial plexus traction and compartment syndrome of the dependent limb after long cases have all been reported in obese patients and the author’s practice is a padding and position check at the start, at an hour and whenever the table moves.

Blocks are harder and more valuable. The ultrasound image is deep and poor, the needle long, and the time taken longer; the supra-inguinal fascia iliaca block and the adductor canal are the lower limb blocks that stay feasible at the extremes of habitus, the interscalene remains feasible for the shoulder but the phrenic palsy is tolerated worse, so a superior trunk approach is preferred. A spinal is harder to place (sit the patient up, ultrasound the midline, use a long needle) and the block height is less predictable because the cerebrospinal fluid volume is reduced, which argues for a smaller dose rather than a larger one. The dose question extends to everything: local anaesthetic maximum doses are calculated on lean or adjusted body weight, not actual weight, which matters when the surgeon’s infiltration and the block together approach the ceiling; antibiotics scale up (cefazolin 3 g at or above 120 kg); opioids scale on lean mass; propofol induction on lean mass and infusion on adjusted mass; suxamethonium on actual weight.

Sleep apnoea is present in a large fraction of arthroplasty patients and undiagnosed in most of them. The Society of Anesthesia and Sleep Medicine guideline’s position is that a patient who screens positive (STOP-Bang 3 or more, with higher scores more specific) is managed as if they have it rather than cancelled for a sleep study: regional anaesthesia where possible, opioid-sparing analgesia, continuation of CPAP where the patient uses it, extubation awake and sitting up, and postoperative monitoring proportionate to the opioid given. For the day-case question this is the deciding factor: treated apnoea with a device and an opioid-sparing plan is compatible with same-day discharge, untreated apnoea with an expected opioid requirement is not. Body mass index on its own was not an independent predictor of same-day discharge failure in the pooled data; ASA grade, which captures the metabolic consequences of obesity rather than the weight, was. The author’s practice is to use a BMI of about 40 as the point above which the day-case pathway needs an individual decision rather than a default, and to let the airway, the apnoea and the diabetes decide rather than the number.

Infection and wound complications rise with obesity and are the surgeon’s reason for a BMI threshold; the anaesthetist’s contribution is the antibiotic dose, the glucose, the temperature and the tissue oxygenation. Venous thromboembolism risk rises too, and the chemoprophylaxis dose is weight adjusted.

The young trauma patient

The young patient with a long bone fracture is the orthopaedic patient in whom the complications that textbooks dwell on actually occur. Compartment syndrome is a disease of young men: in 164 cases from a single centre, 69% followed a fracture, half of those were tibial shaft, most patients were men under 35, and one in ten had a bleeding disorder or was anticoagulated. The reason is physiological. Young muscle is bulky, the fascial compartments are tight, the bleeding into them after a high-energy fracture is brisk, and the patient’s own blood pressure keeps perfusing the compartment and raising its pressure until it exceeds venous and then capillary pressure. The anaesthetic consequence is the subject of the nerve injury and compartment syndrome chapter: a regional technique in a tibial shaft fracture, a tibial plateau fracture, a forearm fracture or a crush is a decision taken with the surgeon, with a low-concentration local anaesthetic, no adjuncts that prolong it, hourly observation, and a pressure monitor where the risk is high.

Fat embolism is the other young-patient complication: it follows long bone and pelvic fractures and reamed nailing, and the patient who is hypoxic, confused and petechial 24 to 72 hours after a femoral fracture has it until proven otherwise (chapter). Early fixation reduces it, which is one reason the young femoral shaft is nailed on the day of injury if the physiology allows (polytrauma sequencing).

Three other things are specific to this patient. The first is that they are often intoxicated, often have a full stomach, and often have a second injury that the fracture distracts from; a rapid sequence induction and a tertiary survey are the defaults. The second is that their pain is severe, their opioid requirement high and their risk of persistent opioid use after discharge real, so the regional technique is doing more work than it would in an older patient, and the discharge prescription is written with an end date. The third is that the operation they are having is often the first of several (external fixation, then definitive fixation, then soft tissue cover, then removal of metalwork), and a patient who has a bad experience of the first anaesthetic is a difficult patient for the next three. The young trauma patient is where the catheter techniques earn their place on duration grounds, and where the block that is withheld for compartment syndrome reasons must be replaced by something, usually a ketamine infusion and a PCA, rather than by nothing.

Edge cases

  • The frail patient with a periprosthetic fracture. Same pathway, longer operation, more blood; the 36-hour target applies and is met less often because the surgeon with the implants is not always available. The fracture is covered on its card.
  • The rheumatoid patient on a JAK inhibitor and prednisolone having a revision shoulder in beach chair. Every problem in this chapter at once: unstable neck in a head holder, a hoarse voice, a continued steroid, a withheld biologic and a long case. Awake fibreoptic intubation, neutral neck, a tube one size smaller, an arterial line, and a planned extubation.
  • The ankylosing spondylitis patient for a spinal fracture. A fused spine that has fractured is unstable through the fracture and nowhere else; the patient is moved as a single unit and positioned in their own kyphosis, and the airway is the one described above.
  • The obese patient on a traction table for a femoral nail. The perineal post and the pudendal nerve, the weight on the contralateral leg and the well-leg compartment syndrome after a long case are the risks; the positioning chapter (a06) covers them.
  • The young patient with a tibial plateau fracture who asks for a block. The honest answer is in the compartment syndrome chapter: sometimes, with conditions, and only after the surgeon has said yes.

Key sources

The frailty literature and the hip fracture pathway standards are consensus built on consistent observational data, and the two randomised trials that bear on the pathway (REGAIN for technique and HIP ATTACK for extreme acceleration) are both negative, which is itself the finding. The rheumatoid cervical spine prevalence is from a single modern series and the older literature gave higher numbers; the airway advice is standard practice. The steroid and biologic advice is from the 2022 ACR/AAHKS guideline and is a change from older teaching. The ankylosing spondylitis neuraxial data are from a small 1996 series, which remains the best there is. The obesity dosing rules are consensus pharmacology. Where the chapter says “the author’s practice”, the evidence stops there.

Part B. Why operations hurt

Part B

Why operations hurt: a first-principles pain model

Post-operative pain is predictable from four things: which tissue was cut, what was left under tension, what will be loaded afterwards, and who the patient is. Bone hurts hard and briefly; a tendon pulled onto bone under tension hurts for as long as it is loaded; a joint that has been re-tensioned aches for weeks; arthroscopic surface work barely registers. The early peak is a poor guide, because the shape of the curve after day 2 is what decides whether a single-shot block, a catheter or nothing is the right plan. Every card in Part C carries a 1-5 score and a day 0 to 7 trajectory built on this model, and this chapter defines them.

The claim

Pain after an orthopaedic operation is not a property of the operation’s name. It is a property of what was done to which tissue, what that tissue is now doing, and who it was done to. A surgeon who says “this is the least painful operation I do” is reporting the first of those four, filtered through the patients who complained to him. A registrar who says “cuff repairs are agony” is reporting the same thing from the other end of the corridor. Both are right about the days they saw and wrong about the days they did not.

The model in this chapter has four questions. Ask them in order and the block, the catheter decision and the oral regimen follow.

  1. TISSUE      what was cut, reamed, stripped or detached
                 (bone, tendon, capsule, muscle, periosteum, nerve, skin and portals)
                        |
  2. TENSION     what was left pulled tight, lengthened or re-tensioned
                 (a repaired tendon, a lengthened arm, a balanced knee, a corrected osteotomy)
                        |
  3. LOAD        what will be loaded in the days after, and how soon
                 (weight-bearing, hand use, physiotherapy, rolling over in bed)
                        |
  4. PATIENT     who it was done to
                 (age, sex, pre-operative pain, opioid exposure, catastrophising, what they expect)
                        |
                        v
            pain SCORE, pain SHAPE over day 0-7, and the PLAN that fits the shape

Tissue: what each kind of cut feels like

Nociceptors are not evenly distributed. Periosteum is dense with them; cancellous bone marrow is sensitive to pressure and inflammation; tendon and ligament carry mechanoreceptors that fire with stretch; synovium and capsule are richly innervated; muscle belly is comparatively quiet unless it is torn or ischaemic; cartilage has no nerves at all, which is why a bone-on-bone joint hurts and a cartilage-covered one does not. The surgeon’s choice of what to cut therefore sets the baseline.

Mechanism tag What the surgeon did How it hurts How long
bone osteotomy, reaming, broaching, drilling for anchors, decorticating a footprint, cement interface hard, deep, inflammatory; responds to NSAIDs; worse with the first loading peaks day 1-2, falls fast once nothing is loaded through it
tendon-tension a tendon or ligament repaired or reattached under tension, or a graft fixed in a tunnel sharp with every movement that loads it; night pain because the patient cannot find a position; aching between plateau for one to two weeks, then slow decline over the healing period
retension the joint re-tensioned or the limb lengthened: reverse shoulder, knee balancing, osteotomy correction, leg length change at the hip deep ache and stiffness pain, worse with range-of-motion exercises, a feeling of the limb being “too tight” weeks, improving as the soft tissues creep
capsule capsular release, labral repair, synovectomy, joint distension sharp with movement in the released direction, settles once the joint is moved regularly days
muscle a muscle split, released, lengthened or widely dissected aching, position-dependent, worse on contraction days to a week
periosteum subperiosteal stripping or plating along a long bone raw and incisional along the whole length of the plate, worse than the fracture it fixed days, then the bone takes over
nerve nerve handling, traction, decompression or transposition burning, dysaesthetic, in the territory rather than the wound unpredictable; may be the longest
tourniquet ischaemia and reperfusion plus cuff-site pressure dull thigh or arm ache after a long tourniquet, separate from the wound 24-48 h
surface arthroscopic portals and irrigation only minimal; swelling more than pain hours
visceral a retroperitoneal or anterior approach to the spine or pelvis abdominal wall and visceral, ileus, referred pain days

Two of these tags do most of the work in the atlas. Bone explains why an anatomic shoulder replacement, a distal radius plate and a primary hip hurt hard for two days and then stop. Tendon-tension explains why a rotator cuff repair, a distal biceps repair and an MPFL reconstruction hurt for two weeks, at night, every time the patient moves.

Tension: what was left pulled tight

The surgeon’s second decision is what the tissues are left doing. A replaced humeral head sized to the one that was removed leaves the cuff and capsule at their original length: nothing pulls except the repaired subscapularis, so after the bone settles there is little left to hurt. That exception matters: in the one direct comparison the anatomic replacement, with its subscapularis repair and younger patients, needed opioids for longer than the reverse, which the folklore calls the more painful of the two. A reverse shoulder deliberately lengthens the arm and tensions the deltoid so that it can lift the arm without a cuff; the deltoid and the capsule spend weeks creeping to the new length and the patient feels every centimetre. A knee replacement is balanced by releasing tight ligaments and choosing insert thickness until the gaps match; the collateral ligaments and the posterior capsule are then held at a new tension through every flexion exercise. An osteotomy that corrects an alignment deformity leaves the soft tissues on the lengthened side stretched. A repaired tendon is the extreme case: by design it is pulled back to bone under enough tension to hold, and the tension is then tested by every movement until it heals.

This is the single most useful question to ask a surgeon who says an operation is painless or painful: what have you left under tension? The answer predicts the shape of the curve better than anything else they can tell you.

Load: what the patient will do to it

A cut bone that is not loaded is quiet by day 3. The same cut bone loaded by weight-bearing is not, which is why the Gerbershagen cohort, 50,523 patients ranked by their worst pain on the first day after 179 different operations, put open reduction of a calcaneal fracture at the top of the whole list, above every major abdominal and thoracic operation, and put foot arthrodesis, metacarpophalangeal arthrodesis and hand resection arthroplasty in the top eleven. Small bones that have to bear the body’s weight or do the hand’s work from day 1 hurt out of all proportion to the size of the incision. Twenty-two of the forty most painful procedure groups in that cohort were orthopaedic or trauma operations on the limbs. Spinal fusion and scoliosis surgery held ranks 2, 3 and 6, with no epidural analgesia used.

The same cohort delivered the finding that should keep every anaesthetist honest: appendicectomy, cholecystectomy, haemorrhoidectomy and tonsillectomy all ranked in the 25 most painful procedures, and laparoscopic appendicectomy patients reported pain equal to knee replacement and sternotomy patients, while receiving almost no opioid because nobody expected them to need it. Expectation sets the regimen, and the regimen sets the pain. “Minor” is a description of the surgeon’s effort, not the patient’s.

Load also explains the gap between pain at rest and pain on movement, which most of the published trials never measured: an updated systematic review of 944 post-surgical analgesic trials found that 53% did not assess movement-evoked pain at all. Blocks and catheters earn their keep on movement-evoked pain, which is the pain that stops physiotherapy, sleep and discharge; a trial that reports only rest pain understates what a continuous technique does for a tendon repair and overstates what it does for a bone cut.

The shape of the curve, not the height of the peak

Put tissue, tension and load together and each operation has a characteristic trajectory. The cards record it as the expected worst pain (0-10) on the evening of surgery, day 1, day 2, day 3 and day 7, with the card’s recommended plan in place.

pain

 4 |   . .  :    .    :          B        peaks as the block recedes, falls fast

The folk wisdom that an anatomic shoulder replacement is painless and a cuff repair is agony turns out to be wrong about the peak and right about the shape. In the only prospective comparison, 102 patients having either an arthroscopic cuff repair or a short-stay shoulder arthroplasty under long-acting interscalene blocks peaked on the same day (day 2) at the same height (mean 4.4 and 5.1, not different) and tracked together for 14 days; what separated them was that the cuff repair patients were still reaching for opioid at a week. The peak is set by the block wearing off and by the bone work both operations share. The tail is set by the tendon.

Two consequences for planning. First, the day 1-2 peak is where the single-shot block ends and the oral regimen has to be already running; it is the same problem for every card with a bone tag, and intravenous dexamethasone plus a pre-emptive oral dose is the answer for all of them. Second, the catheter question is a question about the tail. A catheter that comes out on day 2 has done its job for a bone operation and has barely started for a tendon repair, which is why the atlas marks the catheter as selective for most bone work and gives it its strongest claim for the tendon-tension and retension cards.

Rebound pain: the predictable collapse

When a single-shot block recedes, the pain does not return to where it would have been without the block; for a few hours it is worse. In 972 ambulatory patients who had a peripheral nerve block, half met the definition of rebound pain (well-controlled, 3 or less, while the block worked, then 7 or more within 24 h of placement). The odds were higher after bone surgery (OR 1.82), in women (OR 1.52) and in the young, and lower when intravenous dexamethasone had been given (its absence carried an OR of 1.78). Satisfaction with the block was still 83%, which is the measure of how much patients value the hours it buys.

The practical rule set that follows:

  1. Give intravenous dexamethasone with the block unless there is a reason not to. It prolongs the block and reduces the rebound.
  2. Start the oral regimen before the block recedes, in recovery, not when the patient rings.
  3. Tell the patient what will happen and when, in words. A rebound that was predicted is a symptom; one that was not is an emergency.
  4. For a bone-tagged operation in a young woman going home the same day, assume rebound will happen and write the night plan accordingly.
  5. For a tendon-tagged or retension-tagged operation, the rebound is the start of the plateau, not a blip; that is the catheter conversation.

The patient

Who it was done to modifies everything above. Pre-operative pain, pre-operative opioid use, anxiety and catastrophising raise the whole curve and lengthen the tail; the opioid-tolerant patient needs a separate chapter (A12). Age lowers reported pain and raises the cost of treating it. Sex shifts the rebound odds. Expectation works in both directions: the patient told to expect a painless operation who wakes in pain has lost confidence in the plan; the one told to expect a hard first night who has one takes the next dose and goes back to sleep. The patient-facing line on every card exists for this reason.

The scale the atlas uses

Each card carries a score from 1 to 5. It describes the pain the operation produces with the card’s own recommended plan in place, not the pain of the untreated operation, so a score of 3 for a replacement means “with a working block and a regimen, moderate”, and a score of 5 means “even with a good plan, severe and prolonged”. The scale is deliberately built on what the plan has to be rather than on a number on day 1, because the number on day 1 is the same for a 3 and a 5.

Score Label What the plan has to be Anchors
1 Minimal Simple analgesia. Day case. A block, if used, is for the anaesthetic, not for pain. carpal tunnel release, knee arthroscopy and meniscectomy, minor removal of metalwork
2 Mild to moderate Regular paracetamol and NSAID with a few opioid doses on day 0-1; a single-shot block helps; a catheter is not needed. subacromial decompression, distal radius ORIF, hip arthroscopy, primary THA with spinal and infiltration, lumbar microdiscectomy
3 Moderate A block or neuraxial technique is expected; opioids for two days; worst pain on day 1-2, then a quick fall because the mechanism is bone. ACL reconstruction, hip hemiarthroplasty, ankle ORIF, ACDF, elbow fracture fixation
4 Severe A catheter or a robust multimodal plan; opioids to day 3; rebound after a single-shot block is a real problem; movement-evoked pain limits physiotherapy. primary TKA, anatomic and reverse TSA, Latarjet, high tibial osteotomy, posterior lumbar fusion
5 Severe and prolonged The catheter has its strongest claim; pain persists beyond 72 h and is re-provoked by movement for weeks; the mechanism is tissue under tension or a bone that keeps being loaded. The early peak need not be higher than a 3 or a 4. rotator cuff repair, multiligament knee reconstruction, periacetabular osteotomy, scoliosis correction, amputation

From mechanism to plan

The decision the model exists to make is the block and catheter decision, and it reads straight off the tags.

Two cautions. The evidence for continuous techniques is weaker than the mechanism argument suggests, because most trials measured rest pain over the first 48 hours, which is exactly the window where a dexamethasone-prolonged single shot and a catheter look alike; the trial that added an infusion on top of full multimodal analgesia in shoulder surgery found no difference in morphine use or pain scores at any point to 48 h. And a catheter that falls out, leaks or is never topped up is a single shot with extra steps; the logistics decide more outcomes than the pharmacology.

Why the book is organised this way

PROSPECT, the procedure-specific pain management collaboration, exists because generic guidelines fail: the same drug list applied to every operation treats a cholecystectomy and a cuff repair alike, and the Gerbershagen data show what that costs. Their method is to review the evidence operation by operation and recommend an analgesic skeleton that fits the mechanism; the rotator cuff repair guideline is the worked example that the shoulder cards lean on. This book takes the same step one further back: the mechanism itself is written down for every card, so that when there is no PROSPECT guideline, which is most of orthopaedics, the plan can still be derived rather than guessed. Where a guideline exists, the card cites it. Where it does not, the card says which tags apply and what that implies, and marks the catheter call as author’s judgement. That is the limit of what the model can plainly claim: it predicts the shape of the curve from first principles, and it tells you where to look when the evidence is thin.

Using it at seven in the morning

Five questions, in order, for an operation you have not seen before:

  1. What tissue is being cut, and is any of it bone? If yes, plan for a peak on day 1-2 and for rebound.
  2. What is being left under tension? A repaired tendon, a lengthened limb, a balanced joint, a corrected osteotomy: plan for a tail, and have the catheter conversation.
  3. When will it be loaded? Weight-bearing or hand use from day 1 raises the score by one. A sling, a brace or bed rest lowers it.
  4. Who is the patient? Young, female, anxious, opioid-exposed, or burned by a previous block wearing off: raise the plan, not the score.
  5. What can the system deliver? A day-case patient with nobody at home and a unit that cannot run an ambulatory catheter gets the single shot, the dexamethasone, the written night plan and a phone call, and that is a complete plan rather than a compromise.

Then open the card, and see whether the atlas agrees.
