Part C. The procedure atlas

Upper limb › Shoulder

1 Anatomic total shoulder arthroplasty

Stemmed, stemless, hemiarthroplasty and humeral head resurfacing

4Severe

Dominant mechanism: Bone. Humeral head osteotomy and glenoid reaming over a subscapularis takedown and repair, which is a tendon under tension even in a sling; cuff and capsule left at native length, and the pre-operative pain generator (bone on bone) is removed

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: moderate.

Block
Interscalene brachial plexus block, single shot, with intravenous dexamethasone
Catheter: selective Single shot plus multimodal is the defensible default; a catheter earns its place for revision, opioid-tolerant or chronic pain patients, and anyone with a previous bad night after shoulder surgery
Alternatives: Superior trunk block (phrenic sparing, equivalent analgesia at 24 h); Suprascapular plus axillary nerve blocks (phrenic sparing, weaker); Surgeon-delivered periarticular infiltration as a supplement, not a substitute
Position
Beach chair, 45-70 degrees, head fixed in a holder, operative arm free on a support or held by an assistant
Tourniquet
No
Cement
Sometimes. Polyethylene glenoid is usually cemented (small volume, low pressure); humeral component is usually press-fit, stemless or stemmed; a cemented humeral stem is the exception and the only BCIS-relevant step
Blood loss
200-400 mL; transfusion uncommon with tranexamic acid
Duration
90-150 min skin to skin; stemless and hemiarthroplasty at the short end, revision of a failed hemiarthroplasty well beyond it
Length of stay
1-2 nights. Day case: selected
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV within 60 min of incision (3 g over 120 kg); the surgeon's benzoyl peroxide skin preparation is the Cutibacterium acnes measure, not an extra antibiotic
Tranexamic acid
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV before incision
VTE
Mechanical prophylaxis; chemoprophylaxis only for patients with their own risk factors, since the baseline risk is well below lower-limb arthroplasty
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV at induction and ondansetron 4 mg IV before emergence
Tell the patient
You will wake with a numb, heavy arm that lasts into the night; the shoulder hurts most on the first two days, then settles quickly, and most people are off strong painkillers within a few days.
The trap
Blood pressure at the head, not the arm: in beach chair the cuff overstates brain perfusion pressure by about 1 mmHg for every 1.25 cm between cuff and ear, and deliberate hypotension for a dry field is the mechanism behind the reported strokes

What the surgeon is doing and why

Glenohumeral osteoarthritis is a joint that has worn through its cartilage with the rotator cuff still working. That last clause is the whole operation. The humeral head flattens and grows a collar of inferior osteophytes, the glenoid wears posteriorly and retroverts, the anterior capsule contracts so the arm cannot externally rotate, and the patient’s pain is bone on bone at the centre of the joint. The cuff, if it is intact, still centres the head. An anatomic replacement resurfaces both sides and restores the original geometry so that the intact cuff can go back to doing its job. If the cuff is gone, the same implant will rock the glenoid loose within a few years, which is why a cuff-deficient shoulder gets a reverse instead (see reverse TSA).

The surgeon has four aims, in order:

  1. Get in. The only clean way into the front of the joint is through the subscapularis, so the tendon is taken down (tenotomy, a “peel” off the lesser tuberosity, or a lesser tuberosity osteotomy) and repaired at the end. The three methods heal about as well as each other over two years; the choice is the surgeon’s habit.
  2. Take the head off at the anatomical neck, in the patient’s own retroversion, and measure it. The replacement head is sized to what was removed so that the cuff and capsule end up at their original length. This is the sentence that explains the pain profile: nothing is stretched, lengthened or re-tensioned.
  3. Ream the glenoid flat and correct its version, then implant a polyethylene glenoid, usually cemented, sometimes with a posterior augment if the wear is severe. This is the step with the worst exposure and the hardest retraction.
  4. Seat the humeral component (stemless on the cut surface of the metaphysis, or a short or standard stem down the canal, press-fit in good bone), reduce, check that the head translates about half its width in each direction and that the subscapularis will reach, then repair the subscapularis and close.

A hemiarthroplasty skips step 3 and leaves the native glenoid. Humeral head resurfacing skips the osteotomy as well and caps the head. Both are shorter, bleed less, and leave the glenoid-side pain generator in place, so the post-operative pain pattern is the same shape but the long-term pain relief is less reliable.

The pain logic follows from the anatomy. The dominant mechanism is bone: an osteotomy, reaming, and either impaction or broaching of the metaphysis, all of which hurt in the first 48 hours and then settle because nothing is being loaded through them. The one repaired tendon is the subscapularis, protected by a sling and by the fact that nobody uses it hard for six weeks, but still a tendon pulled onto bone under tension and loaded by every internal rotation the patient forgets not to make; it is a smaller version of the mechanism that dominates rotator cuff repair, not an absence of it. There is no raw subacromial bone surface. And the pre-operative pain generator has been removed, so by the end of the first week most patients are less sore than they were before surgery. The folk ordering puts the reverse, with its lengthened arm and tensioned deltoid, above the anatomic for pain. The one direct comparison, 278 anatomic against 412 reverse replacements, found the opposite: anatomic patients were more often still on opioids at two weeks (62% against 46%), needed more refills, and had slightly higher pain at six weeks (2.8 against 2.2). The model’s explanation is that the anatomic population is younger, which predicts more pain, and that it carries the subscapularis repair, which the reverse often does not.

One honest correction to the folk wisdom that an anatomic replacement is the least painful shoulder operation: in the only prospective comparison, 102 patients having either arthroscopic cuff repair or short-stay arthroplasty under liposomal bupivacaine interscalene blocks had the same early pain, peaking on day 2 at a mean of 4.4 for cuff repair and 5.1 for arthroplasty, with no difference over 14 days and only slightly more opioid use after cuff repair at a week. The difference between the two operations is not the height of the peak. It is the shape of the curve afterwards: bone pain falls away, tendon pain is re-provoked by every movement for weeks. The evidence for that longer tail is modest (more opioid after cuff repair at a week, and the night pain of the second week that every shoulder surgeon describes), so the anatomic replacement sits at a 4 on the book’s scale, the same band as the reverse, with the cuff repair’s 5 resting on the tail rather than the peak.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 Block, induction and airway before the chair goes up

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Everything the surgeon needs (an immobile head, a free arm, a quiet field) is set up now. Once the drapes are on, the head is out of your reach.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Interscalene block (or superior trunk block if the patient’s lungs cannot afford a phrenic palsy) is placed awake or lightly sedated, before induction, with intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg given at the same time; it both prolongs the block and reduces rebound pain. Secure the airway for a case where the head is away from you behind a screen: a tracheal tube is the author’s default, a second-generation supraglottic airway is reasonable in a slim patient with a short case, and the decision is made now, not at the first episode of airway obstruction in the chair. Tape the eyes, protect the contralateral ulnar nerve, put the blood pressure cuff on the non-operative arm, and record a true awake baseline pressure before any drug is given. That baseline is the target for the next two hours.

  2. 2 Beach chair positioning and head fixation

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Sitting the patient up drops the scapula and the deltoid away from the joint and gives the surgeon a vertical humerus to work down, which is the geometry every instrument in the set assumes.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Venous pooling in the legs, sympathetic block from the interscalene spread, and the anaesthetic together produce a predictable fall in pressure as the chair goes up. The hazard is not the number on the cuff but where the brain is: the external auditory meatus sits 20-40 cm above the cuff, so subtract about 1 mmHg for every 1.25 cm of that height when you read it. A cuff mean of 65 mmHg is a brainstem mean in the 40s. Aim to keep cuff pressure near the awake baseline with a vasopressor infusion started early rather than chased with boluses, treat bradycardia-hypotension episodes promptly (they are common in the sitting position with an interscalene block and a vagal reflex is the usual cause), and do not accept a request for deliberate hypotension to dry the field. Check that the head is neutral in the holder and strapped, not rotated or flexed onto the chest, that the endotracheal tube and circuit are not pulling on it, and that the eyes are free of pressure. Then look once more after the surgeon has positioned the arm, because the arm support moves the shoulder girdle and the neck with it.

  3. 3 Skin preparation, antibiotic and tranexamic acid

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Cutibacterium acnes lives in the dermal sebaceous glands of the shoulder, is not reliably cleared by chlorhexidine, and is the organism behind the slow, culture-negative-looking infections that ruin shoulder arthroplasties. Surgeons prepare the skin with benzoyl peroxide for days beforehand and are fastidious about not touching the dermal edge.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Cefazolin 2 g IV finished before the knife, 3 g over 120 kg. Tranexamic acid 1 g IV at the same time: in the pooled trials it cuts the haemoglobin fall by 0.64 g/dL and drain output by about 117 mL, and makes transfusion rare. Nothing else is needed for C. acnes from your side; it is a surgical skin measure.

  4. 4 Deltopectoral approach

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The interval between deltoid and pectoralis major, marked by the cephalic vein, is an internervous plane (axillary nerve laterally, medial and lateral pectoral nerves medially) and gives a direct route to the front of the joint without cutting muscle. The conjoint tendon (short head of biceps and coracobrachialis) is retracted medially with the musculocutaneous nerve a finger’s breadth behind it.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The cephalic vein bleeds if it is torn and is usually preserved or ligated; this is the first blood loss. Retractors on the conjoint tendon are the first traction on the plexus, which is why the arm is kept adducted at this point. If the patient is in a light plane the shoulder girdle will tense and the surgeon will say so; deepen rather than relax, because the subscapularis repair later will be easier to judge with the muscle working.

  5. 5 Subscapularis takedown and anterior capsular release

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The tendon is the door. It is taken down by one of three methods and the anterior capsule beneath it is released from the humeral neck so that the stiff, internally rotated shoulder can be externally rotated enough to deliver the head. The long head of biceps is usually tenodesed or cut here because it is a pain generator and in the way.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    External rotation of the arm to expose the inferior capsule puts the axillary nerve on stretch where it runs under the joint; the surgeon will want the arm held exactly where they put it. There is nothing to do pharmacologically. The capsular release is the moment of maximal nociception before the osteotomy, and in a patient without a working block the pressure and heart rate will tell you so.

  6. 6 Humeral head dislocation and osteotomy

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The head is delivered out of the wound by extension, adduction and external rotation, osteophytes are cleared so the true anatomical neck can be seen, and the head is cut off at that neck in the patient’s native retroversion. The removed head is measured in diameter and height and the replacement is chosen to match.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The largest single bleed of the operation comes from cancellous bone at the osteotomy and from the circumflex vessels at the inferior neck. Forcible extension and external rotation of a stiff arm in an osteoporotic patient is the point at which a humeral shaft fracture happens; a wince from the surgeon here means the case just doubled in length. For a stemless implant the surgeon will test the cut surface for bone quality (a thumb test or a density check) and convert to a stem if it is soft; have no opinion on this except that a cemented stem brings the one cement step that matters.

  7. 7 Glenoid exposure and reaming

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The glenoid is a small, deep target behind the humerus. Exposure needs the humerus retracted posteriorly with a lever, the labrum excised and a circumferential capsular release. The glenoid is reamed to a flat, bleeding surface in corrected version, then drilled or slotted for the pegs or keel.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is the most physiologically demanding step and the one you should be watching rather than charting. The posterior humeral retractor levers against the plexus and the axillary nerve; prolonged or forcible retraction is the usual mechanism of the post-operative neuropraxias. The surgeon needs the arm in exactly the position that opens the glenoid (usually abduction and external rotation) and will ask for it to be held still, so a brief deepening of anaesthesia is often what they mean by “can you give me something”. Reaming throws bone and blood and raises the surgeon’s heart rate more than the patient’s.

  8. 8 Glenoid implantation

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A polyethylene glenoid is cemented into the pegs or keel; some are hybrid with a central press-fit post and cemented peripheral pegs, and a metal-backed or augmented component is used for severe posterior wear.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A small volume of cement, hand-pressurised into pegs with no medullary canal behind them: bone cement implantation syndrome at this step is a theoretical risk rather than a practical one, and this is not the moment for the cement precautions that a hip demands. Note the time; the glenoid cement curing is dead time in which the surgeon prepares the humerus.

  9. 9 Humeral preparation, trial and definitive component

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Stemless: the metaphysis is impacted and a cage or anchor seated on the cut surface. Stemmed: the canal is entered at the cut surface and reamed and broached to size, press-fit in good bone, cemented in poor bone. A trial head goes on, the joint is reduced, and the surgeon checks tension (the head should translate about half its width posteriorly and sit centred), range, and that the subscapularis will reach its repair site.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Press-fit impaction and broaching are hammering, with the transient drops in pressure and the fat and marrow venting that any canal work produces, far less than a femur because the humeral canal is small and not pressurised. If a stem is cemented, treat it as a true cement step: full canal preparation, pressurisation, and a patient whose pressure is already being supported; this is where a frail patient with a fracture hemiarthroplasty gets into trouble, and that case has its own card (proximal humerus fracture). Trial reduction and dislocation are repeated plexus traction. Ask for a 10-second pause if the pressure dips with each reduction; it will.

  10. 10 Subscapularis repair, closure and sling

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The tendon or tuberosity fragment is repaired back to the lesser tuberosity with heavy sutures, often through the stem or through bone tunnels, with the arm in neutral to slight internal rotation so the repair sits without tension. Layered closure of the deltopectoral interval, which has not been cut, and skin. Drains are uncommon. A sling with the arm in neutral protects the subscapularis for six weeks.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The surgeon will want the arm held precisely and motionless for the repair, and this is the point to be reducing anaesthetic depth rather than deepening it; there is no need for neuromuscular block. Give the antiemetic. The sling goes on before the drapes come off and before the patient lightens, because an awake patient with a blocked, flail arm will try to move it with the other hand. Emergence is unremarkable; the arm is insensate and the wound is small.

  11. 11 Recovery, the first night and discharge

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The implant is stable from the moment it is reduced; what the surgeon wants is a protected subscapularis, an early check radiograph, and the deltoid working.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Document deltoid and sensation over the regimental badge area before the block if you can, because afterwards you cannot test the axillary nerve until the block recedes, and a dense interscalene block reads as a plexus injury to anyone who did not know it was there. The block lasts 12 to 24 hours with dexamethasone; the first dose of oral paracetamol and NSAID goes in before the patient leaves recovery, not when the block wears off. Tell the patient and the ward in words that the arm will come back to life overnight with pain that rises over a few hours and that the oral regimen started on time is the treatment, not the trigger for a rescue call. Day 1 physiotherapy is pendular and passive; it does not need the block to still be working. Length of stay is one to two nights; same-day discharge is reasonable in a younger, fitter patient with home support, where the pooled data show no excess readmission or revision, but the cohorts that did well were selected to do well.

Pain plan

The mechanism is bone over one repaired tendon, with a peak on day 1-2 that matches a cuff repair and a tail that is shorter, so the plan is a single-shot block that covers the operation and the first night, with the oral regimen carrying the patient from day 1 and an opioid available for the first week rather than the first two days. The defensible default is an interscalene block with 15-20 mL of ropivacaine 0.5% (or a superior trunk block with the same volume when the patient cannot afford a hemidiaphragm, which gives the same analgesia at 24 h with complete phrenic paresis in 5% rather than 73%), intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg at induction, regular paracetamol and an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor started before the block recedes, and oral opioid as rescue for the first two or three days. PROSPECT’s rotator cuff repair guideline is the nearest procedure-specific evidence and it recommends exactly this skeleton, with intravenous dexamethasone preferred over perineural.

The catheter question is the one the trigger case asked, and the honest answer is that for an anatomic replacement a catheter is a reasonable choice rather than a necessary one. In the one randomised comparison that added a continuous ropivacaine infusion to day 2 on top of dexamethasone and full multimodal analgesia, in a mixed arthroplasty and cuff repair population, morphine use at 24 h was 10 mg with the infusion and 14 mg without, not different, pain scores were the same, and four of the catheters fell out. The catheter earns its place when the patient, rather than the operation, predicts a bad course: an opioid-tolerant or chronic pain patient, a revision or a previous arthroplasty, someone who has had a catastrophic night after a previous single-shot block, or a unit that cannot deliver a reliable oral regimen at 2 am. Rebound pain is the thing to plan against: in 972 ambulatory block patients it occurred in half, and the odds were higher with bone surgery (OR 1.82), younger age and female sex, and lower when intravenous dexamethasone was given (its absence carried an OR of 1.78). Everything on this card that involves bone qualifies.

Escalation: pain above 7 after the block has receded, with the arm neurovascularly intact and the sling correctly on, is treated with the oral opioid that should already be charted; pain that is out of proportion, with a tense swollen deltopectoral wound, is a haematoma and needs the surgeon, not more morphine. A rescue block the next morning is rarely needed and, if the first block was interscalene with a phrenic palsy, a second on the same side within 24 h is not the right reflex.

Pitfalls and variants

  • Stemless versus stemmed. Stemless implants mean no canal work, less bleeding, a shorter case, and an easier future revision; they need good metaphyseal bone, so the surgeon may convert to a stem after the osteotomy. A cemented stem is rare in elective anatomic replacement and common in fracture surgery.
  • Hemiarthroplasty and resurfacing. Shorter, less bleeding, no glenoid cement, same block, same first night. The glenoid is left native, so some of the original pain stays.
  • Conversion to reverse. If the cuff is found to be irreparable or the glenoid cannot hold an anatomic component, the surgeon converts on the table. The case lengthens by an hour, the arm will be lengthened, and the pain plan moves to the reverse card.
  • Beach chair physiology in the patient with cerebrovascular disease, carotid stenosis or uncontrolled hypertension. The margin between cuff pressure and brainstem perfusion is the whole problem. An arterial line transduced at the ear is the honest way to know, and lateral decubitus is an alternative some surgeons will accept.
  • Phrenic palsy. Near-universal after interscalene block, mostly unnoticed, occasionally not. For the patient with COPD, a single lung, contralateral diaphragm palsy or severe obesity, use a superior trunk block or a suprascapular plus axillary combination and expect slightly less analgesia from the latter.
  • Rheumatoid arthritis. Cervical spine instability for the head holder, a cuff that may be thinner than the imaging suggested, steroid cover, and a tendency to bleed more.
  • Post-traumatic arthritis and failed hemiarthroplasty. Scar, retained metal, a long case, more blood loss, more plexus traction: budget for a catheter and for transfusion samples.
  • Diabetes. Dexamethasone 8 mg raises glucose for a day; it is still worth giving for the block, and the ward needs to know.
  • The dense block that looks like a nerve injury. The axillary nerve is the one at risk from retraction; document deltoid function before the block or accept that you cannot assess it until the next day.

Key sources

The evidence on pain after anatomic replacement is thinner than the operation’s frequency deserves. The strongest procedure-specific guidance is PROSPECT’s rotator cuff repair guideline, which the shoulder arthroplasty literature leans on by extrapolation. The two studies that change practice are the 2025 prospective comparison showing early pain after short-stay arthroplasty equal to arthroscopic cuff repair, and the 2024 randomised trial showing no benefit from a continuous infusion once dexamethasone and multimodal analgesia are in place. The beach chair blood pressure advice rests on physiology and case reports, not trials, and will stay that way.

Upper limb › Shoulder

2 Reverse total shoulder arthroplasty

For cuff tear arthropathy, massive irreparable cuff tears, fracture and revision

4Severe

Dominant mechanism: Joint re-tensioned. The arm is deliberately lengthened by 2-3 cm to tension the deltoid, which then carries the whole load of elevation and is stretched with every movement; underneath that is bone (humeral osteotomy, glenoid reaming, baseplate screws, canal preparation) and the stretch on the axillary nerve and plexus that lengthening produces

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: high.

Block
Interscalene brachial plexus block, single shot, with intravenous dexamethasone
Catheter: selective The threshold for a catheter is the same as for an anatomic replacement, since the one direct comparison found the reverse recovery no harder; a continuous technique is the defensible choice for revision, conversion of a failed arthroplasty, fracture, opioid-tolerant or chronic pain patients, and the patient who has had a bad night after a single-shot block before. Single shot with dexamethasone and a written night plan is the default for primary cuff arthropathy in a counselled patient
Alternatives: Superior trunk block (phrenic sparing, equivalent analgesia at 24 h); Suprascapular plus axillary nerve blocks (phrenic sparing, weaker, and the axillary component matters more here than in any other shoulder operation); Surgeon-delivered periarticular infiltration as a supplement
Position
Beach chair, 45-70 degrees, head fixed, operative arm free on a support or held by an assistant; some surgeons work at a lower incline for the anterosuperior approach
Tourniquet
No
Cement
Sometimes. The glenoid baseplate is never cemented (central peg or screw plus locking screws into the scapula); the humeral stem is press-fit in good bone and cemented in osteoporotic bone, fracture and revision, and the cemented stem is the one BCIS-relevant step
Blood loss
300-500 mL in a primary; transfusion uncommon with tranexamic acid, more likely in revision, conversion and fracture
Duration
90-150 min skin to skin for a primary; revision and conversion of a failed anatomic or hemiarthroplasty run two to three hours and are a different operation
Length of stay
1-3 nights; the population is older and frailer than the anatomic population. Day case: selected
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV within 60 min of incision (3 g over 120 kg); Cutibacterium acnes is the organism and the surgeon's benzoyl peroxide skin preparation is the measure against it
Tranexamic acid
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV before incision; the pooled shoulder arthroplasty data show a smaller haemoglobin fall and less drain output
VTE
Mechanical prophylaxis; chemoprophylaxis for the patient's own risk factors, more often met in this older population than in the anatomic one
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV at induction and ondansetron 4 mg IV before emergence
Tell the patient
The arm will be numb and heavy into the night; the shoulder then aches deeply for several days because the arm has been made slightly longer to tighten the main shoulder muscle, and lifting the arm uses that muscle from the first week.
The trap
The reduction is the moment: lengthening the arm by 2-3 cm pulls on the axillary nerve and the plexus and drops the blood pressure on every trial reduction, and a deltoid that does not work afterwards is either the block, a nerve stretched by the lengthening, or an acromial stress fracture weeks later; document deltoid function and regimental badge sensation before the block

What the surgeon is doing and why

An anatomic replacement works only while the rotator cuff centres the humeral head on the glenoid. Take the cuff away and the deltoid, pulling almost vertically, drags the head up into the acromion instead of lifting the arm: the patient shrugs and cannot elevate (pseudoparalysis), the unroofed head wears the acromion and glenoid into one eroded socket (cuff tear arthropathy), and an anatomic implant in that shoulder rocks its glenoid loose within a few years. The reverse geometry solves the mechanical problem rather than the anatomical one. The ball goes on the glenoid side (a glenosphere on a screwed-in baseplate) and the socket on the humerus (a polyethylene insert on a tray or stem). That moves the centre of rotation medially onto the glenoid face, so the deltoid works with a longer lever arm and loads the baseplate in compression rather than shear, and it lets the surgeon drop the humerus distally, lengthening the arm by two to three centimetres so that the deltoid is on stretch and more of its fibres are recruited into elevation. A tensioned deltoid is now the engine and the stabiliser; the implant stays reduced mainly because the deltoid compresses it. That is the mechanism difference from the anatomic card, and it drives the pain profile, the nerve risk, the instability pattern and the stress fracture.

The indications have widened from cuff arthropathy in the elderly to massive irreparable tears, proximal humerus fractures in older patients (see proximal humerus fracture), inflammatory arthritis, osteoarthritis with too much posterior glenoid wear for an anatomic glenoid, failed arthroplasty, and increasingly primary osteoarthritis over 70. The population is older, frailer and more comorbid than the anatomic one, and a good share are revisions.

The operation in order:

  1. Get in. Deltopectoral is the common route, with the subscapularis taken down if it exists. Some surgeons use an anterosuperior approach that splits the anterior deltoid off the acromion: a direct view of the glenoid in a stiff shoulder, at the cost of cutting into the muscle the construct depends on.
  2. Cut the head off, lower and in less retroversion than for an anatomic replacement, to make room for the humeral socket below the glenosphere.
  3. Expose the whole glenoid down to the inferior scapular neck (a circumferential capsular release with the axillary nerve under the inferior capsule), ream, seat the baseplate low with slight inferior tilt, fix it with a central peg or screw and locking screws into the scapular body, and impact the glenosphere onto the taper.
  4. Prepare the humerus (stem, short stem or stemless; press-fit or cemented), assemble a trial tray and insert, and reduce.
  5. Set the tension. The surgeon pulls on the arm, reduces the trial, and judges how hard it was to reduce, how taut the conjoint tendon is, whether the joint gapes on distraction and whether the arm hangs at the right length. Too loose dislocates; too tight stretches the nerves, loads the acromion and limits motion. Every adjustment of insert or stem is another dislocation and reduction.
  6. Fix the definitive components, decide about the subscapularis (surgeons vary: some repair it for stability, some leave it, some have nothing to repair), close, sling.

The pain logic follows. The dominant mechanism is retension: the arm has been lengthened and the deltoid is on stretch from the final reduction, and unlike the subscapularis after an anatomic replacement nobody can rest it, because every elevation from the first physiotherapy session is the deltoid doing its new job. That gives the deep, aching, stiffness-type pain the Part B table assigns to re-tensioned joints, with night pain and a slower fall than pure bone pain. Bone contributes the first 48 hours: osteotomy, reaming, scapular screws, canal preparation. Nerve adds a flavour of its own: in the one prospective EMG study, subclinical lesions were found at 3.6 weeks in 9 of 19 reverse arthroplasties, mainly axillary and mostly resolving, against one in 23 anatomic replacements, with mean arm lengthening of 2.7 cm. Dysaesthesia over the regimental badge area or a burning quality to the early pain is that, not the block.

One correction to folklore. The reverse is widely called the more painful arthroplasty, and the mechanism supports a 4. The largest retrospective comparison does not: 412 reverse patients were less often still on opioids at two weeks than 278 anatomic patients (46% against 62%) and had lower pain at six weeks. The reverse population is older, and younger age predicts severe early pain; and many reverse shoulders have no subscapularis repair to protect. The honest reading is that retension earns the 4 for revision, conversion, fracture, the younger patient with a massive tear and the opioid-tolerant patient, while the uncomplicated elderly cuff arthropathy patient often runs nearer a 3 with a slower tail. The plan is written for the first group and relaxed for the second.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 Assessment, block, airway and baseline pressure

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants an immobile head, a free arm, a working deltoid afterwards and a stable implant, in a patient who is older and sicker than the anatomic patient and often a revision.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Two decisions cannot be made later. The first is the deltoid: a reverse without a working deltoid is a contraindication, and once the block is in you cannot test the axillary nerve until tomorrow, so document deltoid power and regimental badge sensation in words before the block. The second is the catheter (see the pain plan), decided with the indication in front of you: primary cuff arthropathy and conversion of a failed anatomic are not the same operation. Place the interscalene block (or a superior trunk block in the patient who cannot afford a hemidiaphragm) awake or lightly sedated, with intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg at the same time. A tracheal tube is the author’s default: the head is away from you for two hours and the patient is often obese or has a poor chest. Cuff on the non-operative arm, awake baseline pressure recorded before any drug.

  2. 2 Beach chair and head fixation

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The sitting position drops the scapula and lets the surgeon work down a vertical humerus and across to the glenoid face; some sit the patient lower for the anterosuperior approach.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The pressure falls as the chair goes up, and the cuff overstates perfusion at the brain by roughly 1 mmHg for every 1.25 cm between cuff and external auditory meatus. This population carries more cerebrovascular disease than the anatomic one, so the margin matters more. Start a vasopressor infusion early, keep the cuff reading near the awake baseline, treat the bradycardia-hypotension episodes that the sitting position and the block provoke, and decline deliberate hypotension for a dry field; the reported strokes happened at cuff systolics in the 80s and 90s. Check the head is neutral and strapped and the eyes are free, then look again after the surgeon has set the arm.

  3. 3 Antibiotic, tranexamic acid and approach

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Cutibacterium acnes in the dermal sebaceous glands is the organism behind late, indolent shoulder arthroplasty infection; the surgeon prepares with benzoyl peroxide beforehand and avoids the dermal edge. Deltopectoral: the internervous plane between deltoid and pectoralis major, cephalic vein as the marker, conjoint tendon retracted medially with the musculocutaneous nerve behind it, then the subscapularis taken down if it is there and repairable. Anterosuperior: the anterior deltoid is elevated off the acromion and the surgeon looks straight down onto the glenoid, faster in a stiff or revision shoulder but a knife into the engine of the construct.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Cefazolin 2 g IV finished before the knife, 3 g over 120 kg, and tranexamic acid 1 g IV at the same time. The cephalic vein is the first bleed and retractors on the conjoint tendon the first traction on the plexus. In a revision the approach is through scar with retained metal and a tethered plexus; this step alone can take 45 minutes and is where the revision earns its blood loss, so a group and hold is sensible for a revision or conversion and rarely needed for a primary. If the surgeon has split the deltoid, add muscle to this patient’s pain mechanisms: the split aches with every elevation.

  4. 4 Humeral head osteotomy

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The head is delivered by extension, adduction and external rotation, osteophytes are cleared, and the cut is made at the implant’s neck-shaft angle (155 degrees in the Grammont design, 135 in the lateralised designs) and in less retroversion than anatomic, so the humeral socket sits below and lateral to the glenosphere.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The largest single bleed of the operation, from cancellous bone and the circumflex vessels. Forcible external rotation of a stiff, osteoporotic humerus is where a shaft fracture happens and the case doubles in length, and this population is more osteoporotic than the anatomic one.

  5. 5 Glenoid exposure, reaming and baseplate

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The baseplate must sit flush on the inferior glenoid with its central fixation driven into the dense bone at the base of the scapular spine, so the whole glenoid face and the inferior neck must be seen: labrum excised, capsule released all the way round, a retractor under the inferior neck where the axillary nerve crosses. The surface is reamed flat, the baseplate positioned low with a few degrees of inferior tilt (both reduce scapular notching), and the fixation driven into the scapula. Bone loss is built up with graft from the resected head or an augmented baseplate.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The most demanding step for the patient and the one to watch. The posterior humeral retractor levers on the plexus and the inferior retractor sits on the axillary nerve; the surgeon needs the arm still in the position that opens the glenoid, and a request for “something” usually means depth, not relaxant. Scapular screws bleed from cancellous bone and the irrigation hides how much. A revision glenoid with a failed component to remove is the long version of this step.

  6. 6 Glenosphere and humeral preparation

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The glenosphere is impacted onto the baseplate taper and locked. The humerus is reamed and broached for a stem, or the metaphysis impacted for a stemless or short-stem implant. Press-fit in good bone; in osteoporotic bone, fracture and revision the stem is cemented, either now or after the trial.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Humeral canal work vents far less than a femur, but a cemented stem is a real cement step and the one BCIS-relevant moment in shoulder surgery: 16% of 173 cemented shoulder arthroplasties met any-grade criteria in a large series, against 31% of hip hemiarthroplasties, and the patients who do badly are over 75, ASA 3-4 or have renal impairment, which describes much of this population. When cement goes in, the canal is lavaged and dried, the pressure is already supported, the oxygen is up and you are watching end-tidal carbon dioxide as the stem goes home. Press-fit stems carry no such moment and a higher rate of intraoperative fracture in soft bone; that is the trade the surgeon is making.

  7. 7 Trial reduction and deltoid tensioning

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon assembles a trial tray and insert, pulls the arm into traction and reduces the socket onto the glenosphere. The feel of that reduction, the tautness of the conjoint tendon, the gap on distraction and the range through which the insert does not lever off are the information used to pick the insert thickness and, if needed, reseat the stem. Each change is another dislocation and reduction. The target is enough tension to be stable and no more; the systematic review of arm lengthening puts the goal at 0-2 cm beyond the other side, with shortening raising dislocation and excess raising nerve injury.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is the step the trap is about. Reduction stretches the axillary nerve and the plexus by the full length of the lengthening, in a patient whose nerves are often tethered by scar, and the pressure dips with each reduction as the arm is pulled and the joint levered. Do not give a relaxant to make the reduction easier: a reduction that only goes in with the patient paralysed will dislocate on the ward when tone returns, and the surgeon needs the resting tone to judge the tension. When the surgeon says the reduction is “tight”, the mechanism of this card’s pain is being created in front of you.

  8. 8 Definitive components, subscapularis, closure and sling

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The definitive stem or metaphyseal component is seated (impacted or cemented), the tray and insert locked on, and the final reduction tested through the range, with attention to adduction (the insert must not impinge on the scapular neck) and to extension with internal rotation, the position that dislocates a reverse. Surgeons vary on the subscapularis: some repair it for anterior stability, some leave it because a repaired subscapularis limits external rotation and may not heal to a lengthened humerus, and in many cuff arthropathy shoulders there is nothing to repair. The anterosuperior approach needs the deltoid repaired to the acromion and protected for six weeks. A sling, often with a small abduction wedge, goes on.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A cemented stem has its cement step here if not at step 6, with the same precautions. The final reduction is the last stretch on the nerves; note its time, because this is where you start to lighten. Give the antiemetic. The sling goes on before the patient lightens: an awake patient with a dense block will lift the dead arm by the wrist with the other hand, and the position that does it (arm swung across the body) is the dislocating position. Emergence is unremarkable; the arm is insensate.

  9. 9 Recovery, the first night and physiotherapy

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The implant is stable from the final reduction provided the arm stays out of extension, adduction and internal rotation. The surgeon wants early passive and active-assisted elevation because the deltoid is the operation, a radiograph before discharge, and no hand-behind-back for six weeks.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The block lasts 12-24 hours with dexamethasone. The first regular paracetamol and NSAID dose goes in before the patient leaves recovery, and the ward is told that the arm comes back to life overnight with a deep ache rising over a few hours, which the regular regimen treats. A deltoid that does not work when the block has receded is the differential that matters: residual block (commonest, and it has a timescale), an axillary nerve stretched at the reduction (subclinical in nearly half on EMG, usually recovering), or a true injury. Record what you find and when. Day 1 physiotherapy loads the deltoid, and this is where the reverse separates from the anatomic: the first elevation is pain through a stretched muscle, and a patient who cannot do it because the oral regimen was late loses the day.

  10. 10 Later presentations that come to you first

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Three complications present as new pain or a dead arm in the weeks after discharge. The acromial or scapular spine stress fracture is the deltoid’s own tension breaking the bone it hangs from: pooled incidence 5%, usually in the first months, presenting as new pain over the acromion or spine and a sudden loss of elevation, with worse outcomes whether or not it is fixed. Dislocation (about 2% overall, higher in revision and the absent-subscapularis shoulder) is early, anterior, and follows extension-adduction-internal rotation: pushing up from a chair, or the sling off. Scapular notching is the insert eroding the inferior scapular neck in adduction, radiographic rather than painful in the early years.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    You will be asked whether the block caused the weak deltoid at six weeks. It did not; the stress fracture and the stretched axillary nerve are the candidates and the radiograph and an EMG decide. Reduction of an early dislocation is a short general anaesthetic with full relaxation; closed reduction fails more often than it succeeds, so the surgeon may go on to an open revision of the insert.

Pain plan

The mechanism is a lengthened arm with a tensioned deltoid loaded from day 1, over bone work that hurts for 48 hours and nerves that have been stretched; the population is older and less rebound-prone than the anatomic one. The plan is built for the mechanism and relaxed for the patient: the anatomic card’s skeleton with a lower threshold for a continuous technique.

The defensible default is an interscalene block with 15-20 mL of ropivacaine 0.5% (or a superior trunk block with the same volume when the patient cannot afford a hemidiaphragm; it matches interscalene at 24 h with complete phrenic paresis in 5% rather than 73%), intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg at induction, regular paracetamol and an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor where renal function allows (often it does not, which is one reason the oral regimen is weaker here than on the anatomic card), and oral opioid for the first three days. PROSPECT has no arthroplasty guideline; the rotator cuff repair guideline is the nearest and recommends this skeleton with intravenous dexamethasone preferred over perineural.

The catheter. The one randomised comparison in shoulder arthroplasty found that a continuous interscalene infusion lowered day 1 pain and opioid use against a single shot but did not shorten the stay, produced more adverse events and lost 10% of its catheters early; the trial that added an infusion on top of dexamethasone and full multimodal analgesia, in a mixed arthroplasty and cuff repair population, found no difference at all. The author’s reconciliation is the same as on the other shoulder cards: the catheter’s advantage shows when the single shot is bare and shrinks when it is prolonged with dexamethasone and backed by a regimen that is given. What differs here is who sits in the group the catheter helps. Conversion of a failed arthroplasty, revision of a reverse, the fracture reverse, the opioid-tolerant or chronic pain patient, the younger patient with a massive tear, and anyone whose previous shoulder operation produced a catastrophic night: for these the catheter is the defensible choice, because the deltoid will be loaded on day 1 whether or not the pain is controlled. A catheter needs fixation that survives a sling; the common failure is the catheter in the bed.

Rebound pain: half of ambulatory block patients after bone surgery describe it, with younger age, female sex and the absence of intravenous dexamethasone raising the odds. Escalation: pain above 7 after the block has receded with the sling on and the hand warm and moving is treated with the opioid already charted and a check that the regular doses were given; pain out of proportion with a tense, swelling deltopectoral wound is a haematoma for the surgeon; new sharp pain over the acromion in the first weeks with loss of elevation is a stress fracture and goes back to the surgeon.

Pitfalls and variants

  • Primary cuff arthropathy versus everything else. The primary in a 75-year-old is a 90-minute case with 300 mL of blood loss and a course nearer a 3. Conversion of a failed anatomic, revision of a loose reverse and the fracture reverse are two- to three-hour cases through scar, with more bleeding, longer plexus traction, a cemented stem and a catheter-grade pain course. Book them differently.
  • Anterosuperior approach. Splits the deltoid: faster exposure, a deltoid repair to protect, and muscle added to the pain mechanisms.
  • Lateralised designs. Lateralising the glenosphere or the humerus reduces notching and improves rotation but changes how the deltoid is tensioned; surgeons vary and the pain plan does not.
  • Stemless and short-stem reverse. No canal work, no cement, less bleeding, shorter case; needs good metaphyseal bone.
  • Cemented stem. Fracture, revision and osteoporotic bone. BCIS is less frequent than in a hip but it is the same syndrome in the same frail patient; the precautions are the same. The 2016 systematic review found no difference in loosening or revision between cemented and press-fit stems, so the choice is the surgeon’s and the bone’s.
  • Poor tone. Parkinson’s disease, neuromuscular disease and heavy alcohol use take away the deltoid compression that keeps the implant reduced; instability is commoner and the sling matters more.
  • Beach chair physiology with carotid disease, uncontrolled hypertension or a previous stroke. The cuff-to-brain gradient is the problem and this population has more of these patients. An arterial line transduced at the ear is the honest monitor.
  • Renal impairment. Takes away the NSAID and raises the BCIS risk; the oral regimen becomes paracetamol and opioid, which argues for the best block you can place.
  • Rheumatoid arthritis and obesity. Cervical spine for the head holder, steroid cover and osteoporotic bone for the one; airway access in the chair and a diaphragm that cannot afford the phrenic palsy for the other.

Key sources

There is no PROSPECT guideline for shoulder arthroplasty of either geometry; the rotator cuff repair guideline is extrapolated. The mechanism claims rest on small prospective series on arm lengthening and nerve lesions, not trials; the acromial fracture and instability figures are reviews of heterogeneous reports. The block evidence is the 2019 randomised comparison of continuous and single-shot interscalene block in arthroplasty and the 2024 trial showing no added benefit from an infusion once dexamethasone and multimodal analgesia are in place; the catheter advice is the author’s reconciliation of those two with the mechanism. The claim that reverse patients use less opioid than anatomic patients is a single-centre retrospective series: a corrective to folklore, not evidence that the reverse is a mild operation.

  1. Lädermann A, Edwards TB, Walch G. Arm lengthening after reverse shoulder arthroplasty: a review. Int Orthop 2014;38:991-1000
    Seven studies: upper limb lengthening 15-27 mm, acromiohumeral distance averaging 23 mm; shortening raised dislocation risk and reduced anterior elevation; subclinical neurological lesions frequent; 0-2 cm of lengthening the suggested target to avoid neurological impairment
  2. Lädermann A, Lübbeke A, Mélis B, et al. Prevalence of neurologic lesions after total shoulder arthroplasty. J Bone Joint Surg Am 2011;93:1288-1293
    Prospective EMG at 3.6 weeks: subclinical changes in 9 of 19 reverse arthroplasties, mainly axillary nerve, 8 resolving within six months, versus one plexus lesion in 23 anatomic replacements; relative risk 10.9; mean arm lengthening 2.7 cm after reverse
  3. Lau SC, Large R. Acromial fracture after reverse total shoulder arthroplasty: a systematic review. Shoulder Elbow 2020;12:375-389
    25 papers, 208 fractures, overall incidence 5%, stress fractures commoner than traumatic; outcomes worse after fracture whether operated or not

  6. Howard WH, Robinson LT, Vasimalla M, et al. Instability after reverse shoulder arthroplasty: a systematic review of interventions and clinical outcomes. J Shoulder Elbow Surg 2025;34:2735-2745

    60 arthroplasty and cuff repair patients with dexamethasone, magnesium, paracetamol and ketorolac: morphine at 24 h 10 mg with infusion versus 14 mg without, p=0.74, no difference in any secondary outcome
  9. Jones CA, Chambers S, Renshaw AD, et al. Patients undergoing reverse total shoulder arthroplasty have less pain and require fewer opioid pain medications compared to anatomic total shoulder arthroplasty in the early postoperative period: a retrospective review. J Shoulder Elbow Surg 2025;34:454-461
    278 anatomic and 412 reverse: anatomic patients were more often still on opioids at two weeks (62% vs 46%) and needed more refills; VAS at six weeks 2.8 vs 2.2
  10. Kang R, Jeong JS, Chin KJ, et al. Superior trunk block provides noninferior analgesia compared with interscalene brachial plexus block in arthroscopic shoulder surgery. Anesthesiology 2019;131:1316-1326

    Hydrostatic correction of about 2 mmHg per inch between cuff and external auditory meatus; strokes reported after shoulder surgery in beach chair with cuff systolics in the 80s-90s; no deliberate hypotension

Upper limb › Shoulder

3 Arthroscopic rotator cuff repair

With or without subacromial decompression, biceps tenodesis and distal clavicle excision

5Severe and prolonged

Dominant mechanism: Tendon under tension. A retracted, degenerate tendon pulled back onto a decorticated, bleeding footprint under tension and loaded by every movement for weeks; plus raw bone from acromioplasty, an inflamed bursa stripped out, and arthroscopic fluid in the soft tissues

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: high.

Block
Interscalene brachial plexus block with intravenous dexamethasone; continuous catheter favoured by PROSPECT, single shot plus a written night plan the defensible day-case default
Catheter: selective Catheter for large or massive tears, revision repairs, opioid-tolerant or poorly coping patients, and any unit that cannot guarantee the oral regimen overnight; single shot with dexamethasone for small and medium tears in a counselled day-case patient
Alternatives: Superior trunk block (phrenic sparing, equivalent at 24 h); Suprascapular plus axillary nerve blocks (phrenic sparing, PROSPECT grade B, inferior to interscalene); Liposomal bupivacaine interscalene where available, which pushes the peak to day 2
Position
Beach chair in most Australian practice; lateral decubitus with 5-7 kg of arm traction in some hands, which changes the airway access and the plexus traction but not the pain
Tourniquet
No
Cement
No
Blood loss
Minimal into the wound; the fluid you see is irrigation. Haemoglobin is unchanged
Duration
60-150 min; small tears at the short end, massive tears with releases, tenodesis and decompression at the long end, and the irrigation clock runs the whole time
Length of stay
Day case or one night. Day case: yes
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV within 60 min of incision (3 g over 120 kg); anchors are implants and Cutibacterium acnes is the shoulder organism
Tranexamic acid
Not routinely needed for blood loss; some surgeons use TXA 1 g IV for arthroscopic visibility, which is a reasonable request
VTE
Mechanical only in most units; chemoprophylaxis only for the patient's own risk factors
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV at induction and ondansetron 4 mg IV before emergence
Tell the patient
The arm will be numb and heavy for most of the first day; the shoulder then hurts, especially at night, for one to two weeks, and the sling is what protects the repair, not a sign that something has gone wrong.
The trap
The block wears off at 2 am: rebound pain after a single-shot interscalene block is the rule after bone-and-tendon surgery, and the plan has to be written for the first night at home, not for the recovery room

What the surgeon is doing and why

A rotator cuff tear is a tendon that has pulled off bone. Supraspinatus is the usual victim, because it runs under the acromion and over the humeral head at the point of maximum load and minimum blood supply. Once the tendon end is off the greater tuberosity it retracts medially, the muscle behind it atrophies and fills with fat, and the humeral head loses the depressor that kept it centred under the acromion, so the patient gets weakness, night pain, and a head that rides up and impinges. The tissue the surgeon is working with is not healthy tendon that happened to tear; it is a degenerate, retracted, poorly vascular structure that has to be dragged back to where it came from and persuaded to heal to bone over about twelve weeks. Re-tear rates after repair are substantial and rise with tear size and age, which is why the protection afterwards is so cautious and why the surgeon cares about every detail of fixation.

The operation has a fixed logic:

  1. See the problem: diagnostic arthroscopy of the joint, then the subacromial space. The long head of biceps is often cut or tenodesed on the way because it is a pain generator and anchors nothing useful.
  2. Clear the workspace: the subacromial bursa, thick and inflamed, is stripped out so the tendon and the acromion can be seen. Many surgeons then shave the undersurface of the acromion (acromioplasty) and some excise the distal clavicle. The randomised trials show acromioplasty adds nothing to re-tear or function, but it is still common and it leaves a raw bleeding bone surface.
  3. Free the tendon: releases of the capsule and the coracohumeral ligament above and below the tendon so that it can be pulled laterally without excess tension. The more retracted the tear, the more release, the longer the case.
  4. Prepare the footprint: the cortical surface of the greater tuberosity where the tendon used to insert is decorticated with a burr to bleeding bone, because tendon heals to raw bone and not to cortex.
  5. Fix it: suture anchors are placed in the tuberosity (one row at the medial edge, or two rows in a “transosseous-equivalent” bridge), sutures are passed through the tendon, and the tendon is reduced onto the footprint and tied or locked under tension. The tension is the point: a lax repair does not heal and a tight one re-tears, and the surgeon judges it with the arm in a set position.
  6. Protect it: a sling, often with an abduction pillow, for six weeks, with no active use of the repaired tendon. Every movement that loads the tendon in those weeks is pain and risk.

The pain logic is the mirror image of an anatomic shoulder replacement. There the dominant mechanism is bone, with one repaired tendon resting in a sling, and the pain fades once nothing is being loaded through the cut. Here the dominant mechanism is tendon-tension: a repaired, poorly vascular tendon that is pulled onto bone and then loaded, however gently, by every reach and every roll in bed for weeks. Underneath it is bone (the decorticated footprint and the acromioplasty, which hurt like any osteotomy for two or three days), capsule (the releases), and arthroscopy itself (portals, irrigation fluid in the deltoid and subcutaneous tissues, and a shoulder that has been held in traction or abduction for an hour and a half). The early peak is no higher than after arthroplasty: in the one prospective comparison both groups peaked on day 2, at a mean of 4.4 for cuff repair and 5.1 for arthroplasty under long-acting interscalene blocks. The difference is afterwards. Cuff repair patients were still using more opioid at a week, and the night pain that defines this operation runs for one to two weeks. A plan that only covers the first night has covered the easy part.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 Block, airway and the night plan before the patient is asleep

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The whole operation is done through 5 mm portals under irrigation; nothing about it needs your attention as much as the hours after it.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is the operation PROSPECT wrote its shoulder guideline for: interscalene block first choice, intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg with it, paracetamol and an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor started pre-operatively and continued. Decide the catheter question now with the surgeon’s tear size in front of you (see the pain plan). Airway: a tracheal tube is the author’s default in beach chair, because the head is behind a screen and the neck may swell with irrigation fluid over a long case; a second-generation supraglottic device is reasonable for a short repair in a slim patient. Cuff on the non-operative arm, awake baseline pressure recorded, eyes taped and padded, because the surgeon’s arm and the camera cable will be passing over the face.

  2. 2 Positioning: beach chair or lateral decubitus

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Beach chair gives a familiar anatomy and easy conversion to open; lateral decubitus with the arm in longitudinal traction opens the joint and the subacromial space wider and some surgeons will not operate any other way.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Beach chair: the cuff overstates brain perfusion pressure by roughly 1 mmHg per 1.25 cm of height between cuff and ear, so keep the cuff reading near the awake baseline with a vasopressor infusion and treat the bradycardia-hypotension episodes that the sitting position plus interscalene block provoke. Lateral: the airway is now accessed from the side with the patient’s face in a cradle, the dependent arm and eye need padding, the traction (5-7 kg) is a sustained pull on the plexus that you cannot see, and hypotension is less of a problem but a shift in the patient’s position mid-case is harder to correct. In either position, check that the head is neutral once the surgeon has set the arm, because they will move it.

  3. 3 Portals, irrigation pump and the request for a low pressure

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Visibility in the subacromial space depends on the balance between irrigation pump pressure (typically 40-60 mmHg) and the patient’s systolic pressure; bleeding from the bursa and the acromion fogs the view. Surgeons raise the pump, add adrenaline to the irrigation bags, or ask you to lower the pressure.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The request for a systolic of 90 is the central conflict of this operation. In beach chair it is a request for a brainstem perfusion pressure in the 50s, and PROSPECT lists controlled hypotension as not recommended on exactly those grounds. The honest answer is that you will keep the pressure near baseline, that adrenaline in the irrigation (1 mL of 1:1000 per 3 L bag is a common recipe) and a higher pump pressure are the surgeon’s tools, and that a patient with a working interscalene block and an adequate depth of anaesthesia will not be hypertensive. Adrenaline absorbed from the irrigation can produce transient tachycardia and hypertension; a sudden pressure rise shortly after a new bag goes up is that, not light anaesthesia.

  4. 4 Diagnostic arthroscopy, biceps and labrum

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The glenohumeral joint is inspected for the things that change the plan (a subscapularis tear, a SLAP lesion, cartilage loss that would make repair pointless) and the long head of biceps is tenotomised or tenodesed.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Nothing to do but note the time. A tenodesis into the bicipital groove adds an anchor and twenty minutes; a tenotomy adds nothing.

  5. 5 Subacromial bursectomy

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The inflamed bursa is thick, vascular and obscures everything. It is resected with a shaver and radiofrequency device until the acromion, the coracoacromial ligament and the tendon edge can be seen.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is where the fluid starts to go. Irrigation extravasates into the deltoid and the subcutaneous tissues, the shoulder swells, and over a long case in a heavy patient the swelling tracks to the neck. Watch the neck and the airway pressures as a matter of routine from this point, and warm the irrigation or the patient, because 20 L of room-temperature saline through the shoulder is a cooling system.

  6. 6 Acromioplasty and distal clavicle excision

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The undersurface of the acromion is burred flat to remove a spur or a hooked morphology and to make room for the repaired tendon; the coracoacromial ligament is released. Some surgeons excise the distal 5-10 mm of the clavicle if the acromioclavicular joint is arthritic.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Bone work with a burr: bleeding, bone dust, and the pump going up. The pain contribution is a raw cancellous surface under the deltoid that behaves like a small osteotomy for two or three days. Nothing about the step needs intervention, but it is the step most likely to produce the low-pressure request.

  7. 7 Tendon mobilisation and releases

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A retracted tendon will not reach its footprint without releasing the adhesions, the capsule beneath it and the coracohumeral ligament above it. Massive tears need extensive releases, sometimes a margin convergence (side-to-side sutures to bring the tear edges together), and some get a patch or a superior capsular reconstruction instead of a repair.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The length of this step is the length of the case. A tear that the surgeon describes as “retracted to the glenoid” means releases, more anchors, more fluid, more traction, and a pain course at the top of the range. This is the information you need for the catheter decision, and it arrives now if it did not arrive in the pre-operative note.

  8. 8 Footprint preparation

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The greater tuberosity is decorticated with a burr to a bleeding bed, because tendon heals to marrow and not to cortical bone. Some surgeons add bone marrow vents (small drill holes) to bring in a healing response.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Raw bleeding bone, the second of the three bone surfaces this operation creates. It is the reason that cuff repair qualifies as bone surgery for rebound pain purposes, with the higher odds that carries.

  9. 9 Anchors, suture passage and tendon reduction under tension

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Anchors go into the tuberosity, sutures are passed through the tendon with a dedicated instrument, and the tendon is reduced onto the footprint and fixed with knots or a knotless locking mechanism, in single-row or double-row configurations. The surgeon sets the tension with the arm in a specific degree of abduction and rotation and will want it held exactly there for the tying.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The arm position is set by the surgeon or an assistant and must not drift; a shift of 10 degrees changes the tension on a repair that is about to be locked. This is not a request for neuromuscular block (a working interscalene block already provides a flail arm) but for a steady patient and a steady table. The tendon pulled onto bone under tension here is what the patient will feel for the next fortnight; the moment the knots go down, the mechanism this card is built around exists.

  10. 10 Closure, sling and the swollen shoulder

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Portals are closed with a stitch or a strip, a bulky dressing goes on, and the arm goes into a sling, usually with an abduction pillow that takes the tension off the repair.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Put the sling on before the patient lightens; an awake patient with a dense block will otherwise lift the dead arm by the wrist and load the repair. Examine the neck before extubation after a long case in beach chair: subcutaneous fluid tracking from the deltoid to the supraclavicular fossa and anterior neck is common, usually harmless, and occasionally enough to compromise the airway. A patient with a visibly swollen neck, a long case and a difficult airway earns a longer wait and a careful look rather than a reflex extubation.

  11. 11 Recovery and the first night

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The repair is protected by the sling and nothing else; the surgeon wants pendular movements only, cryotherapy and sleep.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The first paracetamol and NSAID dose goes in before the patient leaves recovery. The block lasts 12 to 24 hours with dexamethasone, longer with liposomal bupivacaine, and when it recedes the pain rises over an hour or two to its day 1 and 2 level; half of ambulatory block patients after bone surgery describe exactly this. The written night plan (what to take at bedtime, what to take when the fingers start to tingle, when the opioid is for) is the single intervention that decides whether this patient telephones at 3 am. Night pain persists for one to two weeks because the patient cannot lie on either side without loading the shoulder; sleeping propped up and the sling worn in bed are surgical advice worth repeating. Day case is the norm for small and medium tears with a single-shot block; a catheter patient can also go home if the unit runs ambulatory infusions, or stays a night if it does not.

Pain plan

The mechanism is tendon under tension plus two raw bone surfaces, loaded by movement for weeks, so this is the shoulder operation where a continuous technique has the strongest claim and the operation PROSPECT’s guideline was written for. The guideline recommends interscalene block as first choice, with single-shot and continuous both graded A and the continuous technique favoured; intravenous dexamethasone (grade B) and preferred over perineural; paracetamol with an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor started before surgery; and suprascapular with or without axillary nerve block as a phrenic-sparing alternative that is inferior to interscalene. It recommends against subacromial or intra-articular infusions, stellate ganglion and cervical epidural blocks, gabapentinoids, and controlled hypotension.

Against that stands the randomised trial that added a ropivacaine 0.2% infusion to day 2 on top of dexamethasone, magnesium, paracetamol and ketorolac, in a mixed arthroplasty and cuff repair population, and found no difference in morphine at any time point or in pain scores, with four of thirty catheters falling out. The two are reconcilable: the catheter’s advantage shows when the alternative is a bare single shot, and shrinks when the single shot is prolonged with dexamethasone and backed by a regimen that is actually taken.

The defensible default, then, is a single-shot interscalene block (15-20 mL of ropivacaine 0.5%, or a superior trunk block with the same volume when the patient cannot afford a hemidiaphragm, which matches it at 24 h), intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg, paracetamol and an NSAID started before the block recedes, oral opioid for the nights of the first week, and a night plan written down for the patient. The catheter is the right call for the large or massive tear with extensive releases, the revision repair, the opioid-tolerant or chronic pain patient, the patient who has had a catastrophic rebound night before, and the unit that cannot guarantee a 2 am dose on a ward. If a catheter is placed, it needs a fixation that survives a sling and a patient who knows what a leaking dressing looks like, because the common failure is the catheter in the bed rather than the catheter in the patient.

Rebound pain is the planning target: in 972 ambulatory block patients it occurred in half, with bone surgery (OR 1.82), female sex (OR 1.52) and younger age raising the odds and intravenous dexamethasone lowering them (its absence OR 1.78). Every cuff repair involves bone. Escalation triggers: pain above 7 after the block has gone, with a sling correctly fitted and the hand warm and moving, is treated with the oral opioid that is already charted and a check that the regular analgesia was actually given; pain with a tense, hugely swollen shoulder in the first hours is extravasated irrigation fluid and settles; new severe pain days later with a hot joint is an infection until proven otherwise.

Pitfalls and variants

  • Tear size is the variable that matters. Small tears with one anchor and no releases run 60 minutes and behave like a decompression with a sore tuberosity; massive tears with margin convergence, patches or a superior capsular reconstruction run over two hours and sit at the top of this card’s range. The pre-operative MRI report, not the booking slip, tells you which you have.
  • Open and mini-open repair. Still used for some massive tears and by some surgeons: a deltoid split, more muscle pain, more bleeding, and PROSPECT’s recommendation to prefer the arthroscopic approach is on pain grounds.
  • Lateral decubitus. Changes airway access and brings sustained plexus traction; the dependent brachial plexus and peroneal nerve need padding and the eye on the pillow needs checking. Hypotension matters less, head position matters more.
  • The request for hypotension in beach chair. The reported strokes happened at cuff systolics in the 80s and 90s. Adrenaline in the irrigation and the pump are the surgeon’s levers; the vasopressor infusion is yours.
  • Fluid extravasation. Long case, high pump pressure, heavy patient, lateral position: the neck swells. Inspect before extubation; if in doubt, wait.
  • Hypothermia. Litres of room-temperature irrigation through the shoulder; forced-air warming from the start.
  • Phrenic palsy. Near-universal after interscalene block; use a superior trunk block for the patient with COPD, obesity with poor reserve, or a contralateral problem, and expect slightly less from a suprascapular plus axillary combination.
  • Chronic pain and opioid-tolerant patients. This operation is the one where their course is worst; a catheter and a pre-agreed plan with the pain service are both reasonable.
  • Day-case discharge criteria. A working block is not a reason to delay discharge, but a patient going home with a dense block needs the sling, written instructions, someone at home, and oral analgesia already started.
  • Infection. Cutibacterium acnes and anchors; presentation is late and indolent.

Key sources

This is the best-evidenced shoulder operation for analgesia, because PROSPECT built its guideline on it. The guideline’s preference for a continuous interscalene technique predates the 2024 randomised trial showing no added benefit from an infusion once dexamethasone and multimodal analgesia are in place, and the 2025 prospective comparison showing early pain equal to arthroplasty; the card’s catheter advice is the author’s reconciliation of the three, not a guideline statement. The acromioplasty meta-analysis is cited for the surgical variant, not for pain.

  1. Toma O, Persoons B, Pogatzki-Zahn E, Van de Velde M, Joshi GP. PROSPECT guideline for rotator cuff repair surgery: systematic review and procedure-specific postoperative pain management recommendations. Anaesthesia 2019;74:1320-1331
    Interscalene block first choice (single shot and continuous both grade A, continuous favoured); IV dexamethasone grade B and preferred over perineural; paracetamol plus NSAID or COX-2; suprascapular with or without axillary block as an alternative (grade B); arthroscopic technique recommended; subacromial or intra-articular infusion, stellate ganglion, cervical epidural, gabapentinoids and controlled hypotension not recommended
  2. Lopez R, Schiffman C, Singh J, et al. Early postoperative pain is similar after arthroscopic rotator cuff repair vs. short-stay shoulder arthroplasty: a prospective study. J Shoulder Elbow Surg 2025;34:1199-1207
    50 cuff repairs and 52 arthroplasties, all with liposomal bupivacaine interscalene block: peak mean VAS on day 2 of 4.4 and 5.1, no difference over 14 days; cuff repair used more opioid on days 7 and 8
  3. Rhyner P, Cachemaille M, Goetti P, et al. Single-bolus injection of local anesthetic, with or without continuous infusion, for interscalene brachial plexus block in the setting of multimodal analgesia: a randomized controlled unblinded trial. Reg Anesth Pain Med 2024;49:313-319
    60 arthroplasty and cuff repair patients with dexamethasone, magnesium, paracetamol and ketorolac: continuous ropivacaine 0.2% to day 2 did not change morphine use at 12, 24, 36 or 48 h or pain scores; four catheters fell out
  4. Barry GS, Bailey JG, Sardinha J, Brousseau P, Uppal V. Factors associated with rebound pain after peripheral nerve block for ambulatory surgery. Br J Anaesth 2021;126:862-871
    Rebound pain (NRS 3 or less rising to 7 or more within 24 h) in 49.6% of 972 ambulatory block patients; bone surgery OR 1.82, female OR 1.52, younger age, no IV dexamethasone OR 1.78
  5. Kang R, Jeong JS, Chin KJ, et al. Superior trunk block provides noninferior analgesia compared with interscalene brachial plexus block in arthroscopic shoulder surgery. Anesthesiology 2019;131:1316-1326
    Arthroscopic shoulder surgery, 15 mL ropivacaine 0.5%: pain at 24 h 1.4 vs 1.2, maximum pain 4.7 vs 4.8; complete hemidiaphragmatic paresis 5% vs 73%
  6. Cullen DJ. Why worry about blood pressure during surgery in the beach chair position? APSF Newsletter 2020
    Cuff pressure overstates brain perfusion by about 2 mmHg per inch of height; strokes reported after shoulder surgery with cuff systolics in the 80s-90s; deliberate hypotension should not be used
  7. Does concomitant acromioplasty facilitate arthroscopic repair of full-thickness rotator cuff tears? A meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis of randomized controlled trials
    Randomised trials of repair with and without acromioplasty show no difference in re-tear or function; acromioplasty remains common and adds a raw bone surface

Upper limb › Shoulder

4 Subacromial decompression and ACJ excision

Arthroscopic subacromial decompression, acromioplasty and distal clavicle excision without cuff repair

2Mild to moderate

Dominant mechanism: Bone. A burred acromial undersurface and, if the clavicle is excised, a raw distal clavicle end: two small cancellous bone surfaces under the deltoid that hurt like a minor osteotomy for two or three days; the bursectomy and portals add surface pain; nothing is repaired, tensioned or loaded

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: moderate.

Block
Interscalene or superior trunk block, single shot, with intravenous dexamethasone, chosen for the anaesthetic and the first night as much as for the pain
Catheter: no No mechanism to justify one: no repair, no tension, no loaded tissue, and the pain is largely over by day 3
Alternatives: Suprascapular nerve block (anterior approach) with or without axillary nerve block, phrenic sparing and near-equivalent after the recovery room; General anaesthesia with surgeon-delivered subacromial local anaesthetic infiltration and an oral regimen, which is adequate for an isolated decompression in a patient who declines a block; Liposomal bupivacaine interscalene where available, of no proven benefit over plain bupivacaine with dexamethasone here
Position
Beach chair in most Australian practice; lateral decubitus with arm traction in some hands, which changes airway access and plexus traction but not the pain
Tourniquet
No
Cement
No
Blood loss
Minimal; the fluid in the drapes is irrigation and the haemoglobin does not move
Duration
30-60 min skin to skin; the distal clavicle adds 15-20 min, a biceps tenotomy adds five
Length of stay
Day case. Day case: yes
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV within 60 min of incision (3 g over 120 kg) if any anchor or implant is placed; for a pure decompression with no implant surgeons vary, and the author gives it because Cutibacterium acnes is the shoulder organism and the cost of omission is a septic joint
Tranexamic acid
Not needed for blood loss; some surgeons ask for TXA 1 g IV for arthroscopic visibility, which is a reasonable request
VTE
Mechanical only; the operation is short, the patient walks out, and chemoprophylaxis is for the patient's own risk factors
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV at induction (also the block adjunct) and ondansetron 4 mg IV before emergence
Tell the patient
The arm will be numb and heavy for the rest of the day; the shoulder is sore for two or three days, mostly at night, and most people are on simple painkillers only by the end of the first week.
The trap
