  13. Cullen DJ. Why worry about blood pressure during surgery in the beach chair position? APSF Newsletter 2020
    Hydrostatic correction of about 2 mmHg per inch between cuff and external auditory meatus; strokes reported after shoulder surgery in beach chair with cuff systolics in the 80s-90s; no deliberate hypotension

Upper limb › Shoulder

10 Diagnostic shoulder arthroscopy, debridement and calcific tendinitis

Diagnostic arthroscopy, debridement of partial cuff tears and labral fraying, loose body removal and synovectomy, and calcific tendinitis treated by ultrasound-guided barbotage or arthroscopic removal: the short shoulder list where the block is chosen for the anaesthetic more often than for the pain

2Mild to moderate

Dominant mechanism: Arthroscopic surface. Portals, irrigation fluid in the deltoid and a shoulder held in abduction or traction for an hour: minimal, and the irreducible part shared by every procedure on this card. Debridement adds nothing under tension. Calcific deposit removal adds a tendon incised along its fibres and curetted, residual calcium and hydroxyapatite crystals in an already inflamed bursa, and in many hands a raw acromial surface; that version has a low but long tail measured in months rather than days

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: moderate.

Block
Interscalene or superior trunk block, single shot, with intravenous dexamethasone, used as the anaesthetic with sedation or under a light general anaesthetic: for diagnostic arthroscopy and debridement the block is for the anaesthetic and the fast-track recovery, not for pain; for arthroscopic calcific deposit removal with acromioplasty it is for the pain as well
Catheter: no Never on this card; nothing is repaired under tension, the first-night pain is covered by a single shot and simple analgesia, and the months-long tail after calcific deposit removal is low-grade and not a catheter problem
Alternatives: General anaesthesia with a supraglottic airway and surgeon infiltration of the portals, with no block, for the 20 min diagnostic look where a numb arm for 12 hours is a cost rather than a benefit; Superior trunk block in place of interscalene for any patient who cannot afford a hemidiaphragm (4.8% versus 71.4% paralysis in the ambulatory arthroscopy trial, same surgical anaesthesia); Suprascapular plus axillary nerve blocks as an analgesic supplement under general anaesthesia when a plexus block is declined
Position
Beach chair in most hands, head fixed, arm free or on a support; lateral decubitus with longitudinal arm traction in some, which opens the subacromial space wider and moves the airway to the side
Tourniquet
No
Cement
No
Blood loss
Negligible into the wound; the fluid in the suction is irrigation. Haemoglobin is unchanged
Duration
20-40 min for a diagnostic arthroscopy; 30-60 min for a debridement; 45-90 min for calcific deposit removal with bursectomy, with or without acromioplasty, and longer if a residual cuff defect is repaired. Barbotage in radiology takes 20-30 min
Length of stay
Day case. Day case: yes
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV within 60 min of incision (3 g over 120 kg) is given by most surgeons for any shoulder arthroscopy because an anchor may go in once the findings are known; the case for it in a pure diagnostic look with no implant is habit rather than evidence
Tranexamic acid
Not needed for blood loss; some surgeons ask for TXA 1 g IV for arthroscopic visibility, which is a reasonable request
VTE
Mechanical only; chemoprophylaxis only for the patient's own risk factors
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV with the block or at induction, which also prolongs the block and lowers the odds of rebound pain; ondansetron 4 mg IV before emergence if a general anaesthetic is given
Tell the patient
The arm will be numb and heavy until late tonight; when the feeling returns the shoulder will be sore for a few days and the tablets started before the numbness goes are what control it. If calcium was removed from the tendon, expect a dull ache that improves over months rather than weeks, and expect the first six weeks to feel slower than you hoped.
The trap
A 30 min arthroscopy under a dense interscalene block is sold to the patient as nothing, and half of ambulatory block patients after an operation that touched bone have their pain climb from 3 to 7 or more in the night: the acromioplasty and the curetted tendon in a calcific case make it a bone-and-tendon operation for rebound purposes, and the analgesia has to be charted and taken before the block recedes

What the surgeon is doing and why

This card is the short shoulder list: the operations where the surgeon looks, tidies and leaves, and repairs nothing under tension. They share an anaesthetic logic. The operation itself produces little pain, the portals and the irrigation are the irreducible part, and the block decision is driven more by the kind of anaesthetic and recovery you want than by what the patient will feel on day 1. The exception, and the reason the card does not score a 1, is the calcific shoulder, where the surgeon cuts into a tendon and leaves a chemically irritant deposit behind, and the course is measured in months.

Diagnostic arthroscopy has shrunk as MRI has improved, but it still has a place: the painful shoulder with imaging that does not explain it, the suspected infection, the stiff shoulder where the surgeon wants to see the capsule before committing to a release, and the athlete whose labrum and biceps anchor cannot be read confidently on a scan. The surgeon inspects the glenohumeral joint from a posterior portal in a fixed order, then enters the subacromial space. Anything found is treated, which is why the pre-operative conversation matters: a look can become a tenotomy, a debridement, a decompression or, rarely, a repair, and the pain plan moves card.

Debridement is the surgeon tidying what will not heal and does not need to. A partial-thickness cuff tear involving less than about half the tendon thickness is debrided of its frayed edge rather than repaired, because the remaining tendon is intact at its normal tension and the fraying is the pain generator. Labral fraying is shaved to a stable rim; a degenerate biceps tendon is cut; loose bodies are retrieved; synovitis or a chondral flap is shaved. The point is what is not done: nothing is reattached, nothing is pulled, no bone is decorticated for healing, and the sling afterwards is for comfort. The patient uses the arm within days.

Calcific tendinitis is a different disease wearing a similar operation. Hydroxyapatite is deposited inside the substance of the supraspinatus (less often infraspinatus or subscapularis) by a cell-mediated process that is neither degenerative nor caused by overload; it runs through a formative, a resting and a resorptive phase, and it is the resorptive phase, when the deposit liquefies, swells and leaks crystals into the bursa, that produces the sudden, severe, sleep-destroying pain that brings a 45-year-old to the emergency department convinced the shoulder is septic. Most deposits resorb on their own. The surgeon’s job is to shorten the course in the patient who cannot wait or whose chronic, hard deposit is not resorbing.

Two procedures do that. Barbotage (ultrasound-guided needling and lavage) is done in radiology under local anaesthetic: a needle is passed repeatedly through the deposit, saline is flushed and aspirated until the calcium clouds the syringe, and steroid is usually injected into the bursa afterwards. Against a subacromial steroid injection alone, barbotage plus steroid gave a better Constant score at one year (86 versus 74) and fewer patients needing further treatment; at five years the scores had converged, but 16 of the steroid-only group had needed something else against four. The steroid afterwards is for the flare: with saline instead of methylprednisolone after lavage, the worst pain in the first week was about 12 mm worse on a 100 mm scale, and the steroid did not impair resorption. The first week can be worse than the week before.

Arthroscopic removal is for the deposit that has failed barbotage, shock wave therapy and time. The surgeon does a diagnostic round, clears the bursa, finds the deposit by its bulge and chalky colour (or localises it with a spinal needle), incises the tendon along its fibres and curettes or shaves the calcium out, producing the “snowstorm” that fills the irrigation. What follows varies: some surgeons add an acromioplasty, some repair the residual tendon defect with an anchor, and many leave it. The evidence favours leaving it: in 99 patients whose cuff defect was not repaired, pain and function improved regardless of deposit size, location or completeness of excision, and 23 of the 29 with a follow-up MRI had healed. Complete removal is not the goal either; residual calcium resorbs. Repair of the defect bought better scores at two years in one cohort at the price of worse pain at three and six months, and both decompression and cuff repair were negative prognostic factors for early recovery in another. Which version this surgeon does sets the day-1 pain and the length of the tail.

The pain logic. For a look and a debridement the mechanism is surface: portals, irrigation fluid in the deltoid, an hour in abduction or traction. Nothing is under tension and nothing is healing to bone, so the pain peaks on day 1 when the block recedes and is gone within days; the card scores a 2 rather than a 1 only because the calcific version shares it. Calcific removal adds a tendon incised and curetted (not repaired, not tensioned, so not the mechanism that defines rotator cuff repair), crystals in a bursa that was already inflamed, and often a raw acromial surface, the bone component that raises the odds of rebound pain and the mechanism on the subacromial decompression card. The day-1 peak is no worse than a decompression. The tail is what differs: in the series that measured it, pain fell below 3 out of 10 only at six months and complete resolution took nearly six months on average. That is not a reason for a catheter or an opioid; it is a reason to tell the patient the truth before surgery.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 Barbotage in the radiology department, the procedure that usually comes first

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The radiologist is trying to fragment and wash out a liquefying deposit and to provoke resorption, without an incision and without a general anaesthetic. The needle passes through the deposit many times, saline is flushed and aspirated, and steroid goes into the bursa at the end to blunt the crystal-induced flare of the first week.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    You are rarely involved. When you are, it is for a patient who cannot lie still or tolerate the needling, and the request is for sedation, not a block: a plexus block for a 20 min needle procedure costs the patient a numb arm into the night for no analgesic return. The radiologist’s local anaesthetic in the bursa is the anaesthetic. Tell the patient the week after can be worse than the week before, and that the steroid is what limits it; a diabetic patient will see a glucose rise for a day or two from the depot.

  2. 2 Decide what the block is for before anyone is asleep

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon’s plan sets the pain plan. A look or a debridement produces almost nothing to treat after the first night; a calcific removal with an acromioplasty is a bone-and-tendon operation for rebound purposes; and a look that might become a repair needs a plan that can be upgraded.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    For a debridement in a fit day-case patient the block is the anaesthetic: an interscalene or superior trunk block with intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg and sedation gives a patient who bypasses the recovery room, walks early and goes home hours sooner than after a general anaesthetic (76% versus 16% recovery room bypass and 123 versus 286 min to discharge readiness in the randomised comparison, with no unplanned admissions against four of 25). The honest counter-argument is that the operation does not need the block for pain, and a patient who would rather have a short general anaesthetic with surgeon infiltration of the portals than a flail arm for 12 hours is making a reasonable choice. For calcific removal the block is for the pain as well, and the interscalene first choice in the PROSPECT cuff repair guideline is the nearest evidence. A superior trunk block gives the same surgical anaesthesia with hemidiaphragmatic paralysis in 4.8% rather than 71.4%, and is the block for anyone whose lungs matter. Decide the airway now: a supraglottic airway for a short case in a slim patient; a tube for the long calcific case in a heavy patient, because the neck swells with irrigation and the head is behind a screen.

  3. 3 Positioning: beach chair or lateral, and the pressure question in a short case

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Beach chair gives the surgeon the familiar upright anatomy and an easy conversion to open; lateral decubitus with 5-7 kg of longitudinal traction opens the subacromial space and some surgeons prefer it.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The hazards are the same as for any shoulder arthroscopy and a short case does not shorten them. In beach chair the cuff overstates brain perfusion by roughly 1 mmHg for every 1.25 cm between cuff and ear, and sitting, interscalene sympathetic spread and sedation together drop the pressure in the first 10 minutes; keep the cuff reading near the awake baseline, start a vasopressor infusion early rather than chasing boluses, and treat the vagal bradycardia-hypotension episodes promptly. In lateral the airway moves to the side, the dependent arm, eye and peroneal nerve need padding, and the traction is sustained plexus tension you cannot see. Check the head again after the surgeon sets the arm.

  4. 4 Portals, irrigation pump and the diagnostic round of the glenohumeral joint

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The posterior portal goes in through the soft spot below the posterolateral acromion, the anterior portal through the rotator interval, and the surgeon inspects the joint in a fixed sequence: biceps anchor and tendon, labrum, cartilage, subscapularis, the undersurface of the cuff, the capsule and the axillary pouch. Findings decide the rest of the list.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Nothing to do but listen. A sedated patient with a working block feels pressure, not pain; one who flinches on portal placement needs the skin and capsule topped up by the surgeon, not more sedation. The pump runs at 40-60 mmHg and the surgeon will ask for a low blood pressure if the view is bloody; the answer is the same as on the rotator cuff repair card, that you will hold the pressure near baseline and that adrenaline in the irrigation and the pump are their levers. A surgeon who announces a full-thickness tear or an unstable labrum has just changed the operation, and the day-case plan with it.

  5. 5 Debridement of what will not heal

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A partial-thickness cuff tear on either surface is debrided back to stable tendon with a shaver if less than about half the thickness is involved; a frayed labrum is trimmed to a stable rim; a diseased long head of biceps is tenotomised (or tenodesed, which adds an anchor, 20 min and a different pain profile covered on the SLAP repair and biceps tenodesis card); loose bodies are retrieved; a synovitis or a chondral flap is shaved. None of it is repaired and none of it is under tension.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is the surface-only version of the card: a minute or two of shaver noise per lesion and nothing physiological. Track time and fluid, not nociception. A surgeon who converts to a repair here has converted the pain plan as well, and a day-case debridement patient and a day-case cuff repair patient go home with different nights ahead.

  6. 6 Subacromial space: bursectomy and the acromioplasty decision

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The scope is redirected into the subacromial space, the thick inflamed bursa is resected so that the bursal side of the cuff and the acromion can be seen, and the surgeon decides whether to burr the acromial undersurface. For a calcific deposit the bursa is often florid, because leaked crystals are an intense chemical irritant, and the bursectomy is where the deposit is found.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Irrigation now extravasates into the deltoid and tracks towards the neck over a long case; watch the airway pressures and the supraclavicular fossa. If an acromioplasty is done the card has acquired a raw bone surface, the mechanism behind the higher odds of rebound pain after bone surgery, and the night plan becomes the one written for a decompression. Litres of room-temperature irrigation cool the patient; forced-air warming from the start.

  7. 7 Finding and removing the calcific deposit

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The deposit bulges the bursal surface of the tendon and looks chalk-white or yellow; if it does not, the surgeon localises it with a spinal needle, or by a needle track that weeps toothpaste-like calcium. The tendon is incised along its fibres over the deposit, and a curette and shaver remove as much as comes freely; the surgeon is not trying to remove every grain, because residual calcium resorbs and chasing it enlarges the tendon defect.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The snowstorm of calcium in the irrigation spoils the view and the pump pressure goes up; expect the low-pressure request again. This is the step that creates the tail: an incised, curetted tendon that is not repaired and an inflamed bursa now full of crystal debris. It is not the tendon-under-tension of a cuff repair and does not need the cuff repair’s catheter; it is a low-grade, months-long ache, which is the fact the patient needs to have heard before today.

  8. 8 The residual defect: repair, acromioplasty or leave alone

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Surgeons vary. Most leave a defect under half the tendon thickness alone, because the series that did so had excellent outcomes and most defects heal on MRI; some place an anchor and close it, which gave better scores at two years in one cohort at the cost of worse pain at three and six months; some add an acromioplasty.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    If an anchor and a side-to-side closure go in, the arm will be held still for the knots, the patient leaves with a repair-type sling and protocol, and the day-1 and day-2 pain is closer to a small cuff repair than to a debridement. If the defect is left, the sling is for comfort and comes off in days. Ask which it was before you write the discharge analgesia.

  9. 9 Closure, sling and emergence

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Portals are closed with a stitch or a strip and a bulky dressing goes on. A sling is for comfort after debridement and calcific removal without repair, and for protection after a repair.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Put the sling on before the patient lightens so that an awake patient with a dense block does not lift the flail arm by the wrist. A patient under block and sedation is sitting up talking within minutes and is the one who bypasses the recovery room. After a general anaesthetic for a long calcific case, inspect the neck before removing the airway: subcutaneous irrigation fluid in the supraclavicular fossa is usually harmless and occasionally enough to matter.

  10. 10 Recovery, discharge and the written night plan

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants early movement after a debridement, pendular movement and comfort after a calcific removal, and a radiograph on the day to see what calcium is left.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The first paracetamol and NSAID go in before the patient leaves, not when the arm wakes up. The block lasts 12-24 h with dexamethasone; the patient who was comfortable at discharge is the one who telephones at 2 am if the rebound was not planned for, and in the ambulatory cohort half of all block patients met the definition of rebound pain, with bone surgery and the absence of intravenous dexamethasone raising the odds. A minor operation is not a reason for a minor prescription: the cohort that ranked 179 procedures found many small operations among the most painful on day 1 because little was prescribed for them. Write a short opioid supply for the first two nights, more after a calcific removal with acromioplasty, and tell the calcific patient in words that the dull ache can run for months and is the disease, not a failed operation.

Pain plan

The dominant mechanism is surface, and the plan follows: a single-shot block chosen for the anaesthetic, simple analgesia started before the block recedes, and a few opioid doses for the first night or two. The defensible default for a debridement in a day-case patient is an interscalene or superior trunk block with 15-20 mL of ropivacaine 0.5% and intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg, light sedation, no airway, and a patient who walks out within a couple of hours. The superior trunk block is the author’s preference for this list, because the operation does not need the extra cover the interscalene gives and the diaphragm is spared in nearly everyone. General anaesthesia with a supraglottic airway, surgeon infiltration of the portals and no block is a reasonable alternative for the patient who would rather be asleep without a numb arm, and the pain cost after a pure debridement is small; it was not small in the randomised day-case comparison, where the general anaesthesia group had more pain, more recovery room time and four unplanned admissions, but that trial included cuff surgery and its findings scale with the bone and tendon work done.

For calcific deposit removal the block is for the pain as well. The nearest guideline is PROSPECT’s for rotator cuff repair, and its skeleton applies: interscalene or superior trunk block, intravenous dexamethasone, paracetamol and an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor started pre-operatively and continued for a week, oral opioid for the first two or three nights, and no subacromial infusion. An NSAID has a particular claim because the bursal inflammation is crystal-driven, and the author’s practice is to continue it for a fortnight where there is no contraindication; that is judgement, not trial evidence. There is no argument for a catheter on this card: nothing is under tension, the first night is covered by a single shot, and the long tail after calcific removal is low-grade and not improved by three days of ropivacaine.

Rebound pain is the planning target, as on every shoulder card. A look that stays a look has the lowest odds; a calcific removal with acromioplasty is bone surgery for rebound purposes, and intravenous dexamethasone lowers the odds. Escalation: pain above 7 after the block has gone, with a warm hand and a correctly fitted sling, is treated with the opioid already charted and a check that the regular analgesia was given; a hugely swollen shoulder in the first hours is extravasated irrigation and settles; severe pain at a week in a calcific patient with a hot shoulder and a fever is an infection or a crystal flare and needs the surgeon; and the patient still aching at three months after a calcific removal is on the expected curve and needs reassurance and physiotherapy, not imaging.

Pitfalls and variants

  • The look that becomes a repair. A diagnostic arthroscopy booked as a day case under block and sedation is sometimes a full-thickness tear with anchors by the time the surgeon has finished looking. The block already placed is the right block for the repair; what changes is the night plan, the sling and the counselling.
  • Barbotage versus surgery. Barbotage is cheaper, needs no anaesthetist and works for most resorptive-phase deposits; arthroscopic removal is for the failed, chronic, hard deposit. The flare after barbotage is real and the steroid injected afterwards is what limits it; a dreadful barbotage week is not the same as a failed barbotage.
  • Acromioplasty with calcific removal. Adds a raw bone surface, was a negative prognostic factor for early recovery in the series that looked, and moves the night plan to the decompression version.
  • Repair of the residual defect. Changes the sling, the protocol and the early pain for a two-year functional gain in one cohort and no difference in others. If it is done, treat the first two days as a small cuff repair.
  • The patient with COPD, a single functioning lung or a contralateral phrenic palsy. Superior trunk block rather than interscalene; same surgical anaesthesia, 4.8% rather than 71.4% hemidiaphragmatic paralysis.
  • Septic arthritis on the differential. A diagnostic arthroscopy for a hot shoulder is a washout, not a day case: antibiotics after samples, a general anaesthetic rather than a block in a febrile patient, and admission. The acutely resorbing calcific shoulder mimics it and the radiograph separates them.
  • Frozen shoulder found at arthroscopy. A tight, red, thickened rotator interval in a patient booked for a look often leads to a capsular release and manipulation on the spot; that operation has its own card (frozen shoulder) and a much more block-dependent pain plan.

Key sources

The anaesthetic evidence for this list is about recovery rather than pain: the randomised day-case comparison of interscalene block against general anaesthesia and the superior trunk trial in ambulatory arthroscopy. The calcific tendinitis evidence is orthopaedic and radiological and is cited for the shape of the course, not for analgesic technique. No PROSPECT guideline exists for any procedure on this card; the rotator cuff repair guideline is borrowed, and the NSAID duration and the superior trunk preference are the author’s judgement.

  1. Hadzic A, Williams BA, Karaca PE, et al. For outpatient rotator cuff surgery, nerve block anesthesia provides superior same-day recovery over general anesthesia. Anesthesiology 2005;102:1001-1007
    50 outpatients randomised to interscalene block with ropivacaine 0.75% or fast-track general anaesthesia with bupivacaine 0.25% wound infiltration: recovery room bypass 76% versus 16%, readiness for discharge 123 versus 286 min, less pain, earlier ambulation, no unplanned admissions versus four of 25 after general anaesthesia
  2. Kim DH, Lin Y, Beathe JC, et al. Superior trunk block: a phrenic-sparing alternative to the interscalene block: a randomized controlled trial. Anesthesiology 2019;131:521-533
    126 ambulatory arthroscopic shoulder surgery patients randomised to superior trunk or interscalene block as the surgical anaesthetic: hemidiaphragmatic paralysis in 4.8% versus 71.4%, worst recovery room pain noninferior (median 0 in both), respiratory parameters unaffected, less hoarseness, no difference in opioid consumption or handgrip strength
  3. Toma O, Persoons B, Pogatzki-Zahn E, Van de Velde M, Joshi GP. PROSPECT guideline for rotator cuff repair surgery: systematic review and procedure-specific postoperative pain management recommendations. Anaesthesia 2019;74:1320-1331
    The nearest procedure-specific guideline: interscalene block first choice, intravenous dexamethasone preferred over perineural, paracetamol and NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor, suprascapular with or without axillary block as an alternative, and subacromial infusions and controlled hypotension not recommended
  4. Barry GS, Bailey JG, Sardinha J, Brousseau P, Uppal V. Factors associated with rebound pain after peripheral nerve block for ambulatory surgery. Br J Anaesth 2021;126:862-871
    972 ambulatory block patients, rebound pain (NRS 3 or less rising to 7 or more within 24 h) in 49.6%; bone surgery OR 1.82, female OR 1.52, younger age; absence of intravenous dexamethasone OR 1.78
  5. de Witte PB, Selten JW, Navas A, et al. Calcific tendinitis of the rotator cuff: a randomized controlled trial of ultrasound-guided needling and lavage versus subacromial corticosteroids. Am J Sports Med 2013;41:1665-1673
    48 patients randomised to barbotage plus subacromial steroid or steroid alone: Constant score at one year 86.0 versus 73.9, calcification shrank by 11.6 versus 5.1 mm, four versus 11 patients needed a further barbotage or surgery
  6. de Witte PB, Kolk A, Overes F, Nelissen RGHH, Reijnierse M. Rotator cuff calcific tendinitis: ultrasound-guided needling and lavage versus subacromial corticosteroids: five-year outcomes of a randomized controlled trial. Am J Sports Med 2017;45:3305-3314
    Same 48 patients at five years: Constant score 90 versus 87, no difference; total resorption in 62% and 73%; four versus 16 patients had additional treatment during follow-up
  7. Darrieutort-Laffite C, Varin S, Coiffier G, et al. Are corticosteroid injections needed after needling and lavage of calcific tendinitis? Randomised, double-blind, non-inferiority trial. Ann Rheum Dis 2019;78:837-843
    132 patients, saline or methylprednisolone 40 mg into the subacromial bursa at the end of ultrasound-guided lavage: maximal pain in the first week 11.76 mm worse on a 100 mm scale with saline, steroid improved pain and function to six weeks and three months, and resorption at 12 months was 83% with saline and 74% with steroid
  8. Youn SM, Rhee SM, Cho SH, Kim CH, Lee JU, Rhee YG. Arthroscopic decompression of calcific tendinitis without cuff repair. Bone Joint J 2023;105-B:663-667
    99 patients, deposit removed and the cuff defect left unrepaired: pain and ASES scores improved regardless of deposit location, size, type or whether excision was complete; of 29 with follow-up MRI, 23 had healed and the six with a persisting interstitial defect still had excellent scores
  9. Pang L, Li T, Li Y, et al. Combined arthroscopic rotator cuff repair leads to better clinical outcomes than isolated removal of calcific deposits for shoulder calcific tendinitis: a 2- to 5-year follow-up study. Front Surg 2022;9:912779
    47 shoulders with deposits over 1 cm, 23 repaired and 24 debrided only: the repair group had worse pain at three and six months and worse function at three months, then better pain and function from 24 months, all differences beyond the minimal clinically important difference
  10. Cho CH, Bae KC, Kim BS, Kim HJ, Kim DH. Recovery pattern after arthroscopic treatment for calcific tendinitis of the shoulder. Orthop Traumatol Surg Res 2020;106:687-691
    35 patients: the pain score fell below 3 only at six months, function reached three quarters of maximum at six months, nine had complete and 26 partial deposit removal with full resorption in all by final follow-up, and subacromial decompression and cuff repair were negative prognostic factors
  11. Lee TK, Shin SJ. Functional recovery of the shoulder after arthroscopic treatment for chronic calcific tendinitis. Clin Shoulder Elb 2018;21:75-81
    39 patients after at least six months of failed conservative treatment: complete resolution of pain took 5.7 months on average, scores reached 80 points at six months, and neither cuff repair nor the completeness of calcium removal changed the outcome
  12. Gerbershagen HJ, Aduckathil S, van Wijck AJM, Peelen LM, Kalkman CJ, Meissner W. Pain intensity on the first day after surgery: a prospective cohort study comparing 179 surgical procedures. Anesthesiology 2013;118:934-944
    50,523 patients: 22 of the 40 most painful procedures were orthopaedic or trauma operations on the extremities, and many minor procedures produced unexpectedly high first-day pain because the analgesia prescribed for them was slight

Upper limb › Elbow

11 Total elbow arthroplasty and radial head replacement

Linked cemented total elbow for rheumatoid, post-traumatic and fracture indications; metallic radial head replacement for the unreconstructable radial head

3Moderate

Dominant mechanism: Bone. Distal humeral and proximal ulnar bone cuts, canal reaming and cement in both bones; the triceps reflected or split and repaired to the olecranon; the ulnar nerve mobilised and often transposed, which adds a neuropathic edge; a long tourniquet. Radial head replacement is a shorter version of the same mechanisms with a lateral ligament repair added

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: moderate.

Block
Infraclavicular or supraclavicular brachial plexus block, single shot, with intravenous dexamethasone, under general anaesthesia
Catheter: selective Single shot plus multimodal is the defensible default for a primary total elbow and for a radial head replacement; a catheter earns its place for revision, opioid-tolerant or chronic pain patients and for the rheumatoid patient who cannot take an NSAID, provided the surgeon has agreed that the ulnar nerve check will wait until the block recedes
Alternatives: Axillary block with a separate musculocutaneous and intercostobrachial component (less reliable at the posterior elbow); General anaesthesia with surgeon infiltration and no block when the surgeon insists on an immediate ulnar nerve examination; Continuous infraclavicular or retroclavicular catheter for the selected patient
Position
Supine with the arm across the chest on a padded bolster is the usual position for a total elbow; lateral decubitus with the arm over a padded post is the alternative some surgeons prefer. Radial head replacement is supine on an arm table
Tourniquet
Yes. Sterile tourniquet high on the arm for a total elbow, often approaching 120 min; many surgeons release it before triceps repair and closure. A radial head replacement sits inside a single inflation
Cement
Yes. Both components of a linked total elbow are cemented, usually with antibiotic-loaded cement, into small canals pressurised with a gun; the humeral canal is the only step with bone cement implantation syndrome potential, and it is small. Radial head stems are press-fit, intentionally loose, or cemented depending on the design
Blood loss
200-400 mL for a total elbow, mostly after tourniquet release and into the drain; transfusion uncommon but the rheumatoid patient starts anaemic. Radial head replacement under 100 mL
Duration
120-180 min skin to skin for a primary total elbow, longer for fracture or revision; 60-120 min for a radial head replacement, longer as part of a terrible triad repair
Length of stay
1-3 nights for a total elbow; day case or one night for a radial head replacement. Day case: selected
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV within 60 min of incision (3 g over 120 kg); antibiotic-loaded cement is the surgeon's second measure for a joint with a 2-8% infection rate
Tranexamic acid
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV before incision; the elbow-specific evidence is thin and the practice is borrowed from the hip and shoulder
VTE
Mechanical prophylaxis; chemoprophylaxis only for the patient's own risk factors, since upper limb arthroplasty carries a low baseline risk
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV at induction and ondansetron 4 mg IV before emergence
Tell the patient
The arm will be numb and heavy into the night; the elbow is sore for the first two or three days and then settles, the little finger side of the hand may tingle for a few weeks because the nerve was moved, and the replaced elbow is for daily living, not for lifting.
The trap
Document ulnar nerve function before the block and agree with the surgeon beforehand whether the nerve will be examined before or after the block recedes: the nerve is mobilised in every total elbow, a dense block hides a neuropraxia until the next day, and a surgeon who expected to test it in recovery will not thank you for a perfect block

What the surgeon is doing and why

The elbow is a hinge that has to be stable through a 140 degree arc while the forearm rotates on it, and it is held together by a deep, congruent bony articulation and two collateral ligaments rather than by muscle. Rheumatoid arthritis destroys that in a particular order: synovitis thins the cartilage, erodes the trochlea and the olecranon, stretches the collaterals, and leaves a painful, unstable, often flail joint in a patient with weak muscles, thin skin, long-term steroids and a suppressed immune system. Post-traumatic arthritis and the comminuted distal humeral fracture in an osteoporotic patient over 65 reach the same end point by another route: the articular surface is worn or in pieces that will not hold a screw, and the choice is between a fixation that may fail and a replacement that works on day 1. In the one randomised trial, five of 21 patients allocated to fixation were converted to a replacement on the table because the fragments were too small, the replacement was half an hour quicker (108 versus 140 min), and function was better at six weeks and six months.

The modern total elbow is a linked, semiconstrained hinge: a cemented humeral stem with an anterior flange, a cemented ulnar stem, and a pin-and-bushing coupling that allows a few degrees of varus-valgus play so the cement interfaces share the load. Linking the halves means the collateral ligaments do not matter, which is the point: the surgeon can release them, excise the radial head, and reconstruct a flail joint that will not dislocate. The cost of a hinge is that every load on the hand becomes a torque on two cement mantles in small canals, which is why aseptic loosening leads the failure list (38% of revisions in the pooled 9,308 elbows, less often with linked than unlinked designs) and why the patient is told, for life, not to lift more than 2-5 kg. Unlinked designs keep the ligaments and need them; some surgeons use them for the rheumatoid elbow with good bone, accepting more instability for less loosening.

The surgeon’s aims, in order:

  1. Reach the back of the joint through a posterior midline incision, find the ulnar nerve behind the medial epicondyle, and decide whether it will be transposed anteriorly or released in situ.
  2. Get the triceps out of the way without losing it: reflected off the olecranon as a continuous sleeve (Bryan-Morrey), split in the midline, or left attached with the joint entered on either side of it. Whatever is done here is undone at the end, and the repair is the tendon-tension element of the operation.
  3. Release the capsule and collaterals, excise the radial head, cut the distal humerus to accept the stem and flange, and ream two small curved canals.
  4. Cement both stems with antibiotic-loaded cement, graft behind the anterior flange, and link the hinge.
  5. Repair the triceps through bone tunnels, settle the ulnar nerve, close thin skin over a prominent joint, and splint in extension so the posterior wound is not folded.

Radial head replacement is a smaller operation sharing the joint. A metallic head goes in when the native head is in too many pieces to fix and the elbow needs it for stability: a terrible triad (dislocation with radial head and coronoid fractures), an Essex-Lopresti injury where the interosseous membrane is torn and the forearm will shorten without a radial column, or a medial collateral injury where the head is the secondary valgus stabiliser. The surgeon enters laterally, removes the fragments, sizes the implant to the native head (too long, and the capitellum erodes and the elbow stiffens), seats a press-fit, loose-fit or cemented stem, and usually repairs the lateral collateral complex to the epicondyle.

The pain logic follows from the tissues. The dominant mechanism is bone: cuts and canal preparation in two bones, with cement, which hurts hard for two or three days and settles because nothing is loaded through a replaced elbow in the first week. Behind it sit three contributors. The triceps repair (or the lateral ligament repair in a radial head case) is a tendon under tension, protected but loaded by every push up from a chair. The ulnar nerve has been dissected over 10 cm and often moved, so some patients wake with ring and little finger dysaesthesia that is neuropathic in character and lasts weeks. And the tourniquet has been up for most of two hours. Compared with distal humerus fixation there is less subperiosteal stripping and no two-column plating, so the early curve is kinder; compared with a reverse shoulder, nothing is lengthened or re-tensioned.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 The patient before the block: rheumatoid, elderly, or both

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon needs an elbow that can be operated on for two hours and a patient who can protect it for six weeks. Most elective total elbows are rheumatoid; most fracture total elbows are frail women over 70.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The rheumatoid patient brings the atlantoaxial question (a documented stable neck before a two-hour case with the head turned), temporomandibular and cricoarytenoid involvement that make the airway harder than it looks, long-term steroids needing a supplement, methotrexate and a biologic managed according to the unit’s practice, anaemia of chronic disease, and skin that tears under tape. The fracture patient brings the hip-fracture problems in a different joint: dehydration, delirium risk, and a reason for the fall. Examine and document ulnar nerve sensation and intrinsic power before any block or sedation, because this nerve is handled in every total elbow and the block will hide it for 12-24 h. Agree the nerve-check plan with the surgeon now, not in recovery.

  2. 2 Block, airway and position

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A posterior approach needs the arm across the chest on a bolster with the patient supine, or over a padded post with the patient lateral. Supine is quicker to set up and keeps the airway in front of you; lateral gives a more stable field.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    An infraclavicular or supraclavicular block with intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg, placed before induction. The two approaches performed identically for elbow surgery in the 150-patient randomised trial (supplementation 4.2% against 4.1%, conversion to general anaesthesia 4.2% against 5.5%), and infraclavicular produced fewer paraesthesiae on placement (8.3% against 23.2%), a reasonable tie-breaker in a patient with rheumatoid neuropathy. The high tourniquet site is covered by depth of anaesthesia rather than by the block. A tracheal tube is the author’s default for a two-hour case with the surgeon leaning on the chest; a supraglottic airway is reasonable for a short radial head case. Pad the contralateral ulnar nerve with more care than usual: a bilateral ulnar neuropathy after an elbow replacement is an argument nobody wins. In lateral, the dependent plexus, eye and peroneal nerve need the usual attention.

  3. 3 Sterile tourniquet, antibiotic and tranexamic acid

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The field is the whole elbow and proximal forearm, so the tourniquet goes high and sterile. Infection is the second commonest reason for revision (19%) and the skin over the olecranon is thin, so antibiotic-loaded cement and a prophylactic antibiotic are both used.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Cefazolin 2 g IV finished before inflation, 3 g over 120 kg; tranexamic acid 1 g IV at the same time, on evidence borrowed from the hip and shoulder. Say the inflation time aloud at 90 and 120 min; a total elbow routinely reaches the limit most units set, and the usual answer is release before the triceps repair. Tourniquet pain under general anaesthesia is a slow rise in pressure and heart rate from about 45 min that ignores opioid.

  4. 4 Posterior incision and the ulnar nerve

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A posterior incision curved around the olecranon gives access to both sides. The ulnar nerve is released from the arcade of Struthers through the cubital tunnel into flexor carpi ulnaris, then either moved into an anterior subcutaneous pocket (most surgeons’ routine in the Mayo review) or released in situ and left (the practice in the 83-elbow series, with persistent symptoms in 2.6%). Either way it is dissected free along its whole course at the elbow and retracted for the rest of the case.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Nothing to do; the step is the surgeon’s quietest ten minutes. Severe ulnar neuropathy is quoted at around 5% in the Mayo review and 3-11% across systematic reviews; most is traction and devascularisation from this step and the retractors that follow, and most resolves. This is the injury your documentation and your block agreement were for.

  5. 5 Triceps: reflect, split or spare

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The Bryan-Morrey approach peels the triceps off the olecranon in continuity with the forearm fascia and reflects the sleeve laterally; a midline split goes through it; a triceps-on approach works around it and is favoured for fractures, where the condyles can be removed without touching the insertion. Reflecting and splitting give the best exposure and need a repair; sparing protects extension strength and makes the ulna harder to prepare.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The choice decides a third of the pain course and all of the rehabilitation. A reflected triceps repaired through drill holes will not be allowed to extend against resistance for six weeks and is loaded by every push on a chair arm; triceps insufficiency (about 3%) is that repair failing. A triceps-on elbow can extend from day 1. Ask which was done before writing the discharge analgesia: the repaired-triceps patient has more movement-evoked pain in week 2 than the mechanism tag suggests.

  6. 6 Releases, radial head excision and the distal humeral cut

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon releases the capsule and both collaterals (a linked design does not need them), dislocates the joint, excises the radial head, and cuts the distal humerus to accept the stem and flange. In a fracture the condyles come out as fragments and the cut is half made.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Full capsular release and dislocation is the point of maximum nociception before the bone work; an incomplete block declares itself now. A thin rheumatoid cortex or an osteoporotic humerus can fracture during dislocation or stem preparation, and the surgeon’s reaction tells you the case has lengthened by 30 min and a cerclage.

  7. 7 Canal preparation in two small bones

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The humeral canal is reamed and broached from the cut surface; the ulnar canal is entered at the coronoid base or olecranon tip and reamed along its curve. Both are small and curved, and the ulna is easy to perforate.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Reaming and broaching are the bone mechanism being created. Marrow vents from two canals, but the volumes are small and neither is pressurised yet, so the disturbance is a fraction of a femur’s. Warm the patient: a long case and an open joint lose heat steadily.

  8. 8 Cementing both stems and linking the hinge

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Antibiotic-loaded cement is injected into both canals with a gun, the stems pushed home with a wedge of bone graft trapped behind the anterior flange so it integrates and resists the loads that would loosen the stem, and the halves linked. The surgeon checks the arc of motion without the triceps.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The only cement step of the upper limb that deserves the name, and a modest one: two small canals, hand pressurised. Treat it as the hip card does in miniature: pressure supported before the cement goes in, oxygen up, and the frail fracture patient watched for the fall in end-tidal carbon dioxide and pressure that marks a cement reaction, because that patient is the one most likely to produce it. The cure time is dead time; use it to plan the deflation.

  9. 9 Triceps repair, nerve placement, closure and the extension splint

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The triceps is sutured back to the olecranon through bone tunnels with the arm slightly flexed so the repair sits without tension. The ulnar nerve is checked for kinking at its new entry or along its native course, the tourniquet released, bleeding dealt with, a drain placed by many surgeons, and thin posterior skin closed in layers. An anterior splint holds the elbow in extension so the wound is not folded.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Release here brings a reperfusion dip in pressure, a rise in end-tidal carbon dioxide and a bleeding field the surgeon must now control; after a full-length inflation the pressure takes minutes to recover. The repair wants a still patient and a held arm, not neuromuscular block. Give the antiemetic. The splint goes on before the patient lightens: an awake patient with a dense block and a repaired triceps will otherwise bend the elbow with the other hand.

  10. 10 Recovery, the first night and the nerve

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants the wound dry and flat, the elbow extended for a few days, no resisted extension for six weeks if the triceps was reflected, and to know that the ulnar nerve works.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The hand is examined when the block recedes, at the time agreed in step 1. The oral regimen starts in recovery: paracetamol, an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor if renal function and the rheumatoid drug list allow it, and an oral opioid for the first three nights. In the 972-patient ambulatory cohort half of block patients had rebound pain, with bone surgery (OR 1.82) and no intravenous dexamethasone (OR 1.78) raising the odds; this is bone surgery. A numb little finger and a rising elbow at 2 am is the block wearing off; a tense, swollen posterior wound is bleeding into a closed space over a nerve and needs the surgeon. Length of stay is one to three nights, longer for slow rheumatoid skin.

  11. 11 Radial head replacement: the lateral approach and the ligament

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Usually a trauma patient. Through the Kocher interval the surgeon removes the head fragments, checks the coronoid and ligaments, sizes the implant against the removed head, reams the neck and seats the stem. If the lateral collateral complex has come off the epicondyle (it usually has in a dislocation) it is repaired with anchors or tunnels, and in a terrible triad the coronoid is fixed first through the same wound.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Supine on an arm table with a standard tourniquet, 60-120 min, the same block with dexamethasone. The posterior interosseous nerve runs through supinator a few centimetres distal to the head and is protected by pronating the forearm; a wrist drop afterwards is retraction or an over-long reamer, and another reason to document before the block. The ligament repair is the tendon-tension element and the reason the elbow is splinted. Sizing is the surgical trap: an over-long head (up to about 20% of implants) erodes the capitellum, stiffens the elbow over months and causes 13-23% of revisions.

  12. 12 The radial head patient and discharge

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Early protected motion in a hinged brace, because a stiff elbow after a terrible triad is the usual bad outcome, with the ligament repair protected from varus stress.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Most isolated radial head replacements go home the same day with a working block, oral analgesia started and a written night plan; a terrible triad with coronoid fixation and a ligament repair stays one night. The pain course behaves like a 2 after the first night, because the bone work is small and the early motion is passive.

Pain plan

The dominant mechanism is bone with cement, which argues for a single-shot block with dexamethasone to carry the first night and an oral regimen for the next three days; the two secondary mechanisms (a repaired triceps or ligament, and a handled nerve) argue for a regimen that expects movement-evoked pain in week 2 and a neuropathic flavour in the hand. There is no procedure-specific guideline for the elbow; the nearest PROSPECT evidence is for the shoulder, and this plan is author’s judgement built on the mechanism and on the general ambulatory block data.

The defensible default is an infraclavicular or supraclavicular block with 20-25 mL of ropivacaine 0.5% (equivalent for elbow surgery in the randomised comparison; infraclavicular gave fewer paraesthesiae), intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg at induction, paracetamol and an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor started before the block recedes, and oral opioid for the first three nights. The NSAID decision is harder than usual: rheumatoid patients are often on methotrexate, have renal function that will not tolerate a week of NSAID, and may already be on a COX-2 inhibitor. When the NSAID is off the table the opioid requirement rises and the catheter argument strengthens.

The catheter question has two parts. On pain grounds a primary total elbow sits where the anatomic shoulder sits: a single shot with dexamethasone and a reliable oral regimen is enough for most, and a continuous infraclavicular or retroclavicular catheter (described for total elbow replacement as a technique report, without a trial behind it) earns its place for a revision, an opioid-tolerant or chronic pain patient, or the rheumatoid patient who cannot take an NSAID. On nerve grounds a catheter means no ulnar nerve examination for two days, and that is the surgeon’s call as much as yours. The author’s practice is a single shot for a primary total elbow and for every radial head replacement, and a catheter only after a conversation with the surgeon about the nerve.

Escalation: pain above 7 after the block has gone, with a soft wound, a warm hand and the splint on, is treated with the charted opioid and a check that the regular doses were given. Pain out of proportion in a tense posterior wound is a haematoma over the ulnar nerve and is surgical. Ring and little finger numbness that was absent when the block wore off, or that worsens over days, is a nerve under pressure in its new bed and also surgical. Burning dysaesthesia present from the start and stable is traction neuritis and settles over weeks; a gabapentinoid for it is author’s judgement, not evidence.

Pitfalls and variants

  • Triceps-reflecting versus triceps-on. The reflected sleeve gives the best exposure and the most movement-evoked pain in weeks 1-2, with a repair that fails in about 3%; triceps-on is favoured for fractures and leaves an elbow that extends from day 1. Ask which was done.
  • Unlinked designs. Kept by some surgeons for the rheumatoid elbow with good bone and intact collaterals: less loosening, more instability, and a still arm wanted while the ligaments are balanced.
  • Fracture total elbow. The frail patient over 70 with a comminuted distal humerus, often converted on the table from a planned fixation: the position and tourniquet of the elbow fracture card, a cement step in the frailest patient of the week, and the hip-fracture medical problems.
  • Rheumatoid airway, neck and drugs. Atlantoaxial instability, a stiff temporomandibular joint and cricoarytenoid arthritis, so an airway plan that does not involve extension; a steroid supplement; methotrexate continued in most units and biologics paused by most rheumatologists.
  • Infection and periprosthetic fracture. Infection 2-4% in the Mayo review, up to 8% in some series, 19% of revisions; fracture in 5-30% of primary elbows over their life, usually the thin humeral shaft above the stem, and the revision is a long case with a strut graft.
  • Ulnar nerve. Transposed by most, released in situ by some; symptoms in 3-11%, mostly transient. Document before the block, agree when the nerve will be examined, treat a worsening deficit as surgical.
  • Radial head overstuffing. Sized against the removed head, and 2 mm too long is enough to erode the capitellum; the stiffness presents months later as a revision.
  • Essex-Lopresti. The head must be replaced, not excised, and the wrist may be stabilised under the same anaesthetic, which lengthens the case and moves the tourniquet.
  • Posterior interosseous nerve. At risk in the lateral approach; a wrist drop in recovery needs the block excluded (document before) and then the surgeon.

Key sources

An uncommon operation with a complication literature far larger than its analgesia literature. The failure data come from the 9,308-elbow systematic review and the Mayo narrative review; the ulnar nerve figures from the same review and an 83-patient series that argues against routine transposition; the fracture indication from the single randomised trial of fixation against replacement in the elderly. The block recommendation rests on a randomised comparison of infraclavicular and supraclavicular approaches for ambulatory elbow surgery and on the general rebound-pain cohort; the catheter advice is author’s judgement. Radial head figures come from the 727-patient systematic review and the overlengthening review. The pain score is calibrated against the elbow fracture anchor in the Part B scale, since procedure-specific pain data do not exist.

  2. Prkic A, Welsink C, The B, van den Bekerom MPJ, Eygendaal D. Why does total elbow arthroplasty fail today? A systematic review of recent literature. Arch Orthop Trauma Surg 2017;137:761-769

Upper limb › Elbow

12 Elbow arthroscopy, release and tennis elbow surgery

Diagnostic and therapeutic elbow arthroscopy, arthroscopic and open capsular release for stiffness, and open, arthroscopic or percutaneous lateral epicondylar release

2Mild to moderate

Dominant mechanism: Capsule. Capsular distension, debridement and (in a release) excision, with the joint then pushed through a range it has not had for months; irrigation in the periarticular tissues; a small raw bone surface after osteophyte or capitellar work. Tennis elbow surgery is a tendon origin debrided and sometimes repaired, a surface-and-periosteum operation. Open release adds a muscle split and an ulnar nerve that is handled

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: moderate.

Block
General anaesthesia with surgeon infiltration for diagnostic and loose body arthroscopy and for tennis elbow surgery; a single-shot infraclavicular or supraclavicular block with intravenous dexamethasone added for arthroscopic or open release, where the surgeon wants the arm moved through its new range from day 1
Catheter: rarely A continuous infraclavicular catheter for the formal release of a severely stiff elbow is a defensible author's-judgement option when the surgeon runs an early movement programme and will accept not examining the nerves for two days; it is not needed for arthroscopy or tennis elbow surgery
Alternatives: Local infiltration alone for percutaneous or open tennis elbow release, with or without sedation; Axillary block (misses the posterior elbow unless the musculocutaneous and intercostobrachial nerves are added); Block as the sole anaesthetic in supine or lateral, impractical in prone
Position
Prone or lateral decubitus with the arm over a padded bolster and the elbow flexed to 90 degrees for arthroscopy; supine on an arm table with the arm across the chest for some surgeons and for most open tennis elbow and open release surgery
Tourniquet
Yes. Routine for arthroscopy and open release; 60-120 min. Tennis elbow surgery is 20-40 min under a tourniquet or, percutaneously, none at all
Cement
No
Blood loss
Minimal; the fluid in the drapes is irrigation. Open release bleeds modestly after tourniquet release into a drain
Duration
30-60 min for diagnostic arthroscopy and loose bodies; 90-150 min for arthroscopic or open release of a stiff elbow; 20-40 min for a lateral epicondylar release
Length of stay
Day case for arthroscopy and tennis elbow; day case or one night for a release, depending on the surgeon's movement programme. Day case: yes
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV at induction (3 g over 120 kg) for arthroscopy and open release; many surgeons omit it for a percutaneous or open tennis elbow release with no implant
Tranexamic acid
Not needed; some surgeons ask for tranexamic acid 1 g IV for arthroscopic visibility in a vascular synovitis
VTE
Mechanical only; upper limb day surgery carries a negligible baseline risk
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 4-8 mg IV at induction and ondansetron 4 mg IV before emergence
Tell the patient
The elbow will be swollen and stiff for a few days from the fluid used to see inside it; the pain is worst on the first day and settles over a week, and for a release the movement exercises are the operation, not an optional extra.
The trap
The nerves sit millimetres from the anterior portals and a stiff or rheumatoid elbow pulls them closer: a transient palsy after arthroscopy is common enough that the surgeon may want the hand examined before any block, and a dense block in recovery after a release can hide both a nerve injury and the forearm that is swelling from extravasated irrigation

What the surgeon is doing and why

Three operations share this card because they share a joint, a position and a pain mechanism, and because the hazards they carry for you are the same: nerves that sit within millimetres of the instruments, a forearm that fills with irrigation fluid, and a surgeon who wants the arm moved afterwards.

The elbow is a tight, congruent joint with a capsule that scars readily. Any insult (a fracture, a dislocation, a haemarthrosis, weeks in a splint, rheumatoid synovitis) produces a thickened anterior capsule that blocks extension and a thickened posterior capsule and olecranon fossa osteophytes that block flexion; the patient loses the functional arc of 30-130 degrees and cannot reach their face or their pocket. Loose bodies, osteophytes on the coronoid and olecranon tips, synovitis and osteochondritis of the capitellum in a young thrower are the other reasons to look inside. Elbow arthroscopy is the way in. The joint is distended with 20-30 mL of saline through the lateral soft spot, which pushes the anterior neurovascular bundle away from the capsule, and portals are made above and below the medial and lateral epicondyles with the elbow flexed to 90 degrees, because flexion relaxes the anterior structures and extension brings the radial nerve 3-7 mm closer to the joint. The distances are small whatever is done: the proximal anteromedial portal sits about 4 mm from the ulnar nerve and 7-20 mm from the median nerve, and the proximal anterolateral portal a mean 13.7 mm from the radial nerve. A stiff elbow pulls the nerves onto the capsule and a rheumatoid elbow has a thin, friable capsule with no safe plane, which is why those two diagnoses predicted transient nerve palsy in the 473-case Mayo series (p less than 0.001 and p less than 0.05), where 12 palsies occurred in 10 patients, all temporary, alongside four deep infections (0.8%) and a minor complication rate of 11%, most of it portal drainage. The pooled modern figure across 14,213 arthroscopies is a total complication rate of 8% and a nerve injury rate of 1.95%, mostly transient.

A release for stiffness takes the same route and goes further. Arthroscopically, the surgeon excises the anterior capsule off the humerus (a capsulectomy, not a capsulotomy, because an incised capsule rescars), clears the coronoid and olecranon fossae of osteophytes and scar, releases the posterior capsule, and often decompresses or releases the ulnar nerve through a small medial incision, because an elbow regaining flexion will stretch a nerve that has been sitting in a scarred cubital tunnel. In the 30-patient arthroscopic series the arc went from 68 to 123 degrees with three transient nerve palsies. An open release does the same through a lateral column incision, a medial over-the-top approach, or both: a muscle interval is split, the capsule excised under direct vision, heterotopic bone removed if there is any, and the ulnar nerve transposed. In the 52-patient open series the arc went from 57 to 116 degrees, but 27% needed a manipulation under anaesthesia in the early weeks and five needed a second release, which is the honest description of what the surgeon is fighting: a capsule that wants to scar back, and a movement programme that has to beat it.

Tennis elbow is a degenerate tendon origin, not an inflamed one. The extensor carpi radialis brevis origin on the lateral epicondyle develops angiofibroblastic degeneration and microtears under repetitive load, and after a year of failed non-operative treatment the surgeon excises the degenerate tissue and either decorticates the epicondyle and repairs the origin (the open Nirschl-type procedure), releases it arthroscopically from inside the joint, or simply divides it percutaneously through a 1 cm stab. The three give the same pain relief and function in the pooled 1,622 elbows (VAS 1.45 open versus 1.62 arthroscopic), with more minor complications after open surgery (57% versus 33%, mostly stiffness, haematoma and superficial infection), and percutaneous release under infiltration alone returned 87% of patients to complete pain relief in a 30-elbow series with a three-week return to work.

The pain logic: the dominant mechanism for arthroscopy and release is capsule, which is sharp with movement and settles over days, and in a release it is made worse by the fact that the joint is then deliberately pushed through a range it has not had for months, so the movement-evoked component is the whole point of the operation rather than a side effect. Irrigation fluid in the periarticular tissues adds a tight, swollen elbow for 48 hours. Osteophyte removal and capitellar drilling add a small bone surface. Open release adds a muscle split and a handled ulnar nerve with a neuropathic edge. Tennis elbow surgery is a surface-and-periosteum operation, a decorticated epicondyle and a debrided tendon origin, and it hurts in the way a decompression does: a few bad days, then a sore elbow for weeks that responds to simple analgesia. None of these operations produces the deep bone pain of an arthroplasty or the prolonged tendon-tension pain of a cuff repair; a score of 2 fits all three, with the release at the top of that band.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 Pre-operative neurology, the block decision and the position

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon is about to put instruments within millimetres of three nerves, in a stiff or rheumatoid elbow that has pulled them closer, and will want to know afterwards whether a weak hand is the block or the operation.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Document ulnar, median, radial and posterior interosseous function before anything is given. For a diagnostic or loose body arthroscopy and for tennis elbow surgery the author’s practice is general anaesthesia with surgeon infiltration and no block: the pain is a 2, the case is short, and a dense block buys nothing but a delay in the nerve check. For a release, where the surgeon wants the new range used from the first day, a single-shot infraclavicular or supraclavicular block with intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg is placed before induction, after the surgeon has agreed to examine the hand when it recedes rather than in recovery. The position decides the airway: prone and lateral need a tracheal tube and the usual care of the dependent eye, plexus and the face in a cradle; supine with the arm across the chest accepts a supraglottic airway in a short case.

  2. 2 Positioning and the tourniquet

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Prone or lateral with the arm over a bolster and the elbow hanging at 90 degrees gives the surgeon access to the posterior compartment, gravity working for them, and the forearm free to move; supine with the arm across the chest is quicker but the arm has to be held. The tourniquet keeps the view clear.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    In prone, the bolster is under the mid-humerus and the shoulder is abducted to 90 degrees and the elbow flexed; check that the shoulder is not forced and that the bolster does not press the radial nerve against the shaft of the humerus, because a radial palsy from a bolster is indistinguishable from one from a portal. The tourniquet goes high on the arm, inflated after exsanguination. In lateral, the same hazards as a shoulder in lateral, with the dependent arm on a board and the head neutral. Tourniquet pain under general anaesthesia is a slow rise in pressure and heart rate from 45 min onwards that will not answer opioid; a release can run to 120 min, an arthroscopy for loose bodies to 45.

  3. 3 Antibiotic and the first distension

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The joint is filled through the lateral soft spot with 20-30 mL of saline before any portal is made; a distended joint moves the brachial artery and median nerve away from the anterior capsule and makes the capsule taut enough to pierce cleanly. Deep infection is 0.4-0.8% and most surgeons give an antibiotic for an arthroscopy that may become a release.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Cefazolin 2 g IV before inflation. Nothing else at this step, but note the pump pressure the surgeon sets and the irrigation volume at the start, because this joint holds far less than a shoulder and extravasates earlier.

  4. 4 Anterior compartment: portals, loose bodies, synovectomy

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon enters through a proximal anteromedial or anterolateral portal with the elbow flexed, inspects the coronoid, the radial head and capitellum, removes loose bodies and synovitis with a shaver, and clears coronoid osteophytes with a burr. The trocar is kept flexed and aimed at the centre of the joint because extension brings the radial nerve closer.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The shaver and burr are the moments of risk for the posterior interosseous and median nerves, and a sudden request to stop the patient moving is a request for depth, not neuromuscular block: the surgeon cannot see the nerves and is relying on the elbow not shifting on the bolster. A retractor may be put through a second portal to hold the capsule off the nerves. Irrigation now begins to leave the joint; the forearm and the anterior elbow swell steadily from this point.

  5. 5 Capsulectomy and the formal release

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    For a stiff elbow the anterior capsule is excised from its humeral attachment, with a retractor holding the brachialis and the bundle away; the posterior capsule is released from the posterior compartment and the olecranon fossa cleared of bone and scar. The surgeon then extends and flexes the elbow on the table to confirm the gain and to tear whatever adhesions are left. A medial incision is often added to decompress or transpose the ulnar nerve, because regained flexion stretches a nerve trapped in scar.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is the capsule mechanism being created and the step that fixes the pain course. The manipulation at the end is forceful; in a patient without a block it is the most stimulating moment of the operation, and in an osteoporotic post-traumatic elbow it is when a supracondylar fracture happens. The ulnar nerve work means a neuropathic element in the hand afterwards and another reason the surgeon wanted the pre-operative documentation.

  6. 6 Posterior compartment and the olecranon

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Through a posterior and posterolateral portal the surgeon clears the olecranon fossa, trims the olecranon tip, removes posterior loose bodies and releases the posterior capsule; this is what restores flexion. The ulnar nerve is a few millimetres medial to the posteromedial gutter.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    In prone the surgeon is now working with gravity, the view is good and the step is quick. Check the forearm: by now a release has run 60-90 min of irrigation, and a forearm that is tense and hard rather than soft and swollen has a compartment filling with saline. The surgeon will usually stop the pump and wait; it resolves within hours and the reported experience is that it does not progress to a compartment syndrome, but a forearm that is still tense after the drapes come off is examined and documented before any block, and the block that was placed for a release is the one circumstance in which you cannot use pain to follow it.

  7. 7 Tennis elbow: the lateral epicondylar release

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A different operation, usually supine on an arm table. Open: a 3-5 cm incision over the lateral epicondyle, the interval between extensor carpi radialis longus and the common extensor origin opened, the degenerate grey tissue at the extensor carpi radialis brevis origin excised, the epicondyle decorticated to bleeding bone to provoke a healing response, and the origin repaired or left. Arthroscopic: the same origin released from inside the joint, which avoids the skin incision and the extensor repair. Percutaneous: a stab and a division of the origin, under local infiltration alone, no tourniquet. The lateral collateral ligament is a few millimetres posterior and the surgeon stays anterior to the equator of the radial head to protect it.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    20-40 min under a tourniquet for the open and arthroscopic versions, and the author’s practice is general anaesthesia with surgeon infiltration, or infiltration with sedation for the percutaneous release, because the pain is a 2 that simple analgesia covers. The posterior interosseous nerve is at risk only if the surgeon dissects distally; a wrist drop afterwards is surgical. The decorticated epicondyle is a raw bone surface and the reason the elbow aches for weeks.

  8. 8 Closure, dressing and the splint or no splint

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Portals are closed with a suture rather than a strip because the elbow extravasates and leaks; a bulky dressing goes on. After a release the surgeon decides between a splint in extension overnight, a hinged brace, or nothing, and some use continuous passive motion from day 1. After tennis elbow surgery a sling for comfort and no immobilisation.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Give the antiemetic. The elbow is swollen and the forearm full; a dressing that is already tight will be tighter in two hours. If a release patient has a block, the arm goes into whatever the surgeon wants before the patient wakes, and the forearm is examined one more time at the end.

  9. 9 Recovery and the first night

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants the arm elevated, the swelling down, the nerves checked, and for a release, movement started within 24 h, because the capsule begins to scar back from the first day.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    For the unblocked arthroscopy and tennis elbow patient, paracetamol and an NSAID started in recovery with a few doses of oral opioid for the first two nights; the pain peaks on the evening of surgery and day 1 and settles over a week. For the blocked release patient, the hand is examined when the block recedes at 12-24 h, at the time agreed with the surgeon, and the oral regimen is started in recovery, not when the block wears off. Half of ambulatory block patients describe rebound pain when the block goes, with bone surgery and no intravenous dexamethasone raising the odds; a release has a small bone component and the dexamethasone was given for that. Nearly every patient on this card goes home the same day; a release may stay a night where the surgeon runs a supervised movement programme.

Pain plan

The mechanism is capsule for arthroscopy and release, surface and periosteum for tennis elbow surgery, and neither is a mechanism that a long-acting block changes much after the first night. There is no PROSPECT guideline for any of the three and the analgesia literature is thin, so the plan is author’s judgement built on the mechanism, on the general rebound-pain data and on what the surgeon needs afterwards.

For a diagnostic or loose body arthroscopy and for tennis elbow surgery, the defensible default is general anaesthesia (or sedation for a percutaneous release), surgeon infiltration of the portals or the wound with 10-20 mL of ropivacaine 0.5% or bupivacaine 0.25%, paracetamol and an NSAID started pre-operatively and continued for a week, intravenous dexamethasone 4-8 mg at induction, and an oral opioid for two nights. No block: it would hide the nerve check for the one complication that matters, and it would not change the day 1 pain in an operation whose peak is reached with simple analgesia.

For a release the calculation changes, because the operation only works if the elbow is moved from the first day, and movement through a freshly excised capsule is the one thing a single-shot block makes possible on day 0 and the oral regimen makes tolerable from day 1. The defensible default is a single-shot infraclavicular or supraclavicular block with 20-25 mL of ropivacaine 0.5% and intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg, placed after the surgeon has agreed to a delayed nerve check, with the same oral regimen. A catheter is author’s judgement for the severely stiff elbow (arc under 60 degrees), the revision release, the patient who had a manipulation after a previous release, and the unit that runs continuous passive motion or a twice-daily physiotherapy programme in hospital, provided the surgeon accepts two days without a nerve examination and the forearm is examined by eye and by hand rather than by pain. The catheter’s cost is a flail arm during the exercises that it exists to make possible; the surgeon decides whether the trade is worth it.

Escalation: pain above 7 after the block has receded, or on day 1 in an unblocked patient, is treated with the charted opioid and a check that the regular doses were given. Pain with a tense forearm, pain on passive finger extension, or a hand that is cooler than the other is a compartment filling, and after an arthroscopy it is usually saline rather than blood, but it is examined by a surgeon, not treated with more opioid. Pain that is better on day 1 than on day 3, in a hot swollen joint, is one of the 0.4-0.8% of deep infections.

Pitfalls and variants

  • Prone versus lateral versus supine. Prone and lateral mean a tracheal tube and the bolster hazards; supine with the arm across the chest means an assistant holding the arm and a surgeon who finds the posterior compartment harder. Ask which, because it decides the airway.
  • The rheumatoid elbow. Thin friable capsule, no safe plane, the strongest predictor of nerve palsy in the Mayo series, plus the neck, airway and steroid questions of every rheumatoid patient.
  • The post-traumatic stiff elbow with retained metal or heterotopic bone. The nerves are in scar and may be adherent to the capsule; the surgeon may convert to open, the case lengthens to two hours, and the ulnar nerve is transposed. A supracondylar fracture during the end-of-case manipulation is the disaster that turns a day case into a fixation.
  • Fluid extravasation. The elbow holds 20-30 mL and leaks from the first portal; a release with a high pump pressure fills the forearm. It resolves, but a tense forearm is examined before any block or discharge, and the block placed for a release removes pain as a sign.
