  • Nerve palsy. 1.95% pooled, mostly transient, ulnar commonest; documented before the case, examined after the block recedes, and treated as the surgeon’s problem if it is a posterior interosseous or median palsy after an anterior portal.
  • The ulnar nerve in a release. Decompressed or transposed by most surgeons when flexion is being regained; dysaesthesia in the ring and little fingers afterwards is expected for weeks and is not the block.
  • Osteochondritis dissecans of the capitellum. A young thrower, a short arthroscopy with drilling or a graft, day case; the bone surface adds a little to the first two days.
  • Tennis elbow: open versus arthroscopic versus percutaneous. Same outcome, fewer minor complications arthroscopically, and the percutaneous release needs nothing but infiltration. Iatrogenic lateral collateral instability is the complication that presents late and to the surgeon, not to you.
  • Continuous passive motion and early physiotherapy after a release. Where the surgeon uses it, the block and the regimen have to be matched to a programme, and the catheter question is decided by the programme, not by the operation.
  • Day-case discharge with a block after a release. A flail arm, a splint or brace, written instructions, oral analgesia already started and a named person for the night; the same list as any ambulatory block patient, with the forearm examined and documented before the patient leaves.

Key sources

The complication data for elbow arthroscopy are good: a single-institution series of 473 cases and a meta-analysis of 14,213, agreeing on a transient nerve palsy rate of about 2% and a deep infection rate under 1%. The stiffness data are small single-surgeon series, one arthroscopic and one open, that show the same 50-60 degree gain and the same tendency to recur. The tennis elbow data come from a systematic review of 1,622 elbows showing no difference between open and arthroscopic release and a small series of percutaneous release under local anaesthesia alone. There is no analgesia trial for any of these operations and no PROSPECT guideline; the block, catheter and day-case advice is author’s judgement from the mechanism and from the general ambulatory block literature.

  1. Kelly EW, Morrey BF, O'Driscoll SW. Complications of elbow arthroscopy. J Bone Joint Surg Am 2001;83:25-34
    473 consecutive elbow arthroscopies: serious complications in 0.8% (four deep infections); minor in 11%, including 12 transient nerve palsies in 10 patients (five ulnar, four superficial radial, one posterior interosseous, one medial antebrachial cutaneous, one anterior interosseous), 33 prolonged portal drainage or superficial infections; rheumatoid arthritis (p less than 0.001) and contracture (p less than 0.05) predicted nerve palsy; no permanent nerve injury, haematoma or compartment syndrome
  2. Ahmed AF, D'Hooghe P, Alkhelaifi K, Zikria B. Complications of elbow arthroscopy: a meta-analysis. ISAKOS Congress 2021 abstract
    95 studies, 14,213 patients: total complication rate 8%; nerve injury the commonest at 1.95%, mostly transient (ulnar 1.95%, radial 0.73%, lateral antebrachial cutaneous 0.26%, posterior interosseous and median 0.17% each); superficial infection 1.89%, deep 0.36%
  3. Wheeless' Textbook of Orthopaedics. Elbow arthroscopy
    Portal anatomy: proximal anteromedial portal about 4 mm from the ulnar nerve and 7-20 mm from the median nerve with the elbow flexed; proximal anterolateral portal a mean 13.7 mm from the radial nerve; extension brings the radial nerve 3-7 mm closer to the joint; distension moves the neurovascular structures away from the portals; prone positioning with a sandbag under the arm
  4. Dai J, Zhang G, Li S, Xu J, Lu J. Arthroscopic treatment of posttraumatic elbow stiffness due to soft tissue problems. Orthop Surg 2020;12:1464-1470
    30 arthroscopic releases with capsulectomy and ulnar nerve release: arc improved from 68 to 123 degrees; three transient nerve palsies, five prolonged portal drainage, one medial haematoma
  5. Tan V, Daluiski A, Simic P, Hotchkiss RN. Outcome of open release for post-traumatic elbow stiffness. J Trauma 2006;61(3)
    52 open releases, mean age 35: arc improved from 57 to 116 degrees; 27% needed a manipulation under anaesthesia in the early weeks; five needed a second release; three wound infections, three cubital tunnel syndromes, one complex regional pain syndrome
  6. Moradi A, Pasdar P, Mehrad-Majd H, Ebrahimzadeh MH. Clinical outcomes of open versus arthroscopic surgery for lateral epicondylitis, evidence from a systematic review. Arch Bone Jt Surg 2019;7:91-104
    34 studies, 1,622 elbows: no difference in pain (VAS 1.45 versus 1.62), DASH, satisfaction or return to work (8.9 versus 6.3 months, not significant); complications 57.3% open versus 33.4% arthroscopic, mostly minor (stiffness, haematoma, superficial infection, transient paraesthesia)
  7. Nazar M, Lipscombe S, Morapudi S, et al. Percutaneous tennis elbow release under local anaesthesia. Open Orthop J 2012;6:129-133
    30 elbows released percutaneously as day cases under 5 mL lidocaine 1% and 5 mL bupivacaine 0.5% with adrenaline, no tourniquet: 87% complete pain relief, return to work at a mean of three weeks, one haematoma, no infection or stiffness
  8. Barry GS, Bailey JG, Sardinha J, Brousseau P, Uppal V. Factors associated with rebound pain after peripheral nerve block for ambulatory surgery. Br J Anaesth 2021;126:862-871
    972 ambulatory block patients, rebound pain in 49.6%; bone surgery OR 1.82, female OR 1.52, younger age; absence of intravenous dexamethasone OR 1.78

Upper limb › Elbow

13 Distal biceps repair; ulnar nerve decompression and transposition

Acute and chronic distal biceps tendon repair by single or double incision; in situ cubital tunnel decompression, subcutaneous and submuscular anterior transposition

3Moderate

Dominant mechanism: Tendon under tension. A retracted biceps tendon pulled back 2-5 cm to a decorticated, drilled radial tuberosity and fixed under tension in a young, muscular patient; the forearm is then held flexed and supinated and the repair is loaded by every attempt to turn the hand. Ulnar nerve surgery is a different and smaller mechanism: a nerve freed from its bed, with a neuropathic flavour, plus a muscle split and a medial epicondyle stripped of flexor origin in a transposition

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: high.

Block
Single-shot infraclavicular or supraclavicular brachial plexus block with intravenous dexamethasone, under general anaesthesia, for a distal biceps repair; general anaesthesia or sedation with surgeon infiltration, and no block, for ulnar nerve decompression and most transpositions
Catheter: rarely Not for a primary biceps repair in a counselled day-case patient; the defensible exception is a chronic reconstruction with a graft and a tendon that has been pulled hard, or the patient who has had a bad night after a previous block. Never for ulnar nerve surgery, where the surgeon wants the nerve examined in recovery
Alternatives: Axillary block with musculocutaneous and intercostobrachial supplementation for a biceps repair when the supraclavicular region is unavailable; Surgeon infiltration with sedation for in situ decompression as a sole technique; General anaesthesia with infiltration and no block for a biceps repair when the surgeon insists on an immediate posterior interosseous nerve check
Position
Supine with the arm on a table, forearm supinated for the anterior incision and pronated for the posterior one in a double-incision repair; supine with the arm on a table and the shoulder externally rotated for the medial elbow in ulnar nerve surgery
Tourniquet
Yes. Routine for both; 45-90 min for a biceps repair, 20-45 min for a decompression and longer for a submuscular transposition. Some surgeons release the tourniquet before the final tensioning of the biceps so the muscle is at its true resting length
Cement
No
Blood loss
Minimal under tourniquet; a haematoma in the antecubital fossa after release is the bleed that matters, and the brachial artery and its recurrent radial branches sit in the field
Duration
60-90 min for an acute biceps repair, 90-150 min for a chronic reconstruction with graft; 20-45 min for in situ decompression, 45-90 min for a transposition
Length of stay
Day case for both; a chronic reconstruction may stay a night. Day case: yes
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV at induction (3 g over 120 kg) for a biceps repair with an implant; many surgeons omit it for an in situ decompression
Tranexamic acid
Not needed
VTE
Mechanical only; the baseline risk is negligible for upper limb day surgery
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV at induction (given anyway for the block) and ondansetron 4 mg IV before emergence
Tell the patient
The arm will be numb into the night and the elbow will hurt most on the first and second days when the feeling comes back; the repair is protected by the splint and the no-lifting rule for six weeks, and a patch of numbness on the thumb side of the forearm is common and usually fades.
The trap
The posterior interosseous nerve wraps around the radial neck exactly where the surgeon is drilling, retracting and tying the biceps down; document wrist and finger extension before the block, and agree with the surgeon that a dense block will hide a wrist drop until the next day

What the surgeon is doing and why

Two operations on the front and the inside of the elbow, paired because they share a position, a tourniquet and a day-case pathway, and because they sit at opposite ends of the question this book keeps asking: whether a block helps, and whether it hides something the surgeon needs to see.

The distal biceps tendon inserts on the radial tuberosity, a bump on the medial side of the radius 2 cm below the radial head, and it ruptures in one setting: a man in his forties or fifties, often heavily built or a weight trainer, takes an eccentric load on a flexed elbow and feels a pop. The tendon retracts into the arm, the muscle belly rides up, and the forearm loses much of its supination strength and some flexion strength if nothing is done. Non-operative treatment is reasonable in a sedentary patient; everyone else is repaired within two or three weeks, before the tendon shortens, scars to the brachialis, and can no longer reach the tuberosity without a graft.

The surgeon’s problem is that the tuberosity faces posteriorly and medially and the only ways to it pass the radial nerve. The single anterior incision goes through the antecubital fossa, between brachioradialis and pronator teres, retracts the lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve laterally (it is injured, usually transiently, in about 9% of repairs, and more often through a small incision than an extensile one), finds the recurrent radial vessels and ties them, and reaches the tuberosity with the forearm fully supinated to roll the bone towards the surgeon and the posterior interosseous nerve away. The nerve wraps around the radial neck inside the supinator a finger’s breadth from the tuberosity, and a retractor on the lateral side of the neck, a drill that exits the far cortex, or a cortical button flipped on the wrong side of it, are the mechanisms of a palsy; it happens in about 1.6-2.7% of repairs and mostly resolves. The double-incision technique, which the trial of 91 men found gave a 10% advantage in flexion strength for the same function scores, retrieves the tendon through a small anterior incision, passes it between radius and ulna, and fixes it through a second posterolateral incision with a muscle split of the extensor mass and bone tunnels in the tuberosity; it trades the nerve risk (lateral antebrachial cutaneous neuropraxia 2.2% versus 9.8%, posterior interosseous palsy 0.2% versus 2.7%) for heterotopic ossification and, rarely, a radioulnar synostosis (ossification or synostosis 9.8% versus 3.2%), because the ulnar periosteum and the interosseous membrane are disturbed on the way through.

Whichever route, the fixation is the same idea: the tuberosity is decorticated or a socket drilled into it, the tendon end is whip-stitched, and it is pulled down and fixed with a cortical button, an interference screw, suture anchors, or sutures through bone tunnels. The arm is flexed and supinated to get the tendon to reach; a tendon that has retracted for weeks has to be dragged, and a chronic rupture over about six weeks gets a graft because it will not reach at all. After the repair the forearm is immobilised in flexion and supination, then moved early but unloaded for six weeks, with a no-lifting rule that the patient population finds hard to keep: re-rupture (1.4-2.5%) clusters in the first three weeks and is attributed to non-compliance.

Ulnar neuropathy at the elbow is a nerve compressed or stretched in a tunnel that narrows with flexion. The nerve runs behind the medial epicondyle under the cubital tunnel retinaculum, between the two heads of flexor carpi ulnaris, and is tethered proximally by the arcade of Struthers and the medial intermuscular septum. The surgeon has three choices and the randomised evidence says they are equivalent: simple in situ decompression (open the roof of the tunnel and the fascia of flexor carpi ulnaris and leave the nerve where it is), anterior subcutaneous transposition (free the nerve over 15 cm, divide the septum, move it in front of the epicondyle into a fat pocket), or submuscular transposition (the same, with the flexor-pronator origin detached from the epicondyle and repaired over the nerve). In the 152-patient randomised trial decompression and subcutaneous transposition gave the same proportion of good results at a year (49 of 75 versus 54 of 77), with complications in 9.6% after decompression and 31.1% after transposition, and the meta-analyses agree that there is no difference in outcome. Decompression is therefore the modern default, with transposition kept for a nerve that subluxes over the epicondyle, a revision, or a nerve that has to be moved for an elbow operation.

The pain logic follows. A biceps repair is tendon-tension in its purest form: a strong, retracted tendon fixed to drilled bone under tension in a young muscular patient, then loaded by every attempt to supinate or flex for weeks. The early peak is a bone-and-tendon peak and the course is prolonged by movement, the shape of a cuff repair but in a joint that is easier to rest, so it earns a 3 rather than a 5; the patient demographic (young, male, opioid-naive) puts rebound risk high. Ulnar nerve decompression is a nerve mechanism: a neuropathic ache and dysaesthesia often better the next morning than the day before surgery, with an incision that hurts for a few days. A transposition adds muscle (the flexor-pronator origin taken down and repaired, in the submuscular version) and a bigger wound, and sits at a 2. The card carries the biceps score because the biceps is the operation that needs a plan.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 Documenting the nerves and deciding the block

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon is about to work within a centimetre of the posterior interosseous nerve, retract the lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve for an hour, and in the ulnar case operate on the nerve itself; they will want to know afterwards which deficit is new.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Before any drug, examine and write down wrist and finger extension (posterior interosseous), sensation over the lateral forearm (lateral antebrachial cutaneous), and for the ulnar case little finger sensation, first dorsal interosseous power and a Froment’s sign. For a biceps repair, the author’s practice is a single-shot infraclavicular or supraclavicular block with intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg, placed awake before induction, after the surgeon has agreed that the nerve check will wait for the block to recede. For an ulnar nerve decompression or a subcutaneous transposition, no block: the operation is short, the pain is a 2 that infiltration covers, and the surgeon wants the little finger examined in recovery. A submuscular transposition is the author’s exception, where a block is reasonable if the surgeon accepts the delay.

  2. 2 Position, tourniquet and the airway

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Supine with the arm on a table, the forearm supinated for the anterior approach. The tourniquet goes high on the arm. For the ulnar nerve, the shoulder is externally rotated and the elbow flexed on the table to present the medial side; some surgeons prefer the arm across the chest.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A supraglottic airway and spontaneous ventilation are reasonable for every operation on this card; a tracheal tube for the reflux-prone or the heavily built biceps patient. Cefazolin 2 g IV before inflation for the implant case. The external rotation needed for the medial elbow strains a stiff shoulder and is the position to check after the surgeon has set it. Tourniquet time runs 45-90 min for a biceps repair and under 45 min for a decompression; a submuscular transposition is longer.

  3. 3 Anterior incision and the lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A transverse or S-shaped incision in the antecubital crease, then the interval between brachioradialis and pronator teres. The lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve runs in the subcutaneous fat lateral to the biceps tendon and is retracted laterally for the rest of the case; the recurrent radial vessels cross the field and are ligated.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The nerve retracted here is the commonest complication of the operation (9.2% in 3,091 repairs), and it is a sensory nerve: a numb patch over the lateral forearm that usually resolves. It is also the nerve whose distribution a patient will describe the next day as “the block has not worn off”, which is why the pre-operative sensory map matters. Nothing to do at this step but note the time.

  4. 4 Retrieving the tendon

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The tendon end is found, often retracted into the arm and scarred to the brachialis; the surgeon milks it distally with the elbow flexed, excises the frayed end, and whip-stitches it. A tendon more than a few weeks old may need a separate proximal incision or a graft.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The elbow is flexed hard and the muscle belly pulled on; in an unblocked patient this is a stimulating moment, and in a blocked patient it is the moment the surgeon finds out whether the tendon will reach. If it will not, the case lengthens by an hour for a graft and the pain course shifts up.

  5. 5 Exposing the tuberosity and protecting the posterior interosseous nerve

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    With the forearm in maximal supination, the radial tuberosity rotates into the wound and the posterior interosseous nerve, in the supinator on the far side of the neck, rotates away. A retractor is placed carefully, never levered against the lateral side of the neck. In the double-incision technique the surgeon instead passes a clamp between radius and ulna from the anterior wound to the posterolateral skin and makes the second incision there, splitting the extensor mass with the forearm pronated and staying off the ulna.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is the step the trap is about. A posterior interosseous palsy presents as a wrist drop with intact wrist extension in radial deviation (extensor carpi radialis longus is spared) and no sensory loss; the mechanisms are retraction, a drill exiting the far cortex, and a cortical button that flips into the nerve. The surgeon will want the forearm held in full supination and still; a request for stillness is a request for depth or for a hand on the forearm, not neuromuscular block. In the double-incision technique the pronation and supination of the forearm between the two wounds is where the arm board and the tourniquet get dislodged.

  6. 6 Preparing the tuberosity and fixing the tendon under tension

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The tuberosity is decorticated with a burr, or a socket drilled to the far cortex for a button or a screw, or bone tunnels made for a double-incision repair. The tendon is pulled down with the elbow flexed and the forearm supinated and fixed with a cortical button through the far cortex, an interference screw into the socket, suture anchors, or sutures tied over a bone bridge. Some surgeons let the tourniquet down before the final tensioning so that the muscle is at its resting length and the repair is not set too tight.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The mechanism this card is built around exists from the moment the tendon is fixed: bone drilled and a tendon tied to it under tension in a young patient. The bone component (socket, decortication) is the reason the rebound-pain odds are those of bone surgery. If the surgeon drops the tourniquet before tensioning, expect the reperfusion dip and a bleeding antecubital fossa in the middle of the critical step rather than at the end.

  7. 7 Closure, the splint and the position of the forearm

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Haemostasis after tourniquet release (the recurrent radial vessels and the brachial artery are in the field), layered closure, and a posterior splint with the elbow at about 90 degrees and the forearm supinated so the repair is unloaded. Early protected motion starts at one to two weeks; no lifting for six.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Give the antiemetic. The splint goes on before the patient lightens; a young man with a dense block will otherwise flex and supinate the arm with the other hand to look at it. A tense antecubital fossa in recovery is a haematoma from a recurrent branch and is surgical; it compresses the median nerve and the brachial artery, so a hand that is cooler than the other or a new numb thumb is examined rather than observed.

  8. 8 Ulnar nerve: the medial approach and in situ decompression

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A 4-8 cm incision behind the medial epicondyle, protecting the branches of the medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve that cross it (the usual cause of a painful scar), then division of the cubital tunnel retinaculum, the fascia between the two heads of flexor carpi ulnaris and, proximally, the arcade of Struthers. The nerve is left in its bed and the elbow is flexed on the table to check that it does not subluxate forward over the epicondyle; if it does, the surgeon moves to a transposition.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Surgeon infiltration with 10-15 mL of ropivacaine 0.5% or bupivacaine 0.25% along the wound and a general anaesthetic or sedation; the operation is 20-45 min. The nerve itself should not be stimulated in a decompression, but a tug on it in a lightly sedated patient produces a jolt into the little finger that the patient will remember. A medial antebrachial cutaneous branch cut here gives a numb or painful patch on the medial forearm that outlasts the nerve symptoms.

  9. 9 Ulnar nerve: anterior transposition

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    When the nerve subluxes, or at revision, the nerve is freed over about 15 cm with its vessels where possible, the medial intermuscular septum is excised so the nerve does not kink over it, and it is moved in front of the epicondyle. Subcutaneous: a fascial sling or a fat pocket holds it. Submuscular: the flexor-pronator origin is lifted off the epicondyle, the nerve laid on the muscle bed next to the median nerve, and the origin repaired over it. A medial epicondylectomy is a third option that removes the bone the nerve was riding over.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The submuscular version is the one with a muscle mechanism, a repaired flexor origin protected for a few weeks, and a 90 min tourniquet; it is the one ulnar operation where a block is reasonable, and even here the surgeon usually wants the hand examined in recovery because a nerve devascularised in the move declares itself early. Complications were three times more frequent after transposition than decompression in the randomised trial (31.1% versus 9.6%); a transposition patient in recovery with a new dense ulnar deficit is examined by the surgeon, not attributed to infiltration.

  10. 10 Recovery, the first night and discharge

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants the biceps repair protected and the nerve patient’s hand working, and both patients home the same day.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    For the biceps patient, the oral regimen starts in recovery: paracetamol and an NSAID, and an oral opioid for the first three nights. The block recedes at 12-24 h and this patient is the rebound-pain phenotype of the 972-patient cohort (bone surgery OR 1.82, younger age, and the dexamethasone given to blunt it); the pain rises over an hour or two to its day 1 level, the worst of the course, and the written night plan is what keeps him from the emergency department. The nerve check happens when the block is gone, at the agreed time, and a wrist drop then is a call to the surgeon. For the ulnar patient, paracetamol and an NSAID with a few opioid doses for two nights; the little finger is examined before discharge and the patient told that the tingling may be better tomorrow or may take months, depending on how long the nerve was compressed.

Pain plan

Two mechanisms, two plans. The biceps repair is tendon-tension on a drilled bone in the patient most likely to have rebound pain, and the plan has to cover the first night and expect a hard day 1 and 2. The ulnar nerve operation is a nerve mechanism with a small wound, where the plan has to not hide the hand.

For the biceps repair the defensible default is a single-shot infraclavicular or supraclavicular block with 20-25 mL of ropivacaine 0.5%, intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg, paracetamol and an NSAID started before the block recedes and continued for a week, and an oral opioid for the first three nights, with a written night plan. The patient is young, male and will be at home with a flail arm; he needs the splint explained, the no-lifting rule explained with the re-rupture figure attached to it, and someone with him on the first night. A catheter is rarely justified: the operation is a day case, the joint is splinted and rested rather than moved, and a flail arm for two days in a patient who will not keep still outweighs the gain. The exceptions are author’s judgement: a chronic reconstruction with a graft, a bilateral or revision case, and a patient who has had a catastrophic rebound night before. There is no procedure-specific guideline and no randomised analgesia trial for distal biceps repair; the plan is the mechanism and the general ambulatory block data.

For the ulnar nerve the defensible default is surgeon infiltration, general anaesthesia or sedation, paracetamol and an NSAID for a few days, and a couple of opioid doses for the first two nights, with no block, because the operation’s only serious complication is a nerve that is worse, and that is found by examining the hand in recovery. A submuscular transposition is the exception where a block is reasonable if the surgeon agrees. A patient already on a gabapentinoid or an antidepressant for neuropathic pain continues it.

Escalation for the biceps patient: pain above 7 on the first night with a soft antecubital fossa, warm fingers and the splint on is the block wearing off and is treated with the charted opioid; pain with a tense fossa, a cool hand or a new numb thumb is a haematoma on the median nerve and brachial artery and is surgical; a wrist drop after the block has gone is a posterior interosseous palsy and is the surgeon’s to follow. For the ulnar patient, pain is rarely the problem; a dense new motor deficit is.

Pitfalls and variants

  • Single versus double incision. Same function; the double incision gives more flexion strength, fewer nerve injuries and more heterotopic ossification, and adds a posterolateral muscle split and the pronation-supination shuffle during the case. The anaesthetic is the same.
  • Chronic rupture and graft. Over about six weeks the tendon will not reach; an allograft or autograft is woven in, the case runs to 150 min, the tourniquet is let down and re-inflated, and this is the patient for whom the catheter question is worth asking.
  • Heterotopic ossification. Mostly after double-incision repairs; some surgeons give an NSAID for prophylaxis, which is the regular NSAID you were charting anyway.
  • The weight trainer. Anabolic steroid use is over-represented in distal biceps ruptures; ask, because it changes the airway, the cardiovascular risk and the opioid tolerance.
  • The lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve. Numb lateral forearm in 9% of repairs, more with small incisions; it looks like a residual block to the patient and the ward, and the pre-operative sensory map is what separates them.
  • Posterior interosseous palsy. 1.6-2.7%; retraction, drill and button. Document before, examine after the block, and treat a persisting palsy as the surgeon’s to image and explore.
  • Ulnar nerve decompression versus transposition. Equivalent outcomes, a third of the complications with decompression; transposition for a subluxing nerve or a revision, submuscular for the thin patient whose subcutaneous nerve would sit on the desk edge.
  • The nerve decompressed as part of an elbow operation. Transposition is bundled with total elbow arthroplasty, distal humerus fixation and some releases; there the nerve plan belongs to the main operation’s card.
  • Pre-existing neuropathic pain. A long-compressed nerve with wasting does not recover its motor function and may not lose its pain; set the expectation before surgery and continue the neuropathic agents.

Key sources

The complication data for distal biceps repair are consistent across two systematic reviews and the randomised single-versus-double-incision trial, and they are what the trap and the nerve documentation rest on. The ulnar nerve evidence is better still: one adequately sized randomised trial and two meta-analyses agreeing that decompression and transposition give the same result and that transposition carries more complications. There is no analgesia trial for either operation and no PROSPECT guideline; the block and catheter advice is author’s judgement from the mechanism and the general ambulatory block literature, and the score of 3 for a biceps repair is calibrated against the Part B anchors rather than against measured pain data, which do not exist for this operation.

  1. Amarasooriya M, Bain GI, Roper T, Bryant K, Iqbal K, Phadnis J. Complications after distal biceps tendon repair: a systematic review. Am J Sports Med 2020;48:3103-3111
    72 studies, 3,091 primary repairs: complications 25% overall, 4.6% major; lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve injury the commonest at 9.2% (9.7% with a limited anterior incision versus 5.2% extensile); posterior interosseous nerve injury 1.6%, unaffected by fixation method; superficial radial nerve injury 6% extensile versus 2.1% limited; re-rupture 1.4%; synostosis 0.1%, only after double incision; most nerve injuries resolved
  2. Amin NH, Volpi A, Lynch TS, et al. Complications of distal biceps tendon repair: a meta-analysis of single-incision versus double-incision surgical technique. Orthop J Sports Med 2016;4(10)
    87 studies, 1,283 patients: complications 28.3% single incision versus 20.9% double; lateral antebrachial cutaneous neuropraxia 9.8% versus 2.2%; posterior interosseous palsy 2.7% versus 0.2%; heterotopic ossification 3.2% versus 7.2% and combined ossification or synostosis 3.2% versus 9.8%; re-rupture 2.5% versus 0.6%
  3. Grewal R, Athwal GS, MacDermid JC, et al. Single versus double-incision technique for the repair of acute distal biceps tendon ruptures: a randomized clinical trial. J Bone Joint Surg Am 2012;94:1166-1174
    91 men with acute ruptures randomised: comparable ASES elbow scores; a 10% advantage in flexion strength with the double-incision technique
  4. Bartels RHMA, Verhagen WIM, van der Wilt GJ, Meulstee J, van Rossum LGM, Grotenhuis JA. Prospective randomized controlled study comparing simple decompression versus anterior subcutaneous transposition for idiopathic neuropathy of the ulnar nerve at the elbow: part 1. Neurosurgery 2005;56:522-530
    152 patients randomised, one-year follow-up: excellent or good in 49 of 75 after decompression and 54 of 77 after transposition, not different; complications 9.6% versus 31.1% (risk ratio 0.32); the authors advise simple decompression even when the nerve subluxes
  5. Zlowodzki M, Chan S, Bhandari M, Kalliainen L, Schubert W. Anterior transposition compared with simple decompression for treatment of cubital tunnel syndrome: a meta-analysis of randomized, controlled trials. J Bone Joint Surg Am 2007;89:2591-2598
    Four randomised trials, 335 patients: no difference in motor conduction velocity or clinical scores between transposition (submuscular or subcutaneous) and simple decompression
  6. Macadam SA, Gandhi R, Bezuhly M, Lefaivre KA. Simple decompression versus anterior subcutaneous and submuscular transposition of the ulnar nerve for cubital tunnel syndrome: a meta-analysis. J Hand Surg Am 2008;33:1314.e1-12
    Ten studies, 449 simple decompressions, 342 subcutaneous and 115 submuscular transpositions: odds of improvement with decompression versus transposition 0.75 (95% CI 0.54-1.04), not significant
  7. Barry GS, Bailey JG, Sardinha J, Brousseau P, Uppal V. Factors associated with rebound pain after peripheral nerve block for ambulatory surgery. Br J Anaesth 2021;126:862-871
    972 ambulatory block patients, rebound pain in 49.6%; bone surgery OR 1.82, female OR 1.52, younger age; absence of intravenous dexamethasone OR 1.78

Upper limb › Elbow

14 Elbow fractures: olecranon, distal humerus, radial head

Olecranon tension band and plate fixation; distal humerus two-column ORIF with or without olecranon osteotomy; radial head screw and plate fixation

3Moderate

Dominant mechanism: Bone. Fractured bone reduced and compressed with metal, drilled and plated along two columns in a distal humerus with periosteal stripping; a triceps either split, reflected or an olecranon osteotomy added; the ulnar nerve mobilised in every distal humerus; a tourniquet. The olecranon and radial head are small versions of the same, and the dislocated elbow adds a ligament repair

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: moderate.

Block
General anaesthesia with a single-shot infraclavicular or supraclavicular block and intravenous dexamethasone for olecranon and radial head fixation; for distal humerus ORIF the same block only after the surgeon has agreed to a delayed nerve examination, otherwise general anaesthesia with surgeon infiltration and a block offered the next morning
Catheter: selective A continuous infraclavicular catheter for a distal humerus fixation is defensible when the surgeon runs early motion and has seen the ulnar nerve intact and untethered; the author's practice is a single shot for olecranon and radial head fixation and a case-by-case decision for the distal humerus, with the nerve examination timing written in the notes
Alternatives: Axillary block with a musculocutaneous supplement for radial head and olecranon fixation; General anaesthesia alone with surgeon infiltration and a rescue block in recovery or the next day for the distal humerus where the surgeon wants an immediate nerve check; Low-concentration block (ropivacaine 0.2%) without adjunct where a compartment or nerve concern exists, on the lower-leg guideline's logic
Position
Lateral decubitus or prone with the arm over a padded post for the distal humerus and most olecranon fixations; supine with the arm across the chest for some surgeons; supine on an arm table for the radial head
Tourniquet
Yes. Sterile tourniquet high on the arm; an olecranon fixation sits inside 60 min, a distal humerus runs to the limit and beyond it, with release and re-inflation or completion without it
Cement
No
Blood loss
100-300 mL for a distal humerus after tourniquet release; under 100 mL for the olecranon and radial head
Duration
45-90 min for olecranon tension band or plate; 120-240 min for a distal humerus two-column fixation, longer with an osteotomy and an osteoporotic bone; 60-120 min for radial head fixation, longer in a terrible triad
Length of stay
Day case or one night for the olecranon and radial head; 1-3 nights for the distal humerus. Day case: selected
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV within 60 min of incision (3 g over 120 kg); an open fracture has its own antibiotic pathway and its own card
Tranexamic acid
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV at induction for a distal humerus; not needed for the olecranon or radial head
VTE
Mechanical for the inpatient; chemoprophylaxis only for the patient's own risk factors
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV at induction and ondansetron 4 mg IV before emergence
Tell the patient
The arm will be numb into the night if a block is used; the elbow hurts most on the first two days and then settles, the metal may be felt under the skin at the point of the elbow, and the little finger side of the hand may tingle for some weeks because the nerve was moved out of the way.
The trap
The block that hides the nerve: the ulnar nerve is mobilised in every distal humerus fixation and injured in a quarter to a third, the posterior interosseous nerve sits against the radial neck, and a surgeon who wants to examine the hand in recovery has a legitimate claim; the decision is made with the surgeon before the block, written down, and never defaulted

What the surgeon is doing and why

Three fractures of one joint, grouped because the surgeon’s logic is the same for all of them: the elbow tolerates neither an incongruent joint surface nor six weeks in a cast, so an intra-articular fracture is reduced anatomically, fixed rigidly enough to move within days, and the price is paid in exposure. What differs is how much exposure. An olecranon is subcutaneous and takes 45 min; a distal humerus is a three-dimensional puzzle behind the triceps and takes three hours; a radial head is a small bone on the lateral side with a nerve wrapped around its neck. The anaesthetic question they share is the one in the trap: a block is the best analgesic for all three, and each has a nerve the surgeon may want to examine before the block would allow.

The olecranon is the triceps’ lever arm. A fall onto the point of the elbow breaks it across, the triceps pulls the proximal fragment up, and the joint surface gapes. A tension band (two Kirschner wires down the shaft and a figure-of-eight wire over the dorsal surface) converts the pull of the triceps into compression at the joint line, which is elegant, cheap and works for a simple transverse fracture; it also leaves wires under thin skin that migrate and irritate, and in the pooled comparisons it needed removal in 79 of 236 cases against 41 of 332 after plating, with a complication rate twice that of a plate (RR 0.48 in favour of the plate). A precontoured dorsal plate is used for comminuted, oblique and osteoporotic fractures and is now the commoner choice. In a frail patient a displaced olecranon fracture can be left alone; surgeons vary.

The distal humerus is two columns of bone, medial and lateral, joined by the articular spool of the trochlea and capitellum, and an intercondylar fracture separates the columns from each other and from the shaft. The surgeon has to see the joint surface, reconstruct it, and fix each column with its own plate (parallel or perpendicular, a matter of preference). Seeing the joint from behind means getting past the triceps: a paratricipital approach works on either side of it and gives a limited view; a triceps split or reflection gives more; an olecranon osteotomy (a chevron cut through the olecranon, swung up with the triceps attached) gives the whole articular surface, at the cost of a second fracture that needs its own fixation and fails to unite in a few percent, with complications of 46-55% in comparative series against 27-41% for the paratricipital approach. The ulnar nerve is found and mobilised in every case, because the medial plate goes where the nerve lives; it is injured in a quarter to a third of patients (26.8% with an osteotomy and 33.3% without, in a 134-patient trauma centre cohort, not different), mostly transiently, and many surgeons transpose it. In an osteoporotic patient over 65 with comminution the fragments may not hold screws, and the surgeon converts to a total elbow on the table; the randomised trial of that decision is on the total elbow card. Everything about this operation is long: a tourniquet that runs past its limit, an exposure that strips the periosteum off both columns, and a joint that will be stiff if it is not moved early.

The radial head is the lateral pillar of the elbow and the secondary stabiliser against valgus. A fall on the outstretched hand drives it into the capitellum and splits it (Mason type II, two pieces, displaced) or shatters it (type III). Two or three large fragments are fixed with headless screws or a small plate through a lateral approach, with the forearm pronated to carry the posterior interosseous nerve away from the field; more than three fragments are replaced rather than fixed, because in the one adequate trial replacement gave a better score (92 versus 72) and fewer adverse events (6 of 36 versus 15 of 31). A radial head fracture with a dislocation and a coronoid fracture is a terrible triad: the same lateral approach then fixes the coronoid, replaces or fixes the head and repairs the lateral collateral ligament, which turns a 60 min case into two hours and adds a ligament under tension.

The pain logic is bone, and the trajectory is the Part B anchor for a 3: a hard peak on day 1 and 2 from fractured and drilled bone, compressed with metal, falling quickly because nothing is loaded through the fixation. Behind it are contributors that scale with the operation: periosteal stripping along two columns and a reflected or osteotomised triceps in the distal humerus, which put that operation at the top of the band with a week-2 movement-evoked component; a handled ulnar nerve with a neuropathic edge; a tourniquet; and a ligament repair in the terrible triad. The olecranon and the isolated radial head are small versions, and in a counselled patient they are day cases.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 Neurology, the fasting state and the block conversation

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon needs a documented hand before the nerve is moved, an elbow fixed within a few days of the injury before it stiffens, and to know whether the hand will be examinable in recovery.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Before any drug, examine and write down ulnar (little finger sensation, first dorsal interosseous), median, radial and posterior interosseous (wrist and finger extension) function; a fracture-dislocation often has a deficit already, and that is the fact that protects everybody later. Then the block conversation, which this card exists for. Olecranon and radial head: the author’s practice is a single-shot infraclavicular or supraclavicular block with intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg, under general anaesthesia, with the surgeon’s agreement that the hand will be examined when the block recedes. Distal humerus: the surgeon decides whether they want the ulnar nerve examined in recovery; if they do, the operation runs under general anaesthesia with infiltration and a block is offered once the hand has been seen; if they do not, the block goes in before induction with the agreement written down. The lower-leg guideline’s principle transfers: dense, long blocks that far outlast the surgery are the ones that delay a diagnosis, neither surgeon nor anaesthetist vetoes the other, and the patient’s consent to the chosen technique is documented. A low-concentration block (ropivacaine 0.2%) without adjunct is the compromise that keeps the analgesia and shortens the blind window. The unfasted emergency patient is on the hand trauma card.

  2. 2 Position: lateral or prone with the arm over a post

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The posterior elbow is reached with the patient lateral or prone and the upper arm supported on a padded post so that the forearm hangs at 90 degrees and the surgeon looks down onto the olecranon; the image intensifier comes in from the opposite side. Supine with the arm across the chest is the alternative for an olecranon and for some surgeons’ distal humerus; the radial head is supine on an arm table.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Lateral and prone mean a tracheal tube, the dependent eye, plexus and peroneal nerve padded, the head neutral in a cradle, and a tube that will not be reached once the drapes and the image intensifier are in place. The post under the humerus is the thing to check: it must sit under the mid-shaft, not in the axilla (plexus) and not at the distal shaft where the radial nerve runs in the spiral groove, because a radial palsy from the post looks exactly like one from the surgery. The high sterile tourniquet goes on before the final positioning. A distal humerus runs long enough that a second check of pressure points at 90 min is worth doing.

  3. 3 Tourniquet, antibiotic and tranexamic acid

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The field is bony and the surgeon wants it dry to see the joint surface; the tourniquet is inflated after exsanguination and will be up for the whole of an olecranon fixation and for as long as the surgeon can manage in a distal humerus.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Cefazolin 2 g IV finished before inflation; tranexamic acid 1 g IV for a distal humerus, on borrowed evidence. The distal humerus is the elbow operation that overruns the tourniquet. Say the time at 90 and 120 min; the surgeon’s choices are a release and re-inflation after 10-15 min of reperfusion, or completion of the second column in a bleeding field. Under general anaesthesia the slow rise in pressure and heart rate from 45 min is tourniquet pain and does not answer opioid.

  4. 4 Olecranon: reduction and tension band or plate

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A posterior incision curved around the point of the elbow, the fracture cleaned of haematoma, the joint surface reduced under direct vision and held with a clamp, then either two wires and a figure-of-eight tension band or a dorsal plate with screws into the shaft and the proximal fragment. The joint is moved under the image intensifier to check that nothing crosses the articular surface.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The quick one, 45-90 min, inside a single tourniquet. The ulnar nerve is a centimetre medial to the plate and is protected rather than mobilised in a simple olecranon fracture. Day case in a fit patient with a working block and an oral regimen started; the wires under thin skin are the complaint at six weeks, not the pain on day 1.

  5. 5 Distal humerus: the ulnar nerve and the approach

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A long posterior incision, the ulnar nerve identified proximally and freed from the arcade of Struthers to the flexor carpi ulnaris, held on a sling for the rest of the case and usually transposed at the end. Then the choice: paratricipital windows either side of the triceps for an extra-articular or simple fracture, a triceps split or reflection, or an olecranon osteotomy for the comminuted articular fracture, which gives the whole joint but adds a fracture that will not unite in about 2-4%.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The nerve work is the first hour and the reason for the pre-operative examination. The osteotomy is the step that changes the pain course: a cut olecranon fixed with a tension band or a plate is a second bone operation inside the first, with its own hardware under thin skin, and ulnar neuropathy after a screw-fixed osteotomy ran to 21% in the pooled series. Ask which approach was used before writing the discharge plan: an osteotomy or a reflected triceps means more movement-evoked pain in weeks 1-2 than a paratricipital window.

  6. 6 Distal humerus: articular reconstruction and two-column plating

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The joint surface is rebuilt first, fragment by fragment, held with wires and then compressed with a screw across the trochlea; the reconstructed spool is then attached to the shaft with a plate on each column, parallel (medial and lateral) or perpendicular (medial and posterolateral), with as many screws into the distal fragments as the bone will take. The periosteum is stripped along both columns to seat the plates. The elbow is then moved through its arc under the image intensifier.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The long middle of the operation, usually 90-150 min on its own. Warm the patient, because a long case in lateral with an open joint loses heat steadily. The periosteal stripping is the mechanism that makes this fixation hurt more and for longer than its bone volume suggests. In an osteoporotic patient this is the step at which the surgeon finds that the screws will not hold and converts to a total elbow: cement, a frail patient, and the total elbow card’s cement step in a patient who has already been under anaesthesia for two hours. If the tourniquet has been released, bleeding from the cancellous surfaces is steady rather than brisk, and the blood loss on this card is mostly accrued now.

  7. 7 Radial head: the lateral approach and the posterior interosseous nerve

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A lateral incision over the radial head through the Kocher interval (anconeus and extensor carpi ulnaris) or a common extensor split, the forearm pronated to swing the posterior interosseous nerve away from the radial neck, the fragments reduced and fixed with headless compression screws placed in the safe zone (the 90 degree arc that does not articulate with the ulna) or a low-profile plate. In a terrible triad the coronoid is reached through the same wound before the head is dealt with, and the lateral collateral ligament is repaired to the epicondyle at the end.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Supine on an arm table, 60-120 min, standard tourniquet. The posterior interosseous nerve is the nerve of this operation; a wrist drop after a radial head fixation is a retractor or a plate that is too distal, and another reason the hand was examined before the block. An isolated radial head fixation is a day case; a terrible triad with a ligament repair stays a night and has a tendon-tension element the isolated fracture does not.

  8. 8 Ulnar nerve transposition, tourniquet release and closure

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    At the end of a distal humerus fixation most surgeons move the ulnar nerve into an anterior subcutaneous pocket so that it does not lie on the medial plate, checking that it is not kinked at the septum or the new entry. The tourniquet comes down, bleeding is dealt with, a drain goes in, and the posterior wound over the olecranon is closed in layers. An olecranon fixation is closed over the wires or plate with no drain. A splint holds the elbow at 90 degrees for comfort.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Tourniquet release after a long inflation brings the reperfusion dip and the washout; after a distal humerus the pressure takes minutes to recover. Give the antiemetic. If a block has been placed, the splint and sling go on before the patient lightens.

  9. 9 Recovery: the hand, the first night and the rescue block

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants a working hand, a dry wound, and movement started within days, because a fixed elbow that is not moved becomes a stiff elbow that needs a release.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The hand is examined at the time that was agreed: in recovery if no block was placed, or when the block recedes at 12-24 h if it was. A new ulnar deficit after a distal humerus is in the expected 25-33% and is usually traction; a dense new palsy that was not there before the block is the surgeon’s to see. If the surgeon wanted an unblocked recovery, this is where the block is offered: a single-shot block in recovery once the hand has been documented, or the next morning, gives the patient the first night. Oral paracetamol and an NSAID start in recovery; an oral opioid is charted for the first three nights. In the 972-patient ambulatory cohort half had rebound pain, with bone surgery (OR 1.82) and no intravenous dexamethasone (OR 1.78) raising the odds; every operation on this card is bone surgery and the dexamethasone was given for it. The olecranon and radial head patient go home the same day or the next morning; the distal humerus stays one to three nights, longer with an osteotomy, an older patient or a conversion.

Pain plan

The dominant mechanism is bone, which is moderate, short and NSAID-responsive, so the analgesic shape is a block for the first night and an oral regimen that carries the next three days, with the catheter kept for the long, stripped, early-moved distal humerus. The complication that argues against the block is nerve injury, and the plan has to answer both. There is no procedure-specific guideline for any elbow fracture and no randomised analgesia trial; the plan is the mechanism, the general ambulatory block data, and the principle borrowed from the lower-leg compartment syndrome guideline that a dense block far outlasting the surgery delays a diagnosis and a low-concentration one with good surveillance does not.

The defensible default for an olecranon or radial head fixation is a single-shot infraclavicular or supraclavicular block with 20-25 mL of ropivacaine 0.5% (or 0.2% when the surgeon wants a shorter blind window), intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg, paracetamol and an NSAID started before the block recedes, and an oral opioid for the first three nights with a written night plan. The nerve examination is before the block and again when it recedes, and the surgeon has agreed to that sequence.

For a distal humerus fixation the default is decided with the surgeon, case by case, and written down. If the surgeon has seen the nerve intact and untethered and runs an early motion programme, a single shot or a continuous infraclavicular catheter is reasonable, and the catheter earns its place for the osteotomy, the reflected triceps, the opioid-tolerant patient and the stiff elbow that will need physiotherapy twice a day; the author’s practice is a single shot in most and a catheter after that conversation. If the surgeon wants the hand examined in recovery, the operation runs under general anaesthesia with infiltration of the wound, and the block is offered as a rescue once the hand is documented. A ropivacaine 0.2% block without adjunct is the middle path: most of the analgesia with a shorter, lighter block that lets a dense motor deficit show through.

Escalation: pain above 7 after the block has gone, with a soft wound, warm fingers and the splint on, is treated with the charted opioid and a check that the regular doses were given. Pain out of proportion in a tense posterior wound after a distal humerus is a haematoma over a transposed nerve and is surgical. A tense forearm with pain on passive finger extension is a compartment syndrome until proven otherwise; it is rare after elbow fixation, but the high-energy fracture-dislocation is the patient it happens to and the reason the lower-leg guideline’s logic was applied. Stable ring and little finger dysaesthesia is traction neuritis and settles over weeks; a deficit that worsens over days is a nerve under pressure and is also surgical.

Pitfalls and variants

  • Tension band versus plate for the olecranon. Same fixation principle, twice the complication rate and twice the removal rate with wires; the anaesthetic is identical.
  • Osteotomy versus paratricipital for the distal humerus. The osteotomy gives the view and adds a fracture; complications in comparative series 46-55% against 27-41%, with the same ulnar neuropathy rate, and more movement-evoked pain in weeks 1-2.
  • Conversion to total elbow. The osteoporotic patient over 65 whose fragments will not hold a screw; five of 21 in the randomised trial. Position and tourniquet stay, cement arrives, and the frailest patient of the day gets the longest case.
  • The ulnar nerve. Mobilised in every distal humerus, transposed by most, injured in a quarter to a third, mostly transiently. Documented before, examined at the agreed time, and the timing is the surgeon’s decision as much as yours.
  • The posterior interosseous nerve. The radial head’s nerve; pronation protects it, a distal retractor or plate injures it, and a wrist drop after a block has gone is surgical.
  • Terrible triad. Radial head, coronoid, lateral collateral ligament, sometimes the medial; two hours, a ligament under tension, a hinged brace and one night.
  • The high-energy elbow. A fracture-dislocation with a swollen forearm is the patient in whom a compartment syndrome is possible and a dense long block is the wrong choice; a low-concentration block without adjunct, hourly observations and a documented decision are the guideline’s answer.
  • The post under the arm. A radial palsy from a post at the spiral groove is indistinguishable from a surgical one; check the post sits under the mid-shaft before draping.
  • Heterotopic ossification. Common after distal humerus fixation, more after a head injury; some surgeons give an NSAID for prophylaxis, which is the NSAID you were charting.
  • The open fracture. Its own antibiotic pathway, its own timing and its own card (open fractures).

Key sources

The surgical evidence is reasonable: a meta-analysis of tension band against plate for the olecranon, a systematic review of 1,700 olecranon osteotomies, a 134-patient cohort comparing osteotomy with the paratricipital approach for ulnar neuropathy, a Cochrane review of radial head fixation against replacement, and the single randomised trial of fixation against arthroplasty for the elderly distal humerus. The anaesthetic evidence is not procedure-specific: the block-versus-nerve-check question is answered by analogy with the Association of Anaesthetists’ lower-leg compartment syndrome guideline and by the general data on nerve injury after blocks and on rebound pain, and the catheter advice is author’s judgement. The pain score is the Part B anchor for elbow fracture fixation.
