Upper limb › Wrist and hand

15 Distal radius ORIF

Volar locking plate through the flexor carpi radialis approach; dorsal plating, fragment-specific fixation, K-wires and external fixation as the variants

2Mild to moderate

Dominant mechanism: Bone. A fractured metaphysis reduced, held with a plate and drilled for locking screws, with periosteum lifted off the volar surface and pronator quadratus divided; the fracture itself is the pre-operative pain generator and fixation removes it. Short, bone-dominant, NSAID-responsive, and the rebound at the end of a dense block is the worst moment of the course

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: high.

Block
Supraclavicular, infraclavicular or axillary brachial plexus block as the sole anaesthetic, with intravenous dexamethasone and light sedation, in the day-case patient; the same block under general anaesthesia where the patient or the surgeon prefers it
Catheter: rarely A single shot with dexamethasone and a written night plan is the defensible default; a continuous infraclavicular catheter did not reduce opioid consumption in the one randomised comparison and is reserved for the bilateral, revision or opioid-tolerant patient, or the one for whom rebound pain on a previous occasion was unmanageable
Alternatives: General anaesthesia with surgeon infiltration and no block, which gives more pain at two hours and less at 12-24 h; Block plus general anaesthesia for the anxious patient or the long fragment-specific fixation; Haematoma block or Bier's block for closed reduction and K-wires, not for plating
Position
Supine with the arm on a radiolucent arm table, forearm supinated for the volar approach, the image intensifier at the end of the table; the shoulder abducted to 90 degrees and no further
Tourniquet
Yes. Routine; 45-90 min on the upper arm. A block that covers the wrist does not cover the tourniquet, so the sedation or the general anaesthetic has to
Cement
No
Blood loss
Under 100 mL
Duration
45-90 min for a volar plate; 90-150 min for fragment-specific, dorsal plus volar or an intra-articular reconstruction; 20-40 min for K-wires
Length of stay
Day case. Day case: yes
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV at induction or before inflation (3 g over 120 kg); a plate is an implant
Tranexamic acid
Not needed
VTE
Mechanical only; negligible baseline risk in upper limb day surgery
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV with the block; ondansetron 4 mg IV if a general anaesthetic is given
Tell the patient
The arm will be numb and useless for most of the day and into the night; when the feeling returns the wrist will hurt, worst on the first night and the first day, and the tablets started before the numbness wears off are what control it; after that it settles quickly.
The trap
The block wears off at 2 am and the patient who was comfortable at discharge is the one who telephones: rebound pain after a bone operation under a dense block is the rule, not the exception, and the oral analgesia has to be started in recovery and timed to the block, not to the first complaint

What the surgeon is doing and why

The distal radius is the commonest fracture an anaesthetist meets, and it comes in two patients: the older woman who falls on an outstretched hand onto osteoporotic metaphyseal bone and gets a dorsally angulated, impacted, extra-articular fracture, and the younger patient with a high-energy injury who gets an intra-articular fracture with a displaced lunate facet and a die-punch fragment. The bone is cancellous, it bleeds, and it crushes rather than snaps; the problem the surgeon is solving is that a radius that heals short and dorsally tilted shifts the load onto the ulna and the dorsal lip, and the wrist is weak and painful for life. The thresholds for operating are arguments about millimetres of shortening and degrees of tilt, and in the older patient the honest evidence is that the function at a year is about the same whether the fracture is plated or pinned (the DRAFFT trial, 461 patients, no difference in the patient-rated wrist score at 12 months, with K-wires cheaper) or, in the over-65s, whether it is operated on at all. Surgeons vary, and the volar locking plate is what most of them do.

The volar locking plate exists because the volar cortex is thick, flat and well covered by muscle, and because a plate with screws that lock into it at a fixed angle acts as a scaffold under the subchondral bone and holds a reduction in osteoporotic bone that a conventional screw would pull out of. The surgeon’s sequence is fixed:

  1. Get to the volar surface through the flexor carpi radialis sheath (the “FCR approach”), retracting the tendon and the radial artery laterally and the median nerve and the flexor tendons medially. The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve runs along the ulnar side of the tendon and is the nerve that gets cut.
  2. Lift pronator quadratus off the radius from its radial edge to expose the fracture. This is the muscle mechanism, small but real, and some surgeons repair it at the end.
  3. Reduce the fracture: traction, volar pressure on the dorsal fragments, and often a lever (a periosteal elevator through the fracture) to tease the impacted dorsal cortex and the articular fragments back out to length. Intra-articular fragments are checked with the image intensifier or, in some hands, an arthroscope.
  4. Apply the plate proximal to the watershed line (the ridge where the volar cortex turns distally towards the joint), fix it to the shaft with a cortical screw, confirm the position on the image intensifier, then place the distal locking screws under the subchondral bone, with care that none of them protrudes through the dorsal cortex into the extensor tendons or into the joint.
  5. Check the screws on a tilted lateral view, close pronator quadratus if the surgeon does, close the skin, and put the wrist in a volar slab or a removable splint. Fingers move from the first day; the wrist moves at two weeks.

The complications that present to you are tendon ones: a plate that sits distal to the watershed, or a long screw through the dorsal cortex, irritates and then ruptures a tendon (flexor pollicis longus on the volar side, extensor pollicis longus dorsally) months later; a median nerve that is swollen in the carpal tunnel from the fracture haematoma presents as numbness the next morning and is the surgeon’s to decompress. Complex regional pain syndrome is the other late complication and the distal radius is its commonest cause.

The variants matter less to you than the volar plate. Dorsal plating is used for dorsal shear fractures and dorsal comminution that the volar plate cannot hold, through an incision between the extensor compartments, with more tendon irritation and a longer case. Fragment-specific fixation uses several small plates and pins for a shattered articular surface and takes twice as long. A dorsal and volar combination is the long, intra-articular reconstruction in a younger patient. K-wires are percutaneous, quick, and cheaper, with a cast afterwards. An external fixator spans the wrist for an open or grossly comminuted fracture and is the bridge to definitive surgery. None of them changes the block; the fragment-specific and combined cases change the tourniquet time and the duration of sedation.

The pain logic is bone, and this is the Part B anchor for a 2: a cancellous metaphysis reduced and drilled, a small muscle lifted and sometimes repaired, periosteum raised over a few centimetres, and nothing under tension afterwards. The fracture was the pre-operative pain generator and fixing it removes it, so by day 3 most patients are more comfortable than they were the day before surgery. The course is short and NSAID-responsive. What makes the card worth writing is the shape of the first 24 h under a block: a patient with a dense brachial plexus block has a pain score of 0 at discharge and the worst pain of the whole course at 2 am, and in the 972-patient ambulatory cohort half of block patients had exactly that pattern (a score of 3 or less rising to 7 or more within 24 h), with bone surgery (OR 1.82), younger age and female sex raising the odds and intravenous dexamethasone lowering them. The one randomised comparison of block against general anaesthesia for this operation showed the same thing from the other direction: the block group had less pain and used less opioid at two hours and went home sooner, the general anaesthesia group had lower pain at 12 and 24 h, and total analgesic use and satisfaction were the same. The block does not reduce the pain of a distal radius fixation; it moves it.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 The patient, the fasting state and the block as the anaesthetic

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Most distal radius fixations are semi-elective trauma on a day-surgery list within a week or two of injury; the surgeon wants a fixed wrist, a moving hand and a patient who goes home the same day.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The block is the anaesthetic. A supraclavicular, infraclavicular or axillary block with 20-30 mL of ropivacaine 0.5% or an equivalent, intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg, light sedation, and no airway is the author’s default for the fasted day-case patient, and the operation is then 45-90 min of an awake patient listening to drilling, which some patients want and some do not. The axillary block needs a separate musculocutaneous injection for the lateral forearm and does not cover the tourniquet; the supraclavicular and infraclavicular blocks cover more of the arm and leave the intercostobrachial area to an intercostobrachial injection or the sedation. For the patient who refuses to be awake, the anxious patient, the fragment-specific case over two hours, or the surgeon who wants a still patient for an arthroscopically assisted reduction, the same block goes under a general anaesthetic with a supraglottic airway. The patient having general anaesthesia alone, with infiltration, will have more pain at two hours and less at 2 am, and that trade is worth explaining. Examine and document median, ulnar and radial function before the block; acute carpal tunnel symptoms from the fracture haematoma are common and the surgeon will want to know they predate the block.

  2. 2 Position, arm table and the image intensifier

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Supine with the arm on a radiolucent table, abducted to 90 degrees and supinated, and the image intensifier either at the end of the table or over the arm; the surgeon sits on the axillary side of the arm and the assistant opposite. The tourniquet goes on the upper arm.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    In an awake patient, the position has to be tolerable for 90 min: the shoulder abducted to 90 and no more, the head on a pillow turned slightly away from the field, the drape held off the face on a screen, and the contralateral arm free for the pulse oximeter and the cannula. The image intensifier swings over the arm repeatedly; a sedated patient who turns towards the noise moves the arm. Lead for the patient’s trunk and for you. An awake patient feels the tourniquet from about 30-45 min as a deep ache that the block does not cover, and that is where the sedation is spent.

  3. 3 Tourniquet, antibiotic and the awake patient's first minutes

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The field is small and the surgeon wants it dry for the reduction and the plate position; the tourniquet is inflated after exsanguination and stays up for the fixation.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Cefazolin 2 g IV before inflation. Test the block before the tourniquet goes up, not after: pinprick over the volar wrist in the median and radial territories, and a check that the patient cannot flex the fingers against resistance. A block that is patchy at this point is supplemented now, with a distal median or radial nerve injection at the elbow or a surgeon’s infiltration, rather than discovered at the skin incision.

  4. 4 The FCR approach and pronator quadratus

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A 6-8 cm incision over flexor carpi radialis, the sheath opened, the tendon retracted radially with the radial artery, the floor of the sheath divided, and pronator quadratus elevated off the radius from its radial border to show the fracture. The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve is on the ulnar side of the tendon and is the nerve that the retractor finds.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The dissection is not stimulating under a working block. In an awake patient the first sensation that breaks through is usually the retractor pulling on the proximal forearm, which is musculocutaneous territory in an axillary block without a supplement, or the tourniquet. The pronator quadratus elevation is the muscle mechanism; small, but it is why the forearm aches for a few days.

  5. 5 Reduction

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Traction, direct pressure, and an elevator through the fracture to lever the dorsal and articular fragments back out to length and tilt, checked on the image intensifier in two planes. An impacted osteoporotic fracture that has been there for two weeks is harder to disimpact and may need the dorsal cortex broken through to get the length back.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Traction on the hand is traction on the shoulder in an awake patient; a sedated patient will tense the arm and the surgeon will say so, and the answer is a little more sedation and a hand on the elbow, not a deeper plane than the airway can tolerate. The reduction is the one moment at which a patchy block declares itself. This is also the step that lengthens the case: a fracture that will not come out to length is the one that becomes a fragment-specific or a combined dorsal-volar fixation.

  6. 6 Plate, shaft screw and the distal locking screws

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The plate is positioned proximal to the watershed line and fixed to the shaft through an oval hole so it can be slid before the first screw is tightened; then the image intensifier confirms the position, and the distal locking screws are placed under the subchondral bone in the row that supports the articular surface. Screw length is measured and checked on a tilted lateral view, because a screw that protrudes dorsally will rupture an extensor tendon in months, and a plate distal to the watershed will rupture flexor pollicis longus.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Drilling through the far cortex and the locking of screws is the bone mechanism of this operation and the reason the rebound odds are those of bone surgery. The awake patient hears and feels the drill as vibration and may find it the hardest part. Nothing to do except keep the arm still and the sedation steady; the image intensifier checks are the pauses.

  7. 7 Tourniquet release, closure and the splint

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Pronator quadratus is repaired over the plate by surgeons who believe it protects the flexor tendons, the tourniquet is released, bleeding points are controlled, the skin is closed and a volar slab or removable splint is applied with the fingers free. Some surgeons infiltrate the wound.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Reperfusion after a 60-90 min tourniquet is unremarkable in a fit patient. Ask the surgeon to infiltrate the wound even under a block, because it will outlast nothing but it costs nothing. The splint goes on before any sedation lightens; a patient with a flail arm will otherwise reach for it with the other hand.

  8. 8 Recovery, the rebound and the night plan

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants the fingers moving from the first hour, the hand elevated, and the patient home with a plan for two weeks until the wrist starts to move.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This step decides the operation. The patient leaves recovery with a dense block and a pain score of 0, and the block recedes 12-24 h later, at night. The first dose of oral paracetamol and an NSAID goes in before discharge, not at the first tingle; the opioid is for the first two nights and is explained as the drug for when the hand comes back to life, with a written plan that says what to take at bedtime, what to take when the fingers tingle, and who to telephone. The one randomised trial that compared a single infraclavicular shot with a continuous infraclavicular catheter and with an opioid PCA found that the catheter cut the pain at 9 and 12 h (median 0 versus 2, and 0.5 versus 3) without reducing total opioid use, and the PCA arm used nine times the opioid; the single shot with a plan is what most units do and the catheter is for the exception. Intravenous dexamethasone lengthens the block and lowers the pain at 4 and 8 h in the randomised comparison, raises the glucose for a day, and its absence carried an OR of 1.78 for rebound pain in the ambulatory cohort; it is given. Discharge is the same day; a patient who had a general anaesthetic alone is the one who needs more opioid in recovery and less at 2 am.

Pain plan

The mechanism is bone, short and NSAID-responsive, with a muscle lifted and nothing under tension; the whole problem is timing. The block is the best anaesthetic for the operation and the worst possible teacher of what the operation feels like, because the patient’s first experience of their wrist is at 2 am with no one to ask. The plan is built around that.

The defensible default is a supraclavicular, infraclavicular or axillary block with 20-30 mL of ropivacaine 0.5% (or an equivalent long-acting agent), intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg, paracetamol and an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor started in recovery and continued for five to seven days, and an oral opioid for the first two nights, with a written night plan. The patient and the carer are told in plain words that the hand will come back to life between bedtime and the early morning, that the pain will rise over an hour or two to the worst of the week, that the tablets taken before bed are what blunt it, and that this is expected and not a complication. Sedation rather than general anaesthesia for the fasted day-case patient is the author’s practice; a general anaesthetic with the block for the patient who wants it or the long case.

The catheter question has a randomised answer for this operation, and it is nuanced: a continuous infraclavicular block abolished the rebound window at 9 and 12 h without reducing opioid consumption at all, and the single-shot group’s total opioid was modest (a median of 37.5 opioid-equivalent units against 30 with the catheter, not different). That is a catheter that does one thing well and nothing else, and for a day case it brings a flail arm for two days and a pump to manage at home. The author’s practice is a single shot for nearly all, and a catheter for the bilateral fracture, the revision or malunion osteotomy, the opioid-tolerant patient, and the one who has had an unmanageable rebound night before. The alternative that answers the same problem differently is general anaesthesia with infiltration and no block, which the randomised comparison found gave more pain at two hours and less at 12 and 24 h with the same satisfaction; for a patient who lives alone and will have no one to help at 2 am, that is a defensible choice and not a failure of regional anaesthesia.

Score calibration: this is a 2, the Part B anchor for distal radius ORIF, and the trajectory on the card (1 on the evening under the block, 4 on day 1 when it has gone, then 3, 2, 1) is the shape of a short bone operation with a dense block in front of it. The first-day figure is honest about the rebound; in a patient who had a general anaesthetic alone the evening figure is higher and the day 1 figure a little lower, and the curve meets by day 2. Escalation: pain above 7 after the block has gone with warm, moving fingers and a splint that is not tight is treated with the charted opioid and a check that the paracetamol and NSAID were actually taken; pain with numb fingers in the median distribution that was not there before the block is an acute carpal tunnel syndrome and is surgical; pain out of proportion at a week, with a swollen shiny hand and allodynia, is the start of complex regional pain syndrome and is referred, not reassured.

Pitfalls and variants

  • Volar plate versus K-wires versus nothing. The function at a year is similar for a dorsally displaced fracture in the DRAFFT trial; the K-wire patient has no incision, a cast, and the same block question; the older patient managed in plaster is not on your list.
  • Fragment-specific and combined dorsal-volar fixation. The intra-articular fracture in a younger patient; two hours, a tourniquet that may need a break, and a block under general anaesthesia rather than sedation.
  • Dorsal plating. A longer case through the extensor compartments, more tendon irritation, more swelling; the same block.
  • The axillary block’s gaps. The musculocutaneous nerve (lateral forearm, where the retractor sits) and the intercostobrachial territory under the tourniquet; both are supplemented or the patient is sedated through them.
  • Block for the awake patient. The patient who hears the drill; a headset, a screen and a steady level of sedation are the tools, and a patchy block is converted to a general anaesthetic before the incision, not after.
  • Acute carpal tunnel syndrome. Median numbness from the fracture haematoma, present before surgery in some and appearing the next morning in others; documented before the block, and decompressed by the surgeon if it is progressive.
  • Tendon rupture. Flexor pollicis longus months later from a plate distal to the watershed, extensor pollicis longus from a long dorsal screw; late, surgical, not yours.
  • Complex regional pain syndrome. The distal radius is its commonest precipitant; a swollen, shiny, allodynic hand at one to three weeks is referred early.
  • The older patient on anticoagulants. The commonest patient on the list; the block is a superficial one with a compressible site, and the usual rules apply.
  • The patient who lives alone. The rebound night is the argument for a general anaesthetic with infiltration, or for an overnight stay, not for a weaker block.
  • The unfasted patient on the trauma list. An isolated distal radius fracture in an unfasted patient can wait for fasting or have the block as the sole anaesthetic with no sedation; the urgent unfasted hand is on the hand trauma card.

Key sources

This is the best-evidenced operation in the wrist and hand section for the anaesthetic question, and the evidence is specific: a randomised comparison of brachial plexus block against general anaesthesia for distal radius fixation showing the block moves the pain from two hours to 12-24 h without changing total analgesic use or satisfaction; a three-arm randomised trial showing a continuous infraclavicular catheter removes the rebound window at 9-12 h without reducing opioid consumption; a randomised trial of dexamethasone with the block showing a longer block and lower early pain; and the 972-patient ambulatory cohort that defines rebound pain and its risk factors, of which this operation has most. The surgical evidence (DRAFFT, the complication review) is cited for the variants and the complications, not for pain. There is no PROSPECT guideline for distal radius fracture, and the day-case advice and the catheter exceptions are author’s judgement.

  1. Galos DK, Taormina DP, Crespo A, et al. Does brachial plexus blockade result in improved pain scores after distal radius fracture fixation? A randomized trial. Clin Orthop Relat Res 2016;474:1247-1254
    36 patients randomised to general anaesthesia or brachial plexus block for distal radius fixation: block gave less pain and less opioid at two hours and a shorter recovery stay; general anaesthesia gave lower pain at 12 and 24 h; total analgesic use, satisfaction and function at six and 12 weeks the same
  2. Lee JH, Kim HJ, Kim JK, Cheon S, Shin YH. Does intravenous patient-controlled analgesia or continuous block prevent rebound pain following infraclavicular brachial plexus block after distal radius fracture fixation? A prospective randomized controlled trial. Korean J Anesthesiol 2023;76:559-566
    66 volar plate patients in three arms of 22: single infraclavicular block, block plus opioid PCA, or continuous infraclavicular block; median pain at 9 h 2 with the single shot versus 0 with the catheter, at 12 h 3 versus 0.5; total opioid equivalents 37.5 single shot versus 30 catheter, not different; the catheter controlled the rebound window without reducing opioid use
  3. Kim MK, Park YH, Lee JS, Jung HS. Addition of dexamethasone to brachial plexus block after distal radius fracture surgery. Clin Orthop Relat Res 2023;481:1966-1974
    69 unstable distal radius fractures randomised to block with or without dexamethasone: longer block and lower pain at 4 and 8 h with dexamethasone, higher post-operative glucose, and no difference the authors judged clinically important thereafter
  4. Efficacy of direct versus peripheral adjuvant dexamethasone on duration and rebound pain in regional anesthesia for outpatient distal radius fracture fixation: a prospective randomized controlled blinded study. Hand (N Y) 2024
    50 volar plate patients with supraclavicular ropivacaine blocks, dexamethasone 4 mg perineural (27) or intravenous (23): the perineural route gave a shorter block in this trial, with no demonstrated difference in pain scores or opioid consumption at 24 h
  5. Barry GS, Bailey JG, Sardinha J, Brousseau P, Uppal V. Factors associated with rebound pain after peripheral nerve block for ambulatory surgery. Br J Anaesth 2021;126:862-871
    972 ambulatory block patients, rebound pain (NRS 3 or less rising to 7 or more within 24 h) in 49.6%; bone surgery OR 1.82, female OR 1.52, younger age; absence of intravenous dexamethasone OR 1.78
  6. Costa ML, Achten J, Plant C, et al. UK DRAFFT: a randomised controlled trial of percutaneous fixation with Kirschner wires versus volar locking-plate fixation in the treatment of adult patients with a dorsally displaced fracture of the distal radius. Health Technol Assess 2015;19(17):1-124
    461 adults with dorsally displaced fractures: no clinical difference in the patient-rated wrist evaluation at 12 months between K-wires and a volar plate; K-wires cheaper
  7. Seigerman D, Lutsky K, Fletcher D, et al. Complications in the management of distal radius fractures: how do we avoid them? Curr Rev Musculoskelet Med 2019;12:204-212
    Review of flexor and extensor tendon irritation and rupture with volar plates placed distal to the watershed line, carpal tunnel syndrome and complex regional pain syndrome after distal radius fixation, with the plate position and screw length as the modifiable causes
  8. Gerbershagen HJ, Aduckathil S, van Wijck AJM, Peelen LM, Kalkman CJ, Meissner W. Pain intensity on the first day after surgery: a prospective cohort study comparing 179 surgical procedures. Anesthesiology 2013;118:934-944
    50,523 patients: small hand and foot operations rank among the most painful on day 1, with arthrodesis of the metacarpophalangeal joints at rank 8 and hand resection arthroplasty at rank 11, and patients after minor surgery received little opioid and reported high scores

Upper limb › Wrist and hand

16 Carpal tunnel, trigger finger, de Quervain's and ganglion

Open and endoscopic carpal tunnel release, A1 pulley release, first extensor compartment release and dorsal or volar wrist ganglion excision: the minor hand list, under WALANT by default

1Minimal

Dominant mechanism: Arthroscopic surface. A small incision, a ligament or pulley divided, nothing repaired and nothing under tension; the pre-operative pain generator (a compressed nerve or a catching tendon) is removed. Surface and a little periosteum at a ganglion stalk; the worst day is day 1 and simple analgesia covers it

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: low.

Block
WALANT: lidocaine 1% with adrenaline 1:100,000, buffered, infiltrated by the surgeon with no tourniquet, no sedation and no anaesthetist in most units; where an anaesthetist is involved, the same infiltration with minimal sedation, or a distal nerve block at the wrist or forearm
Catheter: no Never; the block, where one is used, is for the anaesthetic and not for the pain
Alternatives: Intravenous regional anaesthesia (Bier's block) where a tourniquet is wanted and the surgeon does not use adrenaline; Axillary or supraclavicular brachial plexus block for the patient who cannot tolerate an awake procedure or for a bilateral or combined list; General anaesthesia with a supraglottic airway for the child, the patient who cannot lie still, or the patient who refuses to be awake
Position
Supine with the arm on a hand table, palm up for carpal tunnel and trigger finger, thumb up for de Quervain's, palm down for a dorsal ganglion; the patient awake and talking
Tourniquet
No. None under WALANT, which is the point: adrenaline gives the surgeon a dry field and the patient is spared the one part of a short hand operation that hurts. A forearm or upper arm tourniquet for 10-20 min is used by surgeons who prefer it, and it is tolerable awake for that long
Cement
No
Blood loss
Negligible
Duration
10-20 min for carpal tunnel and trigger finger; 15-30 min for de Quervain's; 20-45 min for a ganglion, longer for a volar ganglion wrapped around the radial artery
Length of stay
Day case; office or procedure room in many units. Day case: yes
Antibiotic
None for a clean elective hand procedure without an implant; some surgeons give cefazolin 2 g IV for a ganglion with a joint opened, and this is their preference rather than evidence
Tranexamic acid
Not needed
VTE
None
Antiemetic
None under WALANT; ondansetron 4 mg IV if a general anaesthetic is given
Tell the patient
You will feel pushing but no pain, the hand will be numb for a few hours, and it will be sore for a day or two; paracetamol and an anti-inflammatory are enough for nearly everyone, and the numbness or the catching that brought you in is usually better straight away.
The trap
The adrenaline in the finger is not the hazard; the patient who is told this is nothing and then sent home with no analgesia is, because minor hand operations rank high on the first-day pain scale when nothing is prescribed, and the few who need an opioid are the ones nobody planned for

What the surgeon is doing and why

These are the operations that fill a hand list and that, in most of the world, now happen without an anaesthetist in the room. They are grouped here because they share a mechanism (a structure divided or excised, nothing repaired), a pain score (the Part B anchor for a 1 is carpal tunnel release), and an anaesthetic default that has changed in the last fifteen years. The card exists so that the anaesthetist who is asked to be involved knows what the surgeon is doing with the adrenaline, when the WALANT default breaks, and why the one thing that goes wrong is the discharge analgesia.

Carpal tunnel syndrome is the median nerve compressed under the transverse carpal ligament, a thick band between the hook of the hamate and the pisiform on one side and the scaphoid tubercle and trapezium on the other. The surgeon divides the ligament along its ulnar side (to stay away from the recurrent motor branch, which usually comes off the radial side of the nerve), either through a 2-3 cm palmar incision or endoscopically through a portal at the wrist crease, and that is the operation; the nerve is not touched, the tunnel springs open, and the numbness of a recently compressed nerve often improves overnight. A nerve that has been compressed for years with thenar wasting does not recover its muscle and may keep its numbness, and the patient needs to know that beforehand. The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve and the superficial palmar arch are the structures the surgeon avoids; pillar pain (an ache at the heel of the hand on either side of the incision, from the divided ligament and the shifted carpal arch) is what the patient complains of at six weeks and is the only pain that outlasts the first days.

Trigger finger is a flexor tendon with a nodule that catches on the A1 pulley at the base of the finger. The surgeon makes a 1 cm incision over the pulley, divides it longitudinally, and asks the patient to flex and extend the finger to confirm it no longer catches, which is the reason the patient is awake: the test is the operation’s end point. The digital nerves run either side of the pulley and are a few millimetres from the blade; the radial digital nerve of the thumb crosses the pulley and is the one that gets cut.

De Quervain’s is the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis tendons inflamed in the first dorsal compartment at the radial styloid. The surgeon opens the compartment’s roof and, because the extensor pollicis brevis often lies in its own sub-compartment, looks for and opens that too, with the superficial radial nerve branches lying directly in the subcutaneous fat over the incision and giving the painful neuroma if cut.

A ganglion is a mucin-filled cyst arising from a joint capsule or tendon sheath, most often the dorsal scapholunate ligament of the wrist. Excision is the only one of these operations with a dissection: the cyst is traced to its stalk and the stalk excised with a cuff of capsule, which means the wrist joint is opened and a little periosteum disturbed; a volar wrist ganglion sits against the radial artery and takes longer. Recurrence is common and aspiration is a reasonable first treatment; surgeons vary on both.

WALANT (wide awake local anaesthesia, no tourniquet) is the surgeon’s infiltration of lidocaine with adrenaline, buffered with bicarbonate so it does not sting, in volumes of 20 mL for a carpal tunnel release and 4 mL for a trigger finger, injected at least 25-30 min before the incision so that the adrenaline has produced a dry field. The adrenaline is what removes the tourniquet, and the tourniquet is the only part of a 15 min hand operation that an awake patient cannot tolerate. The old prohibition on adrenaline in the fingers came from early procaine and cocaine preparations; the modern data are a prospective project of 3,110 consecutive cases of adrenaline in the fingers and hand with no digital infarction, and the reported rare ischaemic events involve either a patient with an undiagnosed vasospastic or occlusive disease (one in about 5,000 in a single surgeon’s series, in a patient with severe Raynaud’s and occluded ulnar arteries who also had a digital tourniquet) or an accidental high-dose injection, and phentolamine infiltration reverses the vasoconstriction. The surgeon’s screening question is whether the patient gets cold, pale fingertips; if yes, plain local anaesthetic is used. The technique needs no fasting, no sedation, no cannula, no anaesthetist and no recovery bay, doubles throughput at a quarter of the cost, and lets the surgeon test a tendon or a trigger with the patient’s own muscles. It is the default for every operation on this card.

The pain logic is surface: a short incision, a ligament or pulley divided, no bone except the stalk of a ganglion, nothing tensioned, and a pre-operative pain generator removed. The score is a 1 and the trajectory peaks at a 3 on day 1 with simple analgesia. The only reason to write a pain plan at all is the finding in the 179-procedure cohort that patients after minor operations typically received little or no opioid yet reported high pain scores on day 1, with small hand and foot operations ranking among the most painful of all, and the plan on this card is what prevents that: a non-opioid regimen started before the local anaesthetic wears off, and a small opioid supply for the few.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 Where this happens and who is in the room

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    WALANT hand surgery is done in a procedure room or an office, with the patient walking in and out, in most units; the main theatre and an anaesthetist are kept for the patient who needs a block, sedation or a general anaesthetic.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    If you are involved, the question is why. The reasons are an anxious patient who wants sedation, a patient who cannot lie still or communicate (dementia, a tremor, a child), a surgeon who uses a tourniquet and wants a block or a Bier’s block for it, a combined or bilateral list, or a list in a hospital whose rules put an anaesthetist in every theatre. For the sedated patient the aim is a patient who is calm and can still move the finger on request for the trigger finger test; for the patient who needs a general anaesthetic a supraglottic airway with spontaneous breathing is the whole plan. No fasting is needed for WALANT alone; sedation brings the fasting rules back.

  2. 2 Surgeon infiltration and the 25-30 min wait

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Lidocaine 1% with adrenaline 1:100,000, buffered 10:1 with 8.4% bicarbonate and warmed, is injected slowly through a fine needle, proximal to distal, 20 mL for a carpal tunnel release (10 mL between the median and ulnar nerves and 10 mL under the incision line), 4 mL for a trigger finger, 2 mL for a digital block; then the surgeon waits for the field to blanch, which takes 25-30 min, and the next patient is injected in the meantime.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The dose is well within the 7 mg/kg that the technique’s authors stay under, and for a trigger finger it is trivial. The wait is the step that gets skipped in a hurry, and a field that is injected and cut at 10 min bleeds. The first-dose paracetamol and NSAID can go in during this wait, which is the simplest way to make the discharge analgesia start on time.

  3. 3 The carpal tunnel: open or endoscopic

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Open: a 2-3 cm incision in line with the ring finger, through the palmar fascia, the transverse carpal ligament divided under direct vision along its ulnar border from distal to proximal, with care at the superficial palmar arch distally and the nerve’s recurrent motor branch radially. Endoscopic: a 1 cm portal at the wrist crease, a cannula passed under the ligament, and the ligament cut from beneath with a blade on the endoscope, which spares the palmar skin and gives a quicker return to work at the cost of a blind cut.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The patient feels pushing in the palm and nothing else if the infiltration was adequate; a patient who flinches when the ligament is divided had too little volume in the tunnel, and the surgeon tops it up through the wound. Endoscopic release in an awake patient is tolerable and common. There is no tourniquet pain, no sedation and no airway, and the operation is 10-15 min.

  4. 4 The trigger finger and the awake test

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A 1 cm incision over the metacarpal head, the A1 pulley exposed between the neurovascular bundles and divided along its length, and then the patient is asked to make a fist and open the hand while the surgeon watches the tendon glide. If it still catches, a little more pulley is divided; if the patient cannot flex, the surgeon looks for a reason.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The test is why this is done awake and why a brachial plexus block or a general anaesthetic is the wrong default: a paralysed hand cannot show the surgeon that the trigger is gone. The digital nerve is millimetres from the blade and a numb fingertip the next day is a cut nerve, not a residual local anaesthetic; the volume used is too small to last.

  5. 5 De Quervain's and the superficial radial nerve

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A short transverse or longitudinal incision over the radial styloid, the superficial radial nerve branches found in the fat and held aside, the roof of the first dorsal compartment opened along its dorsal edge (to leave a volar lip that stops the tendons subluxing), and the sub-compartment for extensor pollicis brevis sought and opened. The patient is asked to extend and abduct the thumb to confirm both tendons glide.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Nothing to do; the same awake test as the trigger finger. The painful neuroma of a cut superficial radial nerve branch is the one complication, and it is the surgeon’s.

  6. 6 The ganglion and the opened joint

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A dorsal ganglion is traced between the extensor tendons to its stalk on the scapholunate ligament and excised with a cuff of capsule, which opens the wrist joint; a volar ganglion is dissected off the radial artery, which lies against it and is sometimes damaged. The capsule is left open or loosely closed and the wrist splinted for a few days by surgeons who think it reduces recurrence.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The one operation on the card with a real dissection and a joint opened, so the infiltration volume is larger (20-30 mL in the dorsal wrist) and the case runs 20-45 min; a volar ganglion in a patient with a thin radial artery is the one where the surgeon may ask for a tourniquet and a block. The opened capsule and the disturbed periosteum give this the sorest day 1 of the four operations, which is still a 3 on simple analgesia.

  7. 7 Dressing, hand elevation and the walk out

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A bulky dressing, the fingers free to move, the hand elevated for two days, and no splint for a carpal tunnel or trigger finger. The patient walks out.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Under WALANT there is no recovery stay and no discharge criteria beyond a dressing that is not tight and a patient who has eaten. A sedated patient needs the usual escort. The adrenaline field stays pale for an hour or two and the fingers are checked to be pink before the patient leaves; a finger that is white and cold at the end of the case is infiltrated with phentolamine and watched, and this is rare enough that most hand surgeons have never done it.

  8. 8 The discharge analgesia that is the whole plan

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon’s interest after a minor hand operation is in the hand moving, the dressing staying dry and the patient not telephoning.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The local anaesthetic lasts two to four hours, and the patient who was told this was nothing goes home with no plan and finds the hand hurts at 9 pm. Paracetamol and an NSAID, started before the local wears off and continued for two or three days, is the regimen, and the randomised trial after carpal tunnel release found that ten tablets of paracetamol or ibuprofen gave the same or lower pain scores than ten tablets of oxycodone (mean worst daily pain 2.3-2.8 against 2.8-3.4), with patients using three to five tablets in total over five days and most of the adverse events in the oxycodone group. The authors’ advice is no more than five to ten tablets of anything. A small supply of an oral opioid for the ganglion patient or the patient who has had a hard time before is the author’s practice; a routine opioid prescription for a carpal tunnel or trigger finger release is not.

Pain plan

The mechanism is surface, the score is a 1, and the honest statement is that the anaesthetic is chosen for the surgeon’s needs and the patient’s tolerance, not for the pain. WALANT is the default because it removes the tourniquet, the sedation, the fasting, the cannula and the anaesthetist, and because the awake test is part of the operation for a trigger finger and a de Quervain’s. There is no PROSPECT guideline for any of these operations and there does not need to be; the randomised evidence after carpal tunnel release says non-opioids are as good as oxycodone and the authors of the trial ask for no more than five to ten tablets of whatever is prescribed.

The defensible default is surgeon infiltration with buffered lidocaine and adrenaline, no sedation, no tourniquet, paracetamol and an NSAID started in the waiting room or during the vasoconstriction wait and continued for two to three days, and a written line telling the patient that the hand will hurt when the numbness goes and that the tablets are for that. For the patient who cannot be awake, a general anaesthetic with a supraglottic airway and the same infiltration; for the surgeon who wants a tourniquet, a Bier’s block or a distal nerve block at the forearm, or an axillary block for a bilateral list. A brachial plexus block is never for the pain on this card and should not be sold as such; it is for the anaesthetic, and it costs the patient a numb arm for twelve hours after a 15 min operation.

Rebound pain is not the problem it is after a bone operation under a dense plexus block, because the local anaesthetic wears off in the afternoon with the patient awake and the regimen already started. The escalation triggers are the ones that are not pain: a white, cold finger at the end of a trigger finger release is the adrenaline and is treated with phentolamine; numbness in the distribution of a digital nerve or the palmar cutaneous branch that persists past the local anaesthetic is a cut nerve; pain and swelling out of proportion at a week in a carpal tunnel patient is the start of complex regional pain syndrome, which this group of operations does produce occasionally; and pillar pain at the heel of the hand at six weeks is expected and treated with time.

Pitfalls and variants

  • The patient who gets cold, pale fingers. Raynaud’s, scleroderma, Buerger’s, a previous digital replant or a known occluded ulnar artery: the surgeon uses plain lidocaine and a tourniquet, and this is the one group in whom the adrenaline prohibition still stands.
  • The patient on beta-blockers or with ischaemic heart disease. The adrenaline dose in 20 mL of 1:100,000 is 0.2 mg, infiltrated slowly; a brief tachycardia is common and clinically trivial, and the author’s judgement is that it changes nothing.
  • The anxious patient. Sedation brings fasting, a cannula, an escort and a recovery stay; a conversation and a screen often do the same job. Where sedation is used, keep it light enough for the awake test.
  • The bilateral or combined list. Two carpal tunnels under WALANT are two injections and no extra time; a carpal tunnel with a trapeziectomy is the trapeziectomy’s anaesthetic.
  • Endoscopic release. Same anaesthetic, a blind cut, and an incomplete release or a cut arch that the surgeon converts to open.
  • The tourniquet habit. A surgeon who uses a forearm tourniquet for 10-15 min can still do the operation awake; one who wants it for 30 min needs a Bier’s block or a sedated patient.
  • Steroid injection before surgery. Many patients have had one or more; it does not change the anaesthetic, and it raises the infection risk a little for a trigger finger release in the weeks afterwards.
  • Dementia, tremor and the patient who cannot lie still. The general anaesthetic group, with a supraglottic airway and the same infiltration; the trigger finger test is lost and the surgeon accepts that.
  • The diabetic trigger finger. Commoner, more often multiple, and more likely to recur; the anaesthetic is the same and the NSAID question is renal.
  • Complex regional pain syndrome. Rare, more after a carpal tunnel release than after the others, and referred early rather than reassured.

Key sources

The anaesthetic default on this card rests on the WALANT literature, which is large, consistent and mostly descriptive: the instructional lecture that sets out the recipe, volumes and dose ceiling, and the 3,110-case prospective project it cites for the safety of adrenaline in the fingers, against which stands a single surgeon’s report of one ischaemic digit in about 5,000 blocks in a patient with undiagnosed vascular disease and a digital tourniquet. The analgesia evidence is a randomised trial after carpal tunnel release showing non-opioids match oxycodone, and the 179-procedure cohort’s finding that minor surgery is undertreated. The pain score is the Part B anchor; nothing on the card is sourced beyond that except the numbers quoted, and the sedation, general anaesthetic and tourniquet alternatives are author’s judgement.

  1. Lalonde D, Eaton C, Amadio PC, Jupiter JB. Wide-awake hand and wrist surgery: a new horizon in outpatient surgery. Instr Course Lect 2015;64:249-259
    Lidocaine 1% with adrenaline 1:100,000 buffered 10:1 with 8.4% bicarbonate; 20 mL for carpal tunnel release, 4 mL for trigger finger, 40 mL for a trapeziectomy or Dupuytren's; the authors stay within 7 mg/kg; the Dalhousie project of 3,110 consecutive cases of adrenaline in the fingers and hand without digital infarction; phentolamine reverses adrenaline vasoconstriction in the finger but is seldom needed; twice the carpal tunnel throughput at a quarter of the cost
  2. Sylaidis P. Digital ischaemia after adrenaline-based digital nerve block: update since 1998 publication. Australas J Plast Surg 2023;6(2):1-2
    One digital necrosis in about 5,000 personal adrenaline digital blocks (lidocaine 2% with adrenaline 1:80,000), in a patient with undiagnosed severe Raynaud's and occluded ulnar arteries who also had a finger tourniquet; recommends asking about cold, pale fingertips before injecting and early phentolamine rescue
  3. Ilyas AM, Miller AJ, Matzon JL, Graham JG. A prospective, randomized, double-blinded trial comparing acetaminophen, ibuprofen, and oxycodone after carpal tunnel release. J Hand Surg Am 2018;43:913-919
    105 patients completing the trial after carpal tunnel release under local anaesthesia alone, ten capsules of paracetamol 500 mg, ibuprofen 600 mg or oxycodone 5 mg: mean worst daily pain 2.3-2.8 for the non-opioids and 2.8-3.4 for oxycodone; mean pills consumed 2.7-5.1 over five days; four of five adverse events in the oxycodone group; the authors recommend non-opioids and no more than five to ten tablets
  4. OrthoEvidence ACE report. No significant difference in efficacy between non-opioids and opioids after hand surgery. AAOS 2018
    Interim report of the same randomised trial in carpal tunnel and trigger finger release: no difference in pain, pills consumed or requests for more analgesia over five days
  5. Gerbershagen HJ, Aduckathil S, van Wijck AJM, Peelen LM, Kalkman CJ, Meissner W. Pain intensity on the first day after surgery: a prospective cohort study comparing 179 surgical procedures. Anesthesiology 2013;118:934-944
    50,523 patients: patients undergoing minor surgery typically received no or low doses of opioid yet many reported high scores; small hand and foot operations ranked among the most painful on day 1, and the authors conclude that minor surgery patients should be monitored more closely

Upper limb › Wrist and hand

17 Dupuytren's fasciectomy

Limited (selective) fasciectomy, dermofasciectomy with full-thickness skin graft, and the needle fasciotomy and collagenase alternatives

2Mild to moderate

Dominant mechanism: Arthroscopic surface. A long zigzag palmar and digital incision with wide skin flaps raised off diseased fascia, the cord excised from around the neurovascular bundles, and a finger that has been bent for years straightened and then held straight; a wound-healing and stiffness problem more than a nociceptive one, with a capsular release at the PIP joint and a skin graft donor site in the bigger operations

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: moderate.

Block
Surgeon infiltration under WALANT for a single-ray limited fasciectomy, or an axillary, supraclavicular or infraclavicular brachial plexus block as the sole anaesthetic for multi-ray, revision and dermofasciectomy cases; general anaesthesia only where the patient or the length of the case demands it
Catheter: rarely Not for a primary single- or two-ray fasciectomy; a catheter is author's judgement for the revision multi-ray dermofasciectomy with a PIP release in a patient with previous complex regional pain syndrome, where a sympathetic block over several days is the aim
Alternatives: WALANT with buffered lidocaine and adrenaline, 40 mL per ray, no tourniquet, for the single-ray case in a surgeon who uses it; Bier's block for a short fasciotomy or single-ray release; General anaesthesia with a supraglottic airway plus a block for the two-hour multi-ray case or the patient who will not be awake
Position
Supine with the arm on a hand table, palm up, the hand held flat by a lead hand or an assistant, the surgeon under loupes; the finger will be straightened against resistance during the case
Tourniquet
Yes. Upper arm tourniquet for most surgeons, 60-120 min for a single ray and routinely approaching the limit for multiple rays or a dermofasciectomy; released before closure to find the bleeding points in a palm that cannot tolerate a haematoma. None under WALANT
Cement
No
Blood loss
Negligible under tourniquet; the haematoma after release is the complication, not the loss
Duration
45-90 min for a single-ray limited fasciectomy; 90-180 min for multiple rays, a PIP joint release or a dermofasciectomy with graft; 15-30 min for a needle fasciotomy
Length of stay
Day case; a multi-ray dermofasciectomy may stay one night for elevation and the graft. Day case: yes
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV at induction (3 g over 120 kg) is many surgeons' practice for a fasciectomy with flaps and grafts; omitted by others for a clean single-ray release, and the evidence does not decide it
Tranexamic acid
Not needed
VTE
None
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 4-8 mg IV and ondansetron 4 mg IV if a general anaesthetic is given; nothing under block alone
Tell the patient
The hand will be numb for most of the day and the palm will be sore and tight for about a week; the fingers will feel stiff and the straightening will be held by a splint at night for months, and the hand therapy is what decides the result, not the operation.
The trap
The long tourniquet in an awake patient and the haematoma in the palm: a multi-ray fasciectomy runs the tourniquet to its limit, the block has to cover it or the sedation has to, and the surgeon who closes without releasing the cuff gets a palmar haematoma under a flap that lifts the skin off and starts the stiffness that this operation exists to prevent

What the surgeon is doing and why

Dupuytren’s disease is a fibromatosis of the palmar fascia. Myofibroblasts in the normal longitudinal bands of the palmar aponeurosis lay down collagen, the bands thicken into nodules and then into cords, and the cords shorten over years and pull the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints into flexion. The ring and little fingers go first. The disease is painless, which is the first thing to understand about the pain plan: the patient comes to surgery with a bent finger and no pain, and everything they feel afterwards is the operation. The second thing is that the cord is not a separate structure that can be lifted out: it is the patient’s own fascia, wrapped around the digital nerves and arteries, which it has displaced and spiralled around so that the bundle may lie on top of the cord in the finger where the surgeon expects it to be underneath. The operation is a dissection of two nerves and two arteries out of diseased tissue under magnification, with a knife, in a hand that will scar everything it can.

The surgeon’s choices, in rising order of what they do to the hand:

  1. Needle fasciotomy: a hypodermic needle passed through the skin to divide the cord at several levels, under local anaesthetic, in a clinic room. Quick, cheap, and the contracture recurs earliest, with the highest recurrence of the three in prospective data over three to four years.
  2. Collagenase injection into the cord, with the finger manipulated straight a day or more later. The DISC trial of 672 patients found it did not meet non-inferiority against limited fasciectomy at one year, with more minor complications (skin tears, haematoma, oedema) but fewer moderate or severe ones (2% against 5%), and weak evidence of more recurrence; in the pooled randomised trials recurrence was about equal to needle fasciotomy and well above fasciectomy.
  3. Limited (selective) fasciectomy, the standard operation: a zigzag Bruner incision along the palm and into the finger, skin flaps raised off the cord, the diseased fascia excised from its proximal end to the finger with the neurovascular bundles identified and followed throughout, and the finger straightened. The joints are then assessed: a metacarpophalangeal joint straightens once the cord is gone, a proximal interphalangeal joint that has been flexed for years has a contracted volar plate and collateral ligaments and may need a capsular release, which the surgeon does cautiously because it adds swelling and stiffness. The skin, which has shortened with the cord, is closed with Z-plasties or left open in part (the McCash open palm) to heal by secondary intention. Recurrence is lowest with fasciectomy (about 16% in prospective series with long follow-up) and the hand therapy and night splinting afterwards are what hold the correction.
  4. Dermofasciectomy: the diseased skin is excised with the fascia and replaced with a full-thickness skin graft from the forearm or groin, for recurrent disease or aggressive diathesis, on the principle that the disease does not recur under a graft. A longer case, a donor site, a graft that must be immobilised, and the top of this card’s range.

The complications that reach you are in the 20-year literature review: overall surgical complication rates of 3.6-39.1%, major complications in 15.7%, with digital nerve injury in 3.4%, digital artery injury in 2%, infection in 2.4%, haematoma in 2.1%, and complex regional pain syndrome in 5.5%; wound healing problems in 22.9% and a “flare reaction” (a swollen, red, stiff, painful hand at two to four weeks) in 9.9%. In recurrent disease the nerve and artery injury rate is about ten times higher (20% against 2%), because the bundle is in scar and cannot be found by its usual landmarks.

The pain logic is surface and skin rather than bone or tendon: a long incision with raised flaps, a dissection that touches the nerves along their length, a joint pushed straight that does not want to be, and a palm that swells. The day 1 pain is a 4 and it is the swelling and the tension on the flaps; the pain after that is stiffness pain, worst in the mornings and with therapy, and the operation’s enemy is not nociception but the fibrosis, oedema and flare that make a stiff finger. The two things that matter for a 2-scoring operation are therefore the tourniquet, which hurts an awake patient at the top of a two-hour case, and the hand therapy, which needs a patient who can move the fingers from day 1 and is not frightened of them. Complex regional pain syndrome at 5.5% is the complication the anaesthetic plan can try to influence, and the Dutch guideline’s secondary prevention advice (adequate peri-operative analgesia, shorter operating time, limited tourniquet, regional anaesthesia) is what underlies the choice of a block for the bigger cases.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 The extent of the operation decides the anaesthetic

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A single-ray limited fasciectomy is 45-90 min; a three-ray fasciectomy with a PIP release, or a dermofasciectomy with a graft, is two to three hours with a tourniquet that will reach its limit. The surgeon knows which from the examination and the plan.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    For a single ray in a surgeon who uses WALANT, surgeon infiltration of 40 mL of buffered lidocaine with adrenaline per ray with no tourniquet is the established approach: in the 148-finger series complication rates were the same as under general anaesthesia with a tourniquet, and the range of motion was similar finger by finger. For more than one ray, a revision, a PIP release or a dermofasciectomy, the author’s practice is an axillary, supraclavicular or infraclavicular block as the sole anaesthetic with light sedation and intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg, because the block covers a tourniquet that WALANT cannot replace at those volumes, gives a sympathetic block that may matter for the complex regional pain syndrome risk, and lets the patient go home the same day. A general anaesthetic with a supraglottic airway on top of the block is for the patient who will not be awake for two hours, or where the surgeon wants an immobile hand for the graft. Document the digital nerves before the block: a numb fingertip the next day is one of the 3.4%, and in recurrent disease one of the 20%.

  2. 2 Position, lead hand, loupes and the tourniquet

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Supine with the arm on a hand table and the hand held flat and open on a lead hand or by an assistant; the surgeon works under loupes and needs the fingers held straight against the cord’s pull and then straighter as the cord is released. The upper arm tourniquet is inflated after exsanguination and is the surgeon’s view of the neurovascular bundles.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    An awake patient under a block can lie for 90 min without much complaint and for 150 min with more; the shoulder at 90 degrees, the head turned away, a screen, and the sedation reserved for the second hour. The tourniquet is the limit on the awake technique: the block covers the arm below it, the intercostobrachial injection or the sedation covers the cuff for the first 45-60 min, and after that an awake patient on a long case is uncomfortable whatever is done. Say the time at 60 and 90 min, because a multi-ray fasciectomy in a scarred hand is the operation that drifts past 120 min while the surgeon is still finding a nerve.

  3. 3 Antibiotic and the first incision

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A Bruner zigzag incision in the palm and along the finger, designed so that the flaps can be closed as Z-plasties to lengthen the skin; or a longitudinal incision converted to Z-plasties at the end. The flaps are raised off the cord with the skin thin and adherent over nodules, which is where the skin tears and the buttonholes happen.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Cefazolin 2 g IV before the tourniquet is many surgeons’ practice for an operation with flaps and sometimes a graft, and it is reasonable without being evidence-based. Nothing else to do for the first 20 min of flap raising.

  4. 4 Finding the neurovascular bundles

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon identifies the digital nerves and arteries in the palm, proximal to the disease, where they are in their normal position, and then follows them distally into the cord, releasing the fascia from around them. The spiral cord of the finger wraps the bundle and brings it to the midline and superficial, so the surgeon dissects from known to unknown and never cuts what has not been seen.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is the slow middle of the operation and the step that sets its length; in a revision the bundle is in scar and the dissection can double the time. In an awake patient the surgeon’s silence here is concentration. Movement of the hand is the hazard: a lightly sedated patient who jerks when the tourniquet aches is a cut nerve, so the second hour’s sedation is spent keeping the hand still, and a patient who cannot keep still is converted to a general anaesthetic before this step, not during it.

  5. 5 Fasciectomy and the joint release

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    With the bundles safe, the cord is excised from the palm to its insertion on the flexor sheath, the middle phalanx or the lateral digital sheet; the finger is then straightened. If the PIP joint will not extend, the surgeon decides whether to release the check-rein ligaments and the volar plate, accepting that a released joint swells and stiffens and may lose flexion for extension. Some surgeons accept 30 degrees of residual PIP contracture rather than release.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The joint release is a capsular step that raises the pain and stiffness of the first week and is the reason the card’s day 2 and 3 figures are not lower. The finger straightened for the first time in years is a stretch on a nerve and an artery that have been short for as long; a finger that goes white when straightened has an artery in spasm or a shortened artery, and the surgeon will flex it back, warm it and wait, which is time on the tourniquet.

  6. 6 Dermofasciectomy and the graft

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    In recurrent or aggressive disease the skin is excised with the fascia and a full-thickness graft from the medial forearm, the antecubital fossa or the groin is sewn in, quilted and dressed with a tie-over bolster. The graft needs an immobile bed for a week, so the finger is splinted and the therapy starts later.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A second wound, which may be outside the block (the groin, or the forearm above an axillary block’s reliable territory), and a longer case; the donor site is often the sorest part of the week. For a groin donor site under a brachial plexus block, the surgeon infiltrates the donor site, or the case is done under general anaesthesia. This is the operation at the top of the card’s range and the one for which an overnight stay for elevation is reasonable.

  7. 7 Tourniquet release, haemostasis and closure

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The tourniquet is released before closure and every bleeding point in the palm is found, because a haematoma under a palmar flap lifts the skin off its bed, kills the flap edge and starts the fibrosis; the open palm technique leaves a transverse wound in the palm unclosed to let blood drain and the skin to lengthen. Z-plasties are closed, the finger dressed in a bulky dressing with the fingers extended, and the hand elevated.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Reperfusion after a 90-120 min tourniquet is noticeable but benign in a fit patient; under a block alone the patient feels the warmth and a deep ache in the arm for a few minutes. The dressing goes on before any sedation lightens.

  8. 8 Recovery, day 1 and the therapy that is the operation

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants the hand elevated, the fingers moving within the dressing from day 1, a check of the wound and graft at a week, and night extension splinting under a hand therapist for three to six months; the therapy decides the result.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The block recedes at 12-24 h and the palm is tight and sore when it does, with the rebound pattern that half of ambulatory block patients describe; paracetamol and an NSAID start in recovery and an oral opioid is charted for the first two or three nights. The WALANT patient has no rebound to speak of, because the local wears off in the afternoon with the patient awake. Nearly every patient goes home the same day; the dermofasciectomy patient may stay a night for elevation. Numbness in a fingertip that persists past the block is a nerve injury and the surgeon is told; a cold white finger at any point is an artery and is urgent.

Pain plan

The mechanism is surface and skin with a joint release in some, and the score is a 2: the pain is real for a week, it is swelling and tension rather than bone, and it responds to elevation, movement and simple analgesia. The anaesthetic is chosen for the surgeon’s needs (a dry field, a still hand, a tourniquet or no tourniquet) and for the two things the plan can influence, a comfortable patient who will do the therapy, and a lower risk of complex regional pain syndrome. There is no PROSPECT guideline and no randomised analgesia trial for fasciectomy; the plan is the mechanism and author’s judgement, with the Dutch complex regional pain syndrome guideline as the only external anchor.

The defensible default for a single ray is surgeon infiltration under WALANT where the surgeon practises it, with paracetamol and an NSAID started before the local wears off and continued for a week, and a small supply of oral opioid for the first two nights. For a multi-ray fasciectomy, a revision, a PIP release or a dermofasciectomy, the default is a brachial plexus block as the sole anaesthetic (axillary with a musculocutaneous and intercostobrachial supplement, or supraclavicular or infraclavicular) with 20-30 mL of ropivacaine 0.5%, intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg, light sedation, and the same oral regimen with a written night plan for the rebound. The Dutch guideline’s secondary prevention list for complex regional pain syndrome (adequate peri-operative analgesia, a short operating time, a limited tourniquet, regional anaesthesia) is a reason to choose the block over a general anaesthetic alone for the big cases, and the author treats it as a reason rather than as proof.

A catheter is rarely warranted. The author’s judgement is that it earns its place only for the revision multi-ray dermofasciectomy in a patient who has had complex regional pain syndrome before, where a sympathetic block for several days is the aim, and for that patient a conversation with the pain service before the operation is more useful than a catheter decided on the day. Rebound pain at 2 am after a block is expected and is a tight, throbbing palm; the oral regimen started in recovery is the treatment. Escalation: a tense, bulging dressing with pain out of proportion in the first hours is a haematoma under the flap and is surgical; a finger that is white or blue is an artery; a hand that at two to four weeks is swollen, red, shiny, stiff and painful beyond what the wound explains is either a flare reaction or the start of complex regional pain syndrome, and both are referred to the hand therapist and the surgeon early rather than reassured, with vitamin C, early movement and a short course of a neuropathic agent being author’s judgement rather than evidence.

Pitfalls and variants

  • Needle fasciotomy and collagenase. Clinic-room procedures under local infiltration, no anaesthetist; higher and earlier recurrence, fewer severe complications; the patient who has had collagenase and comes to fasciectomy later has a scarred cord and a harder dissection.
  • Single ray versus multiple rays. The single ray is a WALANT or Bier’s block case; three rays with a PIP release is a two-hour block case with a tourniquet at its limit.
  • Revision surgery. Nerve and artery injury about ten times commoner (20% against 2%); a longer case, a dermofasciectomy more often, and the surgeon’s quietest hour.
  • The PIP joint release. Adds swelling, stiffness and a day of pain; some surgeons do not do it, accepting residual contracture.
  • The open palm. A transverse palmar wound left to heal by secondary intention; it looks alarming on the ward and drains for two weeks, and it is deliberate.
  • Dermofasciectomy. A graft, a donor site outside the block in some cases, a splint for a week, a possible overnight stay.
  • The tourniquet in an awake patient. Tolerable for 45-60 min on sedation alone, and the second hour is where the awake technique fails; the time is said aloud, and a surgeon who wants more than 120 min on a block-alone patient needs to know before the start.
  • Haematoma. The complication the surgeon is most afraid of; the tourniquet comes down before closure, and a bulging dressing in recovery is surgical.
  • Complex regional pain syndrome. 5.5% in the literature review, the highest of any operation in this section, and more after a long tourniquet and a big dissection; the block, the short operation and the early therapy are the modifiable parts.
  • Diabetes, epilepsy, alcohol and the diathesis. Dupuytren’s patients are often older men with these; the NSAID and the sedation are planned around them, and the aggressive diathesis (young, bilateral, ectopic disease) is the one that gets a dermofasciectomy.
  • Anticoagulation. A superficial block at a compressible site is reasonable; the surgeon’s haemostasis is the issue, not the block.

Key sources

The surgical evidence is good: a 20-year review of fasciectomy complications, the 672-patient DISC trial of collagenase against limited fasciectomy, two systematic reviews of randomised trials across the three treatments, and a prospective-data review of recurrence with long follow-up, which together say that fasciectomy corrects most, recurs least and has the most serious complications. The anaesthetic evidence is one retrospective series showing fasciectomy under local anaesthetic with adrenaline matches general anaesthesia with a tourniquet, and the WALANT lecture that gives the volumes. The link between regional anaesthesia, tourniquet time and complex regional pain syndrome rests on a multidisciplinary guideline’s secondary prevention statement, not on a trial in Dupuytren’s patients, and the block, catheter and sedation advice is author’s judgement. The score is calibrated between the carpal tunnel and distal radius anchors.

  1. Denkler K. Surgical complications associated with fasciectomy for Dupuytren's disease: a 20-year review of the English literature. Eplasty 2010;10:e15
    41 studies, 1988-2008: overall surgical complication rates 3.6-39.1%; major complications 15.7%, including digital nerve injury 3.4%, digital artery injury 2%, infection 2.4%, haematoma 2.1% and complex regional pain syndrome 5.5%; flare reaction 9.9%, wound healing complications 22.9%; nerve and artery injury about ten times commoner in recurrent disease (20%) than primary (about 2%)
  2. Dias J, Tharmanathan P, Arundel C, et al. Collagenase injection versus limited fasciectomy surgery to treat Dupuytren's contracture in adult patients in the UK: DISC, a non-inferiority RCT and economic evaluation. Health Technol Assess 2024;28(78):1-262
    672 patients in 31 hospitals randomised to collagenase or limited fasciectomy: collagenase did not meet non-inferiority at one year (Patient Evaluation Measure difference 5.95, widening to 7.18 at two years); collagenase had more complications per participant (0.82 versus 0.60) but fasciectomy had more moderate or severe ones (5% versus 2%); recurrence at least 15.7%, with weak evidence of more after collagenase (OR 1.39); collagenase cheaper by about 1,100 pounds
  3. Cevik J, Rajaram R, Pollock M, Seth I, Rozen WM. Collagenase clostridium histolyticum for Dupuytren's disease: a comprehensive systematic review and comparative analysis against percutaneous needle aponeurotomy and limited fasciectomy. J Plast Surg Hand Surg 2025;60:27-34
    11 randomised trials, 969 patients: collagenase and needle aponeurotomy equivalent for correction (RR 1.01) and recurrence (RR 1.18); recurrence higher with collagenase than limited fasciectomy (RR 6.84, 95% CI 1.59-29.48); more haematoma, local pain and oedema with collagenase
  4. van den Berge BA, Habibi H, Dijkstra PU, et al. Outcomes of limited fasciectomy, needle fasciotomy and collagenase injection for Dupuytren's disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis of individual patient data. J Hand Surg Eur 2025;50:878-890
    15 studies, individual patient data: extension deficit smaller after fasciectomy but not clinically relevant; minor complications commoner after collagenase; major complications no different; recurrence earlier after needle fasciotomy and collagenase than after fasciectomy over 36 months
