Upper limb › Wrist and hand

18 Wrist arthroscopy, TFCC and scaphoid surgery

Diagnostic and therapeutic wrist arthroscopy, TFCC debridement and repair, percutaneous scaphoid screw fixation, and scaphoid non-union grafting from the distal radius, the iliac crest or a vascularised pedicle, including the free medial femoral condyle graft

2Mild to moderate

Dominant mechanism: Bone. A drilled scaphoid with a compression screw across a fracture, or a non-union curetted to bleeding bone and packed with graft; the fracture or non-union was the pre-operative pain generator and fixation removes most of it. Arthroscopy and TFCC repair are surface and a small ligament reattachment at low tension. The iliac crest donor site, when used, is a separate periosteal wound that hurts more than the wrist for three days and is the reason the grafted version behaves like a 3

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: high.

Block
Supraclavicular, infraclavicular or axillary brachial plexus block, single shot, with intravenous dexamethasone, as the anaesthetic with sedation for arthroscopy, TFCC repair and a percutaneous screw; the same block under general anaesthesia for an open graft, and for a free medial femoral condyle graft the block is for the arm while the general anaesthetic covers the knee and the hours
Catheter: rarely A single shot with dexamethasone and a written night plan is the defensible default for everything short of a free vascularised graft, where an infraclavicular or axillary catheter earns its place for the sympathectomy across the anastomosis as much as for the pain; otherwise reserved for the opioid-tolerant or the patient with a previous unmanageable rebound night
Alternatives: General anaesthesia with a supraglottic airway and surgeon infiltration, no block, for the short arthroscopy where a numb arm until 2 am is a cost rather than a benefit; Intravenous regional anaesthesia (Bier's block) for arthroscopy or a percutaneous screw under 45 min in a surgeon's hands who accepts the exsanguinated field; WALANT for percutaneous screw fixation in units that practise it; not for grafting
Position
Supine with the arm on a radiolucent hand table; for arthroscopy the elbow is flexed to 90 degrees in a traction tower with 3-5 kg through finger traps; the image intensifier comes in from the end of the table for every scaphoid case; for a free medial femoral condyle graft the ipsilateral or contralateral knee is prepared and draped at the same time
Tourniquet
Yes. Upper arm, 30-90 min for arthroscopy and screw fixation, up to 120 min for an open graft, with a second thigh tourniquet for a medial femoral condyle harvest. A block that numbs the wrist does not necessarily cover the cuff; a supraclavicular or infraclavicular block does, an axillary block needs the intercostobrachial supplement, and after 60 min sedation has to carry what the block does not. The arm cuff is released before closure of a vascularised graft so the pedicle can be seen to bleed
Cement
No
Blood loss
Under 100 mL at the wrist; an iliac crest harvest is the only part of the list that bleeds, and it bleeds after the wound is closed
Duration
30-60 min for arthroscopy or a percutaneous screw; 60-90 min for a TFCC repair; 90-150 min for an open non-union graft with iliac crest harvest; 120-180 min for a pedicled vascularised graft; 4-6 h for a free medial femoral condyle graft
Length of stay
Day case for arthroscopy, TFCC repair, percutaneous screw and a distal radius graft; one night after an iliac crest harvest; one to three nights after a free medial femoral condyle graft. Day case: selected
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV before inflation (3 g over 120 kg) whenever a screw, an anchor or a graft goes in; many surgeons omit it for a diagnostic arthroscopy and that is defensible
Tranexamic acid
Not needed
VTE
Mechanical only for the day cases; after a free vascularised graft the unit's microsurgical protocol (aspirin or low-dose heparin for the anastomosis) doubles as prophylaxis, and the patient is otherwise mobile
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV with the block; ondansetron 4 mg IV before emergence when a general anaesthetic is given
Tell the patient
The arm will be numb and useless until late tonight, and when the feeling returns the wrist will hurt, worst on the first night and the first day; the tablets started before the numbness wears off are what control it. If bone was taken from your hip, that is the part that will hurt most for a few days and it is sore to walk on.
The trap
The block that makes the wrist numb does not necessarily cover the upper arm tourniquet, and the one that does leaves a young patient with a dead arm until 2 am after a 40 min screw: rebound pain after bone surgery under a dense block is the predictable event, so the analgesia is started in recovery and timed to the block, and after an iliac crest harvest it is the hip, not the wrist, that needs the plan

What the surgeon is doing and why

The wrist on this card is a young one. Scaphoid fractures and TFCC tears belong to men in their twenties and thirties who fell on an outstretched hand, and the anaesthetic problem is not comorbidity but the mismatch between a short operation and a long block in a patient who expects neither to hurt. The surgical logic differs for each of the three things grouped here, and the pain follows the logic.

Wrist arthroscopy is a 2.7 mm scope through dorsal portals named for the extensor compartments they pass between, with the hand hung in finger traps under 3-5 kg of traction to open joint spaces a few millimetres wide. Surgeons vary between wet arthroscopy with a pump and dry arthroscopy, which avoids fluid in the forearm. The scope stages ligament injuries, debrides a central TFCC tear or a synovitis, excises a ganglion from inside, and increasingly assists scaphoid fixation and grafting. Nothing done through the scope alone is under tension afterwards.

The triangular fibrocartilage complex is the load-bearing disc and ligament hammock between the ulnar head and the carpus, and the radioulnar ligaments that run through it into the fovea of the ulna are what hold the distal radioulnar joint together. A central disc tear is avascular and is debrided. A peripheral tear at the ulnar side (Palmer 1B) is vascular and is repaired: outside-in sutures through the capsule, and for a foveal avulsion an anchor or transosseous sutures into the ulna, so that the ligaments that stabilise the DRUJ are back on bone. The pooled series report residual pain around 2 out of 10 at follow-up, complications that are mostly self-limiting, and paraesthesia of the dorsal sensory branch of the ulnar nerve as the characteristic one. The repair is protected by an above-elbow splint that stops forearm rotation for four to six weeks, a bigger imposition than the operation. The tension on the repaired tissue is low.

The scaphoid has a retrograde blood supply entering at its distal end, so a waist or proximal pole fracture cuts the proximal fragment off from its vessels; that is why it fails to unite and why the proximal pole dies. Most undisplaced waist fractures are now cast rather than fixed: in the 439-patient SWIFFT trial, early screw fixation gave no better wrist score at a year than a cast with fixation of the few that failed to unite, and 14% of the surgery group had a potentially serious surgical complication against 1%. Fixation is for the displaced fracture, the proximal pole, the patient who cannot be in a cast, and the non-union. A percutaneous screw is a headless compression screw passed along the central axis of the bone over a guidewire, volar for waist fractures and dorsal for proximal pole fractures, under the image intensifier through a stab incision. The screw compresses the fracture; the pain afterwards is the drilling of a small bone and the fracture itself, which was already hurting.

Non-union is a different operation because the problem is now biological. The surgeon opens the wrist, excises the fibrous non-union and sclerotic bone back to bleeding cancellous bone, corrects the humpback collapse by opening the volar gap, and fills it with graft before fixing it. The graft is the variable that matters to you. Local distal radius bone comes through the same incision. Iliac crest gives a larger, stronger corticocancellous wedge at the price of a second wound that hurts more than the wrist. A pedicled vascularised graft (the 1,2 intercompartmental supraretinacular artery graft from the dorsal distal radius is the common one) brings its own blood supply for an avascular proximal pole and lengthens the case. The free medial femoral condyle graft is a microsurgical operation for the failed, avascular, collapsed non-union: a corticoperiosteal block from the knee on the descending genicular vessels, anastomosed to the radial artery at the wrist; in the series of 49 failed previous repairs with proximal pole necrosis it united 84% at a mean of 16 weeks. The pooled data say the graft source does not change the union rate (88.7% non-vascularised versus 87.5% vascularised across 7,671 patients, distal radius and iliac crest equal), while the comparative studies of pedicled grafts show a small advantage in union and a week or two in time to union with no functional gain. Surgeons choose by the state of the proximal pole and by habit.

The pain logic: the dominant mechanism is bone, because the scaphoid work sets the upper end of the card and it is a drilled bone with a compression screw across a fracture that was already the pain generator. Fixation removes most of the pre-operative pain, so the curve is the distal radius curve: little while the block works, a sharp rise when it recedes on the first night, and a quick fall over three days because nothing is loaded through a screw in a cast. Arthroscopy and TFCC repair sit below that. The iliac crest donor site is the exception that changes the score in practice: periosteum stripped from a muscle-bearing crest that hurts to walk on, with first-day pain averaging 6.3 out of 10 in the pooled craniofacial series and chronic donor-site pain reported anywhere from 3% to 14% depending on the series. A grafted non-union with crest harvest behaves like a 3, and the plan says so.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 Choose the anaesthetic for the operation booked, and for its tourniquet

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon needs a still arm, a bloodless field under a cuff, and an image intensifier for anything scaphoid; the patient needs an anaesthetic that matches 40 minutes of surgery rather than 14 hours of numb arm.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A supraclavicular or infraclavicular block covers the hand, the wrist and the upper arm cuff and is the single technique that does everything; an axillary block covers the wrist well and the cuff poorly unless the intercostobrachial nerve is added, and after 60 min the sedation is carrying the tourniquet whatever block was used. Intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg goes with the block, for duration and for the rebound odds. The honest alternative for a short arthroscopy or percutaneous screw is a general anaesthetic with a supraglottic airway and surgeon infiltration, which trades a worse first evening for an arm that works by dinner; a Bier’s block suits a surgeon who accepts an exsanguinated field for under 45 min. For a free medial femoral condyle graft the decision is different: a tracheal tube for a 4-6 h case with two operative sites, plus a plexus block or catheter for the arm, because the block’s sympathectomy dilates the recipient vessels in the hours after the anastomosis.

  2. 2 Position, traction tower and the image intensifier

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Supine with the arm on a radiolucent hand table; for arthroscopy the elbow is flexed in a traction tower and the fingers hung in traps so that the joint spaces open; for scaphoid work the image intensifier sits at the end of the table and the surgeon turns the wrist through the views that show the screw in all planes.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The shoulder goes to 90 degrees of abduction and no further, the ulnar nerve at the elbow is padded where the tower rests, and the traction (3-5 kg through finger traps for 30-60 min) is tolerated under a block but is a steady pull a sedated patient will fidget against if the block is marginal. Lead for everyone and a patient whose other arm and eyes are out of the beam. The cuff and the cannula go on the non-operative side.

  3. 3 Portals, traction and the dry or wet joint

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The dorsal portals pass between extensor tendons and within millimetres of the dorsal sensory branch of the ulnar nerve at 6R and the superficial radial nerve at 1-2; the surgeon marks the compartments and dissects bluntly to the capsule. Wet arthroscopy distends the joint and clears the view; dry arthroscopy avoids fluid in the forearm and is preferred by many for bone work.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Nothing physiological. A wet case extravasates saline into the forearm over time; a tight forearm at the end of a long wet arthroscopy is fluid, not a compartment syndrome, and it settles, but the distinction depends on a patient who can be examined, which a dense block prevents until morning. Note the traction time.

  4. 4 TFCC: debride the centre, repair the edge

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A central tear is avascular and is shaved to a stable rim; a peripheral tear is repaired with outside-in sutures through the capsule, and a foveal avulsion with an anchor or transosseous sutures into the ulna so that the radioulnar ligaments are back on bone and the DRUJ is stable. The surgeon tests DRUJ stability with the forearm in each rotation before and after, and the repair goes into an above-elbow splint that stops rotation.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The repair is small and at low tension; the sutures go through skin on the ulnar side of the wrist, where the dorsal sensory branch of the ulnar nerve is caught and where the patient will report numbness afterwards that is not your block. If a diagnostic arthroscopy has turned into a repair, the discharge changes from a bandage to a splint above the elbow and the patient needs to hear that before the block wears off.

  5. 5 Percutaneous scaphoid screw

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A guidewire is passed along the central axis of the scaphoid under the image intensifier (volar through a stab incision at the tubercle for a waist fracture, dorsal through the proximal pole for a proximal fracture with the wrist flexed), the length is measured, the track is drilled, and a headless compression screw is advanced until it compresses the fracture and sits below the cartilage at both ends. Arthroscopy is sometimes added to check the reduction and the screw position.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A 30-45 min case under a cuff, with the wrist flexed hard over a bolster for the dorsal approach, the position that stretches the median nerve at the carpal tunnel and the one a blocked patient will not report. The drilling is the only bone work and the only pain. The fracture that needed fixing was already hurting, and the day-1 pain after a screw is no worse than the pre-operative pain in a cast; the rebound is the issue, not the intensity.

  6. 6 Non-union: open, excise, correct and graft

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Through a volar approach the surgeon exposes the non-union, removes the fibrous tissue and sclerotic bone with a burr and curette until both fragments bleed, opens the volar gap to correct the humpback collapse, and packs or wedges graft into the defect before passing a screw; a dorsal approach is used for proximal pole non-unions and for the pedicled 1,2 ICSRA graft, whose vessel runs along the dorsal distal radius under the extensor retinaculum.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is the version with real bone work: a curetted cavity in a small bone and a wedge of graft under compression. Tourniquet time runs to 90-120 min and the cuff is now the dominant discomfort for a sedated patient, so a general anaesthetic on top of the block is the usual pairing. For a pedicled graft the surgeon will ask for the cuff down before closure to confirm the pedicle bleeds, and will want the pressure normal and the patient warm for that check.

  7. 7 The iliac crest harvest

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A corticocancellous wedge from the anterior crest gives the strongest structural graft for a collapsed non-union; the surgeon strips periosteum and muscle origin off the crest, cuts a block with an osteotome or saw, and curettes cancellous bone from between the tables. Bone wax, gelatin sponge and a layered closure follow, and some surgeons leave a drain.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is a second operation in its own right and the one the patient will complain about. Periosteum is stripped off a bone that bears the abdominal wall and the hip abductors, so every step and every cough loads it; the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve runs close to the anterior superior iliac spine and is the neuropraxia that follows; and the cancellous bed bleeds after closure, so the haematoma that tracks down the thigh is the common complication, more so on the anterior crest in the pooled data. First-day pain is above 6 out of 10 and chronic pain at the site is reported in 3-14% of patients. The plan that works is surgeon infiltration of the wound and periosteum with ropivacaine before closure, regular NSAID, and an opioid for three days charted for the hip rather than for the wrist. A transfusion is not expected.

  8. 8 The free medial femoral condyle graft

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    For the failed or avascular non-union with collapse, a block of cortex and periosteum is raised from the medial femoral condyle on the descending genicular vessels through a medial thigh incision under a thigh tourniquet, shaped to fill the scaphoid defect and inset; the pedicle is anastomosed end-to-side to the radial artery and a vein in the anatomical snuffbox, and the graft is fixed with a screw or wires.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Treat it as a free flap, because it is one: a tracheal tube and a 4-6 h case, two tourniquets whose times are tracked separately, active warming from before the first incision with a core temperature above 36.5 degrees because the anastomosis is to a small artery that spasms when cold, euvolaemia, and no vasoconstrictor infusion while the anastomosis is being done or in the hour after it, which is where a plexus block earns its place by dilating the forearm arterial tree without drugs. The surgeon releases the arm cuff before the anastomosis and will not want it re-inflated. A catheter is the author’s preference here: the sympathectomy lasts as long as the infusion runs, the knee is covered by infiltration and the oral regimen, and the patient stays a night or two anyway. The knee donor site is a periosteal wound over a weight-bearing condyle; it hurts to walk on for a few days.

  9. 9 Tourniquet release, immobilisation and emergence

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The cuff comes down before or after closure according to the surgeon’s habit, the wrist goes into a plaster or a thermoplastic splint (a scaphoid cast including the thumb for a screw in poor bone, a sugar-tong splint above the elbow for a TFCC repair, a volar slab for a graft), and a sling for comfort.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Reperfusion after 90-120 min of ischaemia is a transient fall in pressure and a rise in end-tidal carbon dioxide that passes in minutes. The splint goes on while the arm is still blocked, with the fingers free and visible: the patient and the ward are told to watch for a tight cast as the swelling rises overnight, because the block hides the pain that would otherwise warn them. After a graft the patient wakes with a numb arm and a sore hip, which is confusing unless it has been explained.

  10. 10 Recovery, discharge and the night the block ends

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants the cast intact, the fingers moving, the arm elevated, and the patient back in two weeks for a wound check and in six for a radiograph or CT; union is the outcome and smoking is the modifiable enemy of it.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The first paracetamol and NSAID go in before discharge and are timed to the block, not to the first complaint; the block lasts 12-24 h with dexamethasone and the pain rises over an hour or two when it recedes, usually in the small hours. In the ambulatory cohort half of all block patients met the definition of rebound pain, and bone surgery (OR 1.82), younger age and the absence of intravenous dexamethasone raised the odds; nearly everyone on this card is young and has had bone drilled. A written night plan with a short opioid supply is the intervention, and the “minor” label is the trap: in the 179-procedure cohort small extremity operations were among the most painful on day 1 because so little was prescribed for them. The iliac crest patient stays a night and walks with a stick for a few days.

Pain plan

The mechanism is bone for the scaphoid and surface for the rest, so the plan is a single-shot block chosen for the operation and the cuff, intravenous dexamethasone, and an oral regimen started before the block recedes. The defensible default for arthroscopy, TFCC repair and a percutaneous screw is a supraclavicular or infraclavicular block with 20-25 mL of ropivacaine 0.5% (an axillary block with an intercostobrachial supplement is equivalent for a cuff time under an hour), dexamethasone 8 mg IV, sedation rather than a general anaesthetic, regular paracetamol and an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor for three to five days, and an oral opioid for the first two nights. There is no PROSPECT guideline for any operation on this card; the shape is borrowed from the distal radius evidence and the ambulatory rebound cohort. For a short arthroscopy, a general anaesthetic with infiltration and no block is a reasonable choice that moves the worst pain from 2 am to the recovery room and gives the patient a working arm by the evening; say which trade the patient is making.

The catheter question has one clear answer and one judgement. The clear answer is the free medial femoral condyle graft, where an infraclavicular or axillary catheter run for 48-72 h gives a sympathectomy across the anastomosis and covers a long case and a hospital stay; that is the author’s practice, not trial evidence. The judgement is everything else: an open graft with an iliac crest harvest has its pain at the hip, which an arm catheter does not reach, and a percutaneous screw or a TFCC repair does not need three days of ropivacaine for a night of rebound. A continuous block is reserved for the opioid-tolerant patient and the one who has had a catastrophic rebound night before.

The iliac crest needs its own plan on the chart: surgeon infiltration of the periosteum and wound before closure, regular NSAID unless the surgeon objects on union grounds (the evidence that a short course impairs scaphoid union is weak and most hand surgeons accept it), an opioid for three days, and early mobilisation with a stick. Escalation triggers: pain above 7 after the block has gone with warm, moving fingers and a cast that is not tight is treated with the charted opioid and a check that the regular doses were given; pain with tight, pale or tingling fingers is the cast and is split, not medicated; a tense, expanding thigh or flank after a crest harvest is a haematoma and needs the surgeon; and numbness over the lateral thigh after a harvest is the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve and is explained, not investigated.

Pitfalls and variants

  • The booking that grows. A diagnostic arthroscopy for ulnar-sided pain becomes a foveal repair with an above-elbow splint; a percutaneous screw becomes an open graft when the fracture will not reduce closed. The block already placed is right for all of them; the discharge plan and the splint are not.
  • Tourniquet coverage. The axillary block that numbs the wrist perfectly leaves the upper arm cuff to the sedation after about an hour; an infraclavicular or supraclavicular block covers it. Match the block to the cuff time the surgeon states, then add 30 minutes.
  • The dead-arm discharge. A patient with a dense plexus block goes home with a sling, written instructions, someone at home, oral analgesia already started and a telephone number. A dense block is a reason to counsel, not to delay discharge.
  • The dorsal approach and the flexed wrist. A proximal pole screw needs the wrist held in full flexion for the guidewire; the median nerve is stretched at the carpal tunnel and the blocked patient cannot tell you.
  • Ulnar shortening osteotomy. Some surgeons shorten the ulna rather than repair the TFCC for impaction: a plated osteotomy with a different pain profile (periosteum and bone, a 3 for a week), the same block, and a longer tourniquet.
  • Bilateral or re-do scaphoid surgery. Longer, scarred, more graft, and the patient who has been through the rebound night before; the catheter conversation starts here.
  • Children and adolescents. TFCC repair and scaphoid fixation in a 15-year-old are usually done under general anaesthesia with a block placed asleep; the rebound counselling goes to the parent.
  • The free medial femoral condyle graft in a patient who cannot lie flat for six hours, who smokes, or who has peripheral vascular disease. All three are the surgeon’s problems before they are yours, and all three are reasons the operation is uncommon.

Key sources

The scaphoid evidence is strong for whether to operate (SWIFFT) and moderate for how to graft (the 7,671-patient meta-analysis and the smaller pooled comparisons of vascularised grafts), and silent on analgesia; the pain plan is borrowed from the distal radius trials and the ambulatory rebound cohort. The iliac crest figures come from systematic reviews across orthopaedic and craniofacial surgery, with the wide range for chronic pain reflecting how the question was asked. The TFCC evidence is level IV series pooled in systematic reviews, cited for the shape of recovery, not for anaesthetic technique. The catheter advice for the free medial femoral condyle graft and the NSAID position are the author’s judgement.

  1. Dias JJ, Brealey SD, Fairhurst C, et al. Surgery versus cast immobilisation for adults with a bicortical fracture of the scaphoid waist (SWIFFT): a pragmatic, multicentre, open-label, randomised superiority trial. Lancet 2020;396:390-401
    439 adults with waist fractures displaced 2 mm or less: no difference in patient-rated wrist evaluation at 52 weeks between early fixation and cast with fixation of confirmed non-unions; potentially serious surgical complications in 14% of the surgery group versus 1%, cast complications in 18% of the cast group; the trial behind the current preference for casting undisplaced waist fractures
  2. Duncumb JW, Robinson PG, Williamson TR, et al. Bone grafting for scaphoid nonunion surgery: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Bone Joint J 2022;104-B:549-558
    78 studies, 7,671 patients, mean age 28, 88% male: union 88.7% with non-vascularised and 87.5% with vascularised grafts, no difference; distal radius and iliac crest graft sources united equally (86.9% versus 87.6%); studies excluding proximal pole fractures and avascular necrosis reported 96.5% union against 86.8% in the rest
  3. Zhang H, Gu J, Liu H, Yuan C. Pedicled vascularized versus non-vascularized bone grafts in the treatment of scaphoid non-union: a meta-analysis of comparative studies. ANZ J Surg 2021;91:E682-E689
    Seven comparative studies, 413 patients: pedicled vascularised grafts united 1.13 times as often and 1.7 weeks earlier, with no difference in range of motion, grip, Mayo wrist score or re-operation; the authors note the greater technical difficulty and counsel caution
  4. Pulos N, Kollitz KM, Bishop AT, Shin AY. Free vascularized medial femoral condyle bone graft after failed scaphoid nonunion surgery. J Bone Joint Surg Am 2018;100:1379-1386
    49 patients with proximal pole osteonecrosis after failed non-union surgery: 41 (84%) united at a mean of 16 weeks after a free medial femoral condyle graft; 29 had further procedures, most of them planned wire removal
  5. Dimitriou R, Mataliotakis GI, Angoules AG, Kanakaris NK, Giannoudis PV. Complications following autologous bone graft harvesting from the iliac crest and using the RIA: a systematic review. Injury 2011;42 Suppl 2:S3-S15
    92 studies, 6,449 iliac crest harvests: overall complication rate 19.4%; the anterior crest carried more infection, haematoma, fracture and hypertrophic scar than the posterior crest and less chronic donor-site pain and sensory disturbance
  6. van de Wall BJM, Beeres FJP, Rompen IF, et al. RIA versus iliac crest bone graft harvesting: a meta-analysis and systematic review. Injury 2022;53:286-293
    Five comparative studies: chronic donor-site pain after iliac crest harvest 14.2% versus 0% with reamer-irrigator-aspirator harvest (OR 0.08), with lateral femoral cutaneous neuropraxia and scar numbness specific to the crest
  7. Boehm KS, Al-Taha M, Morzycki A, Samargandi OA, Al-Youha S, LeBlanc MR. Donor site morbidities of iliac crest bone graft in craniofacial surgery: a systematic review. Ann Plast Surg 2019;83:352-358
    44 studies, 2,801 craniofacial patients: mean donor-site pain 6.3 out of 10 on day 1 and 1.3 at day 14; acute gait disturbance 45.7%, chronic pain 3.1%, chronic nerve change 1.4%, crest fracture 1.2%
  8. Liu EH, Suen K, Tham SK, Ek ET. Surgical repair of triangular fibrocartilage complex tears: a systematic review. J Wrist Surg 2021;10:70-83
    27 studies of Palmer 1B peripheral and foveal repairs: residual pain scores 2.1 and 1.7 out of 10, DASH about 16, grip 80-93% of the other hand; transosseous sutures slightly better than capsular sutures or anchors; arthroscopic repair better than open; low complication rates
  9. Ma HH, Wang JP, Yang CY. Effectiveness of suture anchor and transosseous suture technique in arthroscopic foveal repair of the triangular fibrocartilage complex: a systematic review. J Orthop Surg Res 2024;19:72
    26 studies, 904 patients aged 21-41: both techniques gave clinically meaningful improvement in function, pain and grip; most complications self-limiting; re-operation 0-20% with anchors and 0-27% with transosseous sutures
  10. Barry GS, Bailey JG, Sardinha J, Brousseau P, Uppal V. Factors associated with rebound pain after peripheral nerve block for ambulatory surgery. Br J Anaesth 2021;126:862-871
    972 ambulatory block patients, rebound pain (NRS 3 or less rising to 7 or more within 24 h) in 49.6%; bone surgery OR 1.82, female OR 1.52, younger age; absence of intravenous dexamethasone OR 1.78
  11. Gerbershagen HJ, Aduckathil S, van Wijck AJM, Peelen LM, Kalkman CJ, Meissner W. Pain intensity on the first day after surgery: a prospective cohort study comparing 179 surgical procedures. Anesthesiology 2013;118:934-944
    50,523 patients: 22 of the 40 most painful procedures were orthopaedic or trauma operations on the extremities, and many minor procedures produced unexpectedly high first-day pain because little analgesia was prescribed for them

Hip and knee › Hip

21 Primary total hip arthroplasty: posterior approach

Posterolateral approach in lateral decubitus; cemented, uncemented and hybrid fixation

2Mild to moderate

Dominant mechanism: Bone. Acetabular reaming and femoral broaching; a capsulotomy and short external rotator release repaired without tension; gluteus maximus split along its fibres rather than cut; the bone-on-bone pain generator is removed and nothing is left under load

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: low.

Block
Spinal anaesthesia with surgeon-delivered periarticular infiltration; single-shot PENG or supra-inguinal fascia iliaca block when infiltration is not on offer or the patient predicts a bad course
Catheter: no No continuous technique has a place in a primary posterior hip; the epidural and the perineural catheter belong on the revision card
Alternatives: Supra-inguinal fascia iliaca block, about 40 mL, single shot (PROSPECT first line); PENG block, single shot, motor sparing and equivalent to supra-inguinal fascia iliaca in the pooled trials; General anaesthesia with a block when the spinal is refused or impossible
Position
Lateral decubitus, operative side up, pelvis held by clamps at the pubis and sacrum, dependent leg flexed and padded, operative leg draped free so it can be flexed, adducted and internally rotated to dislocate
Tourniquet
No
Cement
Sometimes. The cup is almost always uncemented press-fit; the stem is cemented in older or osteoporotic bone and press-fit in good bone; the cemented stem is the one BCIS step and it comes late in the case
Blood loss
300-600 mL in the field with more into the thigh afterwards; haemoglobin falls over 48 h; transfusion uncommon with tranexamic acid
Duration
60-120 min skin to skin; an uncemented hip in slim hands at the short end, a cemented stem adds the curing time, obesity and dysplasia add more
Length of stay
1-3 nights; same day in selected patients on a day-case pathway. Day case: selected
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV within 60 min of incision (3 g over 120 kg); antibiotic-loaded cement in a cemented stem is the surgeon's second measure and is not a reason to omit the systemic dose
Tranexamic acid
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV before incision; the route, a second dose and a higher dose add nothing measurable in the network meta-analysis
VTE
Chemoprophylaxis is routine after hip arthroplasty (low molecular weight heparin, aspirin or a direct oral anticoagulant by unit protocol) with mechanical prophylaxis; the first dose is timed against the spinal, not against the clock
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV at induction (part of the PROSPECT basic regimen) and ondansetron 4 mg IV; omit intrathecal morphine on a day-case pathway
Tell the patient
The new hip is stable the moment it is in; you will stand and walk on it the same day, the thigh and buttock ache for two or three days, and most people are on simple painkillers within a week.
The trap
Cement going down a long femoral canal in a frail patient: the surgeon announces it, the pressure is already supported, a vasopressor is running, and a sudden fall in end-tidal carbon dioxide under general anaesthesia is the right ventricle failing, not a sampling line leak

What the surgeon is doing and why

Osteoarthritis of the hip is a ball and socket that have worn through their cartilage and started to deform each other. The femoral head flattens, grows osteophytes and migrates superiorly; the acetabulum goes sclerotic and cystic beneath it; the capsule thickens and shortens, so the leg sits short, adducted and externally rotated, and the pain is bone grinding on bone with every step and every turn in bed. The joint bears weight, so unlike the shoulder there is no option of leaving the socket alone: both surfaces are replaced and the implant takes full body weight from the first afternoon. That fact sets the whole plan. The surgeon needs a cup that is immediately stable in the pelvis, a stem that is immediately stable in the femur, a head that will not come out when the patient sits on a toilet, and a leg the same length as the other one.

The posterior approach is the commonest way in worldwide because it is extensile, spares the abductors entirely and gives the best view of the femur. The surgeon:

  1. Splits gluteus maximus along its fibres (no muscle is cut) and finds the short external rotators (piriformis, the gemelli, obturator internus and the upper part of quadratus femoris) lying over the back of the joint, with the sciatic nerve a centimetre or two behind them.
  2. Takes the short external rotators and the posterior capsule off the femur as a flap, tagged with sutures so they can be put back. This is the step that gives the posterior approach its reputation for dislocation, and the step whose repair has largely removed it.
  3. Dislocates the hip posteriorly by flexion, adduction and internal rotation, cuts the femoral neck, and removes the head.
  4. Reams the acetabulum to a bleeding hemisphere, corrects the version and inclination, and press-fits a cup one or two millimetres larger than the last reamer; a few surgeons still cement a polyethylene cup in very old bone.
  5. Opens the femoral canal, broaches it to size, and either press-fits a stem that will osseointegrate over weeks or cements a polished or collared stem in a column of pressurised cement.
  6. Trials the head and neck length until the hip is stable through a range of positions and the leg length and offset match the other side, then seats the definitive head and reduces.
  7. Repairs the capsule and the short external rotators back to the greater trochanter and closes the gluteus maximus split.

The anaesthetic reading of that sequence: the two bone steps, reaming and broaching, are the pain generators, and they are moderate and short. No muscle is cut, so there is no muscle mechanism of consequence. The only repaired structures are a thin capsule and small rotators, sutured without tension and not loaded by walking, so the tendon-tension mechanism that dominates the shoulder cards is absent. And the pre-operative pain generator is gone: a patient who has had bone-on-bone pain for two years is, by the end of the first week, better than before surgery. That is why primary hip arthroplasty sits low in the pain ranking despite being a large operation; in the 179-procedure cohort it is not among the 40 highest-scoring operations, in a table led by open calcaneal reduction, spinal fusion and foot arthrodesis. With a spinal and infiltration in place it is a 2 on the Part B scale: regular paracetamol and an NSAID, a few opioid doses on day 0 and 1, and a patient who copes without a catheter.

Two of the surgeon’s decisions are mostly about you. The stem decision (cemented or press-fit) is made on bone quality and age, and it decides whether the case has a bone cement implantation syndrome step. And the leg length and stability trialling decides how many times the hip is dislocated and reduced with the pelvis clamped on its side, which is the moment the operation moves the patient most.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 Spinal, sedation and the decision about general anaesthesia

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon needs a motionless, relaxed patient for 60-120 minutes, a lax hip for the dislocation and the trial reductions, and a patient who can stand that afternoon.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Neuraxial anaesthesia is the ICAROS group’s strong recommendation for hip arthroplasty, on 94 mostly observational studies in which spinal or epidural anaesthesia carried lower odds of death (OR 0.67), pulmonary complications, acute kidney injury, deep vein thrombosis, infection and transfusion than general anaesthesia, with more urinary retention. The evidence is moderate to low quality and no large randomised trial settles it, so a spinal is the defensible default rather than a proven life-saver. A plain or short-acting spinal sized to the case with propofol sedation is the usual technique; intrathecal morphine up to 0.1 mg is a PROSPECT option for inpatients and is left out on a day-case pathway because nausea and pruritus delay discharge more than the analgesia advances it. General anaesthesia with a tracheal tube is the answer when the spinal is refused, the spine is fused or infected, or the patient is anticoagulated; it brings end-tidal carbon dioxide monitoring, the best early warning of a cement event. Decide the airway now: turning a patient lateral on a supraglottic device and then needing a tube is a bad position to be in.

  2. 2 Lateral decubitus positioning

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Side-lying with the pelvis clamped gives the surgeon a stable pelvis to ream against and lets the leg be flexed across the table to dislocate the hip. The clamps must hold the pelvis square, because the cup is placed by eye against the floor and the table, and a pelvis that has rolled forward puts it in the wrong version.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Dependent arm on a board with the axilla free, upper arm supported at shoulder height, head on a pillow that keeps the neck neutral, dependent eye, ear and peroneal nerve checked, legs separated by a pillow. The anterior pelvic clamp sits on the pubis and the posterior on the sacrum; in a slim patient the anterior clamp can press on the femoral vessels and nerve, and in any patient it compresses the abdomen enough to raise the diaphragm. Under sedation with a spinal this is tolerable; under general anaesthesia the dependent lung is underventilated and overperfused, so expect a lower saturation than supine. A hyperbaric spinal followed by an immediate turn onto the non-operative side fixes on the wrong side, so give it a few minutes to set before the turn. The pressure falls as the patient goes over and the clamps come on; have the vasopressor infusion running before that rather than reaching for the metaraminol afterwards.

  3. 3 Antibiotic, tranexamic acid and the baseline

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A joint replacement is a large implant in a dead space; infection is the complication the surgeon fears most and the one that produces the revision card. Blood in the field and in the thigh afterwards is what tranexamic acid prevents.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Cefazolin 2 g IV finished before the knife (3 g over 120 kg); antibiotic-loaded cement in a cemented stem is an addition, not a substitute. Tranexamic acid 1 g IV before incision: in the 34-trial network meta-analysis intravenous, topical and oral routes all cut blood loss and transfusion, no route is better, and a second dose, a larger dose or a different time add nothing measurable. Record the pre-induction pressure, because the AAGBI cement target is a systolic within 20% of it.

  4. 4 Gluteus maximus split, short external rotator release and capsulotomy

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A curved incision over the posterior trochanter, fascia lata opened, gluteus maximus split bluntly along its fibres: no muscle is divided and the abductors are never touched, which is why this approach does not limp. Piriformis and the conjoint tendon are then taken off the posterior femoral neck as one flap with the capsule beneath them, tagged for repair; repairing that layer at the end is the intervention that cut the posterior approach’s dislocation rate from about 4.5% to under 1% in the pooled series. Quadratus femoris is left if it can be, because the medial femoral circumflex artery runs under it and bleeds hard when cut.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The first bleeding is diffuse, from the gluteal split, and from here the loss runs at a steady rate rather than in events. The sciatic nerve lies a centimetre or two behind the rotators and the surgeon works beside it for the next hour; the leg is moved by the surgical team and nobody else. The capsulotomy is the first moment of real nociception: nothing happens under a working spinal, and the heart rate climbs under a general anaesthetic without a block. A sudden pool of dark blood and a call for more suction means the surgeon has gone through quadratus femoris into the circumflex vessels; the loss is a few hundred millilitres over a minute, not a crisis.

  5. 5 Dislocation and femoral neck osteotomy

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    With the leg flexed, adducted and internally rotated the head is levered out of the socket backwards. The neck is cut at the level planned on the template, which is what sets the leg length and offset later, and the head is removed and measured.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The leg is forced across the table against a clamped pelvis; a frail osteoporotic femur fractures here if the hip is stiff and the surgeon impatient, and an ankylosed or protrusio hip may need the neck cut in situ before it will come out. The pressure often dips at the moment of dislocation as the patient’s mass shifts against the clamps. The femoral vein is kinked from now until reduction, which is the mechanical half of the venous thromboembolism story; the spinal’s vasodilatation is half of the protection.

  6. 6 Acetabular exposure and reaming

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The labrum and remaining capsule are excised, osteophytes cleared to find the true floor and rim, and hemispherical reamers of increasing size are run until the whole socket is bleeding cancellous bone at the planned inclination (about 40 degrees) and anteversion (15-20 degrees). The cup goes in one or two millimetres larger than the last reamer, driven home with a mallet, with screws if the fit is doubtful.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Reaming a hemisphere of cancellous bone is the largest single bleed of the case and it continues until the cup seals it; it is also the first of the two bone pain mechanisms. Cup impaction transmits through the pelvis to the clamps and the table, so the whole patient moves, and the head and dependent arm are checked afterwards. A drill or screw through the medial wall can injure the external iliac or obturator vessels: a pressure that falls and keeps falling after the cup is in, with no bleeding in the field, is that until proven otherwise. Hypotension during reaming under a spinal is more often the spinal and the position than blood; a haemoglobin on a gas tells you which.

  7. 7 Femoral preparation: broaching, and the cemented or uncemented decision

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The femoral canal is opened at the piriformis fossa and broaches of increasing size are hammered down it until one is rotationally stable. For an uncemented stem the last broach is the size of the implant and the stem is press-fit into cortical contact. For a cemented stem the canal is broached a size larger, washed with pulsed lavage, dried, plugged distally and filled retrograde from a gun before the stem is pushed in.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Each blow of the broach vents fat, marrow and air into the femoral veins and produces the transient dips in saturation and pressure that pass unnoticed in a well patient. In an uncemented hip this is the only canal event and it is over in ten minutes. In a cemented hip the dangerous step is next, and this is the moment to prepare for it, not when the gun is loaded.

  8. 8 Cementing the stem: bone cement implantation syndrome

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Polished and collared cemented stems rely on a pressurised cement mantle for immediate fixation, so the surgeon pressurises the cement in the canal deliberately and then drives the stem in against it. That pressurisation is what pushes marrow fat and debris into the venous sinusoids and, from there, into the right heart and lungs.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The Donaldson classification is the common language: grade 1 is a saturation below 94% or a systolic fall of more than 20%; grade 2 is a saturation below 88%, a systolic fall of more than 40% or unexpected loss of consciousness; grade 3 is cardiovascular collapse needing resuscitation. In elective cemented hips the pooled intra-operative mortality is about 1 in 1,000, far below the hip fracture figures, but the mechanism is the same and the elderly patient with cardiopulmonary disease on a diuretic is in the risk group the AAGBI hip fracture guidance identifies. That guidance was written for hemiarthroplasty and applies unchanged here: the surgeon tells you before the cement is mixed, washes and dries the canal, vents it, uses a gun retrograde on a plug and avoids heavy pressurisation in the high-risk patient; you confirm that you know cement is coming, have the pressure within 20% of the pre-induction baseline already, have metaraminol or adrenaline drawn up, run the cuff on its fastest cycle or an arterial line in the high-risk patient, and watch the end-tidal carbon dioxide if the patient is ventilated, because a sudden fall is the right ventricle failing against an embolised pulmonary bed. Treat it as acute right heart failure: oxygen, vasopressor to keep the right ventricle perfused, fluid with judgement, adrenaline early if the pressure does not respond, resuscitation for grade 3. The worst of it is in the minutes after the stem goes in and again at reduction, and the vigilance runs through both.

  9. 9 Trial reduction, leg length and stability

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A trial head goes on, the hip is reduced and tested: flexion with adduction and internal rotation (the toilet-seat position), extension with external rotation, and a shuck test for soft tissue tension. Leg length is checked against a mark on the pelvis or by palpating the knees and heels together. A different neck length, offset or a lipped liner is chosen and the trial repeated until the hip is stable and the legs match.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Each reduction is a hard pull on the leg against the clamps; the pressure dips with it and recovers. A patient under a light general anaesthetic or a thin spinal tenses the abductors, the surgeon reads the hip as tight when it is not, and the wrong neck length goes in. A request for relaxation here means neuromuscular block or depth under general anaesthesia, and more sedation and time under a spinal, because the block cannot be deepened. The surgeon is trading stability against length, and in a stiff or dysplastic hip the two conflict; a leg lengthened by more than a couple of centimetres puts the sciatic nerve on stretch, and that is the foot drop that presents to you first.

  10. 10 Definitive head, reduction, capsular and rotator repair

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The definitive ceramic or metal head is impacted onto the trunnion and the hip reduced for the last time. The posterior capsule and short external rotators are sutured back to the trochanter through drill holes or to the tendon stump: the repair that makes the posterior approach safe. Gluteus maximus and fascia lata are closed; most surgeons have given up drains.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The final reduction is the second embolic moment in a cemented hip, as the femoral vein unkinks and releases what was dammed in it. The rotator repair needs the leg held in slight external rotation and the patient still. Give the antiemetic before closure. From here the day is decided by the spinal receding on time and the first oral doses going in before it does.

  11. 11 Recovery, mobilisation and the day-case pathway

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The implant is stable from the moment of reduction; the surgeon wants the patient standing the same day, walking the next morning, and the posterior repair protected from deep flexion with adduction and internal rotation for a few weeks. Many surgeons with a confident repair have dropped formal precautions altogether.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Standing on the afternoon of surgery needs a spinal that has gone, a leg that bears weight, a pressure that survives standing and a bladder that has emptied; that is the argument against intrathecal morphine, heavy spinals, lumbar plexus and femoral nerve blocks here, and for PENG or supra-inguinal fascia iliaca if a block is used at all. Same-day discharge is reasonable under 80 years, ASA 1-2, Timed Up and Go of 10 seconds or less, BMI under 35 and someone at home; in the randomised and matched cohorts that pathway shows no excess reoperation, readmission or emergency visits, and it fails on hypotension, pain and nausea in the first six hours. The inpatient stays one to three nights. A foot drop in recovery is a sciatic nerve stretched by lengthening or a retractor and the surgeon sees it now; a tense swollen thigh with a falling haemoglobin on day 1 is bleeding into the compartment, which a drain does not reliably reveal.

Pain plan

The mechanism is two bone surfaces and a repaired capsule under no tension, in a patient whose pre-operative pain is gone. The plan does not need to carry anyone through a week; it needs to cover the first two nights and start the oral regimen before the spinal recedes. PROSPECT’s basic regimen for everyone is paracetamol with an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor started before or during surgery and a single intravenous dexamethasone dose up to 10 mg; opioids are for rescue.

The block question has an evidence answer and a practical answer, and they differ. The 2026 PROSPECT update recommends a single-shot supra-inguinal fascia iliaca block (about 40 mL) or a PENG block before surgery, finds the two comparable, and places local infiltration below them: it may be considered when a block is not feasible, its benefit is transient and modest, and combining it with a block is not supported. The author’s default for the posterior approach under a spinal differs: surgeon-delivered periarticular infiltration with a dilute long-acting local anaesthetic, no block, and PENG or supra-inguinal fascia iliaca reserved for the patient whose surgeon does not infiltrate, who is having a general anaesthetic, or who predicts a bad course (chronic pain, opioid tolerance, a previous bad arthroplasty night). The reasoning: the spinal already covers the operation and the first hours; in the one randomised comparison, adding a PENG block to infiltration changed neither day 1 opioid use nor pain scores; and on a day-case pathway the only thing a block can add is a reason the leg will not hold the patient at four o’clock. That is a judgement, not a guideline, and a unit whose surgeons do not infiltrate should follow PROSPECT and block. Lumbar plexus, femoral nerve, quadratus lumborum and erector spinae blocks are not recommended or unsupported in the update, and none fits the mechanism.

No catheter. An epidural or a continuous lumbar plexus technique brings motor block, hypotension, urinary retention and a delayed stand to an operation whose pain is a 2; they belong on the revision card, where the mechanism earns them.

Rebound is low because nothing dense wears off suddenly: the spinal recedes over an afternoon with the infiltration behind it, and the first paracetamol and NSAID doses go in before that. Escalation triggers: day 1 pain out of proportion, in the thigh rather than the buttock, with a tense swollen thigh, is a haematoma; new sharp pain on standing with a short externally rotated leg is a dislocation or a periprosthetic fracture and needs a radiograph before any analgesic decision; buttock pain with numbness down the leg and a foot that will not dorsiflex is the sciatic nerve. None of these is treated with more opioid.

Pitfalls and variants

  • Cemented versus uncemented. The cemented stem is the safer choice in old osteoporotic bone and the only BCIS step; the uncemented stem has no cement event but more intra-operative periprosthetic fractures in the same bone. Surgeons vary by age cut-off and training; find out which you have before the femur is opened, not when the gun appears.
  • Hybrid fixation. An uncemented cup with a cemented stem; the cement precautions apply in full.
  • The frail elderly patient. The ICAROS mortality signal for neuraxial anaesthesia is strongest here, the BCIS risk factors (age, cardiopulmonary disease, diuretics, male sex) cluster here, and an arterial line before the cement is the AAGBI’s explicit advice for the higher-risk patient.
  • Dysplastic and protrusio hips. The head may be cut in situ, the cup may need a graft or a high centre, the leg may be lengthened beyond what the sciatic nerve tolerates, and the case runs long; the periacetabular osteotomy and revision cards cover the longer dissection.
  • Ankylosing spondylitis and the fused spine. A spinal may be impossible and the airway difficult; plan the general anaesthetic and the block in advance, not after a failed needle.
  • Anticoagulation. The timing rules are the unit’s; the alternative is a general anaesthetic with a block, not a spinal placed in a hurry.
  • Obesity. The lateral position, the clamps and the depth of the wound cost time, blood and exposure; the cup is harder to orient; the sedated patient breathing spontaneously on their side desaturates.
  • Dislocation precautions. With a repaired posterior capsule and a large head many surgeons impose none; others still ask for no flexion past 90 degrees with adduction and internal rotation for six weeks. Ask what the surgeon wants on the ward instructions, because the physiotherapist will.
  • The direct anterior and direct lateral approaches change the position, the nerve at risk and the muscle pain: see anterior and lateral approaches.
  • The hip fracture patient having a total hip shares every cement and frailty hazard with the elective patient and adds the fracture pathway’s timing: see neck of femur.

Key sources

Primary hip arthroplasty is one of the best-evidenced operations in this book: a PROSPECT guideline updated in 2026, a neuraxial-versus-general consensus built on 94 studies, a network meta-analysis of tranexamic acid, the Donaldson classification and the AAGBI guidance that operationalised it. The weak points are that the neuraxial evidence is observational and the block-versus-infiltration trials are small; the card’s preference for infiltration under a spinal over a routine block is the author’s reconciliation of the PROSPECT recommendation with one negative randomised trial and the demands of same-day mobilisation, and it is labelled as such.

  1. Carella M, Bugada D, Van de Velde M, et al. PROSPECT guideline for total hip arthroplasty: updated systematic review and procedure-specific postoperative pain management recommendations. Anaesthesia 2026 (online ahead of print)
    71 RCTs and 32 reviews to June 2024: paracetamol, NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor and a single IV dexamethasone dose up to 10 mg for all; single-shot supra-inguinal fascia iliaca block (about 40 mL) or PENG block recommended, the two comparable; local infiltration may be considered when a block is not feasible, benefit transient and modest, combining it with a block not supported; intrathecal morphine up to 0.1 mg may be considered for inpatients; lumbar plexus block, quadratus lumborum, gabapentinoids and the direct anterior approach not recommended
  2. Anger M, Valovska T, Beloeil H, et al. PROSPECT guideline for total hip arthroplasty: a systematic review and procedure-specific postoperative pain management recommendations. Anaesthesia 2021;76:1082-1097
    The 2021 recommendations that the 2026 update builds on; same basic regimen, fascia iliaca block recommended, local infiltration as an alternative
  3. Association of Anaesthetists of Great Britain and Ireland, Griffiths R, White SM, Moppett IK, et al. Safety guideline: reducing the risk from cemented hemiarthroplasty for hip fracture 2015. Anaesthesia 2015;70:623-626
    Grades BCIS by the Donaldson criteria; adverse cardiovascular events in about 20% of cemented hip fracture operations, grade 2 about 3%, grade 3 about 1%; risk factors age, cardiopulmonary disease, diuretics, male sex; surgeon to wash and dry the canal, vent, use a cement gun retrograde on a plug and avoid excessive pressurisation in high-risk patients; anaesthetist to be told before cementing, keep systolic within 20% of pre-induction, have metaraminol or adrenaline ready, and read a falling end-tidal carbon dioxide as right heart failure
  4. Donaldson AJ, Thomson HE, Harper NJ, Kenny NW. Bone cement implantation syndrome. Br J Anaesth 2009;102:12-22
    The classification: grade 1 SpO2 below 94% or systolic fall over 20%; grade 2 SpO2 below 88%, systolic fall over 40% or unexpected loss of consciousness; grade 3 cardiovascular collapse needing CPR. Embolic model favoured; pooled intra-operative mortality 0.11% for cemented elective THA and 0.43% for cemented hemiarthroplasty, rising to 4.3% for pathological fractures
  5. Memtsoudis SG, Cozowicz C, Bekeris J, et al. Anaesthetic care of patients undergoing primary hip and knee arthroplasty: consensus recommendations from the International Consensus on Anaesthesia-Related Outcomes after Surgery group (ICAROS) based on a systematic review and meta-analysis. Br J Anaesth 2019
    94 studies, mostly observational: for hip arthroplasty neuraxial anaesthesia carried lower odds of mortality (OR 0.67), pulmonary complications (0.65), acute renal failure (0.69), deep vein thrombosis (0.52), infection (0.73) and transfusion (0.85), with more urinary retention; strong recommendation for neuraxial in hip arthroplasty on moderate-to-low quality evidence, weak for knee

    Meta-analysis: posterior approach dislocation 4.46% without soft tissue repair and 0.49% with it (relative risk 8.21 for omitting repair); with repair, posterior 1.01%, anterolateral 0.70% and direct lateral 0.43%, described as comparable
  7. Fillingham YA, Ramkumar DB, Jevsevar DS, et al. The efficacy of tranexamic acid in total hip arthroplasty: a network meta-analysis. J Arthroplasty 2018;33(10)
    34 trials: intravenous, topical and oral TXA each reduce blood loss and transfusion against placebo with no route clearly superior; repeat doses, higher doses and timing changes do not add
  8. Ferre F, Rey J, Bosch L, et al. Pericapsular nerve group (PENG) block combined with local infiltration analgesia is not superior to local infiltration analgesia for the management of postoperative pain after primary elective total hip arthroplasty: a prospective, randomized, controlled, single-blind trial. BMC Anesthesiol 2022;22:252
    64 patients, PENG plus infiltration against infiltration alone: no difference in day 1 oral morphine equivalents or pain scores; the block was motor sparing
  9. Bodrogi A, Dervin GF, Beaulé PE. Management of patients undergoing same-day discharge primary total hip and knee arthroplasty. CMAJ 2020;192:E34-E39
    Selection: age under 80 (over 80 OR 4.16 for adverse events or readmission), ASA 1-2, Timed Up and Go 10 s or less, BMI under 35, support at home; a 220-patient randomised trial and matched cohorts show no excess reoperation, readmission or emergency visits; intrathecal morphine avoided for nausea and pruritus; hypotension, pain and nausea are the usual reasons discharge fails
  10. Gerbershagen HJ, Aduckathil S, van Wijck AJM, Peelen LM, Kalkman CJ, Meissner W. Pain intensity on the first day after surgery: a prospective cohort study comparing 179 surgical procedures. Anesthesiology 2013;118:934-944
    50,000 patients, worst pain on day 1: hip arthroplasty is not among the 40 highest-scoring procedures, which are led by calcaneal reduction, spinal fusion and scoliosis surgery; regional analgesia was used in only 15% of extremity cases in the cohort

Hip and knee › Hip

22 Primary total hip arthroplasty: anterior and lateral approaches

What changes from the posterior approach: the direct anterior approach (supine, Hueter interval, with or without a traction table) and the direct lateral approach (Hardinge, abductor split)

2Mild to moderate

Dominant mechanism: Bone. Same acetabular reaming and femoral broaching as the posterior approach. The direct anterior approach adds no muscle division and subtracts the rotator release; the direct lateral approach adds a split and repair of gluteus medius and vastus lateralis, which is the one muscle-under-tension mechanism among the three approaches and the reason the lateral hip aches on walking for longer

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: low.

Block
Spinal anaesthesia with surgeon-delivered periarticular infiltration, as for the posterior approach; PENG or supra-inguinal fascia iliaca block when infiltration is not on offer; no block is needed for the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve because its injury is a surgical event, not a pain target
Catheter: no No continuous technique for any primary approach; the direct lateral approach's muscle ache is covered by infiltration and the oral regimen
Alternatives: PENG block, single shot (motor sparing, equivalent to supra-inguinal fascia iliaca in the PROSPECT pooled trials); Supra-inguinal fascia iliaca block, about 40 mL, single shot; General anaesthesia with a block where a spinal is refused or impossible
Position
Direct anterior: supine, on a traction table with the feet in boots and a perineal post, or on a standard table with the operative leg draped free and dropped into extension and external rotation at the femoral step. Direct lateral: lateral decubitus with pelvic clamps as for the posterior approach, or supine in some hands
Tourniquet
No
Cement
Sometimes. Cup almost always press-fit; the stem is cemented or uncemented by the surgeon's choice of bone, as for the posterior approach. Cementing through the anterior approach is harder because the femoral exposure is the approach's weak point, and some surgeons who cement avoid the approach for that reason
Blood loss
300-600 mL for either approach; more with the direct lateral in the pooled comparisons; the anterior approach bleeds from the lateral femoral circumflex vessels early and from the femur late
Duration
60-120 min; the direct anterior approach runs 10-20 min longer than the posterior in the pooled trials, and much longer early in a surgeon's experience
Length of stay
1-2 nights; the direct anterior approach is the one most often run as a day case. Day case: selected
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV within 60 min of incision (3 g over 120 kg); the anterior wound sits in the groin crease in an obese patient and wound complications are the approach's known penalty, so the timing matters
Tranexamic acid
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV before incision, as for the posterior approach
VTE
Chemoprophylaxis routine after hip arthroplasty by unit protocol, with mechanical prophylaxis; timed against the spinal
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV at induction and ondansetron 4 mg IV; no intrathecal morphine on a day-case pathway
Tell the patient
The hip is stable straight away and there are no bending rules to follow after the anterior approach; expect a patch of numb or tingling skin on the outer thigh, which is common and usually fades, and after the lateral approach expect a limp for a few weeks while the muscle repair heals.
The trap
The direct anterior femoral step: the leg is dropped into extension, adduction and external rotation with the pelvis fixed, the exposure is the worst of any approach, and a calcar crack or trochanteric fracture here is the mechanism of the higher early femoral revision rate in the registry; expect the longest and bloodiest minutes of the case at the point the surgeon is least able to see

What the surgeon is doing and why

This card is written as a set of differences from the posterior approach. The disease, the implant, the cup and stem steps, the cemented or uncemented decision, the cement precautions, the tranexamic acid, the neuraxial-versus-general evidence, the analgesic plan and the day-case pathway are the same and are not repeated. What changes is the way in, and the way in decides the position, the nerve at risk, the muscle that hurts afterwards, which step is the dangerous one, and what the patient is allowed to do on day 1.

There are three honest ways into a hip and every surgeon has been trained to trust one of them. The posterior approach comes in behind the joint through the short rotators and spares the abductors. The direct anterior approach comes in from the front between tensor fasciae latae and sartorius (the Hueter interval), then between rectus femoris and gluteus medius: an internervous, intermuscular plane in which no muscle is cut and no tendon detached. The direct lateral approach comes in from the side through the abductors, splitting gluteus medius and vastus lateralis in continuity, peeling the anterior part off the trochanter and repairing it at the end. The three dislocate at comparable rates once the posterior capsule is repaired, and the Australian registry puts all-cause revision at about 2% for all of them, with the difference for any single complication at most about 0.2%. The choice is about what the surgeon can see, what they are used to, and which complication they would rather have.

The direct anterior approach’s bargain: because nothing is cut there is no posterior capsule to protect, so there are no hip precautions, the patient can sit, bend and cross their legs from the first day, early function and pain scores in the small randomised trials are better, and the stay is about half a day shorter. It is the approach most often chosen for a day-case pathway. The costs are on the femur and the skin. The femur lies behind the surgeon’s line of sight, so the leg has to be dropped into extension, adduction and external rotation with the pelvis fixed, the capsule released off the trochanter, and the proximal femur levered up into the wound. That is the weakest exposure of any approach, it is where the calcar cracks and the trochanter fractures, and it is why the registry found more early femoral complications and early major revisions after the anterior approach despite less dislocation and infection. The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve crosses the interval and is stretched or cut in most patients: 81% in the Ottawa series, higher after resurfacing, mild, without effect on function, and rarely fully resolving. The groin-crease wound under an obese abdomen is the wound-complication penalty. And the fluoroscopy most surgeons use for cup position and leg length means a C-arm over the pelvis and a radiation question for whoever stands at the head.

The direct lateral approach’s bargain is the opposite. The surgeon sees both the acetabulum and the femur well, the dislocation rate is the lowest of the three, and no fluoroscope or traction table is needed. The cost is the abductor mechanism: gluteus medius is split and repaired, the superior gluteal nerve crosses the split about 5 cm above the trochanter and is cut if the split is carried too high, and the pooled comparisons show more limping and more stem malposition than the posterior approach, with heterotopic ossification trending higher. A limp that lasts weeks is a muscle repair under load; a limp that never resolves is a superior gluteal nerve palsy or a failed repair.

The pain logic follows. For the anterior approach the mechanism is pure bone, reaming and broaching with no muscle divided and no capsule under tension, so the pain is the posterior approach’s or a little less and the PROSPECT regimen fits it unchanged. For the lateral approach the bone mechanism is joined by a muscle one, a split and reattached gluteus medius loaded by every step, which does not change the first two nights but does change the second week. Both are a 2 on the Part B scale with a spinal and infiltration in place, the lateral at the top of that band and the anterior at the bottom. Neither needs a catheter.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 Position: supine, with or without a traction table

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The anterior approach is done supine because the interval opens best with the hip extended and the surgeon standing on the operative side. A traction table (the feet in boots on telescoping spars with a perineal post) lets one surgeon control extension, adduction, external rotation and traction with a lever and a pedal; a standard table with the operative leg draped free and the contralateral leg in a holder lets the assistant do it by hand and the leg be dropped off the side of the table for the femoral step. Surgeons vary and both are common.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Supine is the one real advantage of this approach from your side: the airway is in front of you, a spinal with sedation is comfortable, the dependent lung problem of lateral decubitus does not exist, and the pressure is steadier. The traction table brings its own list. The perineal post is a pudendal nerve and perineal skin hazard if traction is heavy or prolonged, as on the hip arthroscopy card, though the pulls here are brief; the boots are an ankle and foot hazard, and the contralateral leg left in traction is a peroneal nerve and compartment hazard. The operative-side arm is often placed across the chest on a rest to clear the surgeon’s elbow, so the drip and the cuff go on the other side. The C-arm comes in over the pelvis from the opposite side, so the machine and the lines need to be where it is not going.

  2. 2 Skin, the interval and the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    An oblique or longitudinal incision over tensor fasciae latae, a few centimetres lateral to the anterior superior iliac spine, deliberately placed lateral to where the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve usually runs. The fascia over tensor is opened and the muscle belly swept laterally to find the interval with sartorius and rectus femoris. The nerve is not sought out; the approach stays lateral of it and accepts that its branches cross the field.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Nothing to do except know what the patient will report. Numbness or tingling over the anterolateral thigh after this approach is the rule, not the exception, is usually mild, does not limit function in the series that measured it, and mostly does not fully resolve. Document pre-operative sensation if the patient already has meralgia paraesthetica, because they will blame the operation for it, and have the surgeon consent for it explicitly. A lateral femoral cutaneous nerve block has no analgesic role here and is listed by PROSPECT as not recommended.

  3. 3 Lateral femoral circumflex vessels, capsulotomy and neck cut

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The ascending branches of the lateral femoral circumflex artery and their veins cross the lower end of the interval and are ligated or sealed before the capsule is reached; this is a step peculiar to the anterior approach and a known bleeding point. The anterior capsule is opened as a flap or excised, the neck exposed, and the neck cut made in situ (the head cannot be dislocated out of a small anterior window) before the head is removed with a corkscrew. Many surgeons use the fluoroscope now to check the neck cut level.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The circumflex vessels bleed briskly if a tie slips; it is the one early arterial bleeding point of the case and the surgeon will say so. Blood loss over the case is similar to the posterior approach in the pooled trials. The in situ neck cut means no forcible dislocation and no shifting of the patient’s mass against clamps, so the pressure is steadier here than at the equivalent posterior step.

  4. 4 Acetabular exposure, reaming and the fluoroscope

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The acetabulum is the easy part of this approach: it faces the surgeon, the pelvis is supine and level, and fluoroscopy gives a true anteroposterior view, so cup inclination and anteversion are checked against the image rather than the surgeon’s estimate of where the floor is. Reaming and cup impaction are as for the posterior approach.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Reaming is the largest single bleed of the case and the first bone pain mechanism, exactly as behind. The C-arm swings in over the pelvis, often several times; stand behind the shield or step back, because the scatter from a hip at the head end over a two-hour list is not trivial, and keep the lines, the sedation pump and the warming blanket clear of the arc. In a sedated patient a spinal that is wearing thin becomes apparent at cup impaction, which is the first hard mallet work of the case.

  5. 5 Femoral exposure: extension, external rotation and capsular release

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    This is the step the anterior approach is judged by. The femur lies posterior to the acetabulum with the patient supine, so the proximal femur has to be brought up into the wound: the leg is extended (dropped below table level, or the traction table spar lowered), adducted under the other leg, externally rotated through 90 degrees or more, and the capsule and the conjoint tendon released off the posterior trochanter until a hook under the calcar can lever the femur up and out. The amount of release is the surgeon’s judgement and the source of the approach’s reputation: too little and the femur cannot be prepared safely, too much and the posterior stability the approach is supposed to preserve is lost.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The leg goes into a position that stretches the femoral nerve and vessels over the front of the hip; on a traction table the pelvis is fixed and the force goes through the femur. A stiff hip, an osteoporotic femur or a surgeon early in their experience makes this the longest step of the case and the one where things break: a calcar crack during broaching or a trochanteric fracture during levering is the mechanism behind the registry’s higher early femoral revision rate, and if it happens the surgeon needs a cable, a different stem or a longer exposure, and the case doubles. The surgeon needs relaxation here more than at any other step: neuromuscular block under general anaesthesia, a dense enough block and adequate sedation under a spinal, because a patient who tenses the quadriceps and hip flexors makes the femur impossible to deliver. The pressure falls as the leg is dropped and rotated and recovers.

  6. 6 Broaching and stem insertion with the leg in extension

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Broaches go down the canal with the femur levered up and the leg in extension and external rotation. Most surgeons use short or collared stems designed for this approach because a long straight broach cannot be lined up with the canal through an anterior window, and the collar is a safeguard against subsidence when the fit is less certain. Cementing is possible but awkward, because the gun has to be delivered down a canal that is pointing away from the surgeon.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The canal is vented with each blow as for any femur, and the cement precautions, if a stem is cemented, are unchanged from the posterior card. The exposure is worse and a stem at the wrong version or subsiding is harder to see, so the fluoroscope comes back to check the stem and the leg length. A collared uncemented stem is the usual choice, which makes this the approach where cement is least often used: a BCIS advantage worth noticing in the frail patient.

  7. 7 Trial reduction, leg length by fluoroscopy, and the absence of posterior precautions

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    With the leg brought back to neutral the trial head is reduced by traction and internal rotation (the traction table makes this a pedal and a lever). Leg length and offset are read off the fluoroscopy image against the other side rather than by palpating heels, which is the second real advantage of the supine position. Because no posterior structure was cut, the surgeon tests the hip in extension and external rotation for anterior stability rather than in flexion and internal rotation, and writes no precautions.

    What it means for anaesthesia
