A 2 on the Part B scale, and in the 179-procedure cohort hip arthroscopy does not appear in the 40 highest-scoring operations. The young, female, opioid-naive population is the one with the highest nausea risk and, in the ambulatory block data, the highest rebound risk, which is an argument for an antiemetic plan and an oral regimen started before discharge rather than for a block.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 General anaesthesia, the airway, and the block question decided in advance

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon needs 60-150 minutes of a motionless, relaxed patient on a traction table with a C-arm over the pelvis, and a patient who can go home on crutches that afternoon.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    General anaesthesia with a tracheal tube and neuromuscular block is the author’s default: the surgeon’s request for relaxation at the traction step is a request for muscle relaxation (a tense hip needs more force to distract, and more force is more pudendal and sciatic injury), a tube protects the airway for a long case with the head away from you and a C-arm swinging over the chest, and the end of the case needs an abdominal examination before extubation. A spinal is a reasonable option for the patient who wants one, sized to two hours, with the understanding that a sedated spontaneously breathing patient under a traction and a pump is harder to assess at the end than a ventilated one; the one reported abdominal compartment syndrome under a spinal declared itself as dyspnoea and abdominal pain in the final minutes. The block decision belongs here and is covered in the pain plan; the short version is no fascia iliaca block, a PENG only for the selected patient, and surgeon-delivered infiltration for everyone.

  2. 2 Positioning on the traction table: the post, the boots and the leg

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Distraction needs a counter-force, which is the perineal post against the medial thigh; a large, well-padded post, lateralised against the operative thigh rather than centred on the perineum, spreads the load away from the pudendal nerve. The operative foot goes into a boot with the leg in slight flexion, abduction and internal rotation; the other leg goes into the contralateral boot in abduction to make room for the C-arm, or is left free.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The post is the pudendal nerve: in the pooled series pudendal injury occurred in 4.3% of patients where a post was used and 0.5% where it was not, all resolving within three months. Check that the post is padded, that it sits on the thigh and not the perineum, and that the genitals are clear of it and not trapped; in a man the scrotum and penis go away from the post and are looked at again after the traction is on. The boots are the feet: a loose boot allows the foot to slip and the traction to be applied through the ankle, a tight boot is a skin and a nerve problem; the contralateral foot in a boot under counter-traction is at the same risk. Arms across the chest on a rest, out of the C-arm’s path. Then the thing nobody else will do: look at the whole patient from the end of the table once the traction is on, because the pelvis will have shifted against the post and the head and the arms will have moved with it.

  3. 3 Traction applied and the vacuum broken

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Traction is increased until the joint seal breaks (seen as a crescent of air on the fluoroscope) and the joint space opens 8-10 mm. A stiff, muscular or guarded hip needs more force, and the surgeon cannot work in the central compartment with less than full distraction.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is the moment the surgeon asks for relaxation, and under general anaesthesia the answer is neuromuscular block, because a relaxed hip distracts with less force and the force is the injury. Start the traction clock. The series are consistent that traction time predicts complications: over 60 minutes the rate rose significantly, and hips with pudendal neurapraxia had an hour of traction against 45 minutes in those without. The surgeon’s practice is to release traction when moving to the peripheral compartment and to re-apply it only if needed; your practice is to say the time out loud at 45 minutes and every 15 minutes after that, which is a request that every experienced hip arthroscopist will understand. The pressure often rises as the traction goes on and the pelvis loads the post; a young patient tolerates it and it is not a reason to deepen.

  4. 4 Portals, capsulotomy and the irrigation pump

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Portals under fluoroscopy, then the interportal capsulotomy to create working space. The irrigation pump is set at 40-60 mmHg and flows continuously; the capsulotomy means the fluid is no longer contained in the joint.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve runs across the anterior portal site and is disturbed in 16.5% of patients in the prospective series, persisting at six months in 1.6%; it is a portal injury, not a traction one, and the patient will report numbness over the anterolateral thigh. The capsulotomy opens the hip to the thigh and the pump fills it: from this point the thigh swells, the fluid tracks where the anatomy lets it, and the two reported routes to the abdomen are along the psoas into the retroperitoneum and from there into the peritoneum. Warm the irrigation or the patient, because 20 L of room-temperature fluid through the hip over two hours is the cooling system that the hypothermia in two of the reported compartment syndrome cases reflects. The surgeon’s request for a systolic of 90-100 for a clear view is reasonable in a flat, young, well patient, which is who is on the table; it is not reasonable in the older patient with hypertension having a scope for a different indication.

  5. 5 Rim trimming, labral takedown and repair under traction

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The pincer rim is burred back, the labrum elevated, the rim decorticated to bleeding bone, and the labrum sutured back with anchors so that it seals against the femoral head. This is the longest part of the central compartment work and all of it is under traction.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The capsule and labrum mechanism is created here: a labrum sutured onto raw bone and a capsule held open by instruments, which the patient will feel on every flexion for a week. The anchors are implants, which is the reason for the antibiotic. Bone dust and bleeding from the decorticated rim fog the view, and this is the step that produces the request for a lower pressure and a higher pump; the pump is the surgeon’s lever. The traction clock is running; this step is where it is most often forgotten.

  6. 6 Traction released, cam resection in the peripheral compartment

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The joint is reduced, the hip flexed to 30-45 degrees to relax the anterior capsule and expose the head-neck junction, and the cam burred away under fluoroscopic and arthroscopic control until the head is spherical through flexion and rotation. The neck must not be over-resected (a femoral neck fracture after a scope is a resection of more than about 30% of the neck diameter, and the patient is told to protect it on crutches for that reason) and the retinacular vessels that supply the head run along the posterosuperior neck and are kept out of the field.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Traction off is the moment the perineum and the feet get their blood back; note the total traction time. The cam resection is the bone mechanism, a burr on a neck rather than a reaming, and in a young patient it is well tolerated. The flexed leg in a boot is a different loading of the sciatic nerve and the peroneal nerve at the fibular neck; the knee is checked. This is where the case runs long if the surgeon is thorough, and the fluid keeps running.

  7. 7 Add-ons: psoas release, peritrochanteric work and the fluid problem

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A psoas tenotomy at the lesser trochanter or through the capsule treats a snapping or impinging iliopsoas; trochanteric bursectomy, iliotibial band release and gluteus medius repair are done in the peritrochanteric space with the leg abducted and the traction off; ligamentum teres debridement in the central compartment.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The psoas release is the step most consistently present in the abdominal compartment syndrome reports, because it opens the fluid’s path along the psoas into the retroperitoneum; four of the seven cases reviewed had one. The peritrochanteric space is a large potential space that holds litres. From this point the examination is the abdomen: distension, a tense wall, rising airway pressures on the ventilator, a pressure that falls without a reason in the field, a core temperature that drops. The treatment of the established syndrome is drainage (a paracentesis drained 3 L in one case) or a laparotomy; the prevention is a surgeon who knows the clock and a pump that is not run at pressures and flows that the anatomy cannot drain. Say the fluid volume out loud when the bags are changed, and say the deficit if the pump displays one.

  8. 8 Capsular closure, portal closure and the abdomen before the drapes come off

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The capsulotomy is closed or plicated with two or three sutures (more in the patient with laxity), the portals closed, and a dressing applied; the leg comes out of the boot and the post is removed.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Before the drapes come off and before any plan to extubate, examine the abdomen: a soft, flat abdomen with normal airway pressures and a normal temperature is the common finding, and anything else is not extubated until it is explained. Look at the perineum and the genitals for the pressure marks and the oedema the post leaves; look at both feet. Give the antiemetic. A patient under a spinal who complains of abdominal pain or breathlessness at this point has declared the diagnosis and the ultrasound probe is the next step, not reassurance.

  9. 9 Recovery, the oral regimen and home

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants the patient home on crutches with partial weight bearing for two to six weeks depending on what was done, with hip flexion limited for a repaired labrum and a closed capsule, and a physiotherapy programme that starts within days.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The pain in recovery is capsular and sharp with movement, and settles with the first doses of paracetamol and an NSAID given before the patient leaves, plus a few oral opioid doses for the first two nights. Nausea in this population is the thing that stops discharge; the dexamethasone and ondansetron at induction and emergence are not optional. The anterolateral thigh numbness and the perineal numbness are expected and are explained before they are reported, because a young woman who wakes with a numb perineum and was not told has had a bad day. A quadriceps that will not hold the patient’s weight on the first standing attempt is a block, if one was given, and is the reason the fascia iliaca block was abandoned for this operation. The thigh will be swollen with fluid for a day or two; a thigh that is tense, with pain out of proportion and a numb foot, is a compartment syndrome of the thigh, reported after this operation, and is the surgeon’s problem now.

Pain plan

The mechanism is a capsulotomy, a labrum sutured to a raw rim and a burred femoral neck, in a joint distracted for an hour and filled with fluid: sharp with movement, settling in days, not re-provoked by loading. That is a 2, and the plan is built for a day case: paracetamol and an NSAID started before discharge and continued for a week, a few oral opioid doses for the first two nights, dexamethasone and ondansetron for the nausea that this population produces, and surgeon-delivered local anaesthetic into the joint and the portals at the end of the case.

The block question has a clear negative and an open positive. The negative is the fascia iliaca block: in the randomised sham-controlled trial of 80 patients having arthroscopy for impingement, a pre-operative fascia iliaca block changed neither the pain scores nor the opioid use over 24 hours, and produced more quadriceps weakness and more falls, and the authors could not recommend it; a femoral nerve block carries the same motor cost for the same absent benefit. The open positive is the PENG block: in the pooled trials across hip surgery it gave the same pain scores as fascia iliaca with less opioid at 24 hours, and in the one hip arthroscopy trial that combined it with a lateral femoral cutaneous nerve block it gave lower pain scores and less quadriceps weakness than fascia iliaca, but it is being compared with a block that does not work, and the trials that report motor function after PENG find quadriceps weakness in over a quarter of patients in some series. The author’s practice is no routine block: infiltration for everyone, and a single-shot PENG for the patient who predicts a bad course (chronic pain, a previous bad day-case night, opioid tolerance) or the larger operation (capsular plication, gluteal tendon repair, labral reconstruction), with the patient told that the leg may not hold them for the first evening. That is a judgement, not an evidence statement; there is no PROSPECT guideline for hip arthroscopy and the nearest one, for total hip arthroplasty, addresses a different mechanism.

No catheter. Rebound is moderate because the population is young, female and opioid-naive, which are the ambulatory block predictors, but the thing that wears off is infiltration rather than a dense block, and the first oral doses go in before discharge. Escalation triggers: a thigh that is tense and swollen with pain out of proportion is a thigh compartment syndrome; perineal or anterolateral thigh numbness is expected and settles; abdominal pain or distension at home on the evening of surgery is the compartment syndrome that was missed in theatre and needs an emergency department, not a phone call.

Pitfalls and variants

  • Traction time is the complication rate. Over 60 minutes the rate rises; the surgeon’s practice of releasing traction for the peripheral compartment and your practice of calling the time are the two controls.
  • The perineal post. Padded, large, lateralised onto the thigh; the genitals checked before and after traction. Post-free traction systems exist and the pooled pudendal injury rate without a post is a tenth of the rate with one.
  • Lateral decubitus. Some surgeons scope the hip on its side with traction applied through a boot on a lateral distractor; the airway access, the dependent arm and the post are the lateral-position issues, and the fluid tracks differently.
  • The obese patient. Harder to distract, longer traction, more force, a deeper wound for the fluid to fill; many surgeons will not scope above a BMI of about 35.
  • Fluid extravasation and the abdomen. The capsulotomy, the psoas release, the long case and the high-flow pump are the reported associations; the signs are distension, airway pressure, hypotension and hypothermia; the examination before extubation is the prevention of the catastrophe, and the hernia in the history is a reason to examine twice.
  • Thigh compartment syndrome. Reported after fluid extravasation into the thigh; a tense thigh with disproportionate pain in recovery.
  • The request for hypotension. Reasonable in a flat young patient; the pump pressure is the surgeon’s lever before yours.
  • Hypothermia. Litres of room-temperature irrigation over two hours; forced-air warming from the start and the fluid warmed where the pump allows.
  • The female athlete on the pill. Long traction, immobility on crutches and oestrogen: the one day-case arthroscopy population where chemoprophylaxis is discussed rather than dismissed.
  • Revision arthroscopy and conversion. Scar makes the capsule harder to open and the distraction harder; a scope that fails for adhesions or cartilage loss ends up as a periacetabular osteotomy or a total hip in the following years, and the surgeon will often say so at the time.
  • The dysplastic hip. A labral tear in a shallow socket is the symptom, not the disease; a scope that repairs the labrum without addressing the dysplasia makes it worse, and the right operation is the periacetabular osteotomy.

Key sources

The complication data are good: a 1,615-hip prospective multicentre series with a validated grading scheme and a pooled analysis of pudendal injury. The abdominal compartment syndrome literature is case reports, perhaps a dozen, and the card’s advice to examine the abdomen before extubation is drawn from their common features rather than from any trial. The block evidence is one well-designed negative randomised trial for fascia iliaca and a small, heterogeneous and early literature for PENG; the card’s no-routine-block default is the author’s reading of that and is labelled as such. There is no procedure-specific analgesic guideline.

  1. Larson CM, Clohisy JC, Beaulé PE, et al. Intraoperative and early postoperative complications after hip arthroscopic surgery: a prospective multicenter trial utilizing a validated grading scheme. Am J Sports Med 2016;44(9)
    1,615 hips, mean age 30: overall complication rate 8.3%, almost all minor; lateral femoral cutaneous nerve disturbance 16.5% (persisting beyond 6 months in 1.6%), pudendal perineal numbness 1.4%, foot sensory deficits 0.8%, chondral injury 1.2%, labral puncture 0.9%, no fluid extravasation; traction over 60 min raised the complication rate (p<0.001) and pudendal neurapraxia hips had 61.5 min of traction against 43.8 min; complications more frequent in women
  2. Habib A, Haldane CE, Ekhtiari S, de Sa D, Simunovic N, Belzile EL, Ayeni OR. Pudendal nerve injury is a relatively common but transient complication of hip arthroscopy. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc 2018;26:969-975
    24 studies, 3,405 patients: pudendal nerve injury in 1.8%, all resolving within 6 weeks to 3 months; 4.3% in studies using a perineal post against 0.5% in those without; longer traction times associated
  3. Ciemniewska-Gorzela K, Piontek T, Szulc A. Abdominal compartment syndrome: the prevention and treatment of possible lethal complications following hip arthroscopy: a case report. J Med Case Rep 2014;8:368
    A 53 kg woman under spinal with propofol sedation: at the end of a 2 h case with psoas release, acute dyspnoea, tachycardia, a distended abdomen and a systolic in the 60s-90s; paracentesis drained 3 L of clear fluid with immediate recovery. Reviews seven earlier reports (95-165 min cases, five with capsulotomy, four with psoas release): distension the consistent sign, with hypotension, raised airway pressure, hypothermia, one cardiac arrest and three laparotomies
  4. Behrends M, Yap EN, Zhang AL, Kolodzie K, Kinjo S, Harbell MW, Aleshi P. Preoperative fascia iliaca block does not improve analgesia after arthroscopic hip surgery, but causes quadriceps muscle weakness: a randomized, double-blind trial. Anesthesiology 2018;129:536-543
    80 patients, fascia iliaca block against sham before hip arthroscopy for impingement: pain scores and opioid use over 24 h the same, quadriceps strength deficit greater and falls more frequent in the block group; the authors could not recommend the block
  5. Ying H, Chen L, Yin D, Ye Y, Chen J. Efficacy of pericapsular nerve group block vs. fascia iliaca compartment block for hip surgeries: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Front Surg 2023;10:1054403
    6 randomised trials, 258 patients across hip surgery: pain scores the same at 6, 12 and 24 h; 24 h opioid consumption lower with PENG by about 9 mg morphine equivalent with high heterogeneity; quadriceps weakness after PENG reported in over a quarter of patients in some trials; moderate certainty, described as preliminary
  6. Liu M, Gao M, Hu Y, et al. Pericapsular nerve group block combined with lateral femoral cutaneous nerve block versus fascia iliaca block for hip arthroscopy. J Pain Res 2024 (OrthoEvidence summary)
    78 patients: PENG with lateral femoral cutaneous nerve block gave lower static and dynamic pain scores and less quadriceps weakness than fascia iliaca block over 48 h
  7. Gerbershagen HJ, Aduckathil S, van Wijck AJM, Peelen LM, Kalkman CJ, Meissner W. Pain intensity on the first day after surgery: a prospective cohort study comparing 179 surgical procedures. Anesthesiology 2013;118:934-944
    Hip arthroscopy does not appear in the 40 highest-scoring procedures; the cohort's top of the table is open calcaneal reduction, spinal fusion and foot arthrodesis

Hip and knee › Hip

26 Periacetabular osteotomy

Bernese (Ganz) periacetabular osteotomy for acetabular dysplasia and retroversion in the adolescent and young adult hip

5Severe and prolonged

Dominant mechanism: Bone. Four osteotomies through the pelvis leaving a free acetabular fragment on three screws, loaded through the hip by every protected step for six to eight weeks before it unites; beneath that, iliacus and the abductors stripped off both tables of the ilium, the direct head of rectus femoris taken down or retracted, a capsule re-tensioned by the reorientation, and the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve in the wound

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: high.

Block
General anaesthesia with a continuous regional technique for the first 48 h: a low-concentration lumbar epidural where the pathway tolerates its side effects, or a suprainguinal fascia iliaca or erector spinae catheter with surgeon periarticular infiltration where early walking and simple chemoprophylaxis are the priority; IV dexamethasone and two doses of tranexamic acid in all
Catheter: routine A continuous technique is the author's default for an operation with a score of 5; which one is a pathway decision rather than an evidence verdict. The epidural has the best analgesia on record for the first 48 h and the longest stay; a fascia iliaca or erector spinae catheter, or a single-shot suprainguinal fascia iliaca block with dexamethasone and infiltration, trades about a point of pain on day 0-1 for a day less in hospital and a leg that walks
Alternatives: Single-shot suprainguinal fascia iliaca block with IV dexamethasone plus surgeon periarticular infiltration (the enhanced-recovery pathway in the recent cohorts); Lumbar erector spinae plane catheter (less weakness, numbness and hypotension than an epidural in the one comparison, slightly more pain on day 0); Combined spinal-epidural where the surgeon's first hour can be covered by the spinal and the epidural run from the pubic cut onwards; Surgeon periarticular injection alone on a two-night pathway, accepting day 0-1 pain near 5
Position
Supine on a radiolucent table with the image intensifier on the operative side; the leg is draped free so the hip can be flexed and adducted for the ischial cut and ranged for the impingement check; some surgeons add a small bump under the ipsilateral buttock
Tourniquet
No
Cement
No
Blood loss
Calculated loss 900-1,500 mL, rising about 11% for every hour of surgery; before tranexamic acid a third to a half of patients were transfused, with it 10-30%; cell salvage is routine
Duration
120-180 min for the osteotomy alone in experienced hands; 180-240 min with a concomitant hip arthroscopy or an open femoral osteochondroplasty, and well beyond that early in a surgeon's experience
Length of stay
2-4 nights: two on a block-and-infiltration pathway, three to four with an epidural. Day case: no
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV within 60 min of incision, 3 g over 120 kg; repeat at 4 h or after 1.5 L of loss, both of which this operation can reach
Tranexamic acid
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV before incision and 1 g IV at closure, the two-dose regimen used in the randomised trial
VTE
Chemoprophylaxis (LMWH or aspirin by unit protocol) plus mechanical prophylaxis and early mobilisation; a long pelvic operation in a young patient is not low risk, three of 205 patients in the multicentre cohort had a thromboembolic event, and an epidural catheter sets the timing of every dose
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV at induction and ondansetron 4 mg IV before emergence; a young woman, a long case and an opioid-based rescue plan is the highest-risk phenotype in the book
Tell the patient
This is a big operation on the pelvis: expect a few nights in hospital, crutches with limited weight through the leg for six to eight weeks, and a hip that is sore for weeks rather than days before the benefit arrives.
The trap
The size of the operation is hidden by the age of the patient: calculated blood loss is about a litre and rises with every hour, a third of patients were transfused before tranexamic acid, and the haematocrit in a 20-year-old woman settles a third below her baseline; group and crossmatch, cell salvage, two doses of tranexamic acid and a written plan for the day the catheter comes out are the minimum, not the maximum

What the surgeon is doing and why

Acetabular dysplasia is a socket that is too shallow and faces the wrong way. The femoral head is covered laterally and anteriorly by labrum instead of bone, the load that should spread over a hemisphere is carried on the edge, and the labrum hypertrophies, tears and the cartilage beside it delaminates. Left alone, the hip arrives at arthroplasty in its forties. The periacetabular osteotomy cuts the acetabulum free from the pelvis as a single fragment, rotates it so that bone sits over the head, pushes it medially so that the joint reaction force falls, and fixes it with screws until it unites. It is a reconstruction of the pelvis in a patient who is usually a woman in her late teens or twenties: the multicentre complication cohort had a mean age of 25 and was 70% female. The same osteotomy rotated the other way treats acetabular retroversion.

The Bernese design keeps the posterior column intact, and that one decision explains the operation. Because the ischial and retroacetabular cuts stop short of the posterior column, the pelvic ring stays in one piece, the fragment is held by screws rather than an external fixator, the patient can sit and bear partial weight from the first day, and the birth canal is unchanged. It also explains the two cuts the surgeon cannot see: the ischial cut is made under the capsule by feel and fluoroscopy, and the retroacetabular cut runs down the quadrilateral plate with the sciatic notch a centimetre behind it.

The sequence is fixed. Get onto the pelvis through a modified Smith-Petersen approach, taking the anterior superior iliac spine or the sartorius origin, lifting iliacus off the inner table and working under rectus femoris and iliocapsularis to the capsule. Make four cuts: ischium below the socket, superior pubic ramus medial to the iliopectineal eminence, the supra-acetabular ilium towards the pelvic brim, and the retroacetabular cut down the quadrilateral surface to meet the ischial cut. Mobilise the fragment on a Schanz screw, reorient it under the image intensifier, fix it with three or four screws from the iliac crest, graft the gap, open the joint if the labrum or the head-neck junction needs attention, repair and close. A hip arthroscopy may precede the osteotomy under the same anaesthetic; it adds its own time, not to the osteotomy’s.

The pain logic follows from a free piece of pelvis held by screws. The dominant mechanism is bone, but not the bone of a single cut that is then rested: four cancellous surfaces across the ilium, pubis and ischium, with the fragment loaded through the hip by every protected step for six to eight weeks until it unites, and a pubic ramus that unites slowly or not at all. Beneath that is muscle, from iliacus and the abductors stripped from both tables of the ilium and the rectus origin taken down, so every hip flexion and every transfer hurts; a capsule re-tensioned by the reorientation (in cadaveric testing the osteotomy reduced abduction and internal rotation and increased adduction and external rotation); and nerve, because the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve runs through the wound. The early peak with a working continuous technique is a 3 or 4; the 5 is earned afterwards. In the largest analgesic cohort, patients on a periarticular injection pathway left hospital with a pain score of 4.8, and when patients describe dissatisfaction with this operation, half of it is pain. Compare hip arthroscopy, which treats the labral consequences of the same dysplasia through portals and sits at 2.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 Pre-operative plan: blood, the continuous technique, and chemoprophylaxis timing

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon’s requirements are a still patient on a radiolucent table for two to three hours, a field dry enough to see osteotomes going into bone they cannot see, and a patient who can get out of bed with crutches the next morning.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Three decisions are made in clinic, not on the day. Blood: the calculated loss is 900-1,500 mL in the series that measured it, 11% more for every hour of surgery, and the haematocrit nadir settles at about 0.69 of the pre-operative value, so a 20-year-old woman with a borderline haemoglobin needs iron and a crossmatch, not a group and hold. The analgesic technique: a continuous technique for the first 48 h is the author’s default for a score of 5, and the choice between a lumbar epidural and a peripheral catheter or single-shot block with infiltration is set by the unit’s pathway (see the pain plan), because the epidural changes the length of stay, the bladder catheter and the timing of every anticoagulant dose. Chemoprophylaxis: three of 205 patients in the multicentre cohort had a thromboembolic event, so youth does not exempt this operation from LMWH or aspirin.

  2. 2 Induction, lines, position and the regional technique

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The patient is supine on a radiolucent table with the image intensifier on the operative side, and the leg is draped free so that the hip can be flexed and adducted for the ischial cut and ranged at the end for impingement. Fluoroscopy is used for every cut and for the correction.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A tracheal tube for a two to three hour supine case with a litre of loss and a C-arm over the abdomen; two large cannulae; an arterial line is the author’s practice because the losses come in pulses at the cuts and the pressure needs to be readable while the surgeon is asking for it to be low. Cefazolin 2 g IV and tranexamic acid 1 g IV before the knife, dexamethasone 8 mg IV for the block as much as for nausea. If an epidural is the plan it goes in before induction at L2-3 or L3-4 and is tested; a combined spinal-epidural lets the spinal carry the exposure and the epidural start from the first cut. A suprainguinal fascia iliaca block takes 30-40 mL of ropivacaine 0.375% and six minutes. Warm the patient from the start and pad the contralateral leg with care: one of the nine reoperations in the multicentre cohort was a decompression of the other leg’s peroneal nerve.

  3. 3 Approach: the spine, the iliacus and the rectus origin

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The incision runs along the anterior iliac crest and down towards the thigh. The anterior superior iliac spine is osteotomised with the sartorius and inguinal ligament attached, or the sartorius is released; iliacus is lifted subperiosteally off the inner table down to the pelvic brim; the direct head of rectus femoris is taken down or, in the rectus-sparing modification, retracted; iliocapsularis is elevated off the capsule to expose the front of the joint and the infracotyloid groove. The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve crosses the field under the inguinal ligament, is protected, and still produces dysaesthesia in a proportion of patients.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The first bleeding is from the inner table and the nutrient vessels of the ilium as iliacus comes off, steady rather than dramatic, and the cell salvage should be collecting from now. Retractors on iliacus lie on the femoral nerve. Muscle relaxation makes the inner table reachable; a light patient with a tense iliopsoas is an unworkable field. The muscle mechanism of the pain is created here, and it is the part a fascia iliaca block covers well.

  4. 4 The ischial cut

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The first and blindest cut. A curved osteotome is passed under the capsule along the infracotyloid groove to the ischium below the acetabulum and driven through the medial two-thirds of the ischium, stopping short of the posterior cortex so that the posterior column survives. The surgeon works by feel and by the lateral and anteroposterior images; the sciatic nerve lies posterolateral to the osteotome’s tip, and the hip is flexed and adducted to relax the capsule and the nerve.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The surgeon will ask for the leg in flexion and adduction and for stillness; neuromuscular block is the right answer rather than depth. Nothing bleeds much here. A sciatic palsy after this operation originates at this osteotome or from a posterior column fracture, and the reviews find it more often with the ilioinguinal and two-incision approaches than with this one; it declares itself when the block recedes, so the foot is examined the morning after, not only in recovery.

  5. 5 The pubic cut

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The superior pubic ramus is divided medial to the iliopectineal eminence. Retractors are placed around the ramus to protect the obturator neurovascular bundle beneath it and the femoral vessels in front of it; a corona mortis, the anastomosis between obturator and external iliac systems that crosses the ramus in a proportion of pelves, is the vessel that bleeds here.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Brisk venous bleeding from behind the ramus is the obturator plexus or a corona mortis and is controlled with packing and patience; the arterial bleed that needed embolisation in the adolescent series and the external iliac vein injury in the Stoppa series are the rare versions. A sudden pressure fall here is surgical, not anaesthetic, and the cell salvage, the second cannula and the crossmatched blood are what you brought for it. The retractor on the front of the ramus compresses the femoral vessels: a leg that is pale and pulseless at the end of the case was clamped here.

  6. 6 The supra-acetabular and retroacetabular cuts

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The iliac cut runs from the outer table below the anterior inferior iliac spine towards the pelvic brim and stops a centimetre short of the iliopectineal line. From its end the retroacetabular cut turns down the quadrilateral surface at roughly 120 degrees, behind the socket and in front of the posterior column, to meet the ischial cut from above. The surgeon has the inner table exposed and the outer table only felt; the greater sciatic notch, the superior gluteal vessels and the sciatic nerve are behind the osteotome.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The largest bleed of the operation: cancellous bone on both surfaces of a thick iliac cut, the venous plexus on the quadrilateral plate and the nutrient vessels of the ilium, with the superior gluteal artery as the thing that must not be hit. The request for a lower pressure arrives here. Hold a mean of 60-65 mmHg in a healthy 25-year-old for the minutes it takes, and not lower, because the dysplastic hip is the only abnormal organ in this patient. A cut that strays into the posterior column converts the operation: the pelvic ring is broken, the fragment is unstable, plate fixation and a longer, bloodier case follow, and three of 715 patients in the large single-surgeon series were reoperated for exactly that.

  7. 7 Fragment mobilisation and reorientation

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    With all four cuts complete the fragment is levered free on a Schanz screw and rotated: lateral and anterior coverage are increased, the fragment is medialised to shorten the lever arm of body weight, and version is set so that the socket is neither retroverted (which impinges) nor excessively anteverted. The surgeon checks the correction on a true anteroposterior pelvis, measuring the lateral centre-edge angle, the roof angle and the crossover sign, and adjusts until the numbers are right.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Moving a fragment still attached by soft tissue moves the whole pelvis, and the table and the patient move with it; a deep, relaxed patient and an arterial line watched rather than charted. Fluoroscopy time accumulates over thirty or more exposures. The retension mechanism of the pain is set here: the capsule, the psoas tendon over the front of the joint and the abductors are all at a new length when the fragment is fixed.

  8. 8 Fixation and bone graft

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Three or four long cortical screws from the iliac crest into the fragment, sometimes a transverse screw from the anterior inferior iliac spine, hold the correction. The wedge that opened at the iliac cut is grafted with the bone removed from the anterior spine or the osteotomy. Stability is checked and the posterior column examined on the lateral image.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Drilling and screws bleed little. If the correction has been large the iliac wedge is wide, and the volume of bleeding cancellous surface left under the closure is the volume that drains over the first night.

  9. 9 Arthrotomy, femoral osteochondroplasty and the impingement check

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Over half of these patients have a cam deformity or a labral tear as well, and the surgeon either opens the capsule to resect the head-neck junction and inspect the labrum, or has already dealt with it arthroscopically at the start. The hip is then flexed and internally rotated under the image to make sure the new roof does not impinge, because an over-corrected or retroverted fragment creates the disease the operation was meant to prevent.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A capsulotomy adds the capsule mechanism to the pain and a bleeding femoral neck to the losses; an arthroscopy done first adds irrigation fluid tracking into the iliopsoas and the retroperitoneum, which can make the exposure wet, and the abdomen is felt before the osteotomy begins. The range-of-motion check is a reminder that the leg is free and the patient is about to be moved hard.

  10. 10 Repair and closure

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The anterior spine is reattached with a screw or sutures, rectus is repaired, the abdominal wall muscles are closed to the crest, a drain is often left on the inner table, and the skin closed. Nothing is under tension and nothing is protected by a splint; the protection is the crutches.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Tranexamic acid 1 g IV. Return the salvaged blood, check a haemoglobin and a gas, and count the losses honestly: the suction, the swabs and the cell saver reservoir add up to what the surgeon will describe as moderate. Infiltration of the wound and the periarticular tissues with ropivacaine by the surgeon is the posterior and capsular cover a fascia iliaca block does not provide and is worth asking for; on a periarticular injection pathway it is the whole regional technique. A patient with an epidural is extubated with the infusion running; a patient with a single-shot block is extubated with the first oral doses already given.

  11. 11 Recovery, the first 48 h and the day the catheter comes out

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants protected weight-bearing from day 1 (toe-touch to partial, with crutches, for six to eight weeks until the osteotomies unite), hip flexion limited to protect the rectus repair, and an early radiograph. Nonunion of the pubic ramus is common and usually silent; loss of fixation and migration of the fragment is the reoperation they fear.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Haemoglobin on the evening of surgery and on days 1 and 2, because the fall continues as the haematoma equilibrates; 71% of one large cohort reached a haematocrit below 26. The trajectory on this card has a working continuous technique for 48 h: 3 on the first evening, 4 on day 1, and the 5 on day 2, which is the day the epidural or catheter stops and the patient walks further. Regular paracetamol and an NSAID from the first evening (the surgeon’s view on NSAIDs and union is a conversation to have once per surgeon; most accept a short course), oral opioid for the nights of the first week, and a written plan for day 2. On a block-and-infiltration pathway the figures for days 0 and 1 are about a point higher and the patient goes home a day earlier with the same day 7. Examine the lateral thigh (lateral femoral cutaneous nerve), the quadriceps (femoral nerve, retractor) and the foot (sciatic and peroneal) when the block has receded, against what you recorded before it. Chemoprophylaxis starts on the evening of surgery or day 1 by the epidural rules.

Pain plan

The mechanism is four pelvic osteotomies loaded through the hip for weeks, a large muscle elevation, a re-tensioned capsule and a nerve in the wound, so the plan has to cover lumbar and sacral plexus territory for 48 h and then hand over to an oral regimen that runs for two to three weeks. There is no PROSPECT guideline for this operation and the systematic review of its analgesia found six studies. What exists is a set of institutional cohorts comparing the lumbar epidural that was standard for thirty years against what replaced it, and they agree with each other.

The epidural covers everything: ilium, pubis, ischium, iliacus and the abductors, the capsule, and the posterior cuts that no anterior block reaches. In the 724-patient cohort it gave a pain score of 2.9 over the first 48 h against 4.7 for periarticular injection, and the price was a stay of 3.4 days against 2.2, a bladder catheter, hypotension and legs that do not walk on day 1. The erector spinae cohort measured the side effects directly: weakness in 16% of epidural patients against 4%, numbness in 40% against 10%, and symptomatic hypotension in 11% against 1%, for one point more pain on day 0 and less opioid with the plane block. The suprainguinal fascia iliaca cohorts found stays of 2.9 days against 4.1 and 4.4, earlier physiotherapy milestones, lower daily opioid use and no difference in pain scores at physiotherapy. Removing the epidural on day 1 rather than day 2 shortened stay in one of the six studies.

The defensible default, then, is a continuous technique for the first 48 h, and the author’s judgement is that which technique is a decision about the pathway, not about the evidence. Where the unit runs a three to four night stay with a bladder catheter and a physiotherapist who works around an epidural, a low-concentration lumbar epidural (ropivacaine 0.2% or less with fentanyl) started before induction gives the best analgesia on record for this operation and is stopped on day 1 or 2 rather than left to run. Where the pathway is two nights and walking on day 0 or 1, the choice is a suprainguinal fascia iliaca block with dexamethasone (single shot, or a catheter where the unit can run one), surgeon periarticular infiltration to cover the capsule and the posterior cuts, and an oral regimen started before the block recedes; an erector spinae catheter is the third option, with one comparison behind it. In every version: intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg, paracetamol and an NSAID from the first evening, oral opioid for the first week’s nights, and tranexamic acid twice.

Rebound pain is the planning target for the block pathway. The ambulatory cohort found it in half of all block patients, with bone surgery (OR 1.82), female sex (OR 1.52) and younger age raising the odds and intravenous dexamethasone lowering them; this patient has all three risk factors and a bone that will be loaded the next morning. The written plan for the night the block recedes, and the opioid charted before it does, are the difference between the 2.9-day stay in the cohorts and a 4 am call.

Escalation: pain above 7 on day 1 or 2 with a soft thigh, a warm foot and a working quadriceps is treated with the charted rescue opioid and a check that the regular doses were given; a tense groin and thigh with a haemoglobin falling faster than the drain explains is a haematoma or a vessel, and the surgeon is called before the second unit is given; new quadriceps weakness or a foot drop after the block has receded is a retractor, an osteotome or a posterior column fracture and is the surgeon’s to assess that day; calf pain or breathlessness in the first week is a thromboembolic event until proven otherwise. Pain at the pubis at six to eight weeks is a ramus nonunion and usually settles; pain at the iliac crest or the screws is the commonest reason for a second small operation.

Pitfalls and variants

  • Blood. The losses are proportional to time and to the size of the correction; a surgeon early in their experience, a large correction, a previous pelvic operation or a bilateral staged programme in one admission all push the figure past a litre and a half. Two doses of tranexamic acid, cell salvage and a crossmatch are the floor.
  • The request for hypotension. Cancellous bone bleeds at any pressure; a mean of 60-65 mmHg for the minutes of the iliac and retroacetabular cuts is reasonable in a healthy young patient, lower is not, and the arterial line is what makes the number honest.
  • Concomitant arthroscopy or open osteochondroplasty. Adds 45-90 min, irrigation fluid in the iliopsoas and a capsule mechanism to the pain; it did not raise the complication rate in either large series and does not lengthen the osteotomy itself.
  • Posterior column fracture or an intra-articular cut. A fragment that will not stabilise, a plate, an hour and a litre more, and sometimes a change to non-weight-bearing; it presents to you as a surgeon who has gone quiet and a pressure that is falling.
  • Nerve injury. Lateral femoral cutaneous dysaesthesia is common and sometimes lasting (four neurolyses in 715 patients); femoral palsy is a retractor; sciatic palsy is the ischial osteotome or a posterior column problem, commoner with other approaches. A dense epidural or fascia iliaca block hides all three until day 1 or 2; the pre-block examination is the baseline.
  • Vascular injury. Rare, but the obturator plexus, a corona mortis, the external iliac vein and the superior gluteal artery are all within reach of the osteotomes and retractors, and embolisation has been needed.
  • Nonunion and heterotopic ossification. The pubic ramus commonly fails to unite and is usually silent; heterotopic bone was the commonest minor complication in the multicentre cohort. NSAIDs are a surgeon-by-surgeon conversation, and most accept a short course.
  • Venous thromboembolism. Three of 205 in the multicentre cohort despite a young population; chemoprophylaxis is routine and the epidural sets the timing.
  • The adolescent. The same operation at 14 with open growth plates, often for a neuromuscular or syndromic dysplasia, carries more minor complications and the same blood loss; a concomitant femoral osteotomy doubles the bone and the bleeding and was the predictor of major complications in the adolescent series.
  • Retroversion and the reverse osteotomy. Same cuts, the fragment rotated the other way; same pain, same blood, and more complications when dysplasia and retroversion are corrected in one fragment.
  • Smoking. Raised the odds of a complication by about 70% in the large series.

Key sources

The analgesic evidence for this operation is a set of institutional cohorts, one of them prospective in its block arm, comparing a lumbar epidural with what replaced it: fascia iliaca blocks, an erector spinae catheter and periarticular injection. They agree that the epidural gives the lowest pain scores over the first 48 h and the longest stay, and that the alternatives trade about a point of pain for a day in hospital and legs that work; none is randomised and the systematic review found six studies in total. The blood management evidence is better: a double-blind randomised trial of tranexamic acid and a before-and-after series agree on about 300 mL less loss and a halving of transfusion. The complication figures come from a prospective multicentre cohort of experienced surgeons and a 715-patient single-surgeon series. The pain score and trajectory are the author’s calibration of those cohorts against the Part B scale; the operation is not in the Gerbershagen cohort, and no number on this card is borrowed from it.

Hip and knee › Knee

27 Primary total knee arthroplasty

Conventional, navigated and robotic; cemented and cementless; cruciate-retaining, posterior-stabilised and medial-pivot designs

4Severe

Dominant mechanism: Joint re-tensioned. The collateral ligaments and posterior capsule are re-tensioned by an implant chosen to fill the gaps; underneath that, five femoral cuts and a tibial cut through cancellous bone, a subperiosteal medial release, a split quadriceps tendon, an everted patella and a tourniquet, all loaded by flexion from the first afternoon

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: high.

Block
Spinal anaesthesia, single-shot adductor canal block and surgeon-delivered periarticular infiltration, with IV dexamethasone
Catheter: selective Adductor canal catheter for the opioid-tolerant or chronic pain patient, the stiff or previously operated knee, and the unit that cannot deliver the oral regimen overnight; single shot plus infiltration for the standard patient
Alternatives: General anaesthesia with adductor canal block and infiltration when a spinal is refused or contraindicated; IPACK added to the adductor canal block for posterior knee cover in the first 24 h; Femoral nerve block: equivalent analgesia, weaker quadriceps, not recommended by PROSPECT; Intrathecal morphine 100 micrograms only for an inpatient when neither block nor infiltration is possible
Position
Supine, thigh in a leg holder or against a lateral post with a foot bump so the knee can be held at 90 degrees and beyond; robotic and navigated cases add tracker pins in the femur and tibia
Tourniquet
Sometimes. Still common for the cement step; the randomised evidence shows more day 1 pain and more serious adverse events with a tourniquet and no functional benefit, and surgeons vary from no tourniquet to the whole case
Cement
Yes. Both components cemented in most Australian practice; cementless designs in younger patients with good bone; the cement load is two surfaces, not a canal, so the BCIS risk is low but real in the frail
Blood loss
Measured loss is modest under tourniquet; the true loss including hidden loss is 500-1,000 mL over 48 h; transfusion uncommon with tranexamic acid
Duration
60-120 min skin to skin; robotic registration and pin placement add 15-30 min early in a surgeon's experience
Length of stay
1-3 nights. Day case: selected
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV within 60 min of incision, 3 g over 120 kg, and before tourniquet inflation if one is used
Tranexamic acid
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV before incision; many surgeons add a second dose at closure or a topical dose into the joint
VTE
Chemoprophylaxis is routine (aspirin or LMWH by unit protocol) plus mechanical prophylaxis and early mobilisation; a spinal and an adductor canal block do not change the timing rules
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8-10 mg IV at induction (PROSPECT recommends at least 10 mg) and ondansetron 4 mg IV; intrathecal opioid raises the need
Tell the patient
The knee will be numb for the first evening and then hurts a lot for two or three days, especially when the physiotherapist bends it; that bending is the treatment, the regular tablets are what make it possible, and the strong painkillers are for the nights.
The trap
The block wears off at 2 am on the first night, the adductor canal block never covered the back of the knee, and the physiotherapist arrives at 8 am: the oral regimen, the posterior cover (infiltration or IPACK) and the night plan all have to be in place before the spinal recedes

What the surgeon is doing and why

Knee osteoarthritis wears the medial compartment first in most patients, so the tibia drifts into varus, the medial collateral ligament and posteromedial capsule contract, the lateral structures stretch, and the joint ends up as a stiff, bowed hinge grinding at a single point. A total knee replacement does not restore that knee; it builds a new one. The surgeon cuts both ends of the joint flat, fits a metal femoral component and a tibial tray with a polyethylene insert between them, and then adjusts the insert thickness and the length of the ligaments until the new joint is stable and tracks straight through its arc. The anterior cruciate is sacrificed and the posterior cruciate kept or replaced by a cam and post; the collaterals and the posterior capsule are the only passive stabilisers left, and the whole operation is organised around getting their tension right.

That is why this is the painful arthroplasty. A hip replacement cuts one neck, reams one socket and broaches one canal, deep under a muscle envelope left at its own length; the pain is bone, and it fades once nothing is loaded through the cut (see posterior approach THA). A knee replacement makes five cuts on the femur and one on the tibia, strips the medial periosteum off the tibia, splits the quadriceps tendon to get in, everts the patella on its own tendon, and then deliberately sets the collaterals and posterior capsule to a tension they have not had for years, all under a thin subcutaneous layer with no muscle cover. Within hours the physiotherapist bends it to 90 degrees, because an arthroplasty that is not moved becomes a stiff one, and every flexion loads the tensioned ligaments. The hip is bone pain at rest. The knee is retension pain under movement, and it stays that way for the first week.

The surgeon’s sequence is: get in through a medial parapatellar arthrotomy; clear the osteophytes and release the medial sleeve; make the cuts, referenced off an intramedullary rod or off pinned trackers and a registered plan; balance the flexion and extension gaps by releasing the tight side, adjusting a cut or choosing a thicker insert, or in the robotic workflow by moving the plan so that less tissue is released; deal with the patella; lavage, cement and implant; infiltrate, close and let the tourniquet down.

The pain logic follows that sequence. The dominant mechanism is retension: ligaments and capsule set tight and loaded by every flexion, the deep ache and stiffness pain that the physiotherapists fight for a fortnight. Underneath it is bone, from six cancellous cuts and the cement interface, and periosteum, from the medial release. The posterior capsule is tensioned, so the back of the knee hurts, and the adductor canal block does not reach it. The tourniquet adds an ischaemia-reperfusion contribution the randomised trials can measure on day 1. Compare the unicompartmental replacement, which keeps the cruciates, balances nothing, makes two small cuts and sits two points lower on the scale.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 Pre-operative decisions: spinal or general, block, dexamethasone, tranexamic acid

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Everything the surgeon wants (a still, relaxed leg through the cuts, a dry field, a patient who can bend the knee that afternoon) is decided before the patient reaches the table.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The defensible default is a spinal with sedation, an adductor canal block, intravenous dexamethasone and tranexamic acid, and the surgeon’s infiltration. The ICAROS consensus prefers neuraxial anaesthesia for knee arthroplasty as a weak recommendation on low-level evidence, with lower odds of pulmonary complications (0.69), deep venous thrombosis (0.77), infection (0.80) and transfusion (0.84) and no mortality difference; the practical case for the spinal is that it covers the tourniquet and the cement step without a deep general anaesthetic in an elderly patient. A general anaesthetic with the same block and infiltration is right for the patient who refuses, is anticoagulated, or has a spine that will not give a spinal in reasonable time. Keep the spinal dose modest and avoid long-acting intrathecal opioid on a mobilisation pathway. Dexamethasone 10 mg IV is a PROSPECT recommendation in its own right, not only an antiemetic; it prolongs the block and its absence nearly doubled the odds of rebound pain in the ambulatory cohort. The adductor canal block takes 15-20 mL of ropivacaine 0.5%.

  2. 2 Positioning, tourniquet decision and antibiotic timing

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon needs the knee to flex past 90 degrees against a post or holder with the foot in a bump, and a tourniquet on the thigh if one is being used. The tourniquet is a habit from the days when cementing needed a bloodless surface; many surgeons now use it only for the cement step, and some not at all.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Cefazolin 2 g IV must be in before the cuff inflates, because nothing given afterwards reaches the leg. The tourniquet question deserves one honest sentence to a surgeon who still uses it for the whole case: in 41 randomised trials and 2,819 patients, a tourniquet raised serious adverse events from 29 to 59 per 1,000 (RR 1.73, moderate certainty), raised day 1 pain by 1.25 points, and made no difference to function at a year. In a spinal the cuff is silent for the first hour and then produces the slow rise in blood pressure and the restless patient at 60-90 minutes, which is tourniquet pain through a working spinal and not a failing one; sedation or a small dose of ketamine and a word to the surgeon about time are the treatment. Under general anaesthesia the same rise reads as light anaesthesia and gets more vapour, which is why a long tourniquet case under GA ends in a hypotensive patient when the cuff comes down.

  3. 3 Medial parapatellar arthrotomy and patellar eversion

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The arthrotomy runs through the quadriceps tendon above the patella, along the medial patellar border and down the medial edge of the patellar tendon, so the extensor mechanism can be swung laterally; the patella is everted or subluxed and the knee flexed to deliver the joint. Midvastus and subvastus approaches spare the quadriceps tendon at the cost of exposure.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The first real nociception of the case, and the first test of a borderline spinal. Eversion of the patella in a stiff knee strains the patellar tendon at the tubercle, and the surgeon wants full quadriceps relaxation here, which a spinal provides and a general anaesthetic needs neuromuscular block to match. Without a tourniquet the suprapatellar fat and synovium bleed steadily from here on.

  4. 4 Osteophyte clearance, medial release and tibial delivery

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Osteophytes tent the capsule and mimic contracture, so they come off first. The deep medial collateral ligament and posteromedial capsule are lifted subperiosteally off the proximal tibia with an elevator, which both exposes the tibia and begins the varus correction; the tibia is then delivered forward in flexion with a lever behind it.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is the periosteal contribution to the pain, proportional to the deformity: a 15-degree varus knee needs a long medial sleeve release, a straight knee almost none. The posterior lever sits against the popliteal vessels and the tibial nerve, the structures at risk through the middle of the operation.

  5. 5 Bone cuts: femur and tibia, conventional, navigated or robotic

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The distal femoral cut sets the extension gap and coronal alignment; the tibial cut sets the slope and the other half of the extension gap; the four remaining femoral cuts set the flexion gap and femoral rotation. Conventional instruments reference a rod passed up the femoral canal. Navigation uses pinned trackers and a mapped surface; robotic platforms add a haptic boundary or a guided saw, and in the newer workflows the cuts are planned to produce balanced gaps with the ligaments as they are.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The intramedullary femoral rod is the fat embolism step of the knee: the canal is opened and a rod driven up it, forcing marrow into the venous system as a reamed femur does, less because no pressurised cement follows. A transient fall in end-tidal carbon dioxide and saturation as the rod goes in is the signature. Navigation and robotic systems avoid the rod but add pins through the cortex of femur and tibia, each a small osteotomy with its own pain and a stress riser that has produced fractures through pin sites. Registration takes 10-20 minutes with the limb manipulated through its range, which the sedated spinal patient tolerates and the awake one does not. The saw through cancellous bone is the bone mechanism, finished in minutes.

  6. 6 Soft-tissue balancing: the mechanism this card is built on

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    With trials or spacer blocks in, the surgeon checks that the extension gap and the flexion gap are rectangular and equal, that the knee reaches full extension, and that neither collateral opens more than a millimetre or two to stress. A tight medial side gets more release off the tibia; a tight lateral side in a valgus knee gets a release of the iliotibial band or posterolateral capsule; a flexion contracture gets posterior capsular release or more distal femur; a loose knee gets a thicker insert.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is the retension mechanism being created in front of you. Ligaments and capsule that have been slack or contracted for years are set to a new length and will be loaded by every flexion from this afternoon; that deep, stiff ache, worst with movement on days 1 and 2, is the pain the adductor canal block only partly reaches and the oral regimen has to carry. Robotic balancing adjusts the plan rather than the ligaments and releases less tissue; whether that is less pain in a randomised comparison is not settled and the card does not claim it. The stress tests move the hip as well as the knee, and a lightly sedated patient reacts to them.

  7. 7 Patella and lateral retinacular release

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The patella is resurfaced with a cemented polyethylene button in many practices, after a cut that leaves about 12-15 mm of bone, and left native with its edge denervated by diathermy in others. If it tracks laterally with the trial in, a lateral retinacular release is made from inside the joint.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The lateral release is a raw capsular edge that bleeds after the tourniquet comes down, and it is the usual reason for a larger haemarthrosis.

  8. 8 Cementing and implantation

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Pulsed lavage clears the cancellous surfaces so cement can interdigitate; cement goes onto the tibia, the tray is impacted, then the femoral component, then the insert, and the knee is held in extension under compression until the cement cures. Cementless components are impacted onto a porous metal surface and rely on bone ingrowth.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The cement load is two flat surfaces and a short keel, not a pressurised femoral canal, so bone cement implantation syndrome is uncommon after a knee and almost always mild; it does occur in the frail patient with a cemented stemmed tibial component, and the preparations in the cement chapter apply to that patient. A cement-only surgeon inflates the tourniquet here; a whole-case surgeon is now at 60-90 minutes with the pressure rising. The 10-12 minutes while the cement sets is the moment for the second tranexamic acid dose if the unit uses one and the ondansetron.

  9. 9 Periarticular infiltration, closure and tourniquet release

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon injects a large-volume local anaesthetic mixture around the joint: into the posterior capsule before the final components go in (the only moment the back of the knee is accessible), then the collaterals, the cut capsular edges, the quadriceps, the periosteum round the tibial cut and the subcutaneous tissues at closure. Recipes vary: ropivacaine 0.2-0.375% to a total of 200-300 mg in 100-150 mL is the common skeleton, with adrenaline, ketorolac and sometimes morphine or a corticosteroid added; PROSPECT regards the added value of adrenaline and ketorolac as questionable and the optimal site and volume as unknown. A drain is unusual now, and the tourniquet comes off before or after closure.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The infiltration is half of the analgesic plan, because it is the only thing that covers the posterior capsule and the lateral side; a surgeon who skips it leaves you with a block that covers the front of the knee and nothing else, which is the case for adding an IPACK block before the patient leaves theatre. Watch the arithmetic: 300 mg of ropivacaine in the infiltration plus 100 mg in the block is near the ceiling for a small elderly patient, and tourniquet release delivers the infiltrated dose to the circulation over the following 20 minutes. Release also produces the fall in blood pressure and the rise in carbon dioxide and potassium from the reperfused leg, proportional to inflation time, and the spinal patient who was hypertensive from the cuff is now hypotensive and bleeding into the joint; a vasopressor drawn up and the second tranexamic acid dose in are the preparation.

  10. 10 Recovery, the first night, day 0 physiotherapy and discharge

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants the knee moving the same day: standing with a frame in the afternoon, flexion to 90 degrees within a day or two, full extension from the start. Stiffness at six weeks is the complication they fear most and the one that brings the patient back for a manipulation.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The spinal recedes over two to four hours, the adductor canal block over 12-24 hours with dexamethasone, and the infiltration over a similar period. Day 0 is the quiet day: the trajectory on this card has pain at 3 that evening and 6 on days 1 and 2 with the plan working. Regular paracetamol and an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor go in before the spinal has worn off; the opioid is charted for rescue and for the nights, and the night plan is explained before the patient leaves recovery, because pain arriving at 2 am as the block recedes is the rule after bone surgery: rebound pain in the ambulatory cohort occurred in half of all patients, more often after bone surgery, in women and in the young, and less often with intravenous dexamethasone on board. Day 1 physiotherapy is the real test: movement-evoked pain of 6-7 with a quadriceps that works is what the plan is designed to produce, and it beats a femoral block with a painless knee that buckles. Stay is one to three nights. Same-day discharge is an established pathway for the selected patient; the pooled non-randomised data show more complications in outpatients (16.1% versus 10.5%, no readmission difference) at very low certainty, which reads as a selection problem rather than a verdict (see the day-case chapter).

Pain plan

The mechanism is retension and bone loaded by movement from day 0, with the posterior capsule involved, so the plan has to cover the front and the back of the knee, preserve the quadriceps, and run for three days without a block. PROSPECT’s 2022 guideline for total knee arthroplasty is the strongest procedure-specific evidence in this book. Its skeleton: paracetamol and an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor started before or during surgery and continued; a single-shot adductor canal block; surgeon-delivered local infiltration, with the combination preferred over either alone; intravenous dexamethasone of at least 10 mg; and opioid reserved for rescue. It does not recommend femoral or sciatic blocks, on functional recovery grounds, nor epidural analgesia, gabapentinoids, ketamine, dexmedetomidine or continuous intra-articular infusion. Intrathecal morphine 100 micrograms is allowed only for an inpatient under spinal when neither the block nor infiltration is possible.

The block hierarchy follows from the anatomy. The adductor canal block covers the saphenous nerve and the nerve to vastus medialis, which is the anteromedial knee and the incision, with a quadriceps that still fires; that is the whole argument against the femoral block, which gives the same analgesia and weakens the muscle the physiotherapist needs. The posterior capsule is supplied by tibial and obturator articular branches that no anterior block reaches; the surgeon’s infiltration is the first way to cover it and an IPACK block is the second. The pooled trials of adding IPACK show lower rest pain in the first 12 hours (by about 0.85 points) and on day 1, less opioid to 48 hours and a stay shorter by about 0.4 days, nothing by day 3 and no change in range of motion or quadriceps strength: real, early and modest. The author’s practice is to add IPACK when the surgeon does not infiltrate the posterior capsule, for the opioid-tolerant, and for a same-day discharge.

The catheter decision: an adductor canal catheter is not the default for a primary knee with a good infiltration, because the gain over a single shot with dexamethasone is small and the catheter gets in the way of the mobilisation that is the point of the pathway; this is author’s judgement on top of a guideline that does not mention catheters. It earns its place for the opioid-tolerant or chronic pain patient, the stiff knee that will be worked hard on day 1, the patient with a previous catastrophic night after a block, and the unit that cannot guarantee a 2 am oral dose. An epidural does the same job with a bladder catheter, hypotension and a patient who cannot walk.

Escalation: pain above 7 on day 1 with a quadriceps that fires and a soft calf is treated with the charted rescue opioid and a check that the regular analgesia was actually given; a tense, swollen knee with pain out of proportion in the first 24 hours is a haemarthrosis and needs the surgeon; a tense calf or numb toes under a block that should have receded is compartment syndrome or a vascular injury until proven otherwise. A rescue adductor canal block the next morning does not weaken the leg; a rescue femoral block does.

Pitfalls and variants

  • Tourniquet or not. The randomised evidence is against the whole-case tourniquet; a cement-only tourniquet is the common compromise, and no tourniquet means a wetter field, steady loss through the case and a quieter emergence.
  • Robotic and navigated knees. No femoral rod, so less marrow embolisation; pins in both bones, so pin-site pain and a fracture risk through the tracts; registration adds time under the spinal.
  • Cementless. Younger patients with good bone; impaction rather than cement, no cure time, and a surgeon who may restrict weight-bearing on day 1.
  • Bilateral simultaneous replacement. Two infiltrations and the local anaesthetic ceiling reached easily; double the blood loss and the marrow load; the spinal is dosed for both knees from the start or the case runs under general anaesthesia with bilateral blocks.
  • Valgus knee. The releases are lateral, the common peroneal nerve is at risk when a fixed valgus and flexion deformity is corrected, and a foot drop after a valgus knee is the surgeon’s correction, not the block. Document peroneal function before any block.
  • The stiff or previously operated knee. More release, a longer case, more bleeding, and a pain course at the top of the range; this is the catheter patient.
  • Opioid-tolerant patients. Retension pain under movement is worst in exactly the patient whose opioid receptors are least useful; a catheter, ketamine and a pre-agreed plan with the pain service are all reasonable even though PROSPECT does not recommend ketamine for the standard patient.
  • Diabetes. Dexamethasone 10 mg raises glucose for a day; it is still worth giving, and the ward needs to know.
  • Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity. Infiltration plus block is the largest cumulative dose in elective orthopaedics, delivered to the circulation at tourniquet release; lipid emulsion lives in the theatre.
  • Infection. Cefazolin before the cuff, repeated for a case beyond three hours or a loss beyond 1.5 L, and the infection card for what happens when it fails.

Key sources

PROSPECT’s knee guideline is the backbone and the block hierarchy on this card is its hierarchy; the statements about catheters, IPACK selection and the tourniquet conversation are the author’s reading of the Cochrane review, the IPACK meta-analysis and the rebound pain cohort, not guideline statements. ICAROS favours neuraxial anaesthesia for the knee as a weak recommendation on low-level evidence. The outpatient data are non-randomised and very low certainty. The claim that the knee is the painful arthroplasty rests on the mechanism; the Gerbershagen cohort’s knee replacement figure sits in a figure the author could not read and is not cited.

    Recommends paracetamol and NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor, single-shot adductor canal block plus surgeon local infiltration (the combination preferred), IV dexamethasone 10 mg or more, opioid as rescue; intrathecal morphine 100 micrograms only for inpatients when block and infiltration are impossible; not recommended: femoral and sciatic blocks (functional recovery), epidural, gabapentinoids, ketamine, dexmedetomidine, continuous intra-articular infusion
