28 Unicompartmental knee arthroplasty

Medial and lateral partial knee replacement, mobile and fixed bearing, cemented and cementless, conventional and robotic

3Moderate

Dominant mechanism: Bone. Two small cancellous cuts (one tibial, one femoral) and a cement interface in a single compartment; the cruciates, the collaterals and the patellofemoral joint are left alone, nothing is balanced or re-tensioned, the quadriceps tendon is not split and the patella is not everted

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: moderate.

Block
Spinal or general anaesthesia with a single-shot adductor canal block and surgeon-delivered periarticular infiltration, with IV dexamethasone
Catheter: rarely A catheter has no claim here: the mechanism is bone in one compartment and the operation is a day case; the exception is the opioid-tolerant or chronic pain patient, and even there a good infiltration and a written night plan usually do
Alternatives: Infiltration alone with a general anaesthetic, which some day-case units run; IPACK added for a lateral UKA or when the surgeon does not infiltrate the posterior capsule; Femoral nerve block: not recommended, for the same quadriceps reason as the total knee
Position
Supine with the thigh in a leg holder and the leg hanging free so the knee can be flexed past 110 degrees for the femoral preparation; robotic cases add tracker pins
Tourniquet
Sometimes. Many surgeons use one for the whole of this short case; the Cochrane evidence against it is from total knees and applies by extrapolation
Cement
Yes. Most are cemented, two small surfaces with no canal; cementless designs with a porous tibial tray and femoral pegs are established for the mobile-bearing designs
Blood loss
Under 300 mL; transfusion is exceptional and tranexamic acid makes it rarer
Duration
45-90 min skin to skin; robotic registration adds 10-20 min
Length of stay
Day case or one night. Day case: yes
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV within 60 min of incision, 3 g over 120 kg, before tourniquet inflation
Tranexamic acid
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV before incision
VTE
Mechanical prophylaxis plus chemoprophylaxis by unit protocol, usually aspirin or a short LMWH course; a day case still gets it
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8-10 mg IV at induction and ondansetron 4 mg IV; a day case under spinal gets no intrathecal morphine
Tell the patient
This is the small version of a knee replacement: most people walk the same afternoon, go home that day or the next, and the knee is sore rather than severe for the first few days, with bending starting straight away.
The trap
Treating it like a total knee: a femoral block, an intrathecal opioid or a catheter turns a day case into an inpatient with a weak leg, and the pain after a well-infiltrated partial knee does not justify any of them

What the surgeon is doing and why

A medial unicompartmental replacement is for the knee whose disease is confined to one compartment: full-thickness cartilage loss on the medial tibiofemoral surface with the lateral compartment and, in the classic indication, the anterior cruciate ligament intact. The anterior cruciate matters because it is what keeps the wear pattern anteromedial and the knee kinematically normal; once it is gone the femur rolls back onto the posterior tibia, the wear becomes posteromedial, and a partial replacement in that knee loosens or dislocates its bearing. The medial collateral ligament has to be intact and the varus deformity correctable, because the operation deliberately does not release it. The surgeon’s aim is to resurface the one worn compartment and change nothing else. That sentence carries the whole anaesthetic difference from a total knee.

The operation: a short paramedial incision from the medial pole of the patella to the medial border of the tubercle, a mini-arthrotomy that does not enter the quadriceps tendon or the suprapatellar pouch, and no eversion of the patella. Osteophytes are cleared from the medial femoral condyle and the notch. The tibial plateau is cut: a vertical cut beside the tibial spine and a horizontal cut a few millimetres below the worn surface, removing a thin sliver of medial plateau and the meniscus with it. The femoral condyle is prepared by a saw or mill to accept a resurfacing component, in a mobile-bearing design a spherical one; the amount of bone removed is a few millimetres of distal and posterior condyle. Trials go in and the surgeon checks the gap in flexion and extension with feeler gauges, choosing a bearing thickness that restores the ligaments to their natural tension rather than tightening them; in the mobile-bearing system the bearing has to be snug enough not to dislocate and loose enough not to overcorrect the knee into valgus, which is why overcorrection and bearing dislocation are the characteristic failures. Pulsed lavage, cement on two small surfaces (or a cementless impaction), infiltration and closure. A fixed-bearing design does the same with a polyethylene insert locked to the tray. A lateral unicompartmental replacement does it on the other side through a lateral parapatellar incision for the valgus knee with isolated lateral disease; it is less common, technically harder, and the bearing behaves differently because the lateral compartment is lax in flexion. Robotic systems plan and execute the cuts and are widely used for this operation because precision of component position is what the outcome depends on.

What is not done is the point. No quadriceps split, no patellar eversion, no intramedullary femoral rod in most systems, no medial release, no sacrifice of the cruciates, no balancing of the whole joint, no re-tensioning of collaterals and posterior capsule, no posterior-stabilised box cut, and bone cuts that total a fraction of a total knee’s six. The randomised comparison against total replacement in medial compartment osteoarthritis found the same Oxford Knee Score at five and at ten years, similar reoperation rates, fewer complications on the intention-to-treat analysis, and better cost-effectiveness, so the surgeon choosing it is not trading durability for comfort. The partial knee’s advantages are recovery and the things that produce recovery: a quadriceps that works on day 0, a knee that bends without a tensioned capsule fighting back, and a pain course that is bone, short and modest.

The pain logic follows. The dominant mechanism is bone: two cancellous cuts and a cement interface in one compartment, which hurt for two days and then fade because nothing is loaded through them that was not loaded before. There is a small capsular contribution from the arthrotomy and the osteophyte clearance, and almost no retension, because the collaterals are returned to their own length rather than set to a new one. The posterior capsule is not needled or stretched the way it is in a total knee. That is why the card sits at 3 and the total knee at 4, and why a catheter has no claim here. In the opioid-prescription comparison, patients after a partial knee were less likely to fill a second opioid prescription (50% against 61%) and far less likely to need more than five (6% against 14%).

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 Anaesthetic choice and the day-case decision

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants a patient who stands and walks the same afternoon and goes home that day or the next; the operation is selected for that patient and the pathway is built around it.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Spinal and general anaesthesia are both defensible. A short-acting spinal (a low dose, no intrathecal morphine) covers the tourniquet and the cement and recedes in time for the afternoon walk; a general anaesthetic with the block and infiltration avoids the urinary retention and the motor block that delay discharge in an elderly patient. The neuraxial evidence that favours a spinal for the total knee is weak and mostly about pulmonary and thromboembolic complications in inpatients; for a 60-minute day case in a fit patient it carries less weight, and the author’s practice is to choose by the patient’s preference and by how long the surgeon takes. Either way the plan is PROSPECT’s total knee skeleton scaled down: paracetamol and an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor started before surgery, an adductor canal block, the surgeon’s infiltration, and intravenous dexamethasone 8-10 mg, which prolongs the block and reduces rebound pain. In the Danish day-surgery series, 59% of operated patients went home the same day and pain and nausea were the reasons the others stayed, which tells you where the effort goes: the oral regimen started in recovery and the antiemetic given early.

  2. 2 Positioning, tourniquet and antibiotic

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The leg hangs free from a thigh holder so the surgeon can flex the knee past 110 degrees to reach the posterior femoral condyle through a small incision; a tourniquet is common for the whole of this short case because the field is small and the bone surfaces need to be dry for cement.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Cefazolin 2 g IV before the cuff inflates. The tourniquet time is short, usually under an hour, so the cuff pain and reperfusion physiology that trouble a long total knee are minor here; the Cochrane case against the tourniquet (more serious adverse events, more day 1 pain) comes from total knee trials and applies to the partial knee only by extrapolation, so it is a conversation to have with the surgeon rather than a rule. The hanging leg puts the common peroneal nerve against the holder at the fibular neck; check the padding, because a foot drop after a partial knee is otherwise inexplicable.

  3. 3 Mini-arthrotomy and exposure

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A short paramedial incision and a capsular incision that stops at the medial border of the patella, without entering the quadriceps tendon or the suprapatellar pouch; the patella is retracted laterally, not everted. The surgeon inspects the lateral compartment, the anterior cruciate and the patellofemoral joint, because finding disease there changes the operation to a total knee.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The conversion decision is made here, in the first ten minutes, and the surgeon will say so. A conversion means the quadriceps tendon is now split, the patella everted, the posterior capsule needled, the cuts multiplied and the spinal needs another 60-90 minutes; the pain plan moves to the total knee card, the day case becomes an inpatient, and the oral regimen and the IPACK question are reopened. A short-acting spinal dosed for a partial knee is the one that runs out.

  4. 4 Tibial cut

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A vertical saw cut beside the medial tibial spine and a horizontal cut below the worn surface remove a sliver of medial plateau with the meniscus. The cut is sized to the thinnest bearing that will balance the knee, because every millimetre of tibia removed weakens the plateau and shifts load onto softer bone.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The first of two cancellous surfaces, and the one that bleeds after the tourniquet comes down. The saw blade sits a few millimetres in front of the popliteal vessels at the back of the plateau; the surgeon protects them with a retractor and the complication, when it happens, declares itself at tourniquet release. A vertical cut that runs too far posteriorly is the mechanism of the tibial plateau fracture that occasionally turns a day case into a protected-weight-bearing inpatient.

  5. 5 Femoral preparation and trials

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The distal and posterior medial condyle are prepared with a saw or a spherical mill to seat the femoral component; in the mobile-bearing design the femur is milled to a sphere so the bearing can slide on it. Trial components and feeler gauges set the flexion and extension gaps equal, and the bearing thickness is chosen to restore, not tighten, the medial collateral ligament. Robotic systems execute the cuts to a plan that has already set these gaps.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The gauges are the balancing of this operation, and the thing to notice is what they are not: there is no release. The ligaments are returned to their own length, so the retension mechanism that dominates the total knee is absent, and the patient’s movement-evoked pain on day 1 is the ache of a cut condyle, not a stretched capsule. The flexion needed to mill the posterior condyle rocks the pelvis in a spinal patient and is the moment a lightly sedated patient complains.

  6. 6 Cementing, infiltration and closure

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Pulsed lavage of the two surfaces, cement on both, the tibial component first and then the femoral, a trial bearing while the cement cures, then the definitive bearing. Cementless designs are impacted onto a porous tibial tray and femoral pegs. The surgeon infiltrates the posterior capsule before the components go in, the capsular edges and the subcutaneous tissues after, and closes in layers.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Two small cement surfaces with no canal: bone cement implantation syndrome after a partial knee is a theoretical entity, and this is not a cement-precautions case. The infiltration carries the back of the knee and the lateral side, where the adductor canal block does not reach; ropivacaine 150-200 mg in 60-100 mL is the usual order of magnitude and leaves room under the ceiling for the block. Tourniquet release after a short inflation produces a small blood pressure dip and a modest bleed into the joint; the tranexamic acid should already be in.

  7. 7 Recovery, the afternoon walk and discharge

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants full weight-bearing and active flexion from the first afternoon; the implant is stable from the moment the cement sets, and nothing has been repaired that needs protection. The day-case pathway depends on the patient walking with crutches, passing urine, eating, and understanding the night plan.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The spinal recedes over two to three hours, the block over 12-24 hours with dexamethasone, and the infiltration over a similar period; the trajectory on this card has pain at 2 on the first evening, 4 on days 1 and 2, and 2 by a week. The first oral doses go in before the patient leaves recovery. Rebound pain when the block recedes is less dramatic than after a total knee because the mechanism under it is smaller, but half of all ambulatory block patients describe it after bone surgery and the written night plan (when to take what, which dose is the rescue) is the single thing that keeps the telephone quiet. A patient who cannot pass urine at six hours after a spinal is the usual reason a day case stays; a short-acting local anaesthetic and no intrathecal opioid are the prevention. The Danish series’ 59% same-day discharge is honest about the ceiling: pain and nausea keep two in five overnight even with a good protocol.

Pain plan

The mechanism is bone in one compartment with no re-tensioning, so the plan is a single-shot block that covers the operation and the first evening, a good infiltration for the back and side of the knee, dexamethasone to stretch both, and an oral regimen that starts in recovery and carries the patient from the first night. PROSPECT has no partial knee guideline; its total knee recommendations (paracetamol and an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor, single-shot adductor canal block plus local infiltration, intravenous dexamethasone 10 mg or more, opioid as rescue, no femoral or sciatic block, no epidural, no gabapentinoid) are the nearest evidence and apply with the volume turned down. The adductor canal block is the right block for the same reason it is right for the total knee: the saphenous nerve and the nerve to vastus medialis cover the incision and the medial compartment, and the quadriceps keeps working for the afternoon walk. A femoral block is wrong here for the same reason and more so, because a weak quadriceps on a day-case pathway is a cancelled discharge.

The catheter decision is short: no. There is no tendon under tension, no osteotomy that will be loaded, no re-tensioned capsule, and the patient is meant to be at home; the opioid data show a partial knee needs fewer prescriptions than a total knee, not more. The exception is the opioid-tolerant or chronic pain patient, for whom a planned overnight stay with a good infiltration, ketamine where the unit uses it and a pain service plan is still usually enough without a catheter; a catheter there is author’s judgement, not evidence. IPACK earns a place for a lateral partial knee, where the incision and the compartment are outside the adductor canal block’s territory, and when the surgeon does not infiltrate the posterior capsule.

Escalation triggers: pain above 6 on day 1 with a working quadriceps is treated with the charted rescue opioid and a check that the regular analgesia is actually being taken; a knee that is tense and swollen with pain out of proportion in the first day is a haemarthrosis and needs the surgeon; a patient whose pain on day 2 or 3 is worse than day 1 after a partial knee, with a plateau that hurts on weight-bearing, has a tibial plateau fracture until an X-ray says otherwise. Rebound on the first night is managed by the regimen already written, and a rescue adductor canal block the next morning is rarely needed.

Pitfalls and variants

  • Conversion to total knee. Decided in the first ten minutes on the state of the lateral compartment, the anterior cruciate and the patellofemoral joint. The spinal dose, the day-case plan and the pain plan all change; a short-acting spinal is the one that runs out.
  • Lateral UKA. A lateral parapatellar approach, a valgus knee, a lateral compartment that is lax in flexion and a bearing that dislocates more readily in mobile-bearing designs; the adductor canal block covers less of the incision and IPACK or a wider infiltration is reasonable.
  • Mobile versus fixed bearing. The mobile bearing can dislocate (about 1% in the medium term) and presents as a locked, painful knee days to years later; a fixed bearing cannot, and the long-term results are similar.
  • Cementless. Impaction, no cure time, a case ten minutes shorter, and no cement step at all.
  • Robotic. Pins in the femur and tibia, registration time, and the same pain pattern; the precision argument is strongest for this operation because the component position is the whole outcome.
  • Tibial plateau fracture. Intra-operative or in the first weeks, from a vertical cut that goes too far back or a thin osteoporotic plateau; presents as new weight-bearing pain, and the patient is readmitted for protected weight-bearing or fixation.
  • Overcorrection. A bearing that is too thick sets the knee into valgus and loads the lateral compartment, which then wears; the pain is late, not post-operative.
  • Bilateral partial knees under one anaesthetic. Done in selected patients; two tourniquets, two infiltrations and the local anaesthetic ceiling, but still a shorter and gentler case than one total knee.
  • The ACL-deficient knee. Outside the classic indication; some surgeons do a partial knee with an ACL reconstruction in the young, which adds the ACL card mechanisms (graft harvest site pain, tunnels) to this one.
  • Urinary retention after spinal. The common reason a day case stays; a low-dose, short-acting spinal without intrathecal opioid, or a general anaesthetic, is the prevention.
  • Obesity. Not a contraindication to the operation in current practice, but the leg holder, the tourniquet fit and the day-case criteria all get harder.

Key sources

There is no procedure-specific guideline for the partial knee and the card borrows PROSPECT’s total knee recommendations and turns the volume down; that scaling is the author’s, not PROSPECT’s. The TOPKAT trial settles that the partial knee is not a compromise on outcome, and the opioid-prescription comparison and the Danish day-surgery series are the evidence that its pain course is lighter and that same-day discharge is realistic but not universal. The technique description rests on the Oxford mobile-bearing series and on standard surgical texts; the pain score and trajectory are calibrated against the total knee card and are author’s judgement.

29 Revision total knee arthroplasty

Aseptic revision for loosening, instability, stiffness, wear and malalignment; one-stage and second-stage revision for infection are on the infection card

5Severe and prolonged

Dominant mechanism: Joint re-tensioned. A scarred, stiff joint is re-exposed through a quadriceps snip or a tibial tubercle osteotomy, old components and cement are levered and burred out of bone that has already been cut, metaphyseal cones and stems are impacted into both canals, and a constrained implant re-tensions whatever ligament is left; then the whole construct is loaded by flexion from day 1, often with a healing osteotomy under the patellar tendon

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: high.

Block
Spinal (or general anaesthesia for the long case) with an adductor canal catheter, surgeon-delivered periarticular infiltration where the tissue allows it, and IV dexamethasone
Catheter: routine Continuous adductor canal block is the default: the case runs two to four hours, the pain outlasts a single shot by days, movement is re-provoked by day 1 physiotherapy and most patients arrive opioid-exposed; a single shot is reasonable only for the isolated polyethylene exchange
Alternatives: Epidural for the stiff knee that will be manipulated from day 1, accepting the mobilisation cost; IPACK added to the adductor canal catheter for the posterior capsule when infiltration is not possible; General anaesthesia with the catheter and a long-acting spinal is the pragmatic answer when the case will outrun a single spinal dose
Position
Supine, thigh in a holder, with the leg hanging free; the surgeon will want hyperflexion to deliver the old femoral component and the position changes through the case
Tourniquet
Sometimes. Used by many for the exposure and cement removal and then let down, because inflation times run past two hours; some surgeons operate without one and accept the blood loss
Cement
Yes. Hybrid fixation is the norm: cemented joint-surface components and metaphyseal regions, press-fit or cemented diaphyseal stems; cement removal from the old bed is a major part of the case and the new cement load is large
Blood loss
1,000-2,000 mL measured plus hidden loss; transfusion in a quarter to a half of patients without tranexamic acid and a blood management protocol, around 5% with one
Duration
120-240 min skin to skin; the exposure, cement removal and a hinge each add time, and the second stage of a two-stage infection revision is the longest
Length of stay
3-7 nights. Day case: no
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV within 60 min of incision, 3 g over 120 kg, repeated at 3-4 h and after 1.5 L of loss; for a suspected infection the surgeon may ask for the dose to be held until deep tissue samples are taken
Tranexamic acid
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV before incision and a second dose at 3 h or at closure; topical TXA into the joint by some surgeons; the one intervention with a large measured effect on transfusion in this operation
VTE
Chemoprophylaxis is routine; the long case, the stems in both canals and the slow mobilisation put this patient above the primary knee risk
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8-10 mg IV at induction and ondansetron 4 mg IV; a long case under spinal with sedation still earns both
Tell the patient
This is a bigger operation than the first replacement and it will hurt more and for longer: a local anaesthetic pump through a thin tube in the thigh runs for two or three days, bending starts straight away but under protection, and the strong painkillers are for the nights of the first week.
The trap
Planning this as a long primary: the exposure needed to get a stiff old knee open (a quadriceps snip or a tubercle osteotomy), the cement removal and the stems in both canals turn a 90-minute spinal into a three-hour case with litres of blood loss, and the single-shot block that works for a primary leaves this patient in trouble on night one

What the surgeon is doing and why

A knee replacement fails in one of a handful of ways, and the reason it has failed is what the surgeon is about to undo. Aseptic loosening is a component that has worked free of its bone or cement bed, usually the tibial tray, with bone lost around it to the osteolysis that polyethylene wear debris provokes. Instability is a joint whose collateral balance was never right or has stretched. Stiffness is a fibrosed joint, or one whose components were oversized or malrotated, that will not bend past 70 or 80 degrees. Malalignment and malrotation produce patellar maltracking and pain. Infection has its own card (periprosthetic joint infection); the second stage of a two-stage infection revision is this operation performed through a spacer and scar, and this card covers the mechanics of it.

The surgeon’s problem is a joint that was already cut once. The native landmarks are gone, the bone that is left is sclerotic where cement sat and absent where osteolysis ate it, the soft-tissue envelope is scarred, the quadriceps is short and adherent, and the collaterals may be attenuated or gone. The sequence is fixed:

  1. Get in through the old scar. If the knee flexes to 90 degrees with the patella mobile, a medial parapatellar arthrotomy with a synovectomy and release of the suprapatellar pouch and gutters will do. If it does not, the surgeon extends the exposure: a quadriceps snip (an oblique cut across the proximal quadriceps tendon that lets the extensor mechanism swing without tearing the patellar tendon off the tubercle), or a tibial tubercle osteotomy (a 6-8 cm shingle of anterior tibial cortex with the patellar tendon attached, hinged laterally and fixed back with wires or screws). The randomised comparison in two-stage infection revisions found better function and range with the osteotomy at long follow-up and the same reinfection rate; it adds a healing bone shingle under the patellar tendon and six weeks of protected extension.
  2. Get the old implants out: the femoral component freed at its cement interface with thin osteotomes and saws, the tibial tray lifted, and cement burred, chiselled or ultrasonically removed from the metaphysis and canals. Well-fixed components take a long time to remove without fracturing the condyles.
  3. Grade the bone loss (the AORI classification: contained defects, uncontained ones, loss of a whole condyle or plateau) and rebuild the platform: diaphyseal stems reamed into both canals to carry load past the damaged metaphysis, porous metal cones or sleeves impacted into the metaphyseal defects, metal augments for uncontained loss.
  4. Restore the joint line and balance. The femoral component is positioned to put the joint line back near its native level (a raised joint line gives a patella baja and a knee that cannot bend), the gaps are balanced with augments and insert thickness, and constraint is added in proportion to what the ligaments can no longer do: a posterior-stabilised insert, a condylar-constrained insert whose tall post substitutes for a collateral, or a rotating hinge when no collateral is left.
  5. Cement the joint-surface components and the metaphyseal region, with the stems cemented, press-fit or hybrid by preference; close over a drain, fix the osteotomy, repair the snip, infiltrate what tissue will hold it.

The pain logic follows. The dominant mechanism is retension, as in the primary knee, but of a worse kind: scarred tissue is released and a constrained implant sets the remaining ligaments and the capsule to a tension that the fibrosed envelope resists, and then the knee is bent from day 1 to stop the scar re-forming. Underneath it is more bone than any primary: reamed canals in femur and tibia, impacted cones, burred cement beds, augment cuts, and sometimes an osteotomy that the patellar tendon pulls on with every quadriceps contraction. Periosteal stripping, a long tourniquet, and a quadriceps cut across or lifted on a bone shingle finish the picture. The curve is what earns the 5: the first-night peak is no higher than a primary with the catheter running, but the pain is re-provoked by movement for weeks and the patient usually arrives opioid-exposed from months of a failing knee. In the one direct comparison under continuous adductor canal blocks, revision patients used the same opioid as primaries over 48 hours, but day 1 pain trended higher and rose with the number of previous operations on the knee; the catheter is what made the courses look alike.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 Pre-operative assessment: the failed knee and the patient who owns it

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon needs infection excluded (aspiration, inflammatory markers) before an aseptic revision, old operation notes to know what implants and cement are in, imaging to grade the bone loss, and a plan for exposure, stems and constraint. The case length and blood loss are decided by that plan.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This patient is older than at the primary and has usually been on opioids for the months it took the knee to fail; a pre-operative opioid history and a plan with the pain service belong in the assessment, not the recovery room. Crossmatch for a stemmed revision; a haemoglobin that was acceptable for the primary may not survive a 1.5 L loss. Look for the things that make a cement load dangerous (pulmonary hypertension, severe aortic stenosis, frailty) because this operation reams and cements both canals. Chronic kidney disease matters twice: for the NSAID and for antibiotic-loaded cement. The exposure plan is yours to know: a tubercle osteotomy means six weeks of protected extension and a different conversation with the patient about day 1.

  2. 2 Anaesthetic choice for a case that may run four hours

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants a still, relaxed leg for an exposure that will be forced, a dry field for cement removal, and a knee that bends on day 1.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A spinal with sedation remains the defensible default and covers the tourniquet and the first cement step, but it is dosed for the planned length with a plan for outrunning it: a general anaesthetic from the start for the case booked beyond three hours, or a combined spinal-epidural where the unit runs the epidural for the operation and removes it before mobilisation. The adductor canal catheter goes in before the spinal, with 15-20 mL of ropivacaine 0.5% as the loading dose; this is the author’s practice rather than a guideline, because PROSPECT’s knee guideline does not cover revision surgery. Intravenous dexamethasone 10 mg at induction, tranexamic acid 1 g IV before incision with a second dose planned, an arterial line for a hinge or a two-canal reconstruction, and a warming plan for four hours of open joint.

  3. 3 Positioning, tourniquet decision and antibiotic

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Supine with the thigh in a holder and the leg free; the surgeon will hyperflex the knee to deliver the old femoral component. A tourniquet is common for the exposure and the cement removal, when the field bleeds most and the view matters most, and is usually let down once the new components are in or when the inflation time reaches the surgeon’s limit.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Cefazolin 2 g IV before the cuff; if infection has not been excluded the surgeon may ask you to hold it until deep samples are taken, a conversation for before the patient is asleep. The tourniquet time is the issue: revision inflation times run to two hours in the published cohorts, well past the primary knee trials in which a tourniquet already raised serious adverse events and day 1 pain, and the reperfusion at release (hypotension, a rise in carbon dioxide and lactate, the infiltrated local anaesthetic arriving in the circulation) is proportional. Agree a deflation time with the surgeon before the start. In the spinal patient the cuff pain begins at 60-90 minutes and is not a failing block; sedation, a small dose of ketamine and a conversation about deflation are the answers.

  4. 4 Exposure: arthrotomy, synovectomy, quadriceps snip or tibial tubercle osteotomy

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The old scar is reopened, the arthrotomy repeated, a thick synovectomy done to find the planes, and the gutters and suprapatellar pouch released. If the patella will not translate laterally and the knee will not flex, the surgeon makes a quadriceps snip, or lifts a tubercle osteotomy with the patellar tendon on it. The danger the extensile exposure prevents is the patellar tendon avulsing from the tubercle under the retractor, which is close to unsalvageable.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is the slow, bloody half hour that sets the case length. The quadriceps snip is a cut across a working tendon and the osteotomy is a bone cut under the patellar tendon’s pull: both will hurt with every quadriceps contraction for six weeks, both restrict what the physiotherapist may ask on day 1, and both are the reason the catheter runs beyond the second night. Note which the surgeon did; it changes the brace and the quadriceps instructions.

  5. 5 Component and cement removal

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The femoral component is separated from its cement with thin osteotomes and saws passed along the interface and levered off; the tibial tray is cut free and lifted; cement is removed from the metaphysis and canals with burrs, chisels and ultrasonic tools. The aim is to lose as little bone as possible, and a well-fixed component in osteoporotic bone is where the condyle fractures.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The loss is continuous, hidden under the tourniquet or steady without it, and this is the step in which the first litre goes. A condylar or plateau fracture here converts the plan to a more constrained implant and a longer case; adjust the spinal expectation and the blood plan when it happens. Watch the clock against the agreed tourniquet deflation.

  6. 6 Canal reaming, cones, sleeves and augments

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The femoral and tibial canals are reamed to accept diaphyseal stems that bypass the damaged metaphyseal bone; porous metal cones are impacted into prepared metaphyseal defects, or sleeves broached in, to give the joint-surface components a fixed platform; metal augments make up distal femoral and tibial plateau loss. This is where the registry data show the survival benefit of stems.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Two reamed canals are the marrow embolisation of a bilateral femoral nailing in one knee: the first reamer pass down each canal produces the fall in end-tidal carbon dioxide and saturation that a long bone does, and in a patient with poor right ventricular reserve it is the dangerous moment of the case. Cone impaction is heavy hammering through the metaphysis with a fracture risk of its own. The bone work here is the second mechanism of the pain, and it is more bone than any primary.

  7. 7 Trials, joint line, balancing and the choice of constraint

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Trial stems, cones, augments and components go in; the surgeon sets the joint line to its native level using the fibular head, the epicondyles or the old films, balances the gaps with augments and insert thickness, checks patellar tracking, and chooses the constraint the ligaments demand. A condylar-constrained insert substitutes for an incompetent collateral with a tall post; a rotating hinge takes over when no collateral is reliable, at the cost of transferring every rotational load to the stems.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The retension mechanism is set here and it is harsher than a primary’s: scar tissue that was released will tighten again, and a constrained post or a hinge holds the joint at a tension the capsule resists, so the deep stiff ache that follows is the pain the catheter is for. A hinge means long stems in both canals and a bigger cement step to come. Repeated trial reductions in a spinal patient rock the pelvis and dip the pressure.

  8. 8 Cementing stems, cones and components

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Pulsed lavage, then cement into the metaphyseal regions and onto the joint surfaces, with the stems cemented (full length, with a restrictor and pressurisation), press-fit, or hybrid (cemented metaphysis, press-fit stem). Tibia first, then femur, then the insert, with the knee held in extension until the cement cures.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is the cement step the primary knee does not have: a pressurised cemented stem in a freshly reamed femoral canal is the full bone cement implantation syndrome mechanism of a hip, and a cemented tibial stem adds a second. The preparations in the cement chapter apply in full: pressure supported before the cement goes in, a vasopressor running rather than drawn up, 100% oxygen, and a plan if the end-tidal carbon dioxide falls. The cure time of two components in sequence is 20-25 minutes, when the second tranexamic acid dose goes in and the haemoglobin is checked.

  9. 9 Osteotomy fixation, snip repair, infiltration, drain and closure

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A tubercle osteotomy is fixed back with cerclage wires or screws and protected afterwards; a quadriceps snip is repaired side to side and needs less protection. The surgeon infiltrates the posterior capsule before the final components where it can be reached and the capsular edges at closure; scarred tissue takes the volume unevenly. A drain is usual, the arthrotomy is closed in layers, and a brace may go on for an osteotomy.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Tourniquet release, if the cuff is still up, is the reperfusion of two hours of ischaemic leg: hypotension, a carbon dioxide rise, a potassium and lactate wash, and the infiltrated local anaesthetic arriving in the circulation on top of the catheter loading dose; the ropivacaine arithmetic across block, infiltration and infusion needs doing before the surgeon starts injecting. The bleeding into the joint after release is the second litre in a bad case, and the drain tells you about it overnight. Confirm the brace goes on before the patient lightens, and start the catheter infusion in theatre rather than in recovery.

  10. 10 Recovery, the first week and the quadriceps question

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants early flexion to prevent the scar re-forming, with the limits set by the exposure: free flexion after a standard arthrotomy, protected active extension for six weeks after a tubercle osteotomy, something between after a snip. Full weight-bearing is usual with a stemmed cemented construct.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The trajectory on this card has pain at 3 on the first evening with the catheter running, 6 on days 1 and 2 with physiotherapy, 5 on day 3 and still 4 at a week, which is the shape that makes this a 5. The adductor canal infusion runs for 48-72 hours, which keeps the quadriceps working for the physiotherapy and covers the medial side; the posterior capsule relies on the infiltration and then on the oral regimen. Regular paracetamol and an NSAID (if the kidneys allow it) start in recovery; the opioid is charted for the nights and for physiotherapy sessions, and in an opioid-exposed patient the baseline dose continues with the rescue on top. Ketamine has no guideline support for a primary knee and a reasonable claim here in the opioid-tolerant patient, as author’s judgement. The transfusion decision is usually made on day 1 when the hidden loss declares itself. Stay is three to seven nights, longer with an osteotomy or a complication.

Pain plan

The mechanism is retension of a scarred, constrained joint plus more bone work than any primary, a cut or lifted extensor mechanism, and a long tourniquet, all loaded by physiotherapy from day 1 in a patient who is usually opioid-exposed. The plan has to run for three days, keep the quadriceps working, and not depend on a 2 am oral dose being given. PROSPECT’s primary knee guideline stops at the primary; its skeleton (paracetamol and an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor, adductor canal block, local infiltration, intravenous dexamethasone 10 mg or more, no femoral or sciatic block, no epidural) is the starting point, and the card’s departures from it are the author’s judgement for an operation it does not cover.

The departure that matters is the catheter. A continuous adductor canal block is the default for every revision beyond an isolated polyethylene exchange, because the case runs two to four hours, the pain outlasts a single shot by days, and the only direct comparison showed that with a continuous block in both arms, revision patients consumed the same opioid as primaries over 48 hours while their day 1 pain trended higher and rose with each previous operation on the knee; the catheter is what levelled the courses. The adductor canal catheter keeps the quadriceps working, which matters more after a snip or an osteotomy, not less. An epidural is the alternative for the stiff knee that will be manipulated hard from day 1 and for the patient in whom the catheter cannot be placed; it costs a bladder catheter, hypotension, delayed mobilisation and a conversation about anticoagulant timing, which is why it is second. A femoral catheter gives no more analgesia than the adductor canal and takes the quadriceps away. IPACK is reasonable when the posterior capsule could not be infiltrated.

Rebound pain is the problem of the night the infusion stops rather than the first night; stepping the infusion down rather than off, with the oral regimen running for a day before the catheter comes out, is the practical answer. Escalation: pain above 7 with the infusion running and a quadriceps that fires is a catheter that has migrated (check the site, re-bolus, replace it) before it is a prescription problem; a tense, hugely swollen knee on day 1 is a haemarthrosis and the surgeon’s; a tense calf or numb toes under a block that should only touch the medial leg is a compartment syndrome or a vascular injury until proven otherwise, and the revision knee, with its long tourniquet and its posterior cement removal, is the knee where that happens. A patient who was on long-acting opioids before surgery gets them back on day 0.

Pitfalls and variants

  • Isolated polyethylene exchange. A short case through the old arthrotomy with no stems and no cement: a single-shot adductor canal block, infiltration and a primary-knee plan. Confirm it is really only the insert before the spinal is dosed.
  • Tibial tubercle osteotomy. Better function in the randomised infection-revision comparison, but a healing bone shingle under the patellar tendon: protected extension for six weeks, a brace, a catheter that runs longer, and a tubercle fracture or non-union as the late complication.
  • Quadriceps snip. A quicker exposure with less protection afterwards; the quadriceps is weaker for weeks and the physiotherapy slower.
  • Rotating hinge. Long stems in both canals, the largest cement load, the longest case, and every rotational load on the stems; this is the patient for the arterial line and the full cement precautions.
  • Press-fit versus cemented stems. A press-fit stem means no pressurised cement in the canal but heavy impaction and a fracture risk; end-of-stem pain for months afterwards is a known late problem.
  • Second stage of a two-stage infection revision. The exposure is through a spacer and more scar, antibiotic-loaded cement in large volumes is used, and the pain course starts from a knee already operated on twice; see the infection card.
  • Periprosthetic fracture as the reason for revision. A distal femoral fracture around a loose component is fixed or revised with a distal femoral replacement; the case is longer again and the patient frailer; see the periprosthetic fracture card.
  • The opioid-tolerant patient. Most revisions are; baseline opioid continued, the catheter as routine, ketamine and a pain service plan as reasonable additions, and a week of significant pain stated plainly before surgery.
  • Chronic kidney disease. The NSAID comes out of a regimen that needs it; the catheter and paracetamol carry more, and antibiotic-loaded cement in large volumes is a nephrotoxin.
  • Blood loss. A litre is usual and two is not rare; two doses of tranexamic acid and a blood management protocol took transfusion from 58% to 5% in one revision cohort. Crossmatch, cell salvage where no infection is suspected, and a first-morning haemoglobin.
  • Tourniquet time. Two hours is common and the primary-knee trials already show harm at shorter exposures; agree a deflation point before the start.

Key sources

There is no revision-specific analgesia guideline; PROSPECT’s primary knee guideline is extrapolated and the catheter-as-routine recommendation is the author’s judgement, supported by a single retrospective comparison in which continuous adductor canal blocks levelled the courses of primary and revision patients. The blood loss figures come from a retrospective revision cohort with a historical control. The exposure evidence is a single randomised comparison in infection revisions; the reconstruction evidence is systematic reviews of cones and sleeves and registry data. The pain score and trajectory are calibrated against the primary knee card and are author’s judgement.

  1. Lavand'homme PM, Kehlet H, Rawal N, Joshi GP; PROSPECT Working Group. Pain management after total knee arthroplasty: PROcedure SPEcific Postoperative Pain ManagemenT recommendations. Eur J Anaesthesiol 2022;39:743-757
    The primary TKA guideline, the nearest evidence; paracetamol and NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor, adductor canal block plus local infiltration, IV dexamethasone 10 mg or more, opioid as rescue; femoral and sciatic blocks and epidural not recommended on functional grounds. Revision surgery is outside its scope
  2. Grant AE, Schwenk ES, Torjman MC, Hillesheim R, Chen AF. Postoperative analgesia in patients undergoing primary or revision knee arthroplasty with adductor canal block. Anesth Pain Med 2017;7:e46695
    29 primary and 29 revision knees, all with continuous adductor canal blocks in the same multimodal protocol: 48 h opioid use 53 vs 55 mg IV morphine equivalent, not different; day 1 pain trended higher after revision (4.8 vs 2.8, p=0.06) and rose with the number of previous knee operations
  3. Ortega-Andreu M, Talavera G, Padilla-Eguiluz NG, et al. Tranexamic acid in a multimodal blood loss prevention protocol to decrease blood loss in revision total knee arthroplasty: a cohort study. Open Orthop J 2016;10:439-447
    87 revision knees: two IV doses of TXA within a protocol cut 24 h drain output from 595 to 256 mL, the haemoglobin fall at 48 h from 3.9 to 2.9 g/dL and transfusion from 58% to 5%; tourniquet times about 108 min and operative times 114-136 min in both groups
  4. Bruni D, Iacono F, Sharma B, Zaffagnini S, Marcacci M. Tibial tubercle osteotomy or quadriceps snip in two-stage revision for prosthetic knee infection? A randomized prospective study. Clin Orthop Relat Res 2013;471:1305-1318
    90 patients randomised to tubercle osteotomy or quadriceps snip for exposure at the second stage of a two-stage infection revision: reinfection rates similar; the osteotomy group had better Knee Society scores and range of motion at a minimum of 8 years
  5. AO Recon. Outcomes of revision total knee arthroplasty using metaphyseal sleeves and cones (review compiled from Zanirato 2020 and Roach systematic reviews and the Australian registry)
    Porous metal cones and sleeves give metaphyseal fixation in AORI 2b and 3 defects with a diaphyseal stem; aseptic loosening 2-3%, reoperation 14-19%, new infection 5-9% in the pooled series; registry data link stem extensions to better survival
  6. Ahmed I, Chawla A, Underwood M, et al. Tourniquet use for knee replacement surgery. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2020;12:CD012874
    41 trials, 2,819 patients, mostly primary knees: serious adverse events 59 vs 29 per 1,000 with a tourniquet (RR 1.73) and day 1 pain 1.25 points higher; a two-hour revision inflation is well beyond the trials' exposure
  7. Barry GS, Bailey JG, Sardinha J, Brousseau P, Uppal V. Factors associated with rebound pain after peripheral nerve block for ambulatory surgery. Br J Anaesth 2021;126:862-871
    972 ambulatory block patients: rebound pain in 49.6%; bone surgery OR 1.82, younger age and female sex; absence of IV dexamethasone OR 1.78

Hip and knee › Knee

30 Patellofemoral surgery: PFJ arthroplasty, MPFL reconstruction, tibial tubercle osteotomy

Patellofemoral arthroplasty for isolated patellofemoral arthritis; MPFL reconstruction, tibial tubercle osteotomy and trochleoplasty for patellar instability, alone or combined

4Severe

Dominant mechanism: Bone. Three different operations on one card: a tibial tubercle osteotomy is a cortical bone cut under the patellar tendon that the quadriceps loads with every contraction, and it sets the score; MPFL reconstruction is a hamstring harvest plus a graft set under tension between two drilled tunnels; patellofemoral arthroplasty is a trochlear cut, a patellar cut and cement in a young, lightly loaded joint. Combined procedures stack the mechanisms

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: high.

Block
General or spinal anaesthesia with a single-shot adductor canal block, surgeon infiltration and IV dexamethasone; an adductor canal catheter or an overnight stay for the tubercle osteotomy
Catheter: selective Single shot for isolated MPFL reconstruction and patellofemoral arthroplasty; an adductor canal catheter earns its place for a tubercle osteotomy, a trochleoplasty, and any combined procedure, because the bone-under-tendon-load mechanism outlasts a single shot and the patient is young, female and bone-operated, the three rebound risk factors
Alternatives: Femoral nerve block: not recommended, the quadriceps is what the brace and the rehabilitation depend on; IPACK is not needed for anterior knee surgery; Spinal for the osteotomy in a patient who prefers it; day-case MPFL under general anaesthesia is the norm
Position
Supine, leg on the table with a lateral post or a holder, flexion to 30-90 degrees for tunnels and tensioning; the surgeon moves the knee repeatedly
Tourniquet
Yes. Used by most for the osteotomy and the arthroplasty and by many for MPFL reconstruction; 45-90 min
Cement
Sometimes. Patellofemoral arthroplasty cements a trochlear component and a patellar button, small surfaces, no canal; the instability operations use no cement
Blood loss
Minimal for MPFL reconstruction; 200-400 mL for the osteotomy, mostly into the joint and the anterior compartment after the tourniquet comes down; 200-300 mL for the arthroplasty
Duration
60-90 min for isolated MPFL reconstruction or arthroplasty; 120-180 min for an osteotomy with MPFL reconstruction or a trochleoplasty
Length of stay
Day case for MPFL reconstruction; one to two nights for the osteotomy and the arthroplasty. Day case: selected
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV within 60 min of incision, 3 g over 120 kg, before tourniquet inflation; the graft, the screws and the implant are all foreign bodies
Tranexamic acid
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV before incision for the osteotomy and the arthroplasty; reasonable for MPFL reconstruction, where the haemarthrosis is the main early pain generator
VTE
Mechanical for the day-case patient; chemoprophylaxis for the osteotomy, which is a young patient immobilised in a brace with a cut tibia, and for the arthroplasty
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8-10 mg IV at induction and ondansetron 4 mg IV; the population is young and female and the risk is high
Tell the patient
The ligament operation is sore for a few days and the brace is what protects it; the bone-shift operation hurts much more, mostly when the thigh muscle pulls on the moved bone, and you will be in a brace and on crutches for six weeks.
The trap
Treating the tubercle osteotomy as a sports-knee day case: it is a cortical bone cut that the quadriceps pulls on with every contraction, it hurts more than an ACL reconstruction, and a single-shot block wears off at 2 am in a young woman after bone surgery, which is the rebound pain phenotype

What the surgeon is doing and why

The patellofemoral joint is a sesamoid running in a groove under the pull of the largest muscle in the body. Two diseases bring it to theatre. In the young it dislocates: a shallow trochlea (dysplasia), a tubercle set too far lateral, a patella that sits too high to engage the groove (alta), and a torn medial patellofemoral ligament after the first dislocation combine so that the patella jumps the lateral ridge whenever the quadriceps fires near extension. In the middle-aged, usually after years of maltracking, the joint wears while the tibiofemoral compartments stay good, and the pain is on stairs and on rising from a chair. The operations on this card address each cause in turn, and the surgeon combines them according to which anatomy is at fault.

Medial patellofemoral ligament reconstruction replaces the primary soft-tissue restraint to lateral displacement in the first 30 degrees of flexion. A gracilis or semitendinosus tendon is harvested from the pes anserinus (or an allograft or quadriceps strip used), passed through tunnels or onto anchors in the medial edge of the patella, run deep to the medial retinaculum, and fixed in a tunnel at an anatomic femoral point just anterior and distal to the adductor tubercle, the point that keeps the graft isometric through flexion. The graft is tensioned with the knee at 20-30 degrees, set so the patella can still be pushed a third of its width laterally, and fixed with an interference screw. The femoral point is everything: a tunnel a few millimetres too proximal tightens the graft in flexion, overloads the medial facet and gives a stiff, painful knee. The tendon-tension mechanism here is a graft between two bone tunnels loaded gently by a brace-limited arc; it is a smaller tension load than a cuff repair or an ACL graft because the knee is kept near extension for the first weeks.

A tibial tubercle osteotomy moves the attachment of the patellar tendon. The anterior tibial cortex is cut with a saw in a long oblique plane from the tubercle distally (a Fulkerson anteromedialisation moves the tubercle medially and forward in one cut; an Elmslie-Trillat moves it medially on a flat cut; a distalisation detaches the shingle entirely and moves it down for alta), the shingle with the tendon attached is shifted 8-15 mm, and it is fixed with two or three cortical screws. The periosteum is stripped to make the cut, the cut runs through the thickest cortical bone in the leg, and from the moment the patient wakes the quadriceps pulls on the moved fragment with every contraction. This is a bone cut under load: the mechanism of a high tibial osteotomy, on a smaller scale but on a fragment with a muscle attached to it. In the published cohorts, full weight-bearing waits for six weeks, delayed union occurs in a quarter (42% with distalisation), the screws are painful in a fifth and removed in a quarter, and a tibial fracture through a screw hole is the feared complication.

Trochleoplasty deepens the groove. The surgeon lifts the articular cartilage of the trochlea as a flap on a thin shell of subchondral bone, removes cancellous bone beneath to create a groove, lays the flap back down and fixes it with sutures or anchors. It is reserved for severe dysplasia, done by a few surgeons, and it is cartilage surgery on raw bone in a young patient: a haemarthrosis, a capsule that has been opened widely, and a knee that is stiff and sore for weeks.

Patellofemoral arthroplasty resurfaces the trochlea with a metal onlay (the current generation cuts the trochlea flat with a saw and seats the component on the cut, like the anterior cut of a total knee) and the patella with a cemented polyethylene button, through a medial parapatellar approach with the patella everted. The cruciates and the tibiofemoral compartments are untouched; there is no balancing and no tibial cut. Against a total knee for the same indication, the systematic review finds the same function scores, slightly better flexion, fewer complications (not significant) and a shorter stay, with a revision rate that is not different at five and ten years but carries wide confidence intervals; disease progression in the tibiofemoral compartments is the main reason it fails.

The pain logic depends on which operation is done. Isolated MPFL reconstruction is a 2-3: a hamstring harvest, two drilled tunnels and a graft under modest tension, kept quiet by a brace; the harvest site and the haemarthrosis are the early pain, and it is a day case. Patellofemoral arthroplasty is a 3: a bone cut and cement in an anterior compartment with no balancing and no re-tensioning, a smaller version of the total knee’s bone mechanism in a younger patient. The tubercle osteotomy is a 4 and sets the card’s score: a periosteum-stripped cortical cut that the quadriceps loads with every contraction for six weeks, in a young woman who has often had previous knee surgery, which puts her squarely in the group whose rebound pain after a single-shot block is worst. The Gerbershagen cohort’s lesson applies: the 40 most painful of 179 procedures had median day 1 scores of 6-7 and many were small orthopaedic operations on bone and ligament in the young, with open knee ligament reconstruction at 15th; the size of the incision is no guide to the pain. Combined procedures stack the mechanisms and run two to three hours.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 Which operation, which patient, which plan

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon chooses by the anatomy: MPFL reconstruction alone for instability with normal bony anatomy, an osteotomy added for a lateralised or high tubercle, a trochleoplasty for severe dysplasia, and an arthroplasty for the worn joint. The booking slip may say “patellar stabilisation” for any of these.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Find out whether bone is being cut before the patient is asleep, because that decision is the whole plan: an isolated MPFL reconstruction is a day case under general anaesthesia with a single-shot adductor canal block, infiltration and dexamethasone; an osteotomy or trochleoplasty is an overnight stay with a catheter or a written plan for the second night and chemoprophylaxis; an arthroplasty follows the total knee skeleton. The patient is typically young and female and has often had the knee operated on before; those are the rebound risk factors from the ambulatory cohort (bone surgery OR 1.82, female sex OR 1.52, younger age), and intravenous dexamethasone 8-10 mg is the one thing that lowers them. Spinal anaesthesia is reasonable for the osteotomy and the arthroplasty and unusual for a day-case MPFL reconstruction in a 19-year-old.

  2. 2 Positioning, tourniquet and antibiotic

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Supine with a lateral post or a leg holder so the knee can be flexed to 30 degrees for graft tensioning and to 90 degrees for the tunnels; the osteotomy needs the leg flat with the anterior tibia exposed. A tourniquet is the norm for the osteotomy and the arthroplasty and common for the MPFL reconstruction.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Cefazolin 2 g IV before the cuff. Tourniquet times are 45-90 minutes and the reperfusion at release is modest, but the osteotomy bleeds into the anterior compartment of a young patient’s leg when the cuff comes down, and the tranexamic acid should be in before incision rather than at release. The common peroneal nerve is at the fibular neck beside the osteotomy site and under the lateral post.

  3. 3 Arthroscopy and lateral release

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Most instability and arthroplasty operations begin with an arthroscopy to grade the cartilage, confirm the tracking and treat loose bodies or chondral flaps; a lateral retinacular release or lengthening is added when the lateral structures are tight, less often than it used to be because an isolated release makes instability worse.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Irrigation fluid in the suprapatellar pouch and a haemarthrosis from the release are the early swelling, and they settle. Note the cartilage grade the surgeon calls out: a bare trochlea in a 20-year-old is the knee that gets a trochleoplasty or a later arthroplasty.

  4. 4 Graft harvest for MPFL reconstruction

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The gracilis (or semitendinosus) is harvested through a small incision over the pes anserinus with a stripper, folded double to about 10 cm, and prepared on the back table; a quadriceps tendon strip left attached to the patella is an alternative that avoids the harvest site, and allograft avoids it altogether.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The harvest is the same mechanism as the hamstring harvest for an ACL reconstruction and is the dominant early pain of an isolated MPFL reconstruction: a muscle stripped off its tendon, bleeding into the posteromedial thigh, and sore with hamstring contraction for a fortnight. The infrapatellar branch of the saphenous nerve crosses the harvest site and is cut or stretched in a proportion of patients, which leaves a numb patch over the anterolateral knee that the adductor canal block will mask on day 0. The adductor canal block covers the harvest site.

  5. 5 Patellar and femoral tunnels and graft fixation

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Two blind tunnels or two anchors in the medial patellar edge take the folded graft; the femoral tunnel is drilled at the anatomic point, located on a lateral image with the intensifier, the graft is passed between the layers of the medial retinaculum, tensioned with the knee at 20-30 degrees so the patella still displaces a third of its width, and fixed with an interference screw. The surgeon then runs the knee through its arc to check the graft neither tightens nor slackens.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The image intensifier comes in for the femoral point. A transverse patellar tunnel that breaches the far cortex is a stress riser, and a patellar fracture weeks later is the complication that brings the patient back. The graft set under tension between two tunnels is the tendon-tension mechanism of this operation, but a modest one because the brace keeps the knee near extension and the graft is near-isometric; the retinacular dissection and the haemarthrosis are what hurt on day 1. The surgeon wants the knee held still at the tensioning angle; a twitch here changes the graft tension for good.

  6. 6 Tibial tubercle osteotomy: the cut, the shift and the screws

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Through an anterior incision the periosteum is lifted off the tubercle and the anteromedial tibia, and a saw cut is made from the tubercle distally in an oblique plane 6-8 cm long, thick enough to hold screws and thin enough to hinge; the shingle is shifted medially and forward (or detached and moved down for alta) and fixed with two or three bicortical screws. The surgeon then checks tracking through the arc.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is the bone-under-load mechanism being created: a cortical cut through the thickest bone in the leg, periosteum stripped, and a fragment that the quadriceps will pull on with every contraction from the moment the patient is awake. It is more bone than an ACL reconstruction and it behaves like a small high tibial osteotomy. The anterior compartment starts to fill after tourniquet release; the compartment syndrome risk is small but real, and the block will not hide it if the calf is examined. The screw heads sit under the skin on the front of the tibia and are the commonest reason for a second operation. A fracture through the distal screw hole is the catastrophe, usually after a fall in the brace at six to eight weeks.

  7. 7 Trochleoplasty

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    For severe dysplasia the surgeon lifts the trochlear cartilage on a thin osteochondral flap, excavates a groove in the cancellous bone beneath with a burr, lays the flap into the new groove and fixes it with sutures, vicryl tape or anchors; an MPFL reconstruction nearly always follows in the same sitting.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Raw cancellous bone over a wide area of the distal femur, a joint opened widely, and a cartilage flap that must not be loaded: a haemarthrosis is certain, the pain is bone and capsule for days, stiffness is the main complication, and continuous passive motion or early supervised flexion is the surgeon’s answer to it. This is the second operation on this card that earns a catheter or an overnight stay with a second-night plan.

  8. 8 Patellofemoral arthroplasty: trochlear cut, patellar cut and cement

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Through a medial parapatellar arthrotomy with the patella everted, the trochlea is cut flat with a saw guided off the anterior femoral cortex (or reamed to an inlay in older designs), the patella is cut to leave 12-15 mm of bone, trial components check tracking, and both components are cemented. Nothing is done to the tibia or the cruciates.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    One femoral cut and one patellar cut: the bone mechanism of a total knee without the balancing, the medial release, the tibial cut or the intramedullary rod. Cement on two small surfaces carries no practical bone cement implantation risk. The eversion of the patella and the arthrotomy are the same as a total knee’s and the quadriceps is sore in the same way; the post-operative course is a total knee’s first two days without the retension ache that follows, which is why the stay is shorter.

  9. 9 Infiltration, closure and the brace

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon infiltrates the harvest site, the capsule and the subcutaneous tissues; closes in layers; and fits a hinged brace locked in extension for the MPFL reconstruction, the osteotomy and the trochleoplasty, with flexion released week by week to 90 degrees over four to six weeks. The arthroplasty goes into a total-knee protocol with no brace.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The brace goes on before the patient lightens; a young patient with a numb leg will otherwise flex it. Tourniquet release after a short inflation is unremarkable; the osteotomy bleeds into the anterior compartment and the joint afterwards, and a drain is sometimes used. The local anaesthetic total across the block and the infiltration is far from the ceiling in this population.

  10. 10 Recovery, discharge and the quadriceps

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants isometric quadriceps work from the first week, weight-bearing as tolerated in the brace for the ligament reconstruction and the arthroplasty, protected weight-bearing for six weeks for the osteotomy, and full range of motion by six weeks for all of them. The quadriceps is the structure the rehabilitation is built around; a weak or inhibited quadriceps is a maltracking patella.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The adductor canal block is the right block for every operation on this card because it leaves the quadriceps working; a femoral block has no place in a patient whose rehabilitation is quadriceps activation in a brace. The isolated MPFL reconstruction goes home the same day with a block that lasts 12-24 hours, the oral regimen started in recovery, and a written night plan for the rebound; its trajectory is lower than the card’s, peaking at 4-5 on day 1. The osteotomy stays a night or two with a catheter running 24-48 hours or, where the unit does not run ambulatory catheters, a single shot plus a plan that accepts a hard first night; its trajectory is the card’s, 2 on day 0, 6 on day 1, 5 on day 2, and the quadriceps pulling on the fragment is why it stays at 3 at a week. Regular paracetamol and an NSAID are the backbone; the surgeon’s view on NSAIDs after an osteotomy is worth asking for, because some restrict them for the union and the delayed union rate is already a quarter.

Pain plan

The mechanism depends on the operation and the plan follows it. For isolated MPFL reconstruction the mechanism is a hamstring harvest, two tunnels and a graft under modest tension, so the plan is a day-case one: a single-shot adductor canal block with intravenous dexamethasone, the surgeon’s infiltration, regular paracetamol and an NSAID started before discharge, oral opioid for the first two nights, and the night plan written down. For patellofemoral arthroplasty the mechanism is bone and cement in an anterior compartment with no balancing, and PROSPECT’s total knee skeleton (adductor canal block plus infiltration, dexamethasone, paracetamol and an NSAID, opioid as rescue, no femoral block) applies with a shorter tail. For the tubercle osteotomy and the trochleoplasty the mechanism is bone under load or raw bone under a cartilage flap, in a young patient with every rebound risk factor, and the defensible default is an adductor canal catheter for 24-48 hours or an overnight stay with a plan for the second night; that is author’s judgement, because there is no procedure-specific guideline and no randomised comparison of catheter against single shot for this operation.

The block choice is the same throughout: adductor canal, because the quadriceps is what the brace, the tracking and the rehabilitation depend on, and a femoral block takes it away. The saphenous and vastus medialis territory covers the medial patella, the pes harvest and the anteromedial tibia where the osteotomy is; the lateral side and the tubercle itself rely on the surgeon’s infiltration. IPACK is not needed for anterior knee surgery. Gabapentinoids and ketamine have no evidence here and PROSPECT does not recommend them for the knee; ketamine is a reasonable adjunct in the opioid-exposed patient with several previous operations, which this population often is.

Rebound is the planning target. The osteotomy patient is young, female and has had bone surgery, which in the ambulatory cohort put rebound pain at well over half; the moment the block recedes at 2 am the quadriceps pull on the fragment is unmasked, and a patient without a running catheter or a taken oral regimen will telephone. Escalation triggers: pain above 7 after the block has receded, with a brace correctly fitted, a warm foot and a soft calf, is treated with the charted opioid; a tense anterior compartment, pain on passive toe flexion or numbness in the first web space after an osteotomy is compartment syndrome until proven otherwise, and the adductor canal block does not anaesthetise the deep peroneal territory, so those signs remain readable; a hot, hugely swollen knee at a week is a haemarthrosis or an infection and the surgeon’s.

Pitfalls and variants

  • Combined procedures. Osteotomy plus MPFL reconstruction, or trochleoplasty plus MPFL reconstruction, runs two to three hours, stacks the harvest, the tunnels and the bone cut, and sits at the top of the card’s range; it is the catheter case.
  • Distalisation. The shingle is detached entirely to move the tubercle down for patella alta; delayed union rises to 42% and the fragment is less stable, so weight-bearing is more restricted and the pain tail longer.
  • Quadriceps tendon or allograft MPFL. No pes harvest, so no hamstring pain; the allograft version is the lightest operation on the card.
  • Patellar fracture. Through a transverse tunnel after MPFL reconstruction or a thin patellar cut after arthroplasty; presents weeks later as sudden pain and an extensor lag.
  • Painful hardware. A fifth of osteotomy patients; screw removal is a short second operation under a block, and it is the commonest reason these patients return.
  • The adolescent. Many MPFL reconstructions are in 14-18-year-olds with open physes, in whom the femoral tunnel is placed to spare the distal femoral physis; a paediatric day case with the same block and a parent who needs the night plan explained.
  • Hypermobility and connective tissue disorders. Over-represented in patellar instability; the graft stretches, recurrence is higher, and the patient may carry several previous operations, a chronic pain history and opioid exposure into this one.
  • Patellofemoral arthroplasty conversion. If the tibiofemoral compartments turn out to be worn at arthrotomy the surgeon converts to a total knee; the plan moves to that card and the stay lengthens.
  • NSAIDs and union. Surgeons vary; some restrict NSAIDs after an osteotomy, which removes the main non-opioid from a plan that needs it. Ask before the drug chart is written.

Key sources

No procedure-specific analgesia guideline exists for any operation on this card; PROSPECT’s total knee guideline is borrowed for the arthroplasty and the block choice, and the catheter recommendation for the osteotomy and trochleoplasty is author’s judgement built on the Gerbershagen cohort’s lesson that small bone-and-ligament operations in the young rank among the most painful, and on the rebound pain cohort’s risk factors. The osteotomy complication figures come from a two-centre retrospective cohort and a systematic review of mostly low-quality studies. The arthroplasty comparison is a systematic review of four small trials and five cohorts with wide intervals. The MPFL technique description rests on a published technical note and standard sports surgery texts.

  1. Gerbershagen HJ, Aduckathil S, van Wijck AJ, Peelen LM, Kalkman CJ, Meissner W. Pain intensity on the first day after surgery: a prospective cohort study comparing 179 surgical procedures. Anesthesiology 2013;118:934-944
    50,523 patients, worst pain on day 1 on a 0-10 scale: open calcaneal reduction, spinal fusion and scoliosis surgery ranked highest; open reconstruction of knee ligaments ranked 15th; the 40 highest-ranked procedures had median worst-pain scores of 6-7, and many of them were minor orthopaedic operations on bone and ligament in young patients
  2. Johnson AA, Wolfe EL, Mintz DN, Demehri S, Shubin Stein BE, Cosgarea AJ. Complications after tibial tuberosity osteotomy: association with screw size and concomitant distalization. Orthop J Sports Med 2018;6:2325967118803614
    153 tubercle osteotomies: delayed union 23% (42% with distalisation), painful hardware 21%, reoperation 25% mostly for screw removal, non-union 2%, wound breakdown 2%, DVT 3%, one proximal tibial fracture through a screw hole after a fall at 8 weeks; full weight-bearing at 6 weeks
  3. Saltzman BM, Rao A, Erickson BJ, et al. A systematic review of 21 tibial tubercle osteotomy studies and more than 1000 knees: indications, clinical outcomes, complications, and reoperations. Am J Orthop 2017;46:E396-E407
    1,055 knees, mostly young women with previous knee surgery: pain and outcome scores improve; 21% reoperation for hardware removal
  4. Vella-Baldacchino M, Webb J, Selvarajah B, et al. Should we recommend patellofemoral arthroplasties to patients? A systematic review. Bone Jt Open 2023;4:948-956
    Four RCTs and five cohorts of patellofemoral versus total knee arthroplasty for isolated patellofemoral arthritis: no difference in function scores, better flexion after PFA, fewer complications (RR 0.57, not significant), stay 3.3 vs 4.4 days in cohorts, revision not different at 5 and 10 years but with wide intervals
  5. Raoulis V, Zibis A, Fyllos A, Malahias MA, et al. Reconstruction of the medial patellofemoral ligament using two blind transverse semi-patella tunnels and an implant-free technique for patellar fixation: a technical note. J Orthop Surg Res 2020;15
    Gracilis autograft folded double, femoral tunnel at the Schottle point fixed with an interference screw at 20-30 degrees of flexion, two blind patellar tunnels, graft tensioned so the patella displaces 30-40% of its width laterally; over-tensioning overconstrains the patella; brace locked in extension for a week then to 90 degrees by week 4; patellar fracture through complete transverse tunnels and infrapatellar saphenous branch injury at harvest listed as complications
  6. Lavand'homme PM, Kehlet H, Rawal N, Joshi GP; PROSPECT Working Group. Pain management after total knee arthroplasty. Eur J Anaesthesiol 2022;39:743-757
    The nearest guideline for the arthroplasty on this card: adductor canal block plus local infiltration, IV dexamethasone, paracetamol and NSAID, no femoral block on quadriceps grounds
  7. Barry GS, Bailey JG, Sardinha J, Brousseau P, Uppal V. Factors associated with rebound pain after peripheral nerve block for ambulatory surgery. Br J Anaesth 2021;126:862-871
    972 ambulatory block patients: rebound pain in 49.6%; bone surgery OR 1.82, female OR 1.52, younger age; absence of IV dexamethasone OR 1.78. The tubercle osteotomy patient has all three risk factors

Hip and knee › Knee

31 Knee arthroscopy: meniscectomy, meniscal repair, chondral procedures

Partial meniscectomy, all-inside and inside-out meniscal repair, loose body removal, chondroplasty, microfracture, osteochondral autograft transfer and the two stages of matrix-induced chondrocyte implantation

2Mild to moderate

Dominant mechanism: Arthroscopic surface. Three portals and a joint washed with litres of saline: for a meniscectomy that is all of it, and the pain is a sore, swollen knee for two days. A meniscal repair adds sutures or anchors through the capsule that are loaded by every flexion and a brace; microfracture and an osteochondral autograft add raw subchondral bone, a donor site in the trochlea and weeks of protected weight-bearing, and sit a point higher

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: low.

Block
General anaesthesia with a supraglottic airway and surgeon-delivered intra-articular and portal infiltration; no nerve block for a meniscectomy
Catheter: no No arthroscopic knee procedure earns a catheter; the chondral procedures that hurt most are protected by non-weight-bearing, not by an infusion
Alternatives: Single-shot adductor canal (femoral triangle) block for meniscal repair, microfracture, an osteochondral autograft, the implantation stage of MACI, or the patient who predicts a bad course: motor-sparing, modest, and gone by the next morning; Unilateral spinal with a short-acting agent where general anaesthesia is undesirable, accepting a slower discharge than a general anaesthetic or a peripheral block; Local anaesthetic arthroscopy with sedation in the slim patient with a simple lesion and a quick surgeon; A femoral nerve block gives the same analgesia as an adductor canal block with a quadriceps that does not work, and has no place in a day case
Position
Supine with the thigh in a leg holder and the foot of the table dropped so the knee hangs at 90 degrees, or the leg flat against a lateral post; the surgeon levers the knee into valgus and varus against the holder to open the compartments
Tourniquet
