Sometimes. A thigh cuff is applied by most surgeons and inflated by fewer; the randomised trials show no difference in view, time or complications without it, and the surgeon who inflates it for the whole case is adding cuff pain to a day case for no return
Cement
No
Blood loss
Negligible; the fluid in the suction is irrigation. A lateral release or a synovectomy bleeds into the joint after the cuff comes down and produces the haemarthrosis that brings the patient back
Duration
20-45 min for a partial meniscectomy or loose body; 45-90 min for a meniscal repair or a microfracture; 60-120 min for an osteochondral autograft or the implantation stage of MACI, which is an arthrotomy
Length of stay
Day case for everything on this card. Day case: yes
Antibiotic
Surgeons vary: none for a simple meniscectomy in many units; cefazolin 2 g IV within 60 min of incision (3 g over 120 kg) when anchors, osteochondral plugs or a chondrocyte membrane are implanted
Tranexamic acid
Not needed; some surgeons ask for TXA 1 g IV before a synovectomy or lateral release to limit the haemarthrosis, which is a reasonable request
VTE
Mechanical and early mobilisation only for the patient who walks out; chemoprophylaxis for the patient's own risk factors or for the weeks of restricted weight-bearing that follow a repair or a chondral procedure, by unit protocol
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 4-8 mg IV at induction and ondansetron 4 mg IV; a day-case patient who vomits at home does not take the tablets
Tell the patient
Most people walk out the same day on the leg, are sore and swollen for two or three days and off painkillers within a week; a meniscal repair or a cartilage procedure means crutches and a brace for several weeks, and a few more sore days at the start.
The trap
Reading the booking slip as the operation: a meniscectomy walks out on paracetamol and a block would be for nothing, but a meniscal repair or a microfracture with six weeks on crutches is a different operation through the same portals, and the surgeon decides which it is with the scope in the knee, so the plan has to work for both

What the surgeon is doing and why

The knee is the joint that arthroscopy was built for: two large compartments and a patellofemoral space that a 4 mm scope through an anterolateral portal can see in full, with instruments through an anteromedial portal and the joint kept open by saline. Everything on this card goes through those portals, and that is why a meniscectomy is a 1 and the anchor of the scale. What varies is what the surgeon does inside, and the range runs from trimming a flap of meniscus in twenty minutes to drilling holes in subchondral bone or lifting plugs of cartilage out of the trochlea, which are bone operations wearing arthroscopy’s clothes.

The meniscus is a fibrocartilage ring that spreads load across the tibial plateau and is vascular only in its outer third. A tear in the avascular inner two-thirds will not heal, so the surgeon removes the unstable fragment back to a stable rim (partial meniscectomy): a fast, painless-looking operation whose consequence is a smaller meniscus and more contact stress for the rest of the knee’s life. That consequence is why the operation’s numbers are falling. In the randomised sham-controlled trial in middle-aged patients with a degenerative medial tear and no arthritis, meniscectomy did no better than a skin incision and the sound of a shaver at twelve months. The meniscectomy that remains is for the mechanical tear in a younger knee, the locked knee and the bucket-handle that will not reduce, and the surgeon is increasingly trying to keep the tissue. A tear in the vascular outer third, a root avulsion, or a bucket-handle in a young patient gets a repair: all-inside anchors fired through the meniscus into the capsule, inside-out sutures passed through the meniscus and tied over the capsule through a small posteromedial or posterolateral incision, or a transtibial pull-out suture for a root. The sutures are through capsule and the meniscus has to heal to its rim over weeks, which is why the repaired knee goes into a brace and onto crutches: partial weight-bearing in the first week and full weight-bearing at four to six weeks in most protocols, though the accelerated ones did no worse in the pooled series.

Cartilage is the other reason to be inside. A loose body or a flap of cartilage is removed and the edge trimmed (chondroplasty). A contained full-thickness defect in a young knee is treated with one of three things, in ascending order of what it does to bone. Microfracture perforates the subchondral plate with an awl so that marrow bleeds into the defect and forms a fibrocartilage clot; it is a few minutes of bone work with six weeks of protected weight-bearing to let the clot mature. Osteochondral autograft transfer (OATS, mosaicplasty) harvests cylinders of cartilage and bone from the non-loading margin of the trochlea and presses them into the defect: two bone surfaces, a donor site that gives patellofemoral symptoms in about 6% of knees, and the same weeks of protection. Matrix-induced autologous chondrocyte implantation (MACI) is two operations: a biopsy of cartilage at a first arthroscopy, then weeks later an arthrotomy to glue the cultured cells on a membrane into the prepared defect, which is a mini-open knee with a long rehabilitation and the pain of an arthrotomy, not of a scope. Synovectomy, plica excision and lateral retinacular release are the soft-tissue extras, and the release is the one that bleeds.

The pain logic follows. For a meniscectomy, a loose body or a chondroplasty, the only mechanism is surface: portals, a capsule distended by litres of saline, and fluid in the fat pad and the subcutaneous tissues that makes the knee feel tight for two days. Nothing has been cut that is loaded afterwards, and the patient walks on it that evening. Meniscal repair adds a capsule mechanism (sutures or anchors through the capsule, pulled by every flexion) and a brace, and the small incision of an inside-out repair runs beside the saphenous nerve medially or the peroneal nerve laterally. Microfracture and OATS add bone: a bleeding subchondral plate or a trochlear donor site, which behave like any small osteotomy for two or three days and are then protected by the crutches rather than loaded. None of it reaches the tendon-tension or retension mechanisms that make the ACL reconstruction a 3 or the tibial tubercle osteotomy a 4. The card is a 2 because of the repairs and the chondral work; a straight meniscectomy is the 1 the scale was anchored on.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 Pre-operative plan: the booking, the MRI and the day-case default

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon’s list says “arthroscopy, right knee”; the MRI report and the surgeon’s letter say whether it is a meniscectomy, a repair or a chondral procedure, and the surgeon will often not decide until the scope is in. Everything they want (a relaxed leg to lever into valgus, a view, and a patient who goes home that afternoon) is the same for all of them.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A general anaesthetic with a second-generation supraglottic airway is the default for every procedure on this card in a day-case patient; a unilateral spinal is reasonable when a general anaesthetic is undesirable, and the pooled trials show it costs about forty minutes to discharge readiness and over an hour to voiding against a peripheral block. Decide the block question now, against the worst case the surgeon has described (see the pain plan): no block for a meniscectomy, an adductor canal block offered for a repair or a chondral procedure. Paracetamol and an NSAID before induction. The patient who cannot take an NSAID is the one for whom the block has the most to offer.

  2. 2 Positioning, the leg holder and the tourniquet question

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The thigh is clamped in a holder with the foot of the table dropped, or the leg lies flat against a lateral post, so that the surgeon can apply valgus with the knee near extension to open the medial compartment and the figure-of-four to open the lateral. A thigh tourniquet is applied by habit.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The leg holder is a vice around the thigh above the cuff and the valgus stress is applied through it; a medial collateral ligament sprain from an enthusiastic surgeon in a stiff knee is the positioning injury of this operation, and the contralateral leg needs its own support and padding. The tourniquet is the honest conversation: in sixteen randomised trials and over a thousand patients, no cuff meant less blood loss and less analgesic use, with no difference in the view, the time, quadriceps strength or complications, and in the one trial that randomised inflation the surgeon needed the cuff up in four patients of the non-inflated group. A cuff applied and left down costs nothing; a cuff inflated at 300 mmHg for a 30-minute meniscectomy adds the one mechanism (ischaemia and cuff pain) that the operation otherwise does not have. If a block is planned and the cuff will be inflated, the block goes in before the cuff or at the end, not between the two: an adductor canal block followed immediately by cuff inflation produced quadriceps weakness in eight of a group where the other sequences produced none.

  3. 3 Portals, irrigation and the diagnostic round

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Anterolateral and anteromedial portals beside the patellar tendon, sometimes a superomedial outflow or a posteromedial portal for the back of the joint. Saline runs in by gravity or a pump at 40-80 mmHg to distend the capsule and clear the view; the surgeon inspects the suprapatellar pouch, both compartments, the notch and the cruciates before touching anything, and the diagnosis is made here.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The capsule distending is the first stimulus and a light patient flexes the hip against the holder; the portal incisions are small. The irrigation goes somewhere: into the joint, out of the portals onto the floor, and into the soft tissues around the knee, and over a long case the thigh and calf swell. Extravasation into the calf under a pump is the rare mechanism of a compartment syndrome after a knee scope, and a tense calf at the end of a long case under a working block is examined, not reassured. Adrenaline in the bags is the surgeon’s answer to bleeding when the cuff is down; the transient tachycardia when a new bag goes up is that.

  4. 4 Partial meniscectomy, loose bodies and chondroplasty

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The unstable fragment is resected with a punch and a shaver back to a stable, contoured rim, keeping as much meniscus as possible because every millimetre removed raises contact pressure; a loose body is found and retrieved; an unstable cartilage flap is trimmed to a stable edge. Ten to twenty minutes of work.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Nothing to do but keep the patient still for the surgeon’s lever and note that the booking has resolved into the simplest version of the card. The patient will weight-bear as tolerated from the recovery room, and the pain for the next two days is the swollen joint and the fat pad, not the meniscus, which has no nerve supply in the part that was removed. This is the operation for which a nerve block would be given for nothing.

  5. 5 Meniscal repair

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A peripheral or root tear in a knee worth saving is reduced and fixed. All-inside devices fire a suture with anchors through the meniscus into the capsule from the front; inside-out repair passes long needles through the meniscus and out through the capsule, where the sutures are retrieved and tied over the capsule through a 3 cm posteromedial or posterolateral incision with a retractor protecting the structures behind the knee; a root is fixed with a suture pulled through a tibial tunnel. The surgeon abrades the tear edges and the synovium to bleed, because the repair heals from the vascular rim.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The case lengthens by half an hour, the capsule is now sutured and will be loaded by every flexion for six weeks, and the brace and crutches follow; this is the version that earns the 2 and the adductor canal block. The posteromedial incision sits on the saphenous nerve and its infrapatellar branch, the posterolateral one on the peroneal nerve, and the popliteal vessels lie behind the retractor during inside-out needle passage: a numb medial calf or a foot drop in recovery is surgical anatomy, not the block, which does not reach the peroneal nerve at all. The plan for discharge changes from “walk out” to “crutches, brace and the rehabilitation protocol”, and the patient hears it from the surgeon before leaving.

  6. 6 Chondral procedures: microfracture, osteochondral autograft and the MACI stages

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Microfracture: the defect is debrided to stable walls, the calcified layer removed, and the subchondral plate perforated every 3-4 mm with an awl until marrow bleeds. OATS: cylinders of cartilage and bone are harvested from the trochlear margin and press-fitted into drilled sockets in the defect, usually through a small arthrotomy. MACI: a biopsy of a few hundred milligrams of cartilage from the notch at a first scope, then an arthrotomy weeks later to fix the cultured membrane into the prepared defect with fibrin glue.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Bone, for the first time on this card: a bleeding subchondral plate or two sets of cancellous sockets, which hurt like a small osteotomy for two or three days and then fall quiet under the protection of crutches and, for microfracture, six weeks of restricted weight-bearing. An OATS or a MACI implantation through an arthrotomy is a mini-open knee with a haemarthrosis and an incision through the retinaculum; the adductor canal block covers the medial arthrotomy and the oral regimen has to carry the first two nights. Remember the donor site: the trochlear harvest gives patellofemoral symptoms in about 6% of knees in the pooled series and is the sore spot the patient points to at a week.

  7. 7 Synovectomy, plica, lateral release and the bleeding extras

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    An inflamed synovium or a thickened medial plica is shaved; a tight lateral retinaculum is divided from inside the joint with a radiofrequency device to let the patella track medially. The release cuts the lateral genicular vessels and a raw retinacular edge is left to bleed.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    These are the procedures that produce the tense haemarthrosis at 6 pm: a raw synovial bed or a lateral release that bled only after the cuff came down and the portals closed. A drain is sometimes left; a request for tranexamic acid before the release is reasonable. The pain of a haemarthrosis is pressure and does not respond to opioid as well as it does to the surgeon’s needle.

  8. 8 Intra-articular injection, portal closure and the chondrotoxicity question

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon injects local anaesthetic, often with adrenaline and sometimes a corticosteroid or morphine, into the joint and the portals, and closes the portals with a stitch or a strip. A compressive dressing goes on, and a brace if the meniscus has been repaired.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The injection is the analgesic plan for a meniscectomy, and it works: in the randomised comparison the surgeon’s intra-articular local anaesthetic beat an adductor canal block for pain at one and two hours and matched it after that. Ropivacaine is the agent to prefer; bupivacaine, lidocaine and most corticosteroids are chondrotoxic to cartilage in a dose- and exposure-dependent way, and the chondrolysis literature was built on intra-articular infusion pumps, which have no place in any joint. A single 20 mL dose at the end of the case is a different exposure from an infusion, and a young knee with a fresh cartilage repair is the one where the surgeon’s recipe deserves a glance. Count the total dose if a block has also been given.

  9. 9 Recovery, discharge and the first night at home

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants the meniscectomy walking that afternoon with no restriction; the repair in a brace, partial weight-bearing and range-of-motion exercises from the first week; the microfracture and the chondral graft on crutches with the knee moving but not loaded.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Paracetamol and an NSAID started before the patient leaves, with the first dose at home timed before bed, and a small number of oral opioid doses for the two nights after a repair or a chondral procedure; a meniscectomy patient does not usually need them. The local anaesthetic in the joint lasts into the evening and the knee is at its sorest the next morning, swollen and stiff rather than painful, and ice and elevation are the treatment. A patient going home with an adductor canal block has a leg that works and a numb medial calf that will recover overnight, and is told so. The calls that come back are the haemarthrosis after a release, the calf that is tense rather than sore, and the patient who was told “scope” and sent home with crutches without understanding why.

Pain plan

The mechanism for most of this card is surface, so the plan is the surgeon’s intra-articular and portal infiltration, paracetamol and an NSAID started before induction, and no block. The evidence for adding an adductor canal block to minor arthroscopic knee surgery is real and small: in the pooled trials it lowered resting pain by 1.5 cm at the moment the patient woke and by about half a centimetre at 6 and 8 h, and saved about 7 mg of oral morphine equivalent over 24 h. Against a surgeon’s intra-articular injection it lost at one and two hours and matched it afterwards, with no difference in opioid use. A block that buys half a centimetre on a scale of ten, for an operation whose patients are going home on paracetamol, is the block the scale’s first line describes: for the anaesthetic, not for pain. A landmark-based saphenous injection by the surgeon at the medial condyle, without ultrasound, did nothing at all.

The block earns its place when the operation changes. A meniscal repair, a microfracture, an osteochondral autograft and the implantation stage of MACI all add a mechanism (capsule under suture, or bone) and a night or two of real pain to a patient who is young, cannot bear weight and will not sleep; the author’s practice is to offer a single-shot adductor canal block for these, placed in the femoral triangle rather than the true canal (the femoral triangle injection gave lower pain scores at 12 h with the same quadriceps strength), with 15-20 mL of ropivacaine 0.375-0.5% and intravenous dexamethasone, and to write the oral regimen so that the first doses are in before the block fades the next morning. A femoral nerve block gives the same analgesia and a quadriceps that does not fire, which in a day-case patient on crutches is a fall waiting to happen; the trial that compared the two after meniscectomy found the same pain relief and a better knee score at a month with the adductor canal block. The opioid-tolerant patient, the patient who has had a miserable night after a previous scope, and the patient who cannot take an NSAID are the other three for whom the block is offered regardless of what is found.

No catheter, for anything. Rebound pain is a small problem because the block is small and the surgery is mostly surface; after a chondral procedure in a young patient it is the usual pattern of a sore morning rather than a catastrophic night, and the oral regimen started in recovery covers it. Escalation: pain out of proportion with a tense knee in the first 24 h is a haemarthrosis, usually after a release or a synovectomy, and the surgeon aspirates it; a tense, painful calf is extravasation or a compartment syndrome, rare and surgical; pain with fever and a hot joint from day 3 onwards is a septic arthritis until the aspirate says otherwise.

Pitfalls and variants

  • The surgeon who inflates the cuff for the whole case. The randomised evidence is against it; the cost is cuff pain and quadriceps weakness in a day case that had neither. Raise it once, then put the cuff on and leave the decision to them.
  • The leg holder and the valgus lever. Medial collateral sprain and, in the osteoporotic, a femoral fracture through the holder have both been described; the surgeon’s force, not yours, but the padding and the contralateral leg are.
  • Inside-out repair. A posteromedial or posterolateral incision and long needles passed towards the back of the knee: the saphenous nerve, the peroneal nerve and the popliteal vessels are the things that present to you as numbness, a foot drop or a swelling in recovery.
  • Extravasation and compartment syndrome. Pump pressures above 80 mmHg, long cases, a capsular breach: the calf swells. A tense calf under a working block is examined by pressure measurement, not by waiting for pain.
  • Intra-articular drugs. Ropivacaine rather than bupivacaine, a single dose rather than an infusion, no pain pumps, and a question about the corticosteroid in a knee with fresh cartilage work; the surgeon’s recipe is the surgeon’s, but you count the dose.
  • Local anaesthetic arthroscopy. A 20 mL intra-articular dose with portal infiltration and light sedation is enough for a simple meniscectomy in a slim, calm patient with a quick surgeon; the pump pressure and the lever hurt, and conversion to general anaesthesia with the leg in a holder is awkward.
  • The degenerative meniscus in the middle-aged knee. The sham-controlled trial found no benefit; the operation is still done, the patient’s expectations are the surgeon’s problem, and the pain afterwards is the pain of the arthritis that was already there.
  • Two-stage MACI. The biopsy is a 20-minute scope; the implantation weeks later is an arthrotomy with a long rehabilitation, booked on the same list as a scope and anaesthetised like a mini-open knee, with the block and the opioid plan that implies.
  • Paediatric and adolescent patients. Discoid meniscus saucerisation, osteochondritis dissecans drilling and fixation: the same portals, often a longer non-weight-bearing period, and a parent who needs the night plan.
  • Anticoagulated patients and venous thromboembolism. The operation itself is low risk; the six weeks on crutches after a repair or a chondral procedure is not, and the unit’s protocol decides.

Key sources

The block evidence is a meta-analysis of ten randomised trials and a handful of later trials, consistent with each other: an adductor canal block gives a small, early, motor-sparing benefit after minor arthroscopy, is beaten by the surgeon’s intra-articular injection in the first two hours, and is wasted when done by landmark. The tourniquet evidence is sixteen randomised trials pointing the same way. The rehabilitation statements after meniscal repair come from two systematic reviews that agree there is no consensus; the chondrotoxicity statements rest on the shoulder pain-pump literature and a scoping review of intra-articular drugs, extrapolated to the knee by mechanism rather than by trial. The sham-controlled meniscectomy trial is cited for why the operation is changing, not for anything about its pain. The score and trajectory are the author’s calibration against the Part B scale; the Gerbershagen cohort is not cited because its figures for the individual arthroscopic procedures are in a figure the author could not read.

  1. Sehmbi H, Brull R, Shah UJ, et al. Evidence basis for regional anesthesia in ambulatory arthroscopic knee surgery and anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: part II: adductor canal nerve block, a systematic review and meta-analysis. Anesth Analg 2019;128:223-238
    Ten randomised trials: for minor arthroscopic knee surgery an adductor canal block lowered resting pain by 1.46 cm at 0 h and about 0.5 cm at 6 and 8 h and cut 24 h oral morphine equivalents by 7.4 mg; for ACL reconstruction it gave no benefit over placebo and was no different from a femoral block
  2. Perry M, LeDuc R, Stakenas S, Wozniak A, Francois A, Evans D. Adductor canal nerve block versus intra-articular anesthetic in knee arthroscopy: a single-blinded prospective randomized trial. J Knee Surg 2024;37:220-226
    124 patients: the surgeon's intra-articular local anaesthetic gave lower pain scores than an adductor canal block at 1 and 2 h (2.6 vs 4.0 and 2.2 vs 3.1), the same thereafter, and no difference in opioid consumption
  3. Xin J, Zhang Y, Li Q, et al. Adductor canal block is similar to femoral nerve block for the quality of rehabilitation after arthroscopic partial meniscectomy. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc 2020;28:2334-2342
    150 meniscectomy patients randomised to femoral block, adductor canal block or neither with 30 mL ropivacaine 0.3%: equivalent pain relief, a better knee score at 30 days with the adductor canal block, and the quadriceps spared
  4. Chen B, Tan M, Li Q, et al. Application of ultrasound-guided single femoral triangle and adductor canal block in arthroscopic knee surgery: a prospective, double-blind, randomized clinical study. BMC Anesthesiol 2024;24:182
    20 mL ropivacaine 0.1%: the femoral triangle injection gave lower pain scores at 12 h than the true adductor canal injection, with quadriceps strength preserved in both
  5. Brush PL, Nanavati R, Toci GR, Conte E, Hornstein J. Surgeon-performed saphenous nerve block at the medial femoral condyle for arthroscopic partial meniscectomy and meniscus repair: a randomized control trial. Cureus 2022;14:e26971
    80 patients: a landmark-based saphenous injection by the surgeon without ultrasound made no difference to pain or opioid use at any time point
  6. Zhang L, Tong Y, Li M, et al. Sciatic-femoral nerve block versus unilateral spinal anesthesia for outpatient knee arthroscopy: a meta-analysis. Minerva Anestesiol 2015;81:1359-1368
    Seven trials, 402 patients: a peripheral block got the patient ready for discharge 39 min sooner and voiding 78 min sooner than a unilateral spinal, at the cost of a longer block procedure and more anaesthetic time
  7. Wang J, Xu W, Lv J. Is it better to routinely use tourniquet for knee arthroscopic surgery: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Knee Surg 2020;33:866-874
    16 randomised trials, 1,132 patients: without a tourniquet, less postoperative blood loss and less analgesic consumption; no difference in arthroscopic view, pain scores, quadriceps strength or operating time
  8. Johnson DS, Stewart H, Hirst P, Harper NJ. Is tourniquet use necessary for knee arthroscopy? Arthroscopy 2000;16:648-651
    109 patients randomised to cuff inflated or not: no difference in view, duration, pain, analgesic use or complications; four of the non-inflated group needed the cuff up during the case
  9. Ekinci M, Ciftci B, Demiraran Y, et al. A comparison of adductor canal block before and after thigh tourniquet during knee arthroscopy: a randomized, blinded study. Korean J Anesthesiol 2021;74:514-521
    Block before inflation, after inflation or at the end of surgery: no difference in analgesia or opioid use, but motor block in eight patients when the cuff went up immediately after the block, against none and one in the other groups
  10. Sihvonen R, Paavola M, Malmivaara A, et al. Arthroscopic partial meniscectomy versus sham surgery for a degenerative meniscal tear. N Engl J Med 2013;369:2515-2524

    88 studies: after meniscal repair, range of motion usually starts in the first week, partial weight-bearing in the first week, full weight-bearing at four to six weeks and full range at six weeks; return to play most often at six months
  12. O'Donnell K, Freedman KB, Tjoumakaris FP. Rehabilitation protocols after isolated meniscal repair: a systematic review. Am J Sports Med 2017;45:1687-1697
    15 studies: accelerated protocols with early motion and immediate weight-bearing had the same clinical success as weight- or motion-restricted ones, with no consensus on the ideal restriction
  13. Andrade R, Vasta S, Pereira R, et al. Knee donor-site morbidity after mosaicplasty: a systematic review. J Exp Orthop 2016;3:31
    21 studies, 1,726 patients: donor-site morbidity 5.9% for knee-to-knee osteochondral autograft, mostly patellofemoral symptoms and crepitus, not related to the number or size of plugs
  14. Matsen FA, Papadonikolakis A. Published evidence demonstrating the causation of glenohumeral chondrolysis by postoperative infusion of local anesthetic via a pain pump. J Bone Joint Surg Am 2013;95:1126-1134
    Chondrolysis followed intra-articular infusion of local anaesthetic, with the risk rising with dose: 20 of 48 shoulders on high-flow infusions against 2 of 25 on low-flow, and 11 of 22 on bupivacaine 0.5%; the argument against intra-articular pain pumps in any joint
  15. Pirri C, Sorbino A, Manocchio N, et al. Chondrotoxicity of intra-articular injection treatment: a scoping review. Int J Mol Sci 2024;25:7010
    65 trials: local anaesthetics, with the possible exceptions of ropivacaine and liposomal bupivacaine, and most corticosteroids are chondrotoxic in a dose- and frequency-dependent way; a single intra-articular dose is a different exposure from an infusion

Hip and knee › Knee

32 ACL reconstruction

Hamstring, bone-patellar tendon-bone and quadriceps tendon autografts, with or without lateral extra-articular tenodesis and meniscal repair

3Moderate

Dominant mechanism: Bone. The graft harvest is the dominant early pain: a hamstring tendon stripped from its muscle up the posteromedial thigh, or a bone block sawn from the patella and tibial tubercle, or a strip of quadriceps tendon; then two tunnels drilled through femur and tibia, which is bone and the reason the peak is on day 1 and falls fast. The graft itself is tensioned but then protected, so there is no tendon-under-load mechanism; a lateral tenodesis adds an iliotibial band strip and a lateral incision, and a meniscal repair adds a capsule under suture and a brace

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: high.

Block
General anaesthesia with a single-shot adductor canal (femoral triangle) block, IV dexamethasone, and surgeon-delivered infiltration of the harvest site, portals and tunnel entries; IPACK added for selected patients
Catheter: rarely An adductor canal catheter is for the opioid-tolerant patient, the revision with bone grafting, or the reconstruction that has grown into a multiligament case; the standard day-case ACL does not earn one, and the mechanism is bone that settles in 48 h
Alternatives: Femoral nerve block: the same analgesia as an adductor canal block, a quadriceps that cannot straight-leg raise on the day, a 13% strength deficit still measurable at six weeks, and no place in a day case; IPACK added to the adductor canal block for posterior cover: the combination beat local infiltration alone for 24 h morphine in the one trial and adds nothing to quadriceps function; Spinal anaesthesia with sedation where general anaesthesia is undesirable, with the same block, at the cost of voiding and discharge time; Surgeon infiltration alone, which is the comparator the blocks have been tested against and loses on opioid consumption
Position
Supine with the thigh in a leg holder and the foot of the table dropped, or the leg flat against a lateral post; the knee is hyperflexed past 120 degrees for the femoral tunnel through the anteromedial portal and taken to full extension to set the graft tension
Tourniquet
Sometimes. Applied by most surgeons, inflated by fewer; the pooled randomised trials show pain 0.4 points higher at 24 and 48 h, about 100 mL more drain output and a thinner thigh with the cuff, and no difference in operating time without it
Cement
No
Blood loss
Minimal in the field; a haemarthrosis of 100-300 mL forms after the cuff comes down and the tunnels bleed into the joint, and a drain is unusual
Duration
60-120 min for an isolated reconstruction, depending on graft and fixation; add 20-30 min for a lateral extra-articular tenodesis and 30-45 min for a meniscal repair; revision with tunnel bone grafting is a different, longer operation
Length of stay
Day case in most units; one night for a meniscal repair with a brace, a lateral tenodesis, or a patient without support at home. Day case: yes
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV within 60 min of incision (3 g over 120 kg) and before the cuff if one is inflated; the graft, the buttons and the screws are implants, and some surgeons soak the graft in vancomycin
Tranexamic acid
Not routine; TXA 1 g IV before incision is a reasonable request from a surgeon who wants a smaller haemarthrosis, and the evidence is for comfort rather than transfusion
VTE
Mechanical and early weight-bearing; chemoprophylaxis for the patient's own risk factors (the pill, obesity, previous thrombosis) or for the weeks of restricted weight-bearing after a concurrent meniscal repair, by unit protocol
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV at induction, for the block as much as the nausea, and ondansetron 4 mg IV before emergence; a vomiting day-case patient does not take the night's tablets
Tell the patient
The knee is numb on the first evening and the worst of the pain is the next day, mostly where the graft was taken rather than in the knee itself; it settles fast over three or four days, the tablets taken on time are what keep it that way, and the physiotherapy starts straight away.
The trap
The 2 am rebound: a young, often female patient after bone and tendon surgery with a single-shot block is the exact phenotype in which half of ambulatory block patients go from a 2 to a 7 overnight, and the dexamethasone, the first oral doses before discharge and the written night plan are what stand between the block wearing off and the telephone ringing

What the surgeon is doing and why

The anterior cruciate ligament stops the tibia sliding forward and rotating inward under the femur. When it ruptures, usually in a non-contact pivot in a patient between fifteen and thirty, the knee gives way on cutting and twisting, and each episode of giving way tears a meniscus or shears cartilage. The ligament does not heal; it is replaced. The surgeon harvests a tendon from the same leg, drills a tunnel into the femur at the ligament’s origin and a tunnel through the tibia at its insertion, pulls the graft through both, tensions it with the knee near extension and fixes it at each end, and then waits a year for the graft to turn from a tendon into something like a ligament while the patient rebuilds the quadriceps that the injury switched off. Everything about the pain follows from where the graft came from and from the two tunnels.

The graft is the surgeon’s main choice and the main determinant of what the patient feels on day 1. Hamstring: semitendinosus with or without gracilis, taken through a 3 cm incision over the pes anserinus and stripped from its muscle belly with a tendon stripper passed up the posteromedial thigh, then folded into a four- or five-strand graft. The pain is a muscle and harvest-site pain, an ache and cramping in the back of the thigh, with the infrapatellar branch of the saphenous nerve often cut in the incision. Bone-patellar tendon-bone: the central third of the patellar tendon with a bone block sawn from the patella and another from the tibial tubercle. The pain is bone, at the front of the knee, and the pooled trials put donor-site morbidity (anterior knee pain or difficulty kneeling) at 47% across all grafts, with the odds 69% lower for hamstring and 88% lower for quadriceps tendon than for patellar tendon. Quadriceps tendon: a strip of the tendon above the patella, with or without a patellar bone block, through a short incision, and the least harvest pain of the three. Surgeons choose by the patient’s sport, their own training and the failure data, and the choice arrives on the booking slip.

Two things are commonly added. A lateral extra-articular tenodesis (a strip of iliotibial band passed under the lateral collateral ligament and fixed to the femur, the modified Lemaire) controls the rotational laxity that a single-bundle graft does not, and in the randomised trial of 618 high-risk patients under 25 it cut graft rupture from 11% to 4%, at the cost of a lateral incision and more pain at three and six months. A meniscal repair is done in the same sitting when the meniscus is torn, and it changes the rehabilitation more than the reconstruction does: a brace, restricted weight-bearing and the rules on the knee arthroscopy card.

The pain logic: the dominant mechanism is bone, from two tunnels and, with a patellar tendon graft, two bone blocks, which is why the worst day is day 1 and the fall is fast; underneath it is muscle and harvest-site pain in the thigh for the hamstring graft, a capsule distended by arthroscopy and a haemarthrosis from the tunnels, and the tourniquet if the surgeon inflated it. The graft itself is fixed under tension but is not loaded like a repaired rotator cuff; the surgeon’s rehabilitation protects it for months, so the tendon-tension mechanism that makes rotator cuff repair a 5 is absent. The open ligament reconstruction of the 1990s sat near the top of the 179-procedure cohort on day 1; the arthroscopic operation on this card is a 3, and the thing that makes it feel like a 5 is a block that wears off at 2 am in exactly the patient most likely to rebound. Compare the multiligament reconstruction, which is the same tunnels three or four times over with a catheter and a bed.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 Pre-operative plan: the graft, the day-case default and the night

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon has already chosen the graft, decided whether a lateral tenodesis is going on, and read the MRI for the meniscus; what they want from you is a relaxed leg that can be hyperflexed, a view, and a patient who goes home that evening with a quadriceps that fires.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    General anaesthesia with a supraglottic airway, an adductor canal block placed in the femoral triangle before induction or at the end, intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg, paracetamol and an NSAID before induction, and the surgeon’s infiltration. A spinal is a reasonable alternative in a unit that prefers it, with the same block and a slower discharge. The night plan is written now: this patient is young, the surgery is bone, the block is single-shot, and the rebound cohort says half of them will go from comfortable to a 7 overnight unless the oral regimen is already running. Decide the IPACK question with the surgeon’s list in front of you (see the pain plan).

  2. 2 Examination under anaesthesia, positioning and the tourniquet

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    With the patient asleep the surgeon confirms the diagnosis by Lachman and pivot-shift tests that a guarding patient would not allow, then sets the leg in a holder with the foot of the table dropped or against a lateral post, so that the knee can be taken from full extension to beyond 120 degrees of flexion.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The examination is a rotational force on an unprotected knee and the first stimulus; the leg holder is a clamp on the thigh above the cuff. The tourniquet is applied by habit and the evidence is against inflating it: in the pooled randomised trials the cuff added 0.4 points of pain at 24 and 48 h, 100 mL to the drain, and took 1.8 cm off the thigh circumference, with no saving in operating time. If it is inflated it goes up after the block and not immediately after it, and the harvest site and the tunnels bleed into the joint when it comes down.

  3. 3 Graft harvest

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Hamstring: a small oblique incision over the pes anserinus, the sartorial fascia opened, semitendinosus identified, freed from its bands to the medial gastrocnemius, and stripped off the muscle with an open or closed stripper passed up the thigh; gracilis the same if a second tendon is wanted. Patellar tendon: a longitudinal anterior incision, the central third of the tendon marked, and bone blocks cut from the patella and the tubercle with a small saw and an osteotome. Quadriceps tendon: an incision above the patella and a strip of tendon taken with a harvester, with or without a patellar plug. The graft goes to the back table to be prepared and sized while the surgeon moves inside the joint.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is the mechanism the patient will describe. The stripper is a blind instrument passed up the posteromedial thigh beside the saphenous nerve and the muscle belly, and a premature amputation of the tendon (the stripper cutting it short) adds time and a second graft. The patellar saw is bone work at the front of the knee and the step with the rare patellar fracture. The infrapatellar branch of the saphenous nerve crosses the hamstring incision and its numbness is the commonest permanent sequel of the operation. This is also where the surgeon’s infiltration earns its place: ropivacaine into the harvest site and along the stripper’s track at the end of the case is the part of the pain the adductor canal block covers least well for a hamstring graft, and covers best for the anterior incision of a patellar or quadriceps graft.

  4. 4 Arthroscopy, notch preparation and the meniscus

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Standard portals, a diagnostic round, the torn ligament remnant debrided or preserved as a stump, the intercondylar notch cleared of soft tissue so that the femoral origin can be seen, sometimes a notchplasty. The menisci are examined and a ramp lesion behind the medial meniscus or a root tear is repaired now, before the graft is in.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Irrigation and time. A meniscal repair here changes the discharge plan to a brace and crutches and adds a capsule mechanism to the pain; it is the moment at which an IPACK or a night in hospital becomes reasonable, and it is announced from the scope, not from the booking.

  5. 5 Femoral tunnel

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The tunnel must enter the femur at the ligament’s anatomical origin on the inner wall of the lateral condyle. Through the anteromedial portal the surgeon hyperflexes the knee past 120 degrees so that the guide pin exits the lateral thigh safely away from the peroneal nerve and the vessels, then drills a socket to the graft’s diameter and a narrower channel through the far cortex for a suspensory button. Transtibial and outside-in techniques reach the same spot from different directions.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The hyperflexion is the position that matters: the leg holder or the assistant forces the knee closed, the foot comes towards the buttock, and the guide pin and drill pass out through the lateral thigh. Bone is drilled here for the first time, and the pressure and heart rate will say so in a patient whose block has not taken. The stimulus is brief.

  6. 6 Tibial tunnel

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A guide is set in the footprint of the ligament on the tibial plateau and a pin drilled from the anteromedial tibia, often through or beside the hamstring harvest incision, up into the joint; the tunnel is reamed to the graft diameter.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The second bone cut, and the one closest to the surface and to the harvest site; the tibial tunnel entry is a sore spot the patient points to at a week. The surgeon will want the knee at 90 degrees and still. Marrow and blood from the tunnel start the haemarthrosis.

  7. 7 Graft passage, tensioning and fixation

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The graft is pulled through the tibial tunnel into the femoral socket and fixed on the femur, usually with a suspensory button flipped on the lateral cortex, sometimes with an interference screw. The knee is cycled through its range to settle the graft, then held near full extension with tension applied by hand or a tensioner while an interference screw or a staple fixes the tibial end. The surgeon checks that the knee reaches full extension without the graft impinging on the notch, and that the Lachman test is now firm.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The retension mechanism is created here, but it is a ligament set to a tension and then protected rather than loaded, and the brace or the crutches shield it; this is why the pain falls after day 2 rather than persisting. A graft that is too tight or impinges is the surgeon’s problem now, and an unexpected return to the scope to trim the notch means fifteen more minutes.

  8. 8 Lateral extra-articular tenodesis

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A 5 cm lateral incision over the distal iliotibial band, a 1 cm strip of the band detached proximally and left attached at Gerdy’s tubercle, passed under the lateral collateral ligament and fixed to the femur with a staple or anchor with the knee in flexion and neutral rotation. It is added for the young patient with a high-grade pivot shift, generalised laxity or a pivoting sport, and for revisions.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A second incision, a second fixation into bone and 20-30 min; the lateral side of the knee is outside the adductor canal block’s territory and inside the surgeon’s infiltration. In the randomised trial the tenodesis group had more pain at three months and on the KOOS at six, so the patient who had one and still hurts at the twelve-week review is not unusual.

  9. 9 Infiltration, closure, tourniquet release and the haemarthrosis

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon infiltrates the harvest site, the portals and the tunnel entries with ropivacaine, with or without an intra-articular dose; closes the harvest incision in layers; applies a compressive dressing and cryotherapy. A brace is a surgeon’s choice for an isolated reconstruction and a rule after a meniscal repair or a tenodesis.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Count the ropivacaine: 20 mL in the block and 20-40 mL in the infiltration is a total to know in a 50 kg athlete. If the cuff was up, release brings the haemarthrosis and the fall in pressure; the knee that is tense and painful in recovery after a bloodless case is bleeding from the tunnels and the harvest bed, and a bulky dressing and ice are the surgeon’s answer. The first oral doses go in before the patient leaves recovery.

  10. 10 Recovery, discharge and the first week

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants full extension from day 1, quadriceps activation, weight-bearing as tolerated for an isolated reconstruction, and physiotherapy that starts within days; a knee that stays bent and swollen becomes a stiff one and the cyclops lesion that brings it back for an arthroscopic release.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The adductor canal block with dexamethasone lasts 12-24 h; the trajectory on this card has pain at 2 that evening and 5 on day 1 with the oral regimen running, falling to 2 by a week. The night plan is explained to the patient and the parent or partner in words: the leg will wake up in the small hours, the first tablets have already been taken, the next dose is at the bedside, and the opioid is for the night and the morning after. A straight-leg raise before discharge is the proof that the right block was used; a patient who cannot lift the leg has had a femoral block or a block that has tracked proximally, and goes home on crutches with a locked brace and a warning. A hot, tense knee from day 3 to 10 is a septic arthritis until the aspirate says otherwise; a calf that is sore rather than tense is examined and the threshold for an ultrasound is low in a patient on the pill or on crutches.

Pain plan

The mechanism is bone plus a harvest site, with a day 1 peak and a fast fall, in a patient who is young, often female and going home with a single-shot block: a plan built for the first night and the morning after, not for a week. The block question has two honest answers that have to be held together. In the meta-analysis of ambulatory knee surgery, an adductor canal block gave no measurable benefit over placebo after ACL reconstruction and was no different from a femoral block; the authors asked for trials in the setting of infiltration and harvest-site analgesia, which is where the later trials went. In those, a femoral triangle block with IPACK cut 24 h morphine from 17 to 9.7 mg against the surgeon’s infiltration alone, and the adductor canal block was non-inferior to the femoral block for morphine and pain while preserving a quadriceps that could contract at two and a half times the strength at 45 min. The block therefore earns its place as the motor-sparing way to deliver what a femoral block delivers, on top of infiltration, not as a technique with a large effect of its own.

The femoral block argument is the one to have with a colleague who still uses it. The analgesia is the same. The cost is a quadriceps that does not fire on the day the surgeon wants it to: a 13.4% lower strength symmetry index and a worse symptom score at six weeks in the randomised comparison, a 13% rate of prolonged motor or sensory disturbance in another, and no difference by six or nine months. Add the rebound signal from the spinal trial, where a femoral block gave less pain at 6 h and more pain from day 3 to day 7, and the day-case straight-leg raise that it abolishes, and the adductor canal block wins on everything except the length of the needle. The one dissenting result is a retrospective cohort of 230 femoral and 30 adductor canal blocks that found a larger fast-extension deficit at six months in the adductor canal group; it is small, non-randomised and alone, and it does not change the plan. The saphenous nerve itself is at risk in this operation from the hamstring incision more than from the needle: in 28,196 blocked knee operations there were 18 saphenous injuries, eight after ACL reconstruction with autograft, and the block was the likely cause in five.

The defensible default, then, is a single-shot adductor canal block in the femoral triangle with 15-20 mL of ropivacaine 0.5%, intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg, the surgeon’s infiltration of the harvest site, portals and tunnel entries, paracetamol and an NSAID started before induction, and an oral opioid for two nights. The author’s practice is to add an IPACK (20 mL ropivacaine 0.2%) for the patient who has had a posterior meniscal repair, the opioid-tolerant, and the one going home a long way from help; the Lausanne trials show the combination beats infiltration for opioid use without touching quadriceps function, and that a selective tibial nerve block does the same job. A catheter is for the revision with bone grafting, the reconstruction that has become a multiligament operation, and the patient whose previous knee surgery ended in a bad week.

Rebound pain is the planning target. In the ambulatory cohort it occurred in half of all block patients; bone surgery (OR 1.82), female sex (OR 1.52) and younger age raised the odds and intravenous dexamethasone lowered them (its absence OR 1.78). This operation and this patient tick every box, and the dexamethasone, the first doses before discharge and the written plan are the three interventions that change the night. Escalation: pain above 7 on the first morning with a quadriceps that fires and a soft calf is treated with the opioid that was charted and a check that the regular doses were taken; a tense, hot knee from day 3 is infection until proven otherwise; a calf that is swollen is imaged; pain that is worst at the pes anserinus with a hamstring cramp is the harvest site and settles with heat, gentle stretching and time.

Pitfalls and variants

  • Graft choice is the pain choice. Hamstring: thigh ache and cramp, a numb patch below the knee, and the least kneeling pain; patellar tendon: anterior knee pain and a patellar fracture risk, with donor-site morbidity four times that of a quadriceps graft; quadriceps tendon: the quietest harvest. The booking slip tells you which.
  • Lateral tenodesis. A second incision outside the block’s territory, bone fixation, 20-30 min and a knee that hurts for longer at three and six months in the trial that proved its value; the infiltration has to reach it.
  • Concurrent meniscal repair. Brace, crutches, restricted weight-bearing, a night in hospital in some units, and the IPACK or a longer-acting plan; decided from the scope.
  • The tourniquet. Inflated for the whole case it adds pain at 24 and 48 h and a thinner thigh, which in an athlete whose rehabilitation is the quadriceps is the wrong direction; the conversation is had once, and the cuff goes on either way.
  • Femoral block in a day case. The same analgesia, a leg that cannot straight-leg raise, a six-week strength deficit and a fall risk on the stairs at home; the adductor canal block replaces it.
  • Paediatric and adolescent patients with open physes. Physeal-sparing or all-epiphyseal techniques, a longer operation, a parent who needs the night plan, and the same rebound phenotype.
  • Revision reconstruction. Old tunnels filled with bone graft in a first stage, allograft or a contralateral harvest, a longer and bloodier case; this is the ACL that earns a catheter or a night.
  • Infection. Rare, and more often after hamstring grafts; some surgeons soak the graft in vancomycin. A hot knee in the second week is aspirated, not reassured.
  • Arthrofibrosis and the cyclops lesion. A knee that will not straighten at six weeks is the surgeon’s complication and the manipulation card’s patient; an operation done on a swollen, stiff knee too soon after the injury is the usual cause.
  • Opioid prescribing to the young. A two-night supply with a stop date is the right prescription; the harvest site does not need a week of opioid, and the adolescent athlete is the patient in whom a leftover box does harm.

Key sources

The block evidence is contradictory on its face and consistent on inspection: the pooled ambulatory trials found no benefit from an adductor canal block over placebo after ACL reconstruction, while the trials that compared it with a femoral block found non-inferior analgesia with a working quadriceps, and the Lausanne trials found that a femoral triangle block with IPACK beat infiltration for opioid use. The reading on this card, that the block is the motor-sparing way to deliver a modest effect on top of infiltration and dexamethasone, is the author’s reconciliation. The quadriceps data are randomised and short-term; nobody has shown a lasting deficit. The graft morbidity figures are from a network meta-analysis of randomised trials, the tenodesis data from one large randomised trial, and the tourniquet data from seven small ones. The Gerbershagen ranking refers to open ligament reconstruction and is cited for perspective, not for a number on this card.

  1. Sehmbi H, Brull R, Shah UJ, et al. Evidence basis for regional anesthesia in ambulatory arthroscopic knee surgery and anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: part II: adductor canal nerve block, a systematic review and meta-analysis. Anesth Analg 2019;128:223-238
    Ten randomised trials: for ACL reconstruction an adductor canal block gave no analgesic benefit over control and was no different from a femoral nerve block on any outcome; for minor arthroscopy it gave a modest early benefit. The authors call for trials in the setting of local infiltration and harvest-site analgesia

Hip and knee › Knee

35 Knee manipulation under anaesthesia and arthroscopic arthrolysis

Manipulation for stiffness after total knee arthroplasty; arthroscopic lysis of adhesions with manipulation; open arthrolysis and quadricepsplasty as the rare escalation

3Moderate

Dominant mechanism: Capsule. Immature adhesions in the suprapatellar pouch, the gutters and the fat pad torn by force, with a haemarthrosis from the raw surfaces; underneath it the re-tensioned joint of the primary arthroplasty pushed through an arc it has not used for weeks, hourly, from the afternoon of surgery. No bone is cut, so the pain is sharp with movement and settles in days

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: high.

Block
Spinal anaesthesia, or general anaesthesia with full neuromuscular block, plus a single-shot adductor canal block with IV dexamethasone; the physiotherapy that afternoon is the operation
Catheter: selective An adductor canal catheter (or a low-dose epidural in a unit that runs them on a mobilising patient) for the knee with more than 30 degrees to recover, the second manipulation, the late manipulation beyond three months, any arthrolysis, and the patient whose stiffness came with pain out of proportion; a single shot with a written physiotherapy plan for the early manipulation of a mildly stiff knee
Alternatives: Low-dose epidural infusion for 1-3 days with daily physiotherapy, the technique in the one published series for refractory stiffness; Femoral nerve block: tolerable here because the quadriceps is not asked to lift on day 0, but it delays the active flexion that holds the range; General anaesthesia with a short-acting relaxant and no block for the 10-minute manipulation of a mildly stiff knee, with the oral regimen loaded before the patient wakes
Position
Supine on a flat table with the leg unstrapped; the surgeon stands at the side with the hip flexed to 90 degrees and the knee clear of the table edge. Arthroscopy adds a thigh holder with the knee over the end of the table
Tourniquet
Sometimes. None for a manipulation; some surgeons inflate one for arthroscopic arthrolysis because the fibrous tissue they are resecting is vascular and fogs the view
Cement
No
Blood loss
Nil measured for a manipulation, but the torn adhesions bleed into the joint and a haemarthrosis is expected; arthrolysis loses irrigation fluid rather than blood, and the haemarthrosis afterwards is larger
Duration
5-15 min for a manipulation; 45-90 min for arthroscopic arthrolysis with manipulation; open arthrolysis runs to the length of a revision exposure
Length of stay
Day case or one night for a manipulation; 1-3 nights for arthrolysis or a catheter-based plan. Day case: selected
Antibiotic
None needed for a closed manipulation of a healed wound; cefazolin 2 g IV (3 g over 120 kg) before any arthroscopic or open arthrolysis, because instruments are going into a joint that contains an implant
Tranexamic acid
Not routine; tranexamic acid 1 g IV before the manipulation is a reasonable surgeon's request to limit the haemarthrosis and has no trial behind it
VTE
Mechanical prophylaxis and immediate mobilisation; a patient still inside the chemoprophylaxis window of the index arthroplasty continues it, and a 10-minute procedure does not restart a full course for the patient beyond it
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV at induction and ondansetron 4 mg IV; the patient has to do physiotherapy that afternoon, and vomiting costs range
Tell the patient
The manipulation itself takes minutes and you will feel nothing; the knee will be swollen and sore for a few days afterwards, and the bending you do with the physiotherapists from this afternoon onwards is what keeps the movement we have won.
The trap
The manipulation is over in minutes and the range it gains is lost over the following 48 hours if the knee is not bent through it; the anaesthetic has to deliver a fully relaxed leg for the surgeon and a patient who can do physiotherapy that afternoon and the next morning, and a plan that stops at the recovery room has missed the point of the operation

What the surgeon is doing and why

A knee replacement heals by scar, and a knee that is not moved while it heals scars shut. The suprapatellar pouch, which has to glide 5 cm over the femoral component for the knee to flex, obliterates; the medial and lateral gutters fill; the fat pad fibroses to the front of the tibial tray and tethers the patellar tendon; the posterior capsule, if the knee was never fully straightened, shortens. The patient arrives at six weeks with a knee that flexes to 70 or 80 degrees against a hard end point. Acquired stiffness affects about 3.6-4.0% of knee arthroplasties and manipulation is performed in 2.6-3.6% of them (3.4% in a national database of over half a million knees, cemented and cementless alike). The risk factors in the case-control data are the patient’s rather than the surgeon’s: diabetes, smoking, a pre-operative range under 100 degrees, and youth (age 65 or over was protective, OR 0.17), so the patient on this list is younger than the average arthroplasty patient.

Stiffness is a diagnosis of exclusion. Before the surgeon books a manipulation they have excluded infection (inflammatory markers and an aspiration), component malposition or oversizing, instability, patella baja and a mechanically blocked knee, because manipulating any of those gains nothing and risks a fracture. What is left is arthrofibrosis: immature scar in a joint that was built correctly. The surgeon’s reasoning is mechanical. Young adhesions tear at a force well below the force that breaks the distal femur or avulses the patellar tendon from the tubercle; mature scar does not. That gap is the timing window. Manipulation within 6-12 weeks gains the most range; in a cohort of 84 stiff knees the gain was 28 and 30 degrees when treated within three and six months of the arthroplasty and 21 degrees beyond six months, and every review since 2010 has said the same thing in different numbers. Past three months the surgeon is weighing a smaller gain against a higher fracture risk, and past six they usually move to arthroscopic arthrolysis, which cuts the scar rather than tearing it.

The manipulation itself is a controlled tear. With the patient fully relaxed, the surgeon flexes the hip to 90 degrees, puts a hand on the proximal tibia close to the joint so the lever arm is short, and flexes the knee slowly and steadily, feeling and often hearing the adhesions give in the pouch and the gutters, pausing at each new end point, and stopping when nothing more yields or when the resistance changes character from fibrous to bony. A long lever at the ankle multiplies the moment at the supracondylar femur, which is how the fractures happen, and a sudden jerk is how the patellar tendon comes off the tubercle. If there is a flexion contracture, the heel goes on a bolster and the surgeon presses the distal femur towards the table to stretch the posterior capsule. In the largest cohort, 344 knees manipulated at a mean of 2.9 months, the range improved by 36 degrees and the gain held at five years; the complication rate was 2.3%, and the list of complications (haematoma, wound dehiscence, infection, tibial tubercle fracture, patellar tendon rupture) is the list of what force does to a healing knee.

Arthroscopic arthrolysis is the escalation for the knee that is too late, too tight or has failed one manipulation. Through standard portals the surgeon resects the fibrous mass in the suprapatellar pouch and both gutters with a shaver and a radiofrequency probe, frees the fat pad from the tibial tray and the patellar tendon from the anterior tibia, sometimes releases the posterior capsule, and then manipulates a knee whose scar has already been divided. The gain is the same as manipulation alone (24.8 against 25.4 degrees in the direct comparison), the complication rates are similar, and open arthrolysis gains less than either. Revision arthroplasty for stiffness is the last resort and the worst performer: in the pooled literature 43% of stiffness revisions needed further treatment against 25% of arthroscopic releases and 17% of manipulations, which is why the surgeon tries the small operation first and early.

The pain logic follows from what is torn. The dominant mechanism is capsule: adhesions ripped off the pouch and gutters leave raw, bleeding synovial surfaces and a haemarthrosis, sharp with movement and settling in days, with no bone cut and no tendon repaired. Beneath it is the re-tensioned joint of the primary arthroplasty, pushed hourly through an arc it has not used since surgery; that deep ache is familiar from the first week after the index operation. The score is 3: a block or neuraxial technique is expected, the worst pain is on days 1 and 2 when the knee is being bent through the haemarthrosis, and it falls quickly because nothing is being loaded through a cut. The rebound risk is high for a reason specific to this operation: when a single-shot block recedes at 2 am and the patient stops moving, the price is the range that was won that morning. Manipulated patients end up with less flexion than uncomplicated knees (114 against 125 degrees in one matched cohort) and a higher five-year revision rate (7.5% against 2.7%), which is the measure of how much there is to lose.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 The decision: exclusion, timing and what the surgeon wants

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon manipulates only a knee that is stiff for want of movement, inside the window in which scar tears before bone breaks, and only if the physiotherapy afterwards can be delivered. The booking should carry three things: the current range, the range they expect to reach, and the plan for the afternoon.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Ask for all three. A knee at 75 degrees being taken to 110 is a 10-minute day case with a single-shot block; a knee at 50 degrees at four months, or a second manipulation (which gains about half as much as the first), is a knee with a lot to lose overnight and the catheter conversation starts here. Confirm the inflammatory markers and aspiration have been done, because a manipulation in an infected knee is the operation nobody wanted. Confirm the chemoprophylaxis status from the index operation, which sets the neuraxial timing and the size of the haemarthrosis to expect. Note the bone quality, the steroid history and the age: the fracture risk is an osteoporotic risk, and the patient with rheumatoid disease on prednisolone is the one some surgeons will not manipulate at all.

  2. 2 Anaesthetic technique: a fully relaxed quadriceps and a patient who can bend the knee by lunchtime

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A guarding quadriceps is the force path that breaks the femur: the surgeon is pushing against the muscle rather than the scar, applies more force to get through it, and the force arrives at the supracondylar bone and the tubercle. The surgeon needs a leg with no tone at all for five minutes and then a patient who can flex actively within hours.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Two techniques deliver the first requirement and they differ on the second. A spinal gives perfect relaxation and a quiet patient, and its motor block then delays active physiotherapy by two to four hours; a short-acting or low-dose spinal with no intrathecal opioid narrows that gap. A general anaesthetic with full neuromuscular block (rocuronium, with sugammadex to reverse it completely before the patient wakes) gives the same flaccid leg, a fast wake and an afternoon session two hours later; a general anaesthetic without a relaxant, deepened until the leg goes limp, is the technique in which the surgeon pushes against tone and should be avoided. The author’s practice for a day-case manipulation is the general anaesthetic with full block and an adductor canal block placed before induction with intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg; the spinal is kept for the patient who prefers it or whose airway argues for it. The adductor canal block is chosen over a femoral block because the physiotherapist will ask for active flexion and a straight-leg raise that afternoon. There is no trial of anaesthetic technique for manipulation; this is judgement.

  3. 3 Position, the table and the range measured asleep

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon needs the leg free of straps and the knee clear of the table edge, a flat table so the hip can be flexed to 90 degrees, and a first measurement of range under anaesthesia, which is often 10 degrees more than the clinic figure because the patient is no longer guarding.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Unstrap the leg, take the foot off any footplate and protect the contralateral leg from the surgeon’s weight. The airway in a general anaesthetic has to tolerate the surgeon leaning on the pelvis, which argues for a supraglottic device checked with the hip flexed or a tracheal tube.

  4. 4 The flexion manipulation

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Slow, sustained flexion with the hand high on the tibia and the lever short; the adhesions in the pouch and gutters give with a palpable and audible tearing, the surgeon holds at each new end point for the scar to yield rather than the bone, and stops when the end point turns hard. A sudden jerk or a long lever at the ankle is the mechanism of a supracondylar fracture, a tibial tubercle avulsion or a patellar tendon rupture, and an osteoporotic femur or a recent tubercle osteotomy raises the risk.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Confirm full neuromuscular block before the surgeon starts, not when they comment on the leg; a train-of-four count of zero is the standard for this step in a general anaesthetic. Under a spinal the block height needs to reach the hip flexors, which it will. The manipulation is the one nociceptive moment of the operation and a lightly anaesthetised patient will show it with a pressure and heart rate rise; a brief deepening at the request is correct. Listen: the tearing of adhesions is a series of crepitant releases, a single loud crack followed by a knee that suddenly flexes freely with a soft, abnormal end point is a fracture or an avulsion, and the surgeon will stop and ask for an image intensifier or a radiograph in recovery. A bleeding haemarthrosis begins now.

  5. 5 The extension manipulation and the posterior capsule

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A flexion contracture of more than 10 degrees is addressed with the heel on a bolster and firm pressure over the distal femur, stretching the posterior capsule and the hamstring insertions. The surgeon is more cautious here because the posterior capsule is thick, mature scar yields poorly, and the force goes through the femoral component into the distal femur.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The same requirements: no tone, a short period of deep anaesthesia, and a watch for the crack. Extension loss is also the component of stiffness the physiotherapists find hardest to hold, which is an argument for the catheter when the contracture was the main problem.

  6. 6 Measurement, injection, dressing and no splint

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon measures and records the range achieved, which is the target for the physiotherapist; some inject the joint with local anaesthetic and a corticosteroid, some aspirate the haemarthrosis, and most apply a light dressing with no brace of any kind because the knee has to move within hours. Some put the leg straight onto a continuous passive motion machine in recovery.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Reverse the block completely and wake the patient promptly; this is a case where a 20-minute delay in recovery is a 20-minute delay in the first physiotherapy session. Give the ondansetron. If the surgeon injects local anaesthetic into the joint, add it to the day’s ropivacaine arithmetic alongside the block.

  7. 7 Arthroscopic arthrolysis

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    For the late, the very tight and the previously manipulated knee, the surgeon divides the scar before manipulating it: anterolateral and anteromedial portals, often a superolateral portal to reach the pouch, resection of the fibrous mass in the suprapatellar pouch and the gutters with a shaver and a radiofrequency probe, release of the fat pad from the tray and of the patellar tendon from the anterior tibia, and sometimes a posterior capsular release from inside the joint. The instruments are working next to a polyethylene insert and a metal femoral component, so the surgeon is slow and careful, and the vascular scar bleeds into the view. The manipulation follows with the scar already cut.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is a 45-90 minute arthroscopy of a joint that contains an implant: cefazolin 2 g IV before the knife, a tourniquet in some hands, litres of irrigation and a cold patient, and a larger haemarthrosis afterwards because divided scar bleeds more than torn scar. The pain afterwards is the manipulation’s pain plus portals and a distended joint, and a spinal, if one was chosen, has to be dosed for the length. This is the case in which the author places an adductor canal catheter as routine, because the patient has already failed the small operation once and the stakes for the first 48 hours are higher.

  8. 8 Open arthrolysis and quadricepsplasty

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Rare, and done when the stiffness is extra-articular or the arthroscope cannot reach it: the old arthrotomy is reopened, the pouch and gutters are cleared under direct vision, the quadriceps is freed from the femur, and for the knee that will not flex because the extensor mechanism is short a V-Y quadricepsplasty lengthens the tendon, or the stiffness is treated by revision of oversized or malrotated components. The exposure is that of a revision and the quadriceps has been cut.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is a different operation wearing the same booking: 90-150 minutes, real blood loss, a quadriceps that has been lengthened and will be weak and painful for six weeks, and a catheter as routine, with the revision card’s plan rather than this one’s. A quadricepsplasty also changes what the physiotherapist may ask on day 1, and the surgeon’s instructions on active extension need to reach the ward.

  9. 9 Recovery, the first physiotherapy session and the first night

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants the knee taken through the new arc the same afternoon and several times a day thereafter, either by a physiotherapist or on a passive motion machine, because the torn surfaces will re-adhere within days if left still. The first 48 hours decide whether the manipulation worked.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The first physiotherapy session happens within two to four hours of the manipulation, so the block has to be working and the patient awake, not nauseated and not sedated. The trajectory on this card has pain at 3 that evening with the block working, 5 on day 1 and 4 on day 2 when the knee is being pushed through the haemarthrosis, and 2 at a week. Regular paracetamol and an NSAID go in before the block recedes; the oral opioid is charted for the nights and for 30 minutes before each physiotherapy session, which is the one timing that matters; and the night plan is explained before the patient leaves recovery, because the patient who wakes in pain at 2 am and lies still until morning has lost range by the time the physiotherapist arrives. Observations on the first evening are for the complications that force produces: a knee that will not straight-leg raise is a patellar tendon or tubercle avulsion until proven otherwise, a knee that is tense and far more painful than expected is a haemarthrosis or a fracture, and both need the surgeon and a radiograph that evening.

  10. 10 Discharge and the week

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Day case is reasonable for an early manipulation of a mildly stiff knee with a physiotherapy session completed before discharge, daily outpatient physiotherapy booked and the patient able to do the exercises alone; otherwise one to three nights. The range is checked at a week and at six weeks, and a knee that has drifted back may be manipulated again, with a smaller gain the second time.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The written plan for the week: regular analgesia for five to seven days, the opioid before exercise sessions rather than after, ice and elevation for the haemarthrosis, and the exercises themselves. A catheter patient goes home with the pump if the unit runs ambulatory infusions, or stays until it comes out and the oral regimen has carried a day of physiotherapy. Pain that rises through the week rather than falling, or a knee that becomes hot, is an infection or a haematoma and is the surgeon’s.

Pain plan

The mechanism is torn capsule and synovium with a haemarthrosis, loaded by deliberate hourly flexion from the first afternoon, so the plan is not built to make the patient comfortable at rest; it is built to make a specific afternoon and a specific next morning possible. The skeleton is the primary arthroplasty guideline’s, extrapolated because PROSPECT does not cover manipulation: paracetamol and an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor started before the block recedes, a single-shot adductor canal block, intravenous dexamethasone, and opioid as rescue, with the femoral block and the epidural deprecated on functional grounds. For a manipulation the functional argument is the whole argument: the adductor canal block preserves the quadriceps the physiotherapist needs for active flexion and a straight-leg raise, which is also the test that detects an avulsed tendon.

The catheter decision is author’s judgement on thin evidence. The one series that used a continuous technique, 65 refractory knees manipulated under an epidural that was then run for one to three days with continuous passive motion and daily physiotherapy, gained 31 degrees and succeeded in 74%, and it also recorded a subdural haematoma and a fatal pulmonary embolism, which is the cost of an epidural in a patient who then does not walk. An adductor canal catheter does the same job for the medial knee without the bladder catheter, the hypotension or the immobility, and the author’s practice is to place one for the knee with more than about 30 degrees to recover, the second manipulation, the late manipulation, every arthrolysis, and the patient whose stiffness came with pain out of proportion, in whom the stiffness and the pain are the same disease. For the early manipulation of a mildly stiff knee a single shot with a written physiotherapy plan is enough, and the day case is reasonable.

Rebound is the specific hazard. In the ambulatory block cohort rebound pain occurred in half of all patients, more in the young and in women and less with intravenous dexamethasone on board. What it costs here is range, so the night plan (the oral regimen started before the block recedes, the opioid timed before exercises, a passive motion machine where the unit has one) is part of the operation. Escalation triggers: pain above 7 with a soft knee and a working straight-leg raise is a prescription problem; pain above 7 with a tense, hot, hugely swollen knee is a haemarthrosis and may need aspiration; any loss of active extension is an extensor mechanism injury until the surgeon says otherwise; a crack during the manipulation followed by pain on weight-bearing is a supracondylar or tubercle fracture and the radiograph is taken before discharge, not at the first clinic visit.

Pitfalls and variants

  • The late manipulation.
