Beyond three months the gain is smaller (about 21 degrees against 28-30 degrees earlier) and the scar is tougher, so the force is higher and the fracture risk with it; many surgeons move to arthroscopic arthrolysis, which is a longer case with a bigger haemarthrosis and the catheter case on this card.
  • The second manipulation. Gains about half of the first (16.8 degrees in the French cohort); the patient has already lost one afternoon’s range to a bad night and the plan should assume the catheter.
  • Osteoporosis, steroids and rheumatoid disease. The fracture risk is a bone-quality risk; the surgeon may limit the force, image the knee first, or decline. Steroid cover applies as usual.
  • Flexion contracture as the main problem. The extension manipulation is the harder one to hold and the posterior capsule is not covered by any anterior block; the surgeon’s intra-articular injection and the oral regimen carry it.
  • The painful stiff knee and complex regional pain syndrome. Stiffness with allodynia, colour change and pain out of proportion is a different disease; the epidural series was built for these patients, a catheter and the pain service are both reasonable, and manipulation without a plan for the pain afterwards makes it worse.
  • Anticoagulation. Patients inside the chemoprophylaxis window bleed a larger haemarthrosis and the neuraxial timing rules apply; a patient on long-term anticoagulation needs it paused for an arthrolysis but not necessarily for a closed manipulation, which is the surgeon’s call.
  • Arthroscopy in a joint with an implant. Cefazolin before incision, instruments kept off the polyethylene, and a lower threshold to call a hot knee in the following week an infection.
  • Stiffness after ligament reconstruction or fracture. The same technique on a native knee with a cyclops lesion after an anterior cruciate reconstruction or after a plateau fixation; the fracture risk is in the healing bone rather than the supracondylar femur, and the surgeon often prefers an arthroscopic release first.
  • The day case. Reasonable for the early manipulation with a session done before discharge, daily outpatient physiotherapy booked and a written night plan; not for the arthrolysis or the catheter patient unless the unit runs ambulatory infusions.

Key sources

The surgical evidence is level III and IV throughout: cohorts and systematic reviews of cohorts, consistent on the timing window, the size of the gain and the low but specific complication rate. The one series of a continuous analgesic technique is an epidural cohort of 65 knees from 2006 with two serious complications. There is no trial of anaesthetic technique for manipulation and no procedure-specific analgesia guideline; the block choice is extrapolated from PROSPECT’s primary arthroplasty guideline on functional grounds, and the catheter advice and the general-anaesthetic-with-full-block preference are the author’s judgement from the mechanism and are labelled as such.

  1. Hosanee S, Elebo N, Sikhauli N, Pietrzak JRT. Reluctant knee: understanding and managing stiffness after total knee arthroplasty. Int Orthop 2026;50:2337-2346
    Narrative review: acquired idiopathic stiffness in 3.6-4.0% of knee arthroplasties and manipulation in 2.6-3.6%; stiffness is a diagnosis of exclusion once infection, malposition and instability are ruled out; manipulation within 6-12 weeks gains more range than later; escalation to arthrolysis or revision when it fails
  2. Peretó Villaescusa G, Coelho A, Grillo G, et al. Management of stiffness after total knee arthroplasty: influence of intervention timing and surgical technique on clinical outcomes. Eur J Orthop Surg Traumatol 2026;36
    84 stiff knees, 52 manipulated and 32 arthroscopic arthrolyses: range gain 24.8 versus 25.4 degrees, no difference; gains of 28 and 30 degrees when treated within 0-3 and 3-6 months against 21 degrees beyond 6 months
  3. Roullet CA, Descamps S, Monadjemi S, et al. Manipulation under anesthesia for stiffness after total knee arthroplasty: a French multicenter study with 5 years' follow-up including 344 cases. Orthop Traumatol Surg Res 2025;112:104432
    344 manipulations at a mean of 2.9 months after arthroplasty: range improved by 36 degrees and held at 5 years; a second manipulation gained 16.8 degrees; complications 2.3% (haematoma, wound dehiscence, infection, tibial tubercle fracture, patellar tendon rupture); satisfaction 77.5%
  4. Haffar A, Goh GS, Fillingham YA, Torchia MT, Lonner JH. Treatment of arthrofibrosis and stiffness after total knee arthroplasty: an updated review of the literature. Int Orthop 2022;46:1253-1279
    40 studies: arc above 90 degrees in 70% of manipulation studies, 71% of arthroscopic lysis studies and 30% of revision studies; further treatment for stiffness needed in 17% after manipulation, 25% after arthroscopic lysis and 43% after revision
  5. Fitzsimmons SE, Vazquez EA, Bronson MJ. How to treat the stiff total knee arthroplasty? A systematic review. Clin Orthop Relat Res 2010;468:1096-1106
    20 mostly level IV studies: gains after manipulation and after arthroscopy with or without manipulation are similar, open arthrolysis gains less; manipulation works best early but still works late; arthroscopy with manipulation remains useful a year after the index arthroplasty
  6. Pariente GM, Lombardi AV, Berend KR, Mallory TH, Adams JB. Manipulation with prolonged epidural analgesia for treatment of TKA complicated by arthrofibrosis. Surg Technol Int 2006;15:221-224
    65 refractory stiff knees manipulated under an epidural continued for 1-3 days with continuous passive motion and daily physiotherapy: range 71 to 102 degrees, 74% successful, 14% later revised; two serious complications, a subdural haematoma and a fatal pulmonary embolism
  7. Day W, Maloy GC, Rubin LE, et al. Incidence, timing, and implications of postoperative manipulation under anesthesia following cemented versus cementless total knee arthroplasty. J Arthroplasty 2026;41:1267-1271
    567,715 arthroplasties in a national database: manipulation within six months in 3.4% of both cemented and cementless knees; five-year revision 7.5% after manipulation against 2.7% without
  8. Issa K, Rifai A, Boylan MR, Pourtaheri S, McInerney VK, Mont MA. Do various factors affect the frequency of manipulation under anesthesia after primary total knee arthroplasty? Clin Orthop Relat Res 2015;473:143-147
    156 manipulated knees in 3,182 arthroplasties, case-control: age 65 or over protective (OR 0.17); diabetes (OR 1.72), smoking (OR 1.59), high cholesterol and pre-operative range under 100 degrees raised the odds
  9. Issa K, Kapadia BH, Kester M, Khanuja HS, Delanois RE, Mont MA. Clinical, objective, and functional outcomes of manipulation under anesthesia to treat knee stiffness following total knee arthroplasty. J Arthroplasty 2014;29:548-552
    145 manipulated knees against 1,973 that were not: mean flexion gain 33 degrees; final range 114 against 125 degrees, with no difference in Knee Society scores at a mean of 51 months
  10. Lavand'homme PM, Kehlet H, Rawal N, Joshi GP; PROSPECT Working Group. Pain management after total knee arthroplasty: PROcedure SPEcific Postoperative Pain ManagemenT recommendations. Eur J Anaesthesiol 2022;39:743-757
    The primary arthroplasty guideline, extrapolated here: paracetamol and NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor, single-shot adductor canal block, local infiltration, IV dexamethasone, opioid as rescue; femoral and sciatic blocks and epidural not recommended on functional grounds. Manipulation is outside its scope
  11. Barry GS, Bailey JG, Sardinha J, Brousseau P, Uppal V. Factors associated with rebound pain after peripheral nerve block for ambulatory surgery. Br J Anaesth 2021;126:862-871
    972 ambulatory block patients: rebound pain in 49.6%; bone surgery OR 1.82, female OR 1.52, younger age; absence of IV dexamethasone OR 1.78

Hip and knee › Knee

36 Quadriceps and patellar tendon repair

Acute repair by transosseous tunnels or suture anchors; augmentation; chronic reconstruction with autograft or allograft; the extensor mechanism rupture after knee arthroplasty

4Severe

Dominant mechanism: Tendon under tension. A retracted, usually degenerate tendon pulled back onto a decorticated, bleeding patellar pole and locked there under tension with heavy sutures, then loaded by every quadriceps contraction, every transfer and every step for six weeks; the torn retinaculum repaired on either side; plus drill tunnels through the patella and a tourniquet

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: high.

Block
Spinal anaesthesia or general anaesthesia with a single-shot adductor canal block and IV dexamethasone; surgeon's infiltration of the wound edges and retinaculum
Catheter: selective An adductor canal catheter for the bilateral rupture, the chronic reconstruction with a graft, the repair after knee arthroplasty, and the opioid-tolerant or dialysis-dependent patient; a single shot with a written night plan for the acute unilateral repair in a braced leg that will not be bent for weeks
Alternatives: Femoral nerve block: acceptable for this operation because the quadriceps is braced in extension and not asked to work, at the cost of a numb, weak leg in a locked brace on the first night; General anaesthesia with infiltration only for the short acute repair in a young patient when a block is declined; Epidural for the bilateral repair in the patient who cannot have two catheters
Position
Supine, leg flat on the table with a bump under the ipsilateral buttock in some hands; the surgeon needs full extension for the repair and the ability to flex the knee to 60-90 degrees to test it
Tourniquet
Sometimes. A thigh tourniquet is common for the exposure but it tethers the retracted quadriceps and makes the tendon harder to bring down to the patella, so surgeons inflate it with the tendon pulled distally, or let it down for the reduction, or do without
Cement
No
Blood loss
100-300 mL; the fracture-like haematoma is evacuated at exposure and the decorticated pole bleeds after tourniquet release
Duration
60-90 min for an acute unilateral repair; bilateral repairs and reconstructions with a graft run to 2-3 h
Length of stay
Day case to two nights; the older comorbid quadriceps patient stays, the young patellar tendon patient often goes home. Day case: selected
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV within 60 min of incision (3 g over 120 kg), before the tourniquet; anchors and heavy non-absorbable sutures are implants
Tranexamic acid
Not routine; tranexamic acid 1 g IV before incision is a reasonable request for a bilateral repair or a reconstruction
VTE
Mechanical prophylaxis and chemoprophylaxis by unit protocol for the six weeks in a brace: venous thromboembolism ran at 0-15% in the pooled quadriceps repair series, and the typical patient is obese, immobile and comorbid
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV at induction and ondansetron 4 mg IV; the single intra-operative dose is not a tendon-healing concern on current evidence
Tell the patient
The tendon has been stitched back onto the kneecap and locked straight in a brace; the knee will ache hard for the first few days and then every time the leg is loaded for about six weeks, and the brace is what protects the repair while it heals.
The trap
This is a tendon repaired under tension, not a knee that has had a bone cut: the first night is the easy part, the pain is re-provoked for six weeks by every step in the brace, and the patient who tore the tendon has the disease that makes tendons tear, so expect diabetes, renal failure, steroids or a fluoroquinolone in the history and plan the NSAID, the dexamethasone and the dialysis timing accordingly

What the surgeon is doing and why

The extensor mechanism is a single chain, quadriceps to quadriceps tendon to patella to patellar tendon to tibial tubercle, and it fails at whichever link is weakest for that patient. The two tendon ruptures are different diseases that get the same operation. The quadriceps tendon tears in the older, heavier man, at a mean age of 61 and a body mass index of 30 in the largest series, through a tendon that was already degenerate: in the zone of poor blood supply just above the patella, in a patient with diabetes, renal failure, gout, hyperparathyroidism, long-term corticosteroids, or a recent fluoroquinolone, after a trivial load such as a stumble on a stair. The patellar tendon tears in the younger man, mean age 39.5, under a high eccentric load with the knee flexed, in a tendon that is usually healthier but may carry a tendinopathy or a previous graft harvest. Both are 91-95% male. The two things the anaesthetist needs from that sentence are that the quadriceps patient has the comorbidities that make tendons fail, and that a woman with either rupture almost always has an underlying medical disease (96% in the series), which may not have been diagnosed yet. In dialysis patients the quadriceps and patellar tendons account for three quarters of spontaneous ruptures, and frailty, years on dialysis, a high calcium-phosphate product and a recent quinolone predict them; after knee arthroplasty, testosterone replacement, fluoroquinolones and smoking do.

The injured knee cannot extend against gravity, there is a palpable gap, and the patella sits low (quadriceps rupture) or high (patellar tendon rupture) on the lateral radiograph. The diagnosis is missed at first presentation in a surprising fraction, which matters because the tendon retracts and the muscle shortens, and a repair that is easy at a week is a reconstruction at six. The surgeon’s aim is simple: put the tendon end back onto the bone it came from, at a tension that restores full active extension without over-tightening the patella into the trochlea, and hold it there for the six to twelve weeks that tendon takes to heal to bone.

The sequence, for either tendon, is:

  1. Midline incision over the gap, evacuation of the haematoma, and identification of the torn tendon end and of the medial and lateral retinaculum, which tear with it in a complete rupture (that is why the knee cannot extend at all rather than weakly).
  2. Debridement of the frayed, degenerate tendon end to healthy tissue, which in the older quadriceps rupture can remove a centimetre and increase the gap.
  3. Preparation of the patellar pole: the proximal pole for a quadriceps rupture, the distal pole for a patellar tendon rupture, decorticated with a burr or rongeur to a bleeding cancellous surface, because tendon heals to bone and not to cortex.
  4. Fixation. Two or three heavy non-absorbable locking sutures (Krackow stitches) run up and down the tendon so the tension is shared along its length; then either three longitudinal drill tunnels through the patella with the suture ends passed through and tied over the opposite pole, or two or three suture anchors in the pole with the sutures tied down onto the tendon. The cadaveric studies show anchors form a smaller gap under cyclic load (0.9-4.1 mm against 2.9-10.3 mm for a transpatellar patellar tendon repair) with a similar load to failure, and the clinical reviews show no difference in re-rupture (0-17% with tunnels, 0-15% with anchors) or function. Transosseous tunnels remain the commoner technique, anchors are increasing, and the choice is the surgeon’s.
  5. The tendon reduced onto the pole with the knee in full extension and the sutures tied under tension; the retinaculum repaired on both sides, which adds to the strength more than it appears to; sometimes an augmentation (a cerclage of suture tape or wire from patella to tubercle, or a strip of tendon) to protect the repair while it heals.
  6. The repair tested by flexing the knee to the angle at which it gaps, usually 60-90 degrees, which sets the limit the brace will allow in the first weeks.
  7. Closure over no drain, and a hinged brace locked in extension. Weight-bearing is allowed in the brace from day 1; flexion is restricted and advanced over six weeks; active extension against resistance waits longer.

A chronic rupture (beyond about six weeks) is a different operation: the retracted tendon will not reach, and the surgeon reconstructs with hamstring autograft, Achilles allograft or synthetic mesh, often with a quadriceps lengthening, over two to three hours. The rupture after knee arthroplasty is worse again: direct repair of a patellar tendon rupture around an implant failed in 63% of pooled cases, which is why those patients get a reconstruction with allograft or mesh instead, and they are older, heavier (mean body mass index 34.5 in the European review) and more comorbid than any other patient on this card.

The pain logic is tendon-tension, which puts this operation in a different family from the arthroplasty whose anaesthetic skeleton it borrows. A degenerate tendon has been pulled back onto a raw, bleeding bony pole and locked there with sutures under tension, and from the first transfer out of bed it is loaded by every quadriceps contraction, including the ones the patient makes to steady the leg in its brace. The retinacular repair is loaded the same way. Underneath it is bone, from the decorticated pole and the drill tunnels, which hurts for two or three days and then settles, and a tourniquet. The score is 4: the first night with a block working is unremarkable, the peak is on day 1 and 2 as the block and the infiltration recede and the patient starts moving, and the ache is re-provoked by loading for weeks, so a single-shot block covers the easy part. It is not a 5 because the knee is held still: nobody bends it on day 1, the brace takes most of the load off the repair, and by a week most patients are on simple analgesia and the opioid is for sleep.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 Diagnosis, the patient behind the tendon, and the timing

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants the tendon repaired within a week or two of the injury, before retraction and muscle shortening turn a repair into a reconstruction; it is urgent, not an emergency, and a quadriceps rupture in a dialysis patient waits for a dialysis session rather than the reverse.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The assessment is of the disease that tore the tendon. For the quadriceps rupture: diabetes and its control, chronic kidney disease or dialysis (timing of the last session, potassium, the calcium-phosphate axis and the frailty that goes with years of dialysis), long-term corticosteroids needing cover, gout, hyperparathyroidism, a recent fluoroquinolone course, obesity with its airway and positioning consequences, and anticoagulants in a population where atrial fibrillation is common. A woman with either rupture needs a medical cause looked for if none is known. For the patellar tendon: a young, fit patient, sometimes a bodybuilder on anabolic steroids or testosterone, who will be the rebound pain phenotype. Bilateral simultaneous rupture, which happens in the steroid, renal and gout patients, means a patient who cannot stand at all afterwards and a different plan for both the anaesthetic and the ward. The NSAID decision is made here, because the typical quadriceps patient has the kidneys that forbid it.

  2. 2 Anaesthetic plan: spinal or general, the block, dexamethasone

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon needs a still, fully relaxed leg while the retracted tendon is brought down and tied, a dry field for the suture work, and a patient who can stand in a locked brace the next morning.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A spinal with sedation or a general anaesthetic are both reasonable; the spinal suits the older comorbid quadriceps patient and the general anaesthetic the young patellar tendon patient who wants to go home, and neither has evidence over the other for this operation. The analgesic skeleton is borrowed from the arthroplasty guideline because there is none for tendon repair: paracetamol and an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor where the kidneys allow, a single-shot adductor canal block with intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg, surgeon’s infiltration, and opioid for rescue. The adductor canal block is the author’s default because the patient will stand and transfer in the brace with a quadriceps that fires, which is safer than a femoral block’s numb, weak leg in a locked brace, and because the brace does the job of keeping the quadriceps quiet that the femoral block would otherwise do. A femoral block is acceptable for this operation in a way it is not for an arthroplasty. The single dose of dexamethasone has no evidence of harm to a tendon repair and prolongs the block; it is given.

  3. 3 Positioning, the tourniquet and the retracted quadriceps

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Supine with the leg flat, because the repair is tied in full extension; a tourniquet on the thigh gives a dry field for the suture work but compresses the quadriceps bunched up proximally and tethers it, so that a retracted tendon which would reach the patella with the muscle free will not reach with the cuff up. Surgeons inflate the cuff with the tendon pulled distally, let it down for the reduction, or do without.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Cefazolin 2 g IV before the cuff. The tourniquet time is short, 45-75 minutes, and tourniquet pain through a spinal arrives at the end of it, if at all. Full relaxation matters at the reduction (a general anaesthetic needs neuromuscular block here, a spinal supplies it) because a quadriceps with tone pulls against the surgeon bringing the tendon down and the repair is tied under more tension than it needs. Pad the heel and the contralateral leg; the obese quadriceps patient on a flat table for an hour and a half is a pressure-area patient.

  4. 4 Exposure, haematoma and debridement of the tendon end

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The midline incision opens a haematoma that has been under tension since the injury; the torn tendon end is found retracted, frayed and, in the older patient, visibly degenerate, and it is trimmed back to tissue that will hold a suture. The torn retinaculum on either side is identified for repair later.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The first bleeding of the case, modest under a tourniquet and steady without one. The debridement is the step at which the surgeon learns whether this is a repair or a reconstruction: a tendon that is trimmed back 2 cm and will not reach the pole with the muscle freed means a lengthening or a graft and an extra hour, and the catheter conversation reopens here.

  5. 5 Preparation of the patellar pole and the tunnels or anchors

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The pole is decorticated to bleeding bone, then either drilled with three parallel longitudinal tunnels for the suture ends, or fitted with two or three anchors. Tunnels through a small patella risk a fracture through the drill holes, particularly in the osteoporotic patient; anchors avoid the tunnels but can pull out of poor bone.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is the bone step: a raw cancellous surface and drill holes through the patella, which is the component of the pain that settles in 48 hours and the reason the operation qualifies as bone surgery in the rebound cohort’s terms. Nothing to do but note that a patient with a fractured patella from the drill holes has just acquired a longer case and a tension-band fixation.

  6. 6 Locking sutures, reduction and the repair under tension

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Heavy locking sutures are run along the tendon, passed through the tunnels or anchored, and tied with the knee in full extension and the tendon pulled down onto the pole; the retinaculum is repaired; the surgeon then flexes the knee to find the angle at which the repair gaps, and that angle sets the brace limit. The tension is the point: a lax repair leaves an extension lag and a tight one over-compresses the patella and re-tears.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The leg must not move while the knots go down; a working spinal or full block delivers this without being asked. The mechanism this card is built on exists from this moment: tendon on bone under tension, loaded by every contraction from tomorrow. The test flexion is a brief, sharp nociceptive stimulus that a lightly anaesthetised patient will show. If the surgeon augments with a cerclage, there is more bone work at the tubercle.

  7. 7 Closure, infiltration and the brace

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Layered closure over no drain, infiltration of the wound edges and retinaculum where the surgeon does it, a bulky dressing, and a hinged brace locked at zero degrees that the patient will wear day and night for the first weeks.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Tourniquet release, if the cuff was up, brings the usual reperfusion dip and the bleeding from the decorticated pole; a vasopressor to hand. Add the surgeon’s infiltration to the block in the ropivacaine arithmetic. The brace goes on before the patient lightens, because an awake patient with a dense block and a leg that feels like someone else’s will try to bend it. Give the ondansetron.

  8. 8 Recovery, the first night and standing in a brace with a blocked leg

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Weight-bearing as tolerated in the locked brace from day 1 is the usual instruction, with crutches; no active extension against resistance, no flexion beyond the brace setting, and the brace worn in bed.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The trajectory on this card is 3 on the first evening with the block working, 6 on day 1 and 5 on day 2 as the block recedes and the patient starts transferring, 4 on day 3 and 3 at a week. The regular paracetamol and NSAID (or paracetamol alone, in the renal patient) go in before the block recedes; the opioid is charted for the nights and for the first transfers; and the night plan is explained, because the first night at home or on the ward is when rebound arrives, in half of ambulatory block patients, more in the young and in those without dexamethasone. The first stand is the hazard with a block still working: a numb leg in a locked brace is a fall risk, and the physiotherapist is told which block was done. Observations: a knee that cannot be actively extended against gravity when the block has gone and the brace is off for the check is a failed repair; a tense, hot wound over the next week in a diabetic or renal patient is an infection, which is the common serious complication in the patellar tendon series.

  9. 9 The six weeks and what fails

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The brace is unlocked in stages (commonly 30 degrees more flexion every two weeks), active extension is allowed from about six weeks, and the repair is protected from a fall or a forced flexion throughout. Re-rupture (0-17% in the pooled series), arthrofibrosis, an extension lag, wound infection and venous thromboembolism are the complications.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The pain tail is a tendon tail: an ache with each day’s loading that outlasts the bone pain by weeks, which is why the oral regimen is written for ten days rather than three, with the opioid reserved for sleep after the first week. Venous thromboembolism in a braced, immobile, obese patient with renal disease or diabetes is the medical complication of this operation and the chemoprophylaxis plan is for six weeks, not the inpatient stay. The patient who returns with a re-rupture gets a reconstruction, the longer and more painful operation on this card.

Pain plan

The mechanism is a tendon repaired under tension on a decorticated bone surface and loaded for six weeks, with the loading limited by a brace, in a patient who is either young and fit (patellar tendon) or old, heavy and comorbid (quadriceps). There is no procedure-specific guideline. PROSPECT’s knee arthroplasty guideline is the nearest and its skeleton transfers: paracetamol with an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor where the kidneys allow, a single-shot adductor canal block, surgeon’s infiltration, intravenous dexamethasone and opioid as rescue. The adductor canal block covers the anteromedial knee and the incision; the lateral retinaculum and the tubercle are the surgeon’s infiltration to cover. The arthroplasty guideline’s objection to the femoral block is functional (a weak quadriceps on a knee that must be bent on day 1) and does not apply with the same force here, because the knee is locked straight and the quadriceps is deliberately rested; the author still prefers the adductor canal block because the patient has to stand on the leg in a brace, but a femoral block for this operation is a defensible choice and some surgeons prefer the quieter quadriceps it gives on the first night.

The catheter decision is author’s judgement on no direct evidence. For an acute unilateral repair in a braced leg, a single shot with dexamethasone, infiltration and a written night plan is enough, because the knee is not moved for the first days and the re-provocation is standing and transferring rather than bending. An adductor canal catheter earns its place for the bilateral rupture (two numb legs and no way to stand, so the plan is pain control and bed-based rehabilitation for several days), the chronic reconstruction with a graft, the rupture after arthroplasty (older, heavier, a bigger operation and a worse tissue bed), the dialysis patient who cannot have an NSAID, and the opioid-tolerant patient. An epidural is the alternative for the bilateral case where two catheters are impractical, accepting the immobility that the bilateral brace already imposes.

Rebound: the young patellar tendon patient is the ambulatory cohort’s rebound phenotype (bone surgery, young, often sent home the same day), and intravenous dexamethasone is the single intervention with evidence for reducing it. Escalation triggers: pain above 7 after the block has gone with the brace on and the calf soft is a prescription problem and is treated with the charted opioid; a tense, swollen knee with pain out of proportion is a haematoma under a repair and the surgeon decides whether to evacuate it; calf pain or a swollen leg at any point in the six weeks is a clot; and any loss of active extension is a re-rupture until the surgeon has examined it.

Pitfalls and variants

  • Transosseous versus anchors. Anchors gap less under cyclic load in the laboratory and are not better clinically; tunnels through a small or osteoporotic patella can fracture it; neither changes the anaesthetic.
  • The tourniquet and the tendon. A cuff inflated with the quadriceps retracted makes the reduction harder; expect the surgeon to let it down mid-case or to work without one, and expect the bleeding to be at the end.
  • Bilateral rupture. The renal, steroid and gout patient; both legs braced, no standing for days, catheters or an epidural, a high venous thromboembolism risk and a long stay; the medical disease is usually the bigger problem.
  • Dialysis. Operate the day after a session; potassium and fluid status on the day; no NSAID; cefazolin dosed for renal failure on repeat; the fistula arm protected; expect poor tissue and a higher re-rupture rate.
  • Steroids and diabetes. Steroid cover; glucose control for a day after the dexamethasone, which is still worth giving; a wound that heals slowly and infects more often.
  • Fluoroquinolones. The patient on one when the tendon tore, or given one post-operatively, has the other tendons at risk; the association appears in the arthroplasty disruption data (OR 1.58) and the drug class is avoided afterwards.
  • Chronic rupture and reconstruction. Hamstring autograft, Achilles allograft or mesh, with a quadriceps lengthening: a 2-3 h case, more bleeding, a graft harvest site that hurts in its own right, and the catheter case.
  • Rupture after knee arthroplasty. Direct repair fails in most patellar tendon cases; the operation is a reconstruction in an older, heavier patient with a 16% pooled complication rate; cefazolin timing and the infection risk are those of an arthroplasty revision.
  • The missed diagnosis. A patient presenting weeks late with a “sprain” has a retracted tendon; the booking says repair and the operation becomes a reconstruction, and the surgeon finds out at step 4.
  • Obesity. The quadriceps patient’s mean body mass index is 30 and the post-arthroplasty patient’s 34.5; positioning, pressure areas, airway under sedation, and dosing of the chemoprophylaxis.
  • Anticoagulation. Atrial fibrillation is common in the quadriceps population; the haematoma is bigger, the spinal timing applies, and the brace hides a bleeding wound.
  • The young patient going home. Day case is reasonable for an acute patellar tendon repair with a block, a brace, crutches practised, and a written night plan that assumes rebound.

Key sources

The surgical evidence is case series and systematic reviews of them, consistent on the demographics, the comorbidities, the equivalence of tunnels and anchors in practice, and the poor results of direct repair after arthroplasty. The biomechanical data are cadaveric. There is no analgesia trial and no procedure-specific guideline for extensor mechanism repair; the block choice is extrapolated from PROSPECT’s arthroplasty guideline with the functional argument adjusted for a braced knee, and the catheter advice, the dexamethasone statement and the score are the author’s judgement from the mechanism and are labelled as such.

  1. Garner MR, Gausden E, Berkes MB, Nguyen JT, Lorich DG. Extensor mechanism injuries of the knee: demographic characteristics and comorbidities from a review of 726 patient records. J Bone Joint Surg Am 2015;97:1592-1596
    726 operated extensor mechanism injuries: mean age 61 for quadriceps rupture, 39.5 for patellar tendon rupture, 56 for patellar fracture; 91% and 95.5% of tendon ruptures in men; BMI 30 for quadriceps rupture; 43% of patellar tendon ruptures were over 40; 96% of women with a tendon rupture had a medical comorbidity
  2. Dave U, Rubin J, Morgan JT, et al. Patients have restored extensor mechanism function with low complication rates following quadriceps tendon repair: a systematic review. J Orthop 2025;67:214-222
    Six studies, 324 patients, 89.5% male: full extension in 88.7-100%, flexion 124-133 degrees; re-rupture 0-15.4%, venous thromboembolism 0-15.4%, arthrofibrosis 0-7.7%, infection 0-2%; no outcome difference by fixation technique
  3. VanDerwerker NB, Winzenried AE, Mosiman SJ, Grogan BF, Baer GS, Cotter EJ. Transosseous tunnel suture fixation results in similar rerupture rates and patient-reported outcome measures compared to suture anchors for primary quadriceps tendon repair: a systematic review. Arthroscopy 2025;41:4903-4910
    12 studies, 600 patients, 79.5% transosseous: re-rupture 0-16.7% with tunnels and 0-14.7% with anchors; anchors used 2-3 per repair, tunnels usually 3
  4. Onggo JR, Babazadeh S, Pai V. Smaller gap formation with suture anchor fixation than traditional transpatellar sutures in patella and quadriceps tendon rupture: a systematic review. Arthroscopy 2022;38:2321-2330
    212 cadaveric knees: gap formation under cyclic load 0.9-4.1 mm with anchors against 2.9-10.3 mm with transpatellar sutures for the patellar tendon, 1.5-5.0 against 3.1-33.3 mm for the quadriceps; load to failure similar; knot failure the usual mode with tunnels, anchor pull-out with titanium anchors
  5. Dankert JF, Mehta DD, Remark LH, Leucht P. Transosseous tunnels versus suture anchors for the repair of acute quadriceps and patellar tendon ruptures: a systematic review and meta-analysis of biomechanical studies. J Orthop Sci 2022;28:821-828
    Pooled cadaveric data: for the patellar tendon anchors gap 2.86 mm less after cycling; load to failure not different for either tendon
  6. Davis G, Fellheimer HS, McCormick C, Freedman KB. Repair techniques for acute rupture of the patellar tendon: a systematic review. Orthop J Sports Med 2026;14
    20 studies, 1,161 patients: transosseous, anchor and end-to-end repairs all heal reliably with flexion beyond 130 degrees; the common complications are wound infection, re-rupture and deep vein thrombosis; results are best when the tear is repaired acutely
  7. Vajapey SP, Blackwell RE, Maki AJ, Miller TL. Treatment of extensor tendon disruption after total knee arthroplasty: a systematic review. J Arthroplasty 2019;34:1279-1286
    28 studies: after arthroplasty, direct repair of a patellar tendon rupture failed in 63% and of a quadriceps rupture in 25%; reconstruction with autograft, allograft or mesh had complication rates near 19% for either; extension lag of 30 degrees or more was the commonest failure
  8. Violante B, Compagnoni R, Kroell A, et al. Various surgical techniques result in different outcomes for full extensor mechanism ruptures following total knee replacement: a systematic review by the European Knee Associates (ESSKA-EKA). Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc 2026;34:586-595
    32 studies, 893 ruptures after arthroplasty, mean age 67, mean BMI 34.5: nine techniques, overall complication rate 16%, autograft 38%; all techniques improved extensor lag
  9. Pür B, Demir M, Kaya S, et al. Predicting spontaneous tendon rupture in dialysis: a parsimonious clinical model on the frailty and CKD-MBD axis. Injury 2025;56:112762
    34 spontaneous tendon ruptures in dialysis patients against 68 controls: frailty and dialysis vintage independently predictive, calcium-phosphate product and recent quinolone exposure directionally so; 44% of ruptures were the quadriceps and 32% the patellar tendon
  10. Ayala-Ortiz J, Taylor S, Ghomrawi H, et al. Testosterone replacement therapy is associated with extensor mechanism disruption after total knee arthroplasty. J Knee Surg 2026;39:317-321
    34,911 primary arthroplasties: extensor mechanism disruption in 0.48%; testosterone replacement OR 2.38 (men 3.00), post-operative fluoroquinolone OR 1.58, smoking OR 1.46
  11. Lavand'homme PM, Kehlet H, Rawal N, Joshi GP; PROSPECT Working Group. Pain management after total knee arthroplasty: PROcedure SPEcific Postoperative Pain ManagemenT recommendations. Eur J Anaesthesiol 2022;39:743-757
    The nearest procedure-specific guideline, extrapolated: paracetamol and NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor, adductor canal block, local infiltration, IV dexamethasone, opioid as rescue; tendon repair is outside its scope
  12. Barry GS, Bailey JG, Sardinha J, Brousseau P, Uppal V. Factors associated with rebound pain after peripheral nerve block for ambulatory surgery. Br J Anaesth 2021;126:862-871
    972 ambulatory block patients: rebound pain in 49.6%; bone surgery OR 1.82, female OR 1.52, younger age; absence of IV dexamethasone OR 1.78

Hip and knee › Knee

37 Periprosthetic joint infection: DAIR, one- and two-stage revision, spacers

Debridement with implant retention for the acute infection; explantation, antibiotic-loaded spacer and delayed reimplantation, or single-stage exchange, for the chronic one; the septic patient; the knee as the model, with the hip's differences noted

4Severe

Dominant mechanism: Bone. An inflamed, infected joint that hurt at rest before surgery, then a revision exposure with components and cement levered out of bone, radical debridement of synovium, capsule and infected bone, a spacer or new components cemented in, and for the reimplantation a constrained implant re-tensioning a scarred, twice-operated envelope. Infection is an inflammatory pain generator in its own right and the debridement removes much of it; what is left is bone, muscle and retension, loaded by physiotherapy that is more cautious than after an aseptic revision

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: high.

Block
General anaesthesia (or spinal in the non-bacteraemic patient) with a single-shot adductor canal block and surgeon's infiltration for DAIR; an adductor canal catheter for explantation and reimplantation, with IV dexamethasone discussed with the surgeon case by case
Catheter: selective Single shot for DAIR, which is a synovectomy and a washout; an adductor canal catheter for the first and second stages, which are revisions in every physical sense, unless the patient is septic, the catheter would pass through cellulitis, or the ward cannot look after it; a neuraxial catheter is avoided in the bacteraemic patient and reserved for the chronic, afebrile reimplantation in a unit that runs epidurals
Alternatives: Spinal anaesthesia with a single-shot block for the afebrile chronic infection with a normal white cell count and no bacteraemia, accepting the case length; Epidural for the afebrile reimplantation where a perineural catheter is impractical, with the usual timing rules around the anticoagulant; Ketamine infusion and a pain service plan for the opioid-tolerant patient, which most chronic infection patients are; For the hip: supra-inguinal fascia iliaca or lumbar plexus catheter, as on the revision hip card
Position
Supine with a thigh holder for the knee, as for a revision; lateral for the hip, with the pressure areas of a long case in mind. A septic patient on a vasopressor is positioned with the arterial line in first
Tourniquet
Sometimes. Many surgeons avoid a tourniquet in the infected knee, because the bleeding tissue bed shows them what is viable and the antibiotic needs to reach it; others use one for the explantation and let it down before the spacer goes in
Cement
Yes. Antibiotic-loaded cement is the treatment: a hand-formed, moulded or pre-formed spacer carrying grams of antibiotic per pack at the first stage, and lower-dose antibiotic cement fixing the definitive components at the second stage or in a one-stage exchange; a stem-type hip spacer or a cemented reimplantation stem is a full canal cement step with the usual implications
Blood loss
DAIR 300-600 mL; explantation with cement removal 1-2 L measured plus hidden loss; reimplantation the same again; cell salvage is not used in the presence of infection, so the blood comes from the bank and the tranexamic acid matters more
Duration
DAIR 60-120 min; first-stage explantation and spacer 120-240 min; second-stage reimplantation 180-300 min; one-stage exchange, with a full re-preparation and re-draping between halves, 4-5 h
Length of stay
5-14 nights per stage; the two-stage patient has two admissions and six to twelve weeks of antibiotics between them. Day case: no
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV (3 g over 120 kg), or the organism-directed agent, given before incision when the organism is already known from aspiration; held until the deep tissue samples are taken only when the aspirate was negative or the organism unknown, by agreement with the surgeon before the patient is asleep; never held in the septic patient. Re-dosed at 3-4 h and after 1.5 L of loss
Tranexamic acid
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV before incision and a second dose at 3 h or closure; with cell salvage off the table it is the main blood-sparing measure
VTE
Low molecular weight heparin from the evening of surgery when the bleeding allows, continued through weeks of immobility with a spacer; the infected, immobile, inflamed patient is a high-risk one
Antiemetic
Ondansetron 4 mg IV; dexamethasone 8 mg IV is a discussion with the surgeon, given by many for the block and withheld by some in active infection, without trial evidence either way
Tell the patient
This is a long operation to clear an infection from around the joint replacement, and you will probably need a blood transfusion, weeks of antibiotics and, if the implant has to come out, a second operation to put a new one in; the knee will be very sore for the first few days, with a local anaesthetic pump to help, and the strong painkillers are for the nights.
The trap
Two conversations have to happen before the patient is asleep: whether the antibiotic is given before the knife or after the samples, and whether this patient is bacteraemic, because the first decides the cultures that choose the next six weeks of treatment and the second decides whether a needle goes anywhere near the spine

What the surgeon is doing and why

An infected joint replacement is a biofilm problem. Bacteria on the surface of the implant and the cement live in a matrix that antibiotics do not penetrate at any dose the kidneys will tolerate, so the infection is cured by removing the biofilm physically, and the surgeon’s options are arranged by how much implant has to come out to do that. The diagnosis itself is made by criteria (a sinus to the joint, the same organism in two samples, or a combination of inflammatory markers, synovial cell count and histology), and the patient has usually had an aspiration that names the organism before the operation; when it does not, the operation is also the diagnostic test, which is the antibiotic-timing problem on this card.

The choice of operation is a question of time. An infection that is less than a few weeks old, either early after the index arthroplasty or acute haematogenous from a bacteraemia onto an old implant, has an immature biofilm, and the surgeon can open the joint, strip the synovium, exchange the modular parts, wash out with litres of fluid and leave the fixed components in: debridement, antibiotics and implant retention (DAIR). In the pooled literature DAIR fails in about a third of early post-operative and acute haematogenous infections and in three quarters of late chronic ones, which is why it is not offered to the chronic infection; knees fail more often than hips, Staphylococcus aureus more often than anything else, exchanging the modular parts has not been shown to help, and a planned second DAIR does as well as a single one (about 70% success). A chronic infection needs the implant out. The surgeon then either reimplants in the same anaesthetic (one-stage or single-stage exchange, with a complete re-preparation, re-draping and new instruments between the two halves) or leaves an antibiotic-loaded cement spacer in the joint, treats with systemic antibiotics for six to twelve weeks, and reimplants at a second operation when the markers have settled (two-stage exchange). The two-stage has been the standard for decades on the grounds of a lower reinfection rate; the one randomised trial, 140 infected hips, found the same patient-reported outcome at 18 months, a better outcome at three months and fewer intra-operative complications (8% against 27%) with the single stage, and the same proportion with markers of possible ongoing infection, so the single stage is gaining ground for the patient with a known organism and a reasonable soft-tissue envelope. The knee follows the hip in this, with less trial evidence.

The explantation is a revision in every mechanical sense: the old scar, a stiff joint needing a quadriceps snip or a tubercle osteotomy (an extended trochanteric osteotomy for a well-fixed hip stem), well-fixed components and every fragment of cement levered and burred out of bone, and then something the aseptic revision does not have: a radical debridement of all infected synovium, capsule, sinus track and bone, because tissue left behind is biofilm left behind. The spacer that follows is cement with grams of antibiotic mixed in, hand-formed into a block that holds the joint space (static) or moulded into a crude articulating knee or a stemmed hip that lets the patient move (articulating), eluting antibiotic locally at concentrations no intravenous dose could reach. The reimplantation, weeks later, is the second stage: the spacer comes out of a joint that has been operated on twice, more scar is released, the bone loss is now worse, and a stemmed, often constrained implant is cemented in with antibiotic-loaded cement at a lower dose. In the hip the same logic applies through a lateral position, an extended trochanteric osteotomy and a stem-type spacer or cemented stem that is a full canal cement step.

The patient is the other half of this card. Chronic infection patients arrive anaemic, hypoalbuminaemic, often diabetic or immunosuppressed, usually on opioids for months of a painful joint, and sometimes already with the renal impairment that the spacer will test. The acute haematogenous patient may arrive septic, and the operation is then source control under resuscitation.

The pain logic: the infected joint is an inflammatory pain generator before anything is cut, with rest pain and night pain, and the debridement removes much of that. What the operation adds is bone (components and cement out, canals reamed, a spacer or stems cemented in), muscle and soft tissue from the radical debridement, and at reimplantation the retension of a constrained implant in a scarred envelope, the aseptic revision’s mechanism. The score is 4: a catheter or a robust plan for three days, movement-evoked pain that limits physiotherapy, and rebound when a single shot wears off in a patient who was already opioid-exposed. It is not the aseptic revision’s 5 because the physiotherapy after a spacer is cautious by design (a static spacer is not bent at all) and the inflammatory component falls as the infection clears; the second stage, taken alone, sits on the revision card’s curve.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 Classification, the organism and the patient before the list

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon decides DAIR or exchange on the age of the infection, the fixation of the components, the soft-tissue envelope and the organism; the aspirate result, the sinus, the inflammatory markers and the radiographs are the inputs, and the plan determines the case length, the blood loss and the cement.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Ask which operation, whether the organism is known, and whether the patient is bacteraemic. Then assess the host: haemoglobin (usually low from chronic inflammation, and cell salvage is off the table), albumin, glucose control, renal function with the spacer in mind, the immunosuppressant or biologic, the steroid needing cover, the anticoagulant, and the opioid history, which in a chronic infection is months long. Crossmatch for any exchange. The two-stage patient returning for reimplantation has had six to twelve weeks of antibiotics and a spacer: the creatinine, the haemoglobin, the vancomycin level if still running, and the deconditioning are the baseline, not an abnormality.

  2. 2 The septic patient

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    An acute haematogenous infection onto an old implant can present as sepsis; the surgeon’s job is source control within hours, and the operation does not wait for the markers to be perfect.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is the one patient on the card for whom the antibiotic is never held: blood cultures and the joint aspirate are taken and the antibiotic goes in now, before the patient reaches theatre. Resuscitate with fluid and a vasopressor, place an arterial line before induction and a central line if the pressor is running, and induce for a general anaesthetic in a patient with a compromised circulation. Neuraxial anaesthesia in a bacteraemic patient carries the risk of seeding the epidural space, and the author does not do it; the peripheral block decision is made on the same grounds, a single shot being reasonable and a catheter through or near cellulitis not. The lactate and the urine output are the monitors of the next 12 hours, and the renal protection that the spacer will need starts with not being hypovolaemic now. A septic patient with a DAIR planned can turn into an explantation on the table if the components are found loose; the blood and the time are planned for that.

  3. 3 Antibiotic timing and the tissue samples

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon takes three to five deep tissue samples with separate clean instruments from the interfaces, the synovium and the sinus, and sends the implant for sonication where available; these cultures choose the antibiotic for the next six to twelve weeks. Surgeons worry that a dose of cefazolin before the knife will sterilise the samples.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The evidence is more settled than the folklore. In a small randomised trial and in a 576-patient multicentre cohort, giving the prophylactic dose before incision did not reduce culture positivity (63% with or without it in the cohort), and in the subgroup whose pre-operative aspirate was negative, withholding raised the yield from 29% to 49%. That gives the rule: when the organism is already known from the aspiration, the antibiotic goes in before the knife as for any arthroplasty, because a new implant or a retained one is about to be exposed; when the aspirate was negative or never done, the dose is held until the samples are in the pots, by agreement made before the patient is asleep, and given the moment the surgeon says so. In the septic patient it is never held. The organism-directed agent (vancomycin for a resistant staphylococcus, which needs an hour’s infusion) replaces or joins cefazolin, and the re-dosing interval for a four-hour case with a litre of loss is written on the chart, not remembered.

  4. 4 DAIR: arthrotomy, synovectomy, modular exchange and lavage

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Through the old incision the joint is opened, pus evacuated, the synovium stripped radically from the gutters, the pouch and the posterior capsule, the polyethylene insert (and for a hip the head and liner) exchanged to reach the surfaces beneath, the fixed components checked for loosening, and the joint washed with several litres of fluid, often with an antiseptic soak, before closure over drains. Some surgeons add antibiotic beads or powder.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A 60-120 minute case that bleeds from inflamed synovium throughout, with or without a tourniquet, and that is more painful than its booking suggests because the whole synovial lining has been stripped. The single-shot adductor canal block with the surgeon’s infiltration is the author’s default, with the oral regimen and the opioid planned for an inflamed knee that was painful before. If the components are found loose the case becomes an explantation; that possibility is why the crossmatch exists even for a DAIR.

  5. 5 Explantation and radical debridement

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The revision exposure (snip or tubercle osteotomy for the knee, extended trochanteric osteotomy for the hip) gives access; the components are freed at their interfaces and removed, every fragment of cement is chased out of the metaphysis and canals, and then all infected tissue is excised, including bone that is soft or sequestered. Nothing that could carry biofilm is left.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is the bloody half of the operation, 1-2 L measured with more hidden, through a bed that the surgeon deliberately leaves bleeding; there is no cell salvage, so the bank blood, the two doses of tranexamic acid and a haemoglobin check at the end of the debridement are the plan. A tourniquet, where used, comes down before the spacer and the reperfusion is of a leg that has been inflamed for weeks. The canal reaming and cement removal embolise marrow as in any revision, and the warming has to match a four-hour open wound. An arterial line and a large-bore cannula are the author’s defaults for any explantation; a central line for the patient who arrived septic.

  6. 6 The spacer: antibiotic-loaded cement and what it does to the kidneys

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Cement is mixed with high doses of heat-stable antibiotic, commonly vancomycin and an aminoglycoside (gentamicin or tobramycin) at several grams of each per 40 g pack, and up to 8 g per pack in some units, and formed into a spacer that fills the space, holds the soft tissues out to length, and elutes antibiotic into the joint for weeks. An articulating knee spacer or a stemmed hip spacer allows some movement; a static block does not. The cement cures with the joint held to length.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Two things. First, cement physiology: a knee spacer is a surface cement load and a stemmed hip spacer is a canal cement load, with the full bone cement implantation syndrome mechanism of the cement chapter in a patient who may be anaemic, hypovolaemic and on a vasopressor already. Second, the kidneys. The antibiotic in the spacer is absorbed systemically and in the largest knee series acute kidney injury followed in 14% of patients with normal baseline renal function and 45% of those with chronic kidney disease, with more than 3.6 g of either antibiotic per batch nearly doubling the odds; in the hip series the figures were 7% and 28%. In both series the independent predictors were things the anaesthetist controls: peri-operative hypovolaemia, hypertension, acute atrial fibrillation, intensive care admission and fluid depletion afterwards. A unit using very high doses reported acute kidney injury in 6.6% after the first stage, mostly resolving within a month. The practical rules: no NSAID in the spacer patient, no hypovolaemia at the end of a four-hour case, an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor or receptor blocker held, the creatinine checked daily for the first days, and the systemic aminoglycoside or vancomycin dosed by a team that knows what is in the cement.

  7. 7 One-stage exchange: the second half in the same anaesthetic

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    After the debridement the surgeon changes gloves and gowns, re-prepares and re-drapes, opens new instrument trays, and reimplants definitive components with antibiotic-loaded cement in the same sitting; the patient leaves theatre with a new joint rather than a spacer. The trial evidence for the hip supports it for the patient with a known organism, and the surgeon’s willingness depends on the soft tissues and the bone loss found at step 5.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is a 4-5 hour case: the explantation’s blood loss plus a cemented stemmed reimplantation’s, a second cement step with a canal in the hip, a second tranexamic acid dose, antibiotic re-dosing, and a spinal that will not last; general anaesthesia with a catheter placed beforehand is the practical answer, or a combined spinal-epidural in the afebrile patient in a unit that runs them. The haemoglobin and the temperature at the half-way re-drape decide whether the second half proceeds comfortably.

  8. 8 The interval and the second stage

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    With a spacer in, the patient has six to twelve weeks of intravenous then oral antibiotics, partial or no weight-bearing on a static spacer, and serial markers; when they fall and the wound is quiet, the second stage removes the spacer, releases the scar of two operations, grades the bone loss, and reimplants stemmed, often constrained components with cones or augments, in antibiotic-loaded cement at a lower dose. Repeat tissue samples are taken.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is the revision knee or revision hip card’s operation with a worse starting point: anaemia from weeks of infection and antibiotics, renal function that may not have recovered from the first spacer, deconditioning, a vancomycin or aminoglycoside level that may still be relevant, and an opioid requirement that has grown. The antibiotic question returns: the prophylactic dose is usually given, because a new implant is going in and the organism is known, but some surgeons hold it for the repeat samples, and the conversation is had again. The catheter is routine here as it is for any revision, and the dexamethasone discussion is repeated, with the surgeon’s view carrying more weight in a patient whose infection may not be cleared.

  9. 9 Recovery, the ward and the weeks

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants a dry wound, the drains out when they slow, the antibiotics running, the markers falling and the physiotherapy at the pace the construct allows: full after a DAIR, protected after an articulating spacer, none through the knee after a static one.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The trajectory on this card is 4 on the first evening with the block or catheter working, 6 on day 1, 5 on day 2, 4 on day 3 and 3 at a week, on top of a baseline that was painful before surgery. Regular paracetamol and the opioid the patient was already on, with rescue on top; the NSAID is the drug this patient cannot have for the duration of the spacer and its systemic antibiotics, and the catheter and paracetamol carry more as a result. The ketamine infusion is the author’s practice for the opioid-tolerant two-stage patient, with the usual low-grade evidence. The first-morning haemoglobin decides the transfusion; the creatinine on days 1-3 is the spacer’s report card; the wound that keeps draining after a week is the infection that was not cleared, and the surgeon sees it first.

Pain plan

The mechanism is an inflamed joint cleared of its infection and then subjected to a revision’s bone work, a radical soft-tissue debridement and, at reimplantation, the retension of a constrained implant in scar; the patient is opioid-exposed, often anaemic and renally fragile, and the NSAID is unavailable for as long as the spacer and its systemic antibiotics are in play. PROSPECT’s arthroplasty guideline is extrapolated for the skeleton (paracetamol, adductor canal block, infiltration, intravenous dexamethasone, opioid as rescue, no femoral or sciatic block) and everything beyond it is the author’s judgement, because no guideline covers infection.

For DAIR a single-shot adductor canal block, the surgeon’s infiltration where the tissue will take it, and a written night plan with the pre-existing opioid continued are enough; the operation is a synovectomy and the pain is inflammatory and short. For the explantation and the reimplantation an adductor canal catheter is the author’s default, as for any revision, with three qualifications. In the bacteraemic patient a single shot replaces it, because a catheter is a foreign body left in an infected patient for days; in 1,416 ward catheters the tip was colonised in 28.7%, local inflammation occurred in 3% and a psoas abscess in one patient, with duration beyond 48 h and absence of antibiotic prophylaxis as the risk factors, and every patient on this card is on antibiotics, so the risk is real and small. A catheter does not pass through cellulitis or a sinus. And a neuraxial catheter is reserved for the afebrile chronic reimplantation in a unit that runs epidurals on a mobilising patient; the author does not site one in a patient with a positive blood culture that week.

Dexamethasone is the honest uncertainty: it prolongs the block and reduces rebound, it raises glucose in the diabetic patient for a day, and in active infection some surgeons would rather it were not given. There is no trial. The author gives it for a DAIR in a non-septic patient and asks the surgeon for an explantation.

Rebound and escalation: rebound is high because the single shot recedes onto an inflamed joint in an opioid-exposed patient; stepping the catheter infusion down rather than off and having the oral regimen running for a day beforehand is the practical answer. Escalation triggers: pain above 7 with the catheter running is a migrated catheter before it is a prescription problem; a tense, swollen joint on day 1 is a haematoma in a patient with no cell salvage and two doses of tranexamic acid; new fever, rigors and hypotension on day 2 are the infection that was not cleared or a line; a creatinine that climbs on day 2 is the spacer, and the fluid balance and the nephrotoxins are reviewed that morning, not at the end of the week.

Pitfalls and variants

  • The hip. Lateral position, an extended trochanteric osteotomy for a fixed stem, a stem-type spacer or a cemented reimplantation stem with the full cement precautions, spacer dislocation as the interval complication, and the revision hip card’s catheter choices (supra-inguinal fascia iliaca or lumbar plexus) in place of the adductor canal.
  • Chronic kidney disease. The spacer’s acute kidney injury risk is five times higher; the antibiotic dose in the cement is a conversation with the surgeon and the infectious diseases team before the day, the NSAID is out, and the fluid balance of a four-hour case is managed as if the kidneys were the operation.
  • Diabetes and immunosuppression. Glucose control through the dexamethasone question; biologics usually paused; steroid cover; wound healing and reinfection both worse.
  • Vancomycin. An hour’s infusion that has to start in time to be in before incision when the organism demands it; vancomycin flushing reaction with fast infusion; a level before the second stage.
  • Aminoglycoside in cement plus systemic aminoglycoside: the nephrotoxic combination, and ototoxicity in the elderly.
  • Fungal infection. Amphotericin in the cement, a longer interval, and a sicker host.
  • Culture-negative infection. The antibiotic-timing conversation matters most here, because the samples are the only chance of a name.
  • Cell salvage. Not used with infection in the field; the blood plan is bank blood, two tranexamic acid doses and a haemoglobin that was corrected beforehand where time allowed.
  • The static spacer. No knee movement for weeks, a high venous thromboembolism risk, deconditioning, and a second stage that starts from a stiffer joint.
  • The opioid-tolerant patient. Most chronic infections; baseline opioid continued, the catheter as default, ketamine and a pain service plan, and a long conversation before the first stage about what the two operations will feel like. See opioid-tolerant and chronic pain patients.
  • Anticoagulation. Common in this age group; affects the neuraxial choice and the haematoma risk in a bed that is left bleeding on purpose.
  • Delirium. Elderly, infected, anaemic, long anaesthetic, opioids, and days in bed: the commonest medical complication of the week after an explantation.
  • Infection prophylaxis for the next implant. Cefazolin before incision at the second stage; the antibiotics chapter for the principles.

Key sources

The surgical evidence is uneven: DAIR outcomes rest on large systematic reviews of observational series, the single-stage versus two-stage question has one randomised trial in hips, and the spacer nephrotoxicity data are large single-institution cohorts whose predictors are consistent between hip and knee. The antibiotic-timing evidence is a small randomised trial and a recent large cohort that agree. The catheter infection figures are a prospective multicentre cohort from 2005. There is no analgesia guideline for infected arthroplasty, no trial of dexamethasone in active infection, and no trial of neuraxial technique in bacteraemia; the block, catheter and dexamethasone advice is the author’s judgement from the mechanism and the physiology, and the score is calibrated against the aseptic revision cards.

  1. Abbaszadeh A, Yilmaz MK, Izadi N, et al. Efficacy of debridement, antibiotics, and implant retention in total hip and knee arthroplasty: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Arthroplasty 2026;41:19-38
    81 studies: pooled DAIR failure 35.9%; 34.2% for early post-operative infection, 39.1% for acute haematogenous infection and 73.6% for late chronic infection; knees fail more often than hips; Staphylococcus aureus the organism most linked to failure
  2. Gerritsen M, Khawar A, Scheper H, et al. Modular component exchange and outcome of DAIR for hip and knee periprosthetic joint infection: a systematic review and meta-regression analysis. Bone Jt Open 2021;2:806-812
    65 studies, 6,630 patients: pooled DAIR success 67% (hip 70%, knee 63%); no benefit from exchanging modular components in studies after 2004
  3. Salman LA, Altahtamouni SB, Khatkar H, Al-Ani A, Ahmed G. Success rate of single versus multiple debridement, antibiotics, and implant retention (DAIR) in hip and knee periprosthetic joint infection: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Eur J Orthop Surg Traumatol 2024;34:3859-3872
    Nine studies, 1,104 patients: single DAIR 67% and planned double DAIR 70% success, not different; a third DAIR 50-60%
  4. Blom AW, Lenguerrand E, Strange S, et al. Clinical and cost effectiveness of single stage compared with two stage revision for hip prosthetic joint infection (INFORM): pragmatic, parallel group, open label, randomised controlled trial. BMJ 2022;379:e071281
    140 infected hips randomised: WOMAC at 18 months no different; single stage better at three months; intra-operative events 8% versus 27%; markers of possible ongoing infection 14% versus 11%; single stage cost-effective
  5. Dagneaux L, Limberg AK, Osmon DR, Leung N, Berry DJ, Abdel MP. Acute kidney injury when treating periprosthetic joint infections after total knee arthroplasties with antibiotic-loaded spacers: incidence, risks, and outcomes. J Bone Joint Surg Am 2021;103:754-760
    455 knee spacers with a mean of 8 g vancomycin and 9 g aminoglycoside per construct: acute kidney injury in 14% of patients with normal baseline renal function and 45% of those with chronic kidney disease (OR 5); more than 3.6 g of either antibiotic per batch raised the odds (1.9 and 1.8); hypertension, peri-operative hypovolaemia and acute atrial fibrillation were independent predictors; 2% progressed to chronic kidney disease
  6. Dagneaux L, Limberg AK, Osmon DR, Leung N, Berry DJ, Abdel MP. Renal toxicity associated with resection and spacer insertion for chronic hip PJI. J Arthroplasty 2021;36:3289-3293
    256 hip spacers: acute kidney injury in 7% without and 28% with pre-existing chronic kidney disease; post-operative fluid depletion, intensive care admission and acute atrial fibrillation predicted it; antibiotic dose in the cement did not
  7. Tchouambou Youmbi C, Santos A, Bridger A, Backstein D, Ekhtiari S, Wolfstadt JI. Acute kidney injury following antibiotic-loaded spacer insertion in two-stage knee arthroplasty revision for periprosthetic joint infection: a retrospective cohort study. J Arthroplasty 2026
    152 knees with very high-dose spacers (typically 8 g per 40 g pack, vancomycin and ceftazidime): acute kidney injury in 6.6% after the first stage and 2.6% after the second; 86% resolved within a month
  8. Paul BR, Verhey JT, Sullivan GR, et al. Withholding prophylactic antibiotics improves culture yield in revision total knee arthroplasty for periprosthetic joint infection with negative aspirations: a multicenter retrospective study. J Arthroplasty 2026;41:3090-3095
    576 chronic knee infections: intra-operative culture positivity 63% whether prophylaxis was given before incision or withheld; in patients with a negative pre-operative aspirate, withholding raised the yield from 29% to 49%
  9. Pérez-Prieto D, Portillo ME, Puig-Verdié L, et al. Preoperative antibiotic prophylaxis in prosthetic joint infections: not a concern for intraoperative cultures. Diagn Microbiol Infect Dis 2016;86:442-445
    28 patients randomised to prophylaxis before incision or none: the same number of positive cultures and the same number of culture-negative infections in each group
  10. Capdevila X, Pirat P, Bringuier S, et al. Continuous peripheral nerve blocks in hospital wards after orthopedic surgery: a multicenter prospective analysis of the quality of postoperative analgesia and complications in 1,416 patients. Anesthesiology 2005;103:1035-1045
    1,416 perineural catheters, median 56 h: catheter tip cultures positive in 28.7%, local inflammatory signs in 3%, one psoas abscess (0.07%); catheter duration beyond 48 h and absence of antibiotic prophylaxis were risk factors for local infection
  11. Lavand'homme PM, Kehlet H, Rawal N, Joshi GP; PROSPECT Working Group. Pain management after total knee arthroplasty: PROcedure SPEcific Postoperative Pain ManagemenT recommendations. Eur J Anaesthesiol 2022;39:743-757
    The primary arthroplasty guideline whose skeleton is extrapolated: paracetamol and NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor, adductor canal block, infiltration, IV dexamethasone, opioid as rescue; revision and infection are outside its scope

Trauma › Trauma

39 Neck of femur fracture: hemiarthroplasty, THA, DHS and nail

Intracapsular fractures (cemented hemiarthroplasty, total hip arthroplasty for the fitter patient, cannulated screws) and extracapsular fractures (dynamic hip screw, cephalomedullary nail on a traction table)

3Moderate

Dominant mechanism: Bone. A mobile fracture before surgery; then a neck osteotomy with canal preparation and cement (hemiarthroplasty), or a reamed lag screw track through the fracture with a lateral approach through vastus lateralis (DHS) or a nail entry through gluteus medius at the trochanteric tip (nail). Fixing the fracture removes most of the pre-operative pain generator

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: moderate.

Block
Fascia iliaca block (supra-inguinal) or femoral nerve block in the emergency department, repeated before positioning for the spinal if more than 6 h have passed; PENG block is a reasonable alternative with equivalent dynamic pain relief in the one direct comparison
Catheter: rarely PROSPECT and the UK guideline both advise against routine catheters; a catheter is reasonable only when surgery will be delayed beyond a day and a repeated single shot cannot be organised
Alternatives: PENG block (motor sparing, covers the anterior capsule, weaker for the lateral incision); Low-dose spinal with hyperbaric bupivacaine and no intrathecal opioid; General anaesthesia with the block as the analgesic component; Surgeon's periarticular infiltration for a posterior approach as a supplement
Position
Lateral for hemiarthroplasty and total hip arthroplasty (posterior or anterolateral approach; supine for some surgeons' direct lateral approach); supine on a traction table with a perineal post and the image intensifier in the field for DHS and nail
Tourniquet
No
Cement
Sometimes. Hemiarthroplasty stems are cemented in most units because cemented fixation gives better function, fewer periprosthetic fractures and no excess mortality; this is the cement step with the highest incidence of bone cement implantation syndrome in orthopaedics. DHS and nail use no cement; THA for fracture is cemented or hybrid according to the surgeon
Blood loss
Hemiarthroplasty 200-500 mL in the wound; DHS and nail bleed less into the wound but the extracapsular fracture has already bled into the thigh, so the day 1-2 haemoglobin falls further than the measured loss predicts and transfusion is common
Duration
Cannulated screws 30-45 min; DHS 45-75 min; cephalomedullary nail 45-90 min; hemiarthroplasty 60-90 min; total hip arthroplasty for fracture 90-150 min
Length of stay
Acute stay of a week or more, then rehabilitation; about a quarter of patients are dead within a year in registry and trial cohorts. Day case: no
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV within 60 min of incision (3 g over 120 kg), after the spinal is in; an implant goes into every one of these operations
Tranexamic acid
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV at induction is common practice and reasonable; the hip fracture trial base is smaller than for elective arthroplasty. Draw it up only after the spinal is sited and never on the same tray as the spinal drugs
VTE
Low molecular weight heparin from admission, timed around the neuraxial block (last dose at least 12 h before the spinal, next dose at least 4 h after), continued for 28-35 days; mechanical prophylaxis from admission
Antiemetic
Ondansetron 4 mg IV; dexamethasone 4-8 mg IV is reasonable for block prolongation and antiemesis, with a day of hyperglycaemia in the diabetic patient
Tell the patient
The operation takes away most of the pain of the broken bone; the hip will be sore for a few days when you move, and getting up with the physiotherapists the day after surgery is part of the treatment, not something to wait for.
The trap
The cemented hemiarthroplasty is the one cement step in orthopaedics that kills: have the pressure supported and a vasopressor running before the surgeon tells you the canal is being cemented, because the collapse at pressurisation is a right heart failing against an embolic load, and the time to treat it is before it happens

What the surgeon is doing and why

A hip fracture is two different injuries that share a ward, and the capsule is the line between them. An intracapsular fracture tears the retinacular vessels that run up the neck to the head, so a displaced one in an old patient has a head that will die if it is fixed, and the surgeon replaces it. An extracapsular fracture breaks through cancellous metaphysis outside the capsule, leaves the head alive and bleeds into the thigh rather than the joint; the surgeon fixes it.

                     hip fracture
                          |
          +---------------+----------------+
     intracapsular                     extracapsular
   (head blood supply torn)         (head alive, bleeds into thigh)
          |                                |
   undisplaced  displaced           stable 2-part   unstable, reverse
       |            |               intertroch.     oblique, subtroch.
  cannulated   fit, independent,        |                 |
   screws      cognitively intact:     DHS       cephalomedullary nail
               THA                                  (traction table)
               everyone else:
               cemented hemiarthroplasty

The displaced intracapsular fracture gets a hemiarthroplasty in most patients: a stemmed femoral component with a large head on the native acetabulum, cemented in most units. WHiTE 5 settled the cement argument in 1,225 patients: the cemented stem gave better quality of life at four months, a quarter of the periprosthetic fracture rate (0.5% against 2.1%) and 12-month mortality of 23.9% against 27.8%, so the cement that frightens the anaesthetist does not cost lives overall, and the uncemented stem fractures the osteoporotic femur it is hammered into. The fit, independent, cognitively intact patient gets a total hip arthroplasty, because the native acetabulum wears under a metal head; the price is a longer operation, more blood loss and a higher dislocation rate. The undisplaced fracture gets cannulated screws through a small lateral incision.

For the extracapsular fracture the device depends on whether the lateral femoral wall will hold a plate. A stable two-part intertrochanteric fracture gets a dynamic hip screw: a lag screw up the neck into the head, sliding in a barrel on a lateral plate so the fracture compresses as the patient weight-bears. An unstable, reverse oblique or subtrochanteric fracture gets a cephalomedullary nail from the trochanteric tip down the canal, with a lag screw or blade through it into the head. Both are done on a traction table under image intensification.

The frail patient is the operation. The mean age in the big trials is about 80, a fifth become delirious, and about a quarter are dead within a year, mostly from what they already had. Surgery is the treatment for the pain and for the immobility that causes the pneumonia and the pressure injuries, which is why the Australian clinical care standard and the UK guideline both set a 36-h limit from presentation and treat delay as a harm. HIP ATTACK tested 6 h against 24 h in 2,970 patients: 90-day mortality (9% against 10%) and major complications (22% in both arms) did not change, but delirium, urinary infection, moderate-to-severe pain and length of stay all fell. Hours inside the window buy comfort.
