The pain logic is bone throughout. Before surgery the generator is a mobile fracture that hurts on movement far more than at rest, which is why positioning for a spinal without a block is cruel. After surgery it is the osteotomy and cement interface (hemiarthroplasty), or a reamed track through the fracture plus a lateral incision through vastus lateralis (DHS) or a nail entry through gluteus medius (nail). Nothing is under tension, so the pain falls over two or three days as bone pain does, and the operation has removed most of what hurt before. The score is 3. The patient often cannot tell you, so the plan is written for someone who will not ask.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 Emergency department: block, clock and assessment

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants the patient on a trauma list within 36 h with the implant decision made, which needs the radiographs, the pre-fracture walking and cognition, and the anticoagulant history.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The block goes in here. The Australian standard and PROSPECT both want a fascia iliaca or femoral nerve block from presentation, and the Australian standard measures it before surgery and before any inter-hospital transfer. Supra-inguinal fascia iliaca is the PROSPECT preference; a PENG block matched it for dynamic pain in the one head-to-head trial, with no difference in resting pain or motor block. Paracetamol starts now; an NSAID waits for a renal function result. The admission bundle that matters to you: a 4AT, a frailty score, an ECG, haemoglobin, electrolytes, renal function, a group and hold, the time and dose of the last anticoagulant, and intravenous fluid, because almost every one of these patients is dry.

  2. 2 Optimisation and the reasons to delay

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A delayed operation is a longer time in pain and in bed; the surgeon pushes for the next list, the orthogeriatrician for a patient fit for it, and both are right.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The UK guideline lists the reasons that justify delay and insists they are corrected inside the 36 h rather than used to cancel: haemoglobin under 80 g/L, sodium under 120 or over 150 mmol/L, potassium under 2.8 or over 6.0 mmol/L, uncontrolled diabetes, acute left ventricular failure, a rate over 120, chest sepsis and a reversible coagulopathy. A murmur without symptoms is not on the list; an echocardiogram that costs a day is a worse trade than an arterial line and the assumption that the valve is tight. Anticoagulants: warfarin is reversed with vitamin K 5 mg IV on admission, with surgery at an INR of 1.8 or below and a spinal at 1.5 or below; a factor Xa inhibitor is stopped and the operation planned 24 h after the last dose (48 h if the eGFR is under 60), or sooner if an anti-Xa level is under 50 ng/mL; dabigatran is planned for the next afternoon with a normal thrombin time, or reversed with idarucizumab if surgery cannot wait. A single antiplatelet agent, including clopidogrel, is not a bar to a spinal in the UK guidance. Transfuse to above 90 g/L, or 100 g/L with ischaemic heart disease, before the table rather than during cementing.

  3. 3 Spinal or general: what the decision rests on

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon has no preference beyond a still patient and no delay.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Two large trials took the belief that spinal anaesthesia protects the brain and failed to confirm it. REGAIN randomised 1,600 patients with a mean age of 78: death or inability to walk at 60 days in 18.5% with spinal and 18.0% with general anaesthesia, delirium 20.5% and 19.7%, and 15% of the spinal group converted on the day. RAGA randomised 950 patients over 65 to unsedated regional or general anaesthesia: delirium within a week 6.2% and 5.1%. So the decision is individual. The defensible default is a spinal for the patient who can lie still on a blocked hip for the duration, with a low dose of hyperbaric bupivacaine (the UK specimen protocol uses under 2 mL of 0.5%) and no intrathecal opioid when a block is working, because the hypotension of a full-dose spinal in a dry 85-year-old is the preventable harm of the technique. A general anaesthetic is the right answer for dementia that will not tolerate the position, dual antiplatelet therapy, or a nail that will take 90 min on a traction table; a fixed cardiac output lesion takes either, with an arterial line and a vasopressor infusion from the start. Sedation is propofol in small doses, not midazolam. Target a mean arterial pressure above 70 mmHg.

  4. 4 The second block, the spinal and the drugs on the tray

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The spinal has to be done sitting or lateral, and either position moves the fracture.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    If the emergency department block is more than 6 h old, repeat it before the patient is moved; the UK guideline asks for a block in the department and a block at surgery, and the second is what makes the spinal civilised. Cefazolin 2 g IV goes in once the spinal is sited. Tranexamic acid is drawn up only after the spinal is in and never on the same tray; intrathecal tranexamic acid is a lethal drug error that the hip fracture list has produced more than once.

  5. 5 Positioning: lateral for arthroplasty, traction table for fixation

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Hemiarthroplasty and THA need a lateral position for the posterior or anterolateral approach. DHS and nail need the patient supine on a traction table with the fractured leg in a boot, the pelvis against a padded perineal post, the other leg abducted or scissored out of the way of the image intensifier, and the operative-side arm across the chest.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    On the traction table the hazards are the post and the pull. The perineal post presses on the pudendal nerve and the genitalia; a pudendal neuropraxia and perineal pressure injury follow a long pull against poor padding, so check the padding and ask for traction to be released whenever the surgeon is not reducing. The pull stretches the sciatic nerve and, in a tight boot, the peroneal nerve. The well leg, abducted and elevated, can develop a calf compartment syndrome in a long subtrochanteric nailing. A spinal patient on their side under a drape for 80 min has a face you cannot see; the capnography line on the mask is the sedation monitor. Forced-air warming from the start: the traction table exposes the patient and the spinal has removed thermoregulation below the waist.

  6. 6 Hemiarthroplasty: approach, capsulotomy and removal of the head

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Through a posterior approach (short external rotators divided, capsule opened at the back) or an anterolateral approach (anterior gluteus medius lifted off the trochanter), the surgeon opens the capsule, removes the fractured head with a corkscrew, measures it and cuts the neck. Posterior is faster and spares the abductors at the cost of a higher dislocation rate.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Removing the head is where the blood starts, from the neck and from the haematoma in the capsule; the 2015 safety guideline tells you to watch for cardiorespiratory compromise from this moment, not from the cement. It is also where you should hear the words “we will be cementing” and acknowledge them; the guideline makes that exchange a formal requirement.

  7. 7 Hemiarthroplasty: canal preparation and cement

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The canal is broached, washed with pressurised lavage, dried, plugged distally and filled retrogradely from a cement gun; the stem is inserted and held while the cement cures. The washing, drying and plugging are the surgical half of the cement precautions, because cement pressurised into a canal full of fat and marrow drives both into the femoral veins.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is the step the 2015 AAGBI, BOA and BGS safety guideline was written for. Bone cement implantation syndrome is graded 1 (saturation below 94% or a systolic fall over 20%, in about 20% of cemented hemiarthroplasties), 2 (saturation below 88%, a systolic fall over 40% or loss of consciousness, about 3%) and 3 (cardiac arrest, about 1%); the risk factors are age, male sex, cardiopulmonary disease and diuretic use, which describes most of the list. The mechanism is embolic: fat, marrow and air into the right heart, pulmonary vasoconstriction and acute right ventricular failure. Under a spinal the first sign is confusion or restlessness; under a general anaesthetic it is an abrupt fall in end-tidal carbon dioxide before the pressure moves. The precautions are all before the event: fluid before induction and again before cementing, a vasopressor infusion already running, systolic within 20% of the pre-induction value, stat-cycling non-invasive pressure or an arterial line in the higher-risk patient, adrenaline diluted and drawn up, and the surgeon told not to pressurise with vigour. When it happens: 100% oxygen, fluid, adrenaline in small boluses for the right heart, and the surgeon stops and waits. See bone cement and BCIS.

  8. 8 Hemiarthroplasty and THA: trial, reduction and closure

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The head size matches the one removed, the hip is reduced, stability is tested, and the capsule and rotators or the abductors are repaired. A THA adds acetabular reaming and a cup: 30-60 min more and a further bleed from the acetabular bed.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Reduction needs a relaxed patient; under a general anaesthetic a bolus of relaxant is what the surgeon means when the hip will not go in. Each trial reduction is a tug on the femoral vein and a transient fall in pressure in a patient just cemented. The THA patient follows the elective card for the approach (posterior or anterior and lateral) with the fracture’s blood loss added.

  9. 9 Extracapsular fractures: closed reduction on the traction table

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Before any incision the surgeon pulls on the boot, internally rotates the leg to bring the neck into profile and checks the reduction on two views: neck-shaft angle restored, medial cortex in contact, no varus. A reduction that fails closed means a clamp or an open reduction and a longer case.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Traction on an unblocked fracture is the most painful moment of the day and the whole case for the second block. Under a spinal the patient feels the pull as pressure in the groin; under a general anaesthetic the heart rate tells you the traction has gone on. The C-arm sweeps across the chest and your lines, so secure both before the drapes go on.

  10. 10 Dynamic hip screw: lateral approach, reaming and plate

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A lateral incision from the trochanter down the shaft, through fascia lata with vastus lateralis lifted off the bone, exposes the lateral cortex. A guidewire goes up the neck into the centre of the head under imaging, the track is reamed over it, the lag screw is inserted, the barrel plate slides over it and is screwed to the shaft, and the traction is released so the fracture compresses along the screw.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The bleeding comes from vastus lateralis stripped off bone and from the reamed cancellous track, which is why this 45-min operation has a bigger haemoglobin fall than its length suggests, on top of the unit or more already lost into the thigh. The vastus split and periosteal stripping are the muscle and periosteal components of the pain, and the reason a fascia iliaca block covers a DHS better than a PENG block.

  11. 11 Cephalomedullary nail: entry, reaming, lag screw and locking

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A short incision proximal to the trochanter, through gluteus medius at its tip, admits a guidewire and an entry reamer; the canal is reamed (little for a short nail, to the isthmus for a long one), the nail is driven in, the lag screw or helical blade goes up the neck through it, and the nail is locked distally under imaging.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Reaming the canal through a fresh fracture in an elderly patient is a marrow embolisation step, smaller than a shaft nailing but the same physiology: a fall in saturation and end-tidal carbon dioxide as the reamer passes, more with a long nail; see fat embolism. The entry through gluteus medius is the pain the patient complains of on the stairs for months and the muscle mechanism in this card. Freehand distal locking of a long nail adds 15 min of fluoroscopy at the end.

  12. 12 Recovery, the first night and day 1

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants a check radiograph and full weight-bearing from the day after surgery; every implant on this card is designed to be loaded from day 1, which is the Australian standard’s mobilisation statement.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The haemoglobin next morning is lower than the one in recovery, because the thigh keeps oozing and the fluids redistribute; transfuse to the thresholds above rather than waiting for symptoms the patient cannot report. Delirium touched a fifth of REGAIN patients whichever anaesthetic they had, and its drivers in the first 24 h are yours: unassessed pain, hypoxia, hypotension, a full bladder, anticholinergic or benzodiazepine drugs, and a night without sleep. The things that stop a patient standing on day 1 are also yours: a dense block that has not worn off (the reason both guidelines discourage catheters), postural hypotension in a patient still dry, a haemoglobin under 90 g/L, delirium, and pain not treated overnight.

Pain plan

The mechanism is bone with a muscle component in a patient who often cannot report pain, so the plan is a single-shot block early, a neuraxial or general anaesthetic for the operation, and a regular oral regimen that does not depend on the patient asking. PROSPECT’s hip fracture recommendations are the skeleton: a single-shot femoral or fascia iliaca block (supra-inguinal preferred) before surgery, paracetamol and an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor started pre-operatively and continued where the kidney and the gut permit, spinal or general anaesthesia, and opioid as rescue only. PROSPECT lists the PENG block as not recommended for lack of evidence rather than evidence against it. The author’s view: fascia iliaca covers the lateral incision of a DHS better; PENG preserves quadriceps function and suits the patient who will stand next morning after a nail or a hemiarthroplasty.

The catheter decision is close to settled: PROSPECT advises against catheters except for an expected surgical delay, and the UK guideline notes that continuous blocks may delay remobilisation, the outcome the whole pathway protects. A catheter is reasonable for the patient whose surgery is delayed beyond a day and who cannot be given a repeated single shot.

The oral regimen shape: regular paracetamol from the emergency department, an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor for the first few days where renal function, cardiac failure and gastrointestinal risk allow (a minority here, so the NSAID is a decision rather than a default), and a low-dose short-acting opioid charted regularly for the first 48 h in the patient who cannot ask, with a behavioural pain score as the trigger. Dexamethasone 4-8 mg IV at induction prolongs the block and reduces nausea.

Escalation and rebound: pain rising as the block recedes on the first night is moderate, because the fracture that hurt on movement is fixed, and it answers the regular regimen started on time. Severe pain with a tense thigh is a haematoma in an anticoagulated patient and needs a haemoglobin and the surgeon. Pain in a hemiarthroplasty with a leg that is shortened and rotated is a dislocation. New confusion on night one is delirium until proved otherwise: was the analgesia given, are the saturation and pressure adequate, is the bladder full.

Pitfalls and variants

  • Uncemented hemiarthroplasty. Chosen by some surgeons for severe cardiopulmonary disease to avoid the cement step; WHiTE 5 shows the trade is a four-fold periprosthetic fracture rate and no survival gain, so the honest discussion is a cemented stem with the full precautions.
  • The dual antiplatelet patient. A general anaesthetic with the block as the analgesic is the common answer; the UK guideline does not forbid a spinal but asks for a good reason to avoid the general anaesthetic. A recent stent is a cardiology conversation inside the 36 h.
  • Dementia and a spinal. Lying still on one side under a drape for 80 min is beyond many of these patients, and a spinal that becomes a struggle with deep sedation and an unprotected airway is the worst of both techniques. Decide at the door.
  • The subtrochanteric fracture. The hardest reduction, often open, a long nail reamed to the isthmus, the biggest blood loss and the longest case; plan it as a femoral shaft nailing with an old patient attached.
  • The periprosthetic fracture that presents as a hip fracture is a different operation (see periprosthetic fractures): longer and bloodier.
  • Pathological fracture. A lytic lesion means a long nail or a long-stem replacement, more bleeding and a bigger cement step.
  • The patient who is not for resuscitation. The operation is still the treatment for pain and is still done; the ceiling-of-care conversation is documented before the cement goes in rather than during the arrest. See the orthopaedic patient.

Key sources

The anaesthetic evidence for hip fracture is better than for any other trauma operation. REGAIN and RAGA close the question of whether spinal anaesthesia protects the brain or improves survival: it does not. HIP ATTACK shows that speed inside the 36-h window buys comfort rather than survival. WHiTE 5 shows the cemented stem is the better implant despite the cement step, which puts the burden on the anaesthetist to make the step safe, and the 2015 safety guideline says how. PROSPECT and the two national standards agree on the block, the timing and the oral regimen. The PENG versus fascia iliaca choice rests on one 80-patient trial and is the author’s judgement where the card says so.

  1. Pissens S, Cavens L, Joshi GP, et al. Pain management after hip fracture repair surgery: a systematic review and procedure-specific postoperative pain management (PROSPECT) recommendations. Acta Anaesthesiol Belg 2024;75:15-31
    Single-shot femoral or fascia iliaca block (supra-inguinal preferred) pre-operatively, paracetamol and NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor, spinal or general anaesthesia with spinal possibly giving better immediate pain relief; catheters avoided except for expected surgical delay; PENG block, epidural, local infiltration, dexmedetomidine and clonidine not recommended on current evidence
  2. Neuman MD, Feng R, Carson JL, et al. Spinal anesthesia or general anesthesia for hip surgery in older adults (REGAIN). N Engl J Med 2021;385:2025-2035
    1,600 previously ambulatory patients aged 50 and over, mean age 78: death or inability to walk 3 m at 60 days 18.5% with spinal versus 18.0% with general anaesthesia (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.84-1.27); delirium 20.5% versus 19.7%; 15% of the spinal group received general anaesthesia
  3. Li T, Li J, Yuan L, et al. Effect of regional vs general anesthesia on incidence of postoperative delirium in older patients undergoing hip fracture surgery: the RAGA randomized trial. JAMA 2022;327:50-58
    950 patients over 65 in China, regional anaesthesia given without sedation: delirium within seven days 6.2% with regional versus 5.1% with general anaesthesia, no difference
  4. Borges FK, Bhandari M, Guerra-Farfan E, et al. Accelerated surgery versus standard care in hip fracture (HIP ATTACK): an international, randomised, controlled trial. Lancet 2020;395:698-708
    2,970 patients, median time to surgery 6 h versus 24 h: 90-day mortality 9% versus 10% and the major complication composite 22% in both arms; accelerated surgery reduced delirium, urinary infection, moderate-to-severe pain and length of stay
  5. Griffiths R, White SM, Moppett IK, et al. Safety guideline: reducing the risk from cemented hemiarthroplasty for hip fracture 2015. AAGBI, British Orthopaedic Association and British Geriatric Society. Anaesthesia 2015;70:623-626
    BCIS grade 1 (SpO2 below 94% or systolic fall over 20%) in about 20%, grade 2 (SpO2 below 88%, systolic fall over 40% or loss of consciousness) in about 3%, grade 3 (CPR) in about 1%; risk factors age, male sex, cardiopulmonary disease and diuretics; surgeon warns before canal preparation, washes, dries and plugs the canal, cements retrogradely with a gun and avoids excess pressurisation in high-risk patients; anaesthetist keeps systolic within 20% of pre-induction, has vasopressors ready, uses invasive or stat-mode pressure monitoring in high-risk patients
  6. Griffiths R, Babu S, Dixon P, et al. Guideline for the management of hip fractures 2020. Association of Anaesthetists
    Surgery within 36 h; acceptable reasons for delay are corrected within that window (Hb under 80 g/L, sodium under 120 or over 150, potassium under 2.8 or over 6.0, uncontrolled diabetes, acute LVF, rate over 120, chest sepsis, reversible coagulopathy); warfarin reversed with vitamin K 5 mg IV, operate at INR 1.8 or less and spinal at 1.5 or less; factor Xa inhibitors 24 h after the last dose (48 h if eGFR under 60) or anti-Xa under 50 ng/mL; single antiplatelet agents no bar to spinal; blocks in ED and again at surgery at least 6 h apart and before positioning for the spinal; low-dose spinal without opioid; MAP above 70 mmHg; Hb kept above 90 g/L, or 100 g/L with ischaemic heart disease
  7. Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care. Hip Fracture Clinical Care Standard. ACSQHC 2023
    Seven quality statements: surgery within 36 h of first presentation (reduced from 48 h in the 2016 version); pain assessed on presentation and reassessed within 30 min of analgesia; nerve blocks and multimodal analgesia unless contraindicated, including before inter-hospital transfer; orthogeriatric model of care; mobilisation without weight-bearing restriction on the day of or the day after surgery
  8. Fernandez MA, Achten J, Parsons NR, et al. Cemented or uncemented hemiarthroplasty for intracapsular hip fracture (WHiTE 5). N Engl J Med 2022;386:521-530
    1,225 patients: EQ-5D at 4 months 0.371 cemented versus 0.315 uncemented (adjusted difference 0.055); 12-month mortality 23.9% versus 27.8% (OR 0.80, 95% CI 0.62-1.05); periprosthetic fracture 0.5% versus 2.1%
  9. Koh WU, et al. Comparison of analgesic effect of pericapsular nerve group block and supra-inguinal fascia iliaca compartment block on dynamic pain in patients with hip fractures: a randomized controlled trial. Reg Anesth Pain Med 2025;50:635-640
    80 hip fracture patients, ropivacaine 0.3% in both arms: reduction in dynamic pain on passive hip flexion at 30 min 3.1 with PENG versus 2.9 with supra-inguinal fascia iliaca, no difference in resting pain, Bromage score or opioid use to 48 h

Trauma › Trauma

40 Femoral shaft nailing

Antegrade (piriformis or trochanteric entry) and retrograde reamed intramedullary nailing; traction table or free leg; the polytrauma patient and the damage control decision

3Moderate

Dominant mechanism: Bone. A fractured, mobile long bone with a litre of blood in the thigh; then a reamed canal, an entry point through gluteus medius or the patellar tendon, and a fracture compressed and held rigid by the nail. The fixation itself is the analgesic: a splinted femur hurts far less than a mobile one, and the residual pain is reaming, the entry point and the swollen thigh

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: moderate.

Block
Femoral nerve or fascia iliaca block for the pre-operative period and for traction; the operation itself under general anaesthesia, with a single-shot femoral block or fascia iliaca block as the analgesic component where there is no compartment syndrome concern
Catheter: rarely A single shot covers the first night and the thigh is not a compartment syndrome site in the way the leg is; a catheter is for the patient with bilateral femurs, a floating knee or opioid tolerance, and never in a patient whose other injuries need serial neurological examination
Alternatives: Spinal anaesthesia for the isolated fracture in a fasted, stable patient who can tolerate the traction table; Surgeon's infiltration at the entry point and portals; Multimodal with ketamine for the polytrauma patient without a block
Position
Supine on a traction table with a perineal post for most antegrade nails; supine on a radiolucent table with the leg free and manual traction for the polytrauma patient and for retrograde nailing with the knee flexed over a bolster; lateral on a traction table in a few surgeons' hands
Tourniquet
No
Cement
No
Blood loss
The fracture has already lost 1-1.5 L into the thigh before you meet the patient; the operation adds 300-600 mL, more with reaming of a comminuted fracture and much more in a polytrauma patient with a coagulopathy. Group and hold always; crossmatch for bilateral femurs or a pelvis in the same patient
Duration
60-120 min for an isolated closed fracture on a traction table; longer for a free-leg nailing with an assistant holding traction, a comminuted or segmental fracture, a floating knee or an ipsilateral neck fracture
Length of stay
3-7 nights for an isolated fracture; set by the other injuries in polytrauma. Day case: no
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV within 60 min of incision (3 g over 120 kg) for a closed fracture; for an open fracture the antibiotic was due within an hour of injury and is continued per the open fracture plan
Tranexamic acid
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV at induction, and 1 g IV at injury in the trauma bay if the patient was bleeding (CRASH-2: within 3 h of injury)
VTE
Low molecular weight heparin from the night of surgery or as soon as the bleeding risk allows, continued through the immobile period; mechanical prophylaxis on the other leg from admission. A femoral shaft fracture is a high-risk VTE injury
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV at induction and ondansetron 4 mg IV; the young trauma patient on opioids is the vomiting phenotype
Tell the patient
Once the nail is in, the bone is held still and most of the deep pain of the break goes; the thigh stays swollen and bruised for a couple of weeks and the hip or knee entry point is sore when you walk on it, which you will be asked to do straight away.
The trap
Reaming is a marrow embolisation step, and the patient who cannot afford it is the one with a chest injury or a borderline physiology after resuscitation: in the randomised trial of borderline polytrauma patients, primary nailing carried 6.7 times the odds of acute lung injury compared with external fixation and nailing later, so the question to settle before the reamer is whether this patient should be nailed today at all

What the surgeon is doing and why

A femoral shaft fracture is a high-energy injury in a young patient or a low-energy one in an osteoporotic or pathological femur, and both get the same implant. The femur is the largest tube of bone in the body inside the largest muscle mass, and when it breaks the muscles shorten and angulate the fragments, the thigh fills with a litre or more of blood, and the patient cannot be moved without the fragments grinding. The surgeon’s aim is to restore length, alignment and rotation and hold them with an implant that lets the patient weight-bear at once. A reamed, locked intramedullary nail does that from inside the bone: a load-sharing splint down the canal, locked above and below so the fragments cannot shorten or rotate, inserted through small incisions away from the fracture so the haematoma and periosteum that will heal the bone are left alone. The Canadian trial of 224 polytrauma patients found nonunion five times more likely with an unreamed nail and no excess of lung injury from reaming, which is why nearly every femoral nail is now reamed.

The nail can go in from the top or the bottom. Antegrade nailing enters at the piriformis fossa or the tip of the greater trochanter, through gluteus medius, and is the standard for most shaft fractures. Retrograde nailing enters through the intercondylar notch of the knee, through the patellar tendon, with the knee flexed over a bolster, and is chosen for the obese patient whose trochanter cannot be reached, the patient with an ipsilateral femoral neck or acetabular fracture that needs the hip left alone, the floating knee (ipsilateral tibial and femoral fractures, nailed through one knee incision), the distal third or supracondylar fracture, and the periprosthetic fracture above a knee replacement. Union rates are equivalent; the retrograde knee is sorer for longer.

The second decision is the table. A traction table with a perineal post holds the fracture out to length with the surgeon’s hands free, at the cost of a post pressing on the pudendal nerve and the perineum, a pull on the sciatic and peroneal nerves, and a patient who cannot be turned or reached quickly. The free-leg technique on a radiolucent table, with an assistant pulling, is slower but is the choice for the polytrauma patient who may need a chest drain or a laparotomy, for bilateral femurs, and for retrograde nailing.

The third decision belongs to both of you and is the heart of this card: whether to nail today at all. Bone’s 1989 randomised trial showed that in multiply injured patients delayed femoral fixation carried more ARDS, fat embolism and pneumonia and a longer ICU stay, and early total care became the rule. Then it became clear that the operation itself, reaming a litre of marrow and fat into the circulation during a 2-h case with its own blood loss, is a second inflammatory hit, and that in the patient whose first hit has already primed the lungs, the second hit is what tips them into ARDS. Scalea’s damage control orthopaedics (external fixation in minutes, nailing days later when the physiology has recovered) was the answer, and Pape’s randomised trial of 165 polytrauma patients put numbers on it: in stable patients, primary nailing shortened ventilation; in the 44 borderline patients, primary nailing carried 6.7 times the odds of acute lung injury compared with an external fixator and a nail later. The full physiology of the decision is in the polytrauma card; for this card the rule is that the stable patient is nailed within 24 h and the borderline or unstable patient gets a fixator and a reamer in three to five days’ time.

The pain logic is bone, and it runs backwards from most operations: the patient is in more pain before surgery than after it. The fracture haematoma, the mobile fragments and the muscle spasm hurt in a way splinting cannot fully control, and the nail, by locking the fracture, removes most of that. What remains is the reamed canal (a deep ache for two or three days), the entry point (gluteus medius split at the trochanter, or the patellar tendon and knee joint for a retrograde nail), the locking screw incisions through vastus lateralis, and a thigh swollen with a litre of old blood. The score is 3: a block or neuraxial technique is expected, opioids are needed for two or three days, and the pain falls as bone pain falls. The young patient after a motorcycle crash sits at the top of the range and will need a great deal of opioid in the first 48 h; the older patient after a fall has the same operation with the hip fracture pathway’s problems.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 The trauma bay: splint, block, blood and the decision

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants the fracture splinted in traction to reduce bleeding and pain, the limb’s circulation and skin documented, an ipsilateral femoral neck fracture excluded on a dedicated hip view or CT (it is missed in a meaningful minority of shaft fractures and changes the nail), and the patient’s physiology classified as stable, borderline or unstable.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A femoral nerve or fascia iliaca block in the trauma bay is the analgesic that lets the traction splint go on; the thigh is not the compartment syndrome site that the leg is, so the block is not withheld on those grounds. The femur has already bled a litre or more into the thigh, so a young patient with a normal pressure and a heart rate of 110 is a litre down and compensating; tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 h of injury if there is any bleeding concern, a group and hold or crossmatch, and a lactate and base deficit as the honest measures of how far behind the resuscitation is. Decide the damage control question with the surgeon now, with the lactate, the chest radiograph, the temperature and the coagulation in front of you, not in the anaesthetic room with the patient asleep.

  2. 2 Induction and the unfasted trauma patient

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The isolated closed femoral fracture in a stable patient is nailed on the next available list within 24 h, which is almost never a fasted patient.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Trauma, opioids and pain stop gastric emptying at the moment of injury, so the fasting interval is counted from the crash, not the last meal, and a rapid sequence induction is the default. Spinal anaesthesia is an option for the isolated fracture in a stable, fasted and cooperative patient on a traction table, with a block for the positioning; it is not the choice for a polytrauma patient who may need a laparotomy, a chest drain or a long case. Two large-bore cannulae and an arterial line for anything beyond an isolated fracture. Cefazolin 2 g IV before the incision; for an open fracture the antibiotic was due within an hour of injury and follows the open fracture card. Dexamethasone 8 mg IV at induction.

  3. 3 Positioning: traction table or free leg

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    On the traction table the surgeon puts the foot in a boot, the perineum against the post, adducts the leg to clear the trochanter, swings the C-arm and reduces the fracture with traction and rotation before scrubbing. For a free-leg nailing the patient lies on a radiolucent table with a bump under the buttock and an assistant holds traction by hand.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The post is the injury you can prevent. In the systematic review of 351 traction table patients, mostly femoral shafts, erectile dysfunction occurred in 10%, genital sensory disturbance in 6% and perineal skin necrosis in 3%, with pudendal palsy correlating with the summed pressure on the perineum rather than operative time alone. Pad the post, check the genitalia are not trapped between post and thigh, ask for traction to be released whenever the surgeon is not reducing or imaging, and note the traction time. The pull also stretches the sciatic nerve and the peroneal nerve at the fibular neck; the well leg, abducted and elevated for the C-arm, is at risk of a calf compartment syndrome in a long case. The arm on the operative side is across the chest and must not drag on the plexus. Forced-air warming on the upper body, because the trauma patient arrives cold and the traction table exposes everything.

  4. 4 Entry point: piriformis fossa, trochanteric tip or intercondylar notch

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Antegrade: a 5-cm incision proximal to the trochanter, a guidewire into the piriformis fossa (in line with the canal, but with the medial femoral circumflex artery and the abductors in the way) or the trochanteric tip (easier, used with a bent nail, through gluteus medius), confirmed on two views, then an entry reamer opens the canal. Retrograde: a medial parapatellar or transtendinous incision with the knee flexed 40-50 degrees, a guidewire into the notch just anterior to the posterior cruciate ligament origin, and the entry reamer through the articular cartilage.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Opening the canal is the first marrow venting, smaller than the reaming to come. The trochanteric entry disrupts gluteus medius and is the abductor limp and the hip pain on stairs that follow antegrade nailing for months. The retrograde entry is intra-articular, so the knee will be a haemarthrosis and a stiff, sore joint for weeks.

  5. 5 Reduction and passage of the guidewire across the fracture

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The fracture is reduced with traction, rotation and manipulation of the fragments by a crutch, a mallet or a percutaneous reduction tool, and a ball-tipped guidewire is passed down the canal across the fracture to the distal metaphysis. A fracture that will not reduce closed needs a small open reduction at the fracture site, which disturbs the haematoma and lengthens the case.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is the most physically violent part of the operation and the one that needs a relaxed patient: muscle spasm is what holds the fragments shortened and angulated, so the surgeon’s request for relaxation here is a real one, and a bolus of neuromuscular blocker makes a difference to the reduction. It is also the step most likely to run long. Malrotation is the common malunion after femoral nailing and the surgeon will compare the lesser trochanter profile against the other side, which explains a pause with the C-arm over the well leg.

  6. 6 Reaming

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Flexible reamers are passed over the guidewire in 0.5-mm increments until cortical chatter, to a diameter 1-1.5 mm over the planned nail, so that the nail fits the isthmus tightly and the reaming debris acts as a bone graft at the fracture. Reaming raises intramedullary pressure and forces marrow fat into the venous sinusoids; sharp reamers, slow advancement and a venting hole reduce the peak.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Every pass of the reamer sends marrow fat and debris into the femoral veins and through the right heart; transoesophageal echocardiography shows embolic material in 88% of patients during reaming. In the healthy young patient the lungs filter it with a transient fall in end-tidal carbon dioxide and saturation and nothing else. In the patient with a chest injury, a second fractured femur, a pelvic fracture or a pre-existing lung, this is the second hit: fat embolism syndrome (hypoxaemia, confusion and petechiae 12-72 h later, supportive treatment, 1-10% mortality in the reviews) and ARDS are the consequences. During reaming, watch end-tidal carbon dioxide, saturation and pressure together; an abrupt fall in end-tidal carbon dioxide with a rise in central venous pressure is a large embolic load and the reaming should pause. The Canadian trial found no increase in ARDS with reaming over unreamed nails, so the question is not whether to ream but whether this patient should have had a nail today; see fat embolism.

  7. 7 Nail insertion and proximal locking

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The nail is driven over the guidewire with a mallet, the fracture reduced around it, and locked proximally through a jig (antegrade) or distally through a jig (retrograde). Nail length and rotation are checked under imaging.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Hammering a nail down a reamed canal is a second pressurisation and a second embolic load, smaller than reaming. The blood loss of the operation is mostly from the reamed canal and the entry point, and a comminuted or segmental fracture bleeds more because the reaming debris and the haematoma have nowhere to go; check a haemoglobin in a long case. A nail that incarcerates in a canal reamed too narrow is a long delay and a surgeon reaming again.

  8. 8 Distal locking and release of traction

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Distal interlocking is done freehand under the image intensifier (“perfect circles”), through small lateral incisions and vastus lateralis, two screws in most fractures; the traction is released so the fracture compresses onto the nail, and rotation and length are compared with the other leg.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Freehand locking is 10-20 min of fluoroscopy with the surgeon’s hands in the beam, a still leg and a patient the surgeon wants left alone. Release of traction is the moment to look at the perineum and the well leg, and to feel the calf of the operated leg; a thigh that is tense after nailing is a haematoma, and compartment syndrome of the thigh, rare but real after high-energy fractures and prolonged traction, presents as pain out of proportion and a tense anterior compartment.

  9. 9 Closure, emergence and recovery

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The incisions are small and closed in layers; there is no drain and no cast. The surgeon wants a check radiograph, full weight-bearing as pain allows from day 1 for a stable fracture pattern with a reamed locked nail, and an early rotational profile check.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Emergence from a rapid sequence induction in a full-stomach patient is awake extubation. The oral regimen starts in recovery. The young patient will need substantial opioid in the first 24 h; the haemoglobin on the morning after is the one that counts, after the thigh has finished redistributing. Low molecular weight heparin starts the night of surgery unless the bleeding risk says otherwise; a femoral fracture is a high-risk injury for VTE and the clot is forming in the femoral vein from the night of the crash.

  10. 10 Day 1 and the ward

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants the patient standing on day 1 with physiotherapy, a hip and knee range started, and the other injuries managed.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Fat embolism syndrome declares itself on day 1-3 as confusion, hypoxaemia, a fever and petechiae on the chest and in the axillae, and the ward will call it pneumonia or opioid toxicity; the treatment is oxygen and supportive care, and the diagnosis is yours to make when the night registrar asks. NSAIDs: the case-control literature associates them with femoral nonunion and many surgeons ask for them to be withheld after shaft fractures; the evidence is observational, but it is the surgeon’s call and worth asking before the chart is written.

Pain plan

The mechanism is bone with the operation removing most of the pre-operative generator, so the plan is a block for the pre-operative period and the traction, a general anaesthetic for the operation, and a multimodal regimen with substantial early opioid. There is no PROSPECT guideline for femoral shaft nailing; the nearest is the hip fracture recommendation, and its skeleton (single-shot femoral or fascia iliaca block, paracetamol, an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor if the surgeon permits, opioid rescue) is the author’s starting point here.

The block: a femoral nerve block or fascia iliaca block in the trauma bay covers the anterior thigh and the fracture haematoma, lets the splint and the traction go on, and is repeated before the operation if more than 6 h have passed. It does not cover the posterior thigh or the retrograde knee entry, and a sciatic block in a trauma patient with a possible sciatic nerve injury from the fracture obscures an examination. The catheter decision: a single shot is enough for an isolated fracture, because the nail is the analgesic and the thigh is not the compartment syndrome site the lower leg is. A femoral catheter earns its place for bilateral femurs, the floating knee, the patient who waits days with a fixator on, and the opioid-tolerant patient; it is withheld in the polytrauma patient with a head or spine injury who needs serial neurological examination.

The oral regimen shape: regular paracetamol, an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor for the first few days where the surgeon accepts it (many will not, citing the nonunion association), and an opioid at regular intervals for the first 48 h with a patient-controlled analgesia pump for the young high-energy patient, who will need more than the ward expects. Ketamine at low dose is the author’s adjunct for the opioid-tolerant or the patient without a block. Rebound is moderate: when the block recedes the fracture is fixed and the pain is a sore entry point and a bruised thigh.

Escalation: pain that rises on day 1-2 with a tense thigh is a haematoma or, rarely, a thigh compartment syndrome; pain with new confusion and hypoxaemia is fat embolism syndrome; pain in the calf of either leg is a clot until proved otherwise. For the retrograde nail, a knee that is hot and swollen at a week is a haemarthrosis or a septic knee, and the surgeon sees it first.

Pitfalls and variants

  • The ipsilateral femoral neck fracture. Present in a minority of high-energy shaft fractures and missed on the trauma series; it changes the operation to a retrograde nail with screws into the neck, or a cephalomedullary device, and adds an hour.
  • Bilateral femoral fractures. Two litres in the thighs before the operation, two reamings, a higher fat embolism rate (4.6% against 2.9% in the systematic review), a free-leg technique, and a patient who is borderline by definition. One or both fixators first is a reasonable call.
  • The floating knee. Ipsilateral femoral and tibial fractures, usually nailed through one knee incision (retrograde femur, antegrade tibia); a long case with two reamings and a sore knee for months.
  • The obese patient. The trochanter cannot be reached antegrade, so retrograde nailing; a traction table that may not take the weight; a difficult airway and a difficult arterial line.
  • The older patient after a fall. The same nail with a hip fracture physiology: anticoagulants to reverse, a dry patient, a long reaming of an osteoporotic canal that bleeds, and delirium on the ward. The hip fracture card applies.
  • The pathological fracture. A metastasis in the shaft means a long nail reamed through tumour, with embolisation of tumour and fat together, often a larger blood loss, and a conversation about the rest of the skeleton and the prognosis before the operation.
  • The open femoral fracture. Antibiotics within an hour of injury, debridement, and either a primary nail (most Gustilo I-IIIA fractures) or an external fixator for the contaminated or vascular injury; see the open fracture card.
  • The head-injured patient. Early fixation does not cause secondary brain injury; hypoxia, hypotension and raised intracranial pressure do, and a reaming-induced desaturation is a brain insult in this patient.
  • The perineal post complaint. Numbness of the genitalia or erectile dysfunction after the traction table is a pudendal neuropraxia; it resolves over weeks to months, needs documentation, and is prevented by padding and short traction times.
  • Nail removal. Elective removal of a femoral nail after union is harder than it looks and bleeds more than expected; see removal of metalwork.

Key sources

The evidence on timing is the strongest part of this card and the weakest part of most anaesthetists’ knowledge of it: Bone’s randomised trial for early fixation, Scalea’s series for damage control, and Pape’s randomised trial for the borderline patient between them define who is nailed on the day. The reamed versus unreamed question is settled by the Canadian trial. The fat embolism literature is observational and the incidence has fallen with early fixation. The perineal post review is recent and sobering. There is no procedure-specific analgesia guideline; the block and catheter advice here is extrapolated from the hip fracture recommendations and is the author’s judgement where the card says so.

  1. Bone LB, Johnson KD, Weigelt J, Scheinberg R. Early versus delayed stabilization of femoral fractures: a prospective randomized study. J Bone Joint Surg Am 1989;71:336-340
    178 patients randomised to early or delayed femoral stabilisation: in the multiply injured group, delayed fixation carried more ARDS, fat embolism and pneumonia, a longer stay and more ICU days; the trial that made early fixation the standard
  2. Pape HC, Rixen D, Morley J, et al. Impact of the method of initial stabilization for femoral shaft fractures in patients with multiple injuries at risk for complications (borderline patients). Ann Surg 2007;246:491-499
    165 multiply injured patients randomised to primary nailing within 24 h or external fixation with later conversion: in the 44 borderline patients, primary nailing carried an adjusted odds ratio of 6.69 for acute lung injury; in stable patients primary nailing shortened ventilation
  3. Scalea TM, Boswell SA, Scott JD, et al. External fixation as a bridge to intramedullary nailing for patients with multiple injuries and with femur fractures: damage control orthopedics. J Trauma 2000;48:613-621
    43 patients with initial external fixation compared with 284 primary nailings: temporary external fixation was safe in multiply injured patients, the paper that named damage control orthopaedics
  4. Lempert M, Halvachizadeh S, Ellanti P, et al. Incidence of fat embolism syndrome in femur fractures and its associated risk factors over time: a systematic review. J Clin Med 2021;10:2733
    15 studies, 3,095 patients: fat embolism syndrome fell from 7.9% (1960-1979) to 1.7% (2000-2019); bilateral fractures 4.6% versus unilateral 2.9%; TOE detects embolic material during reaming in 88% of patients; mortality 1-10%; treatment supportive
  5. Attenasio A, Kraeutler MJ, Hong IS, et al. Are complications related to the perineal post on orthopaedic traction tables for surgical fracture fixation more common than we think? A systematic review. Patient Saf Surg 2023;17:5
    10 studies, 351 patients, 83.5% femoral shaft fractures: erectile dysfunction in 10.0%, genital sensory disturbance in 6.3%, perineal skin necrosis in 3.1%; pudendal palsy correlated with summed perineal pressure; risk factors are traction force and time; posts under 9 cm diameter may contribute
  6. Canadian Orthopaedic Trauma Society. Nonunion following intramedullary nailing of the femur with and without reaming: results of a multicenter randomized clinical trial. J Bone Joint Surg Am 2003;85:2093-2096
    224 patients randomised to reamed or unreamed femoral nailing: nonunion 1.7% reamed versus 7.5% unreamed, with no difference in pulmonary complications
  7. Giannoudis PV, MacDonald DA, Matthews SJ, et al. Nonunion of the femoral diaphysis: the influence of reaming and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. J Bone Joint Surg Br 2000;82:655-658
    Case-control study associating NSAID use with femoral diaphyseal nonunion and delayed healing; the paper behind many surgeons' request to withhold NSAIDs after nailing

Trauma › Trauma

41 Tibial shaft nailing and tibial plateau fixation

Infrapatellar and suprapatellar intramedullary nailing of the tibial shaft; open reduction and internal fixation of tibial plateau fractures, staged with a spanning external fixator for high-energy patterns

4Severe

Dominant mechanism: Bone. A reamed tibial canal with an entry through the patellar tendon or the knee (nail), or a crushed articular surface elevated, grafted and plated under periosteal stripping on one or both sides of the proximal tibia (plateau), in a limb whose soft-tissue envelope is thin, bruised and swollen; plus the tourniquet and the raw bone defect that a bone graft fills. The compartment syndrome risk shapes the block, not the pain

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: high.

Block
Single-shot popliteal sciatic and adductor canal (or femoral) blocks with dilute local anaesthetic and no adjuncts, placed after a documented compartment examination and with a surveillance plan the surgeon has agreed; dense long-acting blocks and catheters avoided in the fresh high-energy fracture
Catheter: selective Avoided in the fresh high-energy shaft fracture and the fracture-dislocation plateau in the first 48 h, where the compartment syndrome risk is highest; reasonable for the delayed definitive plateau fixation at 7-14 days with a fixator already on, when the swelling has settled and the window for compartment syndrome has closed
Alternatives: Spinal anaesthesia for the isolated shaft nail in a stable fasted patient, with a short-acting agent so the leg can be examined by the evening; General anaesthesia with multimodal analgesia and ketamine, no block, for the fracture-dislocation plateau in the first 48 h; Surgeon's local infiltration at the entry point and plate incisions
Position
Supine on a radiolucent table; knee flexed over a triangle or bolster for infrapatellar nailing, semi-extended over a small bump for suprapatellar nailing; supine with a bump under the hip and the knee flexed for lateral plateau plating; the leg often brought over the side or a posteromedial approach done with the hip externally rotated
Tourniquet
Sometimes. Not used for nailing (reaming needs the bleeding bone to be seen and a thigh tourniquet obstructs the entry point); commonly used for plateau ORIF at 250-300 mmHg for up to 120 min, deflated before closure in a limb whose circulation is already in question
Cement
No
Blood loss
Shaft nailing 200-400 mL; plateau ORIF 300-600 mL under tourniquet and more once it is released, with a bicondylar dual-incision case bleeding across a long operation. The fracture itself has lost 500 mL or more into the leg
Duration
Shaft nailing 60-120 min; lateral plateau ORIF 90-150 min; bicondylar plateau with dual incisions and bone graft 180-300 min
Length of stay
2-5 nights for a shaft nail; the staged plateau has two admissions or one long one, with the definitive fixation at 7-14 days and a stay of 3-7 nights after it. Day case: no
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV within 60 min of incision (3 g over 120 kg); open fractures were due their antibiotic within an hour of injury and follow the open fracture plan
Tranexamic acid
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV at induction for plateau ORIF; reasonable for nailing
VTE
Low molecular weight heparin from the night of surgery, continued through the non-weight-bearing period for a plateau fracture (6-12 weeks); mechanical prophylaxis on the other leg
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV at induction (it also prolongs whatever block is used, so it is withheld when a short, examinable block is the aim) and ondansetron 4 mg IV
Tell the patient
The first two days after a tibial operation are the hard ones, because the leg swells inside a tight skin; the pain then settles over a week, and the knee stays sore at the front for a long time after a nail, which is normal and not a sign of anything wrong.
The trap
Compartment syndrome is the complication of this bone, it declares itself in the first 48 h, and the thing that hides it is a dense long-acting block that nobody planned a surveillance for: the current UK guidance is that dilute single-shot blocks without adjuncts do not delay the diagnosis when the observation is competent, and that a block placed without that observation does

What the surgeon is doing and why

The tibia is the bone with the worst soft-tissue envelope in the body: a subcutaneous anteromedial border, a thin skin over it with a poor blood supply, and four muscle compartments bound by unyielding fascia behind and lateral to it. Everything that is difficult about tibial fracture surgery follows from that. A shaft fracture bleeds into compartments that cannot expand, so compartment syndrome is the complication of this bone and not of the femur. A plateau fracture crushes the articular surface of the knee and swells the skin over it until the surgeon cannot close an incision, so high-energy plateau fractures are fixed in two stages a fortnight apart. The anaesthetic decisions on this card (the block, the tourniquet, the timing) are all soft-tissue and compartment decisions before they are pain decisions.

    tibial injury
         |
   +-----+------------------------+
 shaft fracture               plateau fracture
   |                               |
 reamed locked nail        low energy (Schatzker I-III,
   |                       lateral split or depression):
 infrapatellar               single-stage ORIF, lateral plate
 (knee flexed, through           |
  patellar tendon)        high energy (IV-VI, medial, bicondylar,
    or                    fracture-dislocation):
 suprapatellar              day 0  spanning external fixator
 (semi-extended,             +/- fasciotomy
  through the joint)        day 7-14  ORIF when the wrinkle
                                      sign returns

Shaft nailing. The nail is a reamed, locked intramedullary splint, as for the femur, inserted from the top of the tibia. The infrapatellar approach flexes the knee to 90 degrees over a bolster and splits or retracts the patellar tendon to reach the entry point; the fracture is reduced by hand against the flexed knee, which is awkward for proximal fractures. The suprapatellar approach nails the tibia semi-extended through a small incision above the patella and a cannula through the patellofemoral joint, which holds the fracture reduced by gravity and gives better alignment (4% against 26% malalignment in the systematic review) at the cost of instruments through the articular cartilage. Anterior knee pain is the signature complaint after tibial nailing whichever route is used, 29% after suprapatellar and 39% after infrapatellar in the pooled studies, not significantly different; it is attributed to the tendon split, the fat pad, the nail tip and the infrapatellar branch of the saphenous nerve, and it lasts for months.

Plateau fixation. The Schatzker classification sorts plateau fractures by energy and side: I-III are lateral split, split-depression and pure depression fractures from a valgus force; IV is the medial plateau, a high-energy injury that is really a fracture-dislocation of the knee with a popliteal artery and a peroneal nerve at risk; V and VI are bicondylar, with VI dissociating the metaphysis from the shaft. The low-energy lateral fracture is fixed in one sitting through a lateral incision: the depressed joint surface is elevated through a cortical window, the void beneath it filled with bone graft or substitute, and a lateral plate buttresses the split. The high-energy fracture arrives with a leg too swollen to open: the surgeon spans the knee with an external fixator on day 0, does a fasciotomy if the compartments are tight, and returns at 7-14 days when the skin wrinkles again to plate both columns through lateral and posteromedial incisions. In the series of 67 high-energy plateaus spanned within 48 h, compartment syndrome occurred in 27%, and in 53% of medial fracture-dislocations; ten cases declared after the frame was on, and three were diagnosed late. Wound breakdown and infection after extensive stripping run at around 20% in the older series, which is the reason for the staging.

The pain logic is bone with two amplifiers. The reamed canal and the entry point (nail), or the elevated, grafted and plated metaphysis (plateau), hurt as bone does for two or three days, then fall. The amplifiers are the tourniquet for a long plateau fixation and the soft-tissue envelope: the leg swells inside skin that cannot stretch, and movement-evoked pain limits the early knee range a plateau fixation needs. The score is 4: the first 48 h need a robust plan, rebound after a single-shot block is high because the bone and the swelling are both at their worst when it wears off, and the plateau patient has a knee that must bend while non-weight-bearing for six to twelve weeks. A catheter would be the obvious answer and is exactly what the compartment syndrome risk argues against in the first two days, which is the tension this card is about.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 Emergency department: splint, compartments, block decision

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants the fracture splinted, the skin and compartments examined and documented, a CT for any plateau fracture, an ankle-brachial index or CT angiogram for a medial plateau or a knee that looks dislocated, and the staging decision made.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The compartment examination before any block is the baseline against which the next 48 h are read: pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch of the toes, a tense compartment, and later paraesthesia; the pressure measurement (a differential of diastolic minus compartment pressure below 30 mmHg is McQueen’s threshold for fasciotomy) belongs to the surgeon. The block decision follows the Association of Anaesthetists’ 2021 guideline: a single-shot peripheral block with a lower concentration of local anaesthetic and no adjuncts is not associated with delayed diagnosis provided surveillance is competent; a dense, long-acting block or a neuraxial technique that lasts well beyond the operation is to be avoided; the patient is told and consents; and neither surgeon nor anaesthetist can veto the other. The retrospective series of 791 tibial fixations found compartment syndrome in 1.6% of blocked and 4.5% of unblocked patients and no excess of missed cases with blocks, with the caveat that all four missed cases in the blocked group had catheters.

  2. 2 Induction and the unfasted, swollen leg

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A closed shaft fracture is nailed within 24 h in a stable patient; a high-energy plateau is spanned the same day and fixed a fortnight later; a low-energy plateau waits for the swelling to settle if the skin is in doubt.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The acute case is a rapid sequence induction counted from the time of injury. A spinal is reasonable for the isolated shaft nail in a stable, fasted patient if a short-acting agent is used so the leg can be examined that evening; it is the wrong technique for a fracture-dislocation plateau in the first 48 h. The delayed definitive plateau fixation with a frame on is an elective anaesthetic with a block or a catheter that the compartment window no longer argues against. Cefazolin 2 g IV; dexamethasone withheld when the aim is a short, examinable block.

  3. 3 Positioning and the tourniquet

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Nailing: supine, knee flexed over a triangle (infrapatellar) or semi-extended over a bump (suprapatellar), the C-arm from the opposite side, no tourniquet because the reamed bone must bleed and a thigh cuff obstructs the entry. Plateau: supine with a bump under the ipsilateral hip and the knee flexed for the lateral approach; the posteromedial approach needs the hip externally rotated and the leg figure-of-four; a thigh tourniquet at 250-300 mmHg is common.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The tourniquet on a plateau fixation runs long, often to its 120-min limit before the surgeon asks for a deflate-and-reinflate, and it is applied to a limb whose circulation is already in doubt; see the tourniquet. A plateau fracture-dislocation with a vascular injury does not get a tourniquet. The peroneal nerve at the fibular neck is the nerve at risk from positioning and from the lateral plate, and a foot drop after surgery is attributed to the block until someone checks the timeline; document the foot before the block.

  4. 4 Nailing: entry point and reaming

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Infrapatellar: a 3-cm incision over the patellar tendon, the tendon split or retracted, an awl or guidewire into the anterior plateau just medial to the lateral tibial spine, and the canal opened. Suprapatellar: a 3-cm incision above the patella, a protective cannula through the patellofemoral joint, and the same entry point reached with the knee at 20 degrees. Flexible reamers are passed over a guidewire across the reduced fracture to 1-1.5 mm over the nail diameter.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Reaming the tibia embolises marrow as the femur does, with a smaller load. The thing that matters at this step is the compartment pressure: reaming raises it, the fracture has already bled into the deep posterior compartment, and a leg that is tense at the end of a nailing is one the surgeon should feel before the drapes come off. The tendon split and the entry through the fat pad are the anterior knee pain that follows.

  5. 5 Nailing: nail insertion, locking and the compartment check

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The nail is driven over the guidewire, locked proximally through a jig and distally freehand under imaging, the fracture compressed by backslapping, and alignment and rotation checked against the other leg.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Freehand distal locking is 10-15 min of fluoroscopy with a still leg. At the end of the case, before the patient wakes, the surgeon examines the compartments, and some will measure pressures in a high-energy fracture; this is the moment the first 48 h of surveillance starts from. A patient waking with a working dilute block will not report pain out of proportion that evening, so the ward observations have to be the palpation, the passive stretch of the toes and the pressure, on a chart, by someone trained to read it.

  6. 6 Plateau: the spanning external fixator

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    For the high-energy fracture, two pins in the femur and two in the tibial shaft, connected by bars across the knee, restore length and alignment by ligamentotaxis and hold the leg still while the swelling settles. A fasciotomy is done at the same sitting if the compartments are tight, and in the medial fracture-dislocation many surgeons release them prophylactically.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A short general anaesthetic, 30-45 min, often at night, in a patient who may have other injuries. No block that lasts beyond the operation: compartment syndrome in this group declares itself in the next 48 h in up to half of medial fracture-dislocations and a fifth of bicondylar fractures, and the frame holding the foot in neutral makes the examination harder, which is how the late diagnoses in the series happened. Analgesia for the first two days is opioid-based and multimodal, with ketamine, and the pain score that matters is the one that rises despite it.

  7. 7 Plateau: the wait and the wrinkle sign

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon waits 7-14 days until the skin over the proximal tibia wrinkles when pinched, the fracture blisters have epithelialised and the swelling has gone; opening earlier costs a wound breakdown and a deep infection in a joint with a plate in it.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The patient is on the ward in a frame, immobile, on opioids; this is the window for VTE, for pin-site infection and for the delirium of an older patient. The definitive operation is then elective in all but name, and the compartment window has closed: a catheter is reasonable for the definitive fixation and the author’s preference for a bicondylar case.

  8. 8 Plateau: approach, elevation of the joint surface and bone graft

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Through an anterolateral incision the surgeon lifts the anterior compartment off the lateral plateau, opens the submeniscal joint, elevates the depressed articular fragments from below through a cortical window with a bone tamp under fluoroscopy, and packs the void with autograft from the iliac crest, allograft or a calcium phosphate substitute. A bicondylar fracture adds a posteromedial incision between the pes anserinus and the medial gastrocnemius to buttress the medial column.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is the long step under tourniquet. An iliac crest graft adds a second painful wound that outlasts the knee, and the surgeon should say in advance whether one is planned, because it changes the block (a fascia iliaca block or infiltration for the crest) and the first week’s pain. The periosteal stripping on two sides of the tibia is the periosteum mechanism, raw and incisional, and the reason the dual-incision plateau sits at the top of this card’s range.

  9. 9 Plateau: plating and tourniquet release

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A lateral locking plate buttresses the lateral column with rafting screws under the elevated joint surface; a medial or posteromedial plate holds the medial column; the construct is checked under imaging and the knee taken through a range to confirm stability.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Tourniquet release after 90-120 min is the reperfusion moment: the fall in pressure, the rise in end-tidal carbon dioxide and potassium, the fall in temperature, and bleeding from bone that was dry a minute ago; the haemoglobin after a bicondylar fixation is lower than the field suggested. Reinflation for closure is a request to refuse in a leg with a compromised envelope.

  10. 10 Closure, splint and the first 48 h

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Layered closure over the plate without tension, sometimes a drain, a bulky dressing and a hinged brace or a splint; the surgeon wants early passive knee range from day 1 and no weight-bearing for 6-12 weeks.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    For the nail, the compartment surveillance runs for 48 h on a chart; the regular regimen starts in recovery and the opioid is given regularly rather than on request. For the plateau, the first two nights are the worst of this card: the leg is swollen in a dressing, the bone defect under the graft aches, and the brace has to move. Rebound after a dilute single-shot block is high and arrives in the small hours; the plan for it is the opioid already charted and a nurse who knows the difference between rebound pain and pain out of proportion. Low molecular weight heparin from the night of surgery.

  11. 11 Day 1 onwards

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Physiotherapy starts the knee moving on day 1 for a plateau (the joint surface is held by the rafting screws and stiffness is the enemy) and the patient walking non-weight-bearing on crutches; the nail patient weight-bears as tolerated from day 1.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Movement-evoked pain limits the physiotherapy on a plateau and is the argument for a catheter once the compartment window has closed; a rescue block on day 2 is reasonable in a patient whose compartments have been examined and recorded as soft. Anterior knee pain after a nail is a weeks-to-months complaint and not an acute problem. The leg that is more painful on day 2 than day 1, with a tense calf, has a compartment syndrome until someone measures the pressure.

Pain plan

The mechanism is bone with a swollen, inelastic envelope and a tourniquet, so the plan is multimodal from the trauma bay with a regional technique chosen for the compartment risk rather than for the pain alone. There is no PROSPECT guideline for tibial fracture surgery; the structure is the author’s, built on the Association of Anaesthetists’ 2021 guideline for lower leg trauma and the regional anaesthesia literature for knee and ankle surgery.

The block: for the shaft nail and the low-energy plateau, a single-shot popliteal sciatic block and an adductor canal block (or a femoral block for the plateau, where the anterolateral incision crosses the femoral territory) with a dilute local anaesthetic and no perineural or intravenous adjunct, placed after a documented compartment examination and with a surveillance chart the surgeon has agreed. The retrospective evidence is that blocks placed this way do not hide compartment syndrome and reduce opioid use; the case reports that frightened a generation of surgeons involved dense blocks and no surveillance. For the high-energy shaft fracture with a tense leg at presentation and the medial plateau fracture-dislocation in the first 48 h, no block that outlasts the operation, and a multimodal general anaesthetic with ketamine as the analgesic backbone; this is the author’s judgement and the surgeon’s, agreed before the case, because the guideline says neither can veto the other and the only way to honour that is to decide together.

The catheter: no, in the first 48 h of a fresh high-energy fracture, because every one of the missed compartment syndromes in the blocked group of the large series had a catheter. Yes, selectively, for the delayed definitive plateau fixation at 7-14 days when the window has closed and the operation is long and movement-evoked pain will limit the knee; a popliteal sciatic catheter with a dilute infusion and the compartments still examined daily.

The oral regimen shape: regular paracetamol, an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor for the first week unless the surgeon withholds it for union, a regular opioid for the first 48-72 h and then as needed, ketamine at low dose for the unblocked patient, and the night plan written for the rebound. Rebound is high: when a dilute block recedes on the first night the bone and the swelling are both at their peak, and the pain is severe for an hour or two until the regular regimen catches up. Escalation: pain that is out of proportion to the operation, pain on passive stretch of the toes, a tense compartment or rising opioid requirement in the first 48 h is a compartment syndrome until the pressure says otherwise; the response is the surgeon and a pressure measurement, not more opioid and not a rescue block.

Pitfalls and variants

  • The medial plateau fracture-dislocation. A knee dislocation that reduced itself: a popliteal artery at risk, a peroneal nerve palsy, compartment syndrome in half, and a surgeon who spans and fasciotomises on day 0. No block, an arterial line, and a vascular surgeon’s number.
  • The open tibial fracture. The commonest open long bone fracture, because the bone is subcutaneous; antibiotics within an hour, debridement, a nail for most Gustilo I-IIIA fractures or a fixator for IIIB and vascular injuries, and the open fracture card.
  • Suprapatellar nailing. Semi-extended, better alignment, instruments through the patellofemoral joint; the same anterior knee pain in the pooled data. A bump under the knee rather than a triangle, and the C-arm comes in lower.
  • The proximal third shaft fracture. Hard to align with an infrapatellar nail (the fragment flexes); many surgeons plate it or use the suprapatellar route. A plated proximal tibia is a bigger soft-tissue dissection and a tourniquet.
  • The distal third and the pilon. A fracture that extends into the ankle joint is a pilon and belongs on the ankle and pilon card: staged, soft-tissue driven, and worse.
  • The fasciotomised leg. If the compartments were released on day 0, the leg comes back for debridement and closure every 48-72 h and a block is now reasonable; see compartment syndrome and fasciotomy.
  • Iliac crest bone graft. A second wound that hurts for longer than the knee and is often forgotten in the plan; infiltration or a fascia iliaca block for the crest, and the patient warned.
  • Intravenous dexamethasone. It prolongs the block by several hours and reduces rebound, which is the wrong trade when the aim is a block that has worn off by the evening examination; withhold it in the fresh fracture and use it for the delayed fixation.
  • The spinal that will not wear off. A plain bupivacaine spinal lasts into the evening and a leg that cannot be examined for 4 h after a high-energy nailing is the neuraxial version of the dense block the guideline warns against; a short-acting agent or a general anaesthetic instead.

Key sources

The regional anaesthesia and compartment syndrome evidence is the point of this card and it has changed: the 2021 Association of Anaesthetists guideline moved the profession from “no blocks in tibial fractures” to “dilute single-shot blocks with surveillance”, and the 2025 series of 791 patients is the largest cohort to find no excess of missed compartment syndrome with blocks, with the catheter caveat. McQueen’s differential pressure threshold is the diagnostic standard. The surgical evidence is observational. There is no procedure-specific analgesia guideline, and the catheter timing advice is the author’s reading of the compartment window rather than a trial result.

  1. Association of Anaesthetists. Regional analgesia for lower leg trauma and the risk of acute compartment syndrome: guideline from the Association of Anaesthetists. Anaesthesia 2021
    Literature of case reports and series: lower-concentration peripheral blocks without adjuncts are not linked to delayed diagnosis when post-injury and post-operative surveillance is effective; dense, long-lasting neuraxial or peripheral blocks are to be avoided; observations by trained staff at set intervals with objective scoring charts; patient consent documented; neither surgeon nor anaesthetist can veto the other's recommendation
  2. Kakalecik J, et al. Relationship between perioperative regional anesthesia and the risk of missing acute compartment syndrome following tibia fractures. Anesth Analg 2025
    791 tibial shaft and plateau fixations at one level 1 centre, 610 with regional anaesthesia: in-hospital compartment syndrome 1.6% with versus 4.5% without; missed compartment syndrome (persistent motor deficit at 3 months) 0.7% versus 1.7%, not different; all four missed cases in the regional group had catheters; opioid use lower with blocks
  3. McQueen MM, Court-Brown CM. Compartment monitoring in tibial fractures: the pressure threshold for decompression. J Bone Joint Surg Br 1996;78:99-104
    116 tibial fractures, 2.6% acute compartment syndrome: a differential pressure (diastolic minus compartment pressure) of 30 mmHg predicted the need for fasciotomy more reliably than absolute compartment pressures of 30 or 40 mmHg
  4. Schatzker J, McBroom R, Bruce D. The tibial plateau fracture: the Toronto experience 1968-1975. Clin Orthop Relat Res 1979;138:94-104
    94 plateau fractures; the six-type classification with type-specific treatment that every plateau card still uses
  5. Compartment syndrome in Schatzker type VI plateau fractures and medial condylar fracture-dislocations treated with temporary external fixation. J Orthop Trauma 2009 (PubMed 19633459)
    67 patients spanned within 48 h: compartment syndrome in 27% overall, 18% of Schatzker VI fractures and 53% of medial fracture-dislocations; ten cases declared after frame placement, including three diagnosed late
  6. Leliveld MS, Verhofstad MHJ, Van Bodegraven E, Van Haaren J, Van Lieshout EMM. Anterior knee pain and functional outcome following different surgical techniques for tibial nailing: a systematic review. Eur J Trauma Emerg Surg 2021;47:763-772
    14 studies, 1,447 patients: anterior knee pain 29% after suprapatellar and 39% after infrapatellar nailing, not significantly different; malalignment 4% versus 26%; no difference in chondropathy, infection, function or quality of life

Trauma › Trauma

42 Ankle and pilon fracture fixation

Malleolar ankle ORIF (lateral, medial, posterior malleolus and syndesmosis) and tibial pilon fractures, staged with a spanning external fixator and fixed when the skin wrinkles

3Moderate

Dominant mechanism: Bone. Malleolar fragments reduced and plated or screwed through small incisions over subcutaneous bone, with a tourniquet; the pilon adds an impacted articular surface elevated and grafted through an envelope that has already been injured once. The mechanism is bone and periosteum under thin skin, and the block that covers it so well is the reason the rebound is the problem

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: high.

Block
