Popliteal sciatic block plus a saphenous (adductor canal) block, single shot, with intravenous dexamethasone, under general anaesthesia or sedation; the ankle is the operation where the block is the anaesthetic as well as the analgesic
Catheter: selective A single shot with dexamethasone and a written night plan is the day-case default for malleolar ORIF; a popliteal catheter earns its place for the pilon, the calcaneus-like high-energy foot, the opioid-tolerant patient and anyone whose previous block ended in a 3 am rebound
Alternatives: Spinal anaesthesia (inferior to blocks for the first 27 h in the AnAnkle trial, with more opioid); General anaesthesia with surgeon's infiltration where a block is refused or contraindicated; Ankle block for isolated distal fibular work in a patient who needs motor function preserved
Position
Supine with a bump under the ipsilateral buttock to internally rotate the leg for the lateral malleolus; the bump removed or the leg externally rotated for the medial side; prone or lateral for a direct posterior malleolar approach, which changes the airway plan; the pilon often needs an anteromedial or anterolateral approach with the leg on a radiolucent platform
Tourniquet
Yes. Thigh tourniquet at 250-300 mmHg for most malleolar fixations, 45-90 min; a pilon fixation runs longer and the tourniquet is often released before the articular reduction is checked; the swollen or vascular leg may get none
Cement
No
Blood loss
Under 200 mL for malleolar ORIF; 200-400 mL for a pilon, mostly after tourniquet release
Duration
Isolated lateral malleolus 45-60 min; bimalleolar or trimalleolar with syndesmosis 60-120 min; pilon ORIF 120-240 min, after a 30-min spanning fixator on day 0
Length of stay
Day case or one night for malleolar ORIF; the pilon has a day-0 fixator admission and a 2-5 night definitive admission at 7-14 days. Day case: selected
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV before the tourniquet is inflated (3 g over 120 kg); open fractures were due their antibiotic within an hour of injury and follow the open fracture plan
Tranexamic acid
Not routinely needed for malleolar ORIF; tranexamic acid 1 g IV at induction is reasonable for a pilon
VTE
Low molecular weight heparin through the immobilised period for a patient with their own risk factors or a pilon; mechanical prophylaxis on the other leg; practice varies for the day-case malleolar patient in a boot, and the decision is made rather than defaulted
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV at induction (prolongs the block, reduces rebound) and ondansetron 4 mg IV
Tell the patient
The foot will be completely numb and floppy for most of the first day; the pain then arrives over an hour or two, usually in the night, and the tablets taken before bed and again when the tingling starts are what get you through it. It settles quickly after the second day.
The trap
The block wears off at 3 am in a day-case patient at home with no analgesia taken and a leg that was pain-free when they left: rebound pain after a popliteal block for ankle fracture surgery affected 44% of patients in the trial that tested it and 15% with intravenous dexamethasone, so the dexamethasone and the written night plan are the operation's analgesia, not the block

What the surgeon is doing and why

An ankle fracture and a pilon fracture both break the distal tibia and fibula at the joint, and they are different operations because of the direction of the force. The malleolar fracture is a rotational injury: the talus twists in the mortise, the fibula breaks at or above the joint line, the medial malleolus or the deltoid ligament fails, and sometimes the posterior malleolus and the syndesmosis go too. The joint surface of the tibia is intact; the mortise is simply unstable, and the surgeon’s job is to put the talus back under the tibia and hold it there with a fibular plate, a medial screw or two, a posterior malleolar screw if the fragment is large, and a syndesmosis screw or suture-button if the fibula will not stay reduced. The soft tissues are bruised but the envelope is usually intact, and the operation is a day case in a fit patient.

The pilon is an axial injury: a fall from a height or a foot on a brake pedal drives the talus up into the tibial plafond and shatters it. The articular surface is impacted and comminuted (Ruedi-Allgower III), the metaphysis is crushed, the fibula is usually broken, and the skin over the front of the ankle, with the thinnest envelope in the lower limb, has taken the same energy. Early open reduction through that skin produced wound breakdown, deep infection and amputation at rates the surgeons of the 1990s called unacceptable, and the answer was staging: a spanning external fixator and a fibular plate on day 0 to restore length and let the swelling go, a CT once the fracture is out to length, and definitive fixation at 7-14 days when the skin wrinkles when pinched and the fracture blisters have healed. The definitive operation is then an anteromedial or anterolateral approach chosen from the CT exit of the fracture line, elevation of the impacted articular fragments, bone graft into the metaphyseal void, and a plate; the worst fractures get a circular frame instead and a year of rehabilitation.

   rotational injury                    axial injury
   (talus twists in mortise)            (talus driven into plafond)
          |                                     |
   malleolar fracture                    pilon fracture
   joint surface intact                  joint surface impacted
   envelope bruised                      envelope injured
          |                                     |
   ORIF when swelling allows             day 0: spanning fixator
   (same day to 7 days),                        +/- fibular plate
   day case, block as anaesthetic        day 7-14: CT, wrinkle sign,
                                                 ORIF or frame

The pain logic is bone and periosteum under a thin skin, and the block question dominates. The fibular plate sits on subcutaneous bone with a strip of periosteum lifted; the medial malleolar screws cross a fracture that is now compressed; the pilon adds an elevated, grafted articular surface and a metaphysis full of bone substitute. All of this is well covered by a popliteal sciatic block with a saphenous block for the medial skin, which is why ankle surgery is the lower-limb operation where the block is the whole anaesthetic. The cost is the rebound: in the AnAnkle trial, blocks beat spinal anaesthesia for pain and opioid use over 27 h and 99% of block patients would choose them again, but the authors noted intense pain as the blocks wore off; in the trial that tested dexamethasone for exactly this, rebound pain affected 44% of ankle ORIF patients with a plain block and 15% with intravenous dexamethasone, lasting about 3 h either way. The Gerbershagen cohort, in which blocks were rarely used, ranked open reduction of the calcaneus the single most painful procedure of 179 and foot arthrodesis seventh; the malleolar ankle is not in that company, but the pilon and the high-energy hindfoot are its neighbours. The score is 3 for the malleolar ankle: a block is expected, opioids are needed on the first two days, and the pain falls quickly because the mechanism is bone. The pilon sits a point higher on duration and the second operation, and the card says so where it matters.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 Presentation: reduce, splint, and decide the day

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A dislocated ankle is reduced in the emergency department before the radiograph, because the skin over the medial malleolus tents and dies within hours; a swollen ankle is elevated in a backslab and fixed within a day if the skin allows or at 5-10 days if it does not. A pilon gets a CT after the spanning fixator, not before, because the fracture is only readable at length.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The reduction in the department is a sedation or a block; a popliteal block for a fracture-dislocation is the kindest reduction and does not hide a compartment syndrome in a malleolar injury, which is not the at-risk pattern the 2021 guideline describes. The fasting state is counted from the injury for the same-day case. The decision between day-of-injury surgery and a delay belongs to the surgeon’s reading of the skin; for the anaesthetist the delayed case is the easier one, fasted and on a planned list, and the day-case plan applies to it.

  2. 2 Block, airway and the night plan

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon needs a still foot, a bloodless field under tourniquet, and a patient who will go home that evening with the leg elevated.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A popliteal sciatic block (20-30 mL of ropivacaine 0.5% or 0.75%) and a saphenous block in the adductor canal (10 mL) with intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg, under sedation or a light general anaesthetic with a supraglottic airway; the block is the anaesthetic, and a general anaesthetic that is only there to stop the patient feeling the tourniquet after 45 min is a small one. The saphenous block is not optional: the medial malleolar incision and the skin over the medial ankle are saphenous territory, and a block that misses it hurts on the medial side the moment the surgeon starts there. Spinal anaesthesia is a legitimate alternative, inferior in the trial for the first 27 h and the wrong choice for a day case. Cefazolin 2 g IV before the tourniquet goes up. The written night plan (what to take at bedtime, what to take when the tingling starts, what the opioid is for) is written now and handed over in recovery; the trial data say the rebound comes in the small hours in a third to a half of patients without dexamethasone.

  3. 3 Positioning and the tourniquet

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Supine with a bump under the ipsilateral buttock internally rotates the leg so the lateral malleolus faces up; the bump comes out for the medial side; a large posterior malleolar fragment needs a posterolateral approach with the patient prone or lateral, or a figure-of-four position. A thigh tourniquet at 250-300 mmHg.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The prone posterior malleolus is a different anaesthetic: a tracheal tube, a turn, pressure areas, and a case that cannot be a day case in an older patient. Tourniquet time for a trimalleolar fixation with a syndesmosis runs to 90 min, and the tourniquet pain that a popliteal block does not cover (the thigh cuff is above it) is what the sedation or general anaesthetic is for; see the tourniquet. The swollen leg with fracture blisters, the diabetic foot and the leg with peripheral vascular disease are the ones the surgeon may not tourniquet, and the field bleeds instead.

  4. 4 Lateral malleolus: fibular plate

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Through a lateral incision the surgeon reduces the fibular fracture to length and rotation, because the fibula is the key to the mortise, and fixes it with a lag screw and a neutralisation plate, or a locking plate in osteoporotic bone, or a posterolateral antiglide plate. The superficial peroneal nerve crosses the field above the joint line and the sural nerve lies behind it.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The plate on subcutaneous bone with a strip of periosteum lifted is the periosteal mechanism and the pain the patient feels on day 1-2; there is no deep muscle to dissect. Nothing to do at this step but note the tourniquet time.

  5. 5 Medial malleolus and deltoid

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The medial malleolus is reduced through a small medial incision and fixed with two partially threaded screws or a tension band; a deltoid ligament rupture with an intact medial malleolus is usually left to heal once the fibula is out to length. The saphenous vein and nerve run across the incision.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is the saphenous territory, and the step that tells you whether the adductor canal block worked: a patient under sedation who flinches as the medial incision is made has a popliteal block and no saphenous block.

  6. 6 Posterior malleolus and syndesmosis

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A posterior malleolar fragment over a quarter of the joint surface, or one that leaves the talus subluxed, is fixed from the front with screws or from behind through a posterolateral approach with a buttress plate. The syndesmosis is then stress-tested under the image intensifier (a hook test or external rotation); if the fibula moves, it is reduced by hand with the foot in neutral and held with one or two screws across both bones or a suture-button.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The syndesmosis reduction needs the foot held still and in neutral while the surgeon images and places the screw; a patient who moves under light sedation here costs a malreduction. The stress test and the imaging add 15-30 min to a case that felt finished.

  7. 7 Closure, splint and emergence

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Layered closure without tension over the fibular plate, a well-padded backslab or boot with the ankle at neutral, and elevation; the surgeon wants the foot above the heart for 48 h and non-weight-bearing for 6 weeks.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Tourniquet release before closure is the surgeon’s call and the moment the field starts to bleed; the reperfusion changes are modest at 60-90 min. Emergence is unremarkable; the foot is numb. The splint goes on before the patient lightens, because a patient with a dense sciatic block will otherwise let the foot drop off the trolley without noticing.

  8. 8 Recovery, discharge and the first night

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The fixation is stable from the moment the screws are in; the surgeon wants elevation, the splint untouched and a clinic review at two weeks.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The first paracetamol and NSAID dose goes in before discharge. The patient goes home with a numb, insensate foot, crutches, a written night plan and someone at home; the discharge criteria are the same as for any day case, and a working block is not a reason to keep the bed. The rebound comes 12-24 h after the block with dexamethasone and 8-12 h without, usually at night, rises over an hour to its peak, lasts about 3 h and responds to the opioid that the patient should already have taken; the trial data make the dexamethasone and the plan the two interventions that decide whether the patient telephones. Day 1-2 is the peak; by day 3 the regular regimen is enough and the opioid is stopped.

  9. 9 The pilon on day 0: spanning fixator and fibular plate

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Two pins in the tibial shaft and one or two in the calcaneus or the talus, connected by bars across the ankle, pull the fracture out to length by ligamentotaxis; many surgeons plate the fibula at the same sitting through the lateral skin, which is usually the least injured side, to set the length. A CT follows.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A 30-60 min general anaesthetic, often at night, in a patient who may have fallen from a height and has a spine and a calcaneus to think about. A popliteal block is reasonable here (the pilon is not the compartment syndrome pattern that the tibial shaft is), but a short one, because the leg will be examined for the next 48 h. Analgesia for the fortnight in the frame is oral and the leg is elevated.

  10. 10 The pilon at 7-14 days: definitive fixation

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    When the skin wrinkles and the blisters have epithelialised, the surgeon opens the ankle through the approach the CT dictates (anteromedial for a medially exiting fracture line, anterolateral for a lateral exit), reconstructs the joint surface from the key fragment outwards, elevates the impacted segments, fills the metaphyseal void with autograft, allograft or substitute, and applies a medial or anterolateral plate. The most comminuted fractures get a circular frame with fine wires instead, and a long rehabilitation.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is the long, elective operation on this card and the one where the catheter has the strongest claim: 2-4 h, a tourniquet to its limit and released, a bone graft (an iliac crest donor site if autograft is used, which needs its own analgesia), and a patient who will be in more pain for longer than the malleolar patient and is not going home that night. A popliteal catheter with a dilute infusion, a saphenous single shot and the usual regimen is the author’s preference; the compartment window of the first 48 h has passed. The haemoglobin after tourniquet release in a long case is worth checking in an older patient.

Pain plan

The mechanism is bone and periosteum under thin skin, fully covered by a popliteal sciatic plus saphenous block, so the plan is built around the block and its rebound. There is no PROSPECT guideline for ankle fracture surgery; the trial evidence is good. AnAnkle randomised 150 ankle fracture patients to popliteal sciatic plus saphenous blocks or spinal anaesthesia, all with paracetamol, ibuprofen and PCA morphine, and found the blocks superior for pain and opioid use over 27 h, with the caveat that the pain as the block wore off was substantial and sometimes intense. The dexamethasone trial randomised 130 bimalleolar and trimalleolar ORIFs with the same blocks to intravenous dexamethasone or saline: rebound pain 15% against 44%, the block 8 h longer, the first analgesic request at 26 h rather than 17 h. The ambulatory rebound cohort of 972 patients adds the risk factors: bone surgery, younger age, female sex, and no intravenous dexamethasone.

The defensible default for malleolar ORIF is therefore a single-shot popliteal sciatic block and a saphenous block with intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg, under sedation or a light general anaesthetic, regular paracetamol and an NSAID started before discharge, oral opioid for the first two nights, and a written night plan that tells the patient to take the bedtime dose whether or not the foot hurts and the next dose when the tingling starts. The catheter is the right call for the pilon’s definitive fixation, for the opioid-tolerant or chronic pain patient, for the patient with a previous catastrophic rebound night, and for the unit that admits its ankle fractures and can run an infusion; it is not needed for the malleolar day case and adds a dislodgement and a leaking dressing to a patient going home on crutches.

Escalation triggers: pain above 7 when the block has worn off, with the splint intact and the toes pink and moving, is rebound and is treated with the opioid already charted; pain that is severe inside the splint with a foot that is cold, pale or paraesthetic is a tight cast or a vascular problem and the splint is split; pain that persists beyond day 3 with a hot ankle is an infection. The malleolar ankle is not a compartment syndrome injury in the way the tibial shaft is, and the 2021 guideline’s caution about dense blocks is aimed at the shaft and the high-energy proximal tibia, not at this card.

Pitfalls and variants

  • The elderly, osteoporotic, diabetic ankle. The fibular plate does not hold, the skin does not heal, and the surgeon may choose a fibular nail, a hindfoot nail through the calcaneus and talus, or a cast. A diabetic neuropathic foot (Charcot) is a different disease with a different operation and a long cast. Blocks are still the right anaesthetic.
  • The open ankle fracture. Common because the medial skin is thin: antibiotics within an hour, debridement, often primary fixation if the wound is clean, and the open fracture card.
  • The fracture-dislocation with skin at risk. Reduced in the department before anything else; a block in the department is the kindest way to do it.
  • The posterior malleolus done prone. A tracheal tube, a prone turn with a fractured ankle, and no day case.
  • The syndesmosis screw that will not hold the foot in neutral. A malreduced syndesmosis is the commonest technical error in ankle fixation and the surgeon’s concern; for you it means a still foot during the imaging and a case that runs 20 min longer than the booking.
  • The calcaneus in the same patient. A fall from a height that produces a pilon often produces a calcaneal fracture or a spine fracture; the calcaneus is the most painful operation in the Gerbershagen cohort and has its own staging and its own catheter decision.
  • Day case criteria. A dense popliteal block is not a reason to delay discharge, but the patient needs crutches they can use, elevation at home, the night plan, the dexamethasone already given, and a telephone number; a patient who lives alone and cannot manage stairs stays the night.
  • Rebound in the opioid-tolerant patient. The worst phenotype for this operation: a catheter or an admission with a planned regimen, not a single shot and a prescription.
  • The patient who refuses the block. A general anaesthetic with surgeon’s infiltration and a spinal both work; the first night is worse and the opioid requirement doubles, which the trial data make explicit.

Key sources

The analgesia evidence for ankle fracture surgery is better than for most trauma operations because the operation is common, short and standardised. AnAnkle is the randomised comparison of blocks against spinal anaesthesia; the dexamethasone trial is the randomised answer to the rebound problem the AnAnkle authors flagged; the ambulatory rebound cohort gives the risk factors. The pilon evidence is surgical and observational, and the staging protocol rests on the wound complication history rather than a trial. The Gerbershagen cohort places the hindfoot and foot arthrodesis among the most painful operations in surgery, with the caveat that few of those patients had a block; it is cited here as context for the high-energy foot rather than as a ranking of the malleolar ankle, which it did not list. The catheter advice is the author’s judgement.

  1. Sort R, Brorson S, Gogenur I, et al. Peripheral nerve block anaesthesia and postoperative pain in acute ankle fracture surgery: the AnAnkle randomised trial. Br J Anaesth 2021;126:881-888
    150 patients randomised to popliteal sciatic plus saphenous blocks with ropivacaine or spinal anaesthesia, all with paracetamol, ibuprofen and PCA morphine: 27-h pain and opioid score median minus 26.5% with blocks versus plus 54.3% with spinal; rebound pain as the blocks wore off was substantial and sometimes intense; 99% of block patients would choose the same again
  2. Gao M, Li Y, Yu J, et al. The effects of intravenous dexamethasone on rebound pain after nerve block in patients with ankle fracture: a randomized controlled trial. J Pain Res 2023;16:1127-1136
    130 bimalleolar and trimalleolar ORIFs with popliteal and adductor canal ropivacaine blocks: rebound pain 44% with saline versus 15% with intravenous dexamethasone; block about 8 h longer, first analgesic request 26 h versus 17 h; rebound lasted about 3 h in both groups
  3. Barry GS, Bailey JG, Sardinha J, Brousseau P, Uppal V. Factors associated with rebound pain after peripheral nerve block for ambulatory surgery. Br J Anaesth 2021;126:862-871
    972 ambulatory block patients, rebound pain in 49.6%: bone surgery OR 1.82, female OR 1.52, younger age, and absence of IV dexamethasone OR 1.78
  4. Gerbershagen HJ, Aduckathil S, van Wijck AJM, Peelen LM, Kalkman CJ, Meissner W. Pain intensity on the first day after surgery: a prospective cohort study comparing 179 surgical procedures. Anesthesiology 2013;118:934-944
    50,523 patients: open reduction of the calcaneus was the single most painful procedure in the cohort, with foot arthrodesis seventh and open ankle ligament reconstruction 54th; 22 of the 40 most painful operations were orthopaedic or trauma procedures on the extremities, in a cohort where regional techniques were rarely used
  5. Jacob N, Amin A, Giotakis N, Narayan B, Nayagam S, Trompeter AJ. Management of high-energy tibial pilon fractures. Strategies Trauma Limb Reconstr 2015;10:137-147
    Ruedi-Allgower classification; early ORIF of type C fractures had unacceptable soft-tissue complication rates; the staged protocol (spanning fixator, definitive fixation at 7-14 days when swelling settles, after a planning CT) from Patterson and Cole and Sirkin; approach chosen from the CT fracture exit; fibular plating optional; long-term outcomes often deteriorate
  6. Association of Anaesthetists. Regional analgesia for lower leg trauma and the risk of acute compartment syndrome. Anaesthesia 2021
    Dilute single-shot blocks without adjuncts are not associated with delayed diagnosis when surveillance is effective; dense long-lasting blocks are to be avoided in the at-risk leg; the at-risk injuries are tibial shaft and high-energy proximal tibia rather than the malleolar ankle

Trauma › Trauma

47 Lower limb amputation

Below-knee and above-knee amputation for vascular disease, infection, trauma and tumour; through-knee and guillotine variants; stump revision

5Severe and prolonged

Dominant mechanism: Nerve. Four or five named nerves cut under tension and left to form neuromas, a deafferented cord segment and cortex that will generate phantom sensation and, in half or more, phantom pain; under that, a tibia or femur transected with a saw, a muscle flap sutured over the bone end under tension so the stump has a shape, and an ischaemic or infected limb that was hurting before the knife

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: high.

Block
Spinal anaesthesia for the operation where coagulation and sepsis allow, with a sciatic (tibial) perineural catheter placed by the surgeon under direct vision before closure or by ultrasound before the spinal; a single-shot femoral or saphenous block for the anteromedial skin
Catheter: routine The author's default is a sciatic or tibial perineural catheter running ropivacaine 0.2% for three to five days, on the grounds of the mechanism and of a frail population that tolerates opioid badly; the pooled evidence shows a modest reduction in acute pain and opioid use and no effect on phantom pain, so the catheter is a judgement, not a proven preventive
Alternatives: Lumbar epidural started before surgery and run for several days, which gives better stump analgesia in the first three days than a perineural catheter but does not prevent phantom pain and sits badly with heparin infusions and antiplatelet drugs; General anaesthesia with pre-operative ultrasound-guided sciatic and femoral blocks when a spinal is contraindicated; Low-dose ketamine infusion for the opioid-tolerant patient and the young trauma amputee, as analgesia rather than as prevention
Position
Supine with the limb on a bolster or held by an assistant, the sound heel padded and off the table, and a tourniquet on the thigh in some hands; above-knee amputation sometimes with a sandbag under the buttock to lift the thigh
Tourniquet
Sometimes. Used for trauma, tumour and infection where the vessels are healthy; in vascular disease surgeons vary, some using a thigh tourniquet for a below-knee amputation to cut blood loss and some refusing it to protect calcified vessels and flap perfusion
Cement
No
Blood loss
200-500 mL for a below-knee amputation, 300-800 mL for an above-knee amputation, more without a tourniquet, in trauma and in tumour resection; the vascular patient arrives anaemic from sepsis and renal disease, so a group and hold always and blood available for an above-knee amputation
Duration
45-90 min for a below-knee amputation, 60-120 min for an above-knee amputation; a guillotine amputation 20-30 min; tumour resections and traumatic amputations with flap reconstruction run far longer
Length of stay
7-14 nights, set by wound healing, comorbidity and the rehabilitation destination rather than by the operation; a revision to a higher level resets the clock. Day case: no
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV within 60 min of incision (3 g over 120 kg) for a clean elective amputation; where infection is the indication the treatment regimen already running is continued and timed to cover the incision, with Gram-negative and anaerobic cover for wet gangrene and diabetic foot sepsis
Tranexamic acid
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV at induction for trauma, tumour and any amputation without a tourniquet; in the patient with a fresh stent or graft or an acute arterial thrombosis the author weighs the thrombotic risk and often withholds it, a judgement rather than evidence
VTE
Low molecular weight heparin from the evening of surgery, continued through the immobile weeks; a mechanical sleeve on the sound leg; a femoral vein that has just been ligated and a patient who will not walk for a fortnight are a high-risk combination, and many vascular patients are already on a heparin infusion that is simply resumed
Antiemetic
Ondansetron 4 mg IV; dexamethasone 4-8 mg IV at induction with the lower dose in the septic diabetic, where the glucose rise is the cost and the antiemetic and analgesic benefit still worth having
Tell the patient
The leg will be numb for the first day or two while the local anaesthetic runs; the stump then aches and is sore to touch for a week or two, and most people feel the missing foot as if it were still there, which is normal, expected, and treated if it hurts.
The trap
The patient is the risk, not the operation: 30-day mortality after major amputation for vascular disease runs between 10 and 17% in the series on this card, the mode of anaesthesia has never been shown to change it, and the decisions that matter (sepsis control, the heparin infusion, the glucose, the heart and the kidneys) are made the day before, so a smooth spinal and a well-placed catheter are the easy part

What the surgeon is doing and why

An amputation is offered when the limb is killing the patient, cannot be saved, or is worse than no limb. Four diseases bring four different patients to the same operation. Peripheral arterial disease with rest pain, tissue loss or wet gangrene after failed or impossible revascularisation is the commonest: that patient is old, diabetic, often on dialysis, usually on an antiplatelet drug or a heparin infusion, with coronary and cerebrovascular disease in proportion to the disease in the leg. Infection (diabetic foot sepsis, necrotising fasciitis, an infected non-union or arthroplasty beyond reconstruction) brings a patient who is septic now and needs source control today. Trauma brings a young patient with a mangled limb, blood loss and other injuries; tumour brings a planned resection with a flap and a long operation.

The surgeon’s aims pull against each other: remove everything dead and infected, leave a stump that will heal on the blood supply the patient has, and build an end that can take a prosthesis. The level is the compromise. A below-knee amputation keeps the knee and roughly halves the energy cost of walking compared with an above-knee amputation, so it is the level every surgeon wants, but it needs a calf with enough perfusion to heal a long posterior flap. An above-knee amputation heals more reliably in poor perfusion and is the level for the patient who will never walk, for a knee fixed in flexion, and for sepsis that has reached the calf. A guillotine amputation, a straight cut through everything with the wound left open, is the sepsis operation: 20 minutes in a patient too sick for more, with the formal amputation days later once the physiology has recovered.

The below-knee operation is the spine of the card. Skin flaps are cut a hand’s breadth below the tibial tubercle: a long posterior flap carrying gastrocnemius and soleus on their sural artery supply, or skew flaps on their own perforators. The anterior and lateral compartments are divided and the anterior tibial vessels tied. The tibia is cut with an oscillating saw and bevelled at the front; the fibula is cut a centimetre or two shorter so it takes no load. The posterior tibial and peroneal vessels are ligated and the deep posterior muscles divided. The nerves are dealt with deliberately: the tibial, superficial and deep peroneal, sural and saphenous nerves are each drawn down under gentle traction and divided sharply so the cut end retracts into muscle well above the bone and away from the socket; the tibial nerve is ligated with its vasa nervorum because it bleeds. The posterior flap is brought forward and sutured to the anterior tibial periosteum or through drill holes under tension (a myodesis) or to the anterior muscles (a myoplasty), so the bone end is padded, the muscles keep a length to contract against, and the stump is cylindrical.

The above-knee operation follows the same logic a storey higher: fish-mouth flaps, the quadriceps divided, the femoral vessels ligated in the adductor canal (where the blood loss happens if it happens), the femur cut as long as the flaps allow, the sciatic nerve drawn down, divided and ligated, and adductor magnus sutured across the end of the femur under tension so it does not drift into abduction.

The pain logic is why this card sits with rotator cuff repair and scoliosis at a 5 rather than with the fractures at a 3. The dominant mechanism is nerve. Four or five named nerves are cut, each will form a neuroma, and a cord segment and a cortical map have lost their input and will reorganise over weeks. The result is three pains the ward will chart as one: stump pain (wound, bone end and neuromas, nociceptive and then neuropathic), phantom sensation (the foot is still there, nearly universal, not painful), and phantom pain (the missing foot hurts, cramps or burns), which in the trials on this card affected half the patients at one week and two thirds or more at a year. Beneath the nerve mechanism is bone (a tibia and fibula or a femur sawn through, worst for two days like any osteotomy), muscle under tension (a myodesis loads the muscle with every contraction and is why the stump aches for weeks rather than days), and a leg that was generating pain for weeks before the knife, so the sensitisation is in place before the first incision. The shape of the curve earns the score: a stump sore to touch and to the socket, and a phantom that appears in week one and may persist for years.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 The decision, the level and the day before

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon has judged the limb unsalvageable and chosen a level from the perfusion, the infection and the patient’s prospects of walking. They want sepsis controlled, the heparin infusion or antiplatelet drug managed, the glucose in range and the heart assessed, because the operation is short and the physiology is what kills.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    In the series on this card 30-day mortality after major amputation for vascular disease ran at 10-17%, and in none of them did the mode of anaesthesia change it. The work is the assessment: a functional history in a patient who has not walked far enough to have angina; renal function and the dialysis schedule; glucose and ketones in the septic diabetic; a haemoglobin low from chronic disease and sepsis; and the anticoagulation, which decides between a spinal and a general anaesthetic. Take the pain history in milligrams: weeks of rest pain on an opioid means a tolerant patient whose baseline dose continues and whose plan is in the opioid-tolerant chapter. Agree the technique and who places the perineural catheter now.

  2. 2 The anaesthetic: spinal or general, and the lines

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon needs 60-90 min of a still, perfused patient, a leg that can be lifted, and bleeding skin edges to judge the flaps by.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Spinal anaesthesia is the author’s default for the vascular amputee who can have one: no airway in a patient with bad lungs, a dense block for the nerve division and the saw, and in the 407-patient single-centre series regional anaesthesia was associated with fewer pulmonary complications (15% against 24%), fewer arrhythmias and a shorter intensive care stay. The obstacles are the ones this population carries: a heparin infusion that must be stopped for the guideline interval, clopidogrel or ticagrelor that cannot be, platelets low from sepsis, and bacteraemia. General anaesthesia with ultrasound-guided sciatic and femoral blocks before induction is the alternative, and in the Japanese nationwide cohort a nerve block technique carried the same mortality and morbidity as general anaesthesia with less delirium. Either way: an arterial line for heart failure, dialysis or sepsis, and a vasopressor running early, because a spinal in a dry septic patient with a stiff aorta drops the pressure further and faster than in an arthroplasty.

  3. 3 Positioning, tourniquet and antibiotic

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Supine, leg on a bolster so the posterior flap can be cut, sound heel off the table, and in some hands a thigh tourniquet. Surgeons vary on the tourniquet in vascular disease: some use it for every below-knee amputation to cut blood loss, others refuse it because calcified vessels do not compress and flap perfusion cannot be judged with it inflated.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The sound heel is the one the patient will stand on, and a pressure ulcer from an hour on the table in a neuropathic diabetic is the start of the second amputation; pad it. Cefazolin 2 g IV before the knife for the clean case; where infection is the indication the treatment antibiotics already running are the prophylaxis, timed so the incision falls inside the cover. Tranexamic acid 1 g IV where blood loss is expected and nothing fresh sits in the arterial tree; with an acute thrombosis or a stent placed days ago the author often withholds it, a judgement.

  4. 4 Skin flaps and the viability test

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The posterior flap is cut long and deep to carry the calf muscles on their supply. The surgeon judges viability by the skin edge, which must bleed bright, or the flap necroses and the amputation is revised higher in a week.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A pale, vasoconstricted, hypotensive patient gives a false read, and a flap condemned for not bleeding at a systolic of 80 is a level lost for nothing. Keep the pressure near the patient’s own baseline and the patient warm through this step; a request to bring the pressure up to judge a flap is a reasonable one.

  5. 5 Muscle division and vessel ligation

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The compartments are divided to bone and the tibial and peroneal vessels (or the superficial femoral vessels in the adductor canal) are isolated and ligated. In vascular disease the arteries are calcified pipes and the veins are what bleed; in trauma and tumour the vessels are healthy and the ligation is the haemostasis of the case.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is the blood loss of an above-knee amputation and the time to have the first unit checked in a patient who started at 90 g/L. A ligature that slips off the femoral vein after the tourniquet comes down is a sudden loss into the thigh.

  6. 6 The nerves: division under tension, ligation and reinnervation

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Each nerve is drawn down several centimetres and cut sharply so the end retracts into muscle above the bone and away from where the socket will press; the tibial and sciatic nerves are ligated for their vessels. Some add targeted muscle reinnervation or a regenerative peripheral nerve interface, because a nerve with a target forms a smaller neuroma; the randomised trial behind this treated established pain, and primary use at amputation rests on observational data.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is the mechanism being created. A nerve pulled and cut is the one step a patient under a receding spinal may feel as a shooting pain into the foot; check the block level before it. A surgeon-placed perineural catheter goes in now, laid along the tibial nerve (below knee) or the sciatic nerve (above knee) and brought out through separate skin, with the first bolus of ropivacaine 0.2% 10-20 mL given before closure so the infusion starts in a blocked limb.

  7. 7 The bone cut

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The tibia is transected with an oscillating saw, bevelled anteriorly and rasped smooth, the fibula cut shorter; the femur is cut as long as the flaps allow. The periosteum is stripped no further than needed, because bare bone under skin is a pressure point and an osteomyelitis in waiting.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Cancellous bone bleeds and is sealed with wax or pressure; this is the bone mechanism, worst for two days and then gone. The saw is the moment the patient under a spinal hears, feels through the table and understands, and it is where the one sentence on the emotional side of this operation belongs: the patient has lost a limb, grieves for it, and rehabilitates faster when the people around them say so plainly and then talk about the prosthesis.

  8. 8 Myodesis, myoplasty and the posterior flap

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The gastrocnemius-soleus flap is brought over the bone end and sutured to the anterior tibial periosteum or through drill holes under tension; above the knee, adductor magnus is fixed through drill holes to the lateral femur. The tension is the point: a muscle sutured at length keeps its bulk and gives the stump a shape a socket will fit, and a floppy stump with bone against skin never takes a prosthesis.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A muscle sutured to bone under tension is loaded by every contraction and every attempt to move the knee or hip, and it is why the stump aches for weeks after the bone pain has gone.

  9. 9 Closure, drain and dressing

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A drain in most hands because the dead space under the flap fills with blood; skin closed without tension; a soft bulky dressing or a rigid removable dressing that protects the stump from the fall every new amputee has in the first week.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The perineural catheter is secured and labelled before the dressing goes on, because a catheter under a crepe bandage is one nobody can inspect for a leak or a disconnected filter. The dressing is applied before the spinal recedes or the patient lightens. The first regular analgesia is charted now, not in recovery.

  10. 10 Emergence, recovery and the first night

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants a warm, pink stump, a dry dressing, the knee straight and the patient sitting up by the evening.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The vascular amputee after a spinal is hypotensive for hours with a coronary and cerebral circulation that cannot afford it; a vasopressor infusion in recovery rather than fluid boluses into a bad heart and bad kidneys is the author’s practice. Start the catheter infusion (ropivacaine 0.2% at 5-8 mL/h) as the spinal or single-shot block recedes, with regular paracetamol and the opioid charted as patient-controlled analgesia for the patient who can use it. Delirium is the common complication of the first night, and the lower delirium rate with a block technique in the Japanese cohort is one of the few outcome differences the anaesthetic has been shown to make.

  11. 11 Days 1-5: the catheter, the flap and the phantom

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants the flap watched for a dusky edge or dehiscence, the drain out at a day or two, the patient transferring to a chair with the knee straight, and the prosthetic rehabilitation conversation started.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The catheter runs three to five days and comes out when the stump tolerates handling; the pooled evidence is that it lowers pain scores modestly and opioid use somewhat while it runs and does nothing to the phantom pain afterwards, so its removal is not a loss. Phantom sensation appears in nearly everyone within days and phantom pain in about half within the week; tell the patient on day 1 what it is, because a patient who was not warned believes the leg has been left in the bed. Early phantom pain is treated as neuropathic pain (a gabapentinoid or a tricyclic, mirror therapy, the pain service), on the author’s judgement.

Pain plan

The mechanism is nerve, with bone and muscle under tension beneath it and a sensitised nervous system before the first incision, so the plan is a dense block for the operation, a continuous technique for the first days, and an honest account of what the plan cannot do. There is no PROSPECT guideline for amputation; the evidence is a set of small randomised trials of phantom pain prevention, one meta-analysis of perineural catheters and a few cohort studies of the mode of anaesthesia, and the recommendations are the author’s reading of them.

The anaesthetic: spinal where coagulation and sepsis allow, general anaesthesia with pre-operative ultrasound-guided sciatic and femoral (or saphenous) blocks where they do not. The catheter: the author’s default is a sciatic or tibial perineural catheter, surgeon-placed before closure or ultrasound-guided before the spinal, running ropivacaine 0.2% for three to five days. The grounds are the mechanism and the patient: a limb that has had four nerves cut, a bone sawn and a muscle flap sutured under tension is as strong a case for continuous analgesia as the book contains, and the vascular amputee tolerates opioid worst of all patients. The evidence is modest. In the pooled analysis of 10 studies and 731 patients a perineural catheter lowered pain scores by a standardised mean difference of 0.30 and morphine use by 0.63, the second effect disappearing when only the randomised trials were pooled, with no effect on mortality, phantom pain or chronic stump pain. An epidural does the acute job better: in the 30-patient comparison an epidural started 24 h before surgery gave lower stump pain for the first three days than a surgeon-placed perineural catheter and the same phantom pain at a year. Its problem is the population (heparin infusions, dual antiplatelet therapy, bacteraemia), which is why the perineural catheter is the default.

What the plan cannot do is prevent phantom pain, whatever the folklore says. The 60-patient Lancet trial of an epidural started 18 h before amputation and continued afterwards found phantom pain in 52% at a week and 75% at a year against 56% and 69% with systemic morphine. The 45-patient trial of ketamine at 0.5 mg/kg/h for 72 h found phantom pain at six months in 47% against 71%, not significant in a trial powered for a large effect, with more stump pain on day 3. The 2025 pooling of 20 trials with follow-up of six months or more found a 0.63-point reduction in phantom pain intensity with low certainty and no individual intervention (ketamine, gabapentin, valproate, calcitonin, epidural or perineural local anaesthetic) that reduced it. Ketamine stays in the plan as analgesia for the opioid-tolerant and the young trauma amputee, not as prevention. The surgical answer, primary targeted muscle reinnervation, has a randomised trial for established pain (phantom pain down about three points at a year against none with neuroma excision) and observational data for prevention, and is the surgeon’s call.

The oral regimen: regular paracetamol; an NSAID only where kidneys and vascular tree allow, which in practice means the trauma and tumour patients; the baseline opioid continued in the tolerant patient and an immediate-release opioid or a patient-controlled pump for the first three to five days; a gabapentinoid or a tricyclic when phantom pain declares itself rather than before. Rebound is high: when the catheter comes out on day 3-5, or a single-shot block recedes overnight in a patient without one, the stump pain arrives in a limb that has already begun to generate phantom pain, and that night needs a written plan.

Escalation: stump pain rising under a tense dressing in the first 24 h is a haematoma under the flap; a dusky edge, a discharging wound and a fever at days 3-7 is a failing flap heading for revision at a higher level, the same anaesthetic in a sicker patient; shooting pain into the missing foot is the neuroma and the phantom, a pain service problem rather than a surgical one.

Pitfalls and variants

  • Below-knee versus above-knee. The below-knee amputation is the one the patient wants and the one that fails to heal in poor perfusion; a proportion of vascular below-knee amputations are revised above the knee within weeks, and that second operation finds a patient sicker, more anaemic and already on opioids. The above-knee amputation bleeds more, hurts the same, and is the level for the patient who will not walk.
  • The guillotine amputation. Twenty minutes in a septic patient who cannot tolerate more, often at night and under general anaesthesia because the coagulation is deranged; the formal amputation follows in three to five days. The physiology is septic shock: vasopressor, arterial line, and intensive care told before the knife.
  • The anticoagulated patient. Heparin infusions for acute ischaemia, clopidogrel for a stent, apixaban for atrial fibrillation: the spinal follows the guideline intervals, and the surgeon-placed perineural catheter in an open wound is the technique that does not care.
  • The dialysis patient. Fluid balance, potassium, a fistula arm that takes no cuff or cannula; dialysis the day before and no NSAID ever.
  • The septic diabetic. Glucose and ketones, treatment antibiotics rather than prophylaxis, a relative contraindication to the spinal while bacteraemic, and dexamethasone at the lower dose.
  • Trauma. A young patient with other injuries, a limb that has been under a field tourniquet for hours (acidosis and potassium when it comes off), blood loss and a long reconstruction with flaps; the catheter and the ketamine both earn their place.
  • The opioid-tolerant patient with weeks of rest pain. The commonest phenotype among the vascular amputees and the one for whom the catheter matters most, because the alternative is an opioid dose the ward will not give.

Key sources

The evidence is better than its reputation and worse than its folklore. The three randomised trials of phantom pain prevention (epidural before and after, epidural against perineural catheter, ketamine for 72 h) are small, old and consistent in finding nothing, and the 2025 meta-analysis of 20 trials agrees. The perineural catheter meta-analysis is the only pooled estimate of what the catheter does and its effect on acute pain is modest; the PLACEMENT feasibility trial was built to answer the question properly and the effectiveness trial has not reported. The mode-of-anaesthesia data are retrospective cohorts in which regional techniques were associated with fewer complications and never with lower mortality.

  1. Nikolajsen L, Ilkjaer S, Christensen JH, Kroner K, Jensen TS. Randomised trial of epidural bupivacaine and morphine in prevention of stump and phantom pain in lower-limb amputation. Lancet 1997;350:1353-1357
    60 patients, epidural bupivacaine and morphine started a median of 18 h before amputation and continued afterwards versus epidural saline with systemic morphine: phantom pain at one week 52% versus 56%, at 12 months 75% versus 69%; no difference in stump pain, phantom pain intensity or opioid consumption at any point
  2. Lambert AW, Dashfield AK, Cosgrove C, Wilkins DC, Walker AJ, Ashley S. Randomized prospective study comparing preoperative epidural and intraoperative perineural analgesia for the prevention of postoperative stump and phantom limb pain following major amputation. Reg Anesth Pain Med 2001;26:316-321
    30 patients, epidural bupivacaine and diamorphine from 24 h before surgery versus a surgeon-placed perineural catheter with bupivacaine 0.25% at 10 mL/h: stump pain in the first three days was significantly lower with the epidural; phantom pain at 12 months 38% versus 50%, not different; all patients had general anaesthesia
  3. Hayes C, Armstrong-Brown A, Burstal R. Perioperative intravenous ketamine infusion for the prevention of persistent post-amputation pain: a randomized, controlled trial. Anaesth Intensive Care 2004;32:330-338
    45 above- and below-knee amputations, ketamine 0.5 mg/kg before induction then 0.5 mg/kg/h for 72 h versus saline: no difference in stump allodynia or morphine use; phantom pain at six months 47% versus 71%, not significant in a trial powered for a large effect; more stump pain in the ketamine group at day 3
  4. Laloo R, Ambler GK, Locker D, Twine CP, Bosanquet DC. Systematic review and meta-analysis of the effect of perineural catheters in major lower limb amputations. Eur J Vasc Endovasc Surg 2021;62:295-303
    10 studies, 731 patients, 350 with a perineural catheter: lower post-operative pain (standardised mean difference -0.30, low certainty) and morphine use (-0.63, moderate certainty, lost when only the randomised trials were pooled); no demonstrable effect on in-hospital mortality, phantom limb pain or chronic stump pain
  5. Bosanquet DC, Ambler GK, Waldron CA, et al. Perineural local anaesthetic catheter after major lower limb amputation trial (PLACEMENT): results from a randomised controlled feasibility trial. BMJ Open 2019;9:e029233
    50 vascular amputees randomised to a surgeon-placed sciatic or tibial perineural catheter with levobupivacaine 0.125% for up to five days or no catheter: a feasibility trial, 18 patients supplied six-month data, costs dominated by length of stay; the effectiveness trial it was designed for has not reported
  6. Abrishami R, Azh N, Farhang Ranjbar M, Motamedgorji N. The role of preemptive perioperative analgesia in prevention of chronic phantom pain: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Med J Islam Repub Iran 2025;39:92
    20 randomised trials with follow-up of six months or longer, mostly vascular lower limb amputations: a pooled reduction of 0.63 points in phantom pain intensity at six months with low certainty; ketamine, gabapentin, valproate, calcitonin and local anaesthetic by epidural or perineural catheter did not individually reduce phantom pain
  7. Chery J, Semaan E, Darji S, Briggs WT, Yarmush J, D'Ayala M. Impact of regional versus general anesthesia on the clinical outcomes of patients undergoing major lower extremity amputation. Ann Vasc Surg 2014;28:1149-1156
    407 major amputations at one centre, 259 under regional anaesthesia: fewer pulmonary complications (15% versus 24%) and arrhythmias (14% versus 25%), shorter intensive care and hospital stay; mortality 10% versus 13% and myocardial infarction 12% versus 9%, neither different; the regional group was older, lighter and less often anticoagulated
  8. Abe H, Sumitani M, Matsui H, et al. Comparing outcomes after peripheral nerve block versus general anesthesia for lower extremity amputation: a nationwide exploratory retrospective cohort study in Japan. Reg Anesth Pain Med 2020;45:399-404
    11,796 below-knee and foot amputations, 747 under peripheral nerve block, propensity matched one to four: 30-day mortality odds ratio 1.11 (0.75-1.64) and composite morbidity 1.15, neither different; delirium odds ratio 0.75 (0.57-0.98) with the block
  9. Lin R, Hingorani A, Marks N, et al. Effects of anesthesia versus regional nerve block on major leg amputation mortality rate. Vascular 2013;21:83-86
    158 above- and below-knee amputations, mean age 74: overall 30-day mortality 17.1%; 15.2% with peripheral nerve blocks versus 17.9% with general or spinal anaesthesia, not different
  10. Dumanian GA, Potter BK, Mioton LM, et al. Targeted muscle reinnervation treats neuroma and phantom pain in major limb amputees: a randomized clinical trial. Ann Surg 2019;270:238-246
    28 amputees with established pain randomised to targeted muscle reinnervation or neuroma excision and burial in muscle: phantom pain fell by 3.2 points with reinnervation against 0.2 with standard treatment at one year (adjusted p=0.06 in the primary analysis, p=0.03 in the longitudinal model); the surgical basis for primary reinnervation at the time of amputation
  11. Hsu E, Cohen SP. Postamputation pain: epidemiology, mechanisms, and treatment. J Pain Res 2013;6:121-136
    Review of mechanisms: cortical reorganisation behind phantom pain, dorsal horn changes after deafferentation, and neuroma ectopic firing behind residual limb pain; the trials of epidural and perineural prevention are inconsistent, with any benefit confined to epidurals started more than 24 h before surgery against non-optimised controls

Trauma › Trauma

48 Osteomyelitis debridement and septic arthritis washout

Excision of chronic osteomyelitis with dead space management and staged reconstruction; arthroscopic and open washout of the native septic joint

3Moderate

Dominant mechanism: Bone. Dead and infected bone cut back to a bleeding bed with a burr, a saw and a reamer, leaving a cavity packed with a carrier; for the septic joint, a capsule that was distended under pressure and is decompressed, then a synovium stripped by a shaver. Both operations remove the pain generator, so the post-operative pain is bone and capsule, short, and smaller than the pain the patient arrived with

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: moderate.

Block
General anaesthesia with multimodal analgesia; a single-shot block placed through clean tissue away from the infected field where the site allows (adductor canal for a knee washout, popliteal sciatic and saphenous for a tibial debridement), never through cellulitis or an abscess; spinal anaesthesia for the lower limb in the well host with chronic infection and no bacteraemia
Catheter: no No catheter: a perineural catheter near an infected field, in a bacteraemic patient, in a limb that may need serial examination and a second washout within 48 h, has nothing to offer that a single shot and the oral regimen do not, and the mechanism does not demand it
Alternatives: Spinal anaesthesia for the well host having a lower limb debridement, with the tourniquet time in mind; Surgeon infiltration of the wound edges and portals with long-acting local anaesthetic; Low-dose ketamine infusion for the chronic osteomyelitis patient on long-term opioids
Position
Supine for most sites, with the limb on a bolster or a radiolucent board and a tourniquet in reach; lateral for the hip and the posterior tibia, prone for the calcaneus and the posterior elbow; a long case with the C-arm in and out
Tourniquet
Sometimes. Common for a tibial, foot or forearm debridement so the surgeon can see dead bone against living, and deflated before the end so the bleeding bed can be judged; not used for the proximal femur, the pelvis or the spine, and avoided over cellulitis
Cement
Sometimes. Antibiotic-loaded polymethylmethacrylate as beads or a spacer, or an absorbable calcium sulphate or calcium sulphate and hydroxyapatite carrier, packed into the cavity; a cement spacer in the induced membrane (Masquelet) technique that is removed at the second stage; none of it is pressurised into a canal and none of it is a cement implantation syndrome risk
Blood loss
100-300 mL for a joint washout; 300-800 mL for a long bone debridement with reaming and saucerisation, most of it after the tourniquet comes down from bone deliberately cut back to a bleeding bed; more with a flap or a resection with a fixator
Duration
30-60 min for an arthroscopic washout; 60-90 min for an open arthrotomy; 90-180 min for a long bone debridement with a carrier and closure; half a day when a free flap or a resection and frame are added
Length of stay
A washout 3-7 nights, set by the sepsis and the antibiotic plan; a chronic osteomyelitis debridement 5-10 nights, with weeks of outpatient antibiotics afterwards and a second stage months later. Day case: no
Antibiotic
For chronic osteomyelitis the patient has usually been off antibiotics for two weeks and the surgeon wants deep samples before the first dose; the randomised evidence from prosthetic joint infection is that a dose of prophylaxis before the incision does not change the culture yield, so whether cefazolin 2 g IV goes in before the knife or after the samples is agreed with the surgeon rather than assumed. For septic arthritis the antibiotics started after the blood cultures and the aspirate, in the emergency department, and are never withheld for theatre
Tranexamic acid
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV for a long bone debridement with reaming and a bleeding bed; not needed for a washout
VTE
Low molecular weight heparin from the evening of surgery; infection, immobility and a swollen limb are a prothrombotic set, and a patient on weeks of antibiotics with a frame is at risk for the whole course
Antiemetic
Ondansetron 4 mg IV; dexamethasone 4 mg IV for the well host having an elective debridement, and omitted in the frankly septic patient, by the author's practice rather than by evidence
Tell the patient
Most of the pain you came in with is from the infection and should be better once the dead bone or the pus is out; the wound and the bone are sore for a few days, and the antibiotics run for weeks afterwards whatever the wound feels like.
The trap
Two patients share this card and the mistake is to treat one like the other: the chronic osteomyelitis patient is a well host whose antibiotics have been deliberately stopped so the samples mean something, and the septic arthritis patient is a sick one whose antibiotics must never wait for theatre; the sampling plan and the antibiotic timing are agreed with the surgeon before the first dose, not discovered at the drug cupboard

What the surgeon is doing and why

Two operations share this card because the same surgeon does both and the same anaesthetist is called, but they are opposite problems. Chronic osteomyelitis is a slow disease in a well patient; septic arthritis is a fast disease in a sick one. The first is a planned excision of dead bone that will fail if the surgeon leaves any behind. The second is a drainage procedure on a time clock that will fail if anyone waits.

Chronic osteomyelitis is bone that has died with bacteria living in it. The organisms, most often Staphylococcus aureus, sit in a biofilm on dead bone (the sequestrum) and on any implant, where they are a thousand times less susceptible to antibiotics than in broth, and the body walls them off with new bone (the involucrum) and drains them through a sinus. Antibiotics alone suppress and do not cure. The disease is classified on two axes that decide the operation: the anatomy (medullary, where the canal is infected after a nail; superficial, where exposed bone sits under a wound; localised, a full-thickness cortical segment that can be excised without destabilising the bone; and diffuse, a through-and-through infection where excision leaves the bone unstable or absent), and the host (a normal host, a compromised one with diabetes, smoking, vascular disease, renal failure or malnutrition, and one so compromised that the treatment is worse than the disease). Fracture-related infection after a plate or a nail is the commonest adult form; the infected arthroplasty has its own card.

The surgeon’s aims run in a fixed order. Take deep samples before any antibiotic muddies them, five or more from separate sites with clean instruments, for culture and histology. Excise every piece of dead and infected bone and soft tissue back to a bleeding margin: the sinus tract in its entirety, the sequestrum, the involucrum where it is involved, the infected canal reamed out, and the cortex burred or sawn back to the point where it bleeds from every surface. Then manage what the excision has created: a dead space that will fill with haematoma and re-infect unless it is filled with something, a bone that may now be unstable, and a soft tissue envelope that may not close. The dead space is packed with a local antibiotic carrier: antibiotic-loaded cement beads or a spacer that must be removed later, or an absorbable calcium sulphate or biocomposite carrier loaded with gentamicin or vancomycin that dissolves over weeks and releases concentrations systemic dosing cannot reach. In the 100-patient prospective single-stage series from a specialist unit, debridement, multiple sampling, culture-specific antibiotics, stabilisation, filling with the biocomposite and primary closure eradicated infection with one operation in 96, with three fractures and six wound leaks, and the result did not depend on the host class or the organism. Where the excision leaves a segmental defect, the induced membrane technique puts a cement spacer in the gap, waits six to eight weeks for a vascular membrane to form around it, and then replaces the cement with bone graft at a second stage; where the bone is unstable, an external fixator or a plate goes on at the same sitting. Soft tissue cover is a local or free flap in many cases.

Septic arthritis is a different disease. Bacteria reach a joint by the blood, a wound, an injection or an adjacent osteomyelitis, and inside a closed synovial cavity the neutrophil enzymes, the pressure of the effusion and the organism destroy cartilage within days. Incidence is rising with an ageing, more diabetic population, and in the French national series of 109,160 episodes the mean age was 62, staphylococci accounted for half, rheumatoid arthritis, complicated diabetes, dialysis and drug addiction each quadrupled the risk, and mortality was 3.2% at a month and 11.4% at a year. The surgeon’s aims are drainage, decompression and debridement: get the pus out, wash the joint with litres of fluid, strip the inflamed synovium so that it stops producing enzyme, and do it today. The knee is done arthroscopically by most surgeons now, with a shaver synovectomy and a drain; the meta-analyses of retrospective comparisons favour arthroscopy over arthrotomy for re-infection and complications in the knee and shoulder, with no difference in mortality, and the 80-patient series that looked for predictors found MRSA, not the approach, behind the failed single washout. A patient who does not improve in 48 h goes back for another look, and a quarter do.

The pain logic is the same for both and it runs backwards from most of the book: the operation removes the pain generator. The chronic osteomyelitis patient has had an aching, discharging limb for months or years and is often on opioids; the septic arthritis patient has a joint distended under pressure that hurts to move a degree. Afterwards the mechanisms are bone (cortex, canal and cancellous bone cut back to a bleeding bed, which behaves like an osteotomy, worst for two days and NSAID-responsive) and capsule (a decompressed joint whose synovium has been shaved, sharp with movement and settling in days). Neither mechanism is loaded, tensioned or lengthened, so the pain falls quickly: a 3, with opioids needed for two or three days and the shape of the curve set by the pre-operative opioid state rather than by the operation. The frame, the flap and the second stage each bring their own pain.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 Which patient this is, and the antibiotic-free interval

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    For chronic osteomyelitis the surgeon has stopped antibiotics for two weeks so that the deep samples grow the organism, has staged the disease from the MRI and the host from the clinic letter, and has a plan for the dead space, the stability and the cover. For septic arthritis the surgeon has a patient diagnosed by aspiration in the emergency department whose joint needs washing out within hours.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The chronic patient is a well host or a compromised one, not a septic one: the assessment is the diabetes, the smoking, the renal function, the nutrition, the months of opioids and the plan for them from the opioid-tolerant chapter. The septic arthritis patient is assessed as a septic patient: lactate, blood cultures, the renal function, the anticoagulant for the atrial fibrillation, the rheumatoid drugs, and the fasting status, which is irrelevant to the timing because the joint will not wait. Look at the limb yourself: cellulitis over the block site rules the block out.

  2. 2 The antibiotic timing conversation

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants an organism and a sensitivity, because weeks of empirical therapy against a biofilm is guessing. For the chronic patient the first antibiotic dose is timed against the sampling; for the septic patient the dose has already been given and the samples will be taken anyway.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The one randomised trial, in prosthetic joint infection, gave prophylaxis either before the incision or after three sets of operative cultures and found the operative cultures matched the pre-operative organism in 82% and 81%, which is equivalence; the authors concluded that prophylaxis should not be withheld for the sake of the cultures. Many bone infection surgeons still ask for the first dose after the samples; in a well host with no implant that is a reasonable request, in a patient with a fresh implant going in it is not, and the trial is the argument. Agree it before the patient is asleep. For septic arthritis the antibiotics (empirical anti-staphylococcal cover, broadened for the immunosuppressed, the dialysis patient and the injecting drug user) went in after the blood cultures and the aspirate and are continued through the operation; the dose is not held because the patient is going to theatre.

  3. 3 Anaesthetic technique, lines and the tourniquet

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A debridement needs a bloodless field to tell dead bone from living, then a perfused one to judge the bleeding margin, so the tourniquet goes up for the excision and comes down before the end. A washout needs a still joint and, for arthroscopy, a pump.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    General anaesthesia for the septic patient and for any case with a flap; spinal anaesthesia is reasonable for a lower limb debridement in the well host without bacteraemia, with the tourniquet time in mind. A single-shot block through clean tissue away from the field (adductor canal for a knee washout, popliteal sciatic and saphenous for a tibial debridement) is the author’s practice where it can be placed cleanly; a needle through cellulitis or into a limb with a tracking abscess is not placed. No catheter. An arterial line for the septic patient and for a long case. Cefazolin 2 g IV at the agreed moment, and tranexamic acid 1 g IV for the long bone case because the bleeding bed is the point of the operation.

  4. 4 Exposure, sinus excision and sampling

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The sinus is excised in continuity with the skin ellipse around it, the bone is exposed through the old scar or the old plate incision, any implant is removed and sent for sonication, and five or more deep samples are taken from separate sites with a fresh instrument each time, for culture and for histology.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is the step the antibiotic timing was about, and if the dose was held for the samples it goes in now, once the surgeon says the last one is taken. Removal of old metalwork is slower than it looks and bleeds from the screw holes; the removal of metalwork card applies to this part.

  5. 5 Debridement to bleeding bone

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Sequestrum is lifted out, the involucrum opened, the canal reamed in a medullary infection, and the cortex burred or sawn back until every surface bleeds, the surgeon’s sign that living bone has been reached. In a localised infection a cortical window or a full-thickness segment comes out; in a diffuse one the bone is resected and the stability decision follows.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The tourniquet comes down for the judgement, and the blood loss of the operation starts then: a reamed canal and a saucerised tibia bleed steadily from cancellous bone and do not stop until the carrier is in and the wound closed. Reaming a chronically infected canal is a marrow embolisation step with an inoculum attached; a rise in temperature and a fall in pressure over the next hour is bacteraemia from the reaming, and the antibiotic cover should be running when it happens.

  6. 6 Dead space management, carriers and stabilisation

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The cavity is filled so that it cannot fill with haematoma: antibiotic-loaded cement beads or a spacer that will be removed in weeks, or an absorbable calcium sulphate or biocomposite carrier that dissolves and needs no second operation. A segmental defect gets a cement spacer for the induced membrane technique, and an unstable bone gets a fixator or a plate.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The carrier is pressed into a cavity by hand and is not a cement implantation syndrome risk; the volume of gentamicin or vancomycin in it is large by systemic standards, and in a dialysis patient with a large cavity the levels are checked afterwards because the carrier elutes into a kidney that cannot clear it. Calcium sulphate leaks serous fluid through the wound for a week or two in a proportion of patients, six of 100 in the specialist series, which is expected and not an infection. A frame adds an hour and the pin sites.

  7. 7 Soft tissue cover and closure

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Dead bone was often dead because the soft tissue over it had failed; the excision leaves exposed bone or a carrier that must be covered with vascular tissue, so a local muscle flap, a fasciocutaneous flap or a free flap is raised, and primary closure is the aim in every case because an open wound re-infects.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A free flap is the plastic surgeon’s day and the usual flap rules apply: warm, filled, a pressure the surgeon is content with, no vasopressor boluses into a fresh anastomosis, and a bed in a unit that will monitor the flap. A local flap adds 30-60 min and a second sore site.

  8. 8 Septic arthritis: the approach and the washout

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The knee is entered through standard arthroscopic portals, the joint is washed with several litres of saline through a pump, the fibrin and the loculations are broken down, the synovium is shaved, and a drain is left; an arthrotomy does the same through a parapatellar incision with a hand and a sucker. The hip is scoped or opened according to the surgeon, the shoulder is scoped, and the small joints are opened. The pooled retrospective evidence favours arthroscopy for the knee and shoulder on re-infection and complications, with no difference in mortality.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A pump and litres of room-temperature saline through a joint in a septic patient is a cooling system, and the patient arrived cold; warm the fluid or the patient. The washout mobilises organisms: a rise in temperature, a fall in pressure and a rising heart rate during the lavage are bacteraemia and are treated as the sepsis they are, with the antibiotic already in and a vasopressor rather than a litre of crystalloid in a patient whose heart is the comorbidity.

  9. 9 The septic patient through the operation

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon’s operation is short; the patient’s physiology is the long part. A quarter to a third of septic knee patients in the national surgical registry suffered a serious adverse event within 30 days, which is the population, not the operation.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Treat the patient as a septic laparotomy with a smaller incision: an arterial line, a lactate before and after, noradrenaline rather than fluid once the first litre is in, glucose in the diabetic, steroid cover for the rheumatoid patient on prednisolone, and a bed decided before induction for the patient on a vasopressor. The dialysis patient, the injecting drug user with endocarditis until proven otherwise and the immunosuppressed patient are the ones who die.

  10. 10 Recovery, the ward and the second look

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants the limb elevated and moved early (a washed-out joint stiffens if it is rested, and the physiotherapy is the treatment), the drain watched, the inflammatory markers falling, and a low threshold for a second washout at 48 h if they are not. The chronic osteomyelitis patient starts culture-specific antibiotics, usually intravenous at first and then oral for weeks, and goes home with an outpatient antibiotic plan and a return date for the second stage.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The regular paracetamol and the NSAID (where the kidneys and the surgeon permit) start in recovery, the opioid is charted for 48 h, and the chronic patient’s baseline opioid continues unchanged. Pain that rises on day 2 with a hot, swollen joint and markers that have not fallen is a failed washout, not a rebound, and the second operation is the same anaesthetic in a patient who is now more septic. A wet dressing over a calcium sulphate carrier is the carrier, not the infection.

Pain plan

The mechanism is bone and capsule with the pain generator removed, so the plan is multimodal and short, built around a single-shot block where one can be placed cleanly and the oral regimen from recovery. There is no PROSPECT guideline for either operation; the plan is standard practice and the author’s judgement, and the card says so.

The block decision follows the field. A block is placed through clean tissue away from the infection, never through cellulitis or lymphangitis and never into a limb with a tracking collection, and it is a single shot. The mechanism does not need a catheter: the bone pain is short, the joint pain is short, and the patient who is septic, who may need a serial examination or a second washout in 48 h, and whose limb may have a frame or a flap on it, is a poor candidate for a line that stays in. Surgeon infiltration of the wound and the portals is asked for in every case.

The oral regimen: regular paracetamol; an NSAID for the well host, withheld for the dialysis patient and the septic one with a rising creatinine; an immediate-release opioid for 48-72 h and then as required; the baseline opioid continued in the chronic patient, with a low-dose ketamine infusion through the case and the first night for the one on a large dose, which is the author’s practice. A frame brings pin-site pain that outlasts the bone pain and responds to the same regimen; a flap brings a donor site that needs its own infiltration.

Rebound is moderate because the mechanism is small: when the block recedes the patient finds a sore bone that was far more sore the week before. Escalation: pain rising on day 1-2 with a hot joint, a fever and markers that are not falling is failed source control and a surgical conversation, not an analgesic one; pain in the calf of a limb with a frame or after a long knee lavage is a compartment syndrome until the compartments have been felt; pain that is unchanged at a week in a patient who was on opioids for a year is the chronic state, and the pain service rather than the ward is the right owner.

Pitfalls and variants
