  • The antibiotic-free interval that nobody told you about. The chronic patient’s antibiotics were stopped on purpose; restarting them on admission for a sore red leg wrecks the samples. The decision about the first dose is the surgeon’s and the conversation is before induction.
  • Fracture-related infection with metal in place. The implant is removed, sonicated and often replaced with a frame; the open fracture card covers the fixator and the removal of metalwork card the extraction, which is the slow part of the day.
  • The induced membrane technique. Two operations separated by six to eight weeks: a cement spacer and a frame or plate at the first, graft from the iliac crest or a reamer-irrigator-aspirator harvest from the femur at the second. The second stage bleeds more than the first, and the crest or the reamed femur is the sorest site.
  • The diabetic foot. Osteomyelitis of the forefoot in a neuropathic, vascular, renal patient: a small operation on the sickest host on the card, often a toe or ray amputation, and a prelude to the amputation card in a proportion.
  • The hip in the adult. A deep joint, a lateral position and an open or arthroscopic washout in a patient who is usually old and septic; the native hip that fails washout becomes a resection arthroplasty, and the arthroplasty that follows months later is in a scarred hip.
  • The injecting drug user. Unusual organisms, a sternoclavicular or sacroiliac joint, endocarditis until an echocardiogram says otherwise, difficult venous access and an opioid tolerance that the ward will under-treat; central access and the pain service on day 1.
  • The rheumatoid patient. The highest risk group in the national data, on immunosuppression and often steroids, with a joint already destroyed, a cervical spine for the airway, and a presentation that mimics a flare and is diagnosed late.
  • Crystal arthropathy. The septic joint that turns out to be gout is washed out anyway, because the aspirate takes 48 h to say which it was.
  • The patient who needs an amputation. A diffuse infection in a host who cannot tolerate reconstruction, an infected non-union after years of frames, a diabetic foot that has reached the ankle; the conversation belongs to the surgeon and the patient, and the anaesthetic is on the amputation card.

Key sources

The osteomyelitis evidence is specialist-unit series and reviews rather than trials: the single-stage biocomposite series and the carrier review are the best description of modern practice, and the pathophysiology review supplies the classification and the biofilm logic. The antibiotic timing argument rests on one randomised trial from prosthetic joint infection, extrapolated here. The septic arthritis comparisons are retrospective, and the two meta-analyses that favour arthroscopy in the knee say so themselves; the registry study finding no difference in 30-day complications is the counterweight. The French national database supplies the incidence, the mortality and the risk factors. The analgesic plan is practice, not evidence.

  1. Rupp M, Walter N, Biehl C, Heiss C. Chronic osteomyelitis: pathophysiology and treatment. Z Orthop Unfall 2026
    Review: biofilm as the reason chronic infection resists antibiotics; the Cierny-Mader classification of anatomical type and host; stage-appropriate radical debridement, dead space management with local antibiotic carriers, soft tissue cover and later bone reconstruction; single-stage protocols and shorter systemic courses
  2. McNally MA, Ferguson JY, Lau ACK, et al. Single-stage treatment of chronic osteomyelitis with a new absorbable, gentamicin-loaded, calcium sulphate/hydroxyapatite biocomposite: a prospective series of 100 cases. Bone Joint J 2016;98-B:1289-1296
    100 patients, 80 of them compromised hosts, treated by debridement, multiple sampling, culture-specific antibiotics, stabilisation, dead space filling with the biocomposite and primary closure: infection eradicated in 96 with one operation, with three fractures and six wound leaks; outcome independent of host class and organism
  3. Ferguson J, Diefenbeck M, McNally M. Ceramic biocomposites as biodegradable antibiotic carriers in the treatment of bone infections. J Bone Jt Infect 2017;2:38-51
    Review of calcium sulphate, calcium phosphate and polyphasic carriers: adequacy of debridement remains the key to cure, local carriers deliver far higher antibiotic concentrations than systemic dosing, fill the dead space, dissolve without a removal operation and allow single-stage surgery with closure; carrier choice keyed to the Cierny-Mader stage
  4. Tetreault MW, Wetters NG, Aggarwal V, Mont M, Parvizi J, Della Valle CJ. The Chitranjan Ranawat Award: should prophylactic antibiotics be withheld before revision surgery to obtain appropriate cultures? Clin Orthop Relat Res 2014;472:52-56
    65 patients with culture-positive prosthetic joint infection randomised to prophylactic antibiotics before the incision or after three sets of operative cultures: operative cultures matched the pre-operative organism in 82% and 81%, statistically equivalent; the authors conclude prophylaxis should not be withheld for fear of the cultures
  5. Acosta-Olivo C, Vilchez-Cavazos F, Blazquez-Saldana J, et al. Comparison of open arthrotomy versus arthroscopic surgery for the treatment of septic arthritis in adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Int Orthop 2021;45:1947-1959
    20 studies, 10,249 patients: arthrotomy carried higher odds of re-infection (OR 1.35) and complications (OR 1.32) and a stay 0.57 days longer than arthroscopy; the knee (OR 1.50) and shoulder (OR 1.24) drove the re-infection difference; the authors rate the evidence insufficient for firm conclusions
  6. Ramirez-Acosta K, Sanchez-Enriquez S, Madrigal-Rodriguez M, et al. Comparative effectiveness of repeated joint aspiration, arthroscopic lavage, and open arthrotomy in adult native knee septic arthritis: a systematic review and network meta-analysis. J Orthop 2025;70:183-195
    25 studies, 21,917 patients, one randomised: arthroscopic lavage had higher clinical success than arthrotomy (OR 2.52) and fewer complications (OR 0.69); repeated aspiration carried more re-intervention (OR 3.35) than arthroscopy; no difference in stay or mortality; the authors propose arthroscopy as the reference standard in the immunocompetent adult
  7. Bovonratwet P, Nelson SJ, Bellamkonda K, et al. Similar 30-day complications for septic knee arthritis treated with arthrotomy or arthroscopy: an American College of Surgeons National Surgical Quality Improvement Program analysis. Arthroscopy 2018;34:213-219
    168 arthrotomies and 216 arthroscopies for the septic knee: no difference in adverse events, return to theatre or readmission at 30 days after adjustment; serious adverse events occurred in a quarter to a third of both groups, a measure of how sick the population is
  8. Jaffe D, Costales T, Greenwell P, Christian M, Henn RF. Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus infection is a risk factor for unplanned return to the operating room in the surgical treatment of a septic knee. J Knee Surg 2017;30:872-878
    80 adult septic knees: a single washout succeeded in 75.8% of arthroscopic and 80.9% of open cases, not different; MRSA was the only independent predictor of an unplanned second washout, with a higher synovial white cell count also associated after arthroscopy
  9. Couderc M, Gomez S, Mathieu S, et al. Longitudinal incidence of native septic arthritis in France: a 13-year analysis of the National Health Data System database. Rheumatology (Oxford) 2026;65(5)
    109,160 adult native joint episodes 2009-2022: incidence rose from 13 to 16.2 per 100,000 adults per year; mean age 62, 65% men, staphylococci in 48%; all-cause mortality 3.2% at one month, 8.4% at six and 11.4% at twelve; risk factors rheumatoid arthritis (OR 4.7), drug addiction (4.5), complicated diabetes (4.4) and dialysis (4.0)

Spine › Spine

51 Lumbar microdiscectomy and decompression

Microdiscectomy, laminotomy, laminectomy and foraminotomy for radiculopathy and stenosis, open, tubular or endoscopic

2Mild to moderate

Dominant mechanism: Muscle. Paraspinal muscle stripped off the lamina and held under a retractor for an hour, a small bone window, and a nerve root that has been retracted; the pre-operative leg pain is removed by the operation and most of what is left is back and wound pain that fades over a week

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: low.

Block
Surgeon infiltration of the wound edges and paraspinal muscles with long-acting local anaesthetic, with regular paracetamol and an NSAID; bilateral erector spinae plane blocks at the operative level are the regional option when opioid sparing matters
Catheter: no No catheter has a place: the pain is mild, short and incisional, and a single-shot technique or infiltration covers the only night that matters
Alternatives: Bilateral erector spinae plane block (ultrasound, at or one level above the surgical level) for multilevel decompression, the opioid-tolerant patient or the patient who cannot have opioids; Spinal anaesthesia with sedation, prone on a frame, as a whole-anaesthetic alternative in selected single-level cases; Surgeon-applied epidural steroid at closure, which some surgeons use for radicular pain and which is their decision
Position
Prone on a Wilson frame, bolsters or a Jackson-type table with the abdomen free, hips flexed for a microdiscectomy to open the interlaminar window, arms up on boards at less than 90 degrees of abduction, head in a foam support with the eyes free
Tourniquet
No
Cement
No
Blood loss
50-150 mL for a single-level microdiscectomy; 200-500 mL for a multilevel laminectomy, almost all of it from epidural veins; transfusion is exceptional
Duration
45-90 min skin to skin for a microdiscectomy; 90-180 min for a two- or three-level decompression; revision through scar adds an hour
Length of stay
Day case or one night for microdiscectomy; one to three nights for multilevel laminectomy in an older patient. Day case: selected
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV within 60 min of incision (3 g over 120 kg); no implant, single dose
Tranexamic acid
Not needed for a single-level microdiscectomy; TXA 1 g IV before incision is reasonable for a multilevel laminectomy or a revision, where epidural venous bleeding is the whole blood loss
VTE
Mechanical prophylaxis and early walking; chemoprophylaxis is withheld in most practice because an epidural haematoma is the complication that matters, and is reserved for the patient's own risk factors after the first day
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV at induction and ondansetron 4 mg IV before emergence; vomiting and straining raise epidural venous pressure in a fresh wound
Tell the patient
The leg pain should be better when you wake up, or within a few days as the nerve settles; what you will feel is a sore back and wound for about a week, and walking is part of the treatment.
The trap
Leg pain that is worse rather than better, new weakness or numbness, or difficulty passing urine after this operation is an epidural haematoma or a retained fragment until the surgeon has looked, and it is a surgical emergency rather than an analgesia problem

What the surgeon is doing and why

A lumbar disc prolapse is nucleus pulposus that has pushed through a tear in the annulus and is sitting on a nerve root in the lateral recess or the foramen. The root is compressed, inflamed and ischaemic, and the patient’s pain is in the leg, in the territory of that root, not in the back. Most prolapses shrink on their own over weeks to months, which is why the operation is offered for pain that has not settled, for progressive weakness, or urgently for cauda equina compression. The surgeon’s aim is narrow: take the fragment off the root and leave everything else alone. The annulus is not repaired, the segment is not fused, and the back pain the patient also has, from the degenerate disc and the facets, is not treated and will still be there afterwards. That sentence is the pain logic of the card and the content of the pre-operative conversation.

Lumbar canal stenosis is the other indication. A degenerate bulging disc, hypertrophied ligamentum flavum and overgrown facet joints have narrowed the canal and the lateral recesses, usually at several levels in an older patient, and the symptom is neurogenic claudication rather than a single root. The operation is a decompression: a laminectomy or bilateral laminotomy with undercutting of the medial facets and removal of the flavum until the dura and the roots are free. It is a bigger bone-and-muscle operation on an older patient, and the version of this card that stays in hospital.

The microdiscectomy has a fixed sequence: localise the level on fluoroscopy; a 2-4 cm midline incision with the paraspinal muscles stripped subperiosteally off the lamina on one side and held with a self-retaining retractor (tubular systems dilate through the muscle instead, endoscopic systems go smaller still); a laminotomy of a few millimetres and excision of the ligamentum flavum, which is the only bone work and it is small; medial retraction of the dura and the traversing root to expose the prolapse; removal of the fragment through the annular defect; haemostasis and closure. Surgeons vary on how much disc they take: a fragmentectomy that removes the loose piece only gives a faster recovery and a higher recurrence; a subtotal discectomy that cleans out the disc space gives more back pain and a lower recurrence.

The far lateral prolapse, which compresses the exiting root outside the foramen, is reached through a paramedian muscle-splitting (Wiltse) approach; no laminotomy is needed, and the step that hurts is the dorsal root ganglion being handled.

The pain follows from what has been done to tissue. The dominant mechanism is muscle: multifidus has been stripped off bone and crushed under a retractor blade, and in a laminectomy across two or three levels that stripping is bilateral and long. Underneath it is a small bone window (the raw cancellous edge of a laminotomy, or the whole posterior arch gone in a laminectomy) and a nerve root that has been retracted for ten or twenty minutes, which produces the transient dysaesthesia and residual leg symptoms that settle over days as the root recovers. Tubular and endoscopic techniques remove most of the muscle mechanism, which is why they are day cases with less analgesia. The pre-operative pain generator, the compressed root, has been removed, so the patient’s dominant symptom is usually gone or much better in recovery. The residual is back and wound pain, worst on day 1, which fades over a week and responds to paracetamol and an NSAID. In the 179-procedure cohort the major spinal operations (fusion and scoliosis) sat at ranks 2, 3 and 6 of all surgery for worst pain on day 1; the discectomy is not among them, and the difference is that between a muscle window and an instrumented, grafted, re-tensioned segment, which has its own card (posterior lumbar fusion).

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 Pre-operative neurology, the scan and the plan for prone

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon operates on the level the MRI shows and the dermatome the patient describes, and will want them to match. A foot drop, a dense sensory loss or any sphincter symptom changes the urgency and the consent.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Document the neurology yourself before anything is given: ankle dorsiflexion and great toe extension (L5), plantar flexion (S1), knee extension (L4), the dermatomal sensory loss, and whether the patient has perineal numbness or retention. A deficit that is new in recovery can only be called new if the baseline is written down. Cauda equina compression (bilateral sciatica, saddle anaesthesia, retention, loss of anal tone) is an emergency decompression on the next available list, with a catheter in and the retention volume recorded. Ask about the shoulders and neck before you plan the arm position. A patient with severe radicular pain cannot lie flat and needs analgesia before the induction, or an induction in the lateral position.

  2. 2 Induction, airway and the turn

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon needs the patient prone, flexed at the hips to open the interlaminar space, motionless, and with epidural venous pressure as low as it can be, because the field is a 2 cm window at the bottom of a muscle well and every vein that bleeds obscures it.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A reinforced or well-secured tracheal tube is the author’s default for any prone case; a supraglottic airway is used by some for short microdiscectomies in slim patients and is a decision made with the surgeon and the frame in mind rather than a habit. Secure the tube and the eyes before the turn, disconnect for the log roll, and reconnect and check bilateral air entry and capnography before anyone touches the drapes. Then the checks, in order: eyes free of any pressure in the head support and visible through its mirror or cut-out; nose and chin clear; neck neutral; arms on boards with the shoulders below 90 degrees of abduction and the elbows flexed and padded, so the plexus is not stretched over the humeral head and the ulnar nerve is not on an edge; abdomen hanging free, so the inferior vena cava is not compressed and the epidural veins do not fill; breasts and genitals clear of the frame edges; knees padded; feet off the end of the table. Recheck the eyes and the arms after the surgeon has adjusted the flexion of the frame, because that is when the head moves. There is no neuromonitoring in a routine microdiscectomy, so the choice between volatile and total intravenous anaesthesia, and the use of relaxant, are matters of habit.

  3. 3 Localisation and the skin incision

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A needle or marker is placed over the intended interlaminar space and a lateral fluoroscopic image confirms the level against the sacrum. Then a short midline incision over that space, or a 1 cm stab for a tube.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Cefazolin finished before the knife. Lead aprons on for the localisation film. The surgeon may ask for a pause while the image is read; a wrong-level operation is the disaster the pause prevents. Heavy patients and transitional lumbosacral anatomy are the reasons the film takes longer than expected.

  4. 4 Muscle stripping and retraction, or tubular dilatation

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The paraspinal muscles are taken off the spinous process and lamina with cautery and a periosteal elevator, one side only for a microdiscectomy, both sides for a laminectomy, and a self-retaining retractor holds them out of the way. Tubular systems pass serial dilators through the muscle to a tube fixed to the table, with the microscope looking down it.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is the mechanism of the post-operative back pain and the moment at which a light patient moves. Muscle stripping is the most stimulating step before the root is touched; deepen or give opioid in anticipation rather than in response. Bleeding is from muscle and is controlled with cautery; a bilateral multilevel exposure in an anticoagulated patient is where the laminectomy blood loss starts. The retractor crushes the muscle it holds, and the longer it stays the more the back hurts tomorrow; a surgeon who releases it periodically is doing the pain plan’s work.

  5. 5 Laminotomy, flavectomy and the bone window

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A high-speed burr or Kerrison punch takes the inferior edge of the upper lamina and the medial facet, and the ligamentum flavum is lifted off the dura and excised. In stenosis surgery this is the operation: a full laminectomy, or bilateral laminotomies from one side, until the dura pulsates and the roots are free in their recesses.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The bone work is brief and does not bleed much; the first epidural vein bleeds when the flavum comes off. The surgeon now wants a still field with low venous pressure, and the things that raise it are an abdomen on the frame, coughing or straining, high positive end-expiratory pressure, and a head-down tilt. A modest reverse Trendelenburg tilt and a tidal volume that does not drive the abdomen into the bolsters are the levers. Deliberate hypotension buys nothing and adds risk to a prone patient’s eyes and spinal cord.

  6. 6 Root retraction and discectomy

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The traversing root and the dural sac are retracted medially with a root retractor, which exposes the prolapse and the posterior longitudinal ligament, and the fragment is removed with pituitary rongeurs. Surgeons vary between removing the loose fragment only and clearing the disc space.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The root under retraction is the nerve mechanism. A lightly anaesthetised patient will move a leg when the root is pulled, which in a 2 cm window under a microscope is dangerous. The epidural veins around the root bleed into the field and the surgeon’s requests for lower pressure usually come now; the honest reply is that venous pressure, not arterial, fills the field and the position and ventilation have already been optimised. Pituitary rongeurs placed deep into the disc space can go through the anterior annulus into the retroperitoneum, where the aorta and the iliac vessels lie: sudden unexplained hypotension or tachycardia during the discectomy, with little blood in the wound, is an anterior vascular injury until proven otherwise. It is rare, often unrecognised until the patient collapses in recovery, and the treatment is a supine patient, a vascular surgeon and blood, not a vasopressor.

  7. 7 Dural tear and repair

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The dura is thin, adherent to a prolapse or to scar, and is torn in about 3% of primary microdiscectomies and a fifth of revisions. The surgeon repairs it with a fine suture if it can be reached, adds a sealant, and may ask for a Valsalva to test the repair.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A tear changes the rest of the day. The surgeon will want a still field for a fiddly repair under the microscope, often with a slight head-up tilt to lower the cerebrospinal fluid pressure at the tear; a sustained inflation to 30-40 cmH2O when asked, to show whether the repair leaks; and a smooth emergence with no coughing or bucking, because every strain tests the repair. The post-operative consequences are a positional headache from cerebrospinal fluid loss, which behaves like a post-dural-puncture headache and is treated as one, and a period of flat bed rest that surgeons vary on: the review evidence is that flat rest beyond 24 h after a watertight repair adds medical complications and length of stay without reducing reoperation, but the instruction is the surgeon’s. A tear in a day-case patient means an admission. Document it on the anaesthetic record for the next anaesthetist who considers a spinal or epidural.

  8. 8 Haemostasis, infiltration and closure

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Epidural veins are controlled with bipolar diathermy and a haemostatic agent, the root is checked to be free, and the wound is closed in layers. Many surgeons infiltrate the muscle and skin with long-acting local anaesthetic; some place a steroid on the root, and a few leave a drain after a multilevel decompression.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The infiltration is most of the pain plan and the moment to confirm it has happened. Reverse any relaxant well before the skin closes. A drain after a microdiscectomy tells you the surgeon was worried about bleeding; a laminectomy in an anticoagulated patient is the typical case.

  9. 9 The turn back and emergence

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Nothing surgical remains, but the wound sits over an opened epidural space and a cauterised venous plexus; an epidural haematoma is the complication of the first hours.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Turn supine with the tube secured and the eyes still protected, then inspect the face, the eyes and the arms before the patient wakes: pressure marks on the forehead and cheeks are common and fade, a swollen eye or a complaint of visual change needs an ophthalmological assessment at once. Aim for an emergence without coughing or straining, which raises epidural venous pressure in a fresh field; a dural repair makes this a priority rather than a preference. Extubate when the patient obeys commands and will move both feet to order.

  10. 10 Recovery, the neurological check and the day-case decision

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants the leg pain gone, the neurology at baseline or better, and the patient walking within hours; mobilisation is the treatment for the back pain and the prevention of thrombosis.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Test ankle dorsiflexion, plantar flexion and knee extension against your pre-operative note; a new deficit, or leg pain that is worse than before with a tense wound or increasing back pain, is a haematoma or a retained fragment and the surgeon is called before any opioid is given, because the opioid will mask the progression. Most patients say the leg pain is gone or changed in character; a residual ache or tingling in the same dermatome is the retracted root and settles over days. Retention is common on the first evening after a prone case with opioids and an inflamed root; a bladder scan at four hours prevents the 2 am catheter. Day-case discharge after a single-level microdiscectomy is established practice: the patient walks, passes urine, has pain controlled on oral analgesia, has someone at home and a written note on the red flags (worsening leg pain, new weakness, saddle numbness, inability to pass urine, a leaking wound or a positional headache). A multilevel laminectomy in an older patient stays one to three nights; a drain, an anticoagulant to restart, a dural tear and a bladder are what keep them in.

Pain plan

The mechanism is stripped and retracted muscle over a small bone window, with the pre-operative pain generator removed, so the plan is a short one: regular paracetamol and an NSAID (or a COX-2 inhibitor) from before the infiltration wears off, a surgeon-infiltrated wound, intravenous dexamethasone at induction for its antiemetic and modest analgesic effect, and oral opioid as rescue for day 0 and 1. The defensible default needs no regional block. Most microdiscectomy patients need a few doses of opioid on the evening of surgery and the following day and then nothing stronger than the oral regimen, and the day-case model depends on exactly that.

The erector spinae plane block is the regional technique with evidence in lumbar surgery, and the evidence is mixed in quality. A 2022 meta-analysis of 15 randomised trials in 980 patients, across discectomy, decompression and fusion, found that a bilateral block reduced opioid consumption at 24 h, lowered pain at rest through the first day and roughly halved nausea and vomiting, with heterogeneity wide enough that no milligram figure can be quoted. PROSPECT, writing for complex spine surgery rather than for discectomy, does not recommend the block for lack of procedure-specific evidence. The author’s reconciliation: a bilateral erector spinae plane block at the operative level, placed after induction and before the turn, is worth its ten minutes for a multilevel laminectomy, for a patient who must be opioid-sparing (obstructive sleep apnoea, the frail, the opioid-tolerant) and for the day-case patient whose surgeon does not infiltrate. For a single-level microdiscectomy with a surgeon who infiltrates, it adds little. The catheter question does not arise.

Ketamine, which PROSPECT recommends intra-operatively for complex spine surgery, has no place in a routine microdiscectomy and a sensible one in the opioid-tolerant patient, who is common in this population after months of sciatica on tapentadol or oxycodone and whose plan is in the opioid-tolerant chapter. Gabapentinoids are not recommended by PROSPECT because of their adverse effects; a patient already taking one for radicular pain continues it rather than starting it.

Rebound pain in the usual sense does not happen, because no dense block wears off. What does happen on the first night is back pain and muscle spasm when the infiltration recedes, worse on movement and relieved by walking, and the patient who has been told to expect it does not mistake it for failure. Escalation triggers: pain out of proportion with a tense wound, any new neurology, leg pain that is worse rather than better, or retention are surgical, and the surgeon is called first. A positional headache is a dural leak, declared or not. Pain unchanged from before surgery, in the same leg and distribution, is a root that has not yet recovered or a fragment that was missed: a conversation for the surgeon, not a reason for a stronger opioid.

Pitfalls and variants

  • Microdiscectomy versus laminectomy. The single-level microdiscectomy in a 40-year-old is a 60 minute day case with 100 mL of blood loss. The three-level laminectomy in a 78-year-old on apixaban is a different operation wearing the same name: two hours prone, bilateral stripping, 400 mL from epidural veins, a drain, a night or three in hospital, and a positioning risk that rises with every decade. Plan the second as a fusion without the instrumentation.
  • Tubular and endoscopic techniques. The muscle is dilated rather than stripped, the wound is 1-2 cm, the pain is less and the day case is routine. Endoscopic transforaminal discectomy is often done under local anaesthesia and sedation, with the patient able to report leg pain when the exiting root is touched, which is the surgeon’s neuromonitoring; oversedation removes that safeguard.
  • Spinal anaesthesia. A single-level discectomy or decompression under spinal with sedation, prone on a frame, is a well-described alternative; its limits are the duration of the block, the patient’s tolerance of the position awake, and the surgeon’s willingness to have a patient who can talk.
  • Revision discectomy. Scar between muscle, dura and root; a durotomy rate of nearly one in five; a longer case; more bleeding; more residual leg pain. Not a day case in most hands.
  • Cauda equina syndrome. Out of hours, a patient in retention, a surgeon in a hurry, and a decompression that may be wider than planned. The urgency is real and the positioning checks are the thing that gets skipped.
  • The obese patient. The frame may not keep the abdomen free, ventilation pressures rise when prone, the epidural veins fill, the field bleeds, and the surgeon asks for hypotension. The answer is the position, not the pressure: a table with the abdomen hanging, reverse Trendelenburg, and a surgeon who accepts a slower dissection.
  • The anterior vascular injury. Rongeurs through the anterior annulus into the iliac vessels or the aorta: rare, under-recognised, and presenting as unexplained hypotension with little blood in the wound, or as collapse in recovery.
  • Postoperative visual loss. Rare after a short prone case, but the risk factors are those of the long fusions (see spine essentials): pressure on the globe, a long case, large blood loss, anaemia, hypotension and a head-down position. A single-level microdiscectomy carries almost none of them, which is why the eye check at the turn is the one that matters.
  • Position-related nerve injury. Brachial plexus from arms abducted beyond 90 degrees, ulnar nerve on the board edge, lateral femoral cutaneous nerve on the iliac crest bolster, and a face or breast pressure mark; all checked at the turn and again after the surgeon adjusts the frame.

Key sources

The evidence base for this operation’s analgesia is thin because the operation does not hurt much, and the spine literature has concentrated on fusions. PROSPECT’s complex spine guideline is cited for what it excludes as much as for what it recommends: single-level discectomy is outside its definition, and its advice on paracetamol, NSAID and opioid-as-rescue transfers downwards while its advice on ketamine and epidural catheters does not. The erector spinae plane block meta-analysis pools heterogeneous trials and shows a real but modest opioid-sparing effect rather than the size of it. The durotomy figures come from a narrative review of largely retrospective series. The Gerbershagen cohort is cited for the contrast between discectomy and fusion, not for a discectomy rank.

  1. Waelkens P, Alsabbagh E, Sauter A, Joshi GP, Beloeil H, on behalf of the PROSPECT Working Group of ESRA. Pain management after complex spine surgery: a systematic review and procedure-specific postoperative pain management recommendations. Eur J Anaesthesiol 2021;38:985-994
    Covers instrumented thoracolumbar surgery, laminectomy at three or more levels and scoliosis, not single-level discectomy: recommends paracetamol, NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor, intra-operative low-dose ketamine and opioids as rescue only; erector spinae and thoracolumbar interfascial plane blocks and wound infusion are not recommended for lack of procedure-specific evidence
  2. Xiao X, Zhu T, Wang L, Zhou H, Zhang Y. Efficacy of postoperative analgesia by erector spinal plane block after lumbar surgery: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Comput Math Methods Med 2022;2022:3264142
    15 randomised trials, 980 patients, discectomy, decompression and fusion mixed: erector spinae plane block reduced 24 h opioid consumption (standardised mean difference -2.27), pain at rest to 24 h, and postoperative nausea and vomiting (RR 0.35), with wide heterogeneity and no milligram figure
  3. Shannon MF, Ramanathan R, Poddar N, et al. Incidental dural tears in minimally invasive spine surgery: a narrative review of incidence, management, and outcomes. AME Surg J 2026;6:7
    Incidental durotomy in about 3% of primary microdiscectomies, open or minimally invasive, and 17-20% of revision microdiscectomies; primary suture plus sealant leaks less than sealant alone; flat bed rest beyond 24 h adds complications and length of stay without reducing reoperation
  4. Gerbershagen HJ, Aduckathil S, van Wijck AJ, Peelen LM, Kalkman CJ, Meissner W. Pain intensity on the first day after surgery: a prospective cohort study comparing 179 surgical procedures. Anesthesiology 2013;118:934-944
    50,523 patients, 179 procedures: spinal fusion and scoliosis surgery sat at ranks 2, 3 and 6 of all operations for worst pain on day 1; single-level discectomy is not among the high-ranked procedures, which is the contrast this card rests on

Spine › Spine

52 Posterior lumbar fusion: PLIF, TLIF and posterolateral

Pedicle screw instrumentation with interbody cage (PLIF, TLIF, MIS-TLIF) or posterolateral bone graft, one to three levels

4Severe

Dominant mechanism: Muscle. Bilateral paraspinal muscle stripped off three or four vertebrae and held under retractors for hours, with pedicle screws through the pedicles, a facetectomy, decorticated transverse processes and an interbody space distracted and re-tensioned; the segment is loaded through the construct from the first stand

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: moderate.

Block
Intrathecal morphine placed by the surgeon under direct vision before closure, or by you before induction, with intra-operative low-dose ketamine infusion, regular paracetamol and an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor
Catheter: selective An epidural catheter placed by the surgeon at closure (PROSPECT grade B) is the catheter option; the author's default is single-shot intrathecal morphine with ketamine and no catheter, reserving the surgeon-placed epidural or a ketamine infusion for the opioid-tolerant, the multilevel and the patient who cannot have an NSAID
Alternatives: Bilateral erector spinae plane blocks at the fused levels, as an adjunct where neuraxial morphine is declined or contraindicated; Surgeon-placed epidural catheter at closure, low-concentration local anaesthetic, for the multilevel or opioid-tolerant patient; Surgeon infiltration of the wound and the iliac crest donor site with long-acting local anaesthetic, always
Position
Prone on a Jackson-type open frame or chest and pelvic bolsters with the abdomen free and the hips extended to preserve lordosis for the fusion; arms up on boards below 90 degrees of abduction; head in a foam support or mirror system with the eyes free; a fluoroscopy arm needs room to swing
Tourniquet
No
Cement
Sometimes. Cement-augmented (fenestrated) pedicle screws in osteoporotic bone; small volumes under fluoroscopy, with the risk of cement into the epidural veins and the lungs rather than a hip-type cement reaction
Blood loss
300-800 mL for a single-level open TLIF; 800-1500 mL for two or three levels or a revision; 100-300 mL for a minimally invasive TLIF; type and screen for single level, crossmatch for multilevel and revision
Duration
150-240 min for a single-level open TLIF or PLIF; 240-360 min for multilevel or revision; minimally invasive single-level TLIF 120-180 min in practised hands
Length of stay
2-4 nights; minimally invasive single-level fusion in a fit patient one night, with same-day discharge reported in selected programmes. Day case: no
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV within 60 min of incision (3 g over 120 kg), repeated at 4 h; metal implants, a long case and a deep wound; many surgeons add vancomycin powder to the wound before closure
Tranexamic acid
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV before incision with either 1 g at 3 h or an infusion for a long case; the pooled lumbar trials show less intra-operative and total blood loss, less drain output and fewer transfusions, with no excess thrombosis
VTE
Mechanical prophylaxis from induction; chemoprophylaxis from day 1 or 2 is common once the surgeon is content the epidural space is dry, because an epidural haematoma under a laminectomy is paralysis; the timing is the surgeon's call and is written down
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV at induction and ondansetron 4 mg IV before emergence; intrathecal morphine adds nausea and pruritus and the second antiemetic is charted, not hoped for
Tell the patient
This is a big operation on the back: the first two days are hard, you will be walking on the first day because that is part of the treatment, and the leg pain should be better while the back pain takes a few weeks to settle.
The trap
Neuromonitoring changes the anaesthetic, not the other way round: once the exposure is done there is no relaxant, the volatile is off or low, and a sudden loss of motor evoked potentials during distraction or screw placement is a call to raise the pressure, check the haemoglobin and the temperature, and tell the surgeon to release what they just did

What the surgeon is doing and why

A lumbar fusion is offered when a motion segment is the pain generator or is unstable: a degenerative or isthmic spondylolisthesis in which one vertebra has slipped forward on the next, a disc that has collapsed and is loading the facets, a recurrent prolapse at a level already operated on twice, or a stenosis so severe that decompressing it would remove the facets and leave the segment unstable. The surgeon’s aim is to turn two vertebrae into one: decompress the nerves, restore the disc height and the lordosis, hold the segment rigid with screws and rods, and pack bone graft where it will fuse over six to twelve months. The hardware is scaffolding. The fusion is the bone, and everything the surgeon does to raw bone (decortication, burring, packing) is in the service of getting it to knit.

Three constructs share the card. A posterolateral fusion puts pedicle screws into the vertebrae above and below, connects them with rods, decorticates the transverse processes and the facets, and lays bone graft across them; the disc is left alone. A posterior lumbar interbody fusion (PLIF) adds a cage into the disc space from behind, which means a bilateral laminectomy and retraction of the thecal sac and both roots to the midline. A transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (TLIF) reaches the same disc through one side, by removing a facet joint and entering the foramen, so the dura is barely retracted and the opposite lamina and facet are left for the posterolateral graft. The TLIF has largely replaced the PLIF because of the durotomy and root injury rates the bilateral retraction carried. The minimally invasive TLIF does the same operation through tubes and percutaneous screws, trading a smaller muscle injury and less blood for a longer time under fluoroscopy.

The sequence of an open TLIF is the spine of the card: a midline incision, bilateral subperiosteal stripping of the paraspinal muscles out to the transverse processes, and self-retaining retractors that stay in for the rest of the case; pedicle screws above and below the disc under fluoroscopy or navigation, often with a stimulated screw test; a unilateral facetectomy and laminotomy; a complete discectomy through the foramen with the endplates scraped to bleeding bone, because a cage fuses to marrow and not to cartilage; distraction across the screws and a cage packed with graft hammered into the disc space; rods contoured into lordosis and compression across the screws so the cage is locked and the segment re-tensioned into its new shape; decortication of the contralateral facet and transverse processes with graft laid over them; a drain in most hands and layered closure.

The graft is where the iliac crest enters the story. Autograft from the posterior iliac crest was the standard and is still used by some surgeons; it adds a raw cancellous surface under gluteal muscle that hurts for weeks and that patients remember long after the back has settled. Most surgeons now use the local bone from the laminectomy and facetectomy, supplemented with allograft or a bone substitute, and reserve the crest for revisions and pseudarthroses. Which the surgeon does is worth a question before the case, because it changes the pain plan.

The pain logic. In the 179-procedure cohort, spinal fusion and scoliosis surgery took three of the top six places of all operations for worst pain on the first day, with median scores of 7, and epidural analgesia was not used in those patients. The dominant mechanism is muscle: multifidus and longissimus stripped bilaterally off three or four vertebrae and crushed under retractors for three hours, which produces an aching, position-dependent back pain that is worst when the patient first stands and turns. Layered on it are bone (screws through four pedicles, a facetectomy, decorticated transverse processes and scraped endplates, each a raw cancellous surface), nerve (a root retracted to place the cage, and in a PLIF two roots and the sac), and retension: the segment has been distracted, lordosed and compressed into a new shape, and every step loads it through the screws from day 1. That last mechanism is why the pain does not fall away as quickly as a laminectomy’s, and why the trajectory stays at 4 on day 3. Compare the microdiscectomy, a one-sided muscle window with nothing re-tensioned, and the deformity correction, the same mechanisms over ten levels.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 The pre-operative conversation, neurology and the opioid history

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon has selected a level and a construct from the imaging and the symptoms, and wants a documented neurological baseline, a known bone quality and a plan for the chronic pain that brought the patient to them.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Write down the leg neurology (L4 knee extension, L5 dorsiflexion, S1 plantar flexion, the dermatomes) because new weakness after a fusion is a screw, a haematoma or a retracted root, and it can only be called new against a baseline. Take the opioid history in milligrams, not adjectives: most of these patients have had months or years of back pain, many are on a long-acting opioid, some on a gabapentinoid, and the plan for them is the one in the opioid-tolerant chapter, with ketamine and the usual dose continued through the day of surgery. Ask what graft the surgeon is taking and whether there is neuromonitoring, because both change the anaesthetic. A haemoglobin, a group and screen (crossmatch for multilevel or revision), and the NSAID question: a surgeon who forbids NSAIDs for fear of non-union removes a grade A recommendation from the plan, and that conversation happens before the day, not in recovery.

  2. 2 Induction, lines, neuromonitoring set-up and the turn

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Three hours prone with the abdomen free, lordosis preserved, a fluoroscopy arm swinging under the table, and a motionless field with low epidural venous pressure. If the surgeon uses motor evoked potentials, the monitoring team needs baselines and an anaesthetic that will not abolish them.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A reinforced tracheal tube, well secured and with a bite block if motor evoked potentials are planned (the tongue and the tube take the bite). Two good cannulae; an arterial line for multilevel, revision, the cardiac patient and any case where the surgeon’s blood loss history says so. A urinary catheter for anything over two hours. The anaesthetic for neuromonitoring: a propofol and remifentanil infusion, no volatile or a low fraction only if the monitoring team accepts the signals they are getting, and no neuromuscular block after the intubating dose, because motor evoked potentials and triggered electromyography of the screws need a working neuromuscular junction. Rocuronium at intubation reversed with sugammadex once the exposure is done gives the surgeon a relaxed patient for the stripping and the monitoring team a clean baseline afterwards; tell the surgeon the patient may move with the first screw stimulation. The turn: eyes taped and then checked in the head support, neck neutral, shoulders below 90 degrees, elbows padded, abdomen free, breasts and genitals clear, knees and shins padded, feet free. Then look again after the surgeon has set the lordosis and the table height.

  3. 3 Antibiotic, tranexamic acid and the marking film

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Metal, a deep wound and hours of exposure; the surgeon marks the levels with a lateral image and counts from the sacrum.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Cefazolin finished before the knife and repeated at 4 h, with vancomycin powder in the wound at closure in many hands. Tranexamic acid 1 g IV before incision, repeated at 3 h or as an infusion; across 49 randomised lumbar trials it reduced intra-operative and total blood loss, drain output and transfusion without an increase in thrombosis, and this operation bleeds from muscle, decorticated bone and epidural veins for its whole length. Lead for everyone; the image intensifier is in and out all day.

  4. 4 Exposure: bilateral muscle stripping and retraction

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The paraspinal muscles are taken off the spinous processes, laminae and facets out to the transverse processes on both sides, over the levels to be fused and the screws’ entry points, and held with self-retaining retractors.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The longest sustained stimulus of the case and the mechanism of most of the post-operative pain; this is the moment for the ketamine to be running and the opioid ahead of the knife. Muscle bleeds steadily and the surgeon controls it with cautery; 500 mL by the end of a multilevel exposure is normal and the time to have the first unit checked. The abdomen must be hanging free: a frame that compresses it fills the epidural veins and the field, and the surgeon’s request for a lower pressure is usually a request for a better position. Relaxant, if used, is reversed by the end of this step.

  5. 5 Pedicle screw placement

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Screws go through the pedicle into the vertebral body above and below the disc, by landmarks and fluoroscopy, navigation or a robot. The medial wall of the pedicle is the spinal canal and the inferior wall is the exiting root; a breached screw is the complication the stimulated screw test exists to catch.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Each screw is stimulated and the monitoring team reports the current at which it fires the leg muscles: a threshold below about 6-8 mA suggests a breach and the surgeon redirects it. The test needs no neuromuscular block, and a patient who twitches is the test working. Fenestrated screws with cement in osteoporotic bone bring a small cement step: the volume is low but the vertebral venous plexus drains straight into the lungs, and a transient fall in end-tidal carbon dioxide or a rise in airway pressure during injection is cement embolism, usually tolerated, occasionally not.

  6. 6 Decompression and facetectomy

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Laminotomy, flavectomy and a unilateral facetectomy (TLIF) or bilateral laminectomy (PLIF) free the roots and open the way to the disc. The bone removed is saved as graft.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Epidural venous bleeding begins here and continues until the cage is in. A durotomy at this step is repaired as on the microdiscectomy card, and in a fusion the repair is under the construct and harder to reach; it adds a Valsalva, a smooth emergence and a line on the record. Root retraction is the nerve mechanism; a PLIF retracts the sac and both roots to the midline for longer than a TLIF retracts one, which is why the PLIF carries the higher durotomy and radiculopathy rates.

  7. 7 Discectomy, endplate preparation and distraction

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The disc is removed through the foramen, the cartilaginous endplates are scraped to bleeding bone, and the disc space is distracted across the screws or with spreaders to restore height and open the foramen.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Distraction is the moment the neuromonitoring team watches most closely, because stretching a root shows as a drop in motor evoked potentials; the usual response is to release the distraction, raise the mean pressure, check the haemoglobin and the temperature, and wait. The instruments in the disc space reach the anterior annulus, behind which lie the iliac vessels and the aorta; sudden hypotension with a quiet wound is the same vascular injury as on the microdiscectomy card and is handled the same way. Blood from the scraped endplates is steady and is the second large contribution to the loss.

  8. 8 Cage insertion, rod placement and compression

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A cage packed with graft is hammered into the distracted disc space, the rods are contoured into lordosis and locked, and the screws are compressed towards each other so the cage is loaded and the segment set in its new alignment.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The hammering transmits through the table and the patient; the monitoring team will see artefact and ask for a pause for a clean trace once the cage is seated. Compression is the retension mechanism being created, and the signals are checked again when the rods are locked. If motor evoked potentials fall and do not recover with pressure, haemoglobin and warmth, the surgeon loosens the construct and looks; that decision is theirs, the physiological optimisation is yours, and both happen in the first minutes.

  9. 9 Posterolateral graft, the iliac crest and the local anaesthetic

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Transverse processes and the remaining facet are decorticated to bleeding bone and graft laid along them; if the crest is harvested, a window is cut in the posterior ilium and cancellous bone curetted out.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Decortication is the last bone bleeding of the case. The crest donor site is the sleeper: it hurts more and for longer than the back in many patients and is not covered by anything placed in the spinal wound, so if the crest is harvested, infiltration of the crest with long-acting local anaesthetic is the one thing to ask for by name. The surgeon-placed epidural catheter or the intrathecal morphine, if given at closure, goes in now under direct vision; agree the dose with the surgeon, because it is their injection and your monitoring.

  10. 10 Closure, drain and the turn back

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Layered closure over a drain in most hands; a vancomycin powder dusting in many. The construct is stable from the moment the rods are locked.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    No relaxant has been given for hours, so none to reverse. Give the second antiemetic. Turn supine and inspect the face, the eyes and the arms before the patient wakes; a swollen or painful eye needs an ophthalmologist now, not in the morning. A smooth emergence without bucking protects a dural repair and keeps the epidural veins from refilling under the wound. Extubate a patient who can move both feet to order; one who cannot is a surgical conversation before they leave the table.

  11. 11 Recovery, the first night and the first stand

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants the neurology confirmed, the drain watched, the patient out of bed on day 1 and the wound dry.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Neurological check against the baseline in recovery and at intervals through the first night, because an epidural haematoma under a laminectomy presents as rising back pain, then new leg pain, then weakness and retention, over hours, and the window for evacuation is short. A patient who has had intrathecal morphine is monitored for respiratory depression for 24 h with the ward told in writing what to watch, and the pruritus and nausea are treated as expected effects. The regular paracetamol and NSAID start in recovery; the rescue opioid is charted, not held in reserve; the ketamine stops at closure. The first stand hurts and is the treatment; a patient who has not been told so will refuse it.

Pain plan

The mechanism is bilateral muscle stripping over a bone-and-nerve operation with a segment re-tensioned and loaded from day 1, so the plan is multimodal from the start and built around a neuraxial opioid rather than a peripheral block. PROSPECT, writing for exactly this operation, recommends paracetamol, an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor (grade A), an intra-operative low-dose ketamine infusion (grade A) and opioids as rescue only, with a surgeon-placed epidural catheter at the end of surgery using a low concentration of local anaesthetic as the regional option (grade B). It does not recommend intrathecal morphine, erector spinae or interfascial plane blocks, lidocaine, dexmedetomidine, magnesium or wound infusion, each for lack of procedure-specific evidence rather than evidence of harm, and it advises against gabapentinoids and methadone for their adverse effects.

The author’s default differs from the guideline on one point and follows it on the rest. Intrathecal morphine, 0.1-0.2 mg given by the surgeon under direct vision before closure or by you with a spinal needle before induction, is the single intervention that most reliably changes the first night: in the 150-patient placebo-controlled trial of instrumented fusion, 0.2 mg reduced pain at rest and on movement over 24 h and opioid use without an excess of respiratory depression, and the meta-analysis of 12 trials across spinal surgery found lower pain scores to 24 h and more pruritus with no significant excess of respiratory depression or retention. Its benefit is gone by 48 h, which is why it is combined with the ketamine infusion (0.5 mg/kg at induction and 10 microg/kg/min to closure in the opioid-dependent trial, which reduced opioid use at 48 h and pain at six weeks) and the oral regimen. The ward must be able to monitor a patient after neuraxial morphine; where it cannot, the plan reverts to the surgeon-placed epidural or to ketamine and opioid alone.

The catheter decision. A surgeon-placed epidural catheter with a low-concentration local anaesthetic infusion is PROSPECT’s grade B regional recommendation and the author’s choice for the multilevel fusion, the opioid-tolerant patient who will not be covered by a single dose of intrathecal morphine, and the patient who cannot have an NSAID. Its limits are the surgeon’s willingness to place it, the risk of masking a haematoma or a new deficit (dilute solutions and a motor check every shift are the answer), and the fact that it comes out on day 2 or 3 when the pain is still a 4. For the routine single-level TLIF the default is intrathecal morphine without a catheter. Bilateral erector spinae plane blocks are the fallback when neuraxial morphine is refused or contraindicated, and an adjunct rather than a substitute. The iliac crest, if harvested, needs its own infiltration.

Escalation: rising back pain in the first 24 h with new leg symptoms, weakness or retention is a haematoma until imaged, and the surgeon is called before any analgesic change. Pain that is manageable at rest and severe on standing is the retension mechanism and the expected course; the oral opioid is timed before physiotherapy, not after. Pain still 6 or more at a week with a dry wound is the chronic pain patient’s baseline reasserting itself: a pain service referral, not a dose escalation.

Pitfalls and variants

  • Open versus minimally invasive TLIF. The tubular version replaces stripping with dilatation and percutaneous screws, cuts blood loss to a few hundred millilitres and stay to a night or two, and in selected programmes goes home the same day; the pain mechanism shifts from muscle towards bone and nerve, and the trajectory falls by about a point. The fluoroscopy time triples.
  • PLIF versus TLIF. The PLIF’s bilateral retraction of the sac is the reason for its durotomy and root injury rates; expect more residual leg dysaesthesia and a slower first week.
  • The iliac crest. A separate wound over gluteal muscle and a raw cancellous bed; the most under-treated pain of this operation. Infiltration at the very least, and a warning to the patient.
  • Neuromonitoring and the anaesthetic. Propofol and remifentanil, no relaxant after exposure, a bite block, and a willingness to raise the mean pressure, transfuse and warm when the signals fall. A volatile anaesthetic with full relaxation gives the monitoring team nothing and the surgeon false reassurance.
  • The opioid-tolerant patient. The commonest phenotype on this list. Continue the baseline opioid, run ketamine, place the intrathecal morphine or the epidural, and involve the pain service before the second bad night rather than after it.
  • Osteoporosis and cemented screws. Small cement volumes into a venous plexus that drains to the lungs; watch the end-tidal carbon dioxide during injection.
  • Revision fusion. Scar, retained metal to remove, a durotomy rate several times the primary, double the blood loss and time, and a patient whose pain predates the first operation. Arterial line, crossmatch, catheter plan.
  • The anterior vascular injury. Instruments through the anterior annulus into the iliac vessels: unexplained hypotension with a quiet wound, turn supine, call the vascular surgeon.
  • Postoperative visual loss. A long prone case with blood loss and a head-down tilt is the described risk profile; the head support, the eye checks, avoiding anaemia and sustained hypotension, and a neutral or head-up table are the modifiable parts (see spine essentials).
  • Chemoprophylaxis timing. A dry epidural space matters more than a day’s delay in enoxaparin; the surgeon’s timing is written, and an epidural catheter changes it.

Key sources

This operation has the best analgesia evidence in the spine, because PROSPECT built its complex spine guideline on it, and its recommendations for paracetamol, NSAID, ketamine and a surgeon-placed epidural are the backbone of the card. The guideline’s decision not to recommend intrathecal morphine rests on the thinness of procedure-specific trials rather than on a negative result; the 150-patient randomised fusion trial and the 12-trial meta-analysis are what the author leans on to use it anyway. The tranexamic acid pooling across 49 trials is large but mixes routes and doses. The neuromonitoring thresholds and anaesthetic rules are consensus practice rather than trial evidence, and the Gerbershagen cohort supplies the rank, not a mechanism.

    Complex spine surgery (instrumented thoracolumbar surgery, laminectomy at three or more levels, scoliosis): paracetamol (grade D), NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor (grade A), intra-operative low-dose ketamine infusion (grade A), opioids as rescue only, and a surgeon-placed epidural catheter at the end of surgery with low-concentration local anaesthetic (grade B); gabapentinoids and methadone not recommended for adverse effects; intrathecal opioids, erector spinae and interfascial plane blocks, lidocaine, dexmedetomidine, magnesium and wound infusion not recommended for lack of procedure-specific evidence
  2. Loftus RW, Yeager MP, Clark JA, et al. Intraoperative ketamine reduces perioperative opiate consumption in opiate-dependent patients with chronic back pain undergoing back surgery. Anesthesiology 2010;113:639-646
    102 opioid-dependent patients having major lumbar surgery: ketamine 0.5 mg/kg at induction then 10 microg/kg/min to closure reduced morphine-equivalent consumption at 48 h and at 6 weeks and lowered pain at 6 weeks, with no excess side effects
  3. Wang J, Sun H, Sun WT, Sun HP, Tian T, Sun J. Efficacy and safety of intrathecal morphine for pain control after spinal surgery: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Eur Rev Med Pharmacol Sci 2021;25:2674-2684
    12 trials: intrathecal morphine lowered pain scores from 2 to 24 h and analgesic consumption, with more pruritus and no significant excess of respiratory depression, nausea or urinary retention; the optimal dose was not established
  4. Yavin D, Dhaliwal P, Whittaker T, et al. Intrathecal morphine following lumbar fusion: a randomized, placebo-controlled trial. Can J Neurol Sci 2016;43(S2):S11 (abstract)
    150 instrumented lumbar fusions, intrathecal morphine 0.2 mg or saline before closure: less pain at rest and on movement over 24 h, lower opioid requirement, no excess respiratory depression (HR 0.86), no change in length of stay
  5. Xiao K, Zhuo X, Peng X, Wu Z, Li B. The efficacy and safety of tranexamic acid in lumbar surgery: a meta-analysis of randomized-controlled trials. Jt Dis Relat Surg 2022;33:57-85
    49 randomised trials, 4,822 patients: tranexamic acid reduced intra-operative and total blood loss, drain output and transfusion, with no difference in deep vein thrombosis; intravenous and topical routes pooled
  6. Cole CD, McCall TD, Schmidt MH, Dailey AT. Comparison of low back fusion techniques: transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (TLIF) or posterior lumbar interbody fusion (PLIF) approaches. Curr Rev Musculoskelet Med 2009;2:118-126
    Technique review: PLIF needs the thecal sac and roots retracted to the midline for a bilateral approach, TLIF goes through a unilateral facetectomy with minimal dural retraction; durotomy and root injury are higher with PLIF; cage migration in 3-10% of early series
  7. Gerbershagen HJ, Aduckathil S, van Wijck AJ, Peelen LM, Kalkman CJ, Meissner W. Pain intensity on the first day after surgery: a prospective cohort study comparing 179 surgical procedures. Anesthesiology 2013;118:934-944
    50,523 patients: spinal fusion and scoliosis surgery occupied ranks 2, 3 and 6 of 179 procedures for worst pain on the first day, with median scores of 7

Spine › Spine

53 Anterior and lateral lumbar fusion: ALIF and LLIF

Anterior lumbar interbody fusion through a retroperitoneal approach; lateral (transpsoas, XLIF) and oblique (OLIF, anterior to psoas) lateral interbody fusion; usually with posterior percutaneous fixation

3Moderate

Dominant mechanism: Visceral. An abdominal wall incision with the retroperitoneum swept and the great vessels retracted (ALIF), or a flank incision with the psoas split and retracted off the lumbar plexus (LLIF); the disc space is distracted and a large cage wedged in, but the posterior muscles are untouched, so the pain is wall-and-viscera plus a bruised psoas and a dysaesthetic thigh, not a stripped back

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: low.

Block
Surgeon infiltration of the abdominal or flank wound with long-acting local anaesthetic, regular paracetamol and an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor, intra-operative ketamine for the opioid-tolerant, and a transversus abdominis plane or quadratus lumborum block on the operative side as the regional option
Catheter: rarely A single-shot fascial plane block covers the wall pain that matters; a catheter has a place only when a posterior stage follows under the same anaesthetic and the opioid-tolerant patient needs a multi-day plan, and then it is the posterior card's epidural, not a wall catheter
Alternatives: Quadratus lumborum block (posterior or anterior approach) on the operative side, which reaches the flank and some of the thigh dysaesthesia for an LLIF; Bilateral transversus abdominis plane blocks for a Pfannenstiel-type ALIF incision; Intrathecal morphine when a posterior instrumented stage is combined, with the ward monitoring that implies
Position
ALIF: supine on a radiolucent table with the lumbar spine extended over a break or a bolster to open the disc space, arms out or across the chest, fluoroscopy lateral and anteroposterior. LLIF: true lateral decubitus, usually left side up, taped to the table at the chest and the pelvis, table broken at the iliac crest to open the flank, the dependent arm on a board and the upper arm on a rest, with the fluoroscopy arm confirming a true orthogonal lateral
Tourniquet
No
Cement
No
Blood loss
100-300 mL for an uncomplicated single-level ALIF or LLIF; a major venous injury at L4-5 turns that into litres in minutes, so a crossmatch and two large cannulae are the default for ALIF and for any multilevel lateral case
Duration
90-150 min for a single-level ALIF or LLIF; 180-300 min for a multilevel lateral construct or an anterior stage followed by posterior percutaneous screws under the same anaesthetic
Length of stay
1-3 nights; 3-5 when a posterior stage is added. Day case: no
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV within 60 min of incision (3 g over 120 kg), repeated at 4 h; some surgeons add metronidazole 500 mg IV for a transperitoneal or bowel-adjacent exposure
Tranexamic acid
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV before incision is reasonable and widely used; the lumbar surgery pooling supports it, though the anterior and lateral approaches contribute little of that evidence
VTE
Mechanical from induction; chemoprophylaxis from day 1 is more readily given than after a posterior laminectomy because no canal has been opened, and the iliac vein that was retracted for an hour is the thrombosis the surgeon fears
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV at induction and ondansetron 4 mg IV before emergence; ileus is the gut's response to retroperitoneal retraction and the opioid dose is part of it
Tell the patient
This fusion is done from the front or the side so the back muscles are left alone; expect a sore abdomen or flank and, after a side approach, a numb or burning thigh and a weak hip for some weeks that almost always recovers.
The trap
The left common iliac vein tears at L4-5, the bleeding is immediate and torrential, and the person who can fix it is the access surgeon who may have already left: know where they are, have blood available, and treat sudden hypotension during disc preparation as a vascular injury until the surgeon says otherwise

What the surgeon is doing and why

The posterior fusion on the previous card reaches the disc by stripping the back muscles, removing a facet and retracting the roots. The anterior and lateral fusions reach the same disc from the front or the side, through the abdomen or the flank, so that none of that happens: the paraspinal muscles are untouched, the canal is never opened, the roots are never retracted, and the surgeon gets a view of the whole disc and both endplates that allows a cage two or three times the size of anything that fits through a foramen. A big cage on the strong ring of cortical bone at the edge of the endplate restores disc height and lordosis better, subsides less and fuses more reliably than a small posterior one, and it decompresses the foramen indirectly by lifting the vertebra off the root. The price is paid in a different currency: between the skin and the disc lie the great vessels, the ureter, the bowel, the sympathetic chain and the hypogastric plexus (anterior), or the psoas and the lumbar plexus running through it (lateral). The pain profile and the catastrophe profile both follow from that.

The anterior lumbar interbody fusion is an operation at L5-S1 and L4-5, occasionally L3-4. The patient is supine with the lumbar spine extended over a break in the table. A 6-7 cm transverse or paramedian incision to the left of the midline, the anterior rectus sheath opened, the rectus mobilised, and the peritoneum swept off the posterior wall by hand into the retroperitoneum, with the ureter identified and carried with it. At L5-S1 the disc lies below the aortic bifurcation and between the common iliac vessels; the median sacral vessels are divided and the superior hypogastric plexus, which lies on the front of the disc and carries the sympathetic supply to the bladder neck, is swept aside without monopolar diathermy because burning it causes retrograde ejaculation. At L4-5 the disc lies behind the left common iliac vein, which has to be mobilised and retracted to the right after the iliolumbar vein that tethers it is ligated; this is the step with the vascular risk, and the reason many spine surgeons work with a vascular or general access surgeon. The disc is excised, the endplates prepared, the space distracted and a large lordotic cage, often with integrated screws, impacted in. Posterior pedicle screws through percutaneous stab incisions, prone, under the same or a second anaesthetic, complete the construct in most hands.

The lateral lumbar interbody fusion (transpsoas, XLIF, DLIF) is an operation at L1-2 to L4-5; L5-S1 is hidden behind the iliac crest. The patient is in true lateral decubitus, taped at the chest and pelvis, with the table broken at the crest to open the space between the ribs and the pelvis. A 3-4 cm flank incision, the abdominal wall muscles split, the retroperitoneum entered and the peritoneum swept forwards, and then the psoas. The lumbar plexus runs within the posterior part of the psoas and migrates forwards at lower levels, so the surgeon passes a stimulating probe and serial dilators through the muscle under directional electromyographic guidance, looking for a corridor that does not fire a quadriceps or an adductor, and then opens a retractor against the muscle for the length of the disc preparation. The disc is removed across its whole width, the contralateral annulus released, and a wide cage placed across both rings of the endplate. The oblique approach (OLIF, anterior to psoas) passes in front of the psoas rather than through it, trading plexus risk for a longer path and the vessels in the way. Both are usually followed by percutaneous posterior screws, prone.

The pain logic. The mechanism is visceral: an abdominal wall or flank incision through muscle, a peritoneum that has been swept and a retroperitoneum retracted for an hour, and a bowel handled from the outside that will be slow for a day or two. Nothing posterior has been stripped, no root has been retracted, and the bone work is confined to the endplates, which are inside the disc and do not hurt the way a decorticated transverse process does. The result is a day 1 peak around 5, driven by the wound and by the first stand, and a quick fall. The lateral approach adds two things of its own: a psoas that has been split and held apart, which gives hip flexor weakness and a deep groin ache for days to weeks, and a lumbar plexus that has been stretched or bruised, which gives the anterior thigh numbness or burning that about one in seven patients has acutely and most lose within three months. That nerve component is the difference between the two approaches for the patient, and the thing to warn them about. When a posterior stage is added, its mechanisms are added with it; the score of 3 on this card is for the anterior or lateral stage alone, and the combined case sits at the posterior lumbar fusion score of 4.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 Pre-operative planning: the vessels, the access surgeon and the two-stage question

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon has studied the vascular anatomy on the imaging (the level of the bifurcation, the position of the left iliac vein), has booked an access surgeon or will do the exposure themselves, and has decided whether the posterior fixation follows under the same anaesthetic.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Ask the three questions that change the day: which level (L4-5 is the vascular step for an ALIF and the level at which the plexus sits furthest forward in the psoas for an LLIF), who is doing the exposure and whether they stay in the building, and whether the patient is turned prone for screws afterwards. A crossmatch for every ALIF and for multilevel lateral cases, because the venous injury happens in seconds. Document leg neurology and hip flexor strength on the operative side before an LLIF, because weakness afterwards needs a baseline. The opioid history matters less than on the posterior card but is still taken in milligrams.

  2. 2 Induction, lines and the anaesthetic that neuromonitoring allows

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The lateral approach depends on directional electromyography to find a safe corridor through the psoas; the anterior approach depends on a vascular field that can be controlled at once if it bleeds.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A tracheal tube; two large cannulae for an ALIF and an arterial line for any case at L4-5 with vein mobilisation, for multilevel lateral work and for the patient with cardiac disease. For an LLIF, no neuromuscular block after the intubating dose, and sugammadex to make sure it is gone before the psoas is entered, because the electromyographic probe needs a muscle that can respond; a volatile anaesthetic is acceptable for electromyography alone, and a propofol infusion is needed only if the surgeon also runs motor evoked potentials. Tell the surgeon which you have done. A urinary catheter for both approaches; a nasogastric tube is the surgeon’s call for a transperitoneal exposure and comes out at the end.

  3. 3 Positioning: supine with extension, or true lateral with the table broken

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The ALIF needs the lumbar spine extended so the disc opens anteriorly and the cage can restore lordosis; the LLIF needs a true lateral so that the fluoroscopy, the retractor and the cage all pass orthogonally, and a table break to lift the iliac crest out of the way of L4-5.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    ALIF: a bolster or table break under the lumbar spine, arms secured where the fluoroscopy arm can swing, the sacrum and heels padded. LLIF: the patient on the side with the hip over the break, taped across the chest and the pelvis so the surgeon can lean on them, the dependent arm on a board, an axillary roll under the thorax rather than in the axilla, the upper arm on a rest, the dependent knee flexed and the legs separated by a pillow, the head in line with the spine. The break then flexes the patient at the flank, which stretches the plexus on the upper side and loads the dependent hip, and the surgeon will want it as open as possible; a compromise the monitoring team can accept is better than a femoral nerve that does not recover. Check the eyes and the dependent ear once the drapes are on.

  4. 4 Incision and the retroperitoneal sweep

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Anterior: the rectus is mobilised and the hand enters the retroperitoneum, sweeping the peritoneum and its contents medially and up until the psoas and then the great vessels are felt. Lateral: a flank incision, the three abdominal wall muscles split in the line of their fibres, and the peritoneum swept forwards with a finger until the psoas is palpable.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Antibiotic and tranexamic acid finished before the knife. The peritoneum is breached in 2-16% of retroperitoneal cases, usually without consequence; a transperitoneal conversion changes nothing for you except a longer ileus. The sweep is the first moment of vagal bradycardia, and the retractor placed afterwards keeps the stimulus going. The bowel is being handled from outside its peritoneum, which is why the gut is slow tomorrow.

  5. 5 ALIF: vessel mobilisation and the exposure of the disc

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    At L5-S1 the surgeon works between the common iliac vessels and divides the median sacral vessels; at L4-5 the left common iliac vein is mobilised off the disc after the iliolumbar vein is ligated, and the great vessels are retracted to the right. Monopolar diathermy is avoided on the front of the disc to spare the hypogastric plexus.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is the step. A torn common iliac vein, a cava or an iliolumbar vein that has pulled off bleeds faster than any orthopaedic injury on this site, with the field filling before the surgeon has said a word. The response is the one you have already set up: blood in the room, a second cannula running, the access surgeon’s hands on the vessel, pressure and packing while the anaesthetic catches up, and an arterial line placed at the start rather than now. Venous air embolism is possible with an open vein in a patient whose spine is extended above the heart; a fall in end-tidal carbon dioxide at this moment is air or hypovolaemia and both are treated by flooding the field and lowering the head. Retractor blades resting on the iliac vein for an hour are the mechanism of the post-operative iliac vein thrombosis. A left-leg arterial occlusion from a retracted iliac artery in an atherosclerotic patient is the quieter catastrophe: a pulse oximeter on the left foot during the exposure tells you before recovery does.

  6. 6 LLIF: the transpsoas corridor under electromyography

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A stimulating probe is advanced through the psoas at the position chosen on the lateral image, usually the anterior half of the disc, and the monitoring team reports the current at which it fires the leg; a high threshold means the plexus is far away, a low one means it is close and the surgeon moves forward. Serial dilators and then a retractor open the corridor and hold the muscle apart.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    No block, as planned, and the patient may twitch; a twitch is the test working. The threshold the surgeon accepts before advancing is their convention; a sustained low one at L4-5 is the moment a surgeon abandons the level or changes approach.
