The time the retractor is open is the mechanism of the thigh dysaesthesia and the hip flexor weakness, because the plexus is being stretched over the blade and the psoas crushed; a reminder of the elapsed time from your side is welcome by most surgeons. The genitofemoral nerve runs on the front of the psoas and is the cause of the groin numbness the patient will mention tomorrow.

  7. 7 Discectomy, endplate preparation and contralateral release

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The disc is removed across its width, the cartilaginous endplates scraped to bleeding bone, and in a lateral approach the far-side annulus released with an elevator pushed across to the opposite edge, so that the cage can sit on both rings of cortical bone.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    In an LLIF the instrument passed across the disc space reaches the far annulus, beyond which lie the opposite psoas, the plexus and, in front, the great vessels; the contralateral release is the vascular step of the lateral approach, and the same signs apply (hypotension with a quiet wound). In an ALIF a curette through the posterior annulus is in the canal, which is rare and presents as a new deficit rather than as bleeding. Bleeding from the endplates is modest and runs into the retroperitoneum, where it is not seen.

  8. 8 Cage insertion and fixation

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Trial spacers set the height, then a large lordotic cage packed with graft is impacted into the distracted space; an ALIF cage is often fixed with integrated screws or a plate. Disc height and lordosis are restored at this moment, and the foramen opens indirectly.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Hammering through a lateral retractor transmits to the plexus; a late drop in electromyographic signal here is the retractor, not the cage. Over-distraction of a stiff segment is the moment of an endplate fracture in osteoporotic bone, which the surgeon sees on the image and which changes the fixation plan. The sympathetic chain runs along the anterolateral vertebral body and is injured by either approach: a warm, dry, pink left leg with a cold right one in recovery is a sympathectomy, benign, and worth explaining before someone diagnoses an arterial occlusion on the wrong side.

  9. 9 Closure, the posterior stage and the turn

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The rectus sheath is repaired or the flank muscles allowed to fall together, usually without a drain. If posterior percutaneous screws follow, the patient is turned prone on a frame and the screws placed through stab incisions under fluoroscopy, with no muscle stripping.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Infiltration of the wound is most of the pain plan for the anterior or lateral stage and the moment to ask for it. The turn to prone for the posterior stage is a full second positioning with all the prone checks, on a patient who has been lateral or extended for two hours and whose fluid balance you now reassess; a psoas or retroperitoneal haematoma declares itself as a falling pressure after the turn, when the retractor is gone and the space can fill. Percutaneous screws need the same stimulated screw test and the same unrelaxed patient as the open version. A patient who had a vascular repair stays supine and goes to a high-dependency bed; the posterior stage waits.

  10. 10 Recovery, the leg check and the ileus

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants the neurology confirmed, the abdomen soft, and the patient mobilised early.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Check both femoral pulses and foot perfusion after an ALIF and compare the sides; a cold, pulseless left leg is an arterial injury or thrombosis and goes back to theatre, while a warm, dry left leg with a cold right one is the sympathectomy. After an LLIF, test hip flexion and knee extension on the operative side against the baseline and tell the patient and the ward that a weak hip and a numb or burning thigh are expected and usually transient, while a dense quadriceps palsy is a femoral nerve injury the surgeon needs to know about today. Ileus is the common complication of the anterior approach: sips, early walking, a minimal opioid load and an antiemetic charted. A rising abdominal girth with a falling haemoglobin is a retroperitoneal haematoma and a surgical conversation.

Pain plan

The mechanism is visceral, wall-and-retroperitoneum, with an untouched posterior column, so the plan is a wall block and an oral regimen, not a neuraxial opioid. PROSPECT’s complex spine guideline is written for instrumented thoracolumbar surgery and its backbone transfers (paracetamol, an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor, intra-operative ketamine for the opioid-tolerant, opioids as rescue); its regional advice, the surgeon-placed epidural, does not, because the surgeon is not in the epidural space. The defensible default for an ALIF is bilateral transversus abdominis plane blocks or a surgeon-infiltrated rectus sheath and wound with long-acting local anaesthetic, dexamethasone at induction, and the oral regimen from recovery. For an LLIF the author’s practice is a quadratus lumborum block on the operative side, placed after induction with the patient already lateral, because it reaches the flank wall and some of the lumbar plexus territory that wound infiltration does not; the evidence for that choice is the fascial plane block literature in abdominal surgery rather than anything spine-specific, and it is author’s judgement. Ketamine is reserved for the opioid-tolerant.

A catheter has no routine place. The wall pain is a single-night problem, the thigh dysaesthesia after an LLIF is neuropathic and responds to time rather than to local anaesthetic, and the psoas ache responds to walking. When a posterior instrumented stage is added under the same anaesthetic, the posterior card’s plan applies, with the wall block added for the anterior stage rather than substituted.

Escalation triggers are vascular and visceral before they are analgesic. Hypotension, a distending abdomen, a falling haemoglobin or a pulseless leg are surgical calls. Anterior thigh pain with a weak quadriceps after an LLIF is a femoral nerve injury and the surgeon decides whether to image the psoas for a haematoma. Abdominal distension with vomiting is ileus, and the opioid is reduced rather than increased. A patient still needing regular opioid at a week after an isolated anterior or lateral fusion has something else going on.

Pitfalls and variants

  • ALIF at L5-S1 versus L4-5. The L5-S1 disc sits below the bifurcation and the exposure is between the iliac vessels; L4-5 needs the left common iliac vein mobilised and is the level at which the venous injury happens. The hypogastric plexus and retrograde ejaculation belong to L5-S1, and the transperitoneal approach carries more of it.
  • The access surgeon. Most spine surgeons use one for the anterior approach, and vascular control at the moment of a tear is the whole reason. Know whether they are staying for the disc work or leaving after the exposure.
  • Transpsoas versus anterior-to-psoas. The oblique approach passes in front of the psoas and spares most of the plexus at the cost of a longer corridor past the vessels; the thigh symptoms fall and the vascular risk rises. Both need the same lateral position and the same unrelaxed patient if electromyography is used.
  • The lumbar plexus at L4-5. The plexus is furthest forward in the psoas at this level and the corridor narrowest; many surgeons will not do a transpsoas L4-5 in a patient with an anteriorly placed plexus on the imaging. Expect the highest thigh symptom and hip flexor rates from this level.
  • Neuromuscular block and electromyography. A relaxed patient makes the directional probe useless and the surgeon falsely confident; an intubating dose is reversed before the psoas is reached and the surgeon is told.
  • The lateral position over hours. Dependent brachial plexus, peroneal nerve at the fibular head, the ear, the eye, and the hip at the break; a multilevel lateral construct is two or three hours of it.
  • Sympathectomy. A warm left leg after either approach, from the chain on the anterolateral vertebral body; benign, often permanent, and misread as an occlusion of the other leg.
  • Vascular injury on the table. Litres in minutes from the iliac vein; the surgeon packs and calls, you transfuse and lower the head; a lateral retractor blade pulling off a segmental artery is the lateral version. The slower presentation is a pseudoaneurysm or an iliac vein thrombosis days later.
  • Anterior column realignment and hyperlordotic cages. The anterior longitudinal ligament is divided to open the disc space to 20-30 degrees for deformity correction; the vessels are directly in front of the release, and the case belongs to the deformity card in its blood and positioning risk.
  • Obesity. Harder to sweep, harder to tape laterally, more thigh symptoms after an LLIF in the 545-patient cohort, and a retractor that has to be longer and held harder.

Key sources

The analgesia evidence for the anterior and lateral approaches is almost entirely borrowed: PROSPECT’s complex spine guideline for the oral and ketamine backbone, and the abdominal fascial plane block literature for the wall block, neither of which studied these operations. The complication rates are better documented: the ALIF systematic review gives the approach-specific picture of retrograde ejaculation and vascular injury, the 545-patient lateral cohort and the NICE safety summary give the thigh symptom, hip flexor and femoral nerve rates and their time course, and the AO technique reference gives the vessel-by-level anatomy. The block choice and the catheter advice are author’s judgement.

  1. Feeley A, Feeley I, Clesham K, Butler J. Is there a variance in complication types associated with ALIF approaches? A systematic review. Acta Neurochir 2021;163:2991-3004
    31 studies, 5,728 ALIF patients: retrograde ejaculation significantly more common after the transperitoneal approach and at L5-S1; vascular injury not different by approach; peritoneal breach in 2-16% of retroperitoneal cases; ileus about 3%; laparoscopic approaches shorter stay
  2. Hulliel AF, Saleh D, Alkadri AZ, et al. Neurological complications after lateral lumbar interbody fusion: incidence, patterns, and risk factors in a 545-patient cohort. Neurol Int 2026;18:178
    545 lateral interbody fusions: any neurological complication 30.6%, acute thigh paraesthesia 14.4%, transient motor weakness 13.2%, hip flexion weakness 2.1%, psoas haematoma 1.4%, femoral palsy 1.3%; obesity and multilevel surgery raised the odds
  3. NICE. Lateral interbody fusion in the lumbar spine for low back pain. Interventional procedures guidance, section 5: safety
    Pooled safety evidence: thigh symptoms in about a quarter and hip flexion weakness in about a fifth of patients across the literature, motor deficits around 3%; neurological events 9% after lateral versus 5% after anterior fusion in a 34-study review, 43% resolved within three months; one aortic laceration in 900 cases; bowel injury rare
  4. Epstein NE. Review of risks and complications of extreme lateral interbody fusion (XLIF). Surg Neurol Int 2019;10:237
    Neural injury after XLIF reported at up to 30-40%, higher than after TLIF, PLIF or ALIF, involving the lumbar plexus and the ilioinguinal, iliohypogastric, genitofemoral, lateral femoral cutaneous and subcostal nerves; major vascular and bowel injury listed
  5. AO Surgery Reference. Retroperitoneal approach for ALIF
    Left-sided 6-7 cm horizontal incision, rectus sheath opened, peritoneum swept by hand, ureter identified; at L5-S1 the disc lies below the bifurcation and the median sacral vessels are divided; at L4-5 the great vessels are retracted to the right and the iliolumbar vein ligated; monopolar diathermy on the anterior longitudinal ligament injures the hypogastric plexus and causes retrograde ejaculation
  6. Waelkens P, Alsabbagh E, Sauter A, Joshi GP, Beloeil H, on behalf of the PROSPECT Working Group of ESRA. Pain management after complex spine surgery: a systematic review and procedure-specific postoperative pain management recommendations. Eur J Anaesthesiol 2021;38:985-994
    Written for instrumented thoracolumbar surgery: paracetamol, NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor, intra-operative low-dose ketamine and opioids as rescue; applies to the combined anterior-posterior case rather than to the anterior approach alone

Spine › Spine

54 ACDF and cervical disc arthroplasty

Anterior cervical discectomy and fusion with cage and plate or stand-alone cage, anterior cervical corpectomy, and cervical disc arthroplasty, one to three levels

3Moderate

Dominant mechanism: Bone. Endplates burred to bleeding bone, a cage or disc wedged into a distracted space and a plate screwed to two vertebral bodies, through an approach that splits no muscle; the pain is a sore front of the neck, a sore throat and painful swallowing from retraction of the oesophagus and larynx, with the pre-operative arm pain gone

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: low.

Block
No regional block; surgeon infiltration of the skin and platysma, regular paracetamol and an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor where the surgeon permits it, and a few doses of oral opioid on the first day
Catheter: no There is nothing for a catheter to cover: the wound is small, the mechanism is bone and retraction, and the pain is gone before most catheters would be removed
Alternatives: Superficial cervical plexus block on the side of the approach for a longer or multilevel case, an adjunct of small and unproven value; Intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg at induction, which some surgeons use as a local retropharyngeal dose instead, for swelling and dysphagia rather than pain; Intra-operative ketamine for the opioid-tolerant patient
Position
Supine with the head on a ring or in gentle traction, the neck in slight extension on a roll between the shoulder blades, the shoulders taped down towards the feet for the lateral image of the lower levels, arms by the sides; the surgeon stands on the patient's right or left and the fluoroscopy arm comes in from the opposite side
Tourniquet
No
Cement
No
Blood loss
50-150 mL for a one- or two-level discectomy; 200-500 mL for a corpectomy, where the vertebral body is removed and the epidural veins behind it bleed
Duration
60-120 min for a single-level ACDF or arthroplasty; 120-180 min for two or three levels; 180-240 min for a corpectomy with a strut and plate
Length of stay
One night for most; selected single-level cases go home the same day; a corpectomy or a multilevel case in a myelopathic patient stays two or three nights. Day case: selected
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV within 60 min of incision (3 g over 120 kg); an implant near the oesophagus
Tranexamic acid
Not routinely needed for a discectomy; tranexamic acid 1 g IV before incision is reasonable for a corpectomy or a multilevel case
VTE
Mechanical only during the stay; chemoprophylaxis is withheld because a wound haematoma in this neck is an airway, and the patient is walking within hours
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV at induction and ondansetron 4 mg IV before emergence; retching strains a fresh anterior neck wound and a plate
Tell the patient
The arm pain should be better straight away; what you will have is a sore throat, a stiff and sore front of the neck, and some difficulty swallowing for a week or two, which is from the surgeon holding the gullet aside and settles.
The trap
A swollen anterior neck in the first 24 h is the airway closing from the outside: by the time the patient is stridulous the larynx is displaced and oedematous, intubation may fail, and the treatment is to open the wound at the bedside and release the haematoma before the anaesthetic, not after

What the surgeon is doing and why

A cervical disc prolapse or a spondylotic bar compresses a root in the foramen (radiculopathy: arm pain, numbness, weakness in one root’s territory) or the cord in the canal (myelopathy: clumsy hands, a stiff-legged gait, hyperreflexia, and a cord that is being slowly strangled). The posterior approach can decompress a foramen but cannot reach a central disc or an osteophyte in front of the cord without moving the cord, so the surgeon goes in from the front, through a plane that contains no muscle to split and no nerve to cut, and removes the disc and the bar under direct vision. Having emptied the disc space, they have two choices. Fill it with a cage and bone and plate it so the level fuses (ACDF), which trades motion at that level for a rigid segment and, over years, more wear at the levels above and below. Or fill it with an articulating implant (cervical disc arthroplasty) that keeps the level moving, which in the pooled randomised trials at four years or more gives fewer index-level reoperations and probably less adjacent segment degeneration, at the cost of needing good bone, no facet arthritis and no instability. The approach, the discectomy and the first week are the same operation whichever is chosen; what differs is the implant and the decades afterwards.

The approach is the Smith-Robinson. A transverse skin crease incision on one side of the neck (surgeons vary on the side; the recurrent laryngeal nerve is more predictable on the left and most right-handed surgeons prefer the right), platysma divided, and then a bloodless plane developed between the carotid sheath laterally and the trachea, oesophagus and strap muscles medially, down to the prevertebral fascia and the front of the spine. Nothing is cut on the way in; the longus colli is elevated off the vertebral bodies on each side and the self-retaining retractor blades are hooked under it, so that the oesophagus and trachea are held to one side and the carotid to the other for the duration. That retraction is the mechanism of almost every complication on the card: the recurrent laryngeal nerve pinned between the retractor and the tracheal tube cuff, the oesophagus stretched and bruised, the pharynx and larynx oedematous, and the sympathetic chain on the longus colli bruised into a Horner’s syndrome.

With the disc exposed and the level confirmed on a lateral image, the annulus is incised and the disc removed back to the posterior longitudinal ligament with curettes and rongeurs, the uncovertebral osteophytes and the posterior bar drilled away under the microscope, the posterior longitudinal ligament opened or left, and the foramina undercut until the root and the dura are free. Distraction pins in the vertebral bodies above and below open the space; the endplates are burred to bleeding bone for a fusion (and left intact for an arthroplasty, which needs a flat seat and a preserved rim); a trial is sized, and the cage, filled with local bone or a substitute, or the arthroplasty, is impacted in. An anterior plate screwed to the two vertebral bodies holds a fusion; a stand-alone cage with integral screws is a lower-profile alternative that some surgeons use to reduce dysphagia. A corpectomy removes the whole vertebral body between two discs for a multilevel myelopathy or a tumour, replaces it with a strut or an expandable cage, and plates across; it is a longer, bloodier operation with the epidural veins behind the body in play.

The pain logic is bone in a muscle-free approach. The endplates have been burred, the uncovertebral joints drilled, two vertebral bodies screwed and a space distracted and wedged, so there is a deep, central, sore neck for two or three days that an NSAID treats. No muscle has been stripped or split, which is why the trajectory falls faster than any posterior spine card. What the patient complains of instead is the retraction: a sore throat, painful and awkward swallowing, a hoarse voice and a stiff front of the neck, which are oedema and bruising of the pharynx, oesophagus and larynx rather than nociception from the operation, which peak at a day or two and which, in a minority, outlast the neck pain by months. The pre-operative arm pain is usually gone in recovery, and a myelopathic patient’s symptoms stop progressing but do not reverse. The pain scale places the ACDF at 3 alongside the ankle fracture and the anatomic shoulder, which is right for the first two days and generous after that.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 The neck, the airway and the cord before anything is given

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon has decided the approach from the imaging and wants the pre-operative neurology written down, because the operation is on the cord’s front door and a deficit afterwards has to be timed.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The airway assessment on this card has two extra questions. First, whether the cord is at risk from laryngoscopy: a myelopathic patient with a tight canal, an unstable segment or a rheumatoid neck can be injured by extension, and the answer is a videolaryngoscope with the neck held neutral, or an awake fibreoptic intubation when the surgeon and the imaging say the canal has no room, with the reasoning in the posterior cervical card. Second, whether the airway itself is abnormal: a large anterior osteophyte, a previous anterior fusion, a retropharyngeal mass or a radiated neck all distort the larynx. Document the neurology: grip and intrinsic hand function, the gait, the reflexes, the dermatome of the radiculopathy, and whether the patient already has a hoarse voice or a swallowing problem. A previous anterior approach on the other side means the contralateral cord may already be silent, and the surgeon has it checked first; a bilateral palsy is an emergency airway.

  2. 2 Induction, the tube and the cuff

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon needs a tracheal tube that will tolerate being pushed sideways by a retractor for two hours, a patient who will not move or cough, and a table position that gives a lateral image of the lowest level.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A standard or reinforced tracheal tube, taped on the side away from the surgeon, with the cuff pressure measured after intubation and again after the retractor goes in, because the retractor compresses the cuff against the larynx and the pressure rises. Deflating and reinflating the cuff to the lowest sealing pressure after the retractor is placed is a widely used manoeuvre aimed at the recurrent laryngeal nerve; the evidence is a randomised trial in which it did not reduce vocal cord immobility and an observational study in which it did, so it costs nothing and proves little. Keep it under 20-25 mmHg either way. Relaxant is at your discretion; if the surgeon runs motor evoked potentials for a myelopathic cord, the anaesthetic is propofol-based and unrelaxed after intubation. An oesophageal temperature probe or a nasogastric tube sits exactly where the surgeon is about to retract and is left out unless the surgeon wants one to palpate the oesophagus.

  3. 3 Positioning, traction and the shoulder tape

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Slight extension on a roll opens the anterior disc spaces and brings the lower cervical spine forward; the shoulders are taped down so that C6-7 and C7-T1 are visible on the lateral image; some surgeons apply a few kilograms of halter or tong traction to open the disc space.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Extension is the step that compromises a myelopathic cord; set it with the surgeon, not for them, and less is more in a tight canal. The shoulder tape pulls on the brachial plexus, and a tape that has been applied too hard is the mechanism of the post-operative shoulder and arm dysaesthesia that gets blamed on the surgery; check that the arms are tucked with the elbows padded and the tape is on the shoulders, not the arms. Eyes taped and padded, because the surgeon and the microscope work beside the face. Confirm the tube is still at the right depth after the extension.

  4. 4 Incision and the approach to the prevertebral space

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Platysma divided, then blunt dissection between the carotid sheath and the visceral column to the front of the spine; the omohyoid is retracted or divided; the superior and inferior thyroid vessels are the obstacles above and below.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Cefazolin finished before the knife. The carotid sheath is being retracted laterally: a carotid sinus reflex produces bradycardia and hypotension when the surgeon’s retractor sits on the bifurcation, and the first episode is usually at this step. Tell the surgeon; they will move the blade. A patient with carotid disease has a sheath that is better not leaned on, which the surgeon knows from the imaging. Bleeding from the thyroid vessels is the first blood loss and is small.

  5. 5 Retractor placement and the hours of retraction

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The longus colli is elevated off the vertebral bodies and the self-retaining retractor is seated under it, holding the oesophagus and trachea medially and the carotid laterally, where it stays until closure.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is the moment the cuff pressure rises and the manoeuvre, if used, is done. The oesophagus is now stretched over the retractor blade: this is the dysphagia mechanism, and the longer the retraction the worse it is. The recurrent laryngeal nerve runs in the tracheo-oesophageal groove on the surgeon’s medial side and is injured by stretch or pressure between the blade and the cuff, at about 2% irrespective of the side of approach; a hoarse voice tomorrow is that, and a bilateral palsy after a two-sided history is the airway emergency. The sympathetic chain lies on the longus colli; a retractor placed too laterally bruises it, and a Horner’s syndrome in recovery is the sign. Movement, coughing or straining with the retractor in place drives the blade into the oesophagus; this is an anaesthetic for a still patient.

  6. 6 Discectomy and decompression under the microscope

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The disc is removed back to the posterior longitudinal ligament, the uncovertebral and posterior osteophytes are drilled under the microscope, the ligament is opened and the cord and roots decompressed.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The burr is a millimetre from the cord and the dura; this is the step for a motionless patient and a steady pressure, and for the neuromonitoring team, if present, to be watching. Epidural venous bleeding from behind the ligament is controlled with haemostatic agents and patience; a surgeon asking for a lower pressure here is asking for lower venous pressure, which a slight head-up tilt gives. A durotomy in front of the cord is uncommon and hard to repair, and its consequence is a cerebrospinal fluid collection in the neck or a fistula to the pharynx; a smooth emergence and a line on the record follow. The vertebral artery runs in the foramen transversarium lateral to the uncovertebral joint, and a burr that drifts laterally is the catastrophe: sudden arterial bleeding in the depth of the wound, packing, an angiogram afterwards.

  7. 7 Distraction, endplate preparation and implant insertion

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Pins in the bodies above and below distract the space; the endplates are burred to bleeding bone for a fusion, or kept intact and squared for an arthroplasty; the trial is sized under the image; the cage or the disc is impacted in; and for a fusion a plate is screwed to the bodies, or a stand-alone cage with integral screws is used.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The distraction and the impaction are the bone mechanism, and the impaction is a hammer on a tube that reaches the cord through the implant; the neuromonitoring team sees artefact and then, if something has gone wrong, a loss. The plate’s screws go into the bodies in front of the cord under the lateral image; a screw that is too long is a cord injury and the image is checked before anything is tightened. An arthroplasty needs the endplates left intact and the implant seated exactly, which means more fluoroscopy and a longer step. Some surgeons place a dose of steroid in the retropharyngeal space before closure for swelling and dysphagia; the umbrella review grades the evidence for that and for intravenous steroid as low confidence, and it is their call.

  8. 8 Haemostasis, drain and closure

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The retractor comes out, the longus colli falls back, haemostasis of the prevertebral space is checked, a drain is placed by most surgeons for a multilevel case or a corpectomy and by some for everything, and platysma and skin are closed.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The retractor coming out is the moment the oesophagus and the cuff are released; recheck the cuff pressure. A smooth emergence without coughing or straining matters more here than almost anywhere: a cough raises venous pressure in a prevertebral space that has just been closed, and the haematoma that follows has nowhere to go but into the airway. Deep extubation is not the answer in a neck that may swell; a tube tolerated with remifentanil or a lidocaine-laden cuff and removed on command, with the patient sitting up, is. Look at the neck before and after extubation and compare it with how it looked at the start; a neck that is already full is an early haematoma and a reason to keep the tube in.

  9. 9 Recovery and the first 24 hours: the neck, the voice and the swallow

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants the neurology confirmed, the neck soft, the drain output low, the patient sitting up and swallowing, and an early radiograph of the implant.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The airway complication of this operation is a retropharyngeal haematoma, which closed the airway in 1.15% of 785 fusions in the retrospective series (literature range 0.2-1.9%), with two thirds presenting within 24 h and the remainder at about three days. Its early signs are a full or tense neck, difficulty swallowing saliva, a change in voice, anxiety and a need to sit forward; stridor and desaturation are late. The response is in the trap line: sit the patient up, call the surgeon, open the skin and platysma at the bedside to let the haematoma out, and only then secure the airway, with a videolaryngoscope and a surgical airway ready, because the larynx will be displaced and oedematous and the intubation may fail. Observation on a ward that can see the neck, with the clip remover at the bedside, is the standard for the first night. Check the arms and legs against the baseline. A hoarse voice is a recurrent laryngeal palsy and a swallow that is painful but safe is retraction; a swallow that is unsafe needs a speech pathologist before the first meal. Day-case discharge of a single-level ACDF or arthroplasty is practised in selected units with a long observation period and a patient who lives near the hospital; it rests on the timing data above, and the first night at home is the one the haematoma series is about.

Pain plan

The mechanism is bone work through a muscle-free approach plus retraction oedema, so the plan is short and oral: regular paracetamol and an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor started in recovery, a few doses of oral opioid on the evening of surgery and the first day, and intravenous dexamethasone at induction, which treats the nausea and does something for the throat. No regional block earns its place. PROSPECT’s complex spine guideline was not written for the anterior cervical spine, but its oral backbone (paracetamol, NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor, opioid as rescue) transfers without difficulty. Many spine surgeons forbid NSAIDs after a fusion for fear of non-union, and some allow a short course or a COX-2 inhibitor; the question is settled before the day and the alternative, if the answer is no, is paracetamol, a short opioid course and the knowledge that the neck pain is over by day 3 whatever is given. An arthroplasty has no fusion to protect and the NSAID objection does not apply.

The catheter question does not arise. The infiltration of skin and platysma by the surgeon is the only local anaesthetic in the operation, and a superficial cervical plexus block on the side of the approach is an adjunct of small value that is reasonable for a multilevel case and unproven for any. Ketamine belongs to the opioid-tolerant patient, who is less common on this list than on the lumbar cards but exists.

The thing the patient complains about is not the pain. The sore throat, the dysphagia and the hoarse voice are retraction effects, worst on day 1 and 2, present in most patients in the first fortnight and in about one in eight at a year in the umbrella review’s pooled figures; they respond to time, soft food, sitting up and a speech pathologist for the ones who aspirate, and not to opioid. The patient who has been told this beforehand copes; the patient who has not reports the operation as a failure.

Escalation triggers are the neck and the cord before they are the pain. Neck swelling, a voice change, drooling or distress in the first 24 h is the haematoma. New arm or leg weakness is a cord or root injury, a screw or a graft in the wrong place, and the surgeon is called before any opioid is given. Pain that rises after day 2, with fever, a wound that leaks or a swallow that worsens, is an oesophageal injury or an infection until proven otherwise.

Pitfalls and variants

  • ACDF versus arthroplasty. Same approach, same retraction, same first week; the arthroplasty keeps the endplates and needs more fluoroscopy, has no non-union to protect from NSAIDs, and in the randomised trials at four years or more has fewer reoperations at the index level. The anaesthetic does not change.
  • One level versus three, and the corpectomy. Retraction time is the variable: a three-level fusion or a corpectomy means two or three hours of oesophageal retraction, more dysphagia, more bleeding from the epidural veins behind a removed body, a drain, and the highest haematoma and airway risk on the card. Many surgeons keep a multilevel or corpectomy patient intubated overnight or observe them in a high-dependency bed; the decision is made before the drapes come off, not at the first stridor.
  • The myelopathic cord. Neutral neck for intubation, modest extension on the table, a mean pressure kept at the patient’s baseline throughout because a compressed cord has no autoregulatory reserve, and neuromonitoring in many hands. A deficit after the operation in a myelopathic patient is the one that was coming anyway or the one the position caused, and the timing of the baseline examination is what tells them apart.
  • Horner’s syndrome. A retractor on the sympathetic chain; a ptosis and a small pupil in recovery, usually transient, and worth telling the patient about before they find it in a mirror.
  • Oesophageal perforation. Rare, from the retractor, the burr or a screw that backs out years later; presents as fever, neck pain, crepitus and a leaking wound, early or very late. Nothing to eat until the surgeon is happy.
  • Vertebral artery injury. A burr lateral to the uncovertebral joint; torrential bleeding in the depth of the wound, packing, an angiogram, and a stroke risk afterwards.
  • Rheumatoid disease and ankylosing spondylitis. Atlantoaxial instability in the first, a brittle and fixed neck in the second; both change the intubation, the extension and the shoulder tape, and the orthopaedic patient chapter carries the detail.
  • Obstructive sleep apnoea and obesity. A thick neck in which swelling is harder to see and an airway that is harder to secure in a hurry; a longer observation and a lower threshold for the high-dependency bed.
  • Day-case discharge. Reasonable for a single-level case in a slim, fit patient with a short retraction time and a surgeon who places a drain or does not; the haematoma timing data say the first night is the risk, and the discharge decision has to say how that night is covered.

Key sources

There is no procedure-specific pain guideline for the anterior cervical spine, and the card’s oral regimen is PROSPECT’s lumbar backbone transferred. The haematoma data come from a single retrospective series and the literature range it quotes, and the cuff manoeuvre rests on one negative randomised trial and one positive observational study cited in a trial protocol whose own results the author has not seen. The dysphagia figures come from an umbrella review that rates almost all of its component reviews as critically low confidence, and the card presents them as orders of magnitude. The arthroplasty-versus-fusion comparison is cited to establish that the early course is the same operation, not for its long-term claims, several of which did not survive the authors’ own sensitivity analysis.

  1. Song KJ, Choi BW, Lee DH, Lim DJ, Oh SY, Kim SS. Acute airway obstruction due to postoperative retropharyngeal hematoma after anterior cervical fusion: a retrospective analysis. J Orthop Surg Res 2017;12:19
    785 anterior cervical fusions: airway obstruction from haematoma in 1.15%, literature range 0.2-1.9%; two thirds presented within 24 h and the rest at a median of 72 h; four needed evacuation, one a cricothyrotomy after failed intubation for laryngeal oedema; no pre-operative risk factor identified
  2. Muthu S, Viswanathan VK, Subramanian V, et al. How common is dysphagia after anterior cervical spine surgery, what drives it, and can it be prevented? An umbrella review of systematic evidence. Global Spine J 2026
    32 systematic reviews: early dysphagia in up to 71%, persistent at 12 months in 12-14%; female sex, multilevel surgery, C3-4, anterior plating and rhBMP-2 raise the risk; zero-profile implants, cuff pressure control and perioperative steroids linked to less early dysphagia in low-confidence reviews; no preventive strategy recommendable as standard
  3. Arts MP, Rettig TCD, de Vries J, Wolfs JFC, in't Veld BA. Maintaining endotracheal tube cuff pressure at 20 mm Hg to prevent dysphagia after anterior cervical spine surgery; protocol of a double-blind randomised controlled trial. BMC Musculoskelet Disord 2013;14:280
    Protocol only; cites a recurrent laryngeal nerve injury rate of about 2% after ACDF irrespective of side, a randomised trial in which cuff pressure adjustment did not reduce vocal cord immobility, and an observational study in which it did; cuff pressure rises with retractor placement
  4. Zhang Y, Ju J, Wu J. Comparison of cervical disc arthroplasty versus anterior cervical discectomy and fusion for the treatment of single-segment cervical degenerative disc disease with a minimum of 4-year follow-up: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. J Orthop Surg Res 2025;20:758
    17 randomised trials, 3,303 patients: arthroplasty had fewer index-level reoperations (OR 0.39) and less adjacent segment degeneration (OR 0.56, not robust to sensitivity analysis); the approach, the discectomy and the early course are the same operation
  5. Waelkens P, Alsabbagh E, Sauter A, Joshi GP, Beloeil H, on behalf of the PROSPECT Working Group of ESRA. Pain management after complex spine surgery: a systematic review and procedure-specific postoperative pain management recommendations. Eur J Anaesthesiol 2021;38:985-994
    Written for instrumented thoracolumbar surgery, not the anterior cervical spine; cited for the oral backbone (paracetamol, NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor, opioid as rescue) that transfers

Spine › Spine

55 Posterior cervical decompression and fusion

Cervical laminectomy, laminoplasty, posterior foraminotomy, and posterior instrumented fusion with lateral mass or pedicle screws, including occipitocervical and atlantoaxial fixation

4Severe

Dominant mechanism: Muscle. The posterior neck muscles stripped off the spinous processes and laminae on both sides over three to six levels and held under retractors for hours, with laminae removed or hinged, lateral masses drilled and screwed, and facets decorticated; the nuchal muscles then have to hold the head up on day 1

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: moderate.

Block
No regional block; intra-operative low-dose ketamine infusion, regular paracetamol and an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor where the surgeon permits it, surgeon infiltration of the wound edges, and oral opioid on days 0-3
Catheter: rarely A surgeon-placed epidural or wound catheter is PROSPECT's lumbar recommendation and has no established place in the cervical spine; the author's default is ketamine and the oral regimen, with a wound catheter only for the opioid-tolerant multilevel patient and only in units that have used one here before
Alternatives: Bilateral cervical erector spinae plane or interfascial plane blocks by the surgeon under direct vision before closure, an adjunct with case series behind it rather than trials; Intravenous lidocaine infusion for the opioid-tolerant where ketamine is contraindicated; Intrathecal morphine is not used here: the surgeon is not in the dura and a lumbar injection for a cervical wound is not the author's practice
Position
Prone with the head fixed in a three-pin skull clamp attached to the table, neck in neutral or slight flexion to open the interlaminar spaces, reverse Trendelenburg to lower venous pressure in the neck, arms tucked at the sides and the shoulders taped down for the lateral image; the face is free of all pressure and the eyes can be inspected
Tourniquet
No
Cement
No
Blood loss
200-500 mL for a laminoplasty or a two- or three-level fusion; 500-1000 mL for a long construct, an occipitocervical fusion or a revision, from the muscle and the epidural venous plexus
Duration
120-180 min for a laminoplasty or a short fusion; 180-300 min for a long construct or occipitocervical fixation; a single-level foraminotomy 60-90 min
Length of stay
2-4 nights; a posterior foraminotomy one night or a selected day case. Day case: no
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV within 60 min of incision (3 g over 120 kg), repeated at 4 h; a long case with implants in a wound that sits in a sweaty crease and has the highest infection rate of the elective spine
Tranexamic acid
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV before incision, repeated at 3 h or infused, for any fusion; not needed for a foraminotomy
VTE
Mechanical from induction; chemoprophylaxis from day 1 or 2 once the surgeon is content the epidural space is dry, because a haematoma under a cervical laminectomy is quadriplegia
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV at induction and ondansetron 4 mg IV before emergence; vomiting after a cervical fusion loads the construct and the wound
Tell the patient
The back of the neck will be very sore and stiff for the first few days and the muscles will feel too weak to hold your head up; that improves day by day, and the hands and walking improve slowly over months if they improve at all.
The trap
The anaesthetic for this operation is decided by the cord, not the airway: in a myelopathic or unstable neck the intubation, the turn and the pinning are three separate opportunities to extend or move a spine that has no room, and each needs the neck held where the surgeon wants it and a check that the patient can still move their feet before the drapes go on

What the surgeon is doing and why

The posterior approach to the cervical spine is chosen when the compression is behind the cord or at many levels, when the canal is congenitally narrow, when the ligament behind the vertebral bodies has ossified over several segments (OPLL), or when the spine is unstable and needs screws. A laminectomy takes the laminae and the ligamentum flavum off the back of the canal so the cord can drift backwards away from whatever is in front of it; a laminoplasty hinges the laminae open on one side like a door and props them with small plates, which enlarges the canal while keeping a roof on it and some of the muscle attachments. A posterior foraminotomy drills a keyhole through the facet to free one root and is the small operation on this card. An instrumented fusion puts screws into the lateral masses (C3-C6), the pedicles (C7 and the upper thoracic spine) or C2, connects them with rods, decorticates the facets and lays graft, and is added to a laminectomy whenever enough bone has been removed to make the spine unstable, or when it was unstable already. At the top, atlantoaxial and occipitocervical fusions fix C1 to C2 or the skull to the upper cervical spine for rheumatoid instability, odontoid fractures and tumours.

The sequence of a laminectomy and fusion is the card’s spine. A midline incision from the occiput to the upper thoracic spine, bilateral subperiosteal stripping of the posterior neck muscles off the spinous processes, laminae and lateral masses, and self-retaining retractors that stay in for hours. Lateral mass screws placed by landmarks and fluoroscopy, each angled up and out away from the vertebral artery in front and the exiting root below. Laminectomy with a high-speed burr and punches, with the dura directly beneath. Decortication of the facets and the laminar remnants, rods contoured and locked, graft laid down, a drain and a layered closure. The laminoplasty replaces the screws and the laminectomy with a hinge and plates and leaves one side of the muscle more intact. The surgeon’s first and last concern is the cord: a myelopathic cord has no room and no reserve, and every step from the intubation onwards can injure it.

The pain logic. The dominant mechanism is muscle, and in the neck it is worse than in the lumbar spine for a reason the lumbar cards do not have: the stripped muscles are the ones that have to hold the head up when the patient sits on day 1. Bilateral stripping of the semispinalis, splenius and multifidus over four to six levels, hours under a retractor, and then the load of a head on a neck that cannot brace; the ache is deep, position-dependent, worse sitting than lying and relieved by a collar that many surgeons do not want worn. Under it is bone (lateral masses drilled, facets decorticated, laminae burred), nerve (a decompressed cord and roots, and the C5 root that may be tethered as the cord shifts back), and retension where a kyphotic neck has been pulled into lordosis across the construct. The nuchal muscle pain is the reason this card’s trajectory stays above the ACDF’s at every point and why it is a 4 while the anterior operation on the same disease is a 3. In the 179-procedure cohort the spinal fusions occupy three of the top six places for worst pain on day 1; the cervical fusion is not separated out, but its mechanism puts it among them. Compare the ACDF, where no muscle is touched and the complaint is the swallow.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 The cord, the airway and the plan for three dangerous moments

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon has a myelopathic, stenotic or unstable neck on the imaging and wants it to arrive on the table without having been extended, flexed or rotated beyond what the canal will tolerate; the baseline neurology is written down because any change afterwards will be attributed to the operation.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Examine and record the neurology yourself: hand function, gait, reflexes, the dermatomal level, and whether the deltoid (C5) is already weak. Then decide the airway from the imaging rather than from the Mallampati score. A stable neck with mild myelopathy is intubated asleep with a videolaryngoscope and manual in-line stabilisation, which limits extension, and the randomised evidence in collared patients shows videolaryngoscopy beats flexible bronchoscopy on first-attempt success and time with the same complication rate. An unstable neck (atlantoaxial subluxation, a fracture, a rheumatoid pannus) or a cord with no room on the sagittal image is intubated awake with a flexible scope or a videolaryngoscope under topical anaesthesia and sedation, so the neurology can be checked after the tube is in and again after the turn. The evidence that awake intubation protects the cord is physiological and observational, and the decision is a judgement made with the surgeon, who may want the neck in a collar until the pins are on. Ask what traction or reduction the surgeon intends, because a halo or tongs change the airway plan entirely. Rheumatoid patients bring a stiff jaw, a cricoarytenoid joint and an atlantoaxial subluxation to the same airway.

  2. 2 Induction, lines, neuromonitoring and the baseline before the turn

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The monitoring team wants baseline somatosensory and motor evoked potentials with the patient supine and the neck in a neutral position, so that a change after the turn or the pinning can be attributed to position and reversed.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A reinforced tube, secured on the side and padded where the face will rest, with a bite block if motor evoked potentials are planned. An arterial line for every fusion, because the cord’s perfusion pressure is the one variable you control and the mean pressure is kept at the patient’s baseline from now until the drapes come off; two cannulae; a urinary catheter. Propofol and remifentanil, no neuromuscular block after the intubating dose, and the baseline signals recorded before anyone moves the patient. In an awake intubation the neurology is checked with the tube in and the patient still awake; induction follows only when the feet still move.

  3. 3 The skull clamp and the turn

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The head is fixed in a three-pin clamp so the surgeon can set the neck’s position exactly and hold it motionless for hours, with the face free; the clamp is attached to the table after the patient is turned.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Pinning is a brief, intense stimulus that produces hypertension and tachycardia, which is bad for a cord with no reserve and a canal full of veins; a bolus of opioid or a deepening before the pins go in, and local anaesthetic at the pin sites, blunt it. The turn is a log roll onto the chest with the head held by the surgeon or the most experienced person in the room, the neck kept in the agreed position, and the tube held by you. Once prone, the surgeon sets flexion or neutral and the clamp is locked; then the checks: eyes free and visible, nose and chin clear, no pressure on the face at all, neck neutral or as agreed, shoulders below 90 degrees if the arms are up (they are usually tucked for a cervical case), elbows padded, abdomen free, breasts and genitals clear, knees padded. Reverse Trendelenburg lowers venous pressure in the neck and is the surgeon’s friend; the head above the heart raises the question of air embolism if a vein is opened, which is a real if rare event in the sitting position and a theoretical one here. The neuromonitoring team repeats the signals once the position is set: a loss after the turn is the position, and the position is changed before anything else.

  4. 4 Exposure: bilateral stripping of the nuchal muscles

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The posterior neck muscles are taken subperiosteally off the spinous processes, laminae and lateral masses from the midline outwards on both sides, over the levels to be decompressed and instrumented, and retractors hold them apart.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Antibiotic and tranexamic acid finished before the knife. This is the pain mechanism and the main bleeding; the muscle bleeds steadily and the surgeon controls it with cautery. The stimulus is sustained, and in an unrelaxed patient the response is a lighter plane rather than movement, which the monitoring team sees as a change in signals before you see it on the pressure. The ketamine infusion is running from now. The C2 spinous process carries the attachment of the semispinalis cervicis, which surgeons try to preserve or reattach because its loss is the axial neck pain that persists for months after a laminectomy that included C2.

  5. 5 Lateral mass or pedicle screw placement

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Screws go into the lateral masses from C3 to C6, into the pedicles at C7 and below, and into the pars or pedicle of C2 or the lateral masses of C1, each trajectory chosen to avoid the vertebral artery in front and the exiting root below and the facet above. Fluoroscopy or navigation confirms them.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The screw that goes wrong goes into the vertebral artery or the root, and the first is a sudden deep arterial bleed that the surgeon controls with the screw itself and packing, followed by an angiogram; the second is a radiculopathy in recovery. A C1-2 construct puts the vertebral artery at risk on both sides and the screws are placed with the artery’s course mapped on the pre-operative CT angiogram. Neuromonitoring is watched during the drilling, and a drop in signals in one arm is a root.

  6. 6 Laminectomy or laminoplasty: the decompression

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The laminae are thinned with a burr and lifted off the dura, or the laminae are cut through on one side and hinged on the other and propped open with plates; the ligamentum flavum is removed; the cord, which has been flattened for months, is seen to pulsate and drift backwards.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The burr is on the dura; this is the moment for a motionless patient and a steady mean pressure, with no rise to drive bleeding and no fall to starve a cord that has just been released. The epidural veins bleed as the flavum comes off and are controlled with haemostatic agents and venous pressure, not arterial. A durotomy here is in the cervical dura with the cord beneath; the repair is fiddly and the Valsalva is requested; a cerebrospinal fluid leak into the wound in the neck is a pseudomeningocele or a fistula. The backward drift of the cord is the mechanism of the C5 palsy: the C5 root, the shortest and most horizontal, is tethered as the cord moves and is stretched, which appears as a deltoid and biceps weakness between two days and six weeks after surgery, in about 5% after laminoplasty, 7% after decompression and fusion and 8% after laminectomy in the pooled data, with permanent weakness in about 1%. Nothing anaesthetic prevents it, and documenting the pre-operative deltoid is the one contribution.

  7. 7 Decortication, rod placement, graft and the correction

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The facets and laminar remnants are decorticated to bleeding bone, rods are contoured into lordosis and locked to the screws, and in a kyphotic neck the construct is used to pull the spine into alignment; graft is laid along the construct.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Decortication is the last bone bleeding. A correction across the construct is a change in the shape of a canal with a cord in it; the monitoring team checks the signals after the rods are locked, and a loss here is a call for a higher mean pressure, a haemoglobin, warmth and a surgeon who loosens the rod. An occipitocervical construct fixes the skull to the neck in a position that the patient will live in: a head fixed in flexion cannot see the horizon, and a head fixed in extension cannot swallow, and the surgeon will spend time on the lateral image at this point for exactly that reason.

  8. 8 Closure, drain, the release from the pins and the turn back

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A drain, a layered closure of a thick muscular wound, and the skull clamp released after the dressings are on.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Give the second antiemetic. The head comes out of the pins with the neck supported, and the turn back is a log roll with the head held; a collar goes on if the surgeon wants one before the patient wakes. Inspect the face and the eyes, and the pin sites, which bleed. Extubation is the fourth dangerous moment: a patient who has been prone for four hours with the head below the heart during any part of it, or who has had a long upper cervical or occipitocervical case, has a swollen tongue, pharynx and larynx, and a tube that comes out of an oedematous airway cannot always go back in. The honest test is a cuff leak and a look at the tongue, and the honest decision for a long upper cervical case is often a night in intensive care with the tube in. Extubate a patient who is awake and moves both feet and both hands to order; one who does not is a surgical conversation before they leave the table.

  9. 9 Recovery and the first night: the cord, the airway and the neck

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants the neurology confirmed and rechecked, the drain output watched, the wound dry, and the patient sitting up and walking on day 1 with or without a collar.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Neurology against the baseline in recovery and then at intervals overnight: a haematoma under a cervical laminectomy presents as rising neck pain and then arm and leg weakness over an hour or two, and the window for evacuation before a permanent cord injury is short. The deltoid is tested on both sides daily for the first week because the C5 palsy is a delayed presentation. The regular analgesia starts in recovery and the opioid is charted for the night and before the first sit-up, which is the moment the nuchal muscles are first loaded. A patient who cannot hold their head up on day 1 is not weak from the cord; they are sore from the muscle, and the distinction is the one the physiotherapist needs to hear.

Pain plan

The mechanism is bilateral stripping of the muscles that hold the head up, over a bone-and-nerve operation, so the plan is multimodal and systemic rather than regional, because there is no block that covers the posterior neck reliably without reaching the cord’s own territory. PROSPECT’s complex spine guideline was written for the thoracolumbar spine and its systemic recommendations transfer: paracetamol, an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor where the surgeon allows it after a fusion (a laminoplasty or a foraminotomy has no fusion to protect), an intra-operative low-dose ketamine infusion (grade A, and the one intervention that most changes the first two days in the author’s judgement), opioids as rescue and no gabapentinoids. Its regional recommendation, a surgeon-placed epidural catheter, has no established place in the cervical spine and the author does not use one here. Intrathecal morphine is not part of the plan because the surgeon is not in the dura and a lumbar injection for a cervical wound is an extrapolation the author is not willing to make.

The defensible default is ketamine at induction and by infusion to closure, surgeon infiltration of the wound edges and the pin sites with long-acting local anaesthetic, dexamethasone at induction, the oral regimen from recovery, and an oral opioid charted for the first three days with a dose timed before the first sit-up and before physiotherapy. Bilateral cervical erector spinae or interfascial plane blocks placed by the surgeon under direct vision before closure are an adjunct with case series behind them and are a reasonable addition in a multilevel or opioid-tolerant patient; the evidence does not yet justify calling them standard. A wound catheter is for the opioid-tolerant multilevel patient in a unit that has used one here, and is otherwise not placed.

The opioid-tolerant patient is common on this list, particularly the rheumatoid patient with years of neck pain, and the plan is the one in the opioid-tolerant chapter: the baseline opioid continued, ketamine, and a pain service involved before the second night.

Escalation: rising neck pain with any new arm or leg weakness in the first 24 h is a haematoma and the surgeon is called before any analgesic change. Shoulder abduction weakness appearing between day 2 and week 6 is a C5 palsy and is explained, not treated. Pain that is worst on sitting and relieved by lying is the nuchal muscle and the expected course, and it is treated with the oral regimen, heat and a soft collar if the surgeon permits one. Pain still 6 or more at a week with a dry wound is the rheumatoid or chronic pain patient’s baseline reasserting itself.

Pitfalls and variants

  • Laminoplasty versus laminectomy and fusion. The laminoplasty keeps a roof and one side’s muscle and has no screws and no non-union to protect, so the NSAID objection falls away and the pain is a notch lower; the fusion is for the unstable or kyphotic neck and sits at the top of this card’s range.
  • The posterior foraminotomy. A single-level muscle-splitting or tubular keyhole through the facet for one root: 60-90 min, little blood, one night or a day case in a fit patient, and a pain score of 2. The airway and positioning rules still apply because the patient is still prone in pins.
  • The myelopathic cord and the mean pressure. A compressed cord has lost its autoregulatory reserve; the arterial line is there so the mean pressure can be held at the patient’s own baseline for the whole case, and a vasopressor infusion started early is better than boluses chasing a dip during the stripping.
  • Awake versus asleep intubation. The collar trials say videolaryngoscopy is the faster, more reliable tool in an immobilised neck; the unstable or room-less canal is still intubated awake in most hands so the cord can be examined with the tube in and after the turn, and the decision is made with the surgeon and the imaging.
  • Rheumatoid arthritis. Atlantoaxial and subaxial instability, a pannus behind the dens, cricoarytenoid stiffness, a small mouth, steroid cover, a tendency to bleed, and a long occipitocervical construct; the orthopaedic patient chapter carries the detail.
  • Ankylosing spondylitis. A fixed, brittle neck that fractures through the ankylosed segment with the slightest extension, including during a laryngoscopy; the neck is positioned exactly where it was and no further, and the pins are placed with that in mind.
  • The upper cervical and occipitocervical construct. Longer, bloodier, the vertebral artery at risk on both sides, a head position the patient must live with, airway oedema from the prone time and the proximity to the pharynx, and the strongest case on the card for leaving the tube in overnight.
  • Postoperative visual loss. A long prone case with blood loss and the head in pins carries the described risk profile, and the pins at least keep the face off the pillow; the head above the heart, a normal haemoglobin and no sustained hypotension are the modifiable parts (see spine essentials).
  • Infection. The posterior neck wound has the highest infection rate of the elective spine; the antibiotic is redosed at 4 h and many surgeons add vancomycin powder.
  • The patient who cannot lift their head on day 1. Muscle, not cord, in a patient whose neurology is otherwise unchanged; the physiotherapist needs to hear it from you.

Key sources

No procedure-specific pain guideline exists for the posterior cervical spine, and the card’s plan is PROSPECT’s lumbar backbone with the regional recommendations stripped out and the reasons given. The C5 palsy figures come from a 155-study meta-analysis and a single-centre laminoplasty series that discusses the mechanism; the airway evidence is a randomised comparison in collared volunteers and patients that says nothing about myelopathy, and the awake intubation advice is physiology and judgement, which the card says. The nuchal muscle mechanism and the day 1 head-holding problem are clinical observation rather than measured outcomes.

  1. Stockman IG, Soliman MA, Quiceno E, et al. Incidence of C5 palsy and recovery rate after cervical spine surgery: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Neurosurgery 2025
    155 studies: C5 palsy after laminectomy 8%, posterior decompression and fusion 7.0%, laminoplasty 5.1% and ACDF 2.6%; permanent palsy 1.4%, 1.0%, 0.3% and 1.1% respectively
  2. Chen G, Wang Y, Wang Z, et al. Analysis of C5 palsy in cervical myelopathy with massive anterior compression following laminoplasty. J Orthop Surg Res 2018;13:26
    118 open-door laminoplasties: C5 palsy in 10.2%, 16.4% when the anterior occupying ratio exceeded 50%; onset 2 days to 6 weeks; recovery over 5-12 months and incomplete in some; mechanisms discussed are root tethering from posterior cord shift, reperfusion injury and thermal injury
  3. Guo N, Wen X, Wang X, et al. Comparison of outcomes between video laryngoscopy and flexible fiberoptic bronchoscopy for endotracheal intubation in adults with cervical neck immobilization: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. PLoS One 2024;19:e0313280
    Six randomised trials, 694 patients in cervical collars: videolaryngoscopy had higher first-attempt success and faster intubation than flexible bronchoscopy with similar complications; the patients were immobilised to simulate difficulty, not studied for cervical pathology
  4. Waelkens P, Alsabbagh E, Sauter A, Joshi GP, Beloeil H, on behalf of the PROSPECT Working Group of ESRA. Pain management after complex spine surgery: a systematic review and procedure-specific postoperative pain management recommendations. Eur J Anaesthesiol 2021;38:985-994
    Written for instrumented thoracolumbar surgery: paracetamol, NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor, intra-operative low-dose ketamine infusion (grade A), opioids as rescue, surgeon-placed epidural catheter (grade B); gabapentinoids not recommended; the cervical spine was not studied
  5. Gerbershagen HJ, Aduckathil S, van Wijck AJ, Peelen LM, Kalkman CJ, Meissner W. Pain intensity on the first day after surgery: a prospective cohort study comparing 179 surgical procedures. Anesthesiology 2013;118:934-944
    50,523 patients: spinal fusion and scoliosis surgery at ranks 2, 3 and 6 of 179 procedures for worst pain on day 1, median 7; the posterior cervical fusion sits with them on mechanism

Spine › Spine

58 Spinal metastasis decompression; vertebroplasty and kyphoplasty

Posterior decompression and instrumented stabilisation for metastatic epidural spinal cord compression (separation surgery); percutaneous vertebral augmentation for osteoporotic and pathological fractures

3Moderate

Dominant mechanism: Muscle. Bilateral paraspinal stripping over four or five vertebrae with a laminectomy and pedicle screws for the decompression, in a patient whose mechanical pain generator (an unstable, collapsing vertebra) is removed by the construct and who arrives on steroids and a baseline opioid; vertebral augmentation is a pedicle cannulation and a cemented fracture, bone-mechanism, minor and short

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: low.

Block
No regional technique as standard for the decompression: general anaesthesia with a low-dose ketamine infusion, the baseline opioid continued, regular paracetamol and a systemic multimodal regimen. For vertebral augmentation, operator-infiltrated local anaesthetic to the periosteum under sedation, or a general anaesthetic
Catheter: no Nothing runs through the epidural space of a patient who has tumour in it, a planned radiotherapy field over the wound, steroids on board and often a coagulopathy; the continuous element of the plan is the ketamine infusion and the baseline opioid, not a catheter
Alternatives: Bilateral erector spinae plane blocks at the operated level before the turn, as an adjunct for the open decompression (author's judgement, no procedure-specific trials); Surgeon infiltration of the paraspinal muscles and skin with long-acting local anaesthetic at closure; Intrathecal morphine 0.1 mg only where the puncture level is free of tumour, the clotting is normal and the ward can monitor it; rarely all three
Position
Prone on a radiolucent frame or bolsters with the abdomen free for both operations; the spine is turned as unstable until the screws are in; fluoroscopy or navigation needs a clear arc, and the sedated augmentation patient needs a position they can hold for an hour
Tourniquet
No
Cement
Yes. Polymethylmethacrylate is the point of vertebroplasty and kyphoplasty, injected under fluoroscopy into a fractured body with no pressurised canal; the decompression uses cement-augmented pedicle screws in osteoporotic or irradiated bone and sometimes cement to fill a corpectomy defect; the hazard is cement leak into the epidural veins and lungs, not a hip-type cement reaction
Blood loss
Decompression and stabilisation 500-1500 mL, with hypervascular metastases (renal, thyroid, hepatocellular, melanoma) at the top of the range and beyond it; in the only randomised trial of pre-operative embolisation the means were 618 mL with and 735 mL without; vertebral augmentation under 50 mL
Duration
Decompression and stabilisation 120-240 min, longer with a corpectomy and reconstruction; vertebroplasty 30-45 min for one level; balloon kyphoplasty 45-90 min for one or two levels
Length of stay
Decompression 5-10 nights, often to rehabilitation or palliative care rather than home; vertebral augmentation day case or one night. Day case: selected
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV within 60 min of incision (3 g over 120 kg), repeated at 4 h for the long decompression; the same single dose for augmentation because cement is an implant; the immunosuppressed, recently admitted or MRSA-colonised patient gets vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg IV started 60-120 min before the knife by the local protocol
Tranexamic acid
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV before incision for the decompression, extrapolated from the lumbar fusion trials; malignancy raises the baseline thrombotic risk and the decision is made for each patient; not needed for augmentation
VTE
The highest-risk group in the book: malignancy, immobility, cord compression, steroids. Mechanical prophylaxis from induction, low molecular weight heparin from day 1 once the surgeon is content the epidural space is dry, and a written bridging plan for the patient already anticoagulated for cancer-associated thrombosis
Antiemetic
The decompression patient is already on treatment-dose dexamethasone and needs no more; ondansetron 4 mg IV before emergence, droperidol 0.625 mg IV as the second agent; for augmentation under sedation, ondansetron 4 mg IV only if opioid has been given
Tell the patient
The operation takes the pressure off the spinal cord and holds the spine still; the aim is to keep you walking and out of pain, and the radiotherapy that follows is what treats the tumour.
The trap
Dexamethasone is treatment, not an antiemetic: the cord compression patient arrives on 16 mg a day or more, must not have it stopped for surgery, is hyperglycaemic and immunosuppressed, and the opioid they take for the fracture pain is their baseline, not their rescue

What the surgeon is doing and why

A spinal metastasis matters to the surgeon for two reasons only: it is pressing on the cord or the roots, or it has eaten enough of the vertebra that the spine is unstable. Pain alone is a radiotherapy and oncology problem. The operation on this card is never a cancer operation; the surgeon is buying walking, continence and the absence of mechanical pain, and the randomised evidence says the purchase is worth making. In the defining trial, 101 patients with metastatic cord compression were randomised to direct decompressive surgery followed by radiotherapy or to radiotherapy alone: 84% against 57% could walk after treatment, those who could walk kept walking for a median of 122 days against 13, and 62% against 19% of the patients who arrived unable to walk regained it.

Two ideas run the decision. The Spine Instability Neoplastic Score grades location, mechanical pain on loading, lytic or blastic bone, alignment, body collapse and posterolateral involvement; a high score is a surgical referral regardless of neurology. The second is separation. Stereotactic radiotherapy can control almost any tumour if there are a few millimetres between tumour and cord, so the surgeon no longer attempts an oncological resection: the operation is a laminectomy, removal of the epidural tumour to create that margin around the dura, and pedicle screws two levels above and two below to hold a spine that tumour and laminectomy have made unstable, with radiotherapy within a fortnight. An irradiated, steroid-treated patient will not fuse, so the construct carries the load alone for the patient’s remaining life.

Steroids come first. Dexamethasone reduces the vasogenic oedema in the compressed cord and buys time: in the one randomised trial, 57 patients given a 96 mg bolus and three days of high-dose oral steroid were ambulant after treatment in 81% of cases against 63% without, and at six months in 59% against 33%, with significant side effects in about one in ten. Most units now use 16 mg a day; the patient has been on it for days by the time they reach you, and it continues through the operation.

The other half of the card is vertebral augmentation. Vertebroplasty injects polymethylmethacrylate through a transpedicular needle into a fractured body; balloon kyphoplasty first inflates a balloon to create a cavity and partly restore height, then fills it with thicker cement at lower pressure. A fracture that does not move does not hurt. For osteoporotic fractures the Cochrane pooling of five sham-controlled trials found vertebroplasty improved pain by 0.7 of 10 points at one month, below any minimal important difference, with no benefit in disability or quality of life. For pathological fractures in cancer the fracture is part of a lytic process that will not heal, and in the CAFE trial 134 cancer patients randomised to balloon kyphoplasty or non-surgical care saw their Roland-Morris disability score fall from 17.6 to 9.1 at one month with kyphoplasty and not move without it. That trial was unblinded and industry funded; one of its 70 kyphoplasty patients had an intra-operative myocardial infarction attributed to the anaesthetic.

The pain logic separates the two procedures and then rejoins them. The open decompression is a posterior midline exposure with bilateral stripping over four or five vertebrae, a laminectomy and screws through four pedicles: the tissue injury of an instrumented fusion, which sits among the most painful operations in the 179-procedure cohort. Three things pull the score down to a 3: the mechanical pain generator, a collapsing vertebra that hurts on every movement, is removed by the construct; the patient arrives on dexamethasone and usually a baseline opioid, so the surgical pain is layered on a system already running; and the percutaneous screw variant leaves the muscle unstripped. Augmentation is bone-mechanism, brief and often net analgesic by recovery. An open five-level stripping in a patient with no mechanical pain beforehand behaves as a 4 for two days, and the plan assumes it.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 The call: urgency, steroids, neurology and the decision

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Cord compression is measured in hours. The surgeon wants the patient decompressed before a progressing deficit becomes complete; a dense paraplegia of more than a day or two rarely recovers. Prognosis under three months argues for radiotherapy alone.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The case jumps the queue and is done within 24 h of a new deficit. Dexamethasone is charted as a continuing drug, not stopped for fasting. Examine and record the neurology yourself (level, power by myotome, sensation, bladder): it is the baseline for every later check. Then the oncology history: the primary (the hypervascular ones and myeloma are under pitfalls), recent chemotherapy (neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, anthracycline cardiomyopathy, bleomycin lung), immunotherapy (adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism, pneumonitis), bevacizumab (impaired healing and bleeding), a calcium, a sodium, a haemoglobin, platelets, clotting, and the anticoagulant most of these patients take for a previous thrombosis. Crossmatch two to four units for a hypervascular primary, two for the rest. The goals-of-care conversation happens before the anaesthetic and is written down.

  2. 2 Pre-operative embolisation for the vascular metastasis

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A renal cell, thyroid, hepatocellular or melanoma metastasis has an arterial supply that can bleed litres when entered, and the decompression enters it. Interventional radiology can embolise the segmental feeders within 24-48 h of surgery.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The evidence is thinner than the practice. In the one randomised trial, 45 patients lost a mean of 618 mL with embolisation and 735 mL without, not significantly different, with no difference in transfusion; the operation was shorter (median 90 against 124 min), and in the hypervascular subgroup the reduction was significant (645 against 902 mL). The author’s reading: worth the delay for a renal or thyroid primary, not for the rest. The embolised patient arrives with a femoral puncture site, a contrast load in a kidney that may already be poor, and a small risk of cord ischaemia if the artery of Adamkiewicz shared a feeder, so repeat the neurological examination after it.

  3. 3 Induction, lines, monitoring and the turn with an unstable spine

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A prone, immobile, warm patient with the abdomen free and a clear fluoroscopy arc, turned without moving a spine that may be held together by soft tissue. Motor evoked potentials, if used, are baselined before the turn.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Reinforced tracheal tube, bite block if potentials are planned, an arterial line before induction for a vascular primary, a poor heart or any deficit, two large cannulae, a urinary catheter, warming and a rapid infuser primed for the hypervascular case. Blood in the room, not the fridge. Cell salvage in malignancy is accepted by many units with a leucocyte depletion filter and refused by others; settle it before the day. Rocuronium at intubation, reversed with sugammadex once the exposure is done, if potentials are followed. The turn: log roll with the neck neutral, a collar for any cervical or upper thoracic lesion, abdomen free so the epidural veins drain, arms below 90 degrees, eyes checked after the turn and again after the fluoroscopy arm has swung. Keep the mean pressure at or above the awake level through the turn: the compressed cord has lost autoregulation and a 60 mmHg mean during the roll is an ischaemic insult you cannot see.

  4. 4 Posterior exposure and pedicle screws two levels above and below

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A midline incision, paraspinal muscle stripped two levels above and two below; some surgeons place percutaneous screws through a short midline window to cut the stripping and the bleeding. Screws go in before the laminectomy so that the spine is held while the decompression destabilises it further, and the construct is long because the bone is poor and the screws carry the load for life. In osteoporotic or irradiated bone the surgeon uses fenestrated screws and injects a few millilitres of cement down each.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The first bleeding, steady rather than dramatic, from stripped muscle in a patient on steroids; a tumour that has broken through the posterior elements is entered now and the bleeding changes character at once. Tranexamic acid, if chosen, is in before the knife.
