Cement-augmented screws are a cement step without the hip’s physiology: small volumes, no pressurised canal, but a direct route into the basivertebral and epidural veins and from there to the lungs. A fall in end-tidal carbon dioxide with a rise in airway pressure during screw cementation is pulmonary cement embolism, handled as in step 10, and the surgeon stops injecting.

  5. 5 Laminectomy and circumferential epidural decompression

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Lamina and spinous process at the lesion are removed, then the epidural tumour is taken off the dura all round, including the ventral space reached through the pedicle; a full corpectomy is reserved for the collapsed body that cannot be reconstructed otherwise. This is separation surgery: a few millimetres for the radiotherapy to work in.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The bleed of the case. Epidural tumour is vascular, the plexus is engorged by any abdominal pressure, and tumour in the body has no vessels to clip; haemostasis is packing, haemostatic agents and cement. Keep the mean pressure up through this step, not down: the author’s practice is a mean of 80 mmHg or above while the cord is handled, extrapolated from the spinal cord injury literature rather than any trial in metastatic disease. A drop in motor evoked potentials during the ventral decompression is the cord being retracted or made ischaemic: tell the surgeon, raise the pressure, check the haemoglobin and the temperature, and wait. Dural tears are commoner than in degenerative surgery because tumour is adherent to dura.

  6. 6 Reconstruction, rods and the decision not to fuse

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    After a corpectomy the gap is filled with an expandable cage or with cement poured into a mould, and the rods are locked to the screws. Decortication and graft are usually omitted: radiotherapy follows within two weeks and the biology will not fuse.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Cement into a corpectomy defect is poured, not pressurised, and a cement reaction here is a case report. This is the quiet part of the case: catch up on blood and warmth, and measure the coagulopathy a two-litre loss has produced rather than assume it.

  7. 7 Closure, emergence and the first night

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Layered closure over a drain in a wound that will be irradiated within a fortnight, with steroid and often chemotherapy working against it; wound breakdown is the commonest complication and the one that delays radiotherapy. The surgeon wants an immediate neurological check and the patient sitting up within a day.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Reverse fully and wake the patient to a neurological examination in theatre against the step 1 baseline; a new deficit is a haematoma or a displaced construct and goes back at once. Dexamethasone continues and is tapered by the oncologists over weeks, not by the ward on day 2; hyperglycaemia gets insulin, not a stopped steroid. The baseline opioid restarts on the day of surgery as a regular drug. Mechanical prophylaxis from induction and low molecular weight heparin from day 1 once the surgeon is content. Stay is a week or more and the destination is as often rehabilitation or palliative care as home; involve those teams on day 1.

  8. 8 Vertebral augmentation: the patient and the decision

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A fractured body that hurts on loading, in an osteoporotic patient who has failed weeks of conservative care or a cancer patient whose lytic fracture will not heal, with a posterior wall intact enough that cement will stay in the body. Kyphoplasty is chosen where height matters or the posterior wall is doubtful, because the balloon cavity takes cement at lower pressure; vertebroplasty is faster and cheaper.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The procedure is small; the patient is not. The osteoporotic fracture patient is in their eighties, has had weeks of immobility and often a chest, and now has to lie prone for 45-90 min. Sedation or a general anaesthetic is decided on whether the patient can lie prone awake, keep still for the one painful moment (cement injection) and protect their own airway face-down with a sedative on board. The author’s practice is a general anaesthetic with a tracheal tube for more than one level, any patient who cannot lie prone comfortably on the trolley beforehand, any difficult airway and the cancer patient with a long comorbidity list; sedation for the single-level fracture in a patient who demonstrates the position first.

  9. 9 Prone positioning and transpedicular access under fluoroscopy

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Prone on bolsters with the fracture extended slightly to open the anterior column. Biplanar fluoroscopy guides a trocar through the pedicle into the anterior third of the body, one or both sides, without breaching the medial pedicle wall and the canal.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The turn is the painful part for the awake patient and is done with their help before the sedation, not after it. Under sedation: nasal oxygen with capnography, the airway visible to you in the prone pillow, and an agreed signal for pain. The operator infiltrates skin, muscle and the periosteum of the pedicle entry; the periosteal injection is the one that matters and the one that is rushed. A trocar through the medial pedicle wall presents as sudden radicular pain in the awake patient and as nothing at all in the anaesthetised one, which is the strongest argument for keeping the single-level patient awake.

  10. 10 Balloon inflation and cement injection

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    For kyphoplasty, a balloon is inflated under fluoroscopy to create a cavity and lift the endplate, then removed, and viscous cement is injected into the cavity. For vertebroplasty, thinner cement goes directly into the trabecular bone under continuous screening, and the operator stops when it reaches the posterior quarter of the body or appears outside it. Leak is the complication the technique is designed around: into the disc (common, harmless), the paravertebral veins and from there the lungs, or the canal and foramina.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Cement injection is the painful moment and the dangerous one. Leak rates depend on how hard anyone looks: 39% after vertebroplasty and 29% after kyphoplasty in the comparative studies, none producing neural compromise, pulmonary embolism or emergency decompression; 20.7% in the metastatic series (28.6% with CT), with pulmonary cement embolism in about 1% and symptomatic complications of any kind in 3.4%; and pulmonary cement embolism in 3.5-23% of osteoporotic augmentations depending on whether the lungs were imaged. The one that matters presents in the room: a fall in end-tidal carbon dioxide, a drop in saturation, hypotension and tachycardia during or minutes after the injection, the picture of any pulmonary embolus. Tell the operator to stop, give oxygen, support the pressure, turn the patient supine if it does not settle, and get an echocardiogram; symptomatic or central emboli are anticoagulated as thrombotic emboli and cement in the heart is a cardiothoracic problem. New radicular pain during injection in the awake patient is cement in the foramen and the injection stops; under general anaesthesia it is found at the wake-up, so the neurological check happens before the patient leaves the room.

  11. 11 Recovery and discharge after augmentation

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The fracture is fixed the moment the cement sets; the operator wants the patient sitting, walking and home the same day or the next.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Relief is immediate when it comes: a patient who could not sit beforehand often sits up in recovery. Pain worse than before, new radicular pain or new weakness is a leak or a canal haematoma and needs imaging. The opioid the patient came in on is reduced over days rather than continued unchanged, because the pain generator has gone and an elderly patient on the same dose will be obtunded by day 2. Day case for the single-level fracture with support at home; one night for the cancer patient and anyone who needed a general anaesthetic for the position.

Pain plan

Two procedures, two plans. For the open decompression the mechanism is muscle stripping with a laminectomy and screws in a patient already on steroid and opioid. The regional options that serve a degenerative fusion are mostly closed: an epidural catheter through a space with tumour in it, under a planned radiotherapy field, with steroid thinning the skin and often a clotting screen that would not pass, is not a technique the author would place. Intrathecal morphine 0.1 mg is possible when the puncture level is clear of tumour on the MRI, the clotting is normal and the ward can monitor it, which is a minority of these patients. The defensible default is systemic: a low-dose ketamine infusion from induction to closure (the opioid-dependent spine trial model of 0.5 mg/kg at induction and 10 microg/kg/min, which cut opioid use at 48 h and pain at six weeks in this phenotype), regular paracetamol, an NSAID only where kidneys, platelets and the oncologist allow (which excludes myeloma and most with a raised creatinine), the baseline opioid continued as a regular drug from the day of surgery, and an immediate-release opioid charted as rescue at a dose scaled to that baseline (see the opioid-tolerant chapter). Bilateral erector spinae plane blocks before the turn are the author’s adjunct for the open exposure, on the general spine literature rather than any trial in metastatic disease; they do not touch the epidural space or mask a deficit. Surgeon infiltration at closure is asked for by name.

For augmentation, the pain is the trocar through the periosteum and the cement injection, covered by the operator’s local anaesthetic or the general anaesthetic, then a fracture that no longer moves: regular paracetamol, the opioid the patient was already taking reduced as the fracture pain goes, and no new drugs.

Rebound is not a feature of either plan, because nothing long-acting is wearing off. Escalation: rising back pain in the first 24 h after a decompression with new leg symptoms or retention is an epidural haematoma until imaged; pain after augmentation that is worse than the pre-operative pain is a leak. Both go to the surgeon, not to the rescue dose.

Pitfalls and variants

  • The hypervascular primary. Renal cell, thyroid, hepatocellular and melanoma metastases bleed from the moment they are entered and do not stop with pressure. Know the primary before the day, ask about embolisation, and have an arterial line, a rapid infuser, blood in the room and an agreement with the surgeon on the loss that shortens the operation.
  • Myeloma. Renal impairment, hypercalcaemia, hyperviscosity, anaemia, a bleeding tendency from paraproteins and thrombocytopenia, and no NSAIDs.
  • The cervical metastasis. An unstable neck in a collar, a possible anterior approach with a retropharyngeal haematoma risk, and an airway that may be secured awake and left in overnight; the posterior cervical fusion and ACDF cards carry the detail.
  • Anterior and lateral approaches. A corpectomy through a thoracotomy or the retroperitoneum brings a double-lumen tube, a chest drain and a visceral pain component; rarer now that separation surgery exists, still done for a solitary metastasis with a long prognosis.
  • The patient on immunotherapy. Checkpoint inhibitors cause adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism and pneumonitis, any of which can present as an unexplained collapse under anaesthesia; the augmentation patient on no steroid may need hydrocortisone.
  • Wound breakdown and infection. Weeks of dexamethasone, thin skin and a wound in a radiotherapy field: the infection rate is several times that of degenerative fusion and prophylaxis is not where the difference is made.
  • Vertebroplasty under sedation in the patient who cannot lie prone. The sedative dose creeps up, the airway is face-down, and the capnograph is the only early warning. Convert to a general anaesthetic beforehand, not halfway through the cement.
  • Cement where it should not be. Into the disc (harmless), the paravertebral veins (watch the capnograph), the canal (a laminectomy at once), the heart (a case report). Injection technique and viscosity are the prevention; your contribution is to notice.
  • The goals-of-care conversation. A patient with weeks to live or a complete paraplegia of several days may be better served by radiotherapy and analgesia, and the anaesthetist is often the person who notices the question has not been asked.

Key sources

The surgical evidence is one trial, stopped early, and it is enough; the steroid evidence is one 57-patient trial of a regimen nobody now uses. Pre-operative embolisation has one randomised trial, negative overall and positive in the hypervascular subgroup, and the advice to embolise the renal and thyroid primaries only is the author’s reading of it. The augmentation evidence runs in opposite directions: a Cochrane review against routine vertebroplasty for osteoporotic fractures, and an unblinded industry-funded trial for kyphoplasty in cancer. The leak and embolism figures depend on the imaging used. The cord perfusion target and the anaesthetic choice for augmentation are author’s judgement.

  1. Patchell RA, Tibbs PA, Regine WF, et al. Direct decompressive surgical resection in the treatment of spinal cord compression caused by metastatic cancer: a randomised trial. Lancet 2005;366:643-648
    101 patients with metastatic cord compression: surgery plus radiotherapy against radiotherapy alone; 84% versus 57% able to walk after treatment, retained walking for a median 122 versus 13 days, 62% versus 19% of non-ambulant patients regained walking, and less steroid and opioid use; stopped early for benefit
  2. Sørensen S, Helweg-Larsen S, Mouridsen H, Hansen HH. Effect of high-dose dexamethasone in carcinomatous metastatic spinal cord compression treated with radiotherapy: a randomised trial. Eur J Cancer 1994;30A:22-27
    57 patients: dexamethasone 96 mg IV then 96 mg a day orally for three days and tapered over ten, against no steroid; 81% versus 63% ambulant after treatment and 59% versus 33% at six months; significant side effects in 11%
  3. Fisher CG, DiPaola CP, Ryken TC, et al. A novel classification system for spinal instability in neoplastic disease: an evidence-based approach and expert consensus from the Spine Oncology Study Group. Spine 2010;35:E1221-1229
    The Spine Instability Neoplastic Score: location, pain, bone lesion quality, alignment, vertebral body collapse and posterolateral element involvement, scored to identify the patient who needs a surgical opinion
  4. Clausen C, Dahl B, Frevert SC, Hansen LV, Nielsen MB, Lønn L. Preoperative embolization in surgical treatment of spinal metastases: single-blind, randomized controlled clinical trial of efficacy in decreasing intraoperative blood loss. J Vasc Interv Radiol 2015;26:402-412
    45 patients having posterior decompression and instrumentation: intra-operative blood loss 618 mL with embolisation versus 735 mL without, not significant; transfusion not different; surgery shorter (median 90 versus 124 min); in the hypervascular subgroup 645 versus 902 mL, significant
  5. Krueger A, Bliemel C, Zettl R, Ruchholtz S. Management of pulmonary cement embolism after percutaneous vertebroplasty and kyphoplasty: a systematic review of the literature. Eur Spine J 2009;18:1257-1265
    Pulmonary cement embolism reported in 3.5-23% of osteoporotic fracture augmentations depending on how hard it is looked for; asymptomatic peripheral emboli need follow-up only, symptomatic or central emboli are treated as thrombotic pulmonary embolism with heparin then six months of anticoagulation
  6. Rose LD, Bateman G, Ahmed A. Clinical significance of cement leakage in kyphoplasty and vertebroplasty: a systematic review. Eur Spine J 2024;33:1484-1489
    Six comparative studies, 532 vertebroplasties and 493 kyphoplasties: cement leak in 39.3% versus 28.9%, with no leak in either group producing neural compromise, pulmonary embolism or emergency decompression
  7. Correia MC, Vieira AM, Duarte F, Rodrigues Pinho A, Serdoura F, Leite MJ. Complications of vertebral augmentation in metastatic spinal fractures: a systematic review of multiple study designs. J Bone Oncol 2026;61:100802
    76 studies, 3,234 patients with metastatic fractures: weighted complication rate 25.5%, symptomatic complications 3.41%, cement leak 20.7% (28.6% when CT was used), pulmonary cement embolism 1.08%, adjacent fracture 0.79%; case reports of tumour seeding along the needle tract and cement in the heart
  8. Buchbinder R, Johnston RV, Rischin KJ, et al. Percutaneous vertebroplasty for osteoporotic vertebral compression fracture. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2018;11:CD006349
    21 trials; against sham in five trials (541 patients) vertebroplasty improved pain by 0.7 of 10 points at one month, below the minimal important difference, with no important benefit in disability or quality of life; serious adverse events included osteomyelitis, cord compression, thecal sac injury and respiratory failure
  9. Berenson J, Pflugmacher R, Jarzem P, et al. Balloon kyphoplasty versus non-surgical fracture management for treatment of painful vertebral body compression fractures in patients with cancer: a multicentre, randomised controlled trial. Lancet Oncol 2011;12:225-235
    134 cancer patients with one to three painful fractures: Roland-Morris disability fell from 17.6 to 9.1 at one month with kyphoplasty and was unchanged with non-surgical care; one intra-operative non-Q-wave myocardial infarction attributed to the anaesthetic; unblinded and industry funded
  10. Loftus RW, Yeager MP, Clark JA, et al. Intraoperative ketamine reduces perioperative opiate consumption in opiate-dependent patients with chronic back pain undergoing back surgery. Anesthesiology 2010;113:639-646
    102 opioid-dependent patients having major lumbar surgery: ketamine 0.5 mg/kg at induction then 10 microg/kg/min to closure reduced morphine-equivalent consumption at 24 h, 48 h and six weeks and pain in recovery and at six weeks, with no excess side effects
  11. Gerbershagen HJ, Aduckathil S, van Wijck AJ, Peelen LM, Kalkman CJ, Meissner W. Pain intensity on the first day after surgery: a prospective cohort study comparing 179 surgical procedures. Anesthesiology 2013;118:934-944
    Spinal fusion and scoliosis surgery sat among the most painful of 179 procedures on day 1; the open instrumented decompression on this card shares their exposure and is scored down only because the mechanical pain generator is removed and the patient is already on opioid and steroid

Spine › Spine

59 Spinal cord stimulator and intrathecal pump implantation

Percutaneous trial leads; permanent implant with percutaneous leads or a paddle lead through a laminotomy and a generator pocket; intrathecal drug delivery system with catheter and pump; revisions and generator changes

2Mild to moderate

Dominant mechanism: Muscle. A midline paraspinal dissection with a small laminotomy for a paddle lead (bone, minor), subcutaneous tunnelling, and a generator or pump pocket in the buttock, flank or abdominal wall that is the site most patients complain about; percutaneous leads and the pump catheter add needle tracks only. The surgical pain sits on top of the chronic pain the device exists to treat, in a patient who is usually opioid-tolerant

Rebound risk when a single-shot block wears off: low.

Block
No regional block: operator-infiltrated local anaesthetic with titrated sedation for trial leads and percutaneous implants (the patient has to report paraesthesia), or general anaesthesia with intra-operative neuromonitoring for paddle leads and most pumps; surgeon infiltration of the pocket; regular paracetamol and an NSAID, the baseline opioid continued
Catheter: no The operation is about placing one hardware item in the epidural or intrathecal space and nothing else goes near it; the pain is a pocket and a short midline wound, treated systemically, with the pain service's plan for the baseline opioid doing the real work
Alternatives: Transversus abdominis plane block on the pocket side for an abdominal pump pocket (author's judgement); Erector spinae plane block at the laminotomy level for a paddle lead under general anaesthesia (author's judgement, no procedure-specific trials); Low-dose ketamine infusion through the case for the opioid-tolerant patient under general anaesthesia
Position
Prone on bolsters for trial leads and stimulator implantation, with the generator pocket in the upper buttock or flank reached without turning; lateral decubitus for the intrathecal pump so that the lumbar puncture site and the abdominal pocket are both in the field; the awake patient has to hold the position and talk for an hour, which is the anaesthetic problem
Tourniquet
No
Cement
No
Blood loss
Under 100 mL; a laminotomy for a paddle lead bleeds a little more; the loss that matters is an epidural haematoma around a lead, so anticoagulants and antiplatelet drugs are managed as for a neuraxial catheter
Duration
Trial lead placement 30-60 min; percutaneous permanent implant 60-90 min; paddle lead through a laminotomy with a generator 90-150 min (shorter asleep with neuromonitoring than awake); intrathecal pump 60-120 min; generator change 30 min
Length of stay
Day case for trials, percutaneous implants and generator changes; one night for paddle leads; one to three nights for a pump started on an intrathecal opioid while the systemic dose comes down. Day case: selected
Antibiotic
Cefazolin 2 g IV within 60 min of incision (3 g over 120 kg), vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg IV over 60-120 min for MRSA carriers, as the NACC infection guideline frames it; surgeons vary on a short post-operative course, which the multicentre series associated with fewer infections and the consensus guideline does not endorse beyond the day of surgery
Tranexamic acid
Not needed
VTE
Mechanical only; chemoprophylaxis, if the patient needs it, timed with the surgeon as for any neuraxial catheter while a lead or an intrathecal catheter is in
Antiemetic
Dexamethasone 4 mg IV and ondansetron 4 mg IV for the general anaesthetic; for the pump started on intrathecal morphine, ondansetron as a regular drug for the first days because neuraxial opioid nausea and pruritus are expected
Tell the patient
The device does not remove the pain; the trial finds out whether it changes it enough to be worth keeping, and the operation itself adds a sore back and a sore pocket for a week or two on top of what you already have.
The trap
The deaths after intrathecal opioid pump implantation were respiratory arrests in the first days in patients with intrathecal and systemic opioid on board together: the starting intrathecal dose is small, the systemic opioid comes down on a written schedule from the pain service, and the first nights are monitored, not assumed

What the surgeon is doing and why

Both devices on this card are answers to the same clinical failure: a patient whose pain has outlasted every operation and every drug, who is usually on a long-acting opioid, and in whom the pain service has decided that a piece of hardware in the spinal canal is the next move. The hardware is different, the surgery is small in both cases, and the anaesthetic problems are almost entirely about the patient rather than the wound.

A spinal cord stimulator delivers current to the dorsal columns through an electrode lying in the posterior epidural space, usually at T8-T10 for leg and back pain and at C2-C5 for the arm. Conventional stimulation produces a paraesthesia that must overlap the painful area, which is why the classic technique is done awake: the patient reports where they feel the tingling and the lead is moved until it matches. The newer paradigms (high frequency, burst, dorsal root ganglion stimulation) are paraesthesia-free or nearly so, and that has changed the anaesthetic, because a lead that does not need the patient’s report can be placed under general anaesthesia with the midline confirmed by electromyography of the legs. There are two kinds of lead. Percutaneous cylindrical leads go in through a Tuohy needle with loss of resistance, exactly as an epidural catheter would, and can migrate. Paddle leads are flat, cover more of the cord, migrate less and need a laminotomy: the surgeon removes the upper part of the lower spinous process and enough lamina to slide a plate into the epidural space under direct vision. The lead is anchored to the fascia, a strain relief loop is left, and it is tunnelled to a generator in a pocket in the upper buttock, the flank or the abdominal wall. Every patient has a trial first, with externalised percutaneous leads for a week or so, and goes on to the implant only if the pain falls by half or more.

An intrathecal pump bypasses the dorsal columns and puts the drug where the receptors are. A catheter is placed through a paramedian lumbar puncture, threaded to the dermatome of the pain, tunnelled around the flank and connected to a programmable pump with a 20-40 mL reservoir in a pocket in the abdominal wall, refilled through the skin every few weeks to months. Morphine and ziconotide are the first-line single agents in the consensus algorithms, with bupivacaine, hydromorphone, fentanyl and clonidine as admixtures; baclofen pumps for spasticity are the same hardware with a different drug and a different withdrawal syndrome. The dose ratio is the point: a milligram of intrathecal morphine does the work of hundreds of milligrams by mouth, which is also why the first days after implantation have killed people.

The complication profile explains most of the anaesthetic planning. In the pooled literature 30-40% of stimulator patients have at least one complication; lead migration is the commonest, infection and pain over the implant the commonest biological ones, and neurological injury is rare. The modern infection rate in a multicentre series of 2,737 implants and revisions was 2.45%, with no independent effect of diabetes, smoking or obesity, no difference between paddle and cylindrical leads or between antibiotics, and fewer infections with an occlusive dressing. An infected stimulator or pump is explanted; the device is lost, and so is the months of work that led to it.

The pain logic is unusual for this book because the wound is not the problem. A one-level laminotomy and a midline dissection are minor bone and muscle; the pocket is a subcutaneous dissection that aches for a week or two and is the thing patients complain about; the needle tracks of a percutaneous system are nothing. All of it lands on a patient whose baseline pain is a 6 or 7, who takes a long-acting opioid, often a gabapentinoid and sometimes a benzodiazepine, and who has had many operations before. The score is a 2 on the scale because the plan is paracetamol, an NSAID and a few rescue doses; the day 1 figure of 4 is the pocket, and the honest statement is that the surgical pain will be hard to distinguish from the pain the device was implanted for.

Steps: what happens and what it means for you

  1. 1 Selection, the trial decision and the opioid plan

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The pain service has excluded a treatable cause, screened the patient psychologically, and decided between a stimulator (focal neuropathic pain, failed back surgery, complex regional pain syndrome, limb ischaemia) and a pump (diffuse or cancer pain, spasticity, or a patient already on high-dose opioid who has failed everything else). The consensus guidelines describe who needs a trial and who does not.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Take the drug history in milligrams and times: the long-acting opioid, the gabapentinoid, any benzodiazepine, any buprenorphine, and the pain service’s plan for all of them around the implant, which is written before the day and not improvised in recovery (see the opioid-tolerant chapter). Anticoagulants and antiplatelet drugs are managed as for a neuraxial catheter, because a lead in the epidural space is one, and the surgeon’s interval is written down. Diabetes control, MRSA screening and decolonisation are the infection measures with the guideline behind them. A patient who already has a stimulator for a revision needs its programmer in the room. For a pump patient, the systemic opioid dose on the day and the planned starting intrathecal dose are both on the chart.

  2. 2 Trial lead placement under local anaesthetic and sedation

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    One or two percutaneous leads are placed through Tuohy needles at T12-L1 or L1-L2 and advanced up the posterior epidural space under fluoroscopy to T8-T10, then stimulated while the patient reports whether the paraesthesia covers the pain. The leads are anchored at the skin, connected to an external generator and left for five to ten days.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The patient must be able to lie prone, lie still for the needle and answer questions during the mapping, and the sedation is titrated to exactly that: enough to tolerate the needle, little enough to describe a tingling in the left calf. Propofol in small increments or a dexmedetomidine infusion both work; a patient who cannot answer is a patient whose lead is in the wrong place. Local anaesthetic by the operator at the needle entry and down to the ligament is the analgesic. Dural puncture happens, presents as a wet needle and a headache, and usually means the trial is deferred. A paraesthesia-free system (high frequency or burst) allows deeper sedation because the lead is placed to anatomical landmarks rather than to the patient’s report; find out which system it is before choosing the sedative.

  3. 3 Permanent implant: awake or asleep

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A successful trial leads to a permanent system within a few weeks. Percutaneous leads are replaced in the same way and tunnelled to a generator; paddle leads need a laminotomy and have traditionally been placed awake for mapping, which is uncomfortable, slow and unreliable.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    The best evidence on the anaesthetic is a prospective, non-randomised, multicentre comparison of 30 paddle lead implants: 19 placed asleep with electromyographic guidance and 11 awake with verbal mapping. Asleep placement took 89 min against 125, gave 83.5% pain-paraesthesia overlap at six weeks against 46.6%, produced fewer stray paraesthesiae, matched the awake group for pain relief at 24 weeks, and had two adverse events against six. The author’s default for a paddle lead is therefore a general anaesthetic with neuromonitoring where the unit can provide it, and awake placement only where it cannot or where the surgeon insists. The neuromonitoring rules apply: a propofol and remifentanil infusion, no neuromuscular block after the intubating dose (sugammadex if the laminotomy needs a relaxed patient early), and a bite block for the motor evoked potentials if those are run as well as electromyography.

  4. 4 Prone positioning

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Prone on bolsters with the thoracolumbar spine flexed to open the interlaminar spaces, the arms up for a thoracic lead or down for a cervical one, a fluoroscopy arc that can swing to lateral, and the pocket site on the buttock or flank prepared in the same field.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    For the asleep patient the prone rules apply: abdomen free, eyes checked after the turn and after every fluoroscopy swing, pressure points padded, arms below 90 degrees. For the awake patient the position is the anaesthetic: a prone pillow with a clear view of the mouth, nasal oxygen with capnography, a chest bolster that leaves the abdomen free, a pillow under the shins, an antisialagogue if the case will be long, and a frank conversation beforehand about lying face-down for an hour. A patient with a hip or knee that cannot be extended, a chest that cannot be loaded or a neck that cannot be turned is a general anaesthetic, decided before the day.

  5. 5 Lead placement and intra-operative testing

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Percutaneous leads are steered up the posterior epidural space to the target level and the midline is confirmed on the anteroposterior image. For a paddle, the surgeon removes the superior edge of the lower spinous process and a window of lamina, opens the ligamentum flavum and slides the plate cranially into the epidural space, where it sits against the dura and can compress the cord if the canal is narrow or the paddle too wide. Testing follows: verbal mapping awake, or electromyography asleep, where symmetrical responses in both legs at the same threshold mean the paddle is midline.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Keep the pressure at the patient’s normal through the paddle insertion, because a cord pressed by a plate in a tight canal is an ischaemic cord. A fall in somatosensory potentials or asymmetric motor responses during insertion is the paddle in the wrong place; the response is to tell the surgeon, who repositions it. Under sedation, the lead passage and the stimulation test are tolerable but the laminotomy is not, so the awake technique is really an awake-mapping technique with the bone work under heavy local and the deepest sedation the patient’s airway will allow face-down. Cervical leads bring the airway into it: a cervical epidural haematoma or an oedematous cord presents as a weak arm and then a weak diaphragm.

  6. 6 Anchoring, tunnelling and the generator pocket

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The lead is anchored to the fascia with a strain relief loop so that spinal flexion does not pull it, tunnelled subcutaneously, and connected to the generator in a pocket sized to the device and placed where the patient will not lie or sit on it.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Tunnelling is the most stimulating step for the sedated patient and the one the operator under-infiltrates; ask for the tunnel track to be infiltrated before the rod goes through. The pocket is the post-operative pain generator: a wide subcutaneous dissection over fascia in a thin patient, a deep one in a heavy patient, and the site most likely to produce pain over the implant for weeks. Surgeon infiltration of the pocket with long-acting local anaesthetic before closure is the one request worth making by name. Blood pressure at the patient’s normal keeps the pocket dry; a pocket haematoma is an infection waiting to happen.

  7. 7 Closure, dressing, programming and the wake-up check

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Layered closure, an occlusive dressing (the one measure associated with fewer infections in the multicentre series), and initial programming of the device before the patient leaves theatre or in recovery.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Wake the asleep patient to a neurological examination of the legs (or the arms for a cervical lead) before they leave the room; new weakness is a haematoma or a misplaced paddle and the imaging is immediate. Dural puncture headache after a paddle implant is treated conservatively first; a blood patch near a fresh lead is the surgeon’s decision. The device is left on or off according to the programmer’s plan, and the patient’s existing analgesia continues unchanged.

  8. 8 Intrathecal pump: trial and drug

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    A single-shot intrathecal dose, a short epidural or intrathecal catheter infusion or, in the terminally ill, no trial at all, as the consensus trialling guidance allows. The drug follows the algorithm: morphine or ziconotide first line, admixtures with bupivacaine or clonidine for mixed pain, baclofen for spasticity.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A single-shot morphine trial in an opioid-tolerant outpatient is a neuraxial opioid in a patient also taking systemic opioid, monitored for 24 h with the same respiratory vigilance as any intrathecal morphine; the consensus documents say what to do with the systemic dose during the trial and the pain service writes it down. Ziconotide trials bring psychiatric and cognitive effects rather than respiratory ones. A baclofen trial in a spastic patient can drop the tone enough to unmask weakness and compromise transfers.

  9. 9 Pump implantation

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    Lateral decubitus, pocket side up. A paramedian intrathecal puncture at L2-L3 or below, the catheter threaded to the target level under fluoroscopy and anchored to the lumbodorsal fascia, tunnelled around the flank to an abdominal pocket, and connected to the pump, which is filled, primed with a bridging bolus to fill the catheter dead space, and secured to the fascia, subfascially in a thin patient.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    A general anaesthetic with a tracheal tube is usual; the lateral position has the standard dependent-side padding and the airway on its side for an hour or more. Cerebrospinal fluid runs freely from a 15-gauge needle and the puncture is the source of the post-dural puncture headache that follows a proportion of these operations, treated conservatively because a blood patch beside a fresh catheter is a surgical decision. The priming bolus matters to you: the catheter dead space is filled with drug at the end of the case and the pump then runs at its programmed rate, so the first intrathecal dose arrives in theatre or recovery, not in a week. Anticoagulant timing is the neuraxial rule again, with a catheter that stays in for life.

  10. 10 The first nights on an intrathecal opioid

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The pump is started at a conservative dose and titrated over days to weeks while the systemic opioid is reduced; the pain service owns both numbers.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    This is the lethal step and the reason the card exists. Device registration data put mortality after intrathecal opioid pump implantation for non-cancer pain at 0.088% at three days, 0.39% at one month and 3.89% at one year, higher than after stimulator implantation or lumbar discectomy; in all nine index cases respiratory arrest caused or contributed to death and no device over-infusion was found, which leaves the drug, the systemic opioid still on board, and the interaction. The defensible plan: the starting dose from the consensus guidance rather than from the trial response, continuous oximetry and capnography where available for at least the first night, a sedation score hourly, naloxone at the bedside, no additional sedatives, a written schedule for reducing the oral opioid rather than a stop, and the patient’s family told what to watch for at home. The pocket and the back hurt more than the patient expected in the first week; treat that with the plan below and not with the pump.

  11. 11 Recovery and discharge for both devices

    What the surgeon is doing and why

    The surgeon wants a dry wound, a device that works, and a patient who understands the restrictions (no bending, twisting or lifting for several weeks after a lead, no lying on the pocket) that keep the lead from migrating.

    What it means for anaesthesia

    Day case for a trial, a percutaneous implant or a generator change; one night for a paddle lead; longer for a pump. The pain the patient reports in recovery is three things at once (the pocket, the back, and the chronic pain the device will or will not treat), and separating them is the first conversation. Infection presents over the following weeks as pocket erythema, a fluctuant pocket, a wound that weeps, fever, or new back pain and meningism; any of them is an urgent review, because an epidural abscess around a lead is a cord compression. Lead migration presents as a change in the paraesthesia pattern or loss of effect and is a surgical revision rather than an anaesthetic problem, but the revision patient is the same patient with another operation on the list.

Pain plan

The wound is minor and the patient is not, so the plan is built on the pain service’s opioid plan with surgical analgesia added rather than the other way around. Regular paracetamol and an NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor where the kidneys allow, started before the block of sedation or the general anaesthetic wears off, cover the laminotomy and the pocket for most patients. The baseline long-acting opioid continues at its usual dose and time on the day of surgery, including buprenorphine; an immediate-release rescue dose is charted at a size scaled to the baseline, which for a patient on 200 mg of oral morphine equivalent a day is not 5 mg. Gabapentinoids and benzodiazepines continue because stopping them produces withdrawal, not analgesia. For the paddle lead under general anaesthesia, a low-dose ketamine infusion through the case is the author’s practice in the opioid-tolerant patient, on the strength of the opioid-dependent lumbar surgery trial (0.5 mg/kg at induction then 10 microg/kg/min to closure, which reduced opioid use to 48 h and pain at six weeks), and an erector spinae plane block at the laminotomy level is a reasonable adjunct without procedure-specific evidence. A transversus abdominis plane block on the pocket side for an abdominal pump pocket is the same category of judgement. Surgeon infiltration of the pocket and the tunnel track is asked for in every case.

For the pump patient the plan inverts: the intrathecal opioid starts low, the systemic opioid is reduced on a written schedule, no sedative is added, and the surgical pain of the first week is treated with paracetamol, an NSAID and the reduced systemic opioid rather than with a faster pump titration. A patient who is sedated on day 1 after a pump has too much opioid in total and the pump is the first thing to question.

Rebound is not a feature. Escalation: new leg weakness, retention or back pain out of proportion after a stimulator is an epidural haematoma or a misplaced paddle until imaged; a pump patient with a falling respiratory rate has an opioid problem and gets naloxone and a pump interrogation, not a sleep; a hot, fluctuant pocket is an infection and goes to the surgeon the same day.

Pitfalls and variants

  • Anticoagulants and antiplatelet drugs. A lead or a catheter in the canal is a neuraxial catheter with no removal date; the neuraxial intervals for stopping and restarting apply, and a patient who cannot stop them is a patient who may not be a candidate.
  • The sedated prone airway. The awake-mapping technique fails when the sedation deepens to keep the patient still; a face-down patient with an obstructed airway and a needle in the epidural space has no good options. Choose the general anaesthetic beforehand for the patient with sleep apnoea, a difficult airway or a body habitus that will not lie prone.
  • Buprenorphine. Continue it; the modern advice is in the opioid-tolerant chapter, and a patient taken off buprenorphine for a stimulator implant is in withdrawal with a sore pocket.
  • Opioid use disorder. The pump is rarely the answer and the stimulator sometimes is; the plan is agreed with addiction medicine, the baseline agonist continues, and the rescue dose is scaled honestly.
  • The existing stimulator at later surgery. Turn it off for the operation, bipolar diathermy or a monopolar return pad placed so that the current path avoids the generator and leads, and MRI only under the device’s conditional rules; the programmer and the representative’s number go in the notes.
  • The baclofen pump patient. A pump that fails, a catheter that fractures or a refill that is missed produces baclofen withdrawal within hours: hyperthermia, rigidity, rhabdomyolysis, seizures and death. Treat as an emergency with oral or enteral baclofen, benzodiazepines and the pump team.
  • Refills and pocket fills. A refill needle that misses the port puts weeks of intrathecal opioid into the subcutaneous pocket at once; the presentation is an overdose within an hour of a clinic visit and the treatment is naloxone, an infusion and observation.
  • Catheter-tip granuloma. An inflammatory mass at the tip of a catheter delivering high-concentration opioid, presenting as loss of effect then new neurological signs; the safety consensus describes it, and it is the differential for a pump patient with new leg symptoms.
  • Cervical leads. The epidural haematoma and the swollen cord present as arm weakness and then a diaphragm; the wake-up check includes the arms and the breathing, and the first night is a monitored one.
  • Dorsal root ganglion stimulation. Leads through the foramen onto the ganglion itself, done awake in most hands because the mapping is precise; the same sedation problem with a longer case.
  • Obesity. The pocket is deep, the tunnelling long, the prone position worse, the lead more likely to migrate and the infection rate, in the large series, not higher. The general anaesthetic is chosen more often.
  • Pain over the implant. Pocket pain for weeks is common enough to be listed among the main biological complications and is not an indication for more opioid; a repositioned generator is the surgical answer when it persists.

Key sources

The infection guidance is consensus with a large retrospective series behind it; the two disagree on post-operative antibiotics and the card says so. The awake-versus-asleep evidence is one small prospective non-randomised comparison and a technique video from the same group, which is thin, but the direction is consistent with the physiology and the author follows it. The intrathecal pump guidance is three consensus documents from one conference, and the mortality figures come from manufacturer registration data cross-referenced with death records, with the mechanism inferred rather than proven. Nothing on this card has a procedure-specific analgesia trial behind it; the pain plan is the opioid-tolerant plan with a laminotomy attached.

  1. Deer TR, Provenzano DA, Hanes M, et al. The Neurostimulation Appropriateness Consensus Committee (NACC) recommendations for infection prevention and management. Neuromodulation 2017;20:31-50
    Consensus best practice for neurostimulation implants: pre-incision weight-based antibiotic, MRSA screening and decolonisation, skin preparation, operating room discipline, and management of established infection by explant
  2. Hoelzer BC, Bendel MA, Deer TR, et al. Spinal cord stimulator implant infection rates and risk factors: a multicenter retrospective study. Neuromodulation 2017;20:558-562
    2,737 implants and revisions: infection 2.45%, lower than the 3-6% of older series; diabetes, smoking and obesity did not independently raise the rate; no difference between paddle and cylinder leads or between prophylactic antibiotics; an occlusive dressing and post-operative antibiotics were associated with fewer infections
  3. Falowski SM, Sharan A, McInerney J, Jacobs D, Venkatesan L, Agnesi F. Nonawake vs awake placement of spinal cord stimulators: a prospective, multicenter study comparing safety and efficacy. Neurosurgery 2019;84:198-205
    30 paddle lead implants, 19 asleep with electromyographic guidance and 11 awake with verbal paraesthesia mapping, non-randomised: operating time 89 versus 125 min, pain-paraesthesia overlap at six weeks 83.5% versus 46.6%, fewer extraneous paraesthesiae, equal pain relief at 24 weeks, two versus six adverse events
  4. Stone LE, Falowski SM. Implantation of a thoracic spinal cord stimulator paddle electrode and generator under general anesthesia with intraoperative neuromonitoring: 2-dimensional operative video. Oper Neurosurg 2019;16:E169
    Technique: removal of the superior part of the lower spinous process for paddle access, a strain relief loop at the spinal incision, generator secured parallel to the body in a pocket chosen to limit discomfort, and neuromonitoring for placement
  5. Eldabe S, Buchser E, Duarte RV. Complications of spinal cord stimulation and peripheral nerve stimulation techniques: a review of the literature. Pain Med 2016;17:325-336
    30-40% of patients have at least one complication; lead migration is the commonest hardware problem, infection and pain over the implant the commonest biological ones; dural puncture headache and neurological injury are rare
  6. Deer TR, Pope JE, Hayek SM, et al. The Polyanalgesic Consensus Conference (PACC): recommendations on intrathecal drug infusion systems best practices and guidelines. Neuromodulation 2017;20:96-132
    Algorithms for intrathecal drug choice in cancer, terminal and non-cancer pain, nociceptive and neuropathic, localised and diffuse; morphine and ziconotide as first-line single agents; 31 consensus points
  7. Deer TR, Pope JE, Hayek SM, et al. The Polyanalgesic Consensus Conference (PACC): recommendations for intrathecal drug delivery: guidance for improving safety and mitigating risks. Neuromodulation 2017;20:155-176
    Safety guidance across all phases of intrathecal therapy: granuloma, respiratory depression, refill errors, withdrawal, and the monitoring that mitigates them
  8. Deer TR, Hayek SM, Pope JE, et al. The Polyanalgesic Consensus Conference (PACC): recommendations for trialing of intrathecal drug delivery infusion therapy. Neuromodulation 2017;20:133-154
    34 consensus points on trialling: single-shot and catheter trials, starting doses and titration, monitoring settings, handling of systemic opioids during the trial, and the populations in whom no trial is needed
  9. Coffey RJ, Owens ML, Broste SK, et al. Mortality associated with implantation and management of intrathecal opioid drug infusion systems to treat noncancer pain. Anesthesiology 2009;111:881-891
    Device registration data: mortality 0.088% at three days, 0.39% at one month and 3.89% at one year after intrathecal opioid pump implantation for non-cancer pain, higher than after spinal cord stimulation or lumbar discectomy; respiratory arrest caused or contributed to death in all nine index cases, with no device over-infusion found
  10. Loftus RW, Yeager MP, Clark JA, et al. Intraoperative ketamine reduces perioperative opiate consumption in opiate-dependent patients with chronic back pain undergoing back surgery. Anesthesiology 2010;113:639-646
    102 opioid-dependent patients having major lumbar surgery: ketamine 0.5 mg/kg at induction then 10 microg/kg/min to closure reduced opioid consumption at 24 h, 48 h and six weeks and pain in recovery and at six weeks, with no excess side effects
